gabelle: The word comes from the Italian gabella, a duty, itself from the Arabic qabila, he received. In France the gabelle first meant an indirect tax on goods such as bed sheets, wheat, spices and wine, and from the 14th century only the crown's tax on salt. When the Albigensian Crusades ended in 1229, France gained the Rhône estuary, and in 1246 Aigues-Mortes became its first Mediterranean port, with salt ponds and storehouses meant to finance the crusades of Louis IX. Charles I extended royal control to the Berre saltworks near Marseilles in 1259.

First levied evenly at 1.66% of the sale price, the gabelle later varied widely. All salt had to be taken to a provincial salt granary, the grenier à sel, bought there at a fixed price and sold at an inflated one. In the pays de grandes gabelles, around Paris and the oldest provinces, a third of the population paid two thirds of all salt revenue and had to buy up to 7 kilograms a year. The pays de petites gabelles of the south-east paid about half that rate, the pays rédimés bought themselves free with a lump sum in 1549 after revolts, and the pays exempts, Brittany among them, had joined the kingdom on condition that the tax would not apply.

The gaps between regions bred smuggling. Smugglers, the faux-sauniers, bought salt where it was cheap and sold it where it was dear, and many people saw them as heroes. The armed customs guards, the gabelous, could search people and homes at will and were despised. Women hid salt under their dresses, and in Laval 2,845 of 4,788 people arrested between 1759 and 1788 were women and children. Sheepherders who let their flocks drink at salty ponds could also be charged.

A smuggler caught unarmed could be sent to the galleys for up to ten years, and an armed one to death; a noble caught buying contraband salt lost his nobility. In 1773 over 3,000 soldiers guarded the Loire between Brittany and Anjou. By the late 18th century about 3,000 people a year were imprisoned, sent to the galleys or executed for offences against the gabelle, while clergy, nobles and high officials were often exempt. After abolishing the tax, the National Assembly freed everyone held under its laws.
gabes: Gabès is the capital of the Gabès Governorate in Tunisia, on the Gulf of Gabès, 327 km south-east of Tunis and 113 km from Sfax. It lies at the delta of the Wadi Qabis, which rises 10 kilometres upstream at Ras al-Oued and is its main source of water. The ancient name Takapes is a Punic Numidian toponym. The prefix Ta, meaning the in Berber, was later dropped, and since Arabic lacks the sound p, Kapes became Kabes and then Gabès. It has a hot arid climate with low rainfall.

The town was a Carthaginian settlement known as Tacapae before it fell under Roman control, and it belonged to the Roman province of Tripolitania. Strabo calls it an important entrepôt of the Lesser Syrtis, and Pliny remarks that the water of a copious fountain there was divided among the cultivators, each having the use of it for a certain interval. Tacapae became a Christian bishopric, and three of its bishops are known: Dulcitius, at the Council of Carthage in 403 and the Conference of Carthage in 411; Servilius, exiled by Huneric in 484; and Caius or Gallus, at the Council of Carthage in 525.

The Umayyad Caliphate conquered the region in the 7th century, bringing Islam to Gabès, and the companion of the Prophet Muhammad Abu Lubaba al-Ansari settled in the city. The Banu Jami were among the dynasties that followed. In the 12th century al-Idrisi praised its economy, dense orchards and markets, and its dates, olives and leather goods. In the 14th century al-Tijani called it the paradise of the world and Little Damascus.

In 1574 it became part of the Eyalet of Tunis. It came under the French protectorate in 1881, which brought a railway, roads and a port. German forces held it in the World War II, until British forces retook it in 1943 in the Mareth Line operations. Tunisia became independent in 1956.

Gabès is a commercial centre and port with industries including chemicals, cement, brick and fishing, and a university. Its oasis is one of the last coastal oases in the world, and was added to the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List on 28 May 2008. The Mosque of Sidi Boulbaba and the Mouradi school are its most notable historical and religious landmarks.
gabo-reforms: The name comes from gabo, the year 1894 in the traditional sexagenary cycle. Corruption in the land tax, military service and the state granaries weighed heavily on the Korean peasantry, and the teachings of Donghak, Eastern Learning, spread widely in the countryside. The Japan-Korea Treaty of 1876, an unequal treaty signed under the pressure of gunboat diplomacy, opened Korean ports to Japan, and rivalry between Japan and China in Korea grew through the Imo Incident of 1882 and the failed coup of 1884. When the Donghak Peasant Revolution broke out in 1894, the government asked China for help, and Japan answered with troops of its own, deposed the government and installed a new one that began a programme of reform.

The reforms came in three stages. From July to October 1894, with little Japanese interference while Japan fought the First Sino-Japanese War, a council under Kim Hong-jip passed 210 measures: power moved from the king to the Uijeongbu, the gwageo examinations gave way to a Japanese bureaucratic system, finances were centralised, and class discrimination, slavery and underage marriage were banned, while widows gained the right to remarry. From December 1894 to July 1895 a cabinet of Kim Hong-jip and Park Yung-hio issued the Hongbeom 14 articles, cutting the tie of subordination to China, and 213 further articles created a modern cabinet, reorganised local districts and reformed the courts, until Park fled to Japan accused of treason.

After Japanese agents assassinated Queen Min on 8 October 1895, a cabinet of Kim Hong-jip and Yu Kil-chun introduced the solar calendar, regnal years independent of China, a postal service and primary schools. Its Short Hair Act, ordering men to cut off the traditional topknot, provoked wide protest, above all among conservative scholars who had formed the Righteous Army.

When King Gojong and the crown prince took refuge in the Russian legation on 11 February 1896, the opposition led to the murders of Kim Hong-jip and other ministers, and the reforms came to an end. The programme has been compared with the Meiji Restoration in Japan: it declared Korea independent, ended the privileges of the yangban, opened office to merit, banned torture and guilt by association and ordered official documents written in Hangul. Historians debate how far Japan shaped it and how much it advanced modernisation.
gaborone: Gaborone lies between Kgale Hill and Oodi Hill, near the confluence of the Notwane and Segoditshane rivers, in the south-eastern corner of Botswana and within 15 kilometres of the South African border. It stands at an elevation of 1,010 metres and has a hot semi-arid climate. Several neighbouring towns, among them Mogoditshane, Mochudi and Tlokweng across the river, are largely commuter towns for the city.

There have been inhabitants along the Notwane River for centuries. Around 1880 the Tlokwa left the Magaliesberg ranges to settle the area and called the settlement Moshaweng. The word Gaborone is said to mean "it does not fit badly" or "it is not unbecoming". Early European colonizers called the place Gaberones, a shortening of "Gaborone's Village", after Chief Gaborone of the Tlokwa, whose home village, now called Tlokweng, lay across the river from the Government Camp, the colonial government's headquarters. The nickname GC comes from Government Camp.

In 1890 Cecil John Rhodes picked Gaberones to house a colonial fort, where he planned the Jameson Raid. In the mid-1960s, when the Bechuanaland Protectorate became an independent nation, the city was planned as its capital. It was chosen because it was not affiliated with any specific indigenous group and was close to fresh water. The name changed from Gaberones to Gaborone in 1969. The city grew very fast, which has caused problems of housing and illegal settlement, and it dealt with conflicts spilling over from Zimbabwe and South Africa in the 1980s.

Gaborone is the capital and largest city of Botswana, with 246,325 inhabitants at the 2022 census, about 10 per cent of the national population. Its centre is a long commercial strip called the Main Mall, with a semicircular area of government offices to its east. It holds the Bank of Botswana, the Botswana Stock Exchange and the headquarters of the Southern African Development Community, formed in 1980. The National Museum and Art Gallery, which opened in 1968, has an exhibit on the San, the earliest inhabitants of southern Africa.
gabriel-bethlen: Gabriel was the elder of the two sons of Farkas Bethlen de Iktár, a Hungarian nobleman who had lost his ancestral estate to the Ottoman occupation, and Druzsiána Lázár de Szárhegy, who came from a Székely noble family. He was born at Marosillye, now Ilia in Romania. Both parents died in 1591, and the two orphaned brothers were placed under the guardianship of their maternal uncle, András Lázár de Szárhegy, a soldier who paid little attention to their formal education.

Little is documented of his youth, since only two documents written between 1593 and 1602 mention him. Modern historians assume that Stephen Bocskai, whom Gabriel called his kin, advanced his career at the court of Sigismund Báthory. He was wounded at the Battle of Sellenberk in 1599, fought against the commander Giorgio Basta's rule, and after the defeat at Tövis in 1602 fled to the Ottoman Empire, where the refugees came to regard him as their leader.

Bethlen persuaded Stephen Bocskai to rise against the commissioners of Emperor Rudolph, and Bocskai was elected prince of Transylvania on 21 February 1605. Bethlen then received the domain of Vajdahunyad and became perpetual ispán of Hunyad County. He was a Calvinist who helped the Jesuit György Káldy translate and print the Bible, composed hymns and from 1625 employed Johannes Thesselius as kapellmeister. He later fell out with Prince Gabriel Báthory and fled to the Ottoman Empire. After Báthory was murdered in 1613, the Ottomans installed Bethlen, and the Diet at Kolozsvár endorsed him on 13 October 1613.

His rule was one of enlightened absolutism. He developed mines and industry, nationalised many branches of foreign trade and built a new palace at Gyulafehérvár. He gave hereditary nobility to Protestant priests, founded the Bethlen Gabor College and sent Transylvanian students to Protestant universities in England, the Dutch Republic and Germany. He also ensured the right of serfs' children to be educated.

In the Thirty Years' War he invaded Royal Hungary in August 1619, took Kassa and Pressburg and was elected King of Hungary at Besztercebánya on 20 August 1620. By the Peace of Nikolsburg of 31 December 1621 he renounced the title in return for religious freedoms for Hungarian Protestants, seven counties and the title of Imperial Prince. Further campaigns in 1623-1624 and 1626 ended with the Peace of Vienna and the Peace of Pressburg. He died on 15 November 1629, and his second wife, Catherine of Brandenburg, became princess regnant.
gabriel-garcia-moreno: García Moreno was born in 1821, the son of a Spanish nobleman and María de las Mercedes Moreno y Morán de Butrón, of a wealthy criollo family of Guayaquil. His father died while he was a boy, and he was raised by his devoutly Catholic mother and tutored by a priest. At fifteen he began to study theology and law at the University of Quito and received minor orders, but his friends and his own interests turned him to a secular career. He graduated in 1844 and worked as a lawyer and a journalist opposed to the Liberal government. After two years in Europe from 1849 he returned, was elected a senator and joined the opposition.

In 1859 a conservative junta chose him as president amid civil war, and a popular election in 1861 confirmed him for a four-year term. He found an empty treasury and a large debt, cut posts and corruption, and attracted foreign investment. His highway programme was funded by the trabajo subsidario, four days of unpaid labour a year or its cash equivalent, which fell most heavily on indigenous people, and he has been criticised for forced labour on the roads. He also reformed the universities and raised the number of primary schools from 200 to 500. He resigned in 1865.

Re-elected in 1869, he founded the Conservative Party and made education compulsory and free in 1871. A new concordat removed the state's power over the appointment of bishops, and the 1869 constitution made the Christian faith the religion of the state and required candidates and voters to be Catholic. The legislature consecrated Ecuador to the Sacred Heart of Jesus. Liberals and some radicals described him as a dictator and objected to his secret police.

After his election to a third term in 1875, García Moreno was assassinated on the steps of the National Palace in Quito on 6 August 1875, struck with a machete by Faustino Rayo while three or four others fired revolvers. The pamphlet La dictadura perpetua by Juan Montalvo is said to have inspired the plot. Pope Leo XIII wrote that he had fallen under the steel of the wicked for the Church. The archbishop of Quito began a beatification process on 20 December 1939, which stalled after the Second Vatican Council.
gabriel-narutowicz: Gabriel Józef Narutowicz was born on 29 March 1865 in Telšiai, then part of the Russian Empire, into a Polish-Lithuanian noble family. His father, a district judge, was sentenced to a year in prison for taking part in the January 1863 Uprising and died when Gabriel was one. His mother, Wiktoria Szczepkowska, raised the sons herself and in 1873 moved to Liepāja so that they would not have to attend a Russian school. After a spell at the Saint Petersburg Imperial University, interrupted by illness, Narutowicz studied at the Zurich Polytechnic from 1887 to 1891. He helped exiled Poles there, was barred from returning to Russia and became a Swiss citizen in 1895.

In Switzerland Narutowicz became chief of works on the River Rhine and a pioneer of electrification. He directed the construction of hydroelectric power plants at Monthey, Mühleberg and Andelsbuch, and from 1907 he was a professor at ETH Zurich, where he was dean of the water construction institute from 1913 to 1919. Invited by the Polish government in September 1919, he returned to take part in reconstruction.

As Minister of Public Works from 23 June 1920 to 26 June 1922 he cut the reconstruction bureaucracy fourfold, and by 1921 almost 270,000 buildings and 300 bridges had been rebuilt. In April 1922 he was credited with the success of the Polish delegation at the Genoa Conference, and on 28 June 1922 he became Minister of Foreign Affairs.

Under the March Constitution the president was chosen by the National Assembly. The left, the representatives of the national minorities and the centrist Polish People's Party Piast backed Narutowicz against Count Maurycy Zamoyski, the candidate of the National Democrats, and in the final round he won 289 votes to 227. Catholic and nationalist groups then campaigned against him, calling him an atheist and a Freemason, and some of the press called him the Jewish president.

On 11 December 1922, the day of his oath, opponents held demonstrations in Warsaw and threw mud at his motorcade. He tried to form a government outside parliament and offered the foreign ministry to Zamoyski. On 16 December 1922 he was shot dead at the Zachęta gallery in Warsaw, where he was viewing an exhibition, by the painter Eligiusz Niewiadomski. Niewiadomski was sentenced to death in a one-day trial and executed on 31 January. Nearly 500,000 people attended Narutowicz's funeral, and he was buried on 22 December in the vault of St. John's Cathedral in Warsaw. The funeral was seen as a manifestation of peace that weakened the far right in the following years.
gabriela-mistral: Lucila Godoy Alcayaga was born in Vicuña, Chile, and grew up in the Andean village of Montegrande, where her older sister Emelina Molina taught her at primary school. Her father, a schoolteacher, deserted the family when she was three, and poverty was a constant presence in her early life. At fifteen she began supporting herself and her mother, a seamstress, as a teacher's aide in Compañía Baja. She won the national literary contest Juegos Florales in Santiago and afterwards rarely used her given name.

Mistral taught at several schools near La Serena, Barrancas, Traiguén and Antofagasta between 1906 and 1912, and then at a liceo in Los Andes for six years. In 1918 Pedro Aguirre Cerda, the Minister of Education, made her director of the Sara Braun Lyceum in Punta Arenas. She moved to Temuco in 1920 and in 1921 became director of Liceo No. 6 in Santiago. In 1922 she accepted an invitation from José Vasconcelos to work in Mexico, where she contributed to the reform of libraries and schools and the founding of a national education system.

Her first book of poems, Desolación, appeared in New York in 1922, with help from Federico de Onís, and Ternura, a collection of lullabies and rondas, followed in Madrid in 1924. In 1925 she was invited to represent Latin America in the Institute for Intellectual Cooperation of the League of Nations, and in 1926 she moved to France, in effect an exile for the rest of her life. Tala was published in Buenos Aires in 1938, with proceeds going to children orphaned by the Spanish Civil War.

Her themes include nature, betrayal, love, a mother's love, sorrow and recovery, and a Latin American identity formed from Native American and European influences. She also wrote about 800 articles on geography, education, politics and fellow writers. Her last volume published in her lifetime, Lagar, appeared in a truncated form in 1954, and Poema de Chile was published after her death, in 1967.

She received the Nobel Prize in Literature on 15 November 1945, the first Latin American and the fifth woman to do so, and King Gustav of Sweden presented it on 10 December. She died of pancreatic cancer on 10 January 1957 in Hempstead, New York, aged 67. Her remains were returned to Chile nine days later, and the government declared three days of national mourning.
gabriele-dannunzio: Gabriele D'Annunzio was born in Pescara, in what is now the Italian region of Abruzzo, the son of Francesco Paolo Rapagnetta D'Annunzio, a wealthy landowner and mayor of the town, and Luisa de Benedictis. His father had been born Rapagnetta and was adopted at 13 by an aunt who had married a merchant and shipowner named D'Annunzio. A story that he was first baptised Gaetano is false; his birth and baptismal records both give Gabriele.

D'Annunzio published Canto novo in 1882, poems of youth, the sea and the Abruzzese landscape, followed by Terra vergine, stories of peasant life. With Intermezzo di rime in 1883 he began a more characteristic manner, expressing every subtle vibration of sensuous life. Critics divided: some called him a corrupter of public morals, others welcomed a breath of new vitality. He was linked with the Decadent movement and influenced by Friedrich Nietzsche. His novels include Il Piacere (1889) and Il fuoco (1900), and his plays La figlia di Jorio (1904). The censor banned his tragedy Francesca da Rimini in December 1901, three weeks into its run.

After the First World War began, D'Annunzio returned to Italy and spoke for entry on the side of the Triple Entente. He volunteered, became a fighter pilot and lost the sight of an eye in a flying accident. On 9 August 1918 he led nine planes on a round trip of 1,100 km to drop leaflets on Vienna.

Angered by the proposal at the Paris Peace Conference to hand over Fiume, now Rijeka, he led 186 grenadiers to seize the city on 12 September 1919. His force grew to some 2,500 men, and Italy refused to annex the city and blockaded it. With the syndicalist Alceste de Ambris he wrote the Charter of Carnaro, which set up a corporatist state with nine corporations and a tenth, D'Annunzio's own invention, for heroes, poets and prophets. It declared music the fundamental principle of the state. Afterwards he retired to Lake Garda, where he built the Vittoriale degli Italiani. Mussolini took up his balcony speeches and ceremonies, though D'Annunzio never joined the fascist government.
gadadhar-singha: Born Gadapani Konwar, and known by the Ahom name Supatphaa, he was the son of Gobar Roja, a descendant of the king Suhungmung. The minister Debera Borbarua made Gobar king in 1675; he reigned only twenty days and was executed after Debera's fall. In 1679 Laluk Sola Borphukan had the minister Atan Burhagohain murdered, installed Sulikphaa, called Lora Roja, as king and began to hunt down the Ahom princes eligible for the throne.

To escape, Gadapani became a fugitive in the Naga hills, perhaps near the present-day Mon district, among the Konyak Naga. During this time his wife Joymoti Konwari was tortured and killed by the henchmen of Sulikphaa and Laluk Sola Borphukan. Little is known of his two years in exile, though the hills are rich in lore and legend about him.

He was formally crowned in March 1682, and bound the leading nobles to himself by marrying their daughters. His first act was to equip an army against the Mughals at Guwahati: the forts at Bansbari and Kajali fell at the first assault, and a naval victory near the mouth of the Bar Nadi delivered the whole enemy fleet to the Ahoms. The campaign ended eighty years of Ahom–Mughal conflict. He also stopped Naga raids on the border villages, partly through marriage alliances with Naga chiefs.

He built roads, among them the Dhodar Ali, 211 km long from Kamargaon to Joypur, and two stone bridges, and had a number of tanks dug. The earliest known copper plates recording grants of land by Ahom kings to Brahmins or Hindu temples date from his reign. Having met the Mughal system of land measurement while hiding in Lower Assam, he brought surveyors from Koch Bihar and Bengal; the survey began in Sivasagar and was completed only after his death.

He died in February 1696 after a reign of fourteen and a half years, leaving two sons, Lai and Lechai. Lai succeeded him under the Hindu name Rudra Singha, and under him the Ahom kingdom reached its zenith; the Tungkhungia house ruled until the end of the kingdom in 1826. Gadadhar Singha was buried at Charaideo. The American Baptist missionary Nathan Brown, who saw the royal tombs there dug open, reckoned his about ninety feet high and so natural in appearance that a stranger would have taken it for an ordinary hill.
gadag: Gadag-Betageri is a city municipal council in Gadag district in the state of Karnataka and the administrative headquarters of the district. The original city of Gadag and its sister city Betageri share one city administration. The Gadag Schist Belt, also called the Gadag Greenstone Belt, lies within the Dharwar Craton of north Karnataka and dates back 2.5 to 3.0 billion years to the Archean Era. Its metavolcanic rock gave rise to the Gadag Gold Field, a gold-bearing zone extending over 40 kilometres, where there is evidence of ancient indigenous gold panning and shallow mining.

Deeper shaft mining began in the British colonial period, in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The hills are covered by red sandy soils farmed for groundnut, sunflower, sorghum and pulses, while the flat plains have black cotton soils, which historically made Gadag one of the main cotton trading centres.

The name Gadag is a palindrome in both Latin and Kannada script. It derives from older Kannada names found in inscriptions of the Chalukya period, where the settlement is recorded as Kratuka, Kratapura, Galadugu and Gadugu. The Gadag style of architecture, marked by ornate pillars with intricate sculpture, began under the Western Chalukya (Kalyani Chalukya) king Someswara I and flourished from about 1050 to 1200 CE, during which some 50 temples were built.

Examples include the Trikuteshwara temple complex at Gadag, the Kasivisvesvara temple at Lakkundi, the Doddabasappa Temple at Dambal and the Amriteshwara temple at Annigeri. The temples of Veera Narayana and Trikuteshwara are places of religious and historic importance. The poet Naranappa, known as Kumara Vyasa and author of the Kannada Mahabharata, the Karnata Bharata Kathamanjari, was born in the nearby village of Koliwada and composed his work before the deity Veera Narayana. Kanaginahal of Gadag is the birthplace of the first co-operative society in Asia.

At the 2011 census Gadag-Betageri had a population of 172,813 and an area of about 54 square kilometres. Kannada is the main language. Gadag Junction is a major railway junction of the South Western Railway on lines towards Hubballi, Hosapete and Solapur. The city has been home to musicians such as Ganayogi Panchakshara Gawai, Puttaraj Gawai, who headed the Veereshwara Punyashrama school of music until late 2010, and Bhimsen Joshi, and to writers including Huilgol Narayana Rao, whose song heralded the birth of the state of Karnataka.
gadara: Gadara stood on a hill 378 metres above sea level overlooking the gorge of the Yarmouk River, with the Golan Heights and the Sea of Galilee in view to the north and north-west. The ridge was reachable from the east but protected by steep falls on the other three sides, and the town was well watered from the Ain Qais spring and cisterns. It is distinct from Gadara or Gadora of Peraea, near Salt.

By the 3rd century BCE Gadara was already of some cultural importance. Polybius called it in 218 BCE the strongest of all places in the region, yet it soon surrendered to the Seleucid king Antiochus III, and under the Seleucids it was also known as Antiochia and Seleucia. The Hasmonean king Alexander Jannaeus captured and damaged it. In 63 BCE Pompey rebuilt it as a semi-autonomous city of the Decapolis; in 30 BCE Augustus placed it under Herod, and after Herod's death in 4 BCE it became part of the province of Syria.

A 2nd-century CE aqueduct brought drinking water through a qanat 170 km long, whose 94 km underground section is the longest known tunnel from ancient times. Gadara was long the seat of a Christian bishop under the archbishop of Scythopolis. After the Battle of Yarmouk in 636 it came under Muslim rule, and around 749 an earthquake largely destroyed it. Besides Menippus, Meleager and Philodemus, its sons included the mathematician Philo of Gadara, who calculated a highly accurate value for π, and the Cynic philosopher Oenomaus of Gadara.

The ruins lie at Umm Qais in Irbid Governorate, near Jordan's borders with Israel and Syria; Ulrich Seetzen identified the site in 1806. The walls can be traced for almost their whole circuit of 3 km, and the remains include a hippodrome, a temple and a basilica, while the paved street still shows the ruts of ancient wheels. A Hellenistic temple of the 3rd century BCE, believed to have been dedicated to Poseidon, was found in 2017, and the Ottoman governor's house, Beit Rousan, is now a museum.
gadsden-purchase: Business-minded Southerners hoped that a railroad linking the South with the Pacific coast would widen trade. They thought the mountains of the southern Mexican Cession blocked a direct route, which might have to swing south into what was still Mexican territory. James Gadsden of South Carolina was influential at the Memphis commercial convention of 1845, which recommended a southern route.

The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo of 1848 had left the Mesilla Valley in dispute, because the Disturnell Map it relied on placed El Paso 36 miles too far north and 100 miles too far east. The valley, a flat desert about 50 by 200 miles, was thought essential for a southern railroad.

Mexico also complained that the United States did not stop Comanche and Apache raids across the border, as Article XI had promised, and the New Mexico governor William Carr Lane claimed the Mesilla Valley for New Mexico in a proclamation.

The Pierce administration, which took office in March 1853, was pro-southern and pro-expansion, and Secretary of War Jefferson Davis favoured a southern railroad route. Gadsden, as United States minister to Mexico, signed a first draft with President Antonio López de Santa Anna on 31 December 1853.

The treaty gave the United States 29,640 square miles (76,800 square kilometres) south of the Gila River and west of the Rio Grande, in present-day southern Arizona and south-western New Mexico, and defined the border between the two countries. Mexico received 10 million dollars. Santa Anna's government was in financial distress, and some historians argue that, after the losses of the Mexican–American War and Lane's expeditions, he preferred to cede land for payment rather than risk seizure. The first plan would have reached far south into Baja California, Sonora, Chihuahua and other states.

In the United States Senate the treaty met strong opposition from anti-slavery senators, who disliked acquiring more possible slave territory. On 17 April 1854 the Senate voted 27 to 18 in favour, three votes short of the two-thirds required, and the treaty was changed. It took effect on 8 June 1854. Many Mexicans saw Santa Anna's sale as a betrayal and watched him squander the money. The Purchase was the last substantial territorial enlargement of the contiguous United States.

The Army took control of the lands in 1854 and established Fort Buchanan in June 1857, and miners and ranchers followed. The Southern Pacific Railroad reached Yuma in 1877, Tucson in March 1880, Deming in December 1880 and El Paso in May 1881, the first railroad across the Purchase. Tucson, Yuma, Nogales and Deming now stand on the land.
gaels: Gaelic culture and the Goidelic language are first recorded in Ireland, which suggests that they developed on the island. Scholars disagree about when Ireland became Celtic. Some link it to the arrival of the Bell Beaker culture from about 2400 BCE, which brought people with Steppe ancestry; the archaeologist J. P. Mallory writes that this offers "a simple and clear model" of Irish Gaelic origins. The linguist Peter Schrijver argues that any date before 1000 BCE is too early, because the earliest Goidelic inscriptions of the 1st century CE still resemble other Celtic languages closely. Medieval works such as the Lebor Gabála Érenn trace the Gaels to Goídel Glas, a Scythian prince whose mother Scota was an Egyptian princess.

From the 4th century the Romans called the Gaels Scoti, a name conjectured to mean raiders, since they were then raiding the west coast of Britain. Christianity reached Ireland in the 5th century, through Patrick, a Romano-British former slave, and through Gaels such as Declán and Finnian. Monks and abbots took over some roles of the aos dána as oral culture was set down in writing. Gaelic missionaries worked in Northumbria and across the Frankish Empire, and Gaelic groups settled in parts of Wales.

In 1542 Henry VIII declared the Lordship of Ireland a kingdom and himself its king. The Nine Years' War (1594–1603) ended in defeat for the Irish Gaelic alliance and brought the independence of the last Irish Gaelic kingdoms to an end. In Scotland the Statutes of Iona of 1609 aimed at the Highland chiefs. Gaelic languages declined steeply from the early 19th century, and revival bodies such as Conradh na Gaeilge and An Comunn Gàidhealach arose to restore their standing.

Traditional Gaelic society was divided into clans, each with its own territory and a chieftain or king. Succession followed tanistry: a relative of the same great-grandfather, elected by freemen, was chosen as deputy and succeeded automatically. Law was the Fénechas, or Brehon law, and oral tradition was kept by shanachies. Most people lived in roundhouses and ringforts. Ogham inscription began in the 4th century. Four seasonal festivals, Samhain, Imbolc, Beltane and Lughnasadh, were observed into modern times, and the Gaels developed their own dress, music, dances and sports, including Gaelic games in Ireland and Highland games in Scotland.
gaero-of-baekje: Gaero was the eldest son of the 20th king, Biyu. He tried to strengthen royal control over the aristocracy by choosing officials from his own Buyeo clan at the expense of the powerful Hae and Jin clans. In 469 a surprise attack retook the city of Cheongmongnyeon, near modern Kaesong, from Goguryeo. In 472 he sent an embassy with tribute to the Northern Wei, but the Wei court, at war with the Southern Dynasties and unwilling to fight the stronger Goguryeo, turned him down.

According to the Samguk sagi, King Jangsu of Goguryeo sent a Buddhist monk named Dorim to the Baekje court in the early 470s as his agent. Dorim won Gaero's favour through the king's passion for the board game baduk and persuaded him to neglect the country's defences in favour of public works.

In 475 Jangsu attacked with 30,000 men and overran Baekje's defences in seven days, taking the Han River valley and the capital, which stood in the area of present-day Pungnaptoseong. Gaero was taken to the Acha Mountain Fortress and killed there by two men who had defected from Baekje to Goguryeo. An army of 10,000 sent by Baekje's ally Silla arrived too late.

He was the last king to rule Baekje from its old heartland in the Han River valley, and after his death Hae Gu of the suppressed Hae clan led a bloody revolt. His son Buyeo Modo became the 22nd king, Munju, and another son, Buyeo Gonji, a military commander who had been sent to Japan in 461, was the father of the 24th king, Dongseong.
gaeta: Gaeta lies in the province of Latina in Lazio, on a promontory stretching towards the Gulf of Gaeta, 133 kilometres south of Rome and 96.5 kilometres north of Naples. In antiquity the site, then called Caieta, was inhabited by the Oscan-speaking Aurunci, and in 345 BCE its territory came under Roman influence. Its mild climate made it a place for seaside villas of the Roman elite, owned by figures such as Scipio Africanus and Gaius Laelius. Lucius Munatius Plancus, consul in 42 BCE, had a villa on Monte Orlando, and his cylindrical travertine mausoleum still stands on the summit. The Emperor Antoninus Pius restored the port.

After the Lombard invasion Gaeta remained under Byzantine suzerainty, but like Amalfi, Sorrento and Naples it became practically independent and traded with the Levant. Around 830 it became a lordship ruled by hereditary hypati. The first, Constantine, helped Pope Leo IV in the naval fight at Ostia in 847, and John I helped crush the Saracens at the Garigliano in 915. Docibilis II first took the title of duke, and after his death in 954 the duchy declined. Pandulf IV of Capua captured the city in 1032, and in 1140 Roger II definitively annexed it to the Kingdom of Sicily.

Because of its strategic position Gaeta was repeatedly attacked in wars for the Kingdom of Naples. Frederick II strengthened its castle in 1227, and Charles I of Anjou rebuilt it in 1279. King Alfonso V of Aragon besieged and took the city in 1435 as his base for conquering the kingdom. A new wall around Monte Orlando followed after 1528. The French took it in 1806 under André Masséna after a defence, and the Austrians in 1815. Pope Pius IX took refuge there after fleeing the Roman Republic. In 1860 to 1861 King Francis II of the Two Sicilies defended the fortress with 12,000 men, and capitulated on 13 February 1861 when the withdrawal of the French fleet made bombardment from the sea possible.

Gaeta is a fishing port and seaside resort with beaches such as Serapo. Its main sights include the Angevine-Aragonese Castle and the cathedral, whose Romanesque marble Paschal candelabrum carries 48 reliefs of the life of Jesus. Its bell tower, 57 metres high, was completed in 1279. The Sixth Fleet of the United States Navy has had its flagship based at Gaeta since 1967. Local cooking includes the tiella, a pie resembling a pizza, and a Latin text of 997 found in the town contains the earliest known use of the word pizza. After Italy surrendered to the Allies, German troops occupied the city and expelled most of its population.
gafsa: Gafsa is the capital of Gafsa Governorate in south-western Tunisia. It is a historic oasis and a centre of the country's mining industry, lying about 335 kilometres from Tunis. Excavations at prehistoric sites around it have yielded artefacts and skeletal remains of the Capsian culture, a Mesolithic civilisation radiocarbon dated to between 10,000 and 6,000 BCE. Its people, known as the Snail eaters for their extensive middens of snail shells, are believed to be ancestors of the modern Berbers.

The city was called Capsa in Latin, and the Capsian culture takes its name from it. It belonged to King Jugurtha, who deposited his treasures there, and Gaius Marius captured and destroyed it in 106 BCE. It was later re-established under a Punic-style magistracy of sufetes before becoming a Roman colonia. Capsa was an important city of Roman Africa, and Roman cisterns can still be seen among its ruins.

The Vandals conquered the city and held it until the death of Genseric in 477. Berbers then occupied it and made it the capital of a Romano-Berber kingdom, until it was subjected to Byzantium under Justinian I. He made Capsa the capital of the province of Byzacena, and in 540 the Byzantine governor Solomon built a new city wall and named the city Justiniana Capsa.

The Arab army of Uqba ibn Nafi conquered Gafsa in 688, despite Berber resistance, and Capsa lost importance to the Muslim foundation of Kairouan. Some historians consider Gafsa the last place in North Africa where African Romance survived as a spoken language, until the 13th century. In the 12th century al-Idrisi described a walled city with markets, date palms, gardens, henna and cotton.

Phosphate mines were discovered at Gafsa in 1886, and the deposit is one of the largest in the world. The Compagnie des phosphates de Gafsa had its own private railway line until 1966. The city had 111,170 inhabitants at the 2014 census. Capsa is now listed by the Catholic Church as a titular see, and it had resident bishops from the 3rd century to the end of the 9th.
gagik-i-of-armenia: Gagik was the second son of King Ashot III the Merciful and Queen Khosrovanuysh, the younger brother of Smbat II and the elder brother of Gurgen I of Lori. The Bagratunis were among the most powerful nakharar, or noble, families of Armenia and had restored Armenian statehood with the coronation of Ashot I in 885. Under his brother Smbat II, Gagik governed several provinces and took part in the defence of the kingdom. Smbat died without an heir in 989, and the nobility and the church recognised Gagik as king.

Gagik bore the titles Shahanshah, King of Kings, and King of the Armenians and Georgians, and the rulers of Vaspurakan, Kars, Lori and Syunik recognised his suzerainty. When King David of Tashir-Dzoraget rebelled in 1001, Gagik took most of his lands, earning David the nickname Anhoghin, the Landless, though they were returned once he submitted. Gagik abolished the principality of Vayots Dzor, annexed most of Artsakh including Khachen, and took the Kogovit and Tsaghkotn cantons from Vaspurakan.

He kept peaceful relations with the Byzantine Empire and allied with the Georgian rulers. In 998 the emir of Atropatene, Mamlan, invaded Armenia, and a joint Armenian and Georgian army defeated him at the Battle of Tsumb. Ani, on trade routes linking Byzantium, Georgia, Persia and the Middle East, grew into a centre of crafts and commerce, its walls were strengthened, and it came to be called the city of a thousand and one churches. His wife, Queen Katramide, sponsored the building and renovation of churches.

Gagik died in 1020 and was succeeded by his son Hovhannes-Smbat. Disputes between Hovhannes-Smbat and his brother Ashot IV weakened the kingdom, and his successors never held his authority. His reign is remembered as the golden age of medieval Armenia.

Among his foundations was the Church of St. Gregory at Ani, built in 1001–10 and loosely modelled on Zvartnots. During Nicholas Marr's excavations in 1906 a statue of Gagik 2.26 metres high, holding a model of the church and wearing a turban and khalat, was found in fragments. It was lost at the end of the First World War; a fragment is in the archaeological museum of Erzurum, and a replica by Hrach Galstyan stands at the History Museum of Armenia in Yerevan.
gagik-ii-of-armenia: Gagik was the son of Ashot, who after the death of King Gagik I in 1020 had fought his brother Hovhannes-Smbat for the throne. A peace left Ani and its surroundings to Hovhannes-Smbat and the rest to Ashot, with the whole kingdom to pass to Ashot or his son. In 1022, under pressure from the pro-Byzantine Catholicos Petros Getadardz, Hovhannes-Smbat willed the Kingdom of Ani to Emperor Basil II. Both brothers died in 1041, and when Emperor Michael IV sent an army to claim the bequest, the general Vahram Pahlavuni drove it back and had the young Gagik proclaimed king.

The chroniclers Matthew of Edessa and Kirakos Gandzaketsi remember Gagik as learned, pious and fond of books. In August 1041 the army of Ani raided the outskirts of Dvin, whose emir Abu'l-Aswar Shawir was hostile, and Grigor Magistros Pahlavuni defeated an invading Seljuk force at the fortress of Bini. Emperor Constantine Monomachos, who came to the throne in 1042, demanded the kingdom, and in 1044 Armenian forces under Vahram Pahlavuni and Gagik repeatedly defeated Byzantine armies before Ani, while the emir of Dvin, invited by the emperor, took Amberd and Khor Virap.

Against Vahram's advice, and urged by the courtier Vest Sargis and the Catholicos, Gagik went to Constantinople to make peace. There he was shown the keys of Ani, which Sargis and the Catholicos had sent to the emperor. According to Matthew of Edessa he refused for a month, saying he had been brought there by deception, before agreeing to give up his kingdom.

In exile Gagik held lands near Caesarea, among them Lycandus and Tzamandos, a palace on the Bosphorus and a pension, and seals call him duke of the theme of Charsianon. He defended the rites of the Armenian Church in a debate before the emperor, and his confession of faith survives in the chronicle of Matthew of Edessa. Metropolitan Mark of Caesarea, who scorned the Armenians, died after Gagik had him tied in a sack with his dog. The three Mandalas brothers, Byzantine lords of the fortress of Kyzistra, later seized Gagik and strangled him. Prince Thoros of the Rubenid dynasty later avenged him.
gahadavala-dynasty: The founder, Chandradeva, was a son of Mahichandra and a grandson of Yashovigraha. The dynasty's inscriptions give Yashovigraha no royal title, which suggests a petty chief who probably served a greater king, possibly the Kalachuri king Karna, while Mahichandra bore the feudatory title nṛpa. Chandradeva probably began as a feudatory and declared independence before 1089. Theories that the family descended from the Pala dynasty or from the Rashtrakutas of Kannauj have been rejected, and the meaning of the name Gahadavala, which appears in only four of the dynasty's inscriptions, is uncertain.

In the late 11th century north-central India suffered Ghaznavid raids and lacked a strong imperial power. Chandradeva took the region around Varanasi from the Kalachuris. His son Madanapala, identified with the Malhi of the Muslim chronicles, was imprisoned by the Ghaznavids according to the historian Salman and released for a ransom, but expeditions led by his son Govindachandra forced the Ghaznavids to make peace.

Govindachandra, king from sometime between 1109 and 1114, made the Gahadavalas the leading power of northern India. He adopted Kalachuri titles and coinage, and his marriage to Kumaradevi, a relative of the Pala king Ramapala, paused the rivalry with the Palas, which revived in the 1140s over western Bihar. After 1194 the Ghurids sacked Varanasi and, according to Hasan Nizami, destroyed many temples. Jayachandra's son Harishchandra still took sovereign titles in an inscription of 1197, but was probably defeated by the Delhi sultan Iltutmish (r. 1211–1236).

Most Gahadavala inscriptions were found around Varanasi, and many record grants made after the king bathed in the Ganga there, so Varanasi was probably the favoured capital and Kanyakubja a capital of honour. The kings ruled through semi-independent feudatory chiefs, and the duties of their officials, the amātyas, are described in the Kṛtya-Kalpataru of the courtier Lakshmidhara. The kings worshipped Vishnu and also honoured Shiva and Surya, while two of Govindachandra's queens, Kumaradevi and Vasantadevi, were Buddhists. The poet Shriharsha, author of the Naishadha Charita, worked at the court of Vijayachandra.
gaius-antonius-hybrida: Hybrida was the younger son of the orator Marcus Antonius and the brother of Marcus Antonius Creticus; his mother is unknown. In 87 BCE he went with Lucius Cornelius Sulla to Greece against Mithridates VI of Pontus, as a military tribune or a legate. When Sulla returned to Italy in 83 BCE he left Hybrida with a small cavalry force in Achaea, where he levied contributions on the province. The young Julius Caesar prosecuted him for this in 76 BCE, but Hybrida refused to appear and escaped punishment by appealing to the plebeian tribunes.

In 70 BCE the censors Gellius and Lentulus expelled him from the Senate for his conduct in Greece, for ignoring a praetor's summons and for squandering his property. He returned as praetor in 68 or 66 BCE and, backed by Caesar and Marcus Licinius Crassus, stood with Catiline for the consulship of 63 BCE. Marcus Tullius Cicero and Hybrida were elected. Deep in debt, Hybrida accepted Cicero's offer of the rich province of Macedonia in exchange for leaving Cicero the effective sole consul.

During the Catilinarian conspiracy he at first stayed on the fence. Late in 63 BCE he was sent to Etruria with the consular army but, through gout or a pretence of it, handed command to his legate Marcus Petreius, whose men destroyed Catiline's army at Pistoria. In Macedonia he plundered the provincials and raided neighbouring peoples. The historian Cassius Dio describes how he fled ahead of his infantry, first leaving it to the Dardanians and then losing near the city of the Istrians to the Bastarnian Scythians.

Replaced quietly by Gaius Octavius in 60 BCE, he was prosecuted in 59 BCE by Marcus Caelius Rufus and Lucius Caninius Gallus. Cicero defended him, but he was fined and exiled and chose Cephallenia, where he acted as governor with the islanders' tacit consent. Caesar recalled him in 47 BCE. His bid for the censorship around 45 BCE failed, and he is last mentioned by Cicero in 44 BCE, when Mark Antony, his nephew and son-in-law, divorced his daughter Antonia Hybrida Minor. The historian Antony Kamm called him a thoroughly disreputable character.
gaius-cassius-longinus: Gaius Cassius Longinus was born about 86 BCE into the old Roman family of the gens Cassia, prominent in Rome since the 6th century BCE. Little is known of his early life, apart from a story that at school he quarrelled with the son of the dictator Sulla, showing his dislike of despots. He studied philosophy at Rhodes under Archelaus of Rhodes and became fluent in Greek. He married Junia Tertia, the daughter of Servilia and so a half-sister of Marcus Brutus, and they had a son born about 60 BCE.

In 54 BCE Cassius joined Marcus Licinius Crassus as quaestor on his campaign against the Parthian Empire. After Crassus's defeat at the Battle of Carrhae in 53 BCE, Cassius led the remaining troops back into Syria and organised its defence. Plutarch's account suggests that Crassus could have avoided the disaster by following Cassius's advice. In 51 BCE Cassius defeated an invading Parthian army under Prince Pacorus and the general Osaces, luring it into an ambush after the Parthians gave up their siege of Antioch.

In the civil war he sided with Pompey and commanded part of his fleet, burning a large part of Caesar's navy off Sicily in 48 BCE. After Pompey's defeat at Pharsalus he was overtaken by Caesar and surrendered, and Caesar made him a legate. Cassius became praetor in 44 BCE with the promise of Syria, but was offended when his junior and brother-in-law Brutus received the more senior city praetorship. He was the moving spirit of the plot against Caesar, though Brutus became its leader, and on 15 March 44 BCE he struck Caesar in the chest. According to some accounts he wanted to kill Mark Antony as well, but Brutus dissuaded him.

Cassius went to Syria, amassed twelve legions and defeated Publius Cornelius Dolabella, who took his own life. The Senate confirmed him as governor. After the Second Triumvirate was formed, he joined Brutus at Smyrna, sacked Rhodes and then met Brutus at Sardis, where their armies proclaimed them imperator. They encamped near Philippi in Macedon against Octavian and Mark Antony. In the two battles there Brutus beat Octavian and took his camp, but Antony overran Cassius, who, unaware of Brutus's success, ordered his freedman Pindarus to help him kill himself, on 3 October 42 BCE. Brutus mourned him as the last of the Romans, and he was buried at Thassos.

Cassius followed Epicurus, probably converting between 48 and 45 BCE, and scholars debate whether this belief shaped his politics. He appears in Shakespeare's Julius Caesar and in Dante's Inferno, where he is chewed in one of the three mouths of Satan.
gaius-cornelius-gallus: Gaius Cornelius Gallus was born into a humble family. His birthplace is uncertain: Jerome calls him Foroiuliensis, and the Forum Iulii it points to is disputed between Fréjus, Cividale del Friuli and Voghera, the last favoured by Jean-Paul Boucher and the first by Ronald Syme. It has also been suggested that the epithet refers instead to his erecting an obelisk in the Forum Iulium of Alexandria.

He moved to Rome at an early age and was taught by the same master as Virgil and Varius Rufus. Virgil owed him much for the restoration of his estate and dedicated his tenth Eclogue to him, and Parthenius of Nicaea dedicated his Erotica Pathemata to him.

In politics Gallus supported Octavian and was rewarded with the prefecture of Egypt. In 30 BCE he led a campaign to put down a revolt at Thebes, and he set up a monument at Philae to glorify what he had done. His conduct brought him into disgrace with the emperor, a new prefect was appointed, and after his recall, according to Cassius Dio, he killed himself.

Gallus was highly regarded by his contemporaries. Ovid, in the Tristia, called him the first of the elegiac poets of Rome and said that he would be known in the West and in the East, and that his Lycoris would be known with him. He wrote four books of elegies chiefly about Lycoris, a poetic name for the notorious actress Cytheris, taking Euphorion of Chalcis as his model and translating some of his works into Latin. He is often thought a key figure in establishing Latin love elegy and an inspiration for Propertius, Tibullus and Ovid.

Almost nothing survives. Until 1978 only a single line was known, quoted by Vibius Sequester about the river Hypanis. In that year a papyrus found at Qasr Ibrim in Egyptian Nubia gave nine lines, arguably the oldest surviving manuscript of Latin poetry. One line complains of Lycoris's bad behaviour, which confirmed the author, and four lines have been read as a compliment to Julius Caesar shortly before his assassination.

Another block seems to say that he does not fear the verdict of critics such as Cato and Viscus. Four poems published by Aldus Manutius in 1590 are generally regarded as forgeries. Wilhelm Adolf Becker made Gallus the central figure of Gallus, or Roman Scenes of the time of Augustus (1838), an account of Roman life.
gaius-gracchus: Gaius Sempronius Gracchus came from a well-connected family. His father, Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, was consul in 177 and 163 BCE and censor in 169 BCE, and his mother Cornelia, daughter of Scipio Africanus, refused a marriage proposal from Ptolemy VIII of Egypt to devote herself to her sons.

He served under Scipio Aemilianus in the Numantine War in 133 BCE and then sat on the land commission distributing public land to poor families that his brother Tiberius had created. In 126 BCE he supported Marcus Fulvius Flaccus's programme, was elected quaestor and went to Sardinia. He returned early without his commander's permission, answered the censors successfully, rebutted a charge of aiding the revolt at Fregellae and won election as tribune.

In 123 BCE Gaius proposed to bar a magistrate deposed by the people from office again, a bill withdrawn at his mother's request, and a law on appeal to the people in capital cases that sent the former consul Publius Popillius Laenas into exile.

He set a maximum price for grain of six and a third asses for a modius, re-enacted his brother's land law and may have authorised colonies at Scolacium and Tarentum. He also moved a law on soldiers' clothing and a law assigning consular provinces before the consular elections. His grain law, a tithe in Asia that benefited the publicani, and his rousing oratory made him widely popular, and he was re-elected for 122 BCE.

In his second tribunate he transferred the jury pool of the extortion court to the equestrians, and his ally Gaius Rubrius carried a law for a colony at Carthage. The senate set the tribune Marcus Livius Drusus against him, and a bill to give citizenship to the Latins and Latin rights to Italian allies failed after opposition from the consul Gaius Fannius. Gaius left Rome to supervise the colony and was defeated when he stood for a third tribunate.

In 121 BCE a tribune moved to repeal the law for Carthage. After an attendant of the consul Lucius Opimius was stabbed to death, the senate passed the first senatus consultum ultimum. Gracchus and Flaccus armed their followers and seized the temple of Diana on the Aventine, and Opimius marched against them with the militia and Cretan archers. Flaccus and his sons were killed, and Gaius either was killed or committed suicide after crossing the Tiber.

A special court tried his supporters, and many were reportedly executed without formal trial. Opimius built a temple of Concord and was acquitted when prosecuted, which legitimised the use of such decrees. Most of Gaius's legislation survived, though the law on Carthage was repealed, and the question of citizenship for Italians was not raised again for some thirty years.
gaius-hostilius-mancinus: Mancinus belonged to the plebeian gens Hostilia, whose first consul was his father, Aulus Hostilius Mancinus, in 170 BCE. His cousin Lucius Hostilius Mancinus, consul in 145, claimed to have been the first Roman soldier through the walls of Carthage, which earned the family the enmity of Scipio Aemilianus. Mancinus was praetor by 140 BCE, probably urban praetor, presiding over the senate's ruling on a border dispute between the Thessalian cities of Narthakion and Melitaia; as the office required a minimum age of thirty-nine, he was born no later than 179 BCE.

Consul in 137 BCE with Marcus Aemilius Lepidus Porcina, he received Hispania Citerior. After several defeats he was surrounded by 4,000 Numantines, possibly near Renieblas, though his army was five times as large, and he sent his quaestor Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, whose father had left a favourable impression on the Numantines, to negotiate. The terms spared the 20,000 Roman soldiers and kept Rome's boundaries in exchange for the army's weapons and baggage, and the Numantines made Mancinus and his staff swear religious oaths.

In Rome, where only a capitulation was thought acceptable, the treaty caused a political storm, and Mancinus was recalled. The consul Lucius Furius Philus, a friend of Scipio, proposed that the man who had made the treaty be returned to the other party, so that breaking the oath would not damage the pax deorum. The assembly approved surrendering Mancinus, who spoke in favour of his own punishment, but rejected the bills against Gracchus and Quintus Pompeius. Mancinus was placed naked and in chains before the gates of Numantia until nightfall, but the Numantines refused him.

Back in Rome, a trial brought by the tribune Publius Rutilius held that his surrender had cost him his citizenship and his seat in the senate. Mancinus then commissioned a statue of himself naked and in chains, mentioned by Pliny the Elder, the earliest known nude statue of a Roman citizen. His readiness to sacrifice himself for his oath won admiration, and Cicero and Plutarch later spoke well of him. A bill restored his citizenship, perhaps soon after 135 BCE, and a rare second praetorship returned him to the senate.
gaius-laelius: Laelius's family background is obscure. According to Polybius he was a friend of Scipio from childhood, or at least from their first days in the army, since he seems to have witnessed Scipio's rescue of his father in a skirmish, probably the Battle of Ticinus in late 218 BCE. Livy suggests that he did not come from a rich family, and no Laelius is mentioned before the Second Punic War, so he may have been of even lower birth than is usually assumed.

In Hispania he was Scipio's loyal second-in-command, the only man to whom Scipio confided all his plans. After the fall of New Carthage he took important hostages and the news of the victory to Rome. He led the left wing at the Battle of Baecula in 208 BCE and defeated a Carthaginian squadron at the Battle of Carteia. In Africa he set fire to the camp of Syphax at the Battle of Utica, and at Cirta his light troops and heavy infantry broke Syphax's army; he criticised Masinissa for taking Syphax's wife Sophonisba as his own.

At Zama in 202 BCE his cavalry on the left routed the Carthaginian horse and then, with Masinissa, attacked Hannibal's veterans from the rear. He brought the news of the victory to Rome, with Syphax and his son Vermina as prisoners. He was quaestor after Zama, plebeian aedile in 197 BCE and praetor of Sicily in 196 BCE, but failed to win the consulship of 192 BCE. As consul he lost the command against Antiochus III the Great to Scipio's brother Scipio Asiaticus and was given Gaul instead, where Placentia and Cremona were repopulated.

Laelius later served on embassies to King Perseus of Macedon in 174–173 BCE and to Transalpine Gaul in 170 BCE. His son Gaius Laelius Sapiens, born about 188 BCE, became consul in 140 BCE and was the friend of Scipio Aemilianus, as his father had been of Africanus. In 160 BCE the elder Laelius gave Polybius much first-hand information about Scipio Africanus. Neither Livy nor Polybius records the year of his death. He appears as Lelio in George Handel's opera Scipione.
gaius-maecenas: Gaius Cilnius Maecenas was a friend and political adviser to Octavian, who later reigned as the emperor Augustus. He prided himself on an ancient Etruscan lineage and claimed descent from the princely house of the Cilnii of Arretium. Horace alludes to this in the opening of his Odes with the phrase "atavis edite regibus", descendant of kings. Tacitus calls him Cilnius Maecenas, and it is possible that Cilnius was his mother's family name, or that Maecenas was a cognomen. His wealth may have been partly inherited, but he owed his position to his connection with Augustus. Despite his wealth and power he chose not to enter the Senate and remained of equestrian rank.

Maecenas first appears in 40 BCE, when Octavian employed him to arrange his marriage with Scribonia and to help negotiate the Treaty of Brundisium and the reconciliation with Mark Antony. In 37 BCE he and Marcus Cocceius Nerva patched up a reconciliation between the two claimants to power by the Treaty of Tarentum. During the Sicilian war against Sextus Pompeius in 36 BCE he held supreme administrative control of Rome and Italy, and he acted for Octavian again before the Battle of Actium, when he crushed the conspiracy of Lepidus the Younger. In his last years he fell somewhat out of favour with Augustus. He died in 8 BCE, leaving Augustus sole heir to his wealth.

Maecenas is best known for supporting young poets, and in many languages his name means a patron of the arts, as in French mécène and German Mäzen. Virgil wrote the Georgics in his honour and introduced Horace to him in 38 BCE. Maecenas gave Horace financial support and an estate in the Sabine Mountains, and Propertius and Varius Rufus were also among his protégés. Some see the patronage as serving the state, reconciling minds to the new order. He wrote prose and verse himself, now lost apart from about twenty fragments, and Augustus, Seneca and Quintilian mocked his strange style. His gardens on the Esquiline Hill, the first of their kind in Rome, became imperial property after his death.
gaius-marius: Marius was born about 157 BCE in Cereatae, a village near Arpinum in south-east Latium, a town that had received full Roman citizenship only in 188 BCE. Plutarch calls his father a labourer, which is almost certainly false: Marius had ties with the nobility in Rome and Arpinum, and came from a locally important family of equestrian status with inherited wealth, probably from large landholdings. His younger brother Marcus Marius also entered public life.

He gained military experience under Scipio Aemilianus at the Siege of Numantia in 134 BCE, was elected tribune of the plebs in 119 BCE and passed a law limiting aristocratic interference in elections. He was barely elected praetor in 115 BCE and then governed Further Spain, campaigning against bandits.

In 109 BCE Marius joined the consul Quintus Caecilius Metellus as a legate in the Jugurthine War, probably as his senior subordinate. By 108 BCE he wished to stand for the consulship. Metellus refused his blessing, but Marius won the respect of the troops by sharing their labours, and Italian traders wrote home that he could end the war quickly. Elected consul for 107 BCE, he took volunteers, among them men without property, the capite censi, and sailed to Africa, leaving his cavalry with his quaestor Lucius Cornelius Sulla.

After a series of Roman defeats by the Cimbri and their allies, Marius was elected consul again for 105 BCE and held the office each year from 104 to 100 BCE. He defeated the Teutones at Aquae Sextiae and the Cimbri at Vercellae.

In his sixth consulship, in 100 BCE, the tribune Lucius Appuleius Saturninus pushed laws that gave land to Marius's veterans, and Marius then withdrew from active public life. In 88 BCE a conflict with Sulla, elected consul and given the command against Mithridates of Pontus, led to Marius's exile to Africa. He returned during the War of Octavius, joined Cinna, seized Rome and purged his opponents. He was elected consul for the seventh time and died on 13 January 86 BCE, within weeks.

Since the 1840s Marius has been credited with sweeping army reforms, but specialists now increasingly dismiss these Marian reforms as a construct of modern scholarship. His lasting example lies elsewhere: his successive consulships gave one man unprecedented power, and his use of the assemblies to overturn senatorial assignments of commands set a pattern for later rivals.
gaius-sempronius-tuditanus: Tuditanus belonged to the plebeian gens Sempronia. His father of the same name was a senator and in 146 BCE sat on the commission of ten that reorganised the political order of Greece; Cicero more than once confused the two men and was corrected by his friend Titus Pomponius Atticus in May 45 BCE. The younger Tuditanus probably first appears in 146 BCE as an officer of Lucius Mummius Achaicus in the war in Greece.

He was quaestor in 145 BCE and praetor in 132 BCE, probably passing through the offices without difficulty as an adherent of the Scipiones. As consul in 129 BCE with Manius Aquillius he was charged by the senate with judging the complaints of dispossessed Roman allies whose estates the Gracchian land commission had annexed. He did not carry out the task and went instead to Illyria, allegedly because war threatened, which also held up further allocations of land.

The sources disagree about his campaign. Livy wrote that he first fought the Iapydes without success and that the defeat was made good by a victory owed to Decimus Junius Brutus Callaicus, while Appian said that he and Tiberius Pandusa seem to have subjugated them. He marked his victories with a dedication to the river god Timavus at Aquileia carrying an inscription in Saturnian verse, of which two fragments were found in 1906, and Pliny the Elder quoted an inscription on his statue that gave the river Arsa as the border of Italy.

Cicero praised the elegance of his style. Belonging to the Optimates, he wrote a partisan treatise on Roman constitutional law, the libri magistratuum, in at least thirteen books, dealing with intercalation, the appointment of the tribunes of the plebs and the nundinae; with the De potestatibus of the Gracchan Marcus Junius Congus Gracchanus it was the earliest work of its kind in Roman literature. Some scholars ascribe to him a further history of Rome from its foundation, since fragments on the Aborigines of Latium and the books said to be King Numa Pompilius's fit poorly in a work on law.
gaius-sextius-calvinus: Gaius Sextius Calvinus had held the office of praetor no later than 127 BCE before he became consul of the Roman Republic. During his consulship he joined M. Fulvius Flaccus in waging war against the Ligures, Saluvii and Vocontii in Transalpine Gaul, and he stayed on in Gaul as proconsul for 123 and 122 BCE. Below the Saluvian oppidum of Entremont he established a garrison, a castellum, at a site of thermal springs that took his name as Aquae Sextiae, the Baths of Sextius.

His campaigns formed an important part of the military operations that led to the annexation of Transalpine Gaul as a Roman province, a process concluded by Domitius Ahenobarbus and Fabius Maximus around 120 BCE. Together with Fulvius Flaccus he opened a line of communication a mile wide linking the territory of Massilia, a longtime ally of Rome on the site of present-day Marseille, with Cisalpine Gaul, which was already under Roman control. In 122 BCE he was granted a triumph for his victories over the three Gallic peoples.

Around 92 BCE a Gaius Sextius Calvinus of praetorian rank restored a small altar dedicated to sei deo sei divae, to whichever god or goddess. The restorer is most often identified as the son of the consul of 124 BCE, but the historian E. Badian believed the elder Sextius himself was responsible for the inscription.

The altar was found in 1829 near Sant'Anastasia, on the lower western part of the Palatine Hill. Made of travertine, it has the hourglass shape that came into use in Rome around the time of the Second Punic War. Known as the Ara Calvini, the Altar of Calvinus, and sometimes as the Ara Dei Ignoti, the Altar of the Unknown God, it is kept in the Antiquario Palatino, the Palatine Hill Museum.
gaius-suetonius-paulinus: Little is known of the family of Gaius Suetonius Paulinus, which probably came from Pisaurum, modern Pesaro, on the Adriatic coast of Italy. He served as praetor in 40 CE and was appointed governor of Mauretania, modern northern Morocco, the following year. With Gnaeus Hosidius Geta he suppressed the revolt led by Aedemon, which arose from the execution of the local ruler Ptolemy by Caligula. He was the first Roman commander to lead troops across the Atlas Mountains, and Pliny the Elder quotes his description of the area in his Natural History.

In 58 CE he became governor of Britain, replacing Quintus Veranius, who had died in office, and continued the policy of aggressively subduing the tribes of Wales. Two future governors served under him: Quintus Petillius Cerialis and Gnaeus Julius Agricola. His reputation came to rival that of Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo. He assaulted the island of Mona, now Anglesey, a refuge for British fugitives and a stronghold of the druids. Meanwhile the south-eastern tribes revolted under Boudica of the Iceni and destroyed Camulodunum, now Colchester, and routed Cerialis's legion.

Suetonius marched along Watling Street to Londinium but judged he lacked the numbers to defend it and ordered it evacuated; the Britons destroyed it and Verulamium. He gathered the XIV Gemina, detachments of the XX Valeria Victrix and the auxiliaries, about ten thousand men, though the prefect of II Augusta, Poenius Postumus, did not answer the call. In a defile in an unidentified place, probably along Watling Street, Roman discipline beat British numbers. Tacitus heard that almost eighty thousand Britons died against four hundred Romans, and that Boudica poisoned herself.

Punitive operations after the victory proved counterproductive, and the procurator Gaius Julius Alpinus Classicianus warned Nero. An inquiry under the freedman Polyclitus found an excuse, the loss of some ships, to relieve Suetonius, and Publius Petronius Turpilianus replaced him. He was not disgraced: a Gaius Suetonius Paulinus was consul in 66 CE, either the general or a son of the same name. In 69 CE he was a senior general of Otho, advised against battle at Bedriacum, was overruled, and was pardoned by Vitellius after claiming he had deliberately lost. His eventual fate remains unknown.
gajah-mada: Little is known of Gajah Mada's early life except that he came from an ordinary family. Early accounts mention him as a commander of the Bhayangkara, the elite guard of the Majapahit king and royal family. When the official Rakrian Kuti rebelled against King Jayanegara in 1321, Gajah Mada and the mahapatih Arya Tadah took the king and his family out of the capital Trowulan, and later helped him return and crush the rebellion.

Jayanegara was murdered in 1328 by the court physician Rakrian Tanca, an aide of Rakrian Kuti; another version holds that Gajah Mada arranged the murder. He was appointed mahapatih in 1334, after the retirement of Arya Tadah, under Queen Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi.

It is said that on his appointment Gajah Mada swore the Palapa Oath, recorded in the Pararaton, a history of the fifteenth or sixteenth century. He vowed not to enjoy palapa, interpreted as rest or pleasure, until he had conquered the Nusantara archipelago, naming among his goals Gurun, Seram, Tanjungpura, Haru, Pahang, Dompo, Bali, Sunda, Palembang and Tumasik, the modern Singapore. Even his close friends were at first doubtful. He took Bedahulu in Bali and Lombok in 1343, sent the navy against the remnants of Sriwijaya at Palembang, installed the prince Adityawarman as ruler of the Minangkabau in Sumatra, and conquered Samudra Pasai, Bintan, Tumasik, Melayu and Kalimantan.

Under Tribhuwana's son Hayam Wuruk, who ruled from 1350, he went on to the east, to Seram, Sumba, Bima, Banda, Ambon, Timor and Dompo. He thereby brought what is now the Indonesian archipelago under Majapahit control. An inscription of 1351 records that he built a caitya for the late King Kertanegara.

In 1357 Sunda was the only neighbouring state refusing to acknowledge Majapahit. Hayam Wuruk meant to marry the Sundanese princess Dyah Pitaloka Citraresmi, and Gajah Mada was sent to receive her at Bubat. He demanded Sunda's submission and said that the princess could be taken only as a concubine. The dispute became the Battle of Bubat, in which the Sundanese king and his party were killed; tradition holds that the princess took her own life. Courtiers blamed Gajah Mada, he was demoted and retired to the estate of Madakaripura in Probolinggo, and he died in 1364. Hayam Wuruk divided his duties among four new mahamantri.

Indonesian nationalists, notably Sukarno and Mohammad Yamin, cited his oath as proof of an ancient unity before Dutch rule. He is a national hero, and Gadjah Mada University in Yogyakarta and the satellite Palapa, launched on 9 July 1976, are named for him. Much of his popular image comes from Yamin's book of 1945, whose picture of him many people dispute.
gal-vihara: The name Gal Vihara, rock monastery, comes from the rock face into which the images were cut; the temple was first called the Uttararama, the northern monastery. According to the Cūḷavaṃsa it was among the more prominent of the hundred temples that Parakramabahu I (1153–1186) built across Lanka, and after the temple was finished his workmen made three caves in the rock: the Vijjadhara Guha, the Nissina Patima Lena and the Nipanna Patima Guha. Only the first is a true cave; the other two were image houses whose walls, once decorated with frescoes, joined the rock and survive only as bases.

To make room for the statues the rock was cut almost 4.6 metres deep, the only place in the country where a natural rock was excavated so far for such a purpose. The size of each image seems to follow the height of the rock at that point. The large seated Buddha, in the dhyana mudra, sits on a lotus seat before a throne carved with makara figures and four small images of the Buddha, a feature presumably owed to Mahayana influence. A smaller seated figure in the Vijjadhara Guha sits between two four-armed deities, identified by the archaeologist HCP Bell as Brahma and Vishnu.

The standing figure, its arms folded and its face sorrowful, has been taken by some for the monk Ānanda mourning beside the reclining Buddha, though the walls show the two once stood in separate chambers. Senarath Paranavithana held that it is the Buddha. The reclining figure shows the parinirvana, its slightly withdrawn left foot marking that the Buddha has died and is not merely lying down. Compared with the sculpture of the Anuradhapura period, the images have broader foreheads and robes carved with two parallel lines, after the Amaravati school.

When Parakramabahu I came to the throne, the Buddhist monks of the island were divided into three fraternities: the Abhayagiri vihāra, the Jetavanaramaya and the Mahavihara. He called a congregation to reconcile them and expelled corrupt monks, and with the elders of each fraternity drew up a katikavata, a code of conduct, which was carved on the polished rock between the Vijjadhara Guha and the standing image. The Uttararama was a centre of Buddhist education until it was abandoned with the fall of the Kingdom of Polonnaruwa.
galapagos-islands: The archipelago lies on the equator in the Eastern Pacific and consists of 127 islands, islets and rocks, of which 19 are large islands with an area over one square kilometre. Isabela, at 4,588 square kilometres, makes up close to three-fifths of the land area, and its Volcán Wolf, at 1,700 metres, is the highest point. The islands rest on the Nazca plate and above the Galápagos hotspot, where a mantle plume creates volcanoes. The cold Humboldt Current brings frequent drizzle.

Whether Polynesians or the Indigenous peoples of South America ever reached the islands is disputed. European discovery is recorded on 10 March 1535, when Tomás de Berlanga, bishop of Panama, sailing to Peru, drifted off course in the Doldrums. The islands were so arid that two men and ten horses died for lack of fresh water, and he left them unclaimed. The name comes from the giant tortoises, galápagos in Spanish, and appears on Abraham Ortelius's map of 1570.

Pirates, mostly English, used the islands as a hideout until the early nineteenth century to attack Spanish treasure fleets from Peru. William Ambrosia Cowley mapped them in 1684 and gave English names to 16 of them. The first known permanent resident was Patrick Watkins, an Irish sailor marooned on Floreana from 1807 to 1809. Ecuador formally occupied the islands on 12 February 1832, and José de Villamil led the settlement. In 1892 the group was renamed the Colón or Columbus Archipelago, still its official name on Ecuadorian maps.

In the early twentieth century the United States wished to buy the islands to guard the Panama Canal, and Chilean diplomacy supported Ecuador's resistance. Protective legislation began in 1930, and the Galápagos Province was created by decree on 18 February 1973.

The islands form Ecuador's Galápagos Province, with Puerto Baquerizo Moreno as capital and a population slightly over 33,450 in 2020. All the islands are part of Galápagos National Park and Marine Reserve. Their endemic species include giant tortoises, finches, flightless cormorants and marine iguanas, and about 180 vascular plant species are endemic. Introduced goats, cats, cattle and plants remain the chief threat to native life.
galata-tower: In 1267 the Genoese, allied with the Byzantine Empire, founded a colony called Pera in Galata, north of the Golden Horn. They later expanded without authorization toward the hill to the north-east and between 1335 and 1349 built walls and towers surrounded by moats on its slopes. The tower now known as the Galata Tower was built in 1348. It was a watchtower and the principal tower of the fortifications meant to protect the colony's coastal section against a siege by land. A cross stood at its summit. A war between the Byzantines and Genoese broke out in August 1348 and ended in 1349, and a decree of Emperor John VI transferred the hill to the Genoese.

After the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople on 29 May 1453, the Genoese of Pera surrendered the colony without resistance. Damage to the tower's summit was halted by an edict of Sultan Mehmed II. Under restoration led by Zağanos Pasha the cross was replaced with the Ottoman flag. An earthquake in 1509 damaged it, and repairs under Mimar Hayreddin were complete by mid-1510. In the 16th century the tower and others along the walls housed Christian prisoners of war working at the Kasımpaşa shipyards. In the 17th century Evliya Çelebi wrote that it had been a dungeon and in his time a supply warehouse. From the 18th century the Mehterhane corps and fire watchers used it as a lookout for fires.

A fire of 27 July 1794 forced repairs that shortened the tower, and its upper section became a coffeehouse, with a drum to announce fires and a dovecote in the attic. Another fire in 1831 led to further repairs. After the roof collapsed in a storm in 1875, two floors were added above the top, again for watching fires. After the republic was proclaimed in 1923 the fire brigade and the Turkish Naval Forces still used it. A restoration between 1965 and 1967 made it a tourist facility, and it has served as a museum and exhibition venue since work in 2020.

The Galata Tower is a cylindrical masonry tower in the Romanesque style, 62.59 m tall to the tip of its roof. It stands on a hill 35 m above sea level in the Beyoğlu district of Istanbul. It has eleven floors, including a basement, ground floor and mezzanine. An elevator runs to the sixth floor, and the eighth floor is an observation terrace. A poem by Pertev above the entrance commemorates repairs of 1831 and 1832. The tower is a symbolic landmark of Beyoğlu and Istanbul, and was included on UNESCO's Tentative List of World Heritage Sites in 2013.
galati: Galați lies in south-eastern Romania, on the left bank of the Danube at the junction of the Siret and the Prut, about 80 kilometres from the Black Sea. It is the capital of Galați County in the historical region of Western Moldavia and one of the larger cities on the Danube. The nearest town is Brăila, 15 kilometres to the south, and the two have long been rivals. The city is built on three terraces, from the low Valley City area to the old town, now the centre, and the higher modern city.
