On 19 July 1956 the US and UK withdrew their offer to finance the Aswan Dam, and Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal Company. The UK, France and Israel secretly agreed to take the canal and topple him, but the Suez Crisis ended in what was seen as his political victory, and his prestige across the Arab world rose. His Cairo radio station, the Voice of the Arabs, spread his ideas of Arab unity. From 1961 he nationalised much of the economy, and the National Charter of 1962 promised universal health care, affordable housing and wider women's rights. Egypt's intervention in North Yemen from 1962 cost 26,000 Egyptian soldiers, and Nasser later called it a miscalculation.

Egypt's defeat in the Six-Day War of 1967 led Nasser to resign, but demonstrations brought him back; he named himself prime minister and began the War of Attrition in January 1968. After the Arab League summit closed on 28 September 1970 he suffered a heart attack and died at 52. His funeral in Cairo drew five to six million mourners. Supporters credit him with making Egypt independent of British influence and widening access to housing, education and health services; critics point to authoritarianism and the dominance of the military over civil institutions. His successor Anwar Sadat later departed from Nasserist policies.
gamay: Gamay, in full Gamay Noir à Jus Blanc, is a purple-coloured grape used to make red wines, grown most notably in Beaujolais and in the Loire Valley around Tours. It is a very old cultivar, mentioned as long ago as the 15th century, and has often been cultivated because it produces abundantly. It is thought to have first appeared in the village of Gamay, south of Beaune, in the 1360s, bringing relief to growers after the decline of the Black Death. Unlike Pinot noir, it ripened two weeks earlier and was easier to cultivate, and it gave a stronger, fruitier wine in much larger quantity.

In July 1395 the Duke of Burgundy, Philippe the Bold, outlawed the cultivation of the grape. He called it the disloyal Gaamez, full of very great and horrible harshness, in part because it occupied land that could be used for the more elegant Pinot noir. Sixty years later Philippe the Good issued another edict against it, stating that the Dukes of Burgundy were known as the lords of the best wines in Christendom and would maintain their reputation.

Gamay is a very vigorous vine that tends not to root deeply on alkaline soils, which stresses the vines and gives grapes of high acidity. Carbonic maceration softens the acidity and gives notes of crushed strawberries and raspberries and of lilac and violets. Its wines are typically light-bodied and fruity, while those meant for modest ageing are made by whole-berry maceration, mostly in the Cru Beaujolais areas, and taste of sour cherries, black pepper and dried berry. Beaujolais nouveau is made from the more alkaline soils of southern Beaujolais.

In the Loire Valley it is typically blended with Cabernet Franc and Côt. It is also grown in the Niagara Peninsula in Canada, around Lake Geneva in Switzerland, in Australia, and in Oregon's Willamette Valley, where Amity Vineyards introduced it in 1988. The name has been attached to other grapes in California: Napa Gamay is now known as Valdiguié. In 1929 Gamay was crossed with Seidentraube to produce the white grape Regner.
gamla-uppsala: Gamla Uppsala lies on the Fyris Wolds, a cultivated plain in the valley of the River Fyris. People have been buried there for about 2,000 years, since the land rose above the water. Cairns reveal settlement in the Nordic Bronze Age, but most grave fields date from the Iron Age and Viking Age. There were once between 2,000 and 3,000 mounds, most now turned into farmland, gardens and quarries; about 250 barrows remain. The Royal Mounds are three large barrows, dated to the 5th and 6th centuries and now called the Eastern, Middle and Western Mounds.

From the 3rd and 4th centuries Gamla Uppsala was an important religious, economic and political centre. Early Scandinavian sources, such as Ynglingatal, speak of the king of the Swedes as the "King at Uppsala". It was the site of the Thing of all Swedes, held at the end of February or early March. Adam of Bremen described the Temple at Uppsala in the 1070s as a pagan centre with wooden statues of Odin, Thor and Freyr; his account is contested. In the 1080s the Christian king Ingi was exiled for refusing to perform the sacrifices, and Blot-Sweyn was elected, until Ingi killed him and regained the throne.

Sweden's first archbishopric was placed at Gamla Uppsala in 1164, but the village had lost its access to navigable water as the land rose, and the archiepiscopal seat moved to Östra Aros, later renamed Uppsala, in 1273. In 1846 Bror Emil Hildebrand excavated the Eastern Mound and found burnt bones and bronze panels that probably adorned a helmet of Vendel type; in 1874 he opened the Western Mound, which held a Frankish sword with gold and garnets.

Gamla Uppsala is a parish and village outside the city of Uppsala. Gamla Uppsala Church, begun probably in the 11th century and finished in the 12th, stands on a site where archaeologists have found the remains of large wooden buildings; some hold that these were the pagan temple, others an early wooden church. The astronomer Anders Celsius was buried there. Pope John Paul II held an open-air mass at the Royal Mounds in 1989, and the Swedish Asatru Society resumed holding blóts there in 2000.
gamprin: Gamprin is a municipality of Liechtenstein, on the Rhine, on the border with the Swiss municipality of Sennwald. It lies in the hilly landscape west of the Eschnerberg and consists of the villages of Gamprin and Bendern, in a scattered settlement that includes the old hamlets of Au, Bühl, Badäl, Salums and Gölla. It covers 6.188 square kilometres. It also has an exclave on the Nendler Berg, and its Gampriner Seele, a lake of 2.6 hectares, is the only lake in Liechtenstein. A flood of the Rhine in 1927 created it.

Settlement here goes back to the Stone, Bronze and Iron Ages, and the archaeological site of Lutzengüetle lies within the parish. The name comes from the Old Romansh camp Rin, a field on the Rhine. It was first mentioned about 1150 as Camporin, and in 1253 as Gamperin. The Bendern Parish Church, dedicated to Mary, has a nave dating from the 8th or 9th century, enlarged in the 14th century, and a Gothic chancel inaugurated in 1481. In 1499, during the Swabian War, Swiss Confederates pillaged the village. The oldest surviving village charter, of 1643, describes the villagers' rights and duties in using pastures and forests, and in 1699 the men of the Unterland swore allegiance to the Prince at Bendern.

In the 18th and 19th centuries Bendern ran one of the five ferries on the Liechtenstein stretch of the Rhine, linking it with Haag on the opposite bank. A wooden bridge was built across the river in 1867–68.

Until 1950 Gamprin had neither a coat of arms nor an official flag. A committee designed them, and the municipality adopted them in 1958. The yellow ribbon stands for the Rhine, and the roses come from the arms of the knight Rüdiger von Limpach, who owned property in Gamprin in the Middle Ages. The municipality contains the Liechtenstein Institute and the LGT Group.
ganapati-kakatiya: Ganapati's father Mahadeva was killed in a conflict with the Seuna, or Yadava, kingdom in 1198–1199, and Ganapati himself was taken captive. During his captivity the kingdom suffered revolts and invasions, and the commander-in-chief Rudra of the Recherla Reddi family appears to have governed in his name. An inscription at Manthena dated 26 December 1199 calls Ganapati the establisher of all the kingdom, which suggests that he had been freed by then. Yadava inscriptions claim that their king Jaitrapala released him out of compassion; the Yadavas may rather have wanted a quiet eastern border while they fought the Hoysalas.

Helped by the decline of the Kalyani Chalukya and Chola empires, Ganapati first turned to coastal Andhra, which the Kakatiyas had lost. The Krishna delta was conquered by 1201, and his general Chaunda plundered the island of Divi, whose Ayya chiefs submitted; Ganapati married two daughters of their chief, and their brother Jayapa became his commander. The Velanati Choda ruler Prithvishvara probably died fighting the Kakatiyas about 1206, and by 1209 Vela-nadu and Kamma-nadu were annexed. At Nellore Ganapati installed the Telugu Choda chief Tikka on the throne.

Repeated campaigns in Kalinga and Vengi from 1212 against the Eastern Ganga kings Ananga Bhima III and Narasimha I had mixed results, and Kakatiya control was probably limited to the land south of the Godavari River. In 1250 an army under Samanta Bhoja won a decisive victory at Palaiyaru and restored Tikka's son Manuma-siddhi II at Nellore. Around 1257, however, the Pandya king Jatavarman Sundara I attacked; the Pandyas captured Nellore and killed Manuma-siddhi II at the Battle of Muttukuru in 1263.

Ganapati continued the removal of the capital from Anumakonda to Orugallu, where he built a fortification of 75 bastions, each protected by a nayaka, comprising a stone fort and a mud fort one within the other. He also subdued the petty chiefs who had been harassing foreign merchants at the port of Motupalli.

Ganapati apparently retired after his defeats by the Pandyas in the late 1250s. He had no male heir and two daughters, Rudrama-devi, married to the Vengi Chalukya prince Virabhadra, and Ganapama-devi. Rudrama began to rule as co-regent in 1259–1260 under the regnal name Rudra-deva Maharaja, though an inscription at Duggi shows that Ganapati was alive at least until 1269. The 17th-century Pratapa-charita says that two sons of his by junior queens, Hari-hara and Murari-deva, rebelled against her; no other source knows these sons. Inscriptions listing distant kings as his vassals follow literary convention and can be dismissed.
gandaki-river: The Gandaki drains a catchment of 46,300 square kilometres, most of it in Nepal. Its upper course, the Kali Gandaki, rises at the Nhubine Himal Glacier in the Mustang region at 6,268 metres, on the border with Tibet. It then runs south through the Kali Gandaki Gorge between Dhaulagiri (8,167 metres) and Annapurna (8,091 metres), one of the deepest canyons in the world, and the river is older than the Himalayas, cutting through the mountains as they rise. Near Devghat the Kali Gandaki is joined by the Trishuli, a larger tributary.

Below Gaindakot the river is called the Narayani or Sapt Gandaki, the Seven Gandakis, after seven tributaries that rise in the Himalaya. In India it enters Uttar Pradesh, passes Kushinagar District and flows about 300 kilometres south-east across Bihar, building an immense megafan across eastern Uttar Pradesh and north-western Bihar.

The river is mentioned as Sadanira in the Shatapatha Brahmana, and in the Mahabharata. Its origin is told in the Shiva Purana. Between Dhaulagiri and Annapurna it flows past Muktinath, whose stones, the saligrama silas found in the riverbed, are of great significance to Hindus, who regard them as a representation of Narayana. Srivaishnavas and followers of Madhvacharya count the Muktinath temple among the 108 Divyakshetrams.

Along the river lie places of archaeological interest. At Lauriya-Nandangarh stands a lion pillar of Ashoka, a single block of polished sandstone 11 metres high, believed to be over 2,300 years old, beside brick stupas said to hold ashes from the Buddha's funeral pyre. Near the Kali Gandaki in Upper Mustang some 10,000 man-made caves have yielded partly mummified bodies and skeletons at least 2,000 to 3,000 years old, and religious paintings, sculptures and manuscripts of the 12th to 14th century. Mahatma Gandhi began the Champaran Satyagraha from his ashram at Bhitiharawa near the river.

Under an agreement signed on 4 December 1959 between Nepal and India, the Gandak Barrage was built at Valmikinagar in 1968–69 to supply irrigation to Nepal, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. Chitwan National Park in Nepal, established in 1973 and a World Heritage Site since 1984, lies beside India's Valmiki National Park around the barrage. The river's valleys also have many hydroelectric stations.
ganden-monastery: Ganden stands about 40 kilometres (25 mi) from Lhasa, at the top of Wangbur Mountain in Dagzê County, at an altitude of 4,300 metres. The monastery lies in a hilly natural amphitheatre, and the kora route around it gives views over the valleys. Its full name is Ganden Namgyal Ling. Ganden means joyful and is the Tibetan name for Tuṣita, the heaven where the bodhisattva Maitreya is said to reside; Namgyal Ling means victorious temple.

Je Tsongkhapa Lozang-dragpa (1357–1419) built the main temple, with large statues and three-dimensional mandalas, and often stayed there. He died at Ganden in 1419, and his disciples entombed his preserved body in a silver and gold encrusted tomb. The name Gelug abbreviates Ganden Lug, the Ganden tradition, and the Ganden Tripa, the throne-holder of Ganden, heads the school. Before he died Tsongkhapa gave his robe and staff to the first Ganden Tripa, Gyeltsabjey (1364–1432). The term of office is seven years, and by 2003 there had been 99 Ganden Tripas. The four colleges of the second Tripa's time were later consolidated into two, Jangtsey and Shartsey, which combine the study of sutra and tantra through memorization, logic and debate.

In the 1860s an assembly of the great monasteries and government officials, organised by the lay aristocrat Shatra, deposed the regent and replaced him with Shatra. Thereafter this assembly, the Tsondu, chose the regents. Ganden, Sera and Drepung held about 20,000 monks in all, supported by estates worked by serfs, and could in effect veto government decisions. Ganden could once support over 5,000 monks; Laurence Waddell reported an estimate of about 3,300 in the 1890s, and there were apparently 2,000 in 1959.

The monastery was destroyed after the 1959 Tibetan uprising. In 1966 Red Guard artillery shelled it and monks had to dismantle the remains, and during the Cultural Revolution (1966–1976) the buildings were reduced to rubble with dynamite. Most of Tsongkhapa's mummified body was burned, but his skull and some ashes were saved by Bomi Rinpoche, the monk forced to carry the body to the fire.

Rebuilding has continued since the 1980s. The red-painted lhakang at the centre reconstructs the sanctum holding Tsongkhapa's reliquary chorten, the Tongwa Donden, Meaningful to Behold. The main sights are the Serdung, with Tsongkhapa's tomb, the Tsokchen Assembly Hall and the Ngam Cho Khang, the chapel where he traditionally taught. A monastery of the same name and tradition was established by Tibetan exiles in 1966 at Mundgod in Karnataka, India, where the colleges Ganden Jangtse and Gaden Shartse have also been re-established.
gandhari-language: Gandhari is an early Middle Indo-Aryan language with features that set it apart from every other known Prakrit. It kept the three Old Indo-Aryan sibilants s, ś and ṣ as distinct sounds, while the other Prakrits merged them into one, and it preserved some old consonant clusters, mostly those with v and r. Intervocalic th and dh were at first written with a special letter, which suggests a sound change, probably to a voiced fricative, then to z and finally to a plain s.

Its grammar is hard to analyse, because final consonants were lost and final vowels weakened until they were no longer told apart, though a rudimentary system of case survived. The Kharoṣṭhī script does not mark long and short vowels, so how the language treated them is unknown. Some of its words, such as the term for sister, descended from Old Indo-Aryan svasṛ-, are shared with the Dardic languages, among them Shina and the Kohistani languages, and Torwali stands closest to Niya Prakrit, the dialect once spoken at Niya.

Gandhari appears on coins, inscriptions and manuscripts. It served as an official language of the Kushan Empire and of Central Asian kingdoms including Khotan and Shanshan, and its inscriptions have been found as far east as Luoyang and Anyang in China. From the 1st century CE a heavily Sanskritised form of the language spread. Most Gandhari manuscripts belong to the Dharmaguptaka school, but virtually all Buddhist schools, the Mahayana included, used it to some degree. When the Kushan monk Lokakṣema began translating Buddhist sutras into Chinese in 147 CE, the earliest of these translations show signs of having been made from Gandhari.

In 1932 E. Waldschmidt noticed that the names in the Chinese translation of the Dīrghāgama, made by the monk Buddhayaśas, were rendered not from Sanskrit but from an unidentified Prakrit also found in the Khotan Dharmapada. In 1946 Bailey identified this language, named it Gandhari, and matched it with the language of most Kharoṣṭhī inscriptions of north-western India.

Until 1994 the only known Gandhari manuscript was a birch-bark Dharmapada found at Kohmāri Mazār near Hotan in 1893. Since then many fragments have come to light in eastern Afghanistan and western Pakistan, including 29 birch-bark scroll fragments in the British Library and palm-leaf folios in the Schøyen Collection. The corpus now counts 391 manuscripts, 901 administrative documents, mainly from Niya, and 1,234 inscriptions, besides coin legends.
gandzasar-monastery: The name Gandzasar means treasure mountain in Armenian and is believed to come from a tradition that the monastery stands on a hill with silver and other metal ores. The site is first mentioned by the 10th-century Catholicos Anania of Moks, who listed Sargis, a monk of Gandzasar, among the participants of a council held at Khachen in 949. Khachkars dated 1174, 1182 and 1202 found around the monastery also point to an earlier church or monastery.

The main church was built between 1216 and 1238 by Hasan-Jalal Dawla, prince of Inner Khachen, and consecrated on 22 July 1240, the Feast of the Transfiguration, with some 700 priests present. The narthex was started in 1240 and finished in 1266 by his son Atabek and Atabek's mother Mamkan. The contemporary historian Kirakos Gandzaketsi described the building in his History of Armenia.

The monastery stands on a hill at 1,270 metres, south-west of the village of Vank. Its walled complex has the church, narthex, living quarters, bishop's residence, refectory and school. The church, named for John the Baptist, has a cruciform plan with two-floored sacristies at the corners and is known for a richly decorated sixteen-sided dome. Reliefs on its exterior show the Crucifixion, Mary with the infant Jesus, Adam and Eve, two patrons holding a model of the church, a bull's head and an eagle, and have been compared to the carvings of Aghtamar. Anatoli Yakobson called it an encyclopedia of Armenian architecture.

In the late 14th century Gandzasar became the seat of the Catholicosate of Caucasian Albania, a see of the Armenian Apostolic Church, and in the 16th century it became subordinate to Etchmiadzin. In the early 1700s its patriarch is said to have had authority over some 900 villages. Under Catholicos Yesayi Hasan-Jalalyan it was a centre of efforts by the Karabakh Armenian meliks to seek Russian protection. A Russian regulation of 1836 moved the diocese of Artsakh to Shusha, and the monastery decayed. The Soviet authorities closed it by 1930, and it reopened on 1 October 1989 under Archbishop Pargev Martirosyan.

During the First Nagorno-Karabakh War Azerbaijani helicopters bombarded the complex on 16 August 1992, and an air strike in January 1993 damaged it seriously. It was refurbished between 2000 and 2002 with funding from Levon Hayrapetyan. After the Azerbaijani offensive of 19 and 20 September 2023, Azerbaijani authorities described it as a Caucasian Albanian monument, which Armenian officials, the Armenian Church and scholars such as Victor Schnirelmann reject, pointing to its Armenian inscriptions.
ganesha: Ganesha is mentioned in Hindu texts between the 1st century BCE and the 2nd century CE, and a few images from the 4th and 5th centuries CE have been documented. An elephant-headed figure on Indo-Greek coins of the 1st century BCE has been proposed as an early depiction, but this is strongly contested. The first terracotta images date from the 1st century CE, and the earliest stone icons were carved at Mathura in Kushan times. The title gaṇapati appears twice in the Rig Veda, but there it refers to Brahmanaspati and Indra, not to Ganesha. The detailed stories of his birth and elephant head come from the later Puranas, composed from about 600 onwards.

Ganesha is identified by his elephant head and four arms. He is also called Ganapati, Vinayaka and Pillaiyar. Hindu texts name him as the son of Shiva and Parvati, though the Puranas give different accounts of his birth. In the most recurrent story Parvati made him from clay to guard her, and Shiva beheaded him when he came between them and replaced the head with an elephant's.

Devotees honour him as Vighneshvara, the Lord of Obstacles, held both to place obstacles in the way of those who need to be checked and to remove them for those who begin something new. He is also the patron of letters and learning. In the Ganapatya tradition he is the Supreme Being, and the Ganesha Purana and Mudgala Purana are its principal texts.

Hindus of all denominations invoke Ganesha at the beginning of prayers and ceremonies, and dancers and musicians, particularly in southern India, begin performances with a prayer to him. He is placed at the doorway of many temples, and the Ashtavinayak, eight shrines near Pune, are dedicated to him. The ten-day festival of Ganesh Chaturthi begins with the bringing in of clay idols, which are immersed in water at its end. In 1893 Lokmanya Tilak turned it from private family celebrations into a public event, to build unity against British rule in Maharashtra.

From about the 10th century he became the principal deity of traders. In Mahayana Buddhism he appears as the god Vināyaka, often dancing. Some Jains worship him, and the earliest known Jain statue dates to about the 9th century.
gang-gam-chan: Kang was born on 22 December 948 into a prominent aristocratic family of the Geumju Kang clan, in Geumju, now Gwanak District in Seoul. His father had served King Taejo of Goryeo and was honoured for helping to found the dynasty. A legend tells that a meteor fell towards the house on the day of his birth, and the place is still called Nakseongdae, site of the falling star. From the age of seven he learned Confucian philosophy, military tactics and martial arts from his father, and after his father died in 964 he travelled around the country.

In 983 Kang took the top score in the civil service examination, and in 992 he joined the court as a deputy under the Minister of Education. When the Liao general Xiao Paiya invaded in 993 he supported negotiation, and the talks of Sŏ Hŭi brought a truce. After General Kang Cho murdered King Mokjong in 1009, Emperor Shengzong of Liao invaded in 1010 with, by the figure given, 400,000 soldiers. Kang urged King Hyeonjong to flee rather than surrender, and the king escaped the burning capital; resistance in the country then forced the Khitans to withdraw.

When Xiao Baiya led 100,000 men into Goryeo in 1018, many officials wanted peace talks, but Kang advised war, since this army was smaller than earlier ones. Serving as acting deputy War minister, he led about 208,000 men towards the border, won the Battle of Heunghwajin by breaking a dam as the Khitans crossed the stream, and in 1019 caught the starving, retreating enemy at Gwiju, where only Xiao and a few others escaped.

Kang retired from the army and the government in 1020, was appointed Supreme Chancellor in 1030 and died on 9 September 1031; he was buried in what is now Cheongju. His victories are often compared with those of General Ŭlchi Mundŏk at the Battle of Salsu and Admiral Yi Sun-sin at Hansan and Myeongnyang. The peace that followed lasted about a century, a balance between Goryeo, Liao and Song in which the Jurchens grew strong. His shrine, Anguksa, stands in Sadang-dong, Gwanak District.
gang-of-four: The Gang of Four was a Maoist faction of four Chinese Communist Party officials who came to prominence during the Cultural Revolution of 1966-1976. Its leading figure was Jiang Qing, the wife of Mao Zedong, a former film actress who had taken no public political role before 1966 and whom Mao placed in charge of the country's cultural apparatus. Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan and Wang Hongwen were party leaders in Shanghai who had played leading roles in securing that city for Mao. Yao Wenyuan's article of 10 November 1965 attacking the play Hai Rui Dismissed from Office is cited as the spark of the Cultural Revolution.

The Cultural Revolution began to lose momentum around the death of Lin Biao in 1971. Premier Zhou Enlai regained his authority and brought Deng Xiaoping back into the leadership at the 10th Party Congress in 1973. Near the end of Mao's life a power struggle developed between the Gang and an alliance of Deng, Zhou and Ye Jianying. After Zhou died in January 1976, the Gang used their newspapers to attack Deng and mobilised their urban militia units. It remains unclear which decisions were Mao's and which the Gang's own.

Mao died on 9 September 1976. Premier Hua Guofeng attacked the radicals' media line at a Politburo meeting, and Jiang Qing insisted that she be named party chairman. Hua won the army over to his side, and on 6 October 1976 he had the four leading radicals arrested in a bloodless coup. Nationwide denunciations began on 21 October. Government media blamed the Gang and Lin Biao for the excesses of the Cultural Revolution, and many Chinese saw the arrests as the sign of a new era.

The four were tried in late 1980 by the Supreme People's Court, with Jiang Hua presiding, and convicted in January 1981 of anti-party activities. The trial was broadcast daily on television. The prosecution separated political errors from crimes, among them the usurpation of state power and the persecution of some 750,000 people, 34,375 of whom died in 1966-1976. Jiang Qing alone argued her own case, saying she had obeyed Mao at all times; Zhang Chunqiao admitted nothing, while Yao Wenyuan and Wang Hongwen expressed repentance.

Jiang Qing and Zhang Chunqiao received death sentences later commuted to life imprisonment, Wang Hongwen life, and Yao Wenyuan twenty years. Jiang Qing died by suicide in 1991 and Wang Hongwen died in 1992; Yao Wenyuan and Zhang Chunqiao died in 2005. The term was later used for Hua Guofeng's four closest collaborators, who were demoted in 1980 for grave errors in the struggle against the Gang.
gangaikondacholapuram: Gangaikonda Cholapuram is a village near Jayankondam in Ariyalur district, about 125 kilometres north-east of Tiruchirapalli International Airport and about 50 km from Thanjavur. The city was planned with the royal palace at its centre and the main Shiva temple to its north-east, as Vastu texts prescribe for Shiva shrines. It had two concentric walls, the outer one built of burnt brick as two parallel walls with a sand-filled core, and their remains form a mound round the palace site. The Madhurantaka Vadavaru channel, about 6 km to the east, irrigated the fields around the capital.

Rajendra I founded the city to commemorate his victory over the Pala dynasty, after a campaign that Chola-era records say crossed Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and Bengal; the defeated kingdoms were required to send pots of Ganges water to be poured into the temple's well. He moved the capital from Thanjavur and laid out the city and its temples by the rules of the Tamil Vastu and Agama sastra texts. The temple, modelled on his father Rajaraja I's temple at Thanjavur, was completed in 1035. Inscriptions name a multi-storeyed palace, the Chola-Keralan Thirumaligai, and gates, streets and highways such as the Rajendran Peruvali.

All the city's temples except the Brihadisvara were destroyed in the late 13th and 14th centuries, for reasons that remain uncertain. The archaeologist S. Vasanthi suggests that the Pandyas, who defeated the Cholas in the late 13th century, may have razed the city, but historians note that this does not explain why the main temple was spared and received grants recorded in about 20 later inscriptions. Another theory blames raids by the Delhi Sultanate, whose armies under Malik Kafur in 1311, Khusrau Khan in 1314 and Muhammad bin Tughlaq in 1327 invaded Chola territory.

The ancient site is a designated heritage town. Its Brihadisvara Temple, second in scale only to the temple at Thanjavur, keeps a Shiva lingam carved from a single block of stone, a lotus-shaped solar altar and bronzes of Bhogasakti and Subrahmanya, and it was reconsecrated in 2017. Traces of other Chola buildings survive as mounds, pillar stumps and brick walls across several kilometres around it.
ganges-yamuna-doab: Doab is a term used in South Asia for the tract of land between two confluent rivers, from the Persian do-ab, literally two bodies of water. The Ganges–Yamuna Doab, also called the Ganga Doab, is the flat alluvial tract between the two rivers, running from the Sivalik Hills to their confluence at Prayagraj. It is similar to an interfluve, and J. S. Grewal defines a doab as the inter-fluvial area between any two rivers. It covers about 60,500 square kilometres, around 805 kilometres in length and 97 in width. In ancient times it was known as Antarvedi. It is the most populated and largest of the doabs of India.

Across the Indo-Gangetic plains the doabs have alternating belts of river, khadir and bangar. Khadir is low-lying floodplain near the rivers, usually very fertile, while bangar is higher land away from the rivers, less prone to flooding but on average less fertile. For many centuries villages in the doabs were officially classified as khadir, khadir-bangar or bangar, and different agricultural tax rates applied according to a tiered scale of land productivity. The British Raj divided the Ganges–Yamuna Doab into three administrative districts: the Upper Doab around Meerut, the Middle Doab around Agra and the Lower Doab around Allahabad.

The Doab is divided into the Upper Doab, from Haridwar to Aligarh, the Middle Doab and the Lower Doab. The Upper Doab includes the districts of Dehradun and Haridwar in Uttarakhand, Saharanpur, Muzaffarnagar, Meerut, Ghaziabad and Bulandshahr in Uttar Pradesh, and Delhi. The Middle Doab includes Aligarh, Agra, Mathura, Firozabad and Mainpuri. The Lower Doab includes Farrukhabad, Kannauj, Etawah, Kanpur, Fatehpur and Allahabad.
ganggangsullae: The dance is thought to have originated in ancient times, when the ancient Koreans believed that the Sun, Moon and Earth controlled the universe. Participants danced under the brightest full moon of the year to wish for a fertile harvest. The etymology of the name is not clear. One reading takes it from indigenous Korean words, in the Jeolla dialect meaning circles or surroundings and patrol, so that it would mean beware of your surroundings. Another takes it as a Hanja phrase meaning that a powerful barbarian is going to invade, a reading tied to the naval commander Yi Sun-sin, though there is little evidence for it.

Under the Confucian policy of the Joseon dynasty the status of women fell sharply, and women were required to cover the face and head and were not allowed out of the house. The dance gave them a chance to go outside and sing together. In the 16th century, during the Japanese invasion of Korea, Admiral Yi Sun-sin is said to have ordered women to dance in military uniform on Mount Okmae, so that Japanese scouts overestimated the strength of the Korean troops.

Ganggangsullae is performed only by women, traditionally at night under the moon. Young and old women go out in traditional Korean clothing, hold hands in a circle and begin to rotate. A lead singer sings a line and everyone answers with the refrain ganggangsullae, a call and response like most Korean folk songs. The songs speak of personal hardships, relationships and desires, and the tempo grows faster: it begins slowly (jinyangjo), moves to a moderate pace (jungmori) and ends fast (jajinmori).

The circle changes into spirals, concentric circles and circles of different sizes, breaks into straight lines and forms a full circle again; the opening circle represents the full moon. Between songs the women play games, among them the gatekeeper play, in which dancers pass under an arch of arms, and the stomping of the roof tile, in which one woman walks along the backs of others. The dance can last until dawn.

The dance is performed mostly in South Jeolla Province, on the south-western coast, and is associated with Chuseok and Daeboreum, as well as New Year's Day and Dano. It was registered as UNESCO intangible cultural heritage from Korea in 2009. It is now taught to younger generations in music classes at local schools, and the Korean pop group ATEEZ includes the dance in its performances.
ganghwa-island: Ganghwa Island lies in the Yellow Sea, in an estuary of the Han River, and belongs to Ganghwa County in Incheon, South Korea. A narrow channel separates it from Gimpo on the mainland and is crossed by two bridges, while the main channel of the Han River separates it from Kaesong in North Korea. Its position controls access to the river, which runs through Seoul, the capital of Joseon and of South Korea.

Before the 10th century the island had several names, among them Haegu, meaning mouth of the sea, and Gangha, meaning below the rivers. In 940, in the Goryeo period, it received its present name, which means a beautiful town by the river. It was originally joined to the mainland and became separate through erosion. Mudflats now surround it, and land reclamation for farming has enlarged it. Its highest mountain is Manisan, at 469 metres.

In the early Goryeo period the island formed part of Ganghwa-hyeon. It became part of Ganghwa-bu in 1377, and in 1914 part of Ganghwa County in Gyeonggi Province. It remained so until 1994, when it was placed under Incheon Metropolitan City. A palace site of Goryeo on the island, Goryeogung, dates from 1232 to 1270.

Its fortifications were repeatedly attacked in the 19th century. The island was the site of the French expedition to Korea of 1866, the American expedition of 1871, the Battle of Ganghwa and the Ganghwa Island incident with Japan in 1875. In 1876 Korea was forced to sign a treaty with Japan, which took its name from the island as the Treaty of Ganghwa.

Stone tombs on the island belong to the UNESCO World Heritage series Gochang, Hwasun and Ganghwa Dolmen Sites. On Manisan stands the Chamseongdan Altar, where Dangun Wanggeom is said to have performed ancestral rites; a foundation day festival is held there each autumn. The Ganghwa Bridge was built to the mainland in 1969 and replaced in 1997, and the Ganghwa Choji Bridge opened in 2002. The island's turnip has been cultivated for more than a thousand years.
gangotri: Gangotri is a town and municipality in the Uttarkashi district of Uttarakhand, 99 km from the district headquarters at Uttarkashi. It stands on the banks of the Bhagirathi, from which the Ganges takes its origin, in the Greater Himalayan Range at a height of approximately 3,200 metres. The source of the Bhagirathi is the Gangotri Glacier. Once the river joins the Alakananda at Devprayag it takes the name Ganga. According to Hindu belief Gangotri is the seat of the goddess Ganga.

A popular Hindu legend says that the goddess Ganga descended here when Shiva released the river from the locks of his hair. Near the river is a stone where, according to tradition, King Bhagiratha performed penance to Shiva in order to bring the Ganga down to earth and absolve the sins of his ancestors. According to another legend, the Pandavas performed the great Deva Yajna here to atone for the deaths of their kinsmen in the battle of the Mahabharata.

The original Gangotri Temple was built by the Nepalese general Amar Singh Thapa and was restored in the 19th century. Hindus believe that ancestral rites on the banks of the Bhagirathi free the spirit of the ancestor from the cycle of rebirth, and that a holy dip in its waters cleanses sins of the present life and of past births.

Gangotri is one of the four sites of the Chota Char Dham pilgrimage circuit. The temple is closed from Diwali each year and reopens on Akshaya Tritiya, and during that time the idol of the goddess is kept at Mukhba village, near Harsil. The ritual duties of the temple are supervised by the Semwal family of pujaris, who come from Mukhba. The 2011 census of India recorded a population of 110 in 47 families, all of whom identified as Hindu.
gangtok: Gangtok stands at an elevation of 1,650 m in the lower Himalayas, on the side of a hill. A promenade called The Ridge runs between the Raj Bhawan, the governor's residence, at one end and the palace at the other. Two streams, the Roro Chu and the Ranikhola, flank the city and flow south to join the Teesta at Singtam. Mount Kanchenjunga is visible to the west. The slopes are prone to landslides, and in June 1997 a landslide disaster killed 38 people and destroyed hundreds of buildings. Most agree that the name means hill top in Tibetan.

Little is known of Gangtok's early history. The earliest records date from the building of a hermitic monastery in 1716, and the town remained a small hamlet until the Enchey Monastery, built in 1840, made it a pilgrimage centre. After the English conquest of Sikkim in the mid-19th century it became the capital of what was left of Sikkim, and after the British defeated the Tibetans it became a major stopover in the trade between Tibet and British India. In 1894 Thutob Namgyal, the Sikkimese monarch under British rule, shifted the capital from Tumlong to Gangtok, and a new palace and other state buildings were built.

After India's independence in 1947 Sikkim became a nation-state under Indian suzerainty, by a treaty that gave India control of its external affairs. Trade through the Nathula and Jelepla passes flourished, but it declined after 1959 and the passes were sealed after the Sino-Indian War of 1962. In 1975, after years of political uncertainty including riots, the monarchy was abolished and, following a referendum, Sikkim became India's twenty-second state, with Gangtok as its capital.

Gangtok is the capital of Sikkim and the seat of the Sikkim High Court. Its residents include Nepalis, who settled in the region under British rule and form the majority, Lepchas, who are native to the land, Bhutias and Tibetans. Hinduism and Buddhism are the most significant religions. The Enchey Monastery is the city's oldest and the seat of the Nyingma order, and the Rumtek Monastery on the outskirts, built in the 1960s on the model of one in Lhasa, is the seat of the Kagyu order. Tourism is the main part of the city's economy.
ganja-azerbaijan: Ganja lies 400 to 450 metres above sea level on the Ganja-Dashkasan plain in the west of Azerbaijan, 375 km from Baku. It stands at the north-eastern foothills of the Lesser Caucasus on the Ganjachay river. The name comes from the Persian word ganj, meaning treasure or treasury; Arabic sources call the city Janza and Armenian sources Gandzak. The tale that its founder found treasure nearby is considered a folk etymology.

The anonymous Arabic history Tarikh Bab al-abwab says Ganja was founded in 859–60 by Muhammad ibn Khalid, the Arab governor of the region under the caliph Al-Mutawakkil, after he unearthed a treasure there. The medieval Armenian historian Movses Kaghankatvatsi supports a 9th-century Arab foundation, while the Persian name suggests an older pre-Islamic town. From the 9th to the 12th century the area was known as Arran, and its urban population mainly spoke Persian. The city was damaged by an earthquake in September 1139, when King Demetrius I of Georgia took it and carried off its gates, and again by the Mongol invasion of 1231. It revived after the Safavids came to power in 1501 and was occupied briefly by the Ottomans in 1578–1606 and 1723–1735.

After the death of Nader Shah in 1747 Ganja became the centre of the Ganja Khanate, whose khans were subordinate to the rule of Iran. Russia, after annexing eastern Georgia in 1801, met strong opposition at Ganja. In 1804 Russian forces under General Pavel Tsitsianov invaded and sacked the city, sparking the Russo-Persian War of 1804–1813. Some western sources claim that up to 3,000 inhabitants were massacred. The Treaty of Gulistan forced Iran to cede the khanate, and the Treaty of Turkmenchay of 1828 made its inclusion in the Russian Empire permanent. It was renamed Yelizavetpol after Alexander I's wife, Elizabeth, and became capital of the Elizavetpol Governorate in 1868, though local Azerbaijanis continued to call it Ganja.

In 1918 Ganja was the temporary capital of the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic. The Red Army occupied Azerbaijan in April 1920, and in May an anti-Soviet rebellion in Ganja was put down, heavily damaging the city. In 1935 it was renamed Kirovabad after Sergei Kirov, and it regained its original name in 1989. A pogrom in November 1988 forced the local Armenian population to leave.

Ganja is a major city of western Azerbaijan, divided into the Kapaz and Nizami districts, which were established in 1980. The poet Nizami Ganjavi was born there, and its old landmarks include the Nizami Mausoleum, the Shah Abbas Caravanserai, the Imamzadeh complex and the Chokak Hamam. Most of its people are Muslim, mainly Shia, and most of its Armenians, Slavs, Jews and Germans have emigrated. The city is known for Ganja silk, and metallurgical and food industries operate there.
ganjifa: The first syllable of the name is linked to the Persian ganj, treasure, while the rest may come from a Chinese word for playing cards, an unproven theory. Cards called kanjifah appear on a Mamluk Egyptian deck in the Topkapı Palace museum, dated by L.A. Mayer to the 15th century, and the Egyptian historian Ibn Taghribirdi wrote that Sultan Al-Malik Al-Mu'ayyad played kanjafah for money as an emir. The earliest Persian reference is a poem by Ahli Shirazi (died 1535) with a verse for each of the 96 cards of the eight-suited pack.

In India, Babur noted in the Baburnama that in 1527 he sent a pack of Ganjifa cards to Shah Hassan, and the earliest surviving rules date to around 1600. In Iran Shah Abbas II (r. 1642–66) banned the game, which then declined. The round shape of most modern cards must have been an Indian innovation, since Persian cards were always rectangular.

Each suit has its own background colour and, in most packs, ten pip cards and two court cards, a king and a vizier. Lavish court sets of ivory inlaid with precious stones or of tortoise shell were called darbar kalam, cheaper sets for the public of wood, palm leaf, stiffened cloth or pasteboard bazâr kalam. The suits of the Mughal pack were slaves, crowns, swords, red gold coins, harps, bills of exchange, white gold coins and cloth. Dashavatara Ganjifa, with 120 cards in ten suits, is played mainly in Sawantwadi and by five players in Bishnupur in West Bengal; it can be extended to 24 suits for further gods.

The game most associated with the cards is a trick-taking game for at least three players, each playing for themself, with no trump suit. The king is always strongest, then the vizier, but in half the suits the pip cards rank upward from one and in the other half downward. A partnership version, sometimes called Dugi, sets one pair to win every trick, while Naqsh, a gambling game, resembles Blackjack with a target of 17. In the 20th century the hand-made cards lost their market to Western printed cards, which manufacturers such as Biermans, with a factory in Calcutta from 1934, sold in India.
gansu: Gansu lies between the Tibetan Plateau and the Loess Plateau, bordering Xinjiang and Qinghai to the west, Sichuan to the south, Shaanxi to the east and Inner Mongolia and Ningxia to the north. The Yellow River passes through the south of the province and flows through Lanzhou. The Qilian Mountains rise in the south, and parts of the Gobi Desert lie within the province. The Hexi Corridor, a natural passage of some 1,000 kilometres from Lanzhou to the Jade Gate, runs between the Gobi to the north and the Qilian Mountains to the south.

The name Gansu is a compound of Ganzhou, around Zhangye, and Suzhou, around Jiuquan, two prefectures of the Sui and Tang periods; the compound was first used under the Song dynasty. Before that the region was known as Longxi or Longyou, after Mount Liupan.

In prehistoric times Gansu was home to Neolithic cultures. The Dadiwan culture flourished in the east from about 6000 BCE to about 3000 BCE, and the Majiayao and Qijia cultures took root there in later millennia. The Yuezhi lived in the far west until the Xiongnu forced them to emigrate around 177 BCE. The state of Qin grew out of the south-east, around Tianshui, and Qin tombs and artefacts have been excavated at Fangmatan.

The Han dynasty extended the Great Wall across the corridor and built the fort towns of Yumenguan and Yangguan along it. The Ming dynasty built the Jiayuguan outpost, begun around 1372 and then at the western edge of China. By the Qingshui treaty of 823 between the Tibetan Empire and the Tang dynasty, China lost much of western Gansu for a significant period. Uyghurs who had migrated from their fallen khaganate set up the Ganzhou Uyghur Kingdom, which lasted from 848 to 1036, and the Western Xia later controlled much of the province.

Along the Silk Road, Gansu was both an economic route and a path of cultural transmission. The Mogao Caves near Dunhuang were begun in 366 CE, when a monk named Le Zun is said to have had a vision and carved the first grotto. The Bingling and Maijishan grottoes also date from the early centuries of Buddhist art. The Dungan Revolt of 1862–77 began in Gansu, and an earthquake on 16 December 1920 killed some 180,000 people.

Gansu is a province of north-western China with Lanzhou as its capital and largest city. Its population is about 26 million, mostly Han, with Hui, Dongxiang and Tibetan minorities. Labrang Monastery, built in 1710 in the south, is one of the six great monasteries of the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism, and the Jiayuguan pass preserves a section of the Great Wall.
gansu-corridor: The corridor lies in the modern western Gansu province, west of the Yellow River's Ordos Loop, which is the meaning of Hexi. It stretches roughly 1,100 kilometres from the Wushao Mountains in the east to Yumen Pass in the west, and is 40 to 100 kilometres wide. The Qilian Mountains run along its south, and the Mazong and Longshou Mountains separate it on the north from the Badain Jaran Desert and the Gobi. Deserts make up about 70% of its area, and fertile land is largely confined to oases along rivers fed by Qilian meltwater. This string of oases made it the most convenient route between China and Central Asia.

Settlement began around 4800 BP, when millet farmers from the Yangshao Culture reached the region. In the 3rd century BCE the Yuezhi lived there, until the Xiongnu defeated them in 176 BCE. The Han general Huo Qubing expelled the Xiongnu at the Battle of Hexi in 121 BCE, and the Han created the Four Commanderies of Hexi: Wuwei, Zhangye, Jiuquan and Dunhuang. This gave them control of the trade routes to Central Asia, laid the foundations for the Silk Road and allowed them to set up the Protectorate of the Western Regions in 60 BCE.

In the Sixteen Kingdoms period the corridor was spared much of the turmoil of the Central Plains, and Buddhist culture flourished, with the Mogao Caves built around this time. The Tang took it in 619, but after the An Lushan Rebellion of 755 the Tibetan Empire occupied it, taking Dunhuang in 786. The Western Xia controlled all of it by the 1070s, and the Mongols under Genghis Khan took it in 1226.

Marco Polo passed through between 1271 and 1275. The Ming took most of it in 1370 to 1372, by which time it had largely lost importance as a trade route. In 1907 Aurel Stein explored the corridor and rediscovered the Mogao Caves.

The corridor covers about 60% of Gansu, with five prefecture-level cities: Wuwei, Jinchang, Zhangye, Jiuquan and Jiayuguan. The Lanzhou–Xinjiang railway through it opened in 1963 and a high-speed line in 2014. The Mogao Caves were listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.
ganzak: Ganzak stood somewhere south of Lake Urmia in north-western Iran. The scholars Minorsky, Schippmann and Boyce placed it at the ruins at Leylan, in Malekan County on the Miandoab plain. The name means treasury and is of Armenian origin, from gandzak; it passed into Persian under the Achaemenid Empire and is related to the Persian word ganj, also meaning treasury.

The Achaemenids built Ganzak, and it was the seat of the satrap of Media. In the 4th century BCE it became part of the lands of the Persian aristocrat Atropates, who had gone over to Alexander the Great and probably made the town his capital. Around 148 BCE his kingdom, Atropatene, became a vassal of the Parthian Empire. In 36 BCE the Romans besieged Ganzak but were defeated by the combined forces of the Atropatenian king Artavasdes I and the Parthian king Orodes II.

Around 224 CE the Sasanian king Ardashir I ended the Atropatenian kingdom, but Atropatene remained a province of its own rather than being merged with Media, and Ganzak stayed its capital. In 591 the Battle of Blarathon was fought near the town between Khosrow II and the usurper Bahram Chobin, who was defeated and fled to Khorasan.

When the Byzantine emperor Heraclius came, the governor of Atropatene, Farrukh Hormizd, offered no resistance, because of an alliance he and the military rebel Shahrbaraz had made with the Byzantines. Heraclius destroyed the fire temple as retribution for the sack of Jerusalem, and Byzantine sources described Ganzak as a large town of about 3,000 houses.

In 651, during the Muslim conquest of Persia, the governor of Atropatene, Isfandyadh, became a vassal of the Rashidun Caliphate, and the province was soon taken into its administration. Ganzak lost its place as capital but survived under Muslim rule until it was destroyed at some point in the late medieval era. The nearby town of Leylan became its successor.
gao: Gao lies on the eastern bank of the Niger River, 320 km east-southeast of Timbuktu, at the junction with the Tilemsi Valley. The climate is arid, with rain only from June to September, and almost all local agriculture depends on the river's annual flood, which reaches Gao later than the upper river and peaks in December. In flood the river is 4 km wide at the city.

Excavations at Gao-Saney show that the site was occupied by about 700 CE, as a centre of manufacturing, iron smelting and trade reaching as far as Mesopotamia. Al-Khwārizmī gives the earliest written mention in the first half of the 9th century, and about 872 al-Yaqubi called the kingdom of Kawkaw the most important and most powerful of the realms of the Sūdān. By the 10th century the ruler was said to be a Muslim and the city had two towns. More than 100 medieval Arabic inscriptions survive from Gao and Gao-Saney, the oldest dated 1042. Towards the end of the 13th century Gao became part of the Mali Empire, and Ibn Battuta stayed there in 1352–53.

In the first half of the 15th century Sunni Sulayman Dama threw off Malian rule, and his successor Sunni Ali Ber, who ruled from 1464 to 1492, expanded Songhai territory and made Gao his capital. Leo Africanus, who visited between 1506 and 1510 under Askiya Muhammad I, found a large town without a wall, full of rich merchants, with a market where many slaves were sold. A survey under Askiya Al-Hajj, who reigned from 1582 to 1586, counted 7,626 houses, suggesting about 45,000 people. After the Moroccan invasion of 1591 the invaders made Timbuktu their capital, and Gao declined. When Heinrich Barth visited in 1854 he found a poor village of about 300 huts.

Gao is the capital of the Gao Region and the largest town in eastern Mali. The Tomb of Askia, a World Heritage Site, is a mosque tomb of some 2,500 square metres with a minaret 12 metres high. The town also has a mosque associated with Kankou Moussa, a museum of the Sahel and the sand dune La Dune Rose. Most people speak Koyraboro Senni, and the population includes Bozo, Fulani, Tuareg, Arab and Bambara groups. The city is regarded as a Songhay cultural capital.
gao-wei: Gao Wei was the son of Gao Zhan, then Prince of Changguang, and his wife Princess Hu. A concubine, Lady Li, had borne Gao Zhan a son, Gao Chuo, hours earlier on the same day, but Gao Zhan announced that Gao Wei was born first and made him his heir. Gao Zhan took the throne as Emperor Wucheng in 561, made Gao Wei crown prince in 562 and married him to a daughter of the general Hulü Guang.

In 565, citing astrological signs, the favourites He Shikai and Zu Ting persuaded Emperor Wucheng to hand the throne to his son. Gao Wei became emperor at the age of eight, while his father kept the real power as Taishang Huang, retired emperor. Gao Wei was thought weak, and his parents favoured his younger brother Gao Yan, Prince of Dongping, and considered deposing Gao Wei, though they never did.

After Emperor Wucheng died around 569, a group of eight officials led the government. Princes tried to send He Shikai, the most powerful of them and the open lover of Empress Dowager Hu, to a provincial post, but she instead had his chief critic, Gao Rui, Prince of Zhao Commandery, strangled. Gao Wei's wet nurse Lu Lingxuan and her son Mu Tipo became the most powerful of his favourites.

Lady Lu worked to make Consort Mu, the mother of Gao Heng, empress. In 572 Gao Wei named Consort Mu Right Empress and Empress Hu Left Empress, and around the new year of 573 Empress Hu was deposed. By spring 573 Mu Tipo, Gao Anagong and Han Zhangluan, called the Three Nobles, controlled the government and openly sold offices, while Gao Wei kept building, tearing down and rebuilding palaces until the treasury was exhausted.

Gao Wei passed the throne to Gao Heng but kept his authority. When Northern Zhou forces neared Yecheng he fled towards Ji Province, meaning to resist south of the Yellow River or else escape to the Chen dynasty, and the city fell. He was captured. Emperor Wu of Northern Zhou at first treated him as an honoured guest, put him at the head of his victory procession in summer 577 and made him Duke of Wen.

Later Emperor Wu, wary of the Gao clan, falsely accused him of plotting rebellion with Mu Tipo and ordered him and almost all of his clan to commit suicide; only two disabled brothers were spared and exiled. The Gao were properly buried north of Chang'an only during the regency of Yang Jian.
gaochang: Gaochang, also called Khocho or Qocho, was an oasis city on the northern rim of the Taklamakan Desert in present-day Xinjiang. One of the earliest cultures of the region was the Iron Age Subeshi culture, from 1100 to 100 BCE, probably linked to the Jushi Kingdom known from Chinese sources. Gaochang itself was built in the 1st century BCE and became a transport hub on the Silk Road. Under the Han dynasty control of the region swayed between the Han and the Xiongnu, until the Jushi leaders pledged allegiance to Han, which set up a military colony and settled colonists from the Hexi region and the central plains.

After the Western Jin fell, Gaochang was ruled by the Former Liang, Former Qin and Northern Liang as a commandery; the Former Liang ruler Zhang Jun created the Gaochang Commandery in 327. Remnants of the Northern Liang fled there in 439 and held power until the Rouran Khaganate conquered them in 460. The Rouran appointed Kan Bozhou king, making a vassal kingdom. The Gaoche later killed King Kan Shougui and installed vassal kings, and in 501 the people of Gaochang chose Qu Jia as king, founding the Qu kingdom that lasted until 640. The Qu rulers later became vassals of the Göktürks and were tied to them by marriage. In 629 King Qu Wentai welcomed the Tang pilgrim Xuanzang with great enthusiasm.

Fearing Tang expansion, Qu Wentai allied with the Western Turks and rebelled against Tang suzerainty. Emperor Taizong sent an army under General Hou Junji in 640, and Qu Wentai apparently died of shock at news of its approach. Gaochang was annexed as a sub-prefecture of Xizhou and the seat of government of Anxi. After the An Lushan Rebellion the Tang withdrew its soldiers in 755, and the Tibetans and then, in 803, the Uyghurs took the area. After 840 remnants of the Uyghur Khaganate settled there and founded the Kingdom of Qocho in 850, whose people practised Buddhism, Manichaeism and Christianity.

In 1209 the Uyghur ruler Barchuq offered Genghis Khan the suzerainty of his kingdom, and the Uyghurs entered Mongol service as bureaucrats, with their script adapted for Mongolian. The Mongols of the Chagatai Khanate conquered the Gaochang area between 1275 and 1318. The city was destroyed in wars of the 14th century, though palace ruins and the inner and outer city walls can still be seen. Gaochang was inscribed in 2014 on the UNESCO World Heritage List as part of the Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor. Nearby lie the Astana tombs and the Bezeklik Thousand Buddha Caves, which show depictions of Uyghur sponsors.
gaoyou: Gaoyou is a county-level city under the administration of Yangzhou, in Jiangsu province, on the north side of the Yangtze River in the Yangtze River Delta. It lies in a plain of rivers and lakes, bordered to the west by the canal and Gaoyou Lake, the third largest lake in Jiangsu, and to the north towards the Huai River. Its name comes from the building of Gaotai and a posting pavilion under King Yingzheng of Qin, and it was a military town on the canal line and a gateway to the two Huai rivers.

Finds at the Longqiuzhuang site show rice growing here 5,500 to 7,000 years ago. A commune, or ting, called Gaoyou was set up under the Qin dynasty, and Gaoyou county, with its seat there, was established in 118 BCE. In 1353 Zhang Shicheng revolted and captured the walled city.

In the next year he founded the Kingdom of Dazhou, and Gaoyou served as its temporary capital until 1356. The city withstood a siege led by Toqto'a, as complicated politics had severely reduced the cohesion of the Yuan army. It was one of 46 important mail posts along the Grand Canal between Beijing and Nanjing, a role it kept until the 1911 Revolution.

The Japanese army captured the walled city on 2 October 1939. After Japan's surrender in August 1945, a large Japanese garrison and puppet troops there refused to lay down arms, and the New Fourth Army fought the Battle of Gaoyou in December. It was the last battle against the Japanese in Central China. The site of the surrender has been listed by the State Council among national anti-war memorial sites. The flood of 1931 drowned about 200,000 people in Gaoyou, which was the worst affected place, and more than 30,000 people starved in the county during the great famine.

Gaoyou is the hometown of the Qing classical scholars Wang Nianshun and Wang Yinzhi, the paleontologist Sun Yunzhu, the writer Wang Zengqi and Wu Sangui. Its economy has depended on agriculture and fish farming, with rapeseed, rice, wheat, fish, crab and shrimp, and it is known for salted duck eggs. Lingtang Hui Ethnic Township, under its administration, is the only ethnic township in Jiangsu.
gapsin-coup: After the Imo Incident of 1882 China intervened directly in Korean affairs. Trade regulations of October 1882 gave Chinese merchants advantages and extraterritorial rights, Yuan Shikai trained a new Capital Guards Command, and King Gojong could not appoint diplomats without Chinese approval. Queen Min's relatives, the Min clan, held key offices and pursued a pro-Chinese policy alongside the conservative Sadaedang, who favoured gradual change on the Chinese model. Against them stood the Enlightenment Party, young and well-educated men mostly of the yangban class, among them Kim Okkyun, Pak Yung-hio, Hong Yeong-sik, Seo Gwang-beom and Philip Jaisohn, who admired Meiji Japan and wanted Korea free of Chinese interference.

Shut out of the offices they needed, the reformers saw their chance when war between France and China over Annam led to the withdrawal of half the Chinese troops from Korea. On 4 December 1884, with the Japanese minister Takezoe Shinichiro promising the help of the legation guards, they struck during a banquet given by Hong Yeong-sik to celebrate the opening of the new national post office. Telling the king falsely that Chinese troops had caused a disturbance, they took him to a small palace and placed him under Japanese guard and killed or wounded several senior Sadaedang officials.

The new government drew up a 14-point programme: an end to tribute to China, equal rights for all, a government close to a constitutional monarchy, land tax reform and a modern police. It had no more than 140 Japanese troops against at least 1,500 Chinese in Seoul, and at Queen Min's secret request the Chinese attacked. Hong Yeong-sik was killed, the Japanese legation was burned and forty Japanese soldiers died.

Gojong voided the reforms and demanded the conspirators back from Japan. Japan instead sent two battalions and seven warships, and the Treaty of Hanseong of 9 January 1885 restored relations, with Korea paying ¥100,000 for the legation. Ito Hirobumi and Li Hongzhang then concluded the convention of 31 May 1885, each side pledging to give notice before sending troops again. China's informal domination of Korea lasted until 1894, with Yuan Shikai remaining in Seoul as Chinese Resident.
garamantian-empire: The Garamantes may have descended from Libyco-Berber tribes, Toubou tribes and Saharan pastoralists who settled in the Fezzan region of southern Libya at least by 1000 BCE. At the Takarkori rockshelter, Final Pastoral peoples created burial sites for several hundred individuals around 3000 BP, with luxury goods from elsewhere, which made way for the Garamantian kingdom. From the 6th century BCE the Garamantes formed a powerful polity in northern Libya, controlling the trade routes between the Niger Bend and the Mediterranean. Their language is unknown; Roger Blench suggests it may have been a Nilo-Saharan language, though they wrote in a Libyan script, which is only partly decipherable.

The earliest written record dates to the 5th century BCE. Herodotus calls them a very great nation who herded cattle and farmed dates, and says they hunted Troglodyte Ethiopians in four-horse chariots to obtain slaves. Some scholars, including Sonja and Carlos Magnavita, regard such raids as possibly a speculative tale, but Roman merchants established themselves at Leptis Magna and Lixus to buy slaves brought from sub-Saharan Africa, and ostraca from the Roman fort at Bu Djem document Garamantian traders and slaves.

Tacitus wrote that the Garamantes aided the rebel Tacfarinas and raided Roman coastal settlements. According to Pliny the Elder, Lucius Cornelius Balbus and other Romans captured fifteen of their settlements in 19 BCE, and in 202 CE Septimius Severus captured the capital, Garama. The Roman traveller Julius Maternus accompanied a Garamantian king on an expedition to Agisymba, about four months from Garama.

The kingdom spanned roughly 180,000 square kilometres. Their decline may have been connected to worsening climate or overuse of water: fossil water is non-renewable, and over centuries the groundwater level fell.

The kingdom rested on a network of tunnels and shafts, known to Berbers as foggaras, that tapped fossil water under the limestone layer beneath the desert sand. Their dating is disputed, between 200 BCE and 200 CE, and a system of slave labour kept them maintained. The Garamantes had about eight major towns. Garama, near modern Germa, had around four thousand people, with another six thousand in villages within 5 kilometres. The king controlled trade routes reaching between the Niger Bend and Lake Chad, with oases such as Ghat and Barkat as bases for traders. Excavated cemeteries show a population of diverse geographical origin, including some individuals of sub-Saharan origin buried among other Garamantes, some perhaps enslaved.
garcia-ii-of-galicia: García was the youngest of the three sons and heirs of Ferdinand I, King of Castile and León, and Sancha of León, whose Leonese inheritance included the lands he was to receive. In the division of his father's estates in 1065 he was given the County of Galicia, raised to the rank of kingdom, which extended south to the Mondego River in Portugal and carried the parias of the Taifa of Badajoz and Seville. His eldest brother Sancho received Castile, and Alfonso, the second son and their father's favourite, received an enlarged León.

García's kingdom was the most troubled of the three. It included lands south of the Duero that had been firmly administered again only since the recapture of Coimbra the year before Ferdinand's death, and the bishops of Lugo and Santiago competed for preeminence. Among his first acts García forced the surrender of nearly all the holdings of the nobleman García Múñoz and planned to restore the bishoprics of Braga, Lamego and Tui. In early 1071 he defeated and killed the rebel Count of Portugal, Nuno Mendes, at the Battle of Pedroso.

Alfonso invaded Galicia and northern Portugal in May or early June 1071, and Sancho likely acquiesced in return for part of the realm. After Sancho defeated Alfonso in 1072, he turned on García, defeated him near Santarém and briefly imprisoned him in Castile before allowing him to flee to Seville. García's independent kingdom of Galicia and Portugal then ceased to exist.

Sancho was assassinated at Zamora in October 1072, and both dethroned brothers returned north. In February 1073 Alfonso invited García to a conference and took him prisoner. Later chronicles place his confinement at the castle of Luna, near León, where he remained until his death, dated by his epitaph to 22 March 1090. He wished to be buried in chains and was shown so on his tomb in the Basílica de San Isidoro, León. The epitaph, since destroyed, called him King of Portugal and Galicia and said he was taken by a trick. His capture and long imprisonment made him a favourite of epic poets.
garcia-ramirez-of-navarre: García Ramírez was born around 1112, the son of Ramiro Sánchez, lord of Monzón, whose father Sancho was an illegitimate son of King García Sánchez III of Navarre. His mother Cristina was a daughter of the Castilian nobleman Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, known as El Cid. He succeeded his father as lord of Monzón and also held Logroño. After the murder of King Sancho IV of Navarre in 1076, Navarre had been divided between Castile and Aragon, and Aragon's kings claimed the Navarrese crown, so that for 58 years the two kingdoms were united.

When the childless Alfonso the Battler died in 1134, the succession to both kingdoms was disputed. His will left them to three crusading orders, which the nobility of Aragon rejected in favour of his brother Ramiro, a monk. The Navarrese were doubtful of Ramiro and wary of King Alfonso VII of León and Castile, and at first preferred Pedro de Atarés.

At an assembly at Pamplona they turned away from Pedro, alienated by his arrogance, and elected García Ramírez, a descendant of their own dynasty. The Bishop of Pamplona gave him his church's treasure to fund his government. In January 1135 the Pact of Vadoluengo made García the adopted son of Ramiro, and in May he declared himself a vassal of Alfonso VII, who recognised his royal status.

Alfonso gave him Zaragoza as a fief before September 1135, but by 1137 García's rule there had closed. In 1136 he had to give Rioja to Castile, and in 1137 he allied with Alfonso I of Portugal against Alfonso VII before peace was confirmed in 1139 or 1140. In 1144 he married Urraca, an illegitimate daughter of Alfonso VII, to strengthen the tie to his overlord. He took part in the Reconquista and was instrumental in the conquest of Almería in 1147, and in 1146 he occupied Tauste, held by Aragon, until Alfonso VII mediated peace.

García's first wife, Margaret of L'Aigle, bore his successor Sancho VI and two daughters who married kings: Blanche, who married Sancho III of Castile, and Margaret, who married William I of Sicily. He refused to acknowledge her son Rodrigo as his own. García died on 21 November 1150 and was buried in the cathedral of Santa María la Real in Pamplona. His election restored the independence of the kingdom, which earned him the name the Restorer. His main monument is the Romanesque monastery of Santa María de la Oliva at Carcastillo.
garcia-sanchez-i-of-pamplona: García Sánchez I, son of Sancho I and Toda Aznárez, was born around 919 and succeeded his father in 925 at the age of six, the second king of the Jiménez dynasty. He reigned at first under the tutelage of his uncle Jimeno Garcés and his mother Toda. Three of his sisters married kings of León: Urraca married Ramiro II, Oneca married Alfonso IV, and Sancha Sánchez married first Ordoño II and later Fernán González, Count of Castile.

Another sister, Velasquita, married Munio Vélaz, a count of Álava. The historian Gonzalo Martínez Díez says these family ties meant that soldiers from Pamplona often fought beside Leonese and Castilian troops against Islam, and Queen Toda's web of alliances raised the kingdom's power.

After Jimeno Garcés died on 29 May 931, another uncle, Íñigo Garcés, probably tried to become regent and may have tried to take the throne. In May 934 the Caliph of Córdoba, Abd-ar-Rahman III, marched against Ramiro II of León and was about to enter Pamplona when Toda sent an embassy asking him to withdraw. He made her come to his camp at Calahorra, where she accepted a pact of submission and vassalage, and in return he invested García with Pamplona and its districts.

In 937 García allied himself with Ramiro II and the governor of Zaragoza, Muhammad ibn Hashim, provoking a caliphal campaign into his lands. In July 939 he fought alongside Ramiro II and Fernán González at the Battle of Simancas, where the Christian armies defeated the caliphate's forces.

After the death of Ramiro II and of Ordoño III of León, Pamplona backed Sancho I of León, García's nephew. When Fernán González installed his own son-in-law Ordoño IV in Sancho's place, relations broke down, and García intervened in León, captured Fernán and restored Sancho. Fernán made territorial concessions to win his release, and the alliance was restored in 964, when he married García's daughter Urraca.

García married his first cousin Andregoto Galíndez, daughter of Galindo Aznárez II, Count of Aragon. As Galindo had no legitimate male heirs, the rights to Aragon passed to Andregoto and then to her first son, as a county within the Kingdom of Pamplona. He repudiated her in 942 and by 943 had married Teresa Ramírez, daughter of Ramiro II of León. His son by Andregoto, Sancho II, succeeded him. A son by Teresa, Ramiro Garcés, became the first King of Viguera. García died on 22 February 970 and was buried in the castle of San Esteban de Deyo at Villamayor de Monjardín.
garcia-sanchez-iii-of-pamplona: García Sánchez III, nicknamed García of Nájera, was born around 1012, the eldest son of Sancho III. As the eldest son he inherited the dynastic rights over the crown of Pamplona, becoming feudal overlord of two of his brothers: Ramiro, who received lands that served as the basis of the Kingdom of Aragón, and Gonzalo, who received the counties of Sobrarbe and Ribagorza. He also had some claim to suzerainty over his brother Ferdinand, who under their father had been Count of Castile, nominally subject to León but under Sancho III's personal control.

García Sánchez inherited the crown after Sancho III died in 1035, bypassing Ramiro, who was the late king's eldest son but illegitimate. He also inherited the County of Álava and a great part of the County of Castile, including La Bureba, Trasmiera, the Montes de Oca, the Encartaciones and Las Merindades. In 1043 he defeated his half-brother in battle, which set the eastern border of the kingdom. He took advantage of the weakness of the Islamic taifa kingdoms that arose after the dissolution of the Caliphate of Córdoba, and pushed the southern border into their territory by taking Calahorra in 1045. In 1038 he married Stephanie of Foix in Barcelona, and they had nine children.

In 1037 he joined Ferdinand in a battle against the Kingdom of León near the river Pisuerga, the Battle of Tamarón, in which Bermudo III of León was defeated and killed, ending a dynasty that went back to Peter of Cantabria. Ferdinand was then crowned King of León.

The brothers' relationship turned sour over the conflicted division of the lands of Castile between León and Pamplona. It led to the Battle of Atapuerca, where García Sánchez died on 1 September 1054. His son Sancho Garcés, called Sancho the Noble, reigned as king of Pamplona from 1054 until his death in 1076. An illegitimate son, Sancho Garcés, lord of Uncastillo, had a grandson, García Ramírez, who became King of Pamplona.
garda-siochana: Policing in Ireland before the creation of the Irish Free State had been the work of the quasi-military Royal Irish Constabulary, with a separate, unarmed Dublin Metropolitan Police. During the Irish War of Independence the provisional government created a security force called the Irish Republican Police. The new state slowly built a single centralised, civilian, nationwide police organisation by incorporating various existing law-enforcement agencies and local units.

In English it was first called the Civic Guard. It became the Garda Síochána in both English and Irish at a time when there was a vogue for naming the institutions of the new state after counterparts in the French Third Republic. The phrase gardiens de la paix had been used since 1870 in French-speaking countries for civilian police, as distinct from the armed gendarmerie.

The first Commissioner, Michael Staines, a Pro-Treaty member of Dáil Éireann, held office for only eight months. His successors Eoin O'Duffy and Éamon Broy shaped the service. Under O'Duffy, to many people's surprise, the viability of an unarmed police service was established. He later led the Blueshirts for a short time before going to Spain to fight with Francisco Franco's Nationalists. Broy, who had helped the Irish Republican Army while serving with the Dublin Metropolitan Police, headed the Garda from 1933 to 1938.

Several episodes brought inquiries and reform. The Sallins Train Robbery of 1976 led to accusations that a Heavy Gang within the force had intimidated and tortured the accused, and one of them later received a presidential pardon. In the 1990s and early 2000s allegations of corrupt policing in County Donegal led to the Morris Tribunal, which found that some gardaí there had invented an informer for the Provisional IRA, made bombs and claimed credit for finding them, and tried to frame the publican Frank McBrearty Junior for murder. Its recommendations on management, discipline, promotion and accountability were largely carried out in the Garda Síochána Act 2005, which also set up a Garda Reserve.

The service is headed by a Commissioner appointed by the Government and answerable to the Minister for Justice. Its headquarters are in Phoenix Park, Dublin, and it is divided into four regions: Dublin Metropolitan, North-Western, Eastern and Southern. It has been a predominantly unarmed force, and more than three-quarters of its members do not routinely carry firearms. Detectives and units such as the Armed Support Units and the Emergency Response Unit are armed.

Members cannot join general trade unions and are represented by four rank-based bodies. The Scott Medal for Bravery, first awarded in 1923 and funded by Colonel Walter Scott of the New York Police Department, is the highest honour. Since 1989 the force has also served on United Nations missions, beginning with a contingent of fifty in Namibia.
gardar-greenland: Garðar was the first Catholic diocese established in the Americas. According to the sagas, Sokki Þórisson, a wealthy farmer of the Brattahlíð area, proposed a separate bishop for Greenland early in the 12th century and won the approval of the Norwegian king Sigurd I Magnusson. Most of the clergy came from Norway. The diocese was first placed under the Archbishopric of Bremen and then under the Archdiocese of Lund, and in 1152 it became, with Iceland, the Isle of Man, Orkney and the Faroe Islands, a suffragan of the new Archdiocese of Nidaros.

Arnaldur, the first bishop, was ordained by the Archbishop of Lund in 1124 and began the cathedral; he returned to Norway in 1150 and became bishop of Hamar. His successors included Jón Knútr, Jón Árnason, who went on pilgrimage to Rome in 1202–1203, met Pope Innocent III and was buried at Garðar in 1209, and Ólafr, who was abroad from 1264 to 1280. Communication with Norway was so poor that Bishop Árni was presumed dead and Jón Skalli was ordained in 1343; Skalli resigned when Árni proved to be alive and never went to Greenland.

After Árni died in 1347 the see stood vacant for 19 years, while the Norwegian cleric Ivar Bardsson led the church. Álfr, ordained in 1365, was the last bishop to reside, until 1378, and when Björn Einarsson Jórsalafari landed in 1385 a priest was administering the diocese. It disappeared in the 15th century, when ships from Norway stopped arriving. Bishops were still named to the see until 1537 and the Reformation in Denmark–Norway, apparently without any of them visiting it. In 1996 Garðar was revived as a titular see.

The settlement of Igaliku stands on the site, which has been studied by archaeologists since the 1830s. The Danish archaeologist Poul Nørlund fully excavated the cathedral in 1926. Its ruin, the main one, is of a cross-shaped sandstone church of the 12th century, up to 27 metres long and 16 metres wide, and the stone foundations of many Norse buildings remain visible, among them two large barns that could have held up to 160 cows.
garden-of-the-hesperides: In Greek mythology the Hesperides are the nymphs who tend the garden in which grow the trees of Hera that bear golden apples. They were also called the Atlantides, from their reputed father Atlas. Their name means originating from Hesperos, the evening, which also shares a root with the English word west. Their parents, number and names vary between sources. They are listed as daughters of Night, of Atlas and Hesperis, of Phorcys and Ceto, or of Zeus and Themis. Apollonius of Rhodes gives three, Aigle, Erytheis and Hespere, while Apollodorus gives four, Aigle, Erytheia, Hesperia and Arethusa. Euripides calls them minstrel maids for their sweet song.

The garden is Hera's orchard in the far west, near the Atlas Mountains, at the edge of the ocean of Oceanus. According to the legend, the goddess Gaia brought branches bearing golden apples as a wedding gift when Zeus and Hera married, and Hera had them planted in her gardens, which extended as far as Mount Atlas. The Hesperides tended the grove, and Hera set the immortal, never-sleeping, hundred-headed dragon Ladon to guard the apples. Pliny the Elder places the garden at Lixus in modern Morocco, and elsewhere says the Hesperides live on two islands in the Atlantic. Diodorus gives a variant in which the Hesperides had flocks of sheep so beautiful that the poets called them golden apples, guarded by a shepherd named Dracon.
