Euesperides, modern Benghazi, might have mythological associations with the garden. Diodorus gives a variant in which the Hesperides had flocks of sheep so beautiful that the poets called them golden apples, guarded by a shepherd named Dracon.

The eleventh Labour of Heracles was to steal the apples. In one version Heracles tricked Atlas into fetching them by offering to hold up the heavens for a while, and then walked away with them; in another he killed Ladon. According to Apollodorus, Eurystheus gave the apples back to Heracles, and Athena returned them to the garden. The Argonauts came to the Hesperian plain the next day, and the Hesperides directed them to a spring that Heracles had struck from a rock near Lake Triton. Heracles appears sitting in bliss in the garden on Attic pottery, especially from the late fifth century BCE.

By Roman times the garden had dwindled to a poetic convention. It returned in Renaissance poetry, where Robert Greene, Shakespeare and John Milton mention it, and Robert Herrick's collection of verse, Hesperides, was published in 1647. Later it was thought the golden apples might have been oranges, and the Greek botanical name for citrus species is Hesperidoeidē.
gardman: Gardman, also called Gardmank' or Gardmanadzor, was one of the eight cantons of the province of Utik', and its central fortress bore the same name. It corresponded roughly to the Gazakh, Shamkir, Aghstafa, Dashkasan, Goygol, Tovuz and Gadabay districts of modern Azerbaijan and the original Tavush Region of Armenia. Armenian historians noted two well-known places there: the fortress of Getabakk', in the present Gadabay district, and a copper mine. The historian Robert H. Hewsen thought the name might be of Georgian origin; others derive it from the Indo-Iranian word gard, meaning stronghold or housing.

Under the Arsacid kings of Armenia, Gardman was the seat of the nakharars, or princes, of Utik', so that Utik' was sometimes called the principality of the Gardmanians, and many Armenian authors counted Gardman as part of Artsakh. It passed to Caucasian Albania in 387, after the partition of Armenia. The local house of Gardman was later replaced by the Mihranid family, which became the ruling dynasty of Arran, and under the Mihranids in the 7th and 8th centuries the name Gardman came to be used for the whole of Utik'.

The Arabs conquered the region in 855. In 982 Gardman and Parisos, the northern district of Artsakh, became the small Armenian kingdom of Parisos, which lasted until 1017 and then became part of the Kingdom of Lori. In 1601 the Melik-Shahnazaryan family, a branch of the House of Khachen, founded the melikdom of Gardman, also known as the Voskanapat melikdom after the village where they lived. Their territorial rights were confirmed after the Russian Empire took the region in the early nineteenth century.
garegin-nzhdeh: Garegin Ter-Harutyunyan, known by his nom de guerre Nzhdeh, was born on 1 January 1886 in the village of Kznut in Nakhichevan, the youngest of four children of a village priest. He studied at a Russian school in Nakhichevan, a gymnasium in Tiflis and for two years at the law faculty of Saint Petersburg Imperial University, then returned to the Caucasus to join the Armenian national movement against the Ottoman Empire. In 1906 he moved to Bulgaria and in 1907 was commissioned lieutenant in the Bulgarian army. In 1908 he joined the Armenian Revolutionary Federation.

After three years in a Russian prison from 1909, Nzhdeh joined General Andranik Ozanian in 1912 in an Armenian battalion of the Bulgarian army in the Balkan wars. In the First World War he served in Armenian volunteer units of the Russian army, and in May 1918 he organised the defence of Karakilisa against Ottoman forces. In 1920, while stationed in southern Armenia, he expelled the Turkic-speaking inhabitants of several settlements.

After Armenia became Soviet on 2 December 1920 he rejected the proposal to place Karabakh and Zangezur in Soviet Azerbaijan and declared Syunik self-governing. The 2nd All-Zangezur Congress declared the Republic of Mountainous Armenia on 26 April 1921, with Nzhdeh as prime minister and minister of defence. After months of fighting the Red Army, it capitulated in July 1921 on Soviet promises to keep the region in Soviet Armenia, and Nzhdeh crossed into Iran. He later lived in Sofia, quarrelled with the Armenian Revolutionary Federation over relations with Turkey, and in 1933 founded the youth movement Tseghakron in Boston.

During the Second World War Nzhdeh proposed supporting the Axis powers if they attacked Turkey, and in 1942 he joined the Armenian National Council in Berlin, which Nazi Germany created to coerce Armenian prisoners of war into joining its Armenian Legion. He was arrested in 1944 and on 24 April 1948 was sentenced to 25 years of imprisonment for counterrevolutionary activities of 1920 and 1921. He died in Vladimir Central Prison on 21 December 1955. Armenia's prosecutor general rehabilitated him on 30 March 1992, and Armenians widely admire him as a national hero. His wartime record has drawn criticism, including from Israel's ambassador in January 2024.
gargano: The Gargano is a historical and geographical sub-region of the province of Foggia in Apulia, a wide, isolated mountain massif of highland and several peaks that forms the backbone of a promontory projecting into the Adriatic Sea. Its highest point is Monte Calvo, at 1,065 metres. The peninsula is partly covered by the Foresta Umbra, the only remaining part in Italy of the ancient oak and beech forest that once covered much of Central Europe. The Latin poet Horace spoke of the oaks of Garganus in his Ode II, ix. Two large salt lakes, Lesina and Varano, lie in the north, and the coast has beaches and resorts such as Vieste, Peschici and Mattinata.

Between the Miocene and the early Pliocene the area was a large island, which also included adjacent parts of peninsular Italy. Its animals, known as the Gargano fauna or Terre Rosse fauna, were unbalanced in the way of island communities and included giant rodents, a marine otter, a ruminant with five horns and flightless and giant birds. Fossils have been recovered from fissures in the limestone, filled with red clays. Paleontologists have argued over whether the animals arrived by a single land bridge or in several waves by rafting or flying. Later, as the ice ages began, sea levels sank and the island became joined to the mainland.

The Gargano is the site of the oldest shrine in Western Europe dedicated to the archangel Michael, the Sanctuary of Saint Michael the Archangel at Monte Sant'Angelo, and pilgrimages (cumpagnie) to it are made on 8 May and 29 September.

Most of the upland, about 1,200 square kilometres, forms the Gargano National Park, founded in 1991. Other sites include the Sanctuary of Saint Pio of Pietrelcina in San Giovanni Rotondo, the Abbey of Saint Mary of Ripalta and the Sanctuary of Saint Nazario, whose pilgrimage falls on 28 July. On Good Friday San Marco in Lamis holds the procession of the Fracchie. The varieties of Southern Italo-Romance spoken here are each particular to their town.
garibald-i-of-bavaria: Garibald, also spelt Garivald, was born around 540 and headed the Agilolfings, a noble family of Frankish origin; he is regarded as the founder of the Bavarian dynasty. After the death of King Theudebald of Austrasia, his successor Chlothar I took the widow Waldrada, daughter of the Lombard king Wacho, but when his bishops objected he gave her to Garibald in marriage in 556. The match brought Garibald prestige and created lasting ties between the Bavarii and the Lombards of Pannonia and Bohemia, which mattered after the Lombards moved into Italy in 568.

Sometime before 585 the Merovingian court tried to bind Garibald more closely by arranging a marriage between his daughter Theodelinda and King Childebert II of Austrasia, while also seeking to marry Childebert's sister to the Lombard king Authari. Both plans failed, and the offended Authari was engaged to Theodelinda in 588. According to the Nuremberg Chronicle, the Frankish king Chilperic, fearing an anti-Frankish axis, sent an army that overran Bavaria and drove Garibald to his son-in-law. Authari married Theodelinda at Verona in May 589 and made her brother Gundoald Duke of Asti. A Frankish invasion of Lombardy in 590, backed by Byzantium, was defeated.

After Authari died in 590, Theodelinda chose his cousin Agilulf as her husband and the next king, and in 591 Childebert made peace with the Lombards and the Bavarii, a peace that lasted for decades. Paulus Diaconus writes that peace with Bavaria came when Childebert named Tassilo king. How Garibald's rule ended is not known for certain, and Tassilo was his son or at least a close relation. Garibald was reportedly also the father of Romilda of Friuli and was an ancestor of several leading figures of the Lombard kingdom.
garifuna: The Garifuna are an Afro-Indigenous people of mixed free African and Amerindian ancestry who originated on the Caribbean island of Saint Vincent, which they call Yurumein, and traditionally speak Garifuna, an Arawakan language. They descend from Indigenous Arawak and Kalinago (Island Carib) people and Afro-Caribbean people. European writers called them Black Caribs, and modern historians have said that British colonial use of the name framed most of the island's Indigenous population as interlopers from Africa without claims to land.

How the African part of the population arrived is debated. In 1795 the British governor William Young wrote that Africans from two Spanish slave ships wrecked near Saint Vincent in 1635, largely Ibibio, had lived independently and integrated with the Indigenous people. Several modern researchers hold that most came from other islands, such as Barbados, Saint Lucia and Grenada, as people escaping slavery, and were taken in by the Caribs.

In 1763 the Treaty of Paris gave Britain control. In the First Carib War, which began in 1769, the Black Carib chief Joseph Chatoyer led a successful defence of the windward side of the island, and a peace agreement of 1773 set boundaries between British and Carib areas. In 1795 the Caribs rebelled again, in the Second Carib War, and gained control of most of the island; a major expedition under General Ralph Abercromby defeated them in 1796.

The British authorities then decided to deport the Caribs, to avoid further slave revolts. In 1797 those with African features, considered the cause of the revolt, were chosen, taken first to Jamaica and then to the island of Roatán in Honduras, while Black Caribs with more Amerindian traits were allowed to remain. More than 5,000 were deported, but only about 2,500 had survived when they landed on Roatán on 12 April 1797. They expanded along the Caribbean coast of Central America, to Belize and Guatemala in the north and Nicaragua in the south, and became known as Garifuna.

Almost all Garinagu are bilingual or multilingual and generally speak the official languages of their countries as a first language, while many speak Garifuna mainly as a cultural language. In 2001 UNESCO proclaimed the language, dance and music of the Garifuna a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in Nicaragua, Honduras and Belize. Most Garinagu are Catholic, and a traditional religion honours the ancestors and Bungiu, or Sunti Gabafu, with a shaman called a buyei at its head.
garigliano: The Garigliano forms where the Gari, also called the Rapido, meets the Liri. Its name is a corruption of Gari-Lirano, roughly the Gari from the Liri. In ancient times the whole course of the Liri and the Garigliano was known as the Liris. The river is about 40 km (25 mi) long, and for most of that distance it marks the border between the Italian regions of Lazio and Campania. In medieval times it was called the Verde and formed the southern border of the Papal States.

The western Roman emperor Majorian fought a Vandal raiding party at the Garigliano in 457. In the 9th and early 10th centuries a band of Saracens settled on its banks and raided Campania and central Italy from there. In 915 a coalition of Pope John X, the Byzantines, Franks, Lombards and Naples defeated them in the Battle of the Garigliano.

In 1503 Spanish and French forces fought a second battle there. The larger French army was almost destroyed at little cost to the Spanish, and its remnants later surrendered at Gaeta. Piero II de' Medici drowned in the battle, so that leadership of the Medici family passed to Giovanni de' Medici, later Pope Leo X.

During the Italian Campaign of World War II, the Liri, Gari and Garigliano rivers stood at the centre of a system of German defensive lines, the best known being the Gustav Line, around which the Battle of Monte Cassino was fought in 1943 and 1944. A boiling water reactor nuclear power plant named Garigliano operated near the town of Sessa Aurunca from 1959 until 1982.
garnet-wolseley: Garnet Joseph Wolseley was born on 4 June 1833 in Dublin into an Anglo-Irish family, the eldest son of Major Garnet Joseph Wolseley of the 25th Foot. His father died in 1840, leaving seven children on an army pension, and Wolseley left school at 14 to work in a surveyor's office. Unable to buy a commission, he appealed to the Duke of Wellington, and in March 1852 he was gazetted ensign in the 12th Foot in recognition of his father's service.

He was badly wounded in the Second Anglo-Burmese War and lost an eye at the Siege of Sevastopol. He fought at the relief of Lucknow in 1857, when he wrote of the sepoys in racist terms, and took part in the Anglo-French expedition to China of 1860. In 1870 he led the Red River Expedition to Fort Garry, though the uprising of the Métis under Louis Riel was settled by negotiation while his force was on the way. At the War Office from 1871 he pressed the Cardwell reforms against the Duke of Cambridge, above all short service and a reserve.

In the Ashanti campaign he defeated Chief Amankwatia's army at the Battle of Amoaful on 31 January 1874, and the campaign made him a household name, with a parliamentary grant of £25,000. He served as governor in Natal, as the first High Commissioner to Cyprus in 1878 and in South Africa, where he forced King Sekhukhune of the Bapedi to submit. In 1882 he defeated Urabi Pasha at the Battle of Tel el-Kebir and was made Baron Wolseley. His Nile Expedition of 1884–85 arrived too late to save General Gordon at Khartoum.

Wolseley became a field marshal in 1894 and Commander-in-Chief of the Forces from 1895, a post whose powers had been cut; he handed it to Earl Roberts on 3 January 1901. The reserves he had championed supplied much of the army for the Second Boer War. He died in March 1913 after falling ill on the French Riviera and was buried in the crypt of St Paul's Cathedral. His efficiency gave rise to the phrase all Sir Garnet, meaning all is in order, and W. S. Gilbert may have modelled Major-General Stanley in The Pirates of Penzance on him.
garonne: The Garonne flows from the central Spanish Pyrenees to the Gironde estuary at the French port of Bordeaux, a length of 529 km, of which 47 km lies in the Val d'Aran in Spain. Its basin covers 56,000 square kilometres. The name comes from Garumna, a Latin form of an Aquitanian name meaning stony river. Three places have been proposed as its source, and by the usual convention of the United States Geological Survey and others it is the Ratera-Saboredo cirque, the most distant point of the basin.

The river follows the Aran Valley northwards into France and passes Toulouse and Agen on its way to Bordeaux. The Ariège, the Tarn and the Lot join it, and just after Bordeaux it meets the Dordogne at the Bec d'Ambès to form the Gironde estuary, which runs about 100 km to the Atlantic. It is one of the few rivers in the world with a tidal bore. The European sea sturgeon, critically endangered, breeds only in its basin.

Umayyad and Aquitanian forces fought the Battle of the River Garonne in 732 beside the river near present-day Bordeaux. The river has long served shipping. Seagoing vessels reach Bordeaux, and it forms part of the Canal des Deux Mers between the Mediterranean and the Atlantic. Before the lateral canal was built between 1838 and 1856, shallow-draught boats used the river as far as Toulouse, though navigation on the upper river was uncertain. The canal now takes boats through 53 locks to Toulouse, where it meets the Canal du Midi.

Floods have been recorded since around 1177, with others in 1220, 1258 and many later years. At Toulouse, where the left bank is inhabited, they were frequent. In 1827 the river rose four metres above its usual level and filled the arches of the Pont de Pierre and Pont Neuf, and the floods of 1835, 1855 and 1875 were higher.

The river passes Vielha, Saint-Gaudens, Muret, Toulouse, Agen, Marmande, Langon and Bordeaux. Upstream of Toulouse it depends mainly on snow and snow melt, and downstream it is fed by rain, as are its main tributaries. The Saint-Martory canal and the lateral canal both draw water from the river.
garoua: Garoua lies on the Benue River in northern Cameroon and serves as the gateway to Benoue National Park. Its neighbourhoods include Commercial Centre, Lopere, Quartier de Marouare, Poumpoumre and Roumde Adjia, with the suburb of Yelwa in the north-west, near Garoua International Airport. The city has a tropical savanna climate, with a wet season and a dry season and heat throughout the year. The coolest months are December and January, with an average temperature of 26.0 °C, and the hottest is April, at 33.0 °C. December, January and February receive no rain at all, while August is the wettest month. The city receives about 997 millimetres of rain a year.

Garoua was established by the Fulani emir Modibbo Adama in the first half of the 19th century. During the steamship era it developed into a major river port, and goods were carried by ship along the Benue between Garoua and Burutu in Nigeria. The population of the city was 30,000 in 1967. By 2022 it had grown to approximately 900,000 people, among them a large Fulbe, or Fulani, population.

Garoua is the capital of the North Region of Cameroon and the fourth largest port in the country. It became a centre of trade in petroleum, cement, hides, peanuts and cotton, and has long been a centre of the cotton industry, with several textile processing facilities and factories. The cotton company Sodecoton has one of its major centres there. Leatherwork and fishing are also notable industries.

Most places of worship are mosques, but there are also Christian churches, including those of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Garoua, the Evangelical Church of Cameroon, the Presbyterian Church in Cameroon and the Cameroon Baptist Convention. The city stands on National Highway 1, at a junction of the road between Maroua and Ngaoundéré. Among its notable natives are the storyteller Goggo Addi, who worked to preserve Fulani cultural heritage, and Ahmadou Ahidjo, the first president of Cameroon.
garsenda-of-forcalquier: Garsenda was the daughter of Rainou, or Rénier, lord of Caylar and Ansouis of the House of Sabran, and of Garsenda, daughter of William IV of Forcalquier. Her mother was William's heiress but died before him, so the inheritance passed to the daughter. Garsenda was only thirteen when her grandfather and Alfonso II signed the Treaty of Aix, under which she would inherit his county and marry Alfonso. The wedding took place at Aix-en-Provence in July 1193. The couple had at least two children: a son and heir, and a daughter, also Garsenda, who married Guillermo II de Montcada and was the mother of Gaston VII, Viscount of Béarn.

William IV and Alfonso both died in 1209, leaving Garsenda the natural guardian of her son. Her brother-in-law, Peter II of Aragon, first gave the regency of Provence to his brother Sancho, who passed Provence and Forcalquier to his own son Nuño Sánchez after Peter's death in 1213. Garsenda's partisans accused Nuño of trying to supplant his nephew. The Provençal nobles at length lined up behind her and removed him, and the regency passed to Garsenda with a council of native nobles. By 1217 or 1220 she had ceded Forcalquier to her son and handed over the government. She retired to the monastery of La Celle around 1225.

Probably during her regency she was the focus of a circle of poets. A tenso between a good lady, named in one chansonnier as the countess of Provence, and an anonymous troubadour opens with her lines Vos q'em semblatz dels corals amadors, in which she declares her love. Some read the troubadour as Gui de Cavaillon, whose vida repeats a probably unfounded rumour that he was her lover. Elias de Barjols wrote songs about her as a widow, and Raimon Vidal praised her patronage.

In 1242 Garsenda travelled to Bordeaux to see her newly born great-granddaughter, Beatrice of England, and the child's parents, bringing sixty knights to the service of Henry III of England, who was then at war in France. Her most recent editors have called her one of the most powerful women in Occitan history.
gascony: Gascony was a province of south-western France that succeeded the Duchy of Gascony, dated 602 to 1453. The region is vaguely defined: it lies between the Atlantic Ocean and the Pyrenees and extends north to the Garonne, with the Adour as its other main river. Most definitions put it east and south of Bordeaux. Its historical capital was Auch. Gascony was historically inhabited by Basque-related people, and the Gascon language, usually classified as a variety of Occitan, has been spoken there from the Middle Ages. The name comes from the same root as the word Basque, through Vasconia, Wasconia and Gasconia.

Before Roman rule the inhabitants were the Aquitanians, who spoke a language related to Basque. Julius Caesar's lieutenants conquered Aquitania in the 50s BCE. In 297 Emperor Diocletian made the territory south of the Garonne the province of Novempopulania, the land of the nine tribes, which corresponds mostly to modern Gascony. It was given to the Visigoths in 416 to 418 and passed to the Franks after their victory in 507. Viking raiders devastated towns including Bayonne and Dax in 842 to 844, until Duke William II Sánchez defeated them at Taller in 982. The duchy then splintered into counties and viscounties such as Fézensac, Armagnac, Astarac, Bigorre and Béarn.

The 1152 marriage of Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine gave Henry control of Aquitaine and Gascony. The duchy functioned as an overseas English possession, sometimes called England's first colony. Philip IV of France confiscated it in 1294, beginning the Gascon War, and Edward I's three expeditions of 1294 to 1298 failed to recover it before the Treaty of Paris in 1303. In 1337 Philip VI of France took Gascony back into his hands, which precipitated the Hundred Years' War. The English were finally defeated at the Battle of Castillon on 17 July 1453, and Gascony remained French. From the 17th century its government was united with Guyenne, with its capital at Bordeaux, until 1792.

Gascony is divided between the region of Nouvelle-Aquitaine, with the departments of Landes, Pyrénées-Atlantiques, south-western Gironde and southern Lot-et-Garonne, and the region of Occitanie, with Gers, Hautes-Pyrénées, south-western Tarn-et-Garonne and western Haute-Garonne. Its towns include Auch, Bayonne, Dax, Lourdes, Mont-de-Marsan, Pau and Tarbes. It was the home of Henry III of Navarre, who became king of France in 1594, and it is the land of d'Artagnan, who inspired the character in Alexandre Dumas's The Three Musketeers.
gaspar-de-carvajal: Gaspar de Carvajal was born in Trujillo and entered the Dominican order in Spain. In 1533 he set out for Peru to work for the conversion of its Native peoples. In 1540 he joined, as chaplain, the expedition of Gonzalo Pizarro, governor of Quito, which was searching east of Quito for La Canela, the supposed Land of Cinnamon. Pizarro sent his second in command, Francisco de Orellana, down the Napo River with fifty men to look for provisions. Unable to return against the current, Orellana's party followed the river until it reached the estuary of the Amazon in 1542.

Carvajal survived the voyage and wrote it up as the Relación del nuevo descubrimiento del famoso río Grande, recording its dates and many notes on the peoples of the riverbanks: their numbers and dispositions, their tactics of war, rituals, customs and utensils. Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo used parts of it in his Historia general y natural de las Indias, but the work itself stayed obscure until José Toribio Medina published it in 1894. For more than four centuries scholars dismissed its reports of large cities, roads and dense populations as fabrication; research by Prümers and others, published in Nature in 2022, found them very likely correct.

Back in Peru, Carvajal became subprior of the Convent of San Rosario in Lima and in 1544 was chosen to mediate, apparently without success, between the viceroy Blasco Núñez Vela and the auditors of the Real Audiencia. He was then sent as a missionary to Tucumán and named protector of the Indians there. In 1553 he became prior of the convent of Huamanga and provincial of Tucumán, and with the Dominicans he brought he founded reducciones de indios and nine Spanish towns. As provincial of Peru from 1557 he wrote to the king about the abuse of Indians in the mines.

In 1565 his province chose him to represent it at the Spanish court and before the Pope, but he probably never crossed the ocean. He died in Lima in 1584. Unknowingly, the expedition he served had carried Old World diseases such as smallpox, malaria and yellow fever into the Amazon. Werner Herzog's 1972 film Aguirre, the Wrath of God shows him as a cowardly chaplain on Lope de Aguirre's later expedition of 1561.
gaspar-de-guzman-count-duke-of-olivares: Gaspar de Guzmán was born in Rome on 6 January 1587, where his father Enrique de Guzmán, 2nd Count of Olivares, from one of Spain's oldest noble families, was ambassador. He returned to Spain in 1599 and became student rector at the University of Salamanca. Through his maternal uncle Baltasar de Zúñiga, a key foreign policy adviser to Philip III, he received a post in the household of the heir, Prince Philip, and rapidly became his most trusted adviser.

When Philip IV came to the throne in 1621 at the age of sixteen, he ordered that every paper needing his signature go first to Olivares, who was then 34 and had no administrative experience. Olivares became a valido, the king's favourite and alter ego. He was created Duke of Sanlúcar la Mayor and kept his inherited countship as well, hence the title Count-Duke.

Olivares came to power wishing to lead a crusade of reform against what he saw as Spain's moral and spiritual decline. He created juntas, small committees, to speed up decisions, though by the 1630s they were packed with his own men.

In foreign policy he helped end the Twelve Years' Truce with the Dutch in 1621 and put the Netherlands first; Spain retook Breda in 1624, at huge expense. A Spanish army sent along the Spanish Road into Germany defeated the Protestant alliance at the Battle of Nördlingen in 1634. France then entered the war, and in 1635 Olivares planned an invasion with four armies and two navies. Spanish forces came within 16 miles of Paris, but resources were overstretched and France counter-attacked in 1637.

At home Olivares proposed the Union of Arms in 1624, under which each of the king's territories would raise a fixed quota of soldiers. Opposition from the provinces, above all Catalonia, defeated it. A state bankruptcy in 1627 and the Dutch capture of the treasure fleet in 1628 hurt royal finances. In 1640 major revolts broke out in Catalonia and Portugal. Most historians doubt the Catalan view that he provoked the Catalan revolt deliberately. Lisbon offered the throne to the House of Braganza.

The revolts, inflation in 1641, resentment among the Castilian nobility and his own failing health, which included mental illness, brought Olivares down. Philip IV dismissed him in January 1643, reluctantly and under pressure from a court intrigue led by Queen Isabel. He retired to Loeches and then to his sister's palace at Toro, and died there in 1645. He had also brought the young Diego Velázquez to the king's attention in 1623, and Velázquez painted at least three portraits of him. For long afterwards In Spain he was remembered as the model of a grasping and incapable favourite, a view that has since changed.
gaston-de-foix-duke-of-nemours: Gaston was born on 10 December 1489 at Mazères in the County of Foix, the second child and only son of John of Foix, Viscount of Narbonne, and Marie d'Orléans. His grandparents were Gaston IV of Foix-Grailly and Queen Eleanor of Navarre on one side, and Charles, Duke of Orléans, and Marie of Cleves on the other; his only maternal uncle was King Louis XII of France. His elder sister, Germaine of Foix, became queen of Aragon as the second wife of Ferdinand II.

He arrived in Italy as commander in 1511, aged 21, and was soon called the Thunderbolt of Italy for his forced marches and sudden offensives. In October 1511 Pope Julius II formed the Holy League with Ferdinand of Aragon and the Republic of Venice to drive the French out of Italy. Facing the Swiss in the north, a Papal and Aragonese army under Ramón de Cardona, Viceroy of Naples, in the south and Venice in the east, Gaston held Milan, reinforced Bologna and in February 1512 relieved Brescia, which he took and sacked.

Marching south through the snow, he threatened Ravenna and invited Cardona to battle. On 11 April 1512 about 23,000 French troops, among them 8,500 German landsknechts, with 54 guns, attacked a smaller army entrenched behind works prepared by the engineer Pedro Navarro. French artillery provoked the Spanish cavalry into failed charges, and after an hour of fighting in the entrenchments two guns sent behind the Spanish lines broke their resistance. Leading a charge against retreating infantry, Gaston fell when his horse stumbled and was shot dead.

Ravenna cost the French up to 9,000 men, and the loss of Gaston and over a third of the army fatally weakened them in northern Italy. When the Swiss and Venetians marched on Milan, his successor Jacques de La Palice fled with his army to the Dauphiné in June. Germaine inherited his claim to the Kingdom of Navarre, and Ferdinand invaded and kept its Spanish lands. An elaborate tomb from the workshop of Agostino Busti, never completed, is mostly on display in the Castello Sforzesco in Milan.
gaston-duke-of-orleans: Gaston Jean Baptiste was born at the Palace of Fontainebleau on 24 April 1608, the third son of King Henry IV of France and his second wife, Marie de' Medici. He was given the title Duke of Anjou at birth and was raised under the royal governess Françoise de Montglat. On 6 August 1626 he married Marie de Bourbon, Duchess of Montpensier, and received the duchies of Orléans and Chartres and the county of Blois as an appanage.

She died on 4 June 1627, six days after giving birth to their daughter Anne Marie Louise, later called the Grande Mademoiselle. As eldest surviving brother of Louis XIII he was known at court as Monsieur, and he was heir presumptive from 1611 until the birth of the king's first son in 1638.

Gaston held nominal command of the army besieging La Rochelle in 1628 and had already begun the political intrigue that would occupy the rest of his life. He twice had to leave France for conspiring against his brother and Cardinal Richelieu. After an unsuccessful war in Languedoc that led to the Battle of Castelnaudary in 1632, he took refuge in Flanders. Reconciled with the king, he plotted again in 1635 and fled, then submitted.

He then conspired with the marquis de Cinq-Mars against Richelieu and deserted him in 1642. After Louis XIII died in 1643 Gaston became lieutenant-general of the kingdom and fought Spain on the northern frontier, and he was created duc d'Alençon in 1646. During the Fronde, from 1648 to 1653, he showed no particular loyalty to the crown and passed easily from one side to the other.

While sheltering from Richelieu in Lorraine, Gaston fell in love with Marguerite of Lorraine, sister of Duke Charles IV, and married her in a secret ceremony at Nancy on the night of 2–3 January 1632, without his brother's permission. The Parlement of Paris declared the marriage void in September 1634, and an assembly of the French clergy held in 1635 that a prince du sang could marry only with the king's consent.

Louis XIII accepted his plea on his deathbed in May 1643, and the couple married a third time that July at Meudon. They had five children, of whom three daughters survived to adulthood. After Louis's death Gaston was called Le Grand Monsieur to tell him from his nephew Philippe. Cardinal Mazarin exiled him to Blois in 1652, and he stayed there until he died on 2 February 1660; his titles passed to his nephew.
gaston-iii-of-foix: Gaston was born on 30 April 1331, the only legitimate child of Gaston II, Count of Foix, and Aliénor of Comminges. The House of Foix-Béarn went back to the marriage in 1252 of Margaret of Béarn, heiress of Gaston VII, Viscount of Béarn, to Roger-Bernard III, Count of Foix, and since Gaston II's reign it had also held the Viscounty of Lautrec. Gaston inherited a fragmented territory that paid homage both to the king of France and to the king of England. In 1344, at 13, he was already out hunting while his mother received the homage of the delegates of Josbaig.

During the Hundred Years' War he played the French and English monarchies against each other to dominate the Pre-Pyrenees, and on 25 September 1347 he claimed sovereignty over Béarn. In October 1352 the capitouls of Toulouse asked him to protect the city from English troops, which let him keep his neutrality and profit from the war. When the Dauphin, the future Charles V of France, allied with the House of Armagnac, his family's old enemy, Gaston attacked in March 1359, and the Treaty of Brétigny of 8 May 1360 paid him 200,000 guilders for the loss of Bigorre.

He ruled without the nobility and the traditional assemblies, through a private council and lawyers of his choosing. He struck gold florins at Morlaàs and from 1367 levied the fouage, a direct tax of 2 francs paid each year by every head of a family, for which censuses were taken. He could muster about 4,000 men and more than 1,000 horses. His repudiation of his wife Agnes in 1362 made an enemy of her brother, Charles II of Navarre, a plot against him took shape from 1378, and in 1380 he likely killed his only legitimate son, Gaston, for attempting to assassinate him.

He held court at the Château Moncade in Orthez and received the Black Prince in 1355, Peter I of Cyprus in 1363–1364 and Charles VI in 1390. From 1387 he dictated his Livre de chasse to his secretaries, a work in French dedicated to Philip the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, which the naturalist Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon, was still using at the end of the 18th century. In it he argued that hunting prepares for war, keeps a man healthy, lets him commune with nature and opens the doors to paradise. He died on 1 August 1391, leaving no legitimate heir.
gaston-iv-of-bearn: Gaston, born around 1060, was the son of Centulle V of Béarn and Beatrix of Bigorre, and he succeeded his father as viscount in 1090. During his rule the borders of Béarn were fixed more firmly: he defeated the viscount of Dax, took control of Orthez, Pays de Mixe and Ostabaret by 1105, and gained Montaner by his marriage to Talesa, daughter of Sancho Ramírez, Count of Ribagorza. Though technically a vassal of the Duchy of Aquitaine, then ruled by William IX, he made Béarn in effect an autonomous territory.

In 1096 Gaston led a Béarnais contingent in the First Crusade under Raymond IV of Toulouse, carrying his own standard and commanding his own men. At the siege of Antioch of 1097–1098 he led one of the divisions in the final battle against Kerbogha, the atabeg of Mosul, and afterwards left Raymond for Godfrey of Bouillon. He and Tancred were sent ahead of the main army to occupy Bethlehem, and at the siege of Jerusalem he was in charge of Godfrey's siege engines. He entered the city on 15 July 1099. He and Tancred sheltered some of its Muslims in the Al-Aqsa Mosque, but other crusaders killed them, to their fury.

In August 1099 he led part of the centre of the crusader army at the battle of Ascalon and then went home. In Béarn he oversaw the building of many churches to shelter pilgrims on the route to Santiago de Compostela and gave property to the abbey of St. Foy for new buildings in Morlàas, though he also upheld his claims against the abbey of St. Vincent de Lucq and the monastery of St. Mont. With Centule II of Bigorre he took part in the conquest of Zaragoza by Alfonso I of Aragon in 1118, and the king made him lord of the city.

Gaston was killed in battle near Valencia against the Almoravid governor of that city. His young son Centulle VI succeeded him, with Talesa as regent. She wished to unite Béarn and Aragon, then roughly equal in power, but Aragon united with Catalonia instead and Béarn began to decline. His descendants Gaston VI and Gaston VII took part in the Albigensian Crusade and the Seventh Crusade.
gaston-thorn: Gaston Thorn was born in Luxembourg City on 3 September 1928, but spent his early childhood in Strasbourg, where his father worked for the French railways. The family returned to Luxembourg at the outbreak of World War II. While still at school he took part in resistance activities during the German occupation and spent several months in prison. After the war he studied medicine in Montpellier, then law in Montpellier, Lausanne and Paris, and practised law in Luxembourg from 1955. He entered politics in 1959 for the liberal Democratic Party, sat in the European Parliament from 1959 to 1969 and chaired his party from 1962 to 1969.

Thorn was Foreign Minister and Foreign Trade Minister from 1969 to 1980 and Prime Minister from 1974 to 1979. His socialist-liberal coalition of the Democratic Party and the Luxembourg Socialist Workers' Party was the first government since World War II not to include the Christian Social People's Party, and he was the first prime minister since the war from outside it, though his party had fewer seats than its partner. He also served as Minister of Economics from 1977 to 1980 and as President of the United Nations General Assembly for its 30th session, in 1975-1976.

In 1980 he was chosen to succeed Roy Jenkins as president of the Commission of the European Communities, and took office on 12 January 1981. France and Britain had opposed his appointment. His term coincided with economic and political crisis, and relations with the British government of Margaret Thatcher declined over her demand for compensation for Britain's budget payments. He reached agreement on a common fisheries policy and laid the basis for the accession of Spain and Portugal; Greece had just joined.

After leaving the commission in 1985 Thorn went into business, chairing Luxembourg's largest media company CLT and serving as president of the Banque Internationale à Luxembourg from 1985 to 1999. He remained active in the International European Movement and Liberal International. He died in Luxembourg City on 26 August 2007 and received a state funeral at Notre-Dame Cathedral on 30 August.
gateway-of-the-sun: The gateway stands at Tiwanaku, about 3,825 metres above sea level near La Paz, a site of the Tiwanaku culture that thrived around Lake Titicaca from about 500 to 950 CE. Older literature calls it the great monolithic Gateway of Ak-kapana. It is about 4 metres wide and is estimated to weigh 10 tons. When European explorers came upon it in the mid-19th century it was lying on its side with a large crack through it. It was a later monument of the site, and its carvings are thought to have astronomical or astrological meaning and perhaps a calendrical purpose.

The frieze on the front belongs to the Southern Andean Iconographic Series. Its central figure stands in the Staff God pose, with 24 lines around its head that some read as the rays of the sun, and holds a stylised spear-thrower in its left hand. Running towards it are 48 subsidiary figures, often called attendants: 32 with human heads and 16 human-like figures with the heads of birds. The figures in the outer parts, cut less sharply, were added later; originally there were 30. Some scholars link the central figure with the Inca god Viracocha or the Aymara weather god Thunupa, while others suggest it may show a ritual practitioner rather than a god. The design below it is thought to represent celestial cycles.

An engraving of the gateway served as the frontispiece of Antigüedades peruanas in 1851. Scholars have compared its images with Inca icons as evidence of Tiwanaku's influence on Inca mythology and art, and its position facing the sun may mark a shift from a lunar to a solar religion. Early investigators such as Arthur Posnansky and Edmund Kiss linked it to mistaken theories of early contact with Nordic Aryans, interpretations now regarded as pseudoarchaeology.
gatling-gun: Richard J. Gatling designed the gun in Indiana in 1861 and patented it on 4 November 1862. He wrote that he made it to reduce the size of armies and so the number of deaths from combat and disease. Inventors had explored grouped barrels since the 18th century, but poor engineering and the lack of a unitary cartridge had defeated earlier designs. Gatling's first version used reloadable steel cylinders, each holding a ball and a black-powder charge with a percussion cap. He later used paper cartridges, because self-contained brass cartridges were not yet fully available. Brass cartridges replaced paper in the 1860s.

The gun had six barrels, in some models up to ten, revolving around a central shaft as a hand crank was turned. Each barrel loaded a cartridge from a hopper on top, fired when it reached a set position and ejected the spent case, then cooled while it turned back to the top. Each barrel had its own firing mechanism, so the gun needed no single reciprocating bolt and did not overheat quickly. Unskilled operators could reach about 200 rounds per minute, and by 1886 a model could fire more than 400.

Because it needed a person to crank it, it was not a true automatic weapon; the Maxim gun of 1883 was the first fully automatic one. Black-powder smoke made concealment impossible until smokeless powder arrived, and the weight of the gun and its carriage made it hard to move over rough ground.

The American Civil War saw its first use in combat. Twelve guns bought personally by Union commanders served in the trenches at the Siege of Petersburg, and eight others were fitted to gunboats. The US Army accepted the gun only in 1866.

It was later used in the Boshin War, the Anglo-Zulu War and by Russia, which called it the Gorloff gun, at Nikopol and Plevna in the Russo-Turkish War. It served most successfully in expanding European colonial empires, defeating massed attacks by the Zulu, the Bedouin and the Mahdists; the British first deployed it in the Anglo-Ashanti wars of 1873 and 1874. At San Juan Hill in 1898 a four-gun battery under Lieutenant John H. Parker fired 18,000 rounds in eight and a half minutes. The US military declared all Gatling models obsolete in 1911, after 45 years of service, and the idea of rotating barrels returned after World War II in the Minigun and the M61 Vulcan.
gattilusio: The family's lordships were founded by two brothers, the Genoese adventurer Francesco Gattilusio and Niccolò Gattilusio, nephews of Oberto Gattilusio. Their father's name is unknown, and the historian Anthony Luttrell argues from heraldic evidence that their mother was a Doria. According to the historian Christopher Wright, their rise came as Byzantine power weakened and the Ottomans expanded after the fall of Gallipoli in 1354. With the Genoese and Venetian republics competing at sea, small semi-autonomous regimes such as theirs took root in the north-eastern Aegean, between the Byzantine, Latin and Ottoman worlds.

In 1354 Francesco helped John V Palaiologos retake Constantinople from John VI Kantakouzenos, and in 1355 he married the emperor's sister Maria. Wright notes that John V commanded a substantial force beyond Francesco's small flotilla and seems to have granted Lesbos freely. From Mytilene the family extended its rule to Imbros, Samothrace, Lemnos, Thasos and the Thracian port of Aenus, guarding the sea routes to Constantinople and the approaches to the Dardanelles, and grew rich on the mining and sale of alum.

The Gattilusi spoke Greek, followed the Orthodox Church and called themselves simply lords. Luttrell counts four successive generations who married into the Palaiologos family; a granddaughter of Francesco I married John VII Palaiologos around 1397, and in 1441 a daughter of Dorino Gattilusio married the future Constantine XI. After the Fall of Constantinople in 1453 the Ottomans removed them from all but Lesbos, held for 4,000 gold pieces a year. Domenico Gattilusio was strangled and succeeded by his brother Niccolò, and in September 1462 an Ottoman fleet took the island and carried Niccolò to Constantinople as a prisoner.

Letters of Demetrios Kydones mention Francesco I and his ties with Byzantium. The family's coins and heraldic plaques join the Gattilusio arms with Palaiologos symbols such as the four Betas and with the Doria eagle. Fortifications on Lesbos and other islands were strengthened under their rule, and surviving mine workings may relate to the alum trade. Excavations in the Castle of Mytilene since 1983 by the University of British Columbia, led by Caroline and Hector Williams, have uncovered what may be the family's burial chapel.
gatun-lake: Gatun Lake, in Spanish Lago Gatún, is a reservoir south of Colón in Panama. Its water is mostly fresh and slightly saline near the locks. It covers about 470 square kilometres and carries ships along 33 kilometres of their passage across the Isthmus of Panama, at roughly 26 metres above sea level.

Rainforest around the lake is impassable in places, and these areas remain practically free from human interference. The largest island in the lake is Barro Colorado Island, which was set aside for scientific study when the lake was formed and is operated by the Smithsonian Institution. Many discoveries about tropical animals and plants originated there.

The lake was created by damming the Chagres River. It came into being on 27 June 1913, when the gates of the spillway at Gatun Dam were closed. The water stood then at about 14.6 metres above sea level and was expected to rise to operating levels within the following six months. When it was made, Gatun Lake was the largest artificial lake in the world.
It supplies the millions of litres of water needed to operate the locks of the Panama Canal each time a ship passes through. It also provides drinking water for Panama City and Colón.

Angling is one of the main recreations on the lake. Peacock bass, a species native to the Amazon, Rio Negro and Orinoco basins, were accidentally introduced around 1967 by a local businessman. Known locally as sargento, they have become the dominant game fish. Their introduction had severe effects on the local species: a Smithsonian report found that native fish populations had still not recovered, and only one quarter the number of native fish species was found in a sampling taken in 2016.
gaudeamus-igitur: The claim that the lyrics date from 1287 rests on a manuscript held in the Bibliothèque nationale de France in Paris. A poem there beginning Subscribere proposui has two verses that closely resemble later verses of the song, though neither the first verse nor the words Gaudeamus igitur appear, and its music bears no relation to the present melody. A German translation of these verses was made in about 1717 and published in 1730 without music. A Latin version in a handwritten student songbook, dating from between 1723 and 1750 and kept in the Berlin State Library, differs considerably from the modern text.

The lyrics endorse the bacchanalian mayhem of student life while keeping in view that everyone will die, in the tradition of memento mori and carpe diem. The song contains humorous and ironic references to sex and death, and many versions are bowdlerized for public ceremonies, while students in private typically sing ribald words. The Neo-Latin word Antiburschius refers to opponents of the politically active German student fraternities of the 19th century. Centuries of use have produced many slightly different versions.

The current Latin text was published at Halle in 1781 in Studentenlieder by Christian Wilhelm Kindleben, who admitted to making significant changes. The present melody first appeared in print in Leipzig in 1782 in Lieder für Freunde der Geselligen Freude, though it was evidently well known earlier. The present text and melody were probably first printed together in Ignaz Walter's operatic setting of Goethe's Faust in 1797.

Johannes Brahms quoted the tune in his Academic Festival Overture, and Franz Liszt wrote a paraphrase and, in 1870, a humoresque on it. Pyotr Tchaikovsky arranged it for male chorus in 1874. Johann Strauss II quoted it in his Studenten-Polka, first performed on 24 February 1862, and Franz von Suppé in his operetta Flotte Bursche of 1863. It is the official anthem of the International University Sports Federation.
gaudiya-vaishnavism: Gaudiya Vaishnavism, also called Chaitanya Vaishnavism, takes its name from the Gauda region of Bengal. Its adherents regard Chaitanya Mahaprabhu (1486–1534) as Krishna himself, appearing in the form of his own devotee, with the mood and complexion of Radha. Chaitanya refused to initiate anyone formally, and he neither founded a community nor named a successor. From the beginning the tradition therefore divided into several lines of succession. In the early years the followers of Nityananda Prabhu, Advaita Acharya and other companions of Chaitanya taught and initiated people in their own districts of Bengal.

Chaitanya asked a few followers, later known as the Six Gosvamis of Vrindavan, to set out his theology in writing. They were Rupa, Sanatana, Gopala Bhatta, Raghunatha Bhatta, Raghunatha dasa and Jiva Goswami. In the next generation Narottama, Srinivasa and Shyamananda, students of Jiva Goswami, spread the teaching across Bengal and Orissa. The tradition calls itself the Brahma-Madhva-Gaudiya Sampradaya and traces Chaitanya's teachers to the school of Madhvacharya. The historian Guy L. Beck notes that this link was first put forward by Baladeva Vidyabhushana in the 18th century and that the Madhva annals do not mention Chaitanya.

The tradition rests chiefly on the Bhagavad Gita and the Bhagavata Purana. It worships Krishna as the source of all divine incarnations, citing the verse of the Bhagavata Purana, 1.3.28, that says Krishna is God himself. Its distinctive doctrine, taught by Chaitanya, is Achintya Bheda Abheda, inconceivable oneness and difference: the soul is identical with God in quality but infinitesimal beside him in quantity. Jiva Goswami set out the theology in his six treatises, the Sat Sandarbhas, and Rupa Goswami wrote the Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu. Believers hold that in the present age, Kali Yuga, chanting the names of Krishna is enough for liberation, and that the highest aim is not release from rebirth but pure love of God.

Worship takes the form of singing the holy names of Radha and Krishna, above all in the Hare Krishna mantra, with kirtan and dancing. Haridasa Thakur, a close associate of Chaitanya, is reported to have chanted 300,000 names a day. Gaudiya Vaishnavas follow a vegetarian diet, avoiding meat, fish, eggs, onion and garlic.

In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when Bengal was the centre of a Hindu religious revival, Gaudiya Vaishnavism inspired new movements such as the Gaudiya Math. International bodies later came out of it, including the Gaudiya Mission and the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, often called the Hare Krishna movement. The scholar Ferdinando Sardella estimates the number of adherents at between 30 and 50 million, mostly in Orissa, Manipur, West Bengal and Bangladesh.
gauja: The Gauja flows through the Vidzeme region of Latvia. It is the only large river of Latvia that begins and ends its flow in the country. About 93.5 kilometres of the Gauja lie within Gauja National Park. There the river flows through the Gauja Valley, which is between 1 and 2.5 kilometres wide and reaches a maximum depth of 85 metres near Sigulda. The sandstone rocks on the banks of the Gauja and of the rivers that join it began to form 370 to 300 million years ago, during the Devonian period.

Before the 13th century the Gauja served as a trade route and as a border river between the Livonian and Latgalian lands. While Livonian languages were still spoken along the river and the sea, it was called Koivo, the Birch River, from the Livonian keùv or the Estonian kõiv. In Latvian the name once meant a great amount or a crowd, and so the river was called the big river. The Livonians suffered greatly during the Great Northern War and from a plague in the 18th century, when the remaining Livonians assimilated with the Latvians.

The Gauja changes its bed rapidly and has a reputation for being deceitful. Its bed is made of unconsolidated sand and gravel that move with the current. In places the bed is pebbly and forms boulder rapids, among them Kazu, Raiskuma, Rakšu and Ķūķu. Within the national park the river bottom is 60 to 120 metres wide and the depth changes quickly, from 0.3 to 7 metres. In low water the current runs at 0.2 to 0.4 metres a second, and in the spring flood at 2 to 3 metres a second.

The river usually freezes over in mid-December, and the ice starts moving in late March, though in warm winters it does not freeze. Much underground water flows into it, so its water is cooler than that of the other large rivers of Latvia, and the river changes level and current speed a good deal through the year.
gaul: Little is written about the peoples of Gaul before the Romans, so their early history rests largely on archaeology. Eastern and southern France shared in the Urnfield culture of the Late Bronze Age, from which the Hallstatt culture developed. The La Tène culture arose in the 7th and 6th centuries BCE, probably under Greek, Phoenician and Etruscan influence, and spread across the whole of Gaul by the late 5th century BCE. In the 4th and early 3rd centuries BCE Gallic tribal confederations expanded into northern Italy, Transylvania and Asia Minor.

Rome intervened in southern Gaul in 154 BCE and again in 125 BCE, when it stayed, and by 121 BCE it held the Mediterranean region called Provincia. Julius Caesar entered Gaul in 58 BCE, ostensibly to help Rome's allies against the migrating Helvetii, and conquered nearly all of it. Vercingetorix tried to unite the Gauls and checked Caesar at Gergovia, but Caesar captured him at the Battle of Alesia in September 52 BCE. The Gallic Wars are said to have killed as many as a million people, probably one in twelve of the Gauls, and to have enslaved another million.

Gaul's inhabitants gradually adopted Roman culture, producing a Gallo-Roman culture, and all received citizenship in 212 CE. From 260 to 273 the Gallic Empire broke away from Rome. After Frankish victories in 486, 507 and 532, Gaul except for Brittany and Septimania came under the Merovingians, the first kings of France.

The basic unit of Gallic politics was the tribe or civitas, which had a council of elders and at first a king; later the executive was an annually elected magistrate. The Gauls were seldom united. Caesar divided the people of Gallia Comata into the Aquitani, the Belgae and the Celtae. The druids presided over sacrifices, kept the agricultural calendar, educated the aristocracy and claimed the right to decide questions of war and peace. The Gaulish language is thought to have survived into the 6th century and helped shape the Vulgar Latin that became French.
gauleiter: The Nazi Party first used the term Gauleiter in 1925, around the time Adolf Hitler re-founded the Party on 27 February, after the lifting of the ban imposed in the aftermath of the Beer Hall Putsch of 9 November 1923. The word comes from Gau, an old term for a region of the German Reich, and leiter, leader. In the early years local activists organised the Party in their home areas and were sometimes chosen by the members themselves, which Hitler officially prohibited only in 1929. The Gaue did not necessarily follow existing administrative divisions. There were 35 in 1928 and 43 by the end of the regime.

Gauleiters were appointed by Hitler, were personally responsible to him and could be dismissed at once. Gauleiter was the third-highest rank in the Nazi political leadership, below Reichsleiter and the Führer. A Gauleiter headed the Gauleitung and had authority over the Kreisleiters, who directed the Ortsgruppenleiters, Zellenleiters and Blockleiters, but he had no direct control over the SA or SS. About 125 men held the position. Many were old fighters of the Kampfzeit, born in the last decade of the 19th century, who had served in the First World War and often in the Freikorps; later appointees were younger and trained as administrators.

After the Nazis took power on 30 January 1933, Gauleiters became the key agents in extending Nazi control over the German states. The Second Law on the Coordination of the States with the Reich of 7 April 1933 created the post of Reichsstatthalter (Reich Governor), which Hitler filled almost exclusively with Gauleiters. After the Anschluss of 12 March 1938 and the seizure of the Sudetenland, the annexed territories were organised into eight Reichsgaue under Reichsstatthalters who were also the local Gauleiters. Gauleiters carried out the Party's persecution of Jews, and on 9 and 10 November 1938 they ordered riots in their Gaue after an address by Joseph Goebbels.

On 1 September 1939 fifteen Gauleiters were appointed Reich Defense Commissioners, charged with civil defence, mobilisation, evacuation and rationing. On 16 November 1942 all 42 territorial Gauleiters became commissioners in their own Gaue, registering men and women between sixteen and sixty for war work and overseeing defensive fortifications built with forced labour. In October 1944 each organised the Volkssturm. Under the Nero Decree of 19 March 1945 many refused to destroy infrastructure, but several ordered bridges, plants and factories destroyed. Of the 43 serving in May 1945, twelve killed themselves, eight were executed as war criminals and sixteen were imprisoned.
gaullism: Gaullism took shape around Charles de Gaulle, who as head of the Free French Forces became the symbol of resistance to the Nazi occupation and the Vichy government. The historian Serge Berstein divides its history into phases. In the first, from 1940 to 1945, it meant those who rejected the armistice with Germany and followed de Gaulle. From 1946 to 1958 it was an opposition to the Fourth Republic, whose unstable parliamentary government Gaullists wanted replaced by a president with pre-eminent constitutional powers. In 1947 de Gaulle founded the Rally of the French People, whose membership reached one million within six months.

Berstein holds that Gaullism is neither a doctrine nor a political ideology, but a pragmatic exercise of power. Its fundamental principle is what de Gaulle called a certain idea of France, which required a strong state able to ensure that the nation's interests came first. De Gaulle disliked the regime of the parties, which he held responsible for the military disaster of 1940, and wanted a strong executive embodying national unity. He admired Louis XIV, Napoleon and Georges Clemenceau as makers of consensus. In foreign policy Gaullists sought independence from allies, which led to France's own nuclear force, the withdrawal of French forces from NATO's command structure and the removal of US bases.

After 1945 Gaullists at first defended the French Empire. De Gaulle later accepted decolonisation, and he ended the Algerian crisis of 1954 to 1962 by granting independence, which he judged to be in France's interest. Social Gaullism also proposed an association of capital and labour in place of class struggle.

De Gaulle returned to power in 1958 and served as president of the new Fifth Republic from 1959 until his resignation in 1969. His followers organised the Union for the New Republic, which became the largest force after the November 1958 elections. His successor Georges Pompidou consolidated Gaullism between 1969 and 1974. The Cross of Lorraine became the symbol of later parties, among them the Rally for the Republic, founded by Jacques Chirac in 1976. Scholars distinguish traditional, social and neo-Gaullism, and the strong presidency was kept by all de Gaulle's successors, including the socialist François Mitterrand.
gauls: The Gauls were a group of Celtic peoples of mainland Europe in the Iron Age and the Roman period, roughly from the 5th century BCE to the 5th century CE, and they spoke Gaulish, a Continental Celtic language. Their culture developed over the first millennium BCE, from the Urnfield culture through the Hallstatt culture of the 8th century BCE to the La Tène culture from around the 5th century BCE. By the 4th century BCE they were spread over much of what is now France, Belgium, Switzerland, southern Germany, Austria and the Czech Republic, controlling trade routes along the Rhône, Seine, Rhine and Danube. Their name Galli is generally derived from a Celtic root meaning power or ability.

Gallic invaders settled the Po Valley in the 4th century BCE and defeated Roman forces under Brennus in 390 BCE. In the early 3rd century BCE they expanded into the Balkans, and in 279 BCE they defeated the Macedonians and killed King Ptolemy Keraunos. Those who crossed to Asia Minor settled in Galatia, and the Seleucid king Antiochus I checked them with war elephants in 275 BCE. Many Gauls served as mercenaries in the armies of Carthage, and Hannibal used them in his invasion of Italy, including at Cannae.

Roman pressure grew after the First Punic War. The Battle of Telamon in 225 BCE began a gradual decline of Gallic power. The Romans conquered the area later called Gallia Narbonensis by 121 BCE, and the Cisalpine Gauls were subdued in the early 2nd century BCE. In 58 BCE Julius Caesar began the Gallic Wars, and a mixed Gallo-Roman culture emerged after the annexation. In the crisis of the third century a Gallic Empire briefly broke away under the Batavian general Postumus.

Gaul was never united under a single ruler. The fundamental unit of politics was the tribe, each with a council of elders and at first a king, later an annually elected magistrate. Among the Aedui the executive was called a Vergobret. Many tribes built large fortified settlements called oppida, such as Bibracte, Gergovia and Alesia, and minted their own coins. They imported Mediterranean wine in large quantities, as the Vix grave's 1.63 m vessel shows. Their religion was polytheistic and overseen by druids, and they produced the Coligny calendar.

The Roman civitates, based on the tribes, later became the basis of the French dioceses, which lasted until the French Revolution. In modern France the Gauls have been evoked as ancestors, in the phrase of Ernest Lavisse's school textbook, our ancestors the Gauls.
gautama-buddha: Siddhartha Gautama was a wandering religious teacher of the eastern Indo-Gangetic Plains who lived in the 6th or 5th century BCE. Buddhist legends place his birth at Lumbini, in what is now Nepal, to royal parents of the Shakya clan. Most scholars accept that he lived, taught and founded a monastic order during the reign of Bimbisara of Magadha and died in the reign of Bimbisara's successor Ajatashatru, making him a contemporary of Mahavira, the Jain tirthankara.

His dates are uncertain. The long chronology of the Sri Lankan chronicles gives 624 to 544 BCE, while most scholars who accept it but date Ashoka's coronation to about 268 BCE put his life at 566 to 486 BCE. The oldest surviving written mention of the Buddha is from the middle of the 3rd century BCE, in the Edicts of Ashoka, whose Lumbini pillar inscription commemorates the emperor's pilgrimage to the birthplace. The earliest biographies already contain supernatural elements, and the scholar Rupert Gethin holds that the life story is not history, nor meant to be.

According to Buddhist tradition, he renounced home life to live as a wandering ascetic and attained nirvana at Bodh Gaya in what is now Bihar. He then taught across the lower Indo-Gangetic Plain and built a monastic order, the sangha. Tradition describes a Middle Way between sensual indulgence and severe asceticism, summarised in the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path. The earliest biographical material in the Pali Nikayas describes a forty-five-year career as a teacher.

He left no writings. His teachings were compiled by the Buddhist community as the Vinaya Pitaka, on monastic discipline, and the Sutra Pitaka, discourses attributed to him, passed down orally in Middle Indo-Aryan dialects. How far later doctrine reflects his own words is disputed. Scholars such as Richard Gombrich and A. K. Warder hold that early texts contain material traceable to him, while others doubt that the beliefs of pre-sectarian Buddhism can be recovered.

Buddhist tradition holds that he died at Kushinagar, in modern Uttar Pradesh, and reached parinirvana. Buddhism later developed into the Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana traditions and spread beyond the Indian subcontinent. It declined in India and largely disappeared there after the 8th century CE, but became more prominent in Southeast and East Asia. Mahayana sutras present Shakyamuni as a transcendent being, and the Hindu tradition incorporated the Buddha as the ninth avatar of Vishnu.

The earliest artistic depictions, at Bharhut and Sanchi, are aniconic, showing an empty throne, footprints, a Dharma wheel or a Bodhi tree. Images in human form became widespread after the first century CE, and those of Gandharan and Central Asian Buddhism were influenced by Hellenistic art, a style known as Greco-Buddhist art.
gautamiputra-satakarni: What is known of Gautamiputra comes from his coins, the Satavahana inscriptions and the royal genealogies of the Puranas. Most Puranas name his predecessor as Shivasvati, a king attested by no coin or inscription; the Vayu Purana calls him Shivasvami, and the Brahmanda Purana does not name Gautamiputra at all. His mother, Gautami Balashri, is known from the eulogy inscription in Cave No. 3 of the Pandavleni Caves at Nashik, dated to the 19th regnal year of his son Vasishthiputra Pulumavi. Since the kings married wives from several royal houses, a prince was most easily identified by his mother.

In the years before his reign the Western Kshatrapas, whom the Satavahanas called Shakas, had expanded at Satavahana expense. His mother's inscription says he defeated the Shakas, Pahlavas and Yavanas, uprooted the Kshaharata family of Nahapana and ruled from Malwa and Saurashtra to the Krishna River and from the Konkan to Vidarbha, his horses drinking the waters of three oceans. Coins of Nahapana restruck by Gautamiputra were found at Jogalthambi. Historians agree that he defeated Nahapana but date the victory differently, and Carla M. Sinopoli doubts that he controlled all the lands claimed; the claim to the south is often read as a literary convention.

His inscriptions describe an empire divided into units called aharas, each under an official, the amatya, and he is styled Lord of Benakataka, a place not securely identified. The eulogy calls him ekabrahmana, read as a peerless Brahmin or as the protector of Brahmins, yet he exempted Buddhist monks from taxes and from interference by royal officers.

The Matsya and Vayu Puranas give him a reign of 21 years, but an inscription of his 24th regnal year survives at Nashik. Some scholars, among them D. R. Bhandarkar and R. G. Bhandarkar, thought he ruled jointly with his son in his last years; K. A. Nilakanta Sastri and H. C. Raychaudhuri rejected the idea. He may have lost territory late in his reign to the Kardamakas, since Rudradaman I claimed to have twice defeated a Satakarni, lord of the Deccan, though which Satakarni is disputed.
gauteng: Gauteng lies on the Highveld, a high-altitude grassland at about 1,500 m above sea level. Its southern border is the Vaal River, which separates it from the Free State, and it also borders North West, Limpopo and Mpumalanga. It is the only landlocked South African province without a foreign border. Between Johannesburg and Pretoria lie low parallel ridges and undulating hills, part of the Magaliesberg Mountains and the Witwatersrand. The Witwatersrand area, also called the Rand or the Reef after its gold reefs, is a conurbation about 120 km wide, historically divided into the East Rand, Central Rand and West Rand. The name comes from the Sotho-Tswana word gauta, meaning gold.

At the Sterkfontein caves some of the oldest hominid fossils have been found, including Mrs Ples and Little Foot. Events in the area were not written down until the 19th century. The first records are from the early 19th century, when settlers from the Cape Colony defeated the chief Mzilikazi and began to establish villages. Pretoria, founded in 1855 as capital of the South African Republic, grew rapidly until the discovery of gold on the Witwatersrand in 1886 led to the founding of Johannesburg. Pretoria remained significant, notably in the Second Boer War. In 1905 the Cullinan Diamond, the largest diamond ever found, was mined at the nearby town of Cullinan.

Many events of the anti-apartheid struggle took place in what is now Gauteng: the Freedom Charter of 1955, the Women's March of 1956, the Sharpeville massacre of 1960, the Rivonia Trial of 1963 and 1964, the Soweto uprising of 1976 and the Boipatong massacre of 1992. The Apartheid Museum documents this era. The province was formed from part of the old Transvaal after South Africa's first multiracial elections on 27 April 1994, first as Pretoria–Witwatersrand–Vereeniging, and was renamed Gauteng on 28 June 1995.

Gauteng is the smallest of South Africa's nine provinces by land area and the most populous. Its capital, Johannesburg, is the country's largest city, and Pretoria is the administrative capital. Soweto is its largest township. The province is governed by a 73-member provincial legislature, and the Constitutional Court sits in Johannesburg. Its southern half is a financial and commercial centre and is home to the Johannesburg Stock Exchange. The Cradle of Humankind, which includes the Sterkfontein caves, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The first FIFA world cup match on African soil took place at Soccer City on 11 June 2010.
gavin-douglas: Gavin Douglas was born at Tantallon Castle in East Lothian, the third son of Archibald, 5th Earl of Angus, and his second wife Elizabeth Boyd. He was a student at the University of St Andrews from 1489, studying chiefly Aristotle's logic, physics and metaphysics, and became a Master of Arts in 1496. He held the living of Monymusk and parishes in East Lothian, and about 1501 became provost of the collegiate church of St Giles in Edinburgh. All his surviving poetry was written before his fortieth year, while he held that post.

His earliest work, The Palice of Honour, dated 1501 and dedicated to James IV, is a dream-allegory of more than 2,000 lines in nine-line stanzas, in the tradition of the courts of love. The Eneados, finished six weeks before the Battle of Flodden, is faithful throughout, adds the thirteenth book written by Mapheus Vegius, and opens each of its 13 books with an original verse prologue, some of them semi-autobiographical. He also wrote the short poem Conscience, and the allegory King Hart is doubtfully his. He wrote in a polished, often aureate Middle Scots, and after the Eneados he is not known to have written more poetry.

After Flodden the Douglases took a leading part in the minority of James V, above all once his nephew Archibald Douglas, 6th Earl of Angus, married the king's widow Margaret Tudor in August 1514. She named Gavin Archbishop of St Andrews, but rivals kept him out; he won the bishopric of Dunkeld only after a bitter struggle and nearly a year's imprisonment under the Regent Albany. In 1517 he helped negotiate the Treaty of Rouen with Francis I.

When Albany returned in November 1521, Douglas was sent to the English court to seek help against the French party, was deprived of his see and could not return. He died of plague in London in 1522 at the house of Lord Dacre and was buried in the church of the Savoy; a brass to him stands in St Giles Cathedral. Because of his family and public life he is the best documented of the early Scottish makars.
gavril-radomir: Gavril Radomir, also given as Gabriel Radomir, was a son of Tsar Samuel, who reigned from 997 to 1014. His Greek name appears as Gavriḗl Romanós. During Samuel's reign Samuel sentenced his cousin Ivan Vladislav and Ivan's entire family to death for treason, and Gavril's intervention saved at least his cousin. He is said to have saved his father's life in the disastrous defeat at the Battle of Spercheios, and he was described as a gallant fighter.

Gavril Radomir was emperor of the First Bulgarian Empire from October 1014 to August or September 1015. Around the time that Emperor Basil II captured the bulk of Samuel's army, Gavril and his forces defeated the army of Theophylact Botaneiates. Having inherited Samuel's war with the Byzantine Empire, he raided Byzantine territory, reaching as far as Constantinople. The Byzantines, however, secured the assistance of Ivan Vladislav, who owed his life to Gavril. Vladislav murdered Gavril while hunting near Ostrovo and then took the throne for himself.

Some sources connect Gavril Radomir with Bogomilism, a medieval dualist sect and popular heretic movement that flourished in the Bulgarian region of Kutmichevitsa during his and his father's reign. He married twice. His possible son Peter Delyan played a role in attempting to secure independence for Bulgaria several decades later.

Ian Mladjov inferred that Agatha, the wife of Edward the Exile, was a granddaughter of Agatha Cryselia, a daughter of Gavril by his short-lived first marriage to a Hungarian princess thought to have been a daughter of Duke Géza of Hungary. According to the Polish–Hungarian Chronicle, that princess was Adelaide, the daughter of Doubravka of Bohemia and Mieszko I of Poland.
gavrilo-princip: Gavrilo Princip was born on 25 July 1894 in the hamlet of Obljaj, near Bosansko Grahovo, in western Bosnia, the second of nine children, six of whom died in infancy. His parents, Petar and Marija, were poor Serb farmers who gave a third of their income to a landlord. At thirteen he went to Sarajevo, where his brother Jovan paid for his schooling at the Merchants' School and then the Sarajevo Gymnasium.

Bosnia had been annexed by Austria-Hungary in 1908, and student groups there took up nationalist and anti-imperial ideas. In 1911 Princip joined Young Bosnia, a secret society with Serb, Croat and Muslim members that sought the liberation of Bosnia and the unification of the South Slavs. After taking part in a demonstration in February 1912 he was expelled from school and walked to Belgrade.

In 1914 Nedeljko Čabrinović showed Princip a newspaper cutting announcing Archduke Franz Ferdinand's visit to Sarajevo. Princip drew Čabrinović and Trifko Grabež into a plot. Milan Ciganović, an associate of the Serbian secret society known as the Black Hand, obtained five Browning pistols, six grenades and vials of poison for them and trained them in Belgrade. The three crossed into Bosnia, and Danilo Ilić recruited further conspirators in Sarajevo.

On 28 June 1914 the conspirators stood along the Appel Quay. Čabrinović threw a grenade that wounded occupants of another car, and the motorcade sped on. After the Archduke decided to visit the injured in hospital, his driver took a wrong turn into a side street where Princip stood. As the car stalled, Princip fired twice, killing Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg. Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July, and the conflict widened to the First World War.

Tried with twenty-four others in October 1914, Princip said he was a Yugoslav nationalist and that he regretted the death of the Duchess. He was too young to be executed, being twenty-seven days short of twenty, and received a sentence of twenty years. Held in the Small Fortress at Theresienstadt, he developed tuberculosis, which led to the amputation of his right arm, and he died on 28 April 1918. In 1920 he and the other conspirators were reburied in Sarajevo.

His memory remains contested. The Habsburg monarchy saw a terrorist, the Kingdom of Yugoslavia and socialist Yugoslavia a hero, and many Serbs still honour him, while many Bosniaks and Croats regard him as a terrorist.
gayatri-devi: Gayatri Devi was born on 23 May 1919 into the Hindu royal family of Cooch Behar. Her father was Maharaja Jitendra Narayan of Cooch Behar, and her mother was Indira Raje, the only daughter of Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III of Baroda. Through her paternal grandmother Suniti Devi she was a descendant of the social reformer Keshub Chandra Sen. Her brother Jagaddipendra Narayan succeeded their father as Maharaja of Cooch Behar. She studied at Glendower Preparatory School in London, at Patha Bhavana of Visva-Bharati University in Shantiniketan and in Lausanne, and later took secretarial courses in London.

She first met Sawai Man Singh II when she was 12 and he came to Calcutta to play polo. They married on 9 May 1940, and she was the third Maharani consort of Jaipur until 1949. She was a keen rider and polo player. The photographer Cecil Beaton photographed her for Vogue and described her as one of the ten most beautiful women in the world. Her only child, Prince Jagat Singh, was born on 15 October 1949.

She started two schools in Jaipur, the Maharani Gayatri Devi Girls' Public School in 1943 and the co-educational Maharaja Sawai Man Singh Vidyalaya in memory of her husband, and she helped revive the art of blue pottery. After India's independence and the abolition of the princely states she entered politics in the Swatantra Party, founded by C. Rajagopalachari. In 1962 she won the Jaipur Lok Sabha seat with 192,909 votes out of 246,516 cast, and she held it in 1967 and 1971 against the Indian National Congress. In 1965 she refused Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri's invitation to join Congress, although her husband was being made ambassador to Spain.

The privy purses were abolished in 1971, ending royal privileges and titles. In July 1975, during the Emergency, she was arrested under the COFEPOSA Act on an accusation of violating tax laws and served five and a half months in Tihar Jail. She then retired from politics and in 1976 published the book of her life A Princess Remembers, written by Santha Rama Rau.

Gayatri Devi died in Jaipur on 29 July 2009, aged 90. After her death her family went to the Delhi High Court to regain 800 kg of gold taken by the government in 1975, which the government held she had possessed illegally under the Gold Control Act of 1968.
