A 2019 exhibition in Mumbai marked her centenary, and in 2013 the designer Sabyasachi made five limited-edition saris in honour of her style.
gayatri-mantra: The mantra is the verse Rigveda 3.62.10, dedicated to Savitr. In recitation it is preceded by the syllable oṃ and the formula bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, known as the mahāvyāhṛti or great mystical utterance, as the Taittiriya Aranyaka prescribes. The verse is composed in the metre called gāyatrī, which in principle has three lines of eight syllables each. The text preserved in the Samhita is one syllable short in its first line. A proposed historical form of vareṇyaṃ, vareṇiyaṃ, would restore the eight syllables, and in practice reciters may keep seven, prolong the final m, or use the reconstructed word. The word Gāyatrī also names the metre, the goddess of the mantra, and other verses in the same metre addressed to other deities.

Translators have rendered the verse in many ways. Ralph T. H. Griffith in 1896 gave it as a prayer that the worshipper may attain the excellent glory of the god Savitar so that he may stimulate our prayers. Stephanie W. Jamison and Joel P. Brereton render the same wish as making our own the desirable effulgence of god Savitar, who will rouse forth our insights.

The mantra is cited widely in Hindu texts, including the listings of the Śrauta liturgy, the Srauta-sutras, the grhyasutras, the Mahabharata, the Harivamsa and the Manusmṛti. Several Upanishads treat it esoterically. It has a significant role in the upanayana ceremony, which marks the start of Vedic study. Traditionally this verse was given only to a Brahmana, while other verses were used for a kshatriya and a vaishya. Reciting it is used as a method of atonement, and practitioners hold that it bestows wisdom through the Sun.

The Buddha knew the mantra. In Majjhima Nikaya 92 he calls the Sāvittī the foremost of metres, and in Sutta Nipata 3.4 he asks a man who claims to be a brahmin for the chant of Sāvitrī, in three lines of four and twenty syllables. Among Balinese Hindus it is the first of seven sections of the Trisandhyā Puja, said three times a day.

In 1827 Ram Mohan Roy published a dissertation on the mantra that analysed it against various Upanishads, and from 1830 the Brahmos used it in private devotion. In the later 19th century Hindu reform movements spread the chant beyond the Brahmin class: in 1898 Swami Vivekananda held that a person became a Brahmana through learning, not birth, and gave the mantra to non-Brahmins in the Ramakrishna Mission. Its use is now very widespread.
gaykhatu: Gaykhatu was born about 1259 to Abaqa and Nukdan Khatun of the Tatars. His name means Surprising in Mongolian, and his Buddhist baghshi gave him the Tibetan name Rinchendorje, which later appeared on his paper money. After the execution of the viceroy of Anatolia, Qonqurtai, in 1284 he fled to Arghun in Khorasan. After Arghun took the throne he was confirmed as governor of Anatolia, stationed at Erzincan, where he learnt Persian and some Turkish. In 1286 he marched against the Karamanid chief Güneri, who had taken Tarsus from the Kingdom of Cilician Armenia, and burned Karaman on 16 January 1287.

News of Arghun's death reached Gaykhatu near Antalya. The main rivals for the throne were his nephew Ghazan and his cousin Baydu. Baydu was nominated by the commander Taghachar, but historians suggest he refused because the throne belonged by custom to a brother or son. Ghazan was busy fighting the rebellion of Nawrūz. Gaykhatu was elected il-khan at Ahlat on 23 July 1291, supported by his wife Uruk Khatun, Arghun's widow. He first punished several emirs who had backed Baydu, then went back to Anatolia against rebellious Turkmen emirs and the Karamanids, and spent 11 months there before returning to Iran in 1292.

In 1292 Gaykhatu threatened the Mamluk sultan Al-Ashraf Khalil with an invasion of the Levant unless Aleppo was returned, and the sultan answered with a threat of his own to take Baghdad; no major battle followed. In 1293 Marco Polo escorted the princess Kökötchin from Kublai Khan's court, and Gaykhatu decided she should marry Ghazan. Polo's party stayed with him for nine months. His vizier from November 1292, Sad al-Din Zanjani, became in effect the real ruler of the Ilkhanate.

In 1294 Gaykhatu wished to refill his empty treasury. Sad al-Din proposed paper money on the Chinese model, and the banknotes copied the Chinese ones so closely that they carried Chinese words, with the Muslim confession of faith added to placate local feeling. They first circulated in Tabriz on 12 September 1294. Merchants refused them, bazaar riots followed, trade stopped and the notes were withdrawn.

Gaykhatu insulted Baydu, who left for his lands near Baghdad. Gaykhatu sent Aq Buqa and Taghachar against him in March 1295, but Taghachar had already changed sides. Gaykhatu fled, begged for mercy and was strangled with a bowstring in March 1295, though some sources give other dates. One story holds that Baydu fought him because of the paper money. Mirkhond called him dissolute, while others praised his generosity to all religions, notably the Nestorian Christians.
gazi-ii-giray: Little is known of Ğazı Giray's youth; he may have been trained in horsemanship among the Circassian Besleni. He is first named in a document on a Tatar raid on Podolia in 1575. From 1578 he fought for the Ottomans in the war against the Safavids, escaping the defeat on the Menla Hasan river in which Adil Giray, the khan's brother, was captured, and was rewarded with 50,000 akçes for a surprise attack near Gence. Captured near Shemakha in 1581, he was held in Alamut Castle, escaped from Tabriz disguised as a dervish and led the Tatar and Circassian troops of Özdemiroğlu Osman Pasha at the capture of Tabriz in 1585.

The Ottomans made him khan in 1588 in place of his brother İslâm II Giray, valuing his knowledge of the empire. Taking up a Swedish offer of an alliance, he besieged Moscow on 13 July 1591 but lifted the siege against its fortifications and came home wounded. After raids on Tula and Ryazan, a treaty of October 1593 brought him 10,000 rubles and a promise to withdraw the Cossacks from the Terek and Don.

In the Long Turkish War he joined Koca Sinan Pasha at the taking of Raab in 1594, was badly defeated by Michael the Brave of Wallachia in 1595, and faced Jan Zamoyski at Cecora that year. After the Ottoman victory at Keresztes in October 1596 the new grand vizier Cığalazade Yusuf Sinan Pasha replaced him with his brother Fetih I Giray. The Tatar army demanded his return, the sultan's envoy Hamdan Agha, an old friend, handed him the letter of confirmation, and Fetih was murdered outside Kefe.

Restored in early 1597, Ğazı Giray campaigned in Hungary again in 1598, failing before Varad, and in 1602, when the Tatars were defeated at Telzayn. In 1601 he had plotters around Devlet Giray shot down at a feast, and he had his wife executed for bewitching him. In his last years he sent his son Toqtamış Giray to Hungary in his place and built the castle of Gazikerman in Circassia. He died of plague in November 1607 and Toqtamış succeeded him.
gbaya-people: The Gbaya, also called Gbeya or Baya, have lived in Central Africa since at least the 16th century, and archaeological research places their origin in the lower valley of the Lobaye River. Besides the Central African Republic and Cameroon, they live in the north of the Republic of the Congo, the north-west of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and South Sudan. Their subgroups include the Bokoto, Kara, Kaka, Buli and Bwaka, and their language belongs to the Adamawa-Ubangi branch of the Niger-Congo family.

In the early 19th century several Gbaya groups moved into what is now eastern Cameroon. Wars with the Fulani of the Sokoto Caliphate brought extensive slave raiding; some clans accepted Fulani rule, while others joined leaders such as Bafio to resist. The French explorer Antoine Mizon reached Gbaya country in 1892 after steaming up the Sangha River. Under German Kamerun the Gbaya resented forced resettlement into larger communities; a campaign of repression had subdued them by 1910, their leaders were hanged, and from 1912 many were made to collect rubber.

In the First World War many Gbaya sided with the French against the Germans, whose retreating troops burned Gbaya villages, while rogue soldiers of the Congolese Force Publique raped and killed local people. In 1928 French conscription of labour for the Congo-Ocean Railway and the preaching of Karnu, who claimed powers that could defeat the French, set off a mass revolt. Karnu was killed early, but the fighting went on for about three years. After independence the Gbaya felt shut out of politics until the 1990s.

Traditionally the Gbaya live in small rural communities and practise swidden farming, clearing and burning forest, farming the land for a few years and then moving on. Cassava is the staple, pounded with mortar and pestle for couscous or cooked as the porridge kam, alongside maize, yams, peanuts and tobacco; coffee and rice came with the French. They brew a honey drink called kuri. Most Gbaya are Christians, about 12 percent follow indigenous beliefs and a small minority are Muslims, and witchcraft, known as dua, is still practised. Estimates of their number range from 685,100 to 1.2 million.
gbe-languages: The Gbe languages form a cluster of about twenty related languages stretching across the area between eastern Ghana and western Nigeria. Estimates of the total number of speakers vary, from four million (H. B. Capo, 1988) to eight million (SIL's Ethnologue, 2005). They were traditionally placed in the Kwa branch of the Niger–Congo family, but have more recently been classified as Volta–Niger languages. Gbe is a dialect continuum, divided by Capo into five clusters: Ewe, Fon, Aja, Gen (Mina) and Phla–Pherá. The Gbe languages are tonal and isolating, with subject–verb–object as the basic word order, and they use serial verb constructions.

The name Gbe, the word for language or dialect in each of them, was proposed by Capo and generally accepted after a working group of the West African Languages Congress at Cotonou in 1980. Ewe is a language of secondary and university education in Ghana, and in 1992 Aja and Fon were two of the six national languages chosen by the government of Benin for adult education.

Most Gbe peoples came from the east to their present homes in several migrations between the tenth and fifteenth centuries. Ewe traditions point to Ketu, in present-day Benin, as the origin of humanity, from which wars pressed the ancestors of the Gbe-speaking peoples westward between the tenth and thirteenth centuries. Many settled in the kingdom of Tado on the Mono river, which was an important West African state until the late fifteenth century. Emigrants from Tado founded the Notsie kingdom, later home to the Ewe, and around 1550 the Allada kingdom, the centre of the Fon people. The Gen probably originate from the Ga-Adangbe, and some Phla–Pherá peoples may be original inhabitants who mixed with migrants.

In the late eighteenth century many Gbe speakers were enslaved and transported to the New World, as the Bight of Benin was a centre of the slave trade; the export of about 5% of the population each year led to population decline. Gbe languages are believed to have played some role in the genesis of several Caribbean creoles, especially Haitian Creole and Sranantongo.

German missionaries began linguistic research around 1840. The Bremen missionary J. B. Schlegel published the first Ewe grammar in 1857, and Diedrich Hermann Westermann became the most influential writer on Gbe in the first half of the twentieth century, using the term Ewe for the whole continuum. Capo published the first internal classification in 1988 and a comparative phonology in 1991, and founded the Laboratory for research on Gbe languages, based in Benin.
gdansk: Gdańsk lies at the mouth of the Motława River on the southern edge of Gdańsk Bay. The low-lying Lower Terrace covers part of the Vistula Fens, while the Upper Terrace is an area of uneven highlands that belongs to the Kashubian Lake District. The name most likely comes from Gdania, the old name of the Motława. Its German form, Danzig, developed from forms such as Danzc and Danczk.

The first written mention is in a biography of Saint Adalbert, which records his visit in 997 to a town called Gyddanyzc, then ruled by Bolesław I the Brave of Poland. The city grew into a trading town and later joined the Hanseatic League. In 1308 the Teutonic Knights, called in to relieve the Polish garrison, seized the town and killed many of its inhabitants; estimates of the dead range from about 60 to about 1,000. In 1454 the Prussian Confederation rejected the authority of the Teutonic Order and appealed to King Casimir IV of Poland, which led to the Thirteen Years' War, and on 16 June 1454 the king granted Danzig extensive privileges.

With considerable autonomy it served as the Polish Crown's main seaport and largest city until the early 18th century. Prussia annexed it in 1793 in the Second Partition of Poland, and it joined the German Empire in 1871. It was a free city from 1807 to 1814 and again from 1920 to 1939. A military clash at Westerplatte on 1 September 1939 was one of the first events of the Second World War. After 1945 the German population fled or was expelled and Poles settled in their place. The Solidarity trade union began in the city in the 1980s.

Gdańsk is the capital of the Pomeranian Voivodeship and Poland's sixth-largest city, with a population of 486,492, and a major seaport. With Gdynia and Sopot it forms a metropolitan area called the Tricity. Parts of the old city destroyed in the war were rebuilt in the 1950s and 1960s. Its landmarks include the Town Hall, the Green Gate, Artus Court, Neptune's Fountain and St. Mary's Church, one of the largest brick churches in the world. St. Dominic's Fair, which dates back to 1260, is still held there.
gdynia: Gdynia is historically and culturally part of Kashubia and Eastern Pomerania. It lies in a conurbation with the spa town of Sopot and the city of Gdańsk, which together form the Tricity, a metropolitan area of around a million inhabitants. In prehistoric times the area was the centre of the Oksywie culture. In the late 10th century the region was united with the emerging state of Poland by Mieszko I, and the district of Oksywie was first mentioned in 1209, as Oxhöft. For centuries Gdynia remained a small fishing village, and by the 20th century it attracted visitors as a seaside resort.

The Polish government decided to build a major seaport at Gdynia in the winter of 1920, during the Polish–Soviet War. German dockworkers in the Free City of Danzig had struck and refused to unload military supplies sent from the West to aid the Polish army, and Poland concluded that it needed a port it controlled economically and politically. A special committee began building the city in 1925, city rights were granted in 1926 and tax privileges for investors in 1927. Growth became rapid after 1928, with a new railway station and post office, and by 1939 the population had grown to over 120,000.

Gdynia was the site of fierce Polish defence during the German invasion of September 1939. The Germans captured the whole city on 14 September and occupied it until 1945, carrying out mass arrests of some 7,000 Poles on 15 and 16 September. The occupiers set up prisons and camps, and Poles were deported to concentration camps or executed. The Red Army captured the city on 28 March 1945 and it was restored to Poland. Settlers arrived from destroyed Warsaw and from Wilno and Lwów, and Greek refugees from the Greek Civil War also came through the port. Protests in and around Gdynia in 1970 contributed to the rise of the Solidarity movement in Gdańsk.

Gdynia is a seaport on the Baltic coast of northern Poland, and the largest city in Poland that is not a voivodeship capital. Its modernist centre, laid out in 1926 by Adam Kuncewicz and Roman Feliński as a grand maritime façade for the newly independent state, is built around an axis that runs from 10 Lutego Street through Kościuszko Square to the Southern Pier. Its architecture shows monumentalism, early functionalism and interwar modernism. The oldest building is the 13th-century church of St Michael the Archangel in Oksywie, and two museum ships, the destroyer ORP Błyskawica and the sailing ship Dar Pomorza, are moored in the harbour. The port is the home of the 3rd Ship Flotilla of the Polish Navy.
ge-hong: Ge Hong was born near Jurong county in 283, the third son of a well-established family originally from Eastern Wu. His ancestor Ge Xi had held the high post of Dahonglu in Eastern Wu, and his great-uncle Ge Xuan was an alchemist of the Three Kingdoms period who studied alchemy and Taoism with Zuo Ci. His father, Ge Ti, served as prefect of Shaoling after the country entered the Jin dynasty and died when Ge Hong was 13. The family declined and Ge Hong had no inheritance. He took up farming and sold firewood to buy paper and brushes, so that he could copy books borrowed from friends. He studied alchemy under Zheng Yin, a disciple of Ge Xuan.

Ge Hong held a number of high posts in the bureaucracy, appraised friends as candidates for office and was chosen for military service, but he was unhappy as an official and general. In 303 he was promoted for helping to calm the peasant uprising led by Shi Bing in Yangzhou. In 306 Ji Han, the new governor of Guangzhou, recommended him as an army official, but after Ji Han was killed Ge Hong went to live in seclusion on Mount Luofu, where he gathered herbal medicine, refined elixirs and recorded cases of illness. He became a disciple of Bao Liang, from whom he learned alchemy, and married Bao Liang's daughter Bao Gu.

In 313 he returned to his hometown but lived in seclusion, and in 317 the Inner and Outer Chapters of the Baopuzi were written. In 326 Wang Dao called him to serve as a zhubo and later as a consulting general. Hearing that Jiaozhi produced cinnabar, he asked Emperor Cheng for the post of magistrate of Gouti, but when he reached Guangzhou he was asked to stay, and he again lived on Mount Luofu refining elixirs.

Ge Hong wrote the Baopuzi, the Emergency Formulae at an Elbow's Length and Essays on Chinese Characters, and took the name Baopuzi, 'embracing simplicity'. He never rejected Confucianism but grew interested in Taoist cultivation and elixirs as the way to immortality. He questioned the traditionalism that valued old writings over new ideas and stressed experiment and results, above all in medicine and alchemy. In the Emergency Formulae he suggested extracts of the plant Artemisia annua for malaria, a method that inspired the work of Tu Youyou, who isolated artemisinin and shared the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. He also recorded the redox reaction of mercury and the change of chalcanthite into a golden bronze-like alloy with iron.
geats: The Geats were a large North Germanic tribe who lived in Götaland, the land of the Geats, in southern Sweden from antiquity until the Late Middle Ages, and are one of the progenitor groups of modern Swedes, with the Swedes and the Gutes. The earliest surviving mention is in Ptolemy in the 2nd century, who calls them Goutai; in the 6th century Jordanes wrote of the Gautigoths and Procopius of the Gautoi. They have often been equated with the Goths of the continent, but the actual relationship remains unclear. Old English and Old Icelandic sources keep Geats and Goths apart, while Jordanes's account of three Scandinavian tribes implies that the Geats were Goths.

Beowulf and the Norse sagas name several Geatish kings, but only Hygelac is confirmed elsewhere, as Rex Getarum in the Liber Monstrorum, in connection with a raid into Frisia in about 516. How the Geats and Swedes came to form one kingdom is much debated: some scholars argue that the Swedes subjugated the Geats at a date from the 6th to the 9th century, others see a gradual merging, and others stress the role of individual rulers.

In the 11th century the Swedish House of Munsö became extinct with the death of Emund the Old, and the Geat Stenkil was elected king of the Swedes. The Geats tended to be more Christian and the Swedes more pagan, which is why the Christian king Inge the Elder fled to Västergötland when deposed in favour of Blot-Sweyn in the 1080s; he retook the throne and ruled until about 1100. Papal letters from the 1160s attest the title rex Sweorum et Gothorum, and Swedish kings styled themselves also kings of the Geats from the 1270s.

The Geats were divided into petty kingdoms with their own things and laws; the largest was Västergötland, where the Thing of all Geats met near Skara. At the Council of Basel in 1434 the Swedish delegation argued that the Geats were Goths and so the Swedes had defeated the Roman Empire, a movement called Göticism. Their name survives in Västergötland and Östergötland, in the götamål dialects, and in the way residents call themselves västgötar and östgötar. Until 1973 the official title of the Swedish king included the Geats, or Goths, and the Wends.
gebelein: The Arabic name Gebelein means Two Mountains. In ancient Egyptian the town was Inerty or Per-Hathor, and in Greek and Latin it was Pathyris or Aphroditopolis.The modern locality is known as Naga el-Gherira. The site's cemeteries have produced finds from the Predynastic Period to the Middle Kingdom, and a temple of Hathor stood on its east hill.

The temple's remains include mud bricks stamped with cartouches and a royal stela of the Second to Third Dynasties. Rulers of the Second Intermediate Period left a stela of Dedumose II, a block of Djedankhre Montemsaf and a stela of a king named Sekhemtawy, and the Hyksos kings Apophis and Khyan are named on a lintel and a black granite block. A brick naming the High Priest of Amun Menkheperre and his wife Isetemkheb probably came from the fort that enclosed the temple, and fragments of a statue of Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II and of its limestone shrine date from the Ptolemaic period.

After the Theban rebellion of 186 BCE a military camp was set up at Gebelein. Rebel forces destroyed it in 88 BCE, and the site was never again inhabited on a large scale. The northern necropolis holds the tomb of Iti and Neferu, a partly rock-cut tomb of the First Intermediate Period.

Interest in the site began in the early 18th century, when it was included in Benoît de Maillet's Description de l'Egypte. Besides official excavations, many objects from Gebelein passed through the antiquities market, and they are now in museums in Turin, Cairo, Berlin and Lyons and in the British Museum. At the end of the 19th century Wallis Budge, Keeper of Egyptology at the British Museum, excavated six naturally mummified bodies from shallow sand graves, the first complete predynastic bodies to be found; one has been on display in the British Museum since 1901.

Between 1890 and 1930 several hundred Demotic and Greek papyri and ostraca on the soldiers and the local temple were found in the ruins, among them the archive of the mercenary Horos son of Nechoutes and the Dryton and Apollonia Archive. The wall paintings and burial equipment of the tomb of Iti and Neferu are mainly in the Museo Egizio in Turin.
gebhard-leberecht-von-blucher: Blücher was born on 16 December 1742 in Rostock, then in the Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin, the son of a retired army captain from an old landowning noble family. At sixteen he joined the Swedish Army as a hussar. Prussian hussars captured him in a skirmish in 1760, and the colonel of their regiment, Wilhelm Sebastian von Belling, a distant relative, had him join it.

In peacetime his ardent spirit led him into excesses, including the mock execution of a priest in 1772. Passed over for promotion, he sent a rude letter of resignation in 1773, and Frederick the Great replied, "Captain Blücher can take himself to the devil". He farmed until Frederick died in 1786, then returned as a major in 1787.

He received the Pour le Mérite in 1789 and became a major general in 1794 after his victory at Kirrweiler. As a cavalry general in 1806 he fought at Auerstedt, but he was defeated at Lübeck and surrendered at Ratekau on 7 November, insisting that the document record a lack of provisions and ammunition. In 1813, aged 71, he returned to high command.

As commander-in-chief of the Army of Silesia he defeated Marshal MacDonald at the Katzbach and Marshal Marmont at Möckern, and his army stormed Leipzig on the last day of the Battle of the Nations. He was made field marshal on 16 October 1813 and, with his chief staff officers, pressed the Coalition sovereigns to carry the war into France.

In 1814 he suffered defeats at Champaubert, Vauchamps and Montmirail, then won at Laon on 9 and 10 March, after which a breakdown cost him his sight for a time. The allies entered Paris, and Frederick William III made him Prince of Wahlstatt. When Napoleon returned in 1815 Blücher commanded the Army of the Lower Rhine. At Ligny on 16 June he lay trapped for hours under his dead horse and the Prussians retreated, but he led his army to join Wellington at Waterloo, where its arrival was decisive. The two armies entered Paris on 7 July.

Blücher retired to Krieblowitz in Silesia and died there on 12 September 1819, aged 76. Napoleon called him very brave but no talent as a general, and admired his readiness to rise again after a defeat. Later Prussian soldiers spoke of a Prussian way of war built on the quick, decisive battle. He was made an honorary citizen of Berlin, Hamburg and Rostock, and statues were raised at Berlin, Breslau, Rostock and Kaub, where his troops crossed the Rhine.
gebre-mesqel-lalibela: Lalibela's regnal name, Gebre Meskel, means Servant of the Cross. His life is recorded in his hagiography, the Gadla Lalibela. According to it, his parents were Jan Seyoum, governor of Bugna in the province of Lasta, and Kirwerna, a housemaid in his service. When Kirwerna became pregnant in 1162 Jan Seyoum was angry, and she fled to the town of Roha to give birth. A swarm of bees was said to have surrounded the newborn, which his mother took as a sign of future power, and he was named Lalibela, meaning that the bees recognise his sovereignty in Old Agaw.

The prophecy of his greatness aroused the hostility of his uncle Tatadim and his brother Kedus Harbe, the rightful sovereign. Forced into exile, Lalibela spent many years in Jerusalem. He returned to Lasta long enough to marry Meskel Kibra, and they fled together after renewed murderous attempts by Harbe.

Lalibela reigned from 1181 to 1221. The Gadla does not explain his rise, which took place in Harbe's lifetime, and Taddesse Tamrat suspects that he took the crown by force of arms. A chronicle from Gojjam says that Harbe's persecution led to a battle between the brothers. Lalibela was allied with the Amhara, who had been promised key court positions, while Harbe rallied the seven clans of the Agaw. After winning, Lalibela exiled the Agaws from Lasta and let the Amhara settle there, hence the Amharic proverb: Amhara settled, Agaw exiled.

A vision is said to have inspired him to build a new Jerusalem as his capital after Saladin's forces took the old Jerusalem in 1187. Many features of the town have Biblical names, including its watercourse, the River Jordan. No details survive about the building of its 11 monolithic churches. The later Gadla says the king carved them with only the help of angels, and the Portuguese embassy of 1520-6 was told by Lalibelian priests that they took 24 years to build.

Tradition says his chief queen, Masqal Kibra, persuaded him to abdicate in favour of his nephew Na'akueto La'ab, who ruled badly, and after 18 months Lalibela took the throne again. Taddesse Tamrat suspects this masks a brief usurpation ended by Lalibela's son Yetbarak. Getachew Mekonnen credits Masqal Kibra with building the church of Bet Abba Libanos as a memorial to him after his death. Around 1210 an embassy from the Patriarch of Alexandria visited his court. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church venerates him as a saint on 19 June, and the town of Roha was later renamed Lalibela in his honour.
gedik-ahmed-pasha: Very little about Gedik Ahmed Pasha appears in primary sources, and it was late in historiography that more was learned of him. Serbia and Albania were both proposed as his birthplace, and Mükrimin Halil Yinanç even claimed, from unnamed Western sources, that he descended from the Byzantine Palaiologos dynasty. Research in the Ottoman archives of Vranje, in south-eastern Serbia, by Aleksandar Stojanovski established that he belonged to the local Serbian feudal families and was born in the village of Punoševce. He served as grand vizier and as kapudan pasha, Grand Admiral of the Ottoman Navy, under the sultans Mehmed II and Bayezid II.

Leading the Ottoman army, he defeated the Karamanids, the last Anatolian principality to resist Ottoman expansion in the region. They had been the strongest principality in Anatolia for nearly 200 years and held Konya, the former Selçuk capital. He also fought the Venetians in the Mediterranean. In 1475 the sultan sent him to help the Crimean Khanate against the Genoese. He took Caffa, Soldaia, Cembalo and other Genoese castles, the Principality of Theodoro with its capital Mangup, and the coast of Crimea, and he rescued the khan, Meñli I Giray, from the Genoese. Crimea and Circassia thereby entered the Ottoman sphere of influence.

In 1479, as sanjakbey of Avlona, he was ordered to lead between 10,000 and 40,000 troops to the siege of Shkodra. Later that year Mehmed II gave him command of the fleet in the war against Naples and Milan, and he conquered the islands of Santa Maura (Lefkada), Kefalonia and Zante (Zakynthos).

Mehmed saw himself as the heir of the Roman Empire and seriously considered conquering Italy, and Gedik Ahmed was sent with a naval force to the heel of the peninsula. After a failed attempt on Rhodes, held by the Knights of St. John, he took the harbour city of Otranto in 1480. For lack of food and supplies he had to return to Albania with most of his troops that year, planning to continue in 1481.

Mehmed II's death prevented the continuation of the campaign. In the struggle over the succession, Gedik Ahmed sided with Bayezid II, who nevertheless did not fully trust him. Bayezid had him imprisoned and later killed on 18 November 1482.
gediminas: Gediminas was born in about 1275. Written sources of the era are scarce, so his ancestry and early life remain obscure and are debated by scholars. Theories make him the son, the brother or the cousin of his predecessor, Grand Duke Vytenis, or even his hostler. Chronicles written long afterwards by the Teutonic Knights, long-standing enemies of Lithuania, claimed that he was Vytenis' hostler who killed his master and took the throne. The Lithuanian Chronicles, also late, made him Vytenis' son, though the two men were almost the same age.

Gediminas inherited Lithuania proper, Samogitia, Navahrudak, Podlasie, Polotsk and Minsk, all threatened by the Teutonic Knights and the Livonian Order. He allied with the Tatars against the Teutonic Order in 1319, and in 1322 he wrote to Pope John XXII asking for protection and offering to be baptised. On 25 January 1323 he sent circular letters to the Hanseatic towns inviting people of every order and profession to settle in his lands. Facing opposition from pagan Lithuanians, Orthodox subjects and the Prussian bishops, he drew back from his promises and refused the papal legates who came to Riga in September 1323. He remained pagan.

He allowed Catholic clergy to minister to Catholics, but about 1339 to 1340 he had two Franciscan friars, Ulrich and Martin, executed for preaching against the Lithuanian religion. In the south and east he took lands from the Ruthenian principalities, though the stages of these campaigns are hard to follow. He defeated Stanislav of Kiev at the Irpin River and then took Kiev, and Halych-Volynia came to his family through the marriage of his son Lubart. He avoided war with the Golden Horde. After first using the newly built Trakai, he re-established a permanent capital at Vilnius in about 1320.

Gediminas died in 1341, presumably killed in a coup. He was cremated in 1342 in a pagan ceremony in which his favourite servant and several German slaves were burned with him. His son Jaunutis succeeded him but was deposed in 1345 by his brother Algirdas.

He founded the Gediminid dynasty. By legend he dreamed of an iron-clad wolf on a hill, and his priest Lizdeika told him that a city must stand there, at the meeting of the Vilnia and the Neris. The tale inspired Adam Mickiewicz.
gediminids: The House of Gediminas was a dynasty of monarchs of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania that reigned from the 14th to the 16th century. The origin of Gediminas himself is much debated. Some sources say he was an ostler of Vytenis, others that he was of peasant stock, and some historians consider him a son or grandson of the Lithuanian or Yatvingian ruler Skalmantas. Most scholars agree that he was Vytenis' brother, though the parentage of Vytenis is explained differently in fake genealogies compiled from the 16th century onwards, and the latest Polish research holds that it cannot be established.

The confirmed rulers began with Gediminas (1316–1341), followed by Jaunutis, Algirdas (1345–1377), Jogaila (1377–1434), Kęstutis, Vytautas (1401–1430), Švitrigaila and Sigismund Kęstutaitis. The line continued with Casimir (1440–1492), John I Albert, Alexander, Sigismund I the Old (1506–1548) and Sigismund II Augustus (1529–1572), and ended with the elective ruler Anna (1575–1586). Overlapping years mark coregency or rival rule. The ruler's title was, by some folkloristic evidence, kunigų kunigas, Duke of Dukes, and later didysis kunigas, Great Duke. Contemporary sources sometimes call Gediminid rulers kings, but Catholic Europe never recognised Lithuania as a kingdom, and modern historians regard the earlier Mindaugas as the only Lithuanian king.

A cadet branch founded by Władysław II Jagiełło, the Jagiellonian dynasty, also reigned in the Kingdom of Poland, the Kingdom of Hungary and the Kingdom of Bohemia. Gediminas' Cap was used at the inaugurations of Gediminid rulers in Vilnius Cathedral and symbolised the dynasty's continuity.

Several other branches ranked among the leading aristocratic houses of Poland and Russia into recent times. The Eastern Orthodox branches were at first partly Ruthenized, but most families, such as the Czartoryski, soon became Roman Catholic and Polonized. Others, including the Golitsyns, Kurakins and Trubetskoys, moved to Muscovy and became thoroughly Russified. In Poland the Olelkowicz-Słucki, Wiśniowiecki and Zbaraski families died out, while the Czartoryski, Sanguszko and others survive. Y-DNA testing of living male-line descendants places the dynasty, and the Jagiellonian dynasty, in haplogroup N-M231.
gediz-river: The Gediz is the second-longest river in Anatolia to flow into the Aegean Sea, after the Büyük Menderes, whose course runs roughly parallel a little over a hundred kilometres to the south. It rises on Murat Mountain and Şaphane Mountain in Kütahya Province, flows generally west for 401 kilometres through the provinces of Uşak, Manisa and İzmir, and enters the sea in the Gulf of İzmir, near the village of Yenibağarası in Foça district. Its basin lies between 38°04' and 39°13' north and covers 2.2 per cent of the area of Turkey. The alluvial plain that bears the river's name lies mostly in Manisa Province, with a smaller section downstream in İzmir Province.

The ancient Greek name of the river was Hermos, Latinized as Hermus. Its name Gediz may be related to the Lydian proper name Cadys, and Gediz is also the name of a town near its sources. It is one of two candidates for the Hittite river name Seha, the other being the Bakırçay. The Hermos divided Aeolia from Ionia, except for Ionic Phocaea, which lay north of it. Its valley was the heartland of the ancient Lydian Empire, and the Lydian capital Sardis overlooked it.

The Gediz Delta is a nature reserve and home to rare bird species, but the reserve suffers from water shortages because of the heavy demands of irrigation projects linked to the Demirköprü Dam. Urbanisation and industrialisation along the basin have brought severe pollution, particularly from sand and gravel quarries and from effluents of the leather industry, and the river's formerly rich fish stocks have declined in recent years.
gedrosia: Gedrosia was the Greek name of an Achaemenid satrapy in coastal Makran, in present-day Balochistan. In the accounts of Alexander the Great and his successors, the area called Gedrosia ran from the Indus River to the north-eastern edge of the Strait of Hormuz. It lay south of Arachosia and Drangiana and east of Carmania, with the Indus forming a natural boundary between it and western India. It was a dry, mountainous country along the north-western shores of the Indian Ocean, and in the Bronze Age people settled in its few oases.

Other people settled on the coast and became known in Greek as the Ichthyophagi, the fish-eaters. According to Arrian, Nearchus, who sailed along the Makran coast with a fleet, recorded them on its barren shores. Another group, the Oreitans, lived in what is now Lasbela District. Gedrosia was conquered by Cyrus the Great or by Darius the Great, though the information about the conquest is comparatively late. Its capital was Pura, probably the modern Bampur. Several scholars have argued that the Persian satrapy of Maka is the same as Gedrosia, but it is more likely that Maka was in modern Oman.

Gedrosia became well known in the West when Alexander the Great tried to cross its desert after his army refused to march further east at the Hyphasis River in 326 BCE. He sent half his forces back by sea under Nearchus and led the rest on a march of 60 days inland. He lost at least 12,000 soldiers, together with livestock, camp followers and most of his baggage train. Some historians say he lost three quarters of his army, though that figure may rest on exaggerated numbers for the force before the march. Two theories explain his choice of the desert route: that he meant to punish his men, or that he wished to succeed where Cyrus the Great had failed.

After Alexander's death the region passed to Seleucus. He later ceded it to the Mauryan Empire in the reign of Chandragupta Maurya, and Gedrosia, together with Saurashtra, was an important part of that empire until it was attacked by the Indo-Greeks from the west.
geez: Geʽez, sometimes called Classical Ethiopic in scholarly writing, is an ancient South Semitic language from what is now Ethiopia and Eritrea. Most linguists believe that it is not the common ancestor of the modern Ethio-Semitic languages but separated early from another unattested common language. Inscriptions in Sabaic have been found in the kingdom of Dʿmt from the middle of the first millennium BCE, and Semitic languages have been present in Eritrea since about 2000 BCE. Geʽez is not regarded as an offshoot of Sabaic. The earliest Geʽez inscriptions, from the Kingdom of Aksum, date to as early as the 4th century, and the oldest known example of the script is on the Hawulti obelisk in Matara, Eritrea. It is unvocalised and contains pagan references.

Geʽez is written with the Ethiopic script, an abugida first developed for this language and called fidäl in languages such as Amharic and Tigrinya that use it. It is read from left to right. The script has been adapted for other languages, chiefly Amharic and Tigrinya, and Tigre in Eritrea. The language distinguishes two genders and two numbers, and nouns have an unmarked nominative and an accusative marked with final -a. The normal word order of a declarative sentence has the verb first. Because it is no longer spoken in daily life by large communities, the early pronunciation of some consonants is uncertain.

Surviving Geʽez literature properly begins in the 4th century with the Christianization of Aksum, during the reign of Ezana. Almost all texts from the early Aksumite period are Christian and translated from Greek, producing an Ethiopic Bible of 81 books. The Book of Enoch survives complete in no other language. The oldest surviving Geʽez manuscript is thought to be the second of the Garima Gospels, dating to the 5th or 6th century. After the decline of Aksum, Geʽez was no longer a living language, replaced by Amharic in the south and by Tigrinya and Tigre in the north. It remained the official written language until the 19th century, in a position compared to that of Medieval Latin in Europe.

In the 14th century the Kebra Nagast, retelling the story of the Queen of Sheba, King Solomon and their son Menelik I, was written, and the first royal chronicles date to the reign of Amda Seyon I. Literature flourished especially under Emperor Zara Yaqob, who himself wrote the Book of Light and the Book of the Nativity. The Fetha Negest, the Laws of the Kings, was translated into Geʽez around 1450 and served as supreme law until a modern constitution replaced it in 1931. Geʽez remains the liturgical language of the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Churches and of the Beta Israel.
gegeen-khan: Shidibala was born on 22 February 1302, the eldest son of Ayurbarwada Buyantu Khan and Radnashiri of the Khunggirad clan. His personal name comes from the Sanskrit Siddhipala, and his regnal name Gegeen Khan means enlightened or bright khan.

Ayurbarwada had promised his elder brother Khayishan that Khayishan's son would be made crown prince, but after Khayishan died his two sons were sent to the borderlands and officers loyal to him were purged. Shidibala's grandmother Dagi installed him as crown prince in 1316, and a year later he became nominal head of both the Secretariat and the Bureau of Military Affairs. His father had at one time considered abdicating in his favour.

Shidibala succeeded his father on 19 April 1320. Dagi reappointed Temuder as senior grand councillor, and Temuder's persecution of his opponents in the censorate alienated the new emperor. In the summer of 1320 Gegeen appointed Baiju, a 21-year-old Jalayir descended from Muqali and well educated in Confucianism, as grand councillor of the left. He was himself educated in Chinese, devoted to both Confucianism and Buddhism, and could cite Tang poems from memory. In 1321 he built a Buddhist temple in honour of the 'Phags-pa Lama west of Dadu and had several censors who reproached him put to death. Islam suffered severe discrimination during his reign.

The deaths of Dagi and Temuder in 1322 gave him full power. He dismantled the Khunggirad faction, deprived Temuder of titles and estates and executed his son, and made Baiju sole grand councillor. They recruited many Chinese scholar-officials, among them Zhang Gui, appointed seven scholars to the Hanlin Academy and revised the Da Yuan Tong Zhi, a collection of the dynasty's codes. To ease the labour burdens of small landowners, landowners were to set aside part of their registered lands to cover corvée expenses.

On 4 September 1323, while Gegeen was at Nanpo on the road from the summer palace at Shangdu to the capital Dadu, Temuder's adopted son Tegshi attacked his encampment with Asud guards and killed Gegeen and Baiju. Five princes were involved. This Coup d'état at Nanpo was the first violent succession struggle in the dynasty, and the first time an emperor was overthrown by a group led by a non-Borjigin.

Tegshi asked Yesün Temür to take the throne, but Yesün Temür purged Tegshi's faction before entering Dadu. Gegeen's marriage to Sugabala produced no children. Chinese records glorified him, and his death was sometimes explained as a struggle between a pro-Confucian faction and the steppe elite.
geghard: According to tradition Gregory the Illuminator founded the monastery in the 4th century at a spring inside a cave that had been sacred in pre-Christian times. For that reason it was first called Ayrivank, the Monastery of the Cave. Nothing of the first buildings has survived. Armenian historians of the 4th, 8th and 10th centuries describe religious buildings together with residential and service structures. The first monastery was destroyed by Arabs in the 9th century, and in 923 Nasr, a vice-regent of an Arabian caliph in Armenia, plundered its property, including manuscripts, and burned its buildings. Earthquakes also damaged it.

The main church, the Katoghike, was built in 1215 under the brothers Zakare and Ivane, generals of Queen Tamar of Georgia. It is built against the mountain, with an equal-armed cross plan inscribed in a square under a dome. West of it stands the gavit, built between 1215 and 1225, whose central dome of stalactite vaulting is the best example of the technique in Armenia. Ramparts of the 12th and 13th centuries protect three sides of the complex, and the cliffs the fourth.

After Prince Prosh Khaghbakian, a vassal of the Zakarians, bought the monastery, the Proshyans made it a family monastery and mausoleum. Rock-cut chambers date from the 1240s onward: the first cave church, with a spring, in the 1240s; the second cave church and a sepulchre in 1283; and the upper zhamatun, the tomb of Papak Proshyan and his wife Ruzukan, in 1288. An inscription names the architect Galdzak. The Proshyans also provided an irrigation system, and the monastery was known as the Monastery of the Seven Churches and of the Forty Altars. Crosses carved in relief, khachkars, cover many of its rock faces.

The name Geghardavank, the Monastery of the Spear, is first recorded in a document of 1250. It comes from the spear that wounded Christ at the Crucifixion, allegedly brought to Armenia by the Apostle Thaddeus. A case was made for it in 1687, and it is now in the treasury at Echmiadzin. Relics of the Apostles Andrew and John were donated in the 12th century, and visitors made grants of land, money and manuscripts over the centuries. The historian Mkhitar Ayrivanetsi lived in one of the cave cells in the 13th century.

The monastery later fell out of use, and its main church sheltered the winter flocks of Karapapakh nomads until a few monks from Ejmiatsin resettled it after the Russian conquest. It is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site and remains a place of pilgrimage.
geislingen-an-der-steige: Geislingen an der Steige, literally Geislingen on the Climb, is surrounded by the heights of the Swabian Alb and lies in five valleys. Its name refers to its position at the climb of a trade route over the Swabian Jura. It is about 50 kilometres from Stuttgart and 27 kilometres from Ulm, and is the second largest town in the district of Göppingen. Its urban area includes Altenstadt, which was incorporated in 1912, and several other communities that were added in the territorial reform of the 1970s.

Although the area had settlements from the Bronze Age, Geislingen was founded by the counts of Helfenstein as a collection station for tolls on the important commercial route between the Rhine valley and the Mediterranean. Their fortified castle existed from 1100, and the place was first mentioned as a civitas in a document of 1237. Two districts are much older than this foundation. Altenstadt, called Altengiselingen in the oldest times, is of Alamannic origin, with first traces of settlement from the 5th century. Rorgensteig was an old parish village, whose church served the citizens of Geislingen until 1393 and whose mills made it the town's first medieval industrial centre.

In 1367 Count Ulrich von Helfenstein ordered that the city seal carry his full coat of arms. The count sold Geislingen in 1396 to the imperial city of Ulm, which owned it until 1802. The Lady Chapel became a parish church around 1393, and the present town church, a Gothic building put up by the Ulm minster's masons' workshop, was built from 1424 to 1428. In 1803 Ulm and Geislingen passed to Bavaria, and in 1810 a land exchange brought them into the Kingdom of Württemberg.

Industrialisation began with the railway. The Fils Valley Railway, built from 1847 to 1850 up the steep Geislinger Steige to the plateau of the Swabian Jura, was designed by the railway engineer Michael Knoll, who was born in the town. The Württembergische Metallwarenfabrik, founded in 1852, became the town's leading maker of kitchen and table goods. The town's economy rests on steel, metal goods and automotive supply.

After the Second World War, 4,400 Estonian refugees lived in the Geislingen camp, which existed from October 1945 to 24 June 1950. They ran their own gymnasium, theatre and symphony orchestra and published the newspaper Eesti Post. A memorial in the cemetery was erected in 1949. Geislingen also has the ruins of Helfenstein Castle and a museum in the half-timbered Alter Bau.
gelao-people: The Gelao, called Klau in their own language, are often considered the indigenous inhabitants of Guizhou. Their ancestors were the Rau peoples, who made up the population of ancient Yelang. They are one of the 56 ethnic groups officially recognised by the People's Republic of China, although many Gelao are classified as Yi, Miao or Zhuang. They number approximately 677,521 and live mainly in the Gelao autonomous counties of western Guizhou, such as those in Zunyi, and in Liupanshui, Anshun, Dafang and Bijie. Others live in western Guangxi, southeastern Yunnan and southern Sichuan. In Vietnam they are an official ethnic group, with 2,636 people in 2009.

Gelao people were long thought to have only a spoken language. In September 2008 a book called the Record of the Nine Heavens was found in Guizhou, kept by a Gelao man surnamed Li who said his ancestors were from the Song dynasty. Its supporters take it as proof of a written language and a long history. Its account of where the Gelao lived deviates from local histories of the Ming and Qing dynasties, and its classical Chinese and Gelao contain many grammatical errors, so a modern forgery is possible. Gelao in western Guizhou, such as around Anshun, once used characters derived from Chinese characters to record folk songs.

Gelao belongs to the Kra-Dai language family, but only a little over a thousand Gelao speak it. Its dialects differ greatly, so Mandarin serves as a lingua franca and is now the main language; many Gelao also speak Miao, Yi or Bouyei. Men traditionally wear a jacket fastened up the side and long trousers, women short jackets and narrow skirts in three parts, and both wear long scarves. Their music includes the jiaohu, a two-stringed fiddle with a body made from a cow horn, and their oral literature includes poetry, proverbs and folk songs. The main religion is Taoism, with a small but significant Buddhist minority. Historical names distinguish subgroups such as the Flowery, Red, Cut-Head, Tooth-Hitting and Water Gelao.
gelderland: The province takes its name from the German city of Geldern and descends from the County of Guelders, which arose in the 11th century out of the Frankish pagus Hamaland around castles near Roermond and Geldern. According to the Wichard saga, the Lords of Pont killed a dragon in 878 and named the town they founded after its death-rattle, Gelre.

The counts acquired the Betuwe and Veluwe regions and, through marriage, the County of Zutphen. Through their control of the Rhine, Waal, Meuse and IJssel rivers they became an important power of the later Middle Ages, committed to the interests of the Holy Roman Empire and to expansion to the south and west.

After the acquisition of the imperial city of Nijmegen in the 13th century, Emperor Louis IV raised the county to a duchy in 1339. From 1379 the duchy was ruled from Jülich and by the counts of Egmond and Cleves. It resisted Burgundian domination, but William, Duke of Jülich-Cleves-Berg was forced to cede it to Charles V in 1543, and it became part of the Burgundian-Habsburg lands.

The duchy rose with the rest of the Netherlands against Philip II of Spain and joined the Union of Utrecht in 1579. After Philip's deposition sovereignty lay with the States of Gelderland, and the princes of Orange were stadtholders. Louis XIV temporarily occupied the province in 1672, and in 1713 the southeastern part, including the ducal capital Geldern, fell to Prussia.

Gelderland was part of the Batavian Republic from 1795 to 1806, of Louis Bonaparte's Kingdom of Holland from 1806 to 1810 and of the French Empire from 1810, and became a province of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in 1815. In the Second World War the Battle of Arnhem was fought there between Allied paratroopers, British XXX Corps and the German II SS Panzer Corps.

Gelderland is in the centre-east of the Netherlands and is the largest province by land area, covering 5,136 km2 of which 176 km2 is water. Its capital is Arnhem, though Nijmegen and Apeldoorn are larger. It has four regions: the Veluwe, the largest forest region in the Netherlands, in the north; the Rivierenland including the Betuwe, with orchards, in the southwest; the Achterhoek in the east; and the city-region of Arnhem and Nijmegen.
geldern: Geldern lies in the plains of the lower Rhineland, west of the Rhine, at an average elevation of 27 metres. The Niers, a tributary of the Meuse, flows through it, and the stream Gelderner Fleuth joins the Niers there. It belongs to the district of Kleve in the Düsseldorf administrative region, and the nearby Dutch province of Gelderland is named after it. Its first coat of arms showed a shield with three medlars, which refers to a local dragon legend; the lion of Guelders has appeared in the present coat of arms since the Middle Ages.

By folk legend the Lords of Pont killed a fire-breathing dragon around 878 and then founded the city. It was first documented around 900. The probable ancestor of the counts of Guelders was Gerhard Flamens, who received Wassenberg as a fief from Emperor Henry II in 1020, and his great-grandson Gerhard IV of Wassenberg was the first to call himself Count of Guelders, from 1096. The counts moved to a castle at the crossing of the Niers, which with its settlement became the origin of the city. It was fortified in the 13th century, received city rights in 1229 and was the residence of the counts and dukes until 1343. The Late Gothic parish church of Mary Magdalene was built between 1400 and 1418.

Geldern often lay in the battlefield of territorial disputes. It was under Spanish rule from 1543 to 1578, when the Dutch occupied it, and returned to Spanish control in 1587. In the War of the Spanish Succession Prussia besieged it from February 1703 and it surrendered on 21 December. At the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713 the Upper Quarter of Guelders was divided among Austria, the United Provinces, Prussia and Jülich, and Geldern, with most of it, fell to Prussia as the seat of administration of Prussian Guelders. Frederick II ordered the fortifications demolished in 1764. The French occupied the town from 1794 to 1814 and secularised the Carmelite monastery in 1802.

In World War II bombing, at the end of 1944 and on 14 February 1945, destroyed about 82 per cent of the city, and the parish church was rebuilt in 1952. The population is mostly Roman Catholic. The present city was formed in 1969, when Kapellen, Vernum, Pont, Veert and Walbeck were incorporated. Schloss Haag, enlarged between 1662 and 1664, survives only in its outer castle.
gelimer: Little is known of Gelimer's early life, and his birth date is unknown. He was the son of Gelarius, grandson of Gento and great-grandson of Geiseric, who led the Vandals in the fall of the Western Roman Empire. He had two brothers, Ammatus and Tzazon, and became a military commander who campaigned successfully against the Moors. Apart from King Hilderic he was the heir expected to inherit the throne. Hilderic had sought better relations with Emperor Justinian I and ended persecutions and allowed a new Chalcedonian bishop to take office at Carthage, which alarmed the Arian Vandal nobility. Gelimer allied with the Moors and persuaded the nobles to depose him.

On 19 May 530 Gelimer imprisoned Hilderic and took the throne. Justinian refused his gifts and rejected his legitimacy, and prevented an alliance with the Ostrogoths. Revolts in Tripolitania and Sardinia followed, and Justinian supported both. Gelimer sent his brother Tzazon with 5,000 Vandals to Sardinia, which deprived him of troops and nearly the whole fleet. The historian J. B. Bury called his actions astounding blunders.

In June 533 Justinian sent Belisarius with an expeditionary force. Gelimer confronted him at Ad Decimum on 13 September 533; his plan to ambush the Byzantines failed when his brother Ammatus arrived early and was killed, which set off a rout. Carthage was captured in the following days. On 15 December 533 the armies met again at Tricamarum, where Tzazon died and the Vandal centre collapsed. Gelimer fled to Mons Pappua, on the border of Numidia, where Pharas besieged him.

In March 534 Gelimer surrendered, ending the Vandal Kingdom. He was taken to Constantinople and appeared in Belisarius's triumph, where according to Procopius he cried out the verse from Ecclesiastes, vanity of vanities. He refused to abandon his Arian faith and so did not receive the title of patrikios. Justinian gave him and his supporters estates in Galatia, where he lived until the end of his life. The year of his death is unknown.
gelon: Gelon was the son of Deinomenes and the first of the Deinomenid rulers. According to Herodotus, his ancestors came from the island of Telos in the Aegean and were among the founders of Gela in southern Sicily; Herodotus infers that his descendants, Gelon among them, were priests of the cult of the Earth Goddesses. Gelon had three brothers, Hieron, Thrasybulus and Polyzalus, and an oracle consulted by Deinomenes was said to have told him that Gelon, Hieron and Thrasybulus were destined to become tyrants. Gelon earned a reputation as a formidable soldier and became commander of the cavalry of his uncle Hippocrates, tyrant of Gela.

After Hippocrates was killed in battle with the native Sicel tribe at Hybla, the common people revolted against his sons. Gelon quelled the revolt on the pretext of helping the sons, but took power himself with the army in 491 BCE. His territory then included Gela, Naxos, Zancle and Camarina. In 485 BCE the exiled aristocracy of Syracuse, the Gamori, asked for his help, and he captured the city with little or no resistance. He left Hieron to rule Gela, and according to Herodotus forced half the citizens of Gela to move to Syracuse.

He conquered Euboea and Megara Hyblaea in 483 BCE, removing their aristocracies and enslaving the rest of the population. Syracuse prospered, with a building programme and a mercenary army of about 10,000, all granted citizenship of Syracuse.

Gelon married Demareta, daughter of Theron, tyrant of Acragas. In 481 BCE Athenian envoys asked for help against Xerxes I; Gelon offered 28,000 men and 200 ships if made commander of the Greek army or navy, was refused, and sent nothing. In 480 BCE a Carthaginian force under Hamilcar landed at Panormus and advanced on Himera, where Theron had defeated the tyrant Terillus. Gelon came to Theron's aid with 50,000 men and 5,000 cavalry. Some of his men entered the Carthaginian camp posing as allies from Selinus and set fire to the ships, and the ensuing battle was a decisive victory, with Carthaginian casualties estimated at 150,000, including Hamilcar.

Gelon shared the spoils with his troops and allies, and a large part went to a new temple in Syracuse. According to Herodotus he told the people of Syracuse they could kill him if they found fault with his conduct, but they kept him as tyrant. He died in 478 BCE after ruling Syracuse for seven years, and was succeeded by his brother Hieron, who ruled for ten years. After Hieron's death a dispute over the succession led to the dissolution of the Syracusan state.
gelug: The Gelug is the youngest of the four major schools of Tibetan Buddhism. Je Tsongkhapa, a philosopher, tantric yogi and lama, travelled Tibet studying under Kadam, Sakya, Drikung Kagyu, Jonang and Nyingma teachers. He merged the Kadam teachings of lojong (mind training) and lamrim (stages of the path) with the Vajrayana teachings of other schools and stressed monasticism and strict adherence to the vinaya, the monastic discipline.

The school is also called Ganden, after the first monastery he established, and New Kadam, because it sees itself as continuing the tradition of Atisha. According to Sam van Schaik, Tsongkhapa did not set out to found a new school; his disciples, above all Khedrup, defined and defended it. After his death in 1419 the order grew quickly as they founded monasteries across Tibet.

Doctrinally the Gelug teaches a form of prasangika Madhyamaka based on Tsongkhapa's works, with an understanding of emptiness reached first through study and reasoning. Its graded path draws on Atisha's A Lamp for the Path to Awakening and on Tsongkhapa's Great Exposition of the Graded Path. It is arguably the only school of Vajrayana Buddhism that requires monastic ordination of its teachers. Its principal tantra is the Guhyasamaja, which Tsongkhapa called the king of tantras. The Ganden Tripa, the Ganden Throne Holder, is the official head of the school, while the Dalai Lama is its most influential political figure.

Sönam Gyatso formed an alliance with the powerful Mongol leader Altan Khan, and as a result was designated the 3rd Dalai Lama; Dalai is the Mongolian translation of the Tibetan Gyatso, ocean, and two earlier figures were recognised afterwards as the 1st and 2nd. He travelled to Mongolia, supported monasteries and the translation of Buddhist texts into Mongolian, and worked against practices such as animal sacrifice. The Gelug became the main religion of the Mongols in the following centuries.

After violent strife among the Tibetan schools, the Gelug became dominant with the military help of the Mongol Güshri Khan, who invaded Tibet in 1642 to defeat the king of Tsang. The 5th Dalai Lama, Ngawang Lobsang Gyatso, was the first of his line to hold full political and spiritual power. He established a theocratic government, opened relations with Qing China and built the Potala Palace in Lhasa. After the annexation of Tibet by the People's Republic of China thousands of monasteries were destroyed or damaged, and the three major Gelug monastic colleges, Sera, Drepung and Ganden, were recreated in India.
gemistos-plethon: Georgios Gemistos was born in Constantinople into a well-educated Orthodox family and studied there and at Adrianople, then the Ottoman capital, before teaching philosophy in Constantinople. Late in life he took the name Plethon, which means much the same as Plato. Some time before 1410 Emperor Manuel II Palaiologos sent him to Mystra in the Despotate of the Morea, where he stayed for the rest of his life, serving as a judge and chief magistrate under Theodore II and being consulted by the rulers of the Morea. There he taught philosophy, astronomy, history and geography. His pupils included Bessarion and George Scholarius, later Patriarch of Constantinople and his enemy.

In pamphlets of 1415 and 1418 Plethon urged Manuel II and his son Theodore to turn the Peloponnese into a cultural island with a centralised monarchy advised by a small body of educated men, a professional native army supported by taxpayers, public ownership of land and regulated trade. He drew on Plato's Republic and believed the Peloponnesians descended from the ancient Hellenes. Neither ruler acted on these plans. Late in life he wrote the Nomoi, or Book of Laws, circulated only among close friends, which turned from Christianity to a worship of the classical gods mixed with ideas attributed to Zoroaster and the Magi. Plethon also held that the human soul is reincarnated.

In 1438 and 1439 Plethon accompanied Emperor John VIII to the Council of Ferrara and Florence, on the strength of his reputation for wisdom. At the invitation of Florentine humanists he lectured on the differences between Plato and Aristotle and wrote De Differentiis, to which Scholarius replied. He is credited with reintroducing much of Plato to the Latin West, and Marsilio Ficino called him the second Plato, though James Hankins doubts the traditional story that he inspired Cosimo de' Medici's Platonic Academy.

After his death the Nomoi came to Scholarius, then Patriarch Gennadius II, who burned it in 1460 but described its contents in a surviving letter. In 1466 Italian disciples headed by Sigismondo Pandolfo Malatesta took his remains from Mystra to the Tempio Malatestiano in Rimini. His claim that Greeks were Hellenes by race and culture has fed debate about Byzantine and modern Greek identity.
general-council-of-andorra: The first parliament of Andorra was established in 1419 as the Consell de la Terra. Its councillors were elected by the population, and the council appointed syndics to manage the administration of the principality. It remained in force for several hundred years but slowly became the fiefdom of a few major families, which caused popular discontent by the nineteenth century. The General Council is sometimes called the General Council of the Valleys, its historical name, to distinguish it from similarly named bodies in the Val d'Aran and in France.

Major reforms were instituted in 1866, masterminded by Guillem d'Areny-Plandolit. The Consell de la Terra was abolished and replaced by the Consell General de les Valls, with a syndic and a vice-syndic; the franchise was extended to all heads of families; and regular elections were laid down, with twelve of the then twenty-four councillors elected every two years. In the 1930s a dispute arose when the council began regularly to call Andorra a republic, which angered the co-princes. They ordered the council dissolved in June 1933 and a special election held, and the voting laws were changed so that all men over twenty-five could vote and all men over thirty stand.

In 1970 the vote was extended to women over twenty-five, and in 1971 the voting age was lowered to twenty-one and the age of candidates to twenty-five. Women gained the right to run for office in 1973, and a referendum on further reform was held in 1978. Later that year a seventh parish, Escaldes-Engordany, was formed, bringing the number of councillors to twenty-eight. In 1982 an Executive Council was created, and in 1984 Mercè Bonell became its first female councillor.

The Council is a unicameral parliament of 28 general councillors elected for four-year terms on party lists. Two come from each of the seven parishes, elected from the list with most votes in the parish, and fourteen are elected from national lists by the largest remainder method of proportional representation. Voters cast two separate ballots, and the same person cannot appear on both a parish and a national list. Originally each parish returned four deputies, but as parishes varied in population from 350 to 2,500 this was felt to be imbalanced, and the national list was introduced for the 1997 elections.

The Council appoints a presiding officer, the Síndic general, and a deputy, the subsíndic. It elects the Head of Government, subject to approval of the Co-Princes, and the Head of Government presides over the Executive Council and appoints its other seven members. Political parties are a recent innovation: the first was formed in 1976 and parties gained legal recognition only in 1992.
general-strike-of-1926: Heavy wartime use had depleted British coal seams: output per miner fell from 310 tons a year in the early 1880s to 199 tons in 1920–1924. In 1924 the Dawes Plan let Germany export coal to France and Italy as reparations, lowering prices, and in 1925 Winston Churchill, as chancellor of the Exchequer, returned Britain to the gold standard, making exports dearer. Mine owners cut wages, and when they proposed further cuts the Miners' Federation of Great Britain answered: "Not a penny off the pay, not a minute on the day."

Stanley Baldwin's Conservative government paid a nine-month subsidy and appointed a royal commission under Sir Herbert Samuel. Its report of 10 March 1926 recommended reorganising the industry, cutting wages by 13.5% and ending the subsidy. The owners then offered longer hours and lower pay, which the miners refused, and they were locked out.

After talks failed, the TUC limited the strike to railwaymen, transport workers, printers, dockers, ironworkers and steelworkers. The government had prepared during the subsidy, stockpiling coal, creating the Organisation for the Maintenance of Supplies and using the Emergency Powers Act 1920, while troops and volunteers kept basic services going. Churchill edited the government's British Gazette, and the TUC published the British Worker.

Police and strikers clashed in Canning Town, Poplar and Tilbury, and on 10 May striking miners derailed the Flying Scotsman at Cramlington; elsewhere, in Plymouth, strikers beat a police team 2–0 at football. Mr Justice Astbury ruled in the High Court that the general strike was not protected by the Trade Disputes Act 1906. On 12 May the TUC General Council called the strike off without any guarantee against victimisation of the strikers.

The miners held out until most returned by the end of November, accepting longer hours, lower wages and district agreements, and many stayed unemployed for years. The Trade Disputes and Trade Unions Act 1927 banned sympathy strikes, general strikes and mass picketing. Union membership fell, and Ernest Bevin, who had coordinated the strike, came to see it as a mistake, while many rank-and-file workers felt betrayed by the TUC. Britain has had no further general strike. The strike appears in novels by H. G. Wells, John Galsworthy, Lewis Grassic Gibbon and Evelyn Waugh.
generalife: The name Generalife is most often derived from the Arabic jannat al-‘arīf, variously rendered Garden of the Architect, Garden of the Artist, Garden of the Gnostic or Garden of the Flautist. Robert Irwin finds this unlikely and considers the true origin unclear. An inscription by Ibn al-Jayyab names the palace Dar al-Mamlakat as-Sa'ida, the House of the Felicitous Kingdom.

In the Nasrid period it was an almunia, a country villa used both as a private retreat and as a farming estate, a kind of royal estate known in al-Andalus since the Umayyad period. Muhammad III contributed to its early decoration and added the mirador chamber in the northern pavilion. According to an inscription it was remodelled in 1319 under Isma'il I, whose vizier and court poet Ibn al-Jayyab composed the inscriptions around the entrance to the Salón Regio. Yusuf III remodelled the southern sections of the palace in the 15th century.

The gardens occupy three large terraces on the hillside, and the palace stands on a fourth terrace above them. Its core is the Patio de la Acequia, a courtyard measuring 12.8 by 48.7 metres, divided into four elongated flowerbeds with a water channel along its long axis. This four-part layout has its roots in the Persian chahar bagh garden. A small mirador, or lookout chamber, projects from the western wall, and is probably the earliest known mirador in Nasrid architecture. Pavilions stand at the north and south ends, and the north pavilion holds the Salón Regio.

Water came from the Acequia Real, which draws on the Darro River about 6.1 kilometres east of the Alhambra. Above the Patio de la Sultana rises the Water Stairway, a four-flight staircase whose balustrades are carved with channels. The Nasrid rulers could reach the palace from the Alhambra by a private covered passage that crossed the ravine between them.

After the Reconquista the Catholic Monarchs added an upper story to the northern pavilion in 1494, and the Patio de la Sultana was redesigned in the 16th century. The Venetian traveller Andrea Navagero described the Generalife in 1524–26, before most later Spanish changes, and modern scholars use his account to reconstruct its original appearance. Leopoldo Torres Balbás and Francisco Prieto Moreno rearranged much of the gardens between 1931 and 1951. A fire in 1958 damaged the northern parts and allowed excavations that recorded the Nasrid paths and soil. Since 1984 the Generalife has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site together with the Alhambra.
generalitat-de-catalunya: The Generalitat has its roots in the General Court of Catalonia, which under James I the Conqueror came to be convoked by the king as representatives of the estates. Under Peter the Great the Courts gained institutional status when the king obliged himself to hold a General Court each year. It sat in three branches, the clergy, the nobility and the towns under direct royal rule, and the union of the three was called Lo General de Cathalunya. The Courts passed the Constitutions of Catalonia, the first being those of 1283. Behind them lay the eleventh-century Peace and Truce of God, a Church movement against feudal violence whose first Catalan assembly met at Toluges in 1027.

The Diputació del General de Catalunya was a permanent council of deputies set up by the Courts in 1359 to collect a new tax of the General, a tribute for the king. It gained considerable political power over the following centuries and took on tasks such as that of prosecutor. In the early 18th century, after the Catalan defeat in the War of the Spanish Succession, the Nueva Planta Decrees abolished it with the Principality's other institutions.

It was restored in 1931, when Francesc Macià declared a Catalan Republic and then agreed with Spanish ministers that it be renamed the Generalitat of Catalonia, the self-government of Catalonia within the Spanish Republic. A statute of autonomy of 1932 gave it a parliament, a presidency and an executive council. Macià presided until 1933 and Lluís Companys from 1933 to 1940. Abolished when the Civil War ended, it continued in exile; Companys was executed on 15 October 1940, and Josep Tarradellas, president in exile, returned in 1977 and was recognised by the Spanish government.

The Generalitat is the whole system of Catalan self-government: the Parliament, the President and the Executive Council. The Parliament is unicameral, with 135 members elected for four years. The Generalitat holds wide powers over culture, environment, communications, transport, commerce and public safety, and shares jurisdiction with Spain over education, health and justice. Catalonia has its own police force, the Mossos d'Esquadra. Its seat is the Palau de la Generalitat in Barcelona, and its powers rest on the Statute of Autonomy of 2006.
generality-lands: After 1648 there were four main Generality Lands, together about a fifth of the Republic's territory. States' Brabant was the northern part of the Duchy of Brabant, the bulk of present-day North Brabant. States' Flanders was the northern part of the County of Flanders, now Zeelandic Flanders, although the largely Protestant lands of Axel and several forts were represented in the States of Zeeland.

States' Overmaas, beyond the Meuse as seen from Brussels, comprised small territories between Maastricht, Liège and Aachen, among them the County of Dalhem, Valkenburg Land and the Herzogenrath Land, while Maastricht itself was a condominium with the Prince-Bishopric of Liège. States' Upper Guelders, a part of Spanish Guelders including Venlo and Echt, came to the Republic by the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713, when another part went to Prussia and a small part around Roermond stayed with the Austrian duchy of Guelders.

The lands were taken in the later years of the Eighty Years' War, and their possession was confirmed by the Treaty of Westphalia in 1648. Most had no provincial government because they had been cut off from their old governments, which remained under Spanish rule. The prefix Staats- marked them as dependent territories under the States, and the Generality claimed sovereignty over them, as over the Dutch colonies, by right of conquest. They were exploited with heavy taxes and levies. Westerwolde and Wedde were a generality land from 1594 to 1619 before joining Groningen, and Drenthe, though a member of the Union, also lacked a seat in the States-General.

The Generality Lands ceased to exist after the French occupation and the proclamation of the Batavian Republic in 1795, when States' Brabant became a département of the Batavian Republic and the other lands went into French départements. Under the United Kingdom of the Netherlands the former States' Brabant formed most of the province of North Brabant, States' Flanders was joined to Zeeland, and most of Upper Guelders and Overmaas became part of the province of Limburg, the rest going to Prussia.
geneva: Geneva lies at the south-western end of Lake Geneva, at 46°12' North, 6°09' East, where the Rhône flows out of the lake. Three mountain chains belonging to the Jura surround it: the Jura main range to the north-west, the Vuache to the south and the Salève to the south-east. The city covers 15.93 square kilometres, and about 91.8 per cent of that land is built up.

The Canton of Geneva covers 282 square kilometres and has a border of only 4.5 kilometres with the rest of Switzerland. Of its 107.5 kilometres of border, 103 are shared with France. The name appears in Latin texts, in Caesar's spelling Genava, and probably comes from a Celtic stem meaning mouth, in the sense of an estuary.

Geneva was an Allobrogian border town, fortified against the Helvetii tribe, when the Roman Republic took it in 121 BCE. It became Christian under the Late Roman Empire. It was connected to the Bishopric of Vienne in the 4th century and acquired its own first bishop in the 5th century.

The medieval county of Geneva was known in Middle Latin as the pagus major Genevensis. After 1400 it became the Genevois province of Savoy, although the province did not extend to the city itself until the reformation of the seat of the Bishop of Geneva. A local holiday, the Jeûne genevois, falls on the first Thursday after the first Sunday in September and by tradition commemorates the day news of the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre of Huguenots reached the city.

Geneva is the second most populous city in Switzerland and the most populous in French-speaking Romandy. It is the capital of the Republic and Canton of Geneva. Its municipal population was 203,856 in January 2021.

The city is the European headquarters of the United Nations, in the Palace of Nations, up the hill from the headquarters of the former League of Nations. It also hosts the World Health Organization, the International Labour Organization, the International Committee of the Red Cross and CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear Research. The whole old city is part of the Inventory of Swiss Heritage Sites, and 82 buildings or sites are listed of national significance, among them the Cathédrale St-Pierre.
genghis-khan: Temüjin was born between 1155 and 1167, and historians favour different dates: 1155, 1162 or 1167, with 1162 accepted by most. He was the eldest child of Yesügei, a chieftain of the Borjigin clan, and Hö'elün. When he was eight his father died and his family was abandoned by its tribe. He married Börte around 1178, and when Merkit raiders kidnapped her he recovered her with armies lent by Toghrul, khan of the Kerait, and his childhood sworn brother Jamukha.

Later his relationship with Jamukha deteriorated into open warfare, and he was badly defeated around 1187.
