george-ii-of-abkhazia: George II, of the Leonid dynasty, became king in 923 and ruled until 957. Although independent and called mepe, king, at home, he also held the Byzantine title of Exousiastes. His first years were troubled: his brother Bagrat claimed the crown and, backed by a party of nobles and by his father-in-law Gurgen II of Tao, staged a coup, and the conflict lasted nearly seven years until Bagrat died suddenly in 930.

To hold central Georgia, George made his son Constantine duke of Kartli in 923, but Constantine revolted in 926. George besieged the rock-hewn city of Uplistsikhe, lured his son out by treachery and had him blinded and castrated, then installed another son, Leon, as duke. Aided by rebellious Kakhetian nobles, George dispossessed Kvirike II, Prince-bishop of Kakheti, in the 930s, and allied with the Bagratids of Tao-Klarjeti, betrothing his daughter Gurandukht to Gurgen Bagrationi.

Kvirike returned to the offensive and stirred up a rebellion in Kartli. George sent a large army under Leon, but the king died during the expedition, and Leon made peace with Kvirike, leaving the campaign without result. Three of his sons by his wife Helen later reigned in Abkhazia: Leon III, Demetrius III and Theodosius III.

George promoted Orthodox Christianity, helped with the support of Constantinople to make Christianity an official religion in Alania, and founded the cathedrals of Khopa, Kiachi and Ckhondidi to counter the Greek cathedrals, making the new sees a mainstay of royal power. The Georgian Chronicles describe him as courageous, faithful to God, a builder of churches and merciful towards the poor, and the 18th-century historian Vakhushti Bagrationi wrote of him in similar terms. His long reign is regarded as the height of the kingdom's culture and political power.
george-ii-of-great-britain: George Augustus was born in the city of Hanover. His parents, George Louis, later George I, and Sophia Dorothea of Celle, both committed adultery, and in 1694 the marriage was dissolved on the pretext that she had abandoned her husband. George spoke only French until the age of four, then learned German, English and Italian.

In June 1705 he visited the Ansbach court under the false name Monsieur de Busch to see Princess Caroline of Brandenburg-Ansbach, and was so taken by her good character that he would think of nobody else. They married on 2 September 1705 at Herrenhausen Palace and had eight children. When his father became King in 1714, George was made Prince of Wales; quarrelling with the King, he became associated with the opposition, and his residence at Leicester House was a meeting place for Sir Robert Walpole and Lord Townshend.

George I died on 22 June 1727 and George II succeeded him as king and elector. He did not go to Germany for the funeral, which the English took as proof of his fondness for England, and he suppressed his father's will, which tried to split the Hanoverian succession. He was crowned at Westminster Abbey on 22 October 1727. He exercised little control over domestic policy, which Parliament largely controlled, and he spent twelve summers in Hanover.

Britain reopened hostilities with Spain in 1739, in the War of Jenkins' Ear, which became part of the War of the Austrian Succession. George took part in the Battle of Dettingen and was the most recent British monarch to lead an army in battle. The Jacobite rising of 1745 failed to depose the King. His son Frederick, Prince of Wales, supported the opposition and died in 1751. In 1756 a French invasion of Minorca began the Seven Years' War.

On 25 October 1760 George rose at six, drank hot chocolate, and was found on the floor of his closet; he was dead before his daughter Amelia arrived. At nearly seventy-seven he had lived longer than any English or British predecessor, and his grandson George III succeeded him.

He donated the royal library to the British Museum in 1757, founded the University of Göttingen in 1737. The province of Georgia, chartered in 1732, was named after him. For two centuries historians tended to view him with disdain, concentrating on his mistresses, short temper and boorishness, but later scholars conclude that he exercised more influence in foreign policy and military appointments than was thought.
george-ii-of-greece: George was born on 19 July 1890 at the royal villa at Tatoi, near Athens, the eldest son of Crown Prince Constantine and Sophia of Prussia. He was a great-grandson of both King Christian IX of Denmark and Queen Victoria. He trained with the Prussian Guard at the age of 18 and served in the Balkan Wars. His grandfather George I was assassinated at Thessaloniki on 18 March 1913, and Constantine became king, making George crown prince at 23. He followed his father into exile in Switzerland in 1917, after the National Schism, and he was in Romania when his younger brother Alexander died in 1920. A rigged referendum restored Constantine that year, and he abdicated again in 1922.

George became king on 27 September 1922, but he was not warmly received. Greece was unstable after a coup, and many refugees were arriving from Asia Minor after the war. He and his wife Elisabeth, daughter of the Romanian king Ferdinand I, were confined to Tatoi and closely watched. After a failed royalist coup in October 1923 he went to Romania. The Second Hellenic Republic was proclaimed on 25 March 1924, and the royal family was banished and stripped of Greek citizenship.

In the next ten years Greece had twenty-three governments and thirteen coups. The monarchy was restored after a rigged referendum, and George returned in November 1935. On 4 August 1936 he endorsed the dictatorship of Ioannis Metaxas, signing decrees that dissolved parliament, banned political parties and abolished the constitution. He ruled jointly with Metaxas, kept full control of the army and was largely responsible for foreign policy, though he distrusted Metaxas's growing power.

Italy began a propaganda campaign against Greece in 1940, and when Hitler suggested George abdicate in return for a guarantee against an Italian attack, the king refused. Metaxas rejected an Italian ultimatum on 28 October 1940, and Greece repelled the invasion and occupied the southern half of Italian Albania. After the German invasion of April 1941 George left for Crete, then Egypt and London, where he headed the government in exile. A referendum on 1 September 1946 gave 68.4 per cent in favour of his return, although Allied observers acknowledged significant fraud. George died of arteriosclerosis on 1 April 1947, aged 56. He had no children, and his younger brother Paul succeeded him.
george-ii-rakoczi: George II Rákóczi was born on 30 January 1621, the eldest son of George I Rákóczi and Zsuzsanna Lorántffy. He was elected Prince of Transylvania during his father's lifetime, on 19 February 1642. On 3 February 1643 he married Sophia Báthory, a granddaughter of Stephen Báthory IX, and their son was Francis I Rákóczi. On taking the throne in October 1648 his first thought was to realise his father's ambitions in Poland.

In early 1649 he allied with the Cossack hetman Bohdan Khmelnytsky and with the hospodars of Moldavia and Wallachia, Vasile Lupu and Matei Basarab, but took no action for several years. By the Treaty of Radnot of 6 December 1656 he allied with Charles X Gustav of Sweden against John II Casimir of Poland, and was to seize Lesser Poland and Mazovia with the salt deposits at Wieliczka and Bochnia. In late January 1657 his army of 25,000 crossed the Carpathian Mountains near Krosno. Its march toward Kraków was marked by atrocities, destruction and looting. In April it joined the Swedish army, and the combined army took Lublin, besieged Brest Litovsk and in June took Warsaw.

Charles X Gustav left to fight Denmark, and Rákóczi withdrew. Polish forces under Stefan Czarniecki pursued him, and he was defeated at Czarny Ostrów on 20 July. At Miedzyboz on 23 July he capitulated to Jerzy Lubomirski, promising to break his alliance with Sweden and pay over four million złotys. On 26 July Tatars of the Crimean Khanate, then Polish allies, attacked him. He abandoned his army to János Kemény, and on 31 July the camp near Trembowla was captured, with 500 Transylvanians killed and about 11,000 taken to the Crimea.

On 3 November 1657 the Diet deposed him at the command of the Ottoman Empire, to which Transylvania was tributary, for an unauthorised war, and replaced him with Francis Rhédey. A new Diet at Medgyes reinstated him in January 1658. He was deposed again by the Turkish Grand Vizier and again reinstated. The Turks then invaded Transylvania, and Rákóczi died at Nagyvárad of wounds received at the battle of Gyalu in May 1660.
george-iii: George was born on 4 June 1738 at Norfolk House in St James's Square, London, two months prematurely and so weak that he was baptised the same day. He was the eldest son of Frederick, Prince of Wales, and Princess Augusta of Saxe-Gotha. After his father's death in 1751 he became Prince of Wales. He was the first monarch of the House of Hanover to be born in Great Britain, to speak English as his first language and never to visit Hanover. In his accession speech in 1760 he declared, "Born and educated in this country, I glory in the name of Britain." He married Princess Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, and they had 15 children.

The early years were politically unstable, chiefly because of disagreements over the Seven Years' War. The Peace of Paris in 1763 gave Britain Canada and the part of Louisiana east of the Mississippi. At home George insisted on the Royal Marriages Act 1772, after his brothers made marriages he disapproved of.

After the Boston Tea Party of 1773 opinion hardened in Britain, and fighting began at Lexington and Concord in April 1775. The King and Parliament ignored the petitions of the Second Continental Congress, and George declared the American leaders traitors. Thomas Paine's Common Sense called him the Royal Brute of Great Britain. Britain later fought revolutionary and Napoleonic France from 1793, and the Acts of Union 1800 created the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. The slave trade was banned in the British Empire in 1807, although the King supported planters who sought to delay abolition.

George suffered from recurrent mental illness. Until the mid-20th century it was thought psychological; in 1966 Ida Macalpine and Richard Hunter proposed porphyria, a view that gained wide acceptance. Since 2010 it has been challenged, and recent scholarship holds that the illness was psychiatric, most probably bipolar disorder. In late 1810, nearly blind from cataracts, he relapsed. The Regency Act 1811 made the Prince of Wales regent, and George lived in seclusion at Windsor Castle until his death on 29 January 1820.

He had reigned for 59 years and 96 days, longer than any earlier king. Two of his sons, George IV and William IV, succeeded him in turn, and the throne then passed to Victoria, the only legitimate child of his fourth son.
george-iv-of-georgia: George IV of the Bagrationi dynasty was the son of Queen Tamar of Georgia and her consort David Soslan. His mother declared him co-regent in 1207. According to the Georgian chronicles, his second name Lasha meant illuminator of the world in the Abkhaz language. He had a princely domain in Javakheti, centred on Alastani, and was known as javakht' up'ali, the Lord of the Javakhians, as a type of silver coin struck in his name suggests.

After Tamar's death George continued her policy of strengthening the feudal Georgian state. His supporters included Sargis Tmogveli, Shalva and Ivane Akhaltsikheli, Sula Surameli and Botso and Memna Jaqeli, while Ivane I Mkhargrdzeli and Varam Gageli opposed him. When the atabeg of Ganja, Muzaffar al-Din Uzbek, stopped paying tribute, the Darbazi approved a campaign. The siege went badly, and fighting won by the Georgians caused heavy casualties, but the atabeg agreed to pay tribute again. In 1219 George campaigned against Erzurum, Nakhchivan and Ahlat and forced them to pay annual tribute.

In the 1210s inflation hurt the vassal states. An inscription at Ani records that Catholicos Epiphanes ordered the tithe cut by two thirds after fees for baptism, marriage and burial had tripled. Pope Innocent III had secured Georgia's participation in the Fifth Crusade, and George, according to the chronicles, prepared a campaign in the Holy Land. A Mongol expedition defeated two Georgian armies in 1221 and 1222, and the king was severely wounded; the invasion cut off his plans.

George went to Bagavan in Armenia to secure his sister Rusudan's marriage to the Shah of Shirvan and ensure her succession. He died there on 18 January 1223, of complications from his wound. Rusudan succeeded him, and he was buried at Gelati monastery.

In 1215 a woman from Velistsikhe, married to another man, bore him a son, David VII, who was later king of Georgia from 1246 to 1270. George gave the child to Rusudan to raise. Bishops, the Catholicos and ministers confronted him, and the woman was sent back to her husband, but George insisted that she was his wife and refused any other marriage arranged by the court.
george-iv-of-the-united-kingdom: George Augustus Frederick was born on 12 August 1762 at St James's Palace, the eldest child of King George III and Queen Charlotte. He was created Prince of Wales a few days after his birth. At eighteen he was given a separate establishment and threw himself into heavy drinking, mistresses and spending. On reaching twenty-one in 1783 he received a grant of £60,000 from Parliament and an annual income of £50,000 from his father, which was far too little for his wants. He quarrelled with his conservative father and allied himself with the Whig Charles James Fox.

When the King's mental health failed in 1788, Fox argued that the Prince was automatically entitled to rule, while William Pitt the Younger held that Parliament alone could choose a regent. In 1795, with his debts rising and his father refusing to help unless he married, he wed his cousin Princess Caroline of Brunswick. They separated after the birth of their only child, Princess Charlotte, in 1796.

After the King's final breakdown, the Prince became Prince Regent on 5 February 1811 under the Regency Act 1811. He left his ministers in full charge of government, and the principle that the prime minister is the person supported by a majority in the House of Commons became established. Lord Liverpool controlled the government for most of the regency and reign, presiding over victory over Napoleon and the peace settlement.

George became king on the death of George III in 1820, obese and possibly addicted to laudanum. He refused to recognise Caroline as queen and had her name omitted from the Book of Common Prayer. He asked for the Pains and Penalties Bill, which would have annulled the marriage, but it proved so unpopular that it was withdrawn. Caroline was excluded from the coronation at Westminster Abbey on 19 July 1821, which cost about £243,000, and she died on 7 August. After Liverpool's retirement, he was forced to accept Catholic emancipation, which he opposed.

His health declined in the late 1820s from gout and dropsy, and by December 1828 he was almost blind. He died on 26 June 1830. His only legitimate child, Charlotte, had died in 1817, and his brother Frederick in 1827, so the throne passed to another brother, William IV.

Called the first gentleman of England for his style and manners, he was widely held in contempt for his way of life, and the prestige of the monarchy dimmed. The Duke of Wellington described him in harsh terms, and in his eulogy as the most accomplished man of his age.
george-maniakes: Maniakes was a Greek general of the Byzantine Empire. He first came to prominence in a campaign of 1030–1031, in which the Byzantine army was defeated at Aleppo but went on to capture Edessa from the Arabs. His chief achievement was the partial reconquest of Sicily from the Arabs, begun in 1038. He was aided by the Varangian Guard, then led by Harald Hardrada, who later became King of Norway, and by Norman mercenaries under William de Hauteville. William earned the nickname Iron Arm by defeating the Emir of Syracuse in single combat. He was also catepan of Italy in 1042, and is known as Gyrgir in Scandinavian sagas.

The expedition in Sicily broke up through quarrels. Maniakes ostracized his admiral Stephen, whose wife was the sister of John the Eunuch, the highest-ranking man at court. He then publicly humiliated Arduin, the leader of the Lombard contingent, and the Lombard troops deserted together with the Normans and Norsemen. Emperor Michael IV, who was also Stephen's brother-in-law, recalled him. The Arabs soon recaptured the island, but his successes there later inspired the Normans to invade Sicily themselves.

Maniakes' achievements in Sicily were largely ignored by the emperor, and he revolted against Constantine IX despite having been appointed catepan of Italy. The person most responsible for inciting him was Romanus Sclerus, like Maniakes one of the wealthy landowners of Anatolia. Their estates bordered each other, and the two were rumoured to have attacked each other in a dispute over land. Sclerus owed his influence with the emperor to his sister Maria Skleraina, and used it to turn Constantine against Maniakes. When Sclerus demanded that he surrender command of the forces in Apulia, Maniakes tortured him brutally.

His troops, the Varangians among them, proclaimed him emperor, and he marched on Constantinople. In 1043 his army clashed with troops loyal to Constantine near Thessalonica. Although initially successful, Maniakes was killed in the melee after receiving a fatal wound, according to the account of Psellus. His death ended the rebellion, and Constantine punished the surviving rebels by parading them in the hippodrome, sitting backwards on donkeys. The town of Maniace in Sicily and the Syracusan fortress Castello Maniace are named after him.
george-martinuzzi: Born Juraj Utješenović at Kamičak Castle near Skradin on 18 June 1482, he was the youngest son of the Croatian lesser nobleman Grgur Utješenović and Anna Martinuzzi, of a Venetian patrician family. Most details of his life before 1528 are uncertain. His father and two eldest brothers died while he was a child, and the Ottomans took the family estates. From 1490 he was raised at the castle of Hunyad by Duke John Corvinus, and around 1503 he moved to the court of Hedwig of Cieszyn, widow of Count Stephen Zápolya, as a page and then a guard. At 24 he entered the Pauline Order, learnt to read and write, and studied at Jasna Góra in Częstochowa.

After the Battle of Mohács in 1526 Hedwig's son John Zápolya was elected king, but Ferdinand of Habsburg claimed the throne. When John fled to Poland after his defeat at Szina in 1528, Martinuzzi went with him and served as his envoy to his supporters in Hungary. In 1532 Alvise Gritti made him provisor of Buda Castle. He centralised the royal revenues, checked the tax collectors and drew income from trade in leather, fleece, wine and grain, which earned him charges of greed. He led the secret talks that produced the Treaty of Várad of 24 February 1538, by which Hungary was to be reunited when one of the two kings died, and urged John to marry Isabella Jagiellon.

After John's death on 22 July 1540 he had the Diet elect the infant John Sigismund king. He defended Buda against Ferdinand's siege in 1541 and called on Suleiman the Magnificent, but the Ottomans then seized Buda. The Treaty of Gyalu of 29 December 1541 left the eastern lands to John Sigismund, and Martinuzzi tried to keep the state intact by friendly relations with Austria without offending the Ottomans. In 1550 he imprisoned Queen Isabella at Gyulafehérvár, drove out the hospodars of Moldavia and Wallachia and beat the Turks at Déva. The Diet of Kolozsvár confirmed the agreement with Ferdinand in August 1551, and on 12 October Pope Julius III made him a cardinal.

When he tried to mediate privately with the Ottomans after their capture of Csanád, the imperial general Giambattista Castaldo accused him of treason. On 16 December 1551 at Alvinc Castle his secretary Marco Aurelio Ferrari stabbed him from behind as he read a letter, and he was finished off by Sforza-Pallavicini and hired men. The pope excommunicated Ferdinand and his generals, but lifted the sentence in 1555 after hearing 116 witnesses.
george-monck: George Monck was born on 6 December 1608 at the family estate of Potheridge in Devon, the second son of Sir Thomas Monck and Elizabeth Smith. The Moncks were one of the oldest families in Devon but relatively poor, and in 1625 his father was imprisoned for debt and died in jail two years later. As a younger son of impoverished gentry Monck became a professional soldier.

He served at the failed attack on Cádiz in 1625 and then spent most of a decade in the Dutch States Army, then thought the best school of war, where he rose to lieutenant colonel and played a decisive part in the storming of Breda in 1637. He returned to England in 1638 and fought in the Bishops' Wars.

After the Irish Rebellion of 1641 Monck served in Ireland under the Earl of Ormond, where he was responsible for several alleged massacres in County Kildare. He was captured fighting for the Royalists at Nantwich in January 1644 and, valued for his ability, stayed a prisoner for two years, writing a military manual. After Charles I's surrender he accepted a post under Parliament and in 1647 became Parliamentarian commander in Eastern Ulster.

Under Oliver Cromwell he fought in the Anglo-Scottish War, where 800 civilians were allegedly killed when Dundee was stormed, and was a General at Sea in the First Anglo-Dutch War. From 1655 to 1660 he commanded the army in Scotland.

When Cromwell died in 1658 Monck backed his son Richard. After army radicals under John Lambert and Charles Fleetwood forced Richard out in 1659, Monck declared for the Rump Parliament against Lambert, and his army marched to the English border while Sir Thomas Fairfax raised a force of his own. Lambert's troops melted away, and Monck entered London on 2 February 1660. The Declaration of Breda, issued by Charles II on 4 April 1660, was largely based on his recommendations. Modern historians question whether the policy was his own or followed a majority opinion already in favour of the monarchy.

In July 1660 Monck was made Duke of Albemarle and given the Privy Council, lands and a pension. After an illness in 1661 he stayed away from front-line politics. He took over the Admiralty's administration in the Second Anglo-Dutch War, remained in London during the Great Plague of 1665, shared command with Prince Rupert in 1666 and was recalled to keep order after the Great Fire of London. Albemarle Sound in North Carolina is named after him. He died on 3 January 1670 of severe oedema, three weeks before his wife Anne Clarges, and was buried in Westminster Abbey.
george-of-antioch: George, born around 1080, was a Greek Orthodox Christian from the Byzantine Empire. Many place his birth at Antioch, where he certainly spent part of his youth, and the historian Sarah Davis-Secord dates his departure to around the Seljuk conquest of the city in 1084. The family then served Alexios Komnenos. According to the 15th-century Egyptian scholar al-Maqrizi, around 1087 they were exiled from Constantinople and their ship was intercepted by Tamim ibn al-Muizz, emir of Ifriqiya, who took them into his service and made George governor of Sousse. After Tamim's son Yahya killed George's brother Simon, they fled to the court of Roger II of Sicily in 1108.

In Sicily George served under Christodulus, the king's chief official, as a tax collector, administrator of the district of Iato and ambassador to the Fatimids of Egypt. The Muslim scholars al-Maqrizi and al-Tijani record that he worked to discredit his mentor, and in 1126 he took Christodulus's place, with power over the army and finances nearly equal to the king's. He was styled ammiratus ammiratorum. He shaped Roger's dress and public appearances on the model of Muslim rulers and brought Arabic back into the diwan.

His early command against Mahdia in 1123 ended in defeat, with 200 of 300 ships lost, but he kept his place. In 1131 he blockaded Amalfi, which Roger then took. From 1140 he raided Mahdia regularly; after taking Tripoli he governed it for half a year and left a local Muslim in charge, and the conquests of Sousse, Sfax and Mahdia created Roger's Kingdom of Africa. In 1147 he bribed Corfu into submission and raided Monemvasia, and in 1149 he harassed the defences of Constantinople. The Greek historian Nicetas Choniates portrayed him as a pillager moved by greed.

George died in 1151 or 1152 and was buried in the church he had sponsored in 1143, later known as the Martorana, whose Greek mosaics and Arabic inscriptions combine the cultures of Norman Sicily. In 2015 it became part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Arab-Norman Palermo. The historian Joshua Birk argues that the court's Arabic character was pushed aside almost at once after his death, as the trial and execution of his successor, Philip of Mahdia, showed.
george-of-podebrady: George was the son of Victor of Kunštát and Poděbrady, a Bohemian nobleman of Moravian ancestry and a leader of the moderate Utraquist wing of the Hussites. His mother is not known by name, and he was probably born out of wedlock, a fact his enemies mocked throughout his life. His father died in 1427. At fourteen George fought at the Battle of Lipany in 1434, which ended the revolutionary phase of the Hussite movement.

During the reign of the young Ladislaus the Posthumous, Bohemia divided between the party faithful to Rome, led by Oldřich II of Rosenberg, and the Hussite party, led by George. In 1448 he marched about 9,000 men from Kutná Hora to Prague and took the capital almost without resistance. In 1451 Emperor Frederick III, as the king's guardian, entrusted him with the administration of Bohemia, and a diet at Prague confirmed the regency.

Ladislaus died suddenly in 1457. Some accused George of poisoning him, but research in 1985 identified acute leukaemia as the cause. On 2 March 1458 the estates of Bohemia unanimously chose George as king, even the supporters of the papal party voting for him. He tried to rule moderately on the basis of the Compacta of Prague, but Pope Pius II declared the Compacta void in 1462. George refused to accept this, while punishing the more extreme Taborites and the members of the new Unitas Fratrum church.

He also proposed a treaty among Christian powers, including Hungary, Poland, France and Burgundy, whose members would settle disputes peacefully and share a common parliament. His brother-in-law Jaroslav Lev of Rožmitál toured European courts with the draft. Nothing came of it, and Pius's successor Paul II proved an equally determined opponent.

Noblemen of the papal party formed an alliance at Zelená Hora on 28 November 1465. On 23 December 1466 Paul II excommunicated George and declared him deposed. Frederick III and Matthias Corvinus of Hungary, George's former ally, joined the rebels in the Bohemian War. Matthias conquered much of Moravia and was crowned king of Bohemia by the papal party at Olomouc on 3 May 1469. George was successful against him but made an agreement in 1470.

George died on 22 March 1471 and was buried in St Vitus Cathedral; his heart and entrails were placed in the Church of Our Lady before Týn. His followers chose Vladislaus II, son of the Polish king, to continue the fight against Matthias. His contemporaries called him the King of two peoples and the Friend of peace. In the 19th century he was praised as the last Czech national monarch, and he is now remembered chiefly for the treaty proposal, seen as an early vision of European unity.
george-of-saxony: George was born at Meissen on 27 August 1471, the eldest son of Albert the Brave of Saxony, founder of the Albertine line of the Wettin family, and of Sidonie, daughter of King George of Poděbrady of Bohemia. His cousin Elector Frederick the Wise of the Ernestine branch became known for protecting Luther. George received a training in theology and other branches of learning and was better educated than most princes of his day. As early as 1488 he was regent of the ducal possessions, which included the Margraviate of Meissen with Dresden and Leipzig, while his father fought in East Frisia for the emperor. On 21 November 1496 he married Barbara Jagiellon, daughter of King Casimir IV of Poland.

Albert settled the succession at Maastricht on 14 February 1499, hoping to prevent further partition of his lands. After his death on 12 September 1500, George succeeded him in his German territories as head of the Albertine line. In 1505 an agreement with his brother Heinrich transferred the governorship of Friesland to George, but the province went on producing revolts, and in 1515 he sold it to the future Emperor Charles V for 100,000 florins. At home he divided the duchy into districts, acted against robber-knights and reorganised the law courts. He sometimes infringed the rights of cities, and he encouraged reforms and Humanism at the University of Leipzig.

From 1517 George gave most of his energy to church affairs. At first he was not hostile to Luther, but he turned against him, and an acrimonious correspondence followed. In 1519 he originated the Disputation of Leipzig. At the Diet of Worms in 1521 he added twelve complaints of his own, mainly about indulgences and annates, to the princes' list of grievances. He helped to put down the revolt of the peasants in 1525, had Lutheran books confiscated, and in 1525 formed the League of Dessau with other rulers to protect Catholic interests. Both his son-in-law Philip of Hesse and his brother Heinrich joined the Reformers.

His surviving sons died without heirs, Frederick shortly after his marriage in early 1539. Under the settlement of 1499 his Protestant brother Heinrich was next in line, and George sought instead to leave the duchy to Ferdinand, brother of Charles V. He died at Dresden on 17 April 1539 before this could be carried out. He is buried with Barbara in the Georgskapelle in Meissen Cathedral, which holds an altarpiece by Lucas Cranach the Elder.
george-orwell: Eric Arthur Blair was born on 25 June 1903 in Motihari, Bengal Presidency, British India, into what he described as a lower-upper-middle-class family. His father, Richard Walmesley Blair, worked in the Opium Department of the Indian Civil Service, and his mother, Ida Mabel Blair, grew up in Moulmein, Burma. When he was one year old his mother took him and his sister Marjorie to England, and in 1904 she settled at Henley-on-Thames. Apart from a brief visit in mid-1907, he did not see his father until 1912.

He attended a convent school in Henley run by French Ursuline nuns, and then, through a scholarship, St Cyprian's School in Eastbourne from September 1911. He hated the school and later wrote the essay Such, Such Were the Joys about it, published after his death. He met Cyril Connolly there. He went on to win a scholarship to Eton. As a child he took a keen interest in natural history, in butterflies, birds and fishing, and his adult diaries are full of observations of nature.

Blair wrote under the pen name George Orwell. For most of his career he was best known for journalism, in essays, reviews, columns and books of reportage: Down and Out in Paris and London, The Road to Wigan Pier (1937), on the living conditions of the poor in northern England, and Homage to Catalonia (1938), on his experiences soldiering for the Republican side in the Spanish Civil War. He later called that war his watershed political experience, and said that everything he had written since 1936 was directed against totalitarianism and for democratic socialism.

Modern readers meet him more often as a novelist, through the allegorical novella Animal Farm (1945), often thought to reflect the degeneration of the Soviet Union and the rise of Stalinism, and Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949), on life under totalitarian rule. Many of his coinages, such as Big Brother, Thought Police, Room 101, Newspeak and doublethink, entered the English language. He was an atheist who identified with the humanist outlook, yet he took part in the life of the Church of England. His works are widely studied in schools in England, and his political legacy is contested, with critics on both left and right claiming or attacking him.
george-padmore: Malcolm Ivan Meredith Nurse was born on 28 June 1903 in Arouca District, Tacarigua, Trinidad. His father, James Hubert Alfonso Nurse, was a local schoolmaster, and his paternal great-grandfather was an Asante warrior sold into slavery at Barbados. After school in Port of Spain he worked for several years as a reporter with the Trinidad Publishing Company. In late 1924 he went to the United States to study medicine at Fisk University, later moving to New York University and then Howard University. He took the name George Padmore for party business, joining the Communist Party in 1927 and working in its American Negro Labor Congress.

In 1929 the Communist International asked Padmore to stay in Moscow to head the Negro Bureau of the Red International of Labour Unions, and he was elected to the Moscow City Soviet. In July 1930 he helped organise a conference at Hamburg that launched the International Trade Union Committee of Negro Workers, and he edited its monthly, The Negro Worker, first in Vienna and then in Hamburg. After the Nazi seizure of power the paper's offices were ransacked and he was deported to England. Disillusioned by the Comintern's pursuit of alliances with colonial powers, he cut his ties in 1933 and was expelled from the movement on 23 February 1934.

In London from 1934 he became the centre of a community of Pan-Africanist writers. He chaired the International African Service Bureau, which grew out of C. L. R. James's group on Ethiopia and included Jomo Kenyatta and Amy Ashwood Garvey. His books included How Britain Rules Africa (1936) and Africa and World Peace (1937). In 1945 he organised the Manchester Pan-African Congress, attended by W. E. B. Du Bois, which helped set the agenda for post-war decolonisation.

Padmore advised Kwame Nkrumah by letter, wrote for his newspaper and published The Gold Coast Revolution (1953) and Pan-Africanism or Communism? (1956). He moved to Ghana at Nkrumah's invitation, but his time there was difficult, and he returned to London for treatment of cirrhosis of the liver. He died on 23 September 1959 at University College Hospital. His ashes were buried at Christiansborg Castle on 4 October 1959.

Nkrumah opened the George Padmore Research Library in Accra on 30 June 1961. The George Padmore Institute, an archive and research centre in North London, was founded in 1991 by John La Rose, and a blue plaque marks his former home at 22 Cranleigh Street in Camden.
george-rooke: George Rooke was the son of Colonel Sir William Rooke and Jane Rooke, née Finch, and joined the Royal Navy as a volunteer in 1672. As a lieutenant in HMS London he fought at the Battle of Solebay in May 1672, when the Dutch under Michiel de Ruyter surprised a combined British and French fleet, and at the Battle of Schooneveld in June 1673. Made captain on 13 November 1673, he carried Prince William of Orange to England in HMS Nonsuch in October 1677.

In HMS Deptford he fought at the Battle of Bantry Bay in May 1689 and cleared Belfast Lough of French shipping so that Marshal Schomberg's army could land in Ulster. As a rear admiral he commanded a division during the French victory at the Battle of Beachy Head in July 1690 and was criticised but cleared at the inquiry. Under Admiral Edward Russell he fought at the Battle of Barfleur in May 1692 and burned twelve French ships in a night attack at La Hogue. Knighted in 1693, he lost part of the Smyrna convoy to Admiral Anne Hilarion de Tourville near Lagos that June.

Rooke joined the Board of Admiralty in 1694 and sat as Tory member for Portsmouth from 1698. In 1700 his Anglo-Dutch squadron, with a Swedish fleet under Hans Wachtmeister, attacked Copenhagen and helped King Charles XII of Sweden land in Denmark. His expedition against Cádiz in August 1702 made little progress, and he abandoned it as the passage into the harbour was too strongly guarded before turning to the treasure fleet at Vigo Bay. In December 1703 he brought Archduke Charles of Austria to Windsor Castle, and in August 1704 a bombardment directed by Admiral George Byng preceded the landing at Gibraltar.

Suffering badly from gout, Rooke retired from the navy in January 1705 and left Parliament in 1708. He died at Lawrence House in Canterbury on 24 January 1709 and was buried at St Paul's Church there. He married three times and had one son by his second wife, Mary Luttrell. In November 2004 Peter Caruana, Chief Minister of Gibraltar, unveiled a statue of him for the 300th anniversary of the capture. The badge of HMS Hogue, a chess rook, came from his arms.
george-seferis: Georgios Seferiadis, who wrote as Giorgos Seferis, was born on 13 March 1900 (28 February in the old style) in the Aidin Vilayet of the Ottoman Empire. His father, Stelios Seferiadis, was a lawyer and later a professor at the University of Athens, as well as a poet and translator, a Venizelist and a supporter of demotic Greek over the formal katharevousa. In 1914 the family moved to Athens, and from 1918 to 1925 Seferis studied law at the Sorbonne in Paris.

In September 1922, while he was in Paris, Smyrna was taken by the Turkish Army after a two-year Greek campaign in Anatolia, and many Greeks, including his family, fled. He did not visit Smyrna again until 1950. The sense of exile from his childhood home shaped much of his poetry, notably his interest in the story of Odysseus.

Seferis entered the Greek Ministry of Foreign Affairs in 1926 and held posts in the United Kingdom from 1931 to 1934 and Albania from 1936 to 1938. In the Second World War he accompanied the Greek government-in-exile to Crete, Egypt, South Africa and Italy and returned to liberated Athens in 1944. Later postings included Ankara, London, a ministry to Lebanon, Syria, Jordan and Iraq, and the embassy in London, his last post before retirement.

His collections began with Strophe in 1931 and Mythistorema in 1935, and Log Book III in 1955. He first visited Cyprus in November 1953 and was struck by its likeness to his childhood summer home at Skala. Log Book III, mostly written there, ended six or seven years without poems. In the dispute among the United Kingdom, Greece and Turkey over the island's status he worked through his diplomatic post for a settlement.

In 1963 Seferis received the Nobel Prize for Literature for his eminent lyrical writing, inspired by a deep feeling for the Hellenic world of culture. He was the first Greek to win it. His Hellenism lay in a unifying strand of humanism in the continuity of Greek literature rather than in nationalism.

After the Regime of the Colonels took power in 1967, he made a statement on the BBC World Service on 28 March 1969, declaring that this anomaly must end. He died in Athens on 20 September 1971, of pneumonia aggravated by a stroke, and did not see the junta fall. Crowds at his funeral sang Mikis Theodorakis's setting of his poem Denial, then banned.
george-the-pious: George was born at Ansbach on 4 March 1484, the second of eight sons of Margrave Frederick the Elder and Sophia of Poland, a daughter of Casimir IV. From 1506 he lived at the court of his uncle, King Vladislaus II of Bohemia and Hungary, who treated him as an adopted son, gave him the Duchy of Oppeln in 1515 and in 1516 made him a member of the regency for Hungary and tutor of his son Louis II. At the court of Hungary he led the German party against the Magyar party of the Zápolyas.

By treaties with their dukes, pledges from the king of Bohemia, who could not redeem his debts, and the acquisition of Jägerndorf, George came to hold all of Upper Silesia. Luther's stand at the Diet of Worms in 1521, the Nuremberg preachers of 1522 and Luther's New Testament won him to the Reformation, earlier than any other German prince, and in 1524 he met Luther during the secularisation of Prussia by his brother Albert. Queen Maria of Hungary supported his efforts at court.

In Franconia his elder brother Casimir, co-regent of the family lands, held to the old church. Only after Casimir's death could George, with councillors such as Johann von Schwarzenberg and the state assembly of 1528, carry out the Reformation there. He stripped churches and cloisters of their treasures, using 50,000 florins to pay Casimir's debts, and with Nuremberg developed the church order of Brandenburg-Nuremberg of 1533, later brought into his Silesian lands. He met Elector John of Saxony at Schleitz in 1529, which led to the articles of Schwabach, and opposed the emperor at the Diet of Augsburg in 1530, refusing King Ferdinand's offers of Silesian lands.

George would not approve armed resistance to the emperor, even in self-defence. He helped the sons of Joachim I bring the Reformation to the Electorate of Brandenburg, and the colloquy of Regensburg in 1541 was the last religious meeting he attended. Married three times, he left daughters who married into the houses of Württemberg and Brandenburg, and his son George Frederick became margrave and regent of the Duchy of Prussia. He died on 27 December 1543 and appears in Jan Matejko's painting Prussian Homage.
george-town-penang: George Town is the capital of the Malaysian state of Penang. Its jurisdiction covers about 306 square kilometres, the whole of Penang Island and nine surrounding islets. The island is mountainous down the middle, and the city centre lies on the largest coastal plain, at the north-eastern cape. Before the British arrived the cape was known as Tanjung Penaga after the penaga laut trees that grew there, and the city was named for King George III.

In 1771 Francis Light, a former Royal Navy captain, was instructed by the East India Company to establish trade relations in the Malay Peninsula. The sultan of Kedah, a Siamese vassal state threatened by the Bugis of Selangor, offered Penang Island in exchange for British military protection. Light saw it as a convenient magazine for trade that could check Dutch and French ambitions, and he established George Town as an entrepôt in 1786, the first British settlement in Southeast Asia. As a free port and a conduit for the spice trade it grew rapidly and drew trade from Dutch posts. During the Napoleonic Wars the British enlarged Fort Cornwallis against the threat of French invasion.

George Town became capital of the Straits Settlements in 1826 and lost that status to Singapore in 1832. Immigrants came from across Asia, and by the 1891 census about 68 per cent of its 51,627 people were ethnic Chinese. The Penang High Court was established in 1808 and Penang Free School, the oldest English school in Southeast Asia, in 1816. The first newspaper in Malaysia, the Prince of Wales Island Gazette, appeared there in 1806. After the Second World War the British dissolved the Straits Settlements in 1946, and the Penang Secessionist Committee formed in 1948 to resist merger with Malaya, fearing for the free port. George Town was declared a city shortly before independence in 1957, the first in the country.

At the 2020 census the city had 794,313 inhabitants and the wider conurbation 2,843,344. Malay, English, Hokkien, Mandarin and Tamil are in common use, and Penang Hokkien is the unofficial lingua franca. In 2008 UNESCO designated nearly 260 hectares of the city centre a World Heritage Site for its unique architectural and cultural townscape. The city is known for its street food and for the Chingay procession introduced in 1919.
george-tupou-i: George Tupou I, originally Tāufaʻāhau, was born on 4 December 1797 to Tupouto'a and Hoamofaleono. A series of civil wars in the 18th century had fractured Tonga. In 1820 he received a disputed inheritance of land in Haʻapai, and from this base he expanded his power to take in Vavaʻu, Tongatapu and other islands. He is regarded as the first king of modern Tonga.

Tupou gained control of Vavaʻu in 1833 and took nominal control of Tongatapu when he gained the title of Tu'i Kanokupolu in 1845. His rival Laufilitonga held the title of Tuʻi Tonga from 1827, and Tupou acquired it after Laufilitonga's death in 1865. In 1852 he combined the positions of sacred king, Tu'i Tonga, and secular chief, and became head of the Free Church of Tonga, which Reverend Shirley Waldemar Baker was chosen to administer. He called an assembly of chiefs for the first time in 1859; it drew up a law code issued in 1862. In 1865 he invited James Egan Moulton to Tonga to found Tupou College. In 1875 he promulgated the Constitution of Tonga, which formally made Tonga a constitutional monarchy.

In Fiji, Tupou first visited in 1842 and in 1853 met Seru Epenisa Cakobau, then appointed Enele Maʻafu and Lualala to administer the Tongans there. Maʻafu conquered Vanua Balavu in 1854, and Tupou defeated Cakobau's enemies at the Battle of Kaba in 1855. In 1859 William Thomas Pritchard forced Maʻafu to renounce his territorial claims. After the death of Tupou's heir Vuna in January 1862 Maʻafu took most of the Tongan warriors back to Tonga, and Tupou planned an invasion of Fiji that Pritchard persuaded him to abandon in April. Maʻafu controlled the northern and eastern parts of a Fijian confederacy formed in 1867, and when the parliament of Tonga gave up its claims to Fiji in 1869 he became a Fijian chief.

Tupou died in 1893 at the age of 95 and was buried in Malaʻekula. He was succeeded by his great-grandson George Tupou II. Charles St Julian, who advised him on constitutional development, was dismissed by Tupou, who preferred advice from officials in New Zealand, and St Julian then criticised him in an article in The Sydney Morning Herald, claiming that Tupou sought to conquer Samoa and Fiji.
george-v: George was born on 3 June 1865 at Marlborough House, London, the second son of Albert Edward, Prince of Wales, and Alexandra, a daughter of King Christian IX of Denmark. As a younger son he was not expected to become king. In 1877 he and his elder brother, Prince Albert Victor, joined the training ship HMS Britannia, and he served in the Royal Navy until 1892. Albert Victor's death in January 1892 made George second in line to the throne, and the next year he married his brother's former fiancée, Princess Victoria Mary of Teck. After his father became Edward VII in 1901, George was created Prince of Wales.

George became king on 6 May 1910. He insisted that his wife be called Queen Mary, and he objected to the anti-Catholic wording of the Accession Declaration, which Parliament shortened. The Parliament Act 1911 established the supremacy of the House of Commons.

He held a council on 4 August 1914 to declare war on Germany, whose Kaiser, Wilhelm II, was his first cousin. Because of anti-German feeling he changed the name of the royal house in 1917 from Saxe-Coburg and Gotha to Windsor. The monarchies of Russia, Austria-Hungary, Germany, Greece and Spain fell to war and revolution. On 22 June 1921, at the opening of the Parliament of Northern Ireland, he appealed for conciliation, and a truce followed within weeks. He appointed the first Labour ministry in 1924.

George was seriously injured in a fall from his horse in France in October 1915, and heavy smoking aggravated chronic bronchitis. After a serious illness in November 1928 he convalesced at Bognor, which later gained the suffix Regis. He took to his bedroom at Sandringham House on 15 January 1936 and died on 20 January; his eldest son succeeded him as Edward VIII.

He enjoyed stamp collecting and game shooting and lived a conventional life. The historian David Cannadine describes him and Queen Mary as an inseparably devoted couple who upheld character and family values. In a series of crises he acted as a force for neutrality and moderation, seeing his role as mediator rather than final decision maker.
george-v-of-hanover: George was born in Berlin on 27 May 1819, the only legitimate son of Prince Ernest Augustus, Duke of Cumberland, a son of George III, and Princess Frederica of Mecklenburg-Strelitz. He spent his childhood in Berlin and in Great Britain. He lost the sight of one eye after an illness in 1828 and of the other after an accident in 1833.

When Queen Victoria succeeded to the British throne in 1837, the personal union of Britain and Hanover ended because Hanover's semi-Salic law barred a woman, and George became Crown Prince of Hanover. Because he was totally blind there were doubts about his fitness, but his father decided that he should succeed. He married Princess Marie of Saxe-Altenburg on 18 February 1843.

George succeeded his father on 18 November 1851. From his father and his uncle Duke Charles of Mecklenburg he had learned a high and autocratic view of royal authority, and during his fifteen years as king he often quarrelled with the Hanoverian Landtag. Unlike his father he disliked Prussia, which bordered Hanover on the west and east, and he generally supported Austria in the Diet of the German Confederation. He supported industry: in 1856 a company named after him and his wife founded an iron and steel works that gave the city Georgsmarienhütte its name.

In June 1866 Prussia demanded an alliance and the submission of Hanoverian troops. Against the wishes of his parliament George refused and joined the Austrian side. The Hanoverian army of 20,600 men, though tactically successful at the Battle of Langensalza, was hopelessly outnumbered and surrendered on 29 June 1866. Prussia annexed Hanover on 20 September 1866. George rejected an abdication in favour of his son proposed by Queen Marie.

George went into exile in Austria and never renounced his rights or accepted the annexation. From 1866 to 1870 he maintained the Guelphic Legion, partly at his own expense, hoping a Franco-Prussian war would restore his kingdom. Prussia then confiscated his private assets, which Otto von Bismarck had managed as the Guelph Fund against Guelph activities. He was made honorary general in the British Army in 1876 and died in Paris on 12 June 1878. He was buried in St George's Chapel at Windsor Castle.
george-vi: George VI was born Albert Frederick Arthur George on 14 December 1895 at York Cottage on the Sandringham Estate, the second son of Prince George, Duke of York, later King George V. Queen Victoria was told that the child had been born on the anniversary of the death of Prince Albert and was won over by the proposal to name him Albert. He was known in the family as Bertie. As second son he was not expected to inherit the throne.

He attended the Royal Naval College, Osborne, from 1909 and served as a turret officer on HMS Collingwood at the Battle of Jutland, where he was mentioned in dispatches. Later he transferred to the Royal Air Force and became the first member of the British royal family certified as a fully qualified pilot. He was made Duke of York in 1920 and married Lady Elizabeth Bowes-Lyon on 26 April 1923 at Westminster Abbey.

George V died on 20 January 1936 and Edward VIII abdicated on 11 December 1936 to marry Wallis Simpson, after the prime minister, Stanley Baldwin, advised that he could not remain king and marry a woman with two living ex-husbands. Albert accepted the throne reluctantly, writing in his diary that he broke down and sobbed like a child when he told his mother. He took the name George VI to emphasise continuity with his father and restore confidence in the monarchy. His first act was to make Edward Duke of Windsor, and he was forced to buy Balmoral Castle and Sandringham House from him. The coronation took place at Westminster Abbey on 12 May 1937, and no Durbar was held in Delhi.

After the invasion of Poland in September 1939 the United Kingdom and the Dominions other than Ireland declared war on Nazi Germany. The King and Queen resolved to stay in London despite the bombing. Two German bombs exploded in a courtyard at Buckingham Palace on 13 September 1940 while they were there, and the family was portrayed as sharing the dangers and rationing of the rest of the country. George VI became known as a symbol of British determination to win the war. The empire declined after 1945, with the independence of India and Pakistan in 1947, and he relinquished the title of Emperor of India in June 1948 and became the first Head of the Commonwealth after the London Declaration of 1949.

Smoking-related health problems troubled the later years of his reign. George VI died at Sandringham House on 6 February 1952, aged 56, of a coronary thrombosis, and was succeeded by his elder daughter, Elizabeth II. He had engaged the speech therapist Lionel Logue in the mid-1920s to treat a stutter, which he learned to manage to some degree.
george-viii-of-georgia: George was the third son of Alexander I of Georgia and his second wife Tamar, daughter of Alexander I of Imereti. In 1433 his father, seeking to strengthen the crown against the great lords, named his four sons Vakhtang, Demetrius, George and Zaal co-rulers. After Alexander's abdication in 1442 Vakhtang IV became King of Kings, and George governed Kakheti, Hereti and neighbouring lands under him with the title of mtavari, prince. On Vakhtang's death in 1446 he took the throne and drove his elder brother Demetrius into exile.

Although sovereign in name over the whole realm, George held real power only in Kartli. In Samtskhe the atabeg Qvarqvare II Jaqeli overthrew his brother Aghbugha II in 1447, seized Vardzia and royal estates, and proclaimed a separate church. George restored Shirvan to tribute after besieging Qabala, while in 1456 Uzun Hasan of the Aq Qoyunlu ravaged Somkhiti and Kartli. He did not intervene when Constantinople fell in 1453 or Trebizond in 1461.

After the papal nuncio Ludovico da Bologna reached Georgia in 1456, George corresponded from 1459 with Pope Pius II, the Doge Pasquale Malipiero and Duke Philip III of Burgundy about a crusade against the Ottomans, but European states held back. His cousin Bagrat, whom he had made Duke of Samokalako in 1455, then rebelled with the backing of Samtskhe, Mingrelia, Guria, Abkhazia and Svaneti. While George was occupied in Samtskhe, Uzun Hasan's generals defeated the Georgian army and laid waste to eastern Georgia.

Held by the atabeg until early 1466, George was deposed when Bagrat was crowned King of Georgia as Bagrat VI that February. He won his freedom by promising to pardon Samtskhe, guarantee its autonomy and give up his claims in the west, and was crowned King of Kakheti at the Bodbe Monastery. Allied with the peasantry, the lesser nobility and, from about 1467, with Bagrat against Constantine, he secured recognition of Kakheti as a kingdom. His reforms there curbed the nobles and brought a long peace. The Georgian Chronicles confuse his reign, and the division of the kingdom was formally recognised only in 1490.
george-washington: George Washington was born on 22 February 1732 (11 February 1731 in the old style calendar) at Popes Creek in Westmoreland County, Virginia, the first of six children of Augustine and Mary Ball Washington. When his father died in 1743 he inherited Ferry Farm and ten slaves, while his half-brother Lawrence inherited the estate renamed Mount Vernon. Without the formal schooling his half-brothers had in England, he learned mathematics and land surveying and became a talented draftsman and mapmaker.

Lawrence's service as adjutant general of the Virginia militia inspired him to seek a commission. His report was published in Virginia and London. On 6 January 1759 he married Martha Dandridge Custis, a wealthy widow, and became one of the wealthiest men in Virginia.

After the war began with Lexington and Concord on 19 April 1775, the Second Continental Congress created the Continental Army on 14 June, and John Adams nominated Washington as its commander-in-chief. He led a poorly organised force against disciplined British troops. He won at Boston in March 1776 but was forced to retreat from New York City in November. He crossed the Delaware River and won at Trenton in late 1776 and Princeton in early 1777, then lost at Brandywine and Germantown. In 1781 he led a combined French and American force to a decisive victory at Yorktown, and the Treaty of Paris of 1783 recognised American independence.

He presided over the Constitutional Convention of 1787. Elected unanimously by the Electoral College in 1789 and 1792, he was inaugurated on 30 April 1789 at Federal Hall in New York City. President against grander styles proposed by the Senate. He stayed neutral in the rivalry between Thomas Jefferson and Alexander Hamilton in his cabinet, and adopted neutrality during the French Revolution while supporting the Jay Treaty with Britain.

Washington's farewell address of 1796 stressed national unity and the dangers of regionalism, partisanship and foreign influence. In 1798 President Adams made him commanding general of the army during the Quasi-War, though he did not take the field. He died on 14 December 1799, and Henry Lee III eulogised him as first in war, first in peace and first in the hearts of his countrymen.

At least 577 slaves lived and worked at Mount Vernon during his lifetime. From the 1760s he gradually grew to oppose slavery, partly because his shift from tobacco to grain left him with a costly surplus of slaves, and in a letter of 1778 he wrote of his desire to get quit of Negroes. His will provided for the eventual manumission of his slaves.
george-washington-goethals: Goethals was born in Brooklyn, New York, on 29 June 1858, to Flemish immigrants from Stekene in Belgium, the carpenter John Louis Goethals and Marie Le Barron. After three years at the College of the City of New York he entered the United States Military Academy at West Point in 1876 and graduated second in his class of 52 in June 1880, commissioned in the Corps of Engineers. He taught civil and military engineering at West Point from 1885 to 1889, where he tutored Charles Young, the third African-American graduate of the academy.

His first independent command was the completion of the Muscle Shoals Canal on the Tennessee River near Florence, Alabama. There he persuaded doubtful superiors to accept a single lock with a lift of twenty-six feet, the Riverton Lock, which set a world record and encouraged high-lift locks elsewhere, including Panama. He served as chief of engineers of the United States Volunteers in the Spanish-American War and joined the first Army General Staff in 1903.

After the chief engineers John Findley Wallace and John Frank Stevens had resigned in turn, President Theodore Roosevelt decided that army engineers should build the canal, and in February 1907 appointed Goethals, whom Secretary of War William Howard Taft had recommended. The canal was finished two years ahead of its target date of 10 June 1916. Congress thanked him and promoted him to major general, and with William Crawford Gorgas he received the first Public Welfare Medal of the National Academy of Sciences. President Wilson then made him the first civil governor of the Canal Zone.

In the First World War, after supply blunders in the winter of 1917, he became Acting Quartermaster General on 19 December 1917, reorganised the corps along functional lines and from April 1918 directed the new Purchase, Storage and Traffic Division, which took control of army purchasing, storage and transport.

He retired on 1 March 1919, headed an engineering firm and became the first consulting engineer of the Port of New York Authority, whose Goethals Bridge between Staten Island and Elizabeth, New Jersey, bears his name. He died of lung cancer at his apartment in Manhattan on 21 January 1928 and was buried at West Point. A monument to him was built in Panama City in 1954.
george-washington-williams: Williams was born free on 16 October 1849 in Bedford Springs, Pennsylvania, the eldest of four sons of Thomas Williams, a labourer, and Ellen Rouse Williams. He had little schooling and learned barbering in a house of refuge. At 14 he ran away to join the Union Army under an assumed name and fought in the last battles of the Civil War. He then went to Mexico, where he served as a lieutenant in the Republican Army under General Espinosa against Emperor Maximilian.

Back in the United States in 1867, he re-enlisted and served with the 10th Cavalry, the Buffalo Soldiers, in the Indian Territory until a lung wound in 1868 ended his service. After a short time at Howard University he entered the Newton Theological Institution near Boston in 1870, and in 1874 became its first African American graduate. He married Sarah A. Sterrett that spring; they had one son.

Ordained a Baptist minister, Williams held pastorates including the Twelfth Baptist Church of Boston and in Washington, DC, where with the support of Frederick Douglass and William Lloyd Garrison he founded a weekly journal, The Commoner, which ran to eight issues. In Cincinnati he read law under Alphonso Taft and passed the bar. In 1880 he became the first African American elected to the Ohio legislature, but a bill on a Black church's burial ground cost him re-election after one term. President Chester A. Arthur's nomination of him as minister to Haiti in 1885 was not confirmed.

His History of the Negro Race in America 1619–1880 appeared in 1882 and is considered the first overall history of African Americans; in it he used the phrase crime against humanity of slavery. He also wrote a history of Black troops in the Civil War.

Writing for S. S. McClure's Associated Literary Press, Williams met Leopold II in 1889 and was at first impressed. In the Congo in 1890 he found forced rubber production, mutilation and many deaths, and on 18 July 1890 he wrote his open letter from Stanley Falls, naming Henry M. Stanley's part and calling for an international commission. The king's side tried to discredit him. Taken ill in Cairo on his way home, he died of tuberculosis and pleurisy in Blackpool on 2 August 1891 and was buried in Layton Cemetery, where a tombstone was placed in 1975.
george-william-duke-of-brunswick-lunebur: George William was born on 26 January 1624 at Herzberg am Harz, the second son of George, Prince of Calenberg. Among his sisters was Queen Sophia Amalie of Denmark. In 1648, when his elder brother Christian Louis inherited the Principality of Lüneburg from their uncle Frederick IV, he gave Calenberg to George William as an appanage. In 1658, to be freed from his engagement to Princess Sophia of the Palatinate, George William gave up his claim on Lüneburg to his youngest brother Ernest Augustus, who married Sophia, and promised to stay unmarried and to hold only Celle for his lifetime.

On the death of Christian Louis in 1665 George William took Celle and gave Calenberg to his brother John Frederick. The same year he entered a morganatic marriage with his long-time mistress Eleanor, Countess of Wilhelmsburg, and their only child, Sophia Dorothea, was born in 1666. In 1676, breaking his promise, he legitimised her and declared the marriage valid in church and state, which alarmed his relatives, who feared for the planned union of the Lüneburg lands. In 1682 Ernest Augustus and Sophia agreed to their son George Louis marrying Sophia Dorothea; their son, born the next year, became George II of Great Britain.

From 1675 to 1676, in the Swedish-Brandenburg War, he commanded the allied forces against Sweden in the campaign against Bremen-Verden. When Julius Francis, Duke of Saxe-Lauenburg, died in 1689 leaving only daughters, George William, one of the senior male-line claimants, occupied the duchy with his troops. Of the other claimants only Christian V of Denmark, his sister's son, took up arms, and by the Hamburg Comparison of 9 October 1693 the two agreed that George William would keep Saxe-Lauenburg in personal union.

George William died at Wienhausen on 28 August 1705, aged 81, and Celle and Saxe-Lauenburg passed to his nephew and son-in-law George Louis. Emperor Leopold I had held the Lauenburg exclave of Hadeln in imperial custody; in 1728 Emperor Charles VI enfeoffed George II with Saxe-Lauenburg, and Hadeln followed in 1731.
george-william-duke-of-legnica: George William was the only surviving son of Duke Christian of Legnica-Brzeg and Louise, daughter of Prince John Casimir of Anhalt-Dessau. His grandfather, Duke John Christian of Brieg, had fallen out of favour with Emperor Ferdinand II, and Christian spent years in exile in Poland and the Duchy of Prussia during the Thirty Years' War. When Christian stood for the Polish throne after the abdication of John II Casimir Vasa in 1668, he saw to it that his son spoke Polish and wore Polish clothes.

The deaths of his uncles George III of Brzeg and Louis IV of Legnica in 1663 and 1664 left George William the only heir to the still large Duchy of Legnica-Brzeg, and he was carefully educated: he learned German, French and Latin, understood Italian, Spanish and Polish, and studied theology, philosophy and rhetoric.

George William succeeded his father at twelve in 1672, under his mother's regency. Fearing the claims of Emperor Leopold I as king of Bohemia, Christian had placed his son under the tutelage of Prince John George II of Anhalt-Dessau and Elector Frederick William of Brandenburg, and Louise sent the boy to the Viadrina University in Frankfurt on the Oder. Her open support for the Catholic faith set the Protestant estates against her. In 1673 George William received the estates' homage at Brzeg, and on 14 March 1675, after doing homage to Leopold I in Vienna, he took up the government himself.

He died on 21 November 1675 of a fever, the first sign of smallpox, that began soon after a hunt, and was buried in the church of St. John in Legnica, where his mother built a mausoleum. Leopold I took over the duchy through a deputy, despite the claims of Count August of Legnica, and introduced Counter-Reformation measures. The Piast line ended with the death of his sister Karolina in 1707, and his crypt names him the last of the Piast dukes of Silesia.
george-william-elector-of-brandenburg: George William was born on 13 November 1595 in Cölln on the Spree, today part of Berlin, a member of the Hohenzollern dynasty. He was the son of John Sigismund, Elector of Brandenburg, and Anna of Prussia, and his maternal grandfather was Albert Frederick, Duke of Prussia. In 1616 he married Elisabeth Charlotte of the Palatinate. Their only son, Frederick William, later became known as the Great Elector. The elder of their two daughters, Louise Charlotte, married Jacob Kettler, Duke of Courland, and the younger, Hedwig Sophie, married William VI, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel.

In 1619 George William inherited the Margravate of Brandenburg and the Duchy of Prussia, then a vassal of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, although Sigismund III Vasa did not confirm his ownership until September 1621. Possession of Prussia involved him in the Polish-Swedish War of 1621 to 1625, since Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden was married to his sister Maria Eleonora. During the Thirty Years' War the Calvinist elector tried to stay neutral between the Catholic Emperor Ferdinand II and his mostly Lutheran opponents. When the war shifted to northern Germany in 1625 this did not protect his lands from looting by imperial troops.

He was forced to take sides when Gustavus intervened in the Empire in 1630, but this replaced one set of plunderers with another, as Gustavus could not support so large an army and his unpaid troops became mutinous. After Gustavus was killed at Lützen in November 1632, George William joined the Swedish-backed Heilbronn League, until the defeat at Nördlingen on 6 September 1634. The League was dissolved after the Peace of Prague of 1635, by which time the population of Brandenburg had been decimated by the war.

Leaving his Catholic and pro-imperial chief minister Schwarzenberg to run the government, George William withdrew late in his reign to the relatively untouched region of Prussia. He lived in retirement there until his death at Königsberg on 1 December 1640. He was succeeded by his son Frederick William, who was far more accomplished.
george-xi-of-kartli: George was the son of Vakhtang V, ruler of Kartli, and his first wife, Princess Rodam Qaplanishvili-Orbeliani. Like many Georgian rulers he had to accept Islam nominally and take the name Shahnawaz II before Shah Solayman I would confirm him as viceroy. He married first Tamar, a daughter of Prince David Davitishvili, and in 1687 Khoreshan, a daughter of the Imeretian Prince George Mikeladze.

After nearly half a century of peace with Persia, relations worsened, and George tried to centralise royal authority and weaken Persian influence. He patronised Catholic missionaries, and after the Ottoman defeat at Vienna he wrote to Pope Innocent XI on 29 April 1687 vowing to be a Catholic king. In 1688 he led a failed coup against the Persian governor of Kakheti and sought Ottoman support in vain, and Shah Solayman gave his crown to the Kakhetian prince Erekle I. George fled to Racha in western Georgia and made several attempts to return, helping his brother Archil II regain the crown of Imereti for a time.

Strife in Georgia and across the Safavid empire led Shah Soltan Hosayn to make peace with him in 1696. Appointed beglarbeg of Kerman in 1699, George restored the shah's authority there by 1700 with his brother Levan, and in 1703 was restored as king of Kartli, though not allowed to go home; his nephew, the future Vakhtang VI, governed Kartli in his place. In 1704 he was sent against the Afghan rebellion as viceroy of Kandahar and commander-in-chief of the Persian armies.

He put down the Afghan revolts and ruled with uncompromising severity, sending the Ghilji chieftain Mirwais Hotak in chains to Isfahan. Mirwais won the shah's favour, returned and planned a coup. On 21 April 1709, while most of the Georgian troops were away on a raid, he invited George to a banquet at his estate at Kokaron and had him killed, and his small escort was massacred. Mirwais sent the cross and psalms found on him to Isfahan as proof of his covert defection; Catholic missionaries held that he died a faithful Catholic. A punitive expedition under his nephew Kaikhosro ended in October 1711 with the destruction of nearly all its 30,000 men.
george-xii-of-georgia: George was the son of King Heraclius II and his second wife, Queen Anna, a daughter of the prince Zaal Abashidze. His mother died in December 1749, when he was three, and his elder half-brother Vakhtang, the presumptive heir, died in February 1756, which made George the heir. He was named heir to the throne of the two Georgias in 1766 and received territories in southern Georgia, populated largely by Armenians and Turkmens.

He governed the Armenian province of Pambak and tried to repopulate it. In April 1770 he fought beside his father against the Ottomans and led the left flank at the Battle of Aspindza on 20 April. The Treaty of Georgievsk of 24 July 1783 placed Georgia under Russian protection and recognised him as heir.

Two days after Heraclius died he was recognised as King of Kartli-Kakheti on 14 January 1798, at Kazakh. He had to sign a decree naming his half-brother Iulon as heir, hoping to replace it with one for his eldest son David. His stepmother, Queen Dowager Darejan, and her sons opposed him, and the court divided between supporters of Russia and those who feared it.

In 1798 he considered an Ottoman protectorate, which brought Russia to meet his diplomats' demands, and Lezgin raiders ravaged Kakheti from July to September. Persia under Fath-Ali Shah demanded his submission, and in April 1800 an army of 10,000 gathered under Abbas Mirza. On 7 September 1799 George instructed his envoys to offer Georgia to Russia on the status of a Russian province, if his house kept the crown.

Illness and suspicion marked his last years. He suffered from edemas and feared assassination, and a reform plan presented by his son Ioane on 10 May 1799 could not be carried out. Emperor Paul I secretly ordered General Knorring to secure annexation after George's death. George died on 28 December 1800 without learning that Paul had signed the decree incorporating Kartli-Kakheti into the Russian Empire.

Historians have judged him a poor monarch who could not meet his kingdom's crises, and Donald Rayfield has argued that a more capable successor to Heraclius might have kept Georgia united. David Marshall Lang wrote that he lacked the qualities to lead in his situation. His descendants were regarded by part of the Georgian nobility as heirs to the throne, and in 1865 a great-grandson received the title Prince Gruzinsky from the Russian government.
georges-bidault: Georges Bidault was born in Moulins, Allier, on 5 October 1899. He studied at the Sorbonne and became a history teacher. In 1932 he helped found the Catholic Association of French Youth and the left-wing anti-fascist newspaper l'Aube, for which he wrote a column and protested against the Munich Agreement in 1938. In the Second World War he joined the army, was captured in the Fall of France and held briefly. After his release in July 1941 he taught at the Lycée du Parc in Lyon and joined the Liberté group of the Resistance, which merged with Combat. Jean Moulin recruited him to organise a covert press and the Combat newspaper.

Bidault took part in forming the National Council of the Resistance and became its president after the Gestapo captured Moulin. In 1944 he drew up a Resistance Charter recommending an extensive programme of post-war reform. After the liberation of Paris he represented the Resistance in the victory parade, and on 25 August Charles de Gaulle appointed him foreign minister of the provisional government. He initiated the Popular Republican Movement (MRP). From April to June 1945 he led the French delegation to the San Francisco Conference that founded the UN, where France gained a permanent seat on the Security Council.

On 19 June 1946 the National Constituent Assembly elected him president of the provisional government. His coalition of socialists, communists and the MRP passed pension and workmen's compensation laws, and an act of 22 August 1946 extended family allowances to practically the whole population. He resigned after the elections of 29 November, and Léon Blum succeeded him. He was later foreign minister under Paul Ramadier and Robert Schuman, and in April 1947 endorsed Ramadier's decision to expel the Communists from the government. In 1949 he was premier again, but his government lasted only eight months. He was foreign minister during the siege of Dien Bien Phu in 1954.

In 1961 Bidault became president of the Executive Council of the Rally for French Algeria and opposed de Gaulle's policy of Algerian independence. He established a National Resistance Council within the far-right paramilitary Organisation armée secrète, although in his memoirs he said he was never involved with it. In June 1962 he was accused of conspiring against the state and lost his parliamentary immunity. He went into exile in Brazil, moved to Belgium in 1967 and returned to France in 1968 under an amnesty. He died of a stroke at Cambo-les-Bains in January 1983.
georges-clemenceau: Georges Benjamin Clemenceau was born on 28 September 1841 in Mouilleron-en-Pareds in the Vendée, a remote, rural and poor department. His father, Benjamin Clemenceau, came from a line of physicians but lived off his lands, was a political activist and was arrested in 1851 and 1858. He instilled in his son a love of learning, devotion to radical politics and a hatred of Catholicism. In Paris the young Clemenceau co-founded a weekly, Le Travail, in 1861 and was held for 77 days in Mazas Prison in 1862 after posting notices calling a demonstration. He qualified as a doctor of medicine on 13 May 1865, and in 1869 he married Mary Eliza Plummer in New York City.

After the defeat at Sedan in 1870 Clemenceau became mayor of the 18th arrondissement of Paris and was elected to the National Assembly. When the Paris Commune seized power in March 1871 he tried without success to find a compromise between its leaders and the government. From 1876 he sat in the Chamber of Deputies for the 18th arrondissement, and his energy and cutting eloquence made him leader of the radicals. After his defeat in 1893 he confined himself for nearly a decade to journalism. On 13 January 1898 he published Émile Zola's J'Accuse...! on the front page of L'Aurore, which he owned and edited, and during the Dreyfus Affair he published 665 articles defending Dreyfus.

In 1906 he became Minister of the Interior, reformed the police, supported scientific policing under Alphonse Bertillon and founded the mobile squads nicknamed the Tiger's Brigades. After the war began, his newspaper was censored and, renamed L'Homme enchaîné, criticised the government's lack of transparency while defending the union sacrée. In November 1917, at one of the darkest hours of the war, he became prime minister, governing from the Ministry of War and discouraging internal disagreement. His government passed a general eight-hour day law in April 1919, extended to all classes of workers by later measures.

At the Paris Peace Conference Clemenceau sought the Rhine as France's frontier and was under strong pressure to make Germany's reparations bill large. On 19 February 1919 the anarchist Émile Cottin fired on his car, and a bullet that stayed in his body for the rest of his life struck him between the ribs. The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919, and he defended it in the French Parliament against critics who thought its compromises inadequate. He resigned as prime minister after the presidential election of 17 January 1920 and took no further part in politics.
He was a long-time friend of Claude Monet and persuaded him to complete his donation of the Water Lilies paintings to the French state. He died on 24 November 1929.
georges-danton: Georges Jacques Danton was born on 26 October 1759 in Arcis-sur-Aube, in Champagne, to Jacques Danton, a respectable but not wealthy lawyer, and Madeleine Camus. At thirteen he entered the seminary in Troyes and then a boarding school nearby. He settled in Paris in 1780 as a clerk, passed the barrister examination at Reims in 1783, and in 1787 became a prosecutor. That year he married Antoinette Gabrielle Charpentier, and the couple lived on the Left Bank near the Café Procope.

In the spring of 1789 Danton spoke to crowds at the Palais Royal, and his powerful voice earned him the nickname The Thunderer. He led the militia of the Cordeliers district and in 1790 became president of the Club de Cordeliers. After the monarchy was suspended in August 1792, the Girondin ministers wanted a man committed to the insurgents, and Danton was made Minister of Justice on 10 August. His part in the September Massacres has long been disputed. Against the invading armies he called for daring, and yet more daring.

In 1793 his wife died on 10 February while he was on a mission in Belgium. He supported the Revolutionary Tribunal in March and was among the first members of the Committee of Public Safety, installed on 6 April.
