In March 1793 the National Convention sent him to Leuven to investigate General Dumouriez. On 1 June he urged the Convention to break up the Commission of Twelve. He declined to rejoin the committee in September and withdrew to Arcis-sur-Aube in October.

Returning to Paris in November 1793, Danton attacked religious persecution and called for clemency, and a group called the Indulgents formed around him. Robespierre answered his plea for an end to the Terror on 25 December. He was accused of financial misdeeds, above all involvement in the scandal over the liquidation of the French East India Company, though no hard evidence against him is recorded. On 30 March 1794 two committees decided to arrest him, with Desmoulins and others. Tried from 3 to 5 April before the Revolutionary Tribunal, he was guillotined on 5 April 1794.

Historians have long disagreed about him. Thiers and Mignet saw a gigantic revolutionary, Lamartine a man without principles, and Robinet a generous patriot. He left little writing, so most evidence is secondhand. Georg Büchner made his last days the subject of the play Dantons Tod.
georges-de-la-tour: Georges de La Tour was born on 13 March 1593 in Vic-sur-Seille, in the Diocese of Metz, a town technically part of the Holy Roman Empire but ruled by France since 1552. Baptism records show that he was the son of Jean de La Tour, a baker, and Sybille de La Tour, née Molian, and the second of seven children. His education is unclear. It is assumed that he travelled early in his career to Italy or the Netherlands, and he may have trained under Jacques Bellange in Nancy.

His paintings reflect the naturalism of Caravaggio, which probably reached him through the Dutch Caravaggisti of the Utrecht School, and he is often compared to Hendrick Terbrugghen. In 1617 he married Diane Le Nerf, from a minor noble family, and in 1620 he set up a studio in her home town of Lunéville in the Duchy of Lorraine.

La Tour worked for the Dukes of Lorraine in 1623–4 and received the title Painter to the King of France in 1638, but the local bourgeoisie were his main market and he achieved a certain affluence. He is not recorded in Lunéville between 1639 and 1642 and may have travelled again, and Anthony Blunt saw the influence of Gerrit van Honthorst in his work afterwards. He took part in a Franciscan-led religious revival in Lorraine and came to paint almost entirely religious subjects, treated with the influence of genre painting.

His early work includes genre scenes of cheats, as in The Fortune Teller, and fighting beggars, derived from the Dutch Caravaggisti and probably from Bellange. He often painted several versions of one subject, and his surviving output is relatively small.

La Tour is best known for nocturnal light effects, developed further than his predecessors had done, and carried from the genre subjects of the Dutch Caravaggisti into religious painting. Unlike Caravaggio, his religious paintings lack dramatic effects. In a second phase of his style, perhaps from the 1640s, he used chiaroscuro, careful geometrical compositions and very simplified forms, and his work moved towards greater simplicity and stillness.

His son Étienne, born in 1621, was his pupil, and it is difficult to tell their hands apart in versions of La Tour's compositions, as with the Education of the Virgin in the Frick Collection. La Tour and his family died in an epidemic in Lunéville in 1652. He was forgotten after his death, and some of his work was confused with that of Vermeer. The German art historian Hermann Voss rediscovered him in 1915, and he later inspired writers such as René Char, André Malraux, Pascal Quignard and Charles Juliet.
georges-eugene-haussmann: Georges-Eugène Haussmann was born on 27 March 1809 in the Beaujon neighbourhood of Paris, the son of Nicolas-Valentin Haussmann and Ève-Marie-Henriette-Caroline Dentzel, both of Alsatian families. His maternal grandfather, Georges Frédéric Dentzel, was a general and a baron of Napoleon's First Empire. He studied law and also music at the Paris Conservatory, and joined his father as an insurgent in the July Revolution of 1830.

From 1831 he served in public administration as a deputy prefect at several posts, but his arrogance, dictatorial manner and habit of impeding his superiors kept him from promotion. He was later a prefect in Var, Yonne and Gironde, and in 1853 Emperor Napoleon III appointed him in Paris.

Napoleon III and Haussmann launched public works that hired tens of thousands of workers to improve the city's sanitation, water supply and traffic circulation. The boulevard system was planned partly to let troops and artillery move easily, but its main purpose was to relieve congestion and link landmark buildings. A decree annexed eleven surrounding communes and raised the arrondissements from twelve to twenty.

The engineer Eugène Belgrand built an aqueduct from the Vanne River, raising the water supply from 87,000 to 400,000 cubic metres a day. The sewers were rebuilt, and gas pipes served thousands of new streetlights. With Adolphe Alphand he laid out four major parks, the Bois de Boulogne, the Bois de Vincennes, the Parc des Buttes Chaumont and the Parc Montsouris. By his own estimate one in five streets in central Paris was his creation by 1870. He became a senator in 1857 and took the title baron, which was never officially sanctioned.

Opposition grew as the Empire liberalised from 1860. Costs of expropriation rose from 70 million francs to about 230 million, and in 1858 the Cour des Comptes ruled that the fund for the works was making illegal disguised loans. In 1867 Jules Ferry mocked his accounts as Les Comptes fantastiques de Haussmann. Critics forced his dismissal in 1870. He died in Paris on 11 January 1891, aged 81. Boulevard Haussmann and the Haussmann-Saint-Lazare station bear his name.
georges-lemaitre: Georges Henri Joseph Édouard Lemaître was born on 17 July 1894 in Charleroi, Belgium, the eldest of four children of an industrialist who owned a glassworks. He attended Jesuit schools and in 1911 began studying engineering at the Catholic University of Louvain. In the First World War he volunteered for the Belgian army, fought in the Battle of the Yser and received the Belgian War Cross. Afterwards he turned to physics and mathematics, took his doctorate in 1920 and prepared for the priesthood. He was ordained on 22 September 1923 by Cardinal Mercier, who supported his scientific work.

Lemaître spent 1923 to 1924 at Cambridge with Arthur Eddington and the next year at the Harvard College Observatory with Harlow Shapley. In 1927 he published a report arguing, independently of Alexander Friedmann, that the equations of general relativity implied a universe that is not static, and linking this to a proportional relation between the recession velocity of galaxies and their distance. It had little impact because the journal was little read, and Einstein is reported to have said his calculations were correct but his physics abominable. Edwin Hubble published better data in 1929, and in 2018 the International Astronomical Union recommended the name Hubble-Lemaître law.

In 1931 Lemaître proposed that the universe expanded from a single initial quantum, which he called the primeval atom, now regarded as the first formulation of the Big Bang theory. With Manuel Sandoval Vallarta he showed that cosmic rays are charged particles deflected by the Earth's magnetic field. He argued throughout his career for a positive cosmological constant and was an early user of computers in physics.

Lemaître held that science and religion were not in conflict but should not be mixed. He was professor of physics at Louvain from 1927 until he retired in 1964, and from 1960 president of the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, a post he held until his death. The Royal Astronomical Society gave him its first Eddington Medal in 1953. In 1965 he learned of the discovery of the cosmic microwave background, which convinced most experts of the Big Bang's validity. He died on 20 June 1966.
georges-thierry-dargenlieu: Georges Thierry d'Argenlieu was born in Brest on 7 August 1889 into a family of navy officers and entered the École navale at 17. As a midshipman on the Du Chayla he took part in the campaign in Morocco that led to the Treaty of Fez in 1912, received the Legion of Honour and befriended Hubert Lyautey. In the First World War he served in the Mediterranean, joined the Secular Order of Discalced Carmelites while on leave in Malta in 1915, was promoted lieutenant de vaisseau in 1917 and the next year distinguished himself commanding the patrol boat Tourterelle in the rescue of a troop transport.

After the war he studied theology at the Angelicum in Rome and in 1920 entered the Carmelite novitiate at Avon, taking the name Louis of the Trinity. Ordained a priest at Lille in 1925, he was elected Prior Provincial of the re-established province of Paris in 1935.

Mobilised as a reserve officer in September 1939, he was captured defending the arsenal of Cherbourg in the Battle of France, escaped from the prisoner train after three days and joined Charles de Gaulle on 30 June 1940. Meant to serve as a chaplain, he became a fighting officer by special permission of his superiors, since the Free French Naval Forces had few officers. He was badly wounded at Dakar on 23 September 1940, fired on in an unarmed boat while trying to win over the Vichy governor.

In November 1940 he directed operations in Gabon, and he became chancellor of the new Ordre de la Libération. He rose to counter admiral in 1941, and on 14 June 1944 he carried de Gaulle to France aboard the destroyer La Combattante. He reached Indochina on 31 October 1945 as High Commissioner.

On 23 November 1946 he ordered the French forces in Haiphong to make themselves complete master of the city, which led to the Haiphong Massacre, in which about 6,000 Vietnamese civilians were killed. As his actions grew more controversial he was replaced by Émile Bollaert in March 1947.

Back in France he served as inspector general of the naval forces before retiring to a monastery. Ill, he resigned as chancellor of the Ordre de la Libération in 1958 and returned to monastic life. He died in Brest on 7 September 1964 and was buried at Avrechy. His memoirs of the war and of Indochina were published in 1973 and 1985.
georgetown-guyana: Georgetown is on the east bank of the Demerara River estuary, on Guyana's Atlantic coast, in flat coastal plains. The city is surrounded by cane fields and marshy swamps, with savannah to the east and south. Its land lies as much as 2 metres below the high-tide level, and a retaining wall known as the seawall keeps the ocean out, while a network of canals with kokers, or sluices, built by the Dutch and later the British, drains the city. It is laid out in a north-south, east-west grid interlaced with these canals. It has a hot, trade-wind tropical rainforest climate, moderated by the north-east trade winds, and rarely sees temperatures above 31 degrees Celsius.

In 1748 Governor Laurens Storm van 's Gravesande built a guard post at the mouth of the Demerara River, and English planters later built houses around it, forming a small village. The town was established in 1782 during a brief French occupation of the Dutch colony of Demerara, under the name Longchamps. In 1784 the name was changed to Stabroek, after Nicholaas Geelvinck, Lord of Stabroek, then President of the Dutch West India Company. In 1789 the population was 780, of whom 239 were white, but the town grew quickly, reaching around 8,500 by 1807. American traders built a wharf that became known as American Stelling.

Under British rule the city took the name Georgetown in 1812, in honour of King George III. A ward one fourth of a mile broad and one mile long retains the name Stabroek. Georgetown gained official city status on 24 August 1842, in the reign of Queen Victoria. A large fire, the Great Fire, caused widespread damage in 1945.

Georgetown is the capital and largest city of Guyana, the seat of its government and the home of the Secretariat of the Caribbean Community, CARICOM. The 2022 census recorded 125,683 people. It is known for its colonial architecture, with many wooden buildings and markets. These include the tall painted-timber St. George's Anglican Cathedral, State House (built 1852), the neo-Gothic City Hall (1889), the Victoria Law Courts (1887), the Parliament Building (1829-1834) and Stabroek Market (1792), whose cast-iron clock tower dominates the skyline. The Georgetown Cenotaph, built in 1923, is the site of Remembrance Day services each November.
georgi-dimitrov: Georgi Dimitrov was born in Kovachevtsi, in what is now Pernik Province, the first of eight children of refugee parents from Ottoman Macedonia. His father was a rural craftsman who had been forced by industrialisation to become a factory worker. His mother, Parashkeva Doseva, was a Protestant Christian who wanted him to be a pastor, but he was expelled from Sunday school at age 12.

He trained as a compositor and became active in the labour movement in Sofia. By 1900 he was secretary of the Sofia branch of the printers' union. His brother Nikola joined the Bolsheviks, and Konstantin, a trade union leader, was killed in the First Balkan War in 1912.

Dimitrov joined the Bulgarian Social Democratic Workers' Party in 1902 and sided with the faction of Dimitar Blagoev, which in 1919 became the Bulgarian Communist Party. He was elected to parliament in 1913 and opposed the Balkan Wars and the First World War, for which he received prison sentences. In September 1923 he and Vasil Kolarov led a failed uprising against the government of Aleksandar Tsankov, which cost possibly five thousand lives among communist supporters, and he escaped into exile. A court sentenced him to death in absentia in 1926. From 1929 he headed the Central European section of the Comintern in Germany.

After the Reichstag fire on 27 February 1933 Dimitrov was arrested on 9 March. At the trial, which ran from September to December in Leipzig, he refused counsel and defended himself against Hermann Göring and the other Nazi accusers. On 23 December the court acquitted him and two other Bulgarians, Vasil Tanev and Blagoy Popov, for insufficient evidence, and they were expelled to the USSR. Dimitrov became the head of the Comintern, and the 7th World Congress of 1935 elected him General Secretary. In November 1937 Stalin told him to lure the German communist Willi Münzenberg to the USSR so that he could be arrested, and Dimitrov did not object.

Dimitrov returned to Bulgaria in 1946 after 22 years in exile and became prime minister after a referendum abolished the monarchy. In 1947 he signed the Bled accord with Josip Broz Tito, planning a federation of the Southern Slavs, but the plan fell apart over the future of the joint country and the Macedonian question, and it was abandoned after the Stalin and Tito split of 1948.

He died on 2 July 1949 at the Barvikha sanatorium near Moscow. Speculation that he had been poisoned has never been confirmed. His embalmed body lay in the Georgi Dimitrov Mausoleum in Sofia until 1990, when it was buried in the central cemetery, and the mausoleum was demolished in 1999.
georgian-orthodox-church: The Georgian Orthodox Church is an autocephalous Eastern Orthodox church in full communion with the other Orthodox churches. It asserts an apostolic foundation and traces its roots to the Christianization of Iberia and Colchis, in modern eastern and western Georgia, by the apostle Andrew in the 1st century and by Saint Nino in the 4th. Modern historians consider the Andrew account mythical, the product of a late tradition from 9th-century Byzantine legends. In the 4th and 5th centuries the Church of Iberia was strictly subordinate to Antioch, where its bishops were consecrated, and around 480 the Byzantine government recognised its chief prelate as a catholicos instead of an archbishop.

Between the 11th and early 13th centuries the Bagrationi dynasty united western and eastern Georgia in one kingdom, relying on the church's prestige and granting it tax immunity and large appanages. In 1103 King David the Builder convened the council of Ruisi-Urbnisi, which condemned Armenian Miaphysitism more strongly than before. Georgian monasticism began in the 6th century with the Thirteen Assyrian Fathers, who founded David Gareja, and its golden age lasted from the 9th to the 11th century, with monasteries abroad such as Iviron on Mount Athos.

The Mongol invasions of the 13th century and Tamerlane's in the 14th and 15th gravely disrupted Georgian Christianity. In the west the Catholicate of Abkhazia emerged under the kings of Imereti and lasted until 1795. After the Russian Empire annexed Kartl-Kakheti in 1801, its authorities abolished the church's autocephaly on 18 July 1811 and replaced the Georgian liturgy with Church Slavonic. On 25 January 1990 the Patriarch of Constantinople recognised autocephaly again.

The church is governed by the Holy Synod, the body of bishops, headed by the Catholicos-Patriarch of All Georgia. The first head of the church to carry the title of patriarch was Melkisedek I, from 1010 to 1033. Eastern Orthodoxy was the state religion for most of Georgia's history until 1921, when Soviet forces occupied the country. The constitution recognises the church's special role in Georgia's history and states its independence from the state, and relations are further regulated by the Concordat of 2002.
georgians: Georgians call themselves Kartveli, their land Sakartvelo and their language Kartuli. The Greeks and Romans knew western Georgians as Colchians and eastern Georgians as Iberians. Most historians agree that the ancestors of modern Georgians lived in the southern Caucasus and northern Anatolia from the Neolithic. Western tribes established the kingdom of Colchis, dated to about 1350 BCE, and eastern tribes formed their kingdom in the 7th century BCE. Between the 6th and 4th centuries BCE, Kartlian tribes consolidated around Mtskheta and founded the Kingdom of Kartli, or Iberia, under Pharnavaz I. By the mid-4th century both Lazica and Iberia were officially Christian.

Arabs invaded south-eastern Georgia in 645. The Bagrationi dynasty rose in the 9th century, and Bagrat III, supported by David III of Tao, was crowned first king of a unified Georgia in 1008. Under David IV (r. 1089–1125), who defeated Turkish forces at the Battle of Didgori in 1121, and Tamar (r. 1184–1213), Georgia reached its height, commonly called the Georgian Golden Age. Jalal ad-Din captured Tbilisi in 1226, and the Mongol invasions followed. The kingdom collapsed into anarchy by 1466 and split into three kingdoms and five principalities.

In 1783 the Treaty of Georgievsk made eastern Georgia a Russian protectorate under Heraclius II. Russia annexed eastern Georgia in 1801, abolished the Bagrationi dynasty and ended the autocephaly of the Georgian Orthodox Church. Georgia declared the Democratic Republic of Georgia on 26 May 1918, and the Red Army occupied it in February 1921. The Supreme Council declared independence from the Soviet Union on 9 April 1991.

Georgian is a Kartvelian language with no known relation to any other language family, with its own writing system and a written tradition dating back to the 5th century. Svans, Mingrelians and the Laz speak related Kartvelian languages. The Church was crucial to the development of a written language, and most of the earliest works were religious texts. Most Georgians are Eastern Orthodox Christians belonging to the Georgian Orthodox Church. There are about 5 million Georgians in the world.
georgios-kondylis: Georgios Kondylis was born at Proussos on 14 August 1878 and was nicknamed Keravnos, Greek for thunderbolt. He enlisted in the army as a volunteer in 1896 and fought with the Greek expeditionary corps in Crete. After his commissioning he led his own guerrilla band in the Macedonian Struggle (1904–1908) and was promoted to captain during the Balkan Wars. In the First World War he supported the Provisional Government of National Defence of Eleftherios Venizelos, and he was notorious for his cruel suppression of a loyalist revolt in Chalkidiki in September 1916. A firm Venizelist, he opposed the restoration of King Constantine I in 1920 and fled to Constantinople, where he organised the Democratic Defence.

Kondylis returned after the 1922 Revolution as a major general, suppressed the royalist revolt of 1923 and left the army for politics. Elected to Parliament in 1923 for Rodope, he later founded the National Republican Party, renamed the National Radical Party in 1928. He was war minister from March to June 1924. On 22 August 1926 he overthrew the dictatorship of Theodoros Pangalos in a bloodless coup and formed a government, calling elections for November, in which his party did not take part.

During these years he moved to the right. He became war minister again in 1932 in return for supporting the Populist government, and as minister he was instrumental in crushing the Venizelist revolt of March 1935. He then became the real power in the country, dismissing pro-republican soldiers and civil servants and condemning Venizelos to death in absentia.

On 10 October 1935 Kondylis and other officers forced Prime Minister Panagis Tsaldaris to resign, and he made President Alexandros Zaimis name him premier. The same day he forced Zaimis out, declared himself Regent and abolished the Republic. A plebiscite on 3 November produced an official 98 per cent for the return of George II, a total likely obtained through fraud, since voters dropped a blue paper in the ballot box for the monarchy and a red one for the republic, and those choosing the republic risked beatings.

George returned on 25 November and kept Kondylis as prime minister, but the two quarrelled, as the king was not content to be a puppet, and Kondylis resigned five days later. In the January 1936 elections he worked with Ioannis Rallis and had fifteen MPs elected. He died of a heart attack in Athens on 1 February 1936.
georgios-papadopoulos: Georgios Papadopoulos was born on 5 May 1919 in Elaiohori, a village in Achaea in the Peloponnese, the eldest son of a local schoolteacher. He completed the Hellenic Military Academy in 1940 and in 1941 saw action as an artillery second lieutenant against the Italian and German forces that attacked Greece. Most historians believe he later joined the collaborationist Security Battalions at Patras, a claim that the Greek historians Evanthis Hatzivassiliou and Leonidas Kallivretakis contest. In autumn 1944 he helped create the nationalist secret organisation IDEA. He served in the KYP intelligence service from 1959 to 1964 and became a colonel in 1967.

On 21 April 1967, a month before the general elections, Papadopoulos and other middle-ranking officers carried out a coup, exploiting the conflict between the young King Constantine II and the former prime minister Georgios Papandreou. The king appointed a government nominally headed by Konstantinos Kollias, but Papadopoulos was from the start its strongman. After the king's failed counter-coup of 13 December he replaced Kollias as prime minister, and on 21 March 1972 he named himself regent. Political prisoners, communists above all, were tortured. On 13 August 1968 Alexandros Panagoulis failed to kill him with a bomb, and Papadopoulos pardoned him after a death sentence.

He was among the more moderate members of the junta, but hardliners including Dimitrios Ioannidis thwarted attempts to liberalise it in 1969 and 1970. After an abortive naval coup in early 1973 he abolished the monarchy on 1 June 1973 and declared Greece a republic with himself as president, confirmed by a controversial referendum.

After the student uprising at the National Technical University of Athens on 17 November 1973, which his government put down with the army, Ioannidis overthrew him on 25 November and held him under house arrest. After democracy returned in 1974 he was arrested and tried for high treason, mutiny, torture and other crimes. On 23 August 1975 he was sentenced to death, later commuted to life imprisonment.

He refused to seek parole or amnesty and died in hospital in Athens on 27 June 1999, aged 80. In Greece the junta's leaders are known as the Aprilianoi, after the month of the coup, and the regime's methods and effects are still fiercely debated.
georgios-papandreou: Papandreou was born Georgios Stavropoulos at Kalentzi in Achaea, the son of an Orthodox archpriest, Father Andreas Stavropoulos. He studied law in Athens and political science in Berlin, and his thinking was strongly influenced by German social democracy. He opposed the monarchy and the communists. He volunteered in the First Balkan War, and the Liberal leader Eleftherios Venizelos made him governor of Chios. In 1916 he accompanied Venizelos to Crete and then rallied support on Lesbos for Venizelos's insurgent government in Thessaloniki against King Constantine I.

He was imprisoned in 1921 for an article calling on the king to abdicate, and again under the dictatorship of Theodoros Pangalos. As education minister in 1930 to 1932 he reformed the school system and built many schools for refugees' children. In 1938 the dictator Ioannis Metaxas exiled him. After Italian forces imprisoned him in the Second World War he fled to the Middle East and in 1944 headed the government in exile. Under his premiership came the Lebanon conference of May 1944 and the Caserta Agreement of September 1944. He entered Athens in October as prime minister of a government of national unity and resigned in January 1945 after the Dekemvriana, the conflict between EAM and non-EAM forces.

In 1961 Papandreou founded the Centre Union, which won a minority vote in 1963 and formed a government after the elections of 1964. His government made free education available at all levels and lengthened compulsory schooling. His relationship with the young King Constantine II worsened, and when the defence minister Petros Garoufalias refused to leave his post over the ASPIDA scandal in the army, Papandreou clashed with the king and resigned in July 1965. The coup of April 1967 installed a military regime, and Papandreou was put under house arrest. He died on 1 November 1968. His son Andreas Papandreou later became prime minister.
georgios-tsolakoglou: Georgios Tsolakoglou was born in Rentina, Thessaly, in April 1886, of Aromanian origin. His grandfather Dimitrios Tsolakoglou, proestos of Agrafa and a member of the Filiki Eteria, was executed for treason on the orders of Hurshid Pasha in 1822. Tsolakoglou served in the Balkan Wars, the First World War, the Allied intervention in the Russian Civil War of 1919 and the Asia Minor Campaign, and as a lieutenant general he led the Western Macedonia Army Section in the Greco-Italian War.

After German units cut off the army at the Metsovon Pass and took Ioannina, Tsolakoglou, with the corps commanders Panagiotis Demestichas and Georgios Bakos and the metropolitan of Ioannina, replaced the army section's commander, Ioannis Pitsikas, on 20 April 1941 and signed a surrender protocol with Sepp Dietrich. Against the orders of the commander-in-chief Alexandros Papagos, he formalised the surrender at Larissa the next day; at Benito Mussolini's insistence the ceremony was repeated on 23 April with the Italians. On 26 April he wrote to Adolf Hitler offering to head a government of generals, an offer Hitler called a gift from Heaven.

Appointed prime minister on 30 April 1941, he led a cabinet of generals and a few others, sworn in by Damaskinos after Archbishop Chrysanthus of Athens refused. He failed to keep the Italians out of Greece, and Bulgaria annexed parts of Macedonia and Thrace and expelled Greeks while his letters of protest went unanswered. His special courts against black marketeers did not stop the Great Famine of 1941–42, which killed about 300,000 Greeks as the occupiers requisitioned food.

By November 1942 the Germans and Italians considered him untrustworthy, and on 2 December he retired, citing his health, in favour of Konstantinos Logothetopoulos. In his memoirs he wrote that he had never regretted surrendering the army and was proud of it. A Special Collaborators Court tried him in 1945, and he died of leukaemia in prison in 1948.
georgius-agricola: Agricola was born Georg Pawer, the second of seven children of a clothier and dyer in Glauchau, in the Electorate of Saxony. His teacher at Leipzig, the humanist Petrus Mosellanus, urged him to take the Latin name that was popular among Renaissance scholars. He studied at Leipzig from 1514 to 1518 and at 24 became head of the Greek School of Zwickau, where he served from 1519 to 1522. In 1523 he went to Italy, enrolled at the University of Bologna and completed his medical studies. In 1524 he joined the Aldine Press in Venice and took part in an edition of Galen until 1526.

Agricola settled in 1527 at Joachimsthal, a mining town in the Bohemian Ore Mountains where silver had been found in 1516. The town had some 15,000 people and hundreds of shafts. Agricola found his post as physician undemanding and spent his spare time comparing earlier writings on minerals with his own observations. The result was a dialogue, Bermannus, published in 1530 and praised by Erasmus. In 1533 he moved to Chemnitz as town physician and soon became its lord mayor, serving as burgomaster in 1546, 1547, 1551 and 1553. He also wrote a work on Greek and Roman weights and measures (1533), at a time when the Holy Roman Empire had no uniform ones.

Between 1544 and 1548 he published works on the origins of subterranean things, on the waters and air of the earth's interior and on minerals, ores and metals, De Natura Fossilium (1546). He held that a fatty matter fermented by heat produced fossil shapes, not that fossil shells had belonged to living animals. De re metallica, in twelve books, appeared in 1556. It describes prospecting, surveying, washing ores, water mills, hoisting machines and methods now obsolete such as fire-setting, and Agricola states that he excluded what he had not seen himself or read or heard of.

Agricola died on 21 November 1555, according to his friend the poet Georg Fabricius of a four-day fever. A firm Catholic in a Protestant city, he was refused burial in Chemnitz on the urging of the Protestant superintendent, and his friend Julius von Pflug, Bishop of Naumburg, had the body carried more than 50 kilometres to Zeitz and buried in the cathedral. Words derived from his work include fluorspar and bismuth. In 1912 Herbert Hoover and his wife Lou Henry Hoover published an English translation of De re metallica.
georgy-lvov: Prince Georgy Yevgenyevich Lvov was born on 2 November 1861 (21 October, Old Style) in Dresden, into one of the oldest Russian noble families, which traced its roots to the Rurik princes of Yaroslavl. His reform-minded father spent almost all his income on his children's education. The family lived at Popovka in Tula Governorate, a few miles from Leo Tolstoy's home, and counted Tolstoy among their closest friends. After the abolition of serfdom they fell deep into debt, and chose to turn Popovka into a profitable farm, laying off their servants and working the land themselves while Georgy studied law at the University of Moscow. All debts were repaid by the late 1880s.

When war between Japan and Russia began in January 1904, thirteen provincial zemstvos formed a medical brigade of 360 doctors and nurses under Lvov to help the Red Cross on the Manchurian front. The relief mission won high praise from military leaders and made him a national hero. In 1906 he was elected to the First Duma for the Constitutional Democratic Party. In 1914 he became chairman of the All-Russian Union of Zemstvos, and in 1915 he was a leader of the Union of Zemstvos and a member of Zemgor, the committee that helped supply the army and tend the wounded in the First World War.

After the February Revolution and the abdication of Nicholas II, Lvov headed the Provisional Government founded by the Duma on 2 March 1917, serving as prime minister from 15 March to 20 July. His government introduced universal adult suffrage, freedom of press and speech, the abolition of capital punishment and the removal of legal restrictions of religion, class and race. Unable to rally enough support, he resigned in July 1917 in favour of his war minister, Alexander Kerensky.

After the October Revolution he was arrested but escaped, and in October 1918 travelled to the United States for the anti-Bolshevik Provisional Siberian Government, arriving after the First World War had ended. He moved to France, headed the Russian political meeting in Paris from 1918 to 1920, lived in poverty, wrote his memoirs and died in March 1925.
gepids: The Gepids lived in the area of modern Romania, Hungary and Serbia, roughly between the Tisza, the Sava and the Carpathian Mountains. They are first mentioned by Roman sources in the third century, and neither Tacitus nor Ptolemy named them. The historian Malcolm Todd called them the most shadowy of the major Germanic peoples of the migration period. Everything about their origins comes from Gothic legends, described as malicious and convoluted, recorded in the Getica of Jordanes after 550.

According to Jordanes the Goths and Gepids left the island of Scandza together in three ships under the king Berig, and the Gepids, in the last and slowest ship, were mocked as gepanta, meaning sluggish. Little is known of their language, which was probably a dialect of Gothic.

In the fourth century the Gepids were among the peoples incorporated into the Hunnic Empire, where they became an important part. Attila prized Ardaric, king of the Gepids, above the other chieftains, and a countless host under Ardaric formed the right wing of Attila's army at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains in 451. After Attila died in 453, civil war among his sons let the subject peoples rebel. According to Jordanes, Ardaric was the first to take up arms, and at the Nedao River in Pannonia in 454 a united army of Gepids, Rugii, Sarmatians and Suebi routed the Huns and their allies.

The Gepids then became the dominant power in the eastern Carpathian Basin and ruled over much of Dacia. Emperor Marcian confirmed them as allies of the empire and granted an annual subsidy of 100 pounds of gold. After the Ostrogoths left Pannonia in 473, they captured Sirmium. They reached the height of their power after 537, when King Cunimund minted gold coins at Sirmium and the Gepids and Heruls plundered Moesia in 539. Justinian I, angered by their expansion, allied with the Lombards in 551, and under Alboin the Lombards inflicted a disastrous defeat on the Gepids at Asfeld in 552. In 567 the Lombards and Avars overran the kingdom.

Many Gepids followed Alboin to Italy in 568, according to Paul the Deacon, while others stayed in the area of the old kingdom. In 630 Theophylact Simocatta reported that a Byzantine army attacked a Gepid feast and captured 30,000 Gepids. Few archaeological sites can be attributed to them with certainty. Rich burials include the treasures found at Apahida and Someșeni.
gerald-durrell: Gerald Malcolm Durrell was born in Jamshedpur in British India on 7 January 1925, the youngest of the children of Lawrence Samuel Durrell, a civil engineer, and Louisa Florence Durrell, née Dixie. The family moved to England after his father died in 1928. In March 1935 they left for the Greek island of Corfu and stayed four years, until the outbreak of the Second World War forced them back to Britain.

Back in Bournemouth by early 1940 he was taught by a tutor, Harold Binns, a veteran of the First World War, who gave him a love of poetry and good writing. He spent the next two years exploring the countryside and reading books from the local library.

In 1946 Durrell received an inheritance from his father's will, and he used it to fund collecting trips. He visited the British Cameroons in 1947 and 1948 with the ornithologist John Yealland, returned in 1949 with Ken Smith, and went to British Guiana in 1950. These trips cost more than they earned. He married Jacquie in 1951, and she persuaded him to write down his stories. After a radio talk on his search for the hairy frog he wrote The Overloaded Ark, which sold well.

An expedition to Argentina and Paraguay followed in 1953 and produced The Drunken Forest. My Family and Other Animals became a bestseller. He planned it meticulously in three parts, one for each of the family's villas, and wrote 120,000 words in six weeks. The Amateur Naturalist, written with his second wife Lee, became his most successful book, selling well over a million copies.

Durrell wanted his own zoo, one meant for the study and captive breeding of animals rather than as a showcase. Hugh Fraser, the owner of Les Augrès manor on Jersey, agreed to a lease signed on 17 October 1958. The zoo opened on 26 March 1959, and in 1963 its control passed to the Jersey Wildlife Preservation Trust. An appeal in 1970 raised funds to buy the property.

In 1984 he founded the Durrell Conservation Academy to train people in captive breeding. He was diagnosed with liver cancer and cirrhosis in 1994, had a liver transplant, and died on 30 January 1995. His ashes were divided between Corfu and Jersey Zoo. Princess Anne, the Trust's patron, said that his ability to put his enthusiasm for wildlife on the page was his most important talent.
gerald-templer: Gerald Walter Robert Templer was born in Colchester on 11 September 1898, the only child of Lieutenant-Colonel Walter Francis Templer of the Royal Irish Fusiliers. After Wellington College and Sandhurst he was commissioned into his father's regiment in 1916 and served on the Western Front from late 1917; acute diphtheria took him home just before the German Spring Offensive, in which his battalion suffered over 770 casualties, and he returned for the Hundred Days Offensive. Between the wars he served in Persia, Iraq and Egypt, attended the Staff College at Camberley, and in 1936 commanded a company in Palestine during the Arab revolt, earning the Distinguished Service Order.

In the Second World War he served in the intelligence staff of the British Expeditionary Force in France, then commanded a brigade, a division and, from September 1942, as the army's youngest acting lieutenant-general, II Corps. In 1943 he gave up that rank to command a division on active service, led the 56th (London) Infantry Division in Italy and fought at Anzio, and in August 1944 was badly injured by a land mine. As Director of the Military Government in the British Zone of Germany in 1945 he dismissed the mayor of Cologne, Konrad Adenauer.

Winston Churchill appointed him High Commissioner for Malaya on 22 January 1952. He relied on intelligence, rewards for surrender, curfews and food control, and defoliants sprayed on the insurgents' crops. His troops also used internment in the New Villages, forced relocation, collective punishment and Dayak headhunters to decapitate suspected guerrillas, a practice he defended privately to the Colonial Secretary Oliver Lyttleton and which The Daily Worker exposed in April 1952. Some historians see his campaign as a model of winning hearts and minds; other scholars call that a myth, pointing to its reliance on coercion.

Templer became Chief of the Imperial General Staff on 29 September 1955 and advised the government during the Suez Crisis. He was made a field marshal on 27 November 1956 and retired in 1958. In retirement he worked to found the National Army Museum in London, whose study centre bears his name, and he was Constable of the Tower and Lord Lieutenant of Greater London. He died of lung cancer at his home in Chelsea on 25 October 1979. Many of his counter-insurgency methods were later imitated by the United States in Vietnam.
geraldine-of-albania: Geraldine was born in Budapest, a daughter of Count Gyula Apponyi de Nagy-Appony, Grand Marshal of the Hungarian Court, and Gladys Virginia Stewart, an American. The Apponyi family had been great landowners in Upper Hungary since the 13th century. When Austria-Hungary collapsed in 1918 the family moved to Switzerland, returning to Hungary in 1921.

After her father died in 1924 her mother took the three children to Menton in the south of France, and when she married a French officer the children were returned to Hungary for schooling. Geraldine attended the Sacred Heart boarding school at Pressbaum, near Vienna, and lived at the family's chateau at Oponice, in present-day Slovakia, until 1938. With the family fortune spent, she worked as a shorthand typist and in the gift shop of the Budapest National Museum, where her uncle was director.

King Zog I of the Albanians, who had seen a photograph of her, met her on New Year's Day 1938. She visited Albania and the two were engaged within days. Known as the White Rose of Hungary, she was raised to the rank of Princess Geraldine of Albania before the wedding, held in Tirana on 27 April 1938 with Galeazzo Ciano, son-in-law of Mussolini, as witness. She was Roman Catholic and Zog was Muslim.

Her tiara carried a white rose for the bride and the heraldic goat for the groom, and the couple drove to their honeymoon in a scarlet Mercedes-Benz 540K given by Adolf Hitler. Zog was deposed on 7 April 1939, and the family fled via Greece and Turkey to France and then England, where they lived at the Ritz Hotel in London, at Ascot and for most of the war at Parmoor House in Buckinghamshire. Their only child was Leka.

In 1946 the couple went to Egypt and in 1952 to France. Zog died in Hauts-de-Seine in 1961, and the royalist government in exile proclaimed Leka King Leka I. Geraldine took the title Queen Mother and upheld his claim, moving to Spain, Saudi Arabia, Rhodesia and South Africa.

After a change in the law she settled in Albania, and she died at a military hospital in Tirana on 22 October 2002, aged 87, after at least three heart attacks. She was buried in the Sharra cemetery and later reburied in the Royal Mausoleum in Tirana. The Albanian government awarded her the Mother Teresa Medal posthumously, and a statue of her by Sándor Kligl was inaugurated in Tirana on 1 February 2022.
gerard-of-cremona: Gerard was born in Cremona in northern Italy. Dissatisfied with the philosophies of his Italian teachers, he went to Toledo, and no detailed information survives on when, though it was no later than 1144. He went to learn Arabic so that he could read Ptolemy's Almagest, which had a high reputation among scholars but was not yet known in Latin translation in the West. Toledo had been a provincial capital in the Caliphate of Cordoba and remained a seat of learning. Alfonso VI of Castile conquered it from the Moors in 1085, which made it safely available to a Catholic.

Its rulers protected the large Jewish and Muslim quarters, and the city stayed an important centre of Arab and Hebrew culture, with Mozarabic culture common in the area. It was full of libraries and manuscripts, and was one of the few places in medieval Europe where a Christian could be exposed to Arabic language and culture. One of the great scholars associated with it was Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra, Gerard's contemporary.

In Toledo Gerard devoted the rest of his life to making Latin translations from Arabic scientific literature. He is regarded as the most important translator of the Toledo School of Translators, which transmitted Arab and ancient Greek knowledge in astronomy, medicine and other sciences to Western medieval Europe in the 12th century. Some of the books he obtained in the Toledo libraries had been written in Greek and were well known in Byzantine Constantinople but unavailable in Greek or Latin in the West.

In all he translated 87 books from Arabic. The historian Edward Grant ranks him above every other western translator and says that his translations alone would have drastically altered the course of western science.

His Latin version of the Arabic Almagest, made about 1175, was the most widely known in Western Europe before the Renaissance, although an earlier translation from the Greek had been made in Sicily about 1160 under Henricus Aristippus. The Almagest formed the basis for Western astronomy until Copernicus. Gerard also edited the Tables of Toledo, partly the work of al-Zarqali of Cordoba, and rendered al-Farabi's book on the sciences as De scientiis.

His other translations include Euclid's Elements, Archimedes' On the Measurement of the Circle, Aristotle's On the Heavens, al-Khwarizmi's On Algebra and Almucabala, Jabir ibn Aflah's Elementa astronomica and works of al-Razi. He also composed original treatises on algebra, arithmetic and astrology, and created anatomical terms. A second translator, Gerard de Sabloneta, worked in the 13th century and is probably responsible for some works credited to Gerard.
gerard-of-csanad: Most information about Gerard survives in his legends, which contain many conventional elements of medieval saints' biographies. He was born in a noble Venetian family. Sources written centuries later associate it with the Sagredo or Morosini families. His parents, also named Gerard and Catherine, waited three years for his birth and baptised him George, since he was born on the feast of Saint George, 23 April. At the age of five he fell seriously ill, and his recovery was attributed to the prayers of the Benedictine monks of the San Giorgio Monastery in Venice, to which his family sent him. He studied there and was later sent away to study grammar, music, philosophy and law.

Gerard left Venice on a pilgrimage to the Holy Land around 1020. Modern historians connect his departure with armed conflicts between the Orseolos and their opponents. A storm forced him to break his journey in a monastery near Istria, where Rasina persuaded him to go to Hungary. In Pécs, Bishop Maurus and Abbot Anastasius of Pécsvárad urged him to stay, and King Stephen I of Hungary, meeting him at Székesfehérvár, argued that preaching in Hungary would serve God best. Gerard agreed and became tutor to the king's heir, Emeric, though that role is mentioned only in his Long Life. He then lived for several years as a hermit in the Bakony Hills near Bakonybél, where he wrote homilies and commentaries that were later lost.

Around 1030 Stephen I made him the first bishop of the new Diocese of Csanád, formed after the royal army under Csanád defeated the chieftain Ajtony, who had ruled the Tisza, Danube and Mureș region. The Annales Posonienses give 1030, though historians do not all trust the date. Twelve Benedictine monks accompanied him, seven of whom spoke Hungarian and interpreted for him. As a missionary bishop he baptised many converts. The Long Life says he built churches in every city of his diocese.

Gerard was killed on 24 September 1046 during the Vata pagan uprising, with Bystrik and Buldus. Accounts differ. In one he was stoned, pierced with a lance and thrown from a cliff into the Danube. In another he was hauled in a cart to a hilltop in Buda, now Gellért Hill, and rolled down it. Gerard was canonised in 1083, together with Stephen and Emeric. He is one of the patron saints of Hungary, and his feast day is 24 September.
gerard-of-roussillon: Girart was a son of Leuthard I, Count of Fézensac and Paris, and his wife Grimildis, and became Count of Paris himself in 837. No authentic historical source calls him a man of Roussillon: the name in his title comes from a castle he built on Mont Lassois, near Vix and Châtillon-sur-Seine. He took the side of Lothair I against Charles the Bald, fought at the Battle of Fontenay in 841 and followed Lothair to Aix-en-Provence.

In 843 Girart married Bertha, and they had two children, Thierry and Ava. In 855 he became governor of Provence for Lothair's son Charles of Provence. He may have hoped to become the titular ruler of the northern part of the kingdom, and he went on administering it under Lothair II until that king's death in 869. In 870 Bertha defended Vienne against Charles the Bald without success. Around 860 Girart founded the abbey of Pothières.

Girart withdrew with his wife to Avignon, where he died. The story of his piety, Bertha's heroism and his wars with Charles passed into romance, so distorted that in the epic Girart de Roussillon he becomes an opponent of Charles Martel, who is married to Bertha's sister. The earliest chanson de geste about him dates from the second half of the 12th century and survives at the Bibliothèque nationale de France. Monks of Pothières wrote a romance in alexandrines between 1330 and 1349, dedicated to Odo IV, Duke of Burgundy, and Queen Jeanne de Bourgogne, which Jehan Wauquelin turned into prose in 1447.

Southern French traditions made him a son of Garin de Monglane. They appear in Girart de Vienne by Bertrand de Bar-sur-l'Aube, on the siege of Vienne by Charlemagne, and in Aspramonte by Andrea da Barberino, where as Girart de Fraite he leads an army of infidels against Charlemagne. In the genealogy of the Matter of France he is a son of Doon de Mayence.
gerardo-machado: Machado was born in 1871 as the oldest child of a family in the central province of Las Villas, today Villa Clara. His father, Gerardo Machado y Castellón, served with Cuban rebels in all three of the major wars of rebellion against Spain and attained the rank of major in the Ten Years' War. In 1895 Cubans launched a War of Independence against Spain. Machado joined the Cuban Liberation Army, fought in the middle provinces and rose to brigadier general, one of the youngest Cuban generals of the war.

After the war he turned to politics and business, and was elected mayor of Santa Clara. During the administration of José Miguel Gómez (1909–1913) he was appointed inspector of the armed forces and later Secretary of the Interior.

Running as a Liberal Party candidate in 1924, Machado defeated Mario García Menocal of the Conservative Party by an overwhelming majority, with the slogan 'Water, roads, and schools'. He took office on 20 May 1925. His first term coincided with prosperity, and he embarked on an ambitious public works programme that included the Carretera Central, running over 1,126 kilometres from Pinar del Río to Santiago de Cuba, and the Capitolio, built in 1926–1929 as the home of the Cuban Congress.

Having promised not to seek re-election, Machado pushed constitutional amendments in 1927 that allowed him to do so, and was re-elected without opposition in 1928. His detractors said he became despotic. Falling sugar prices and the crash of 1929 added to the instability. Students formed the Directorio Estudiantil Universitario in 1927; after protests and the death of Rafael Trejo on 30 September 1930, Machado closed the university. Killings of opponents by the police and army are attributed to his regime, though the extent of his own involvement is disputed.

In May 1933 the US ambassador Sumner Welles began to negotiate with the opposition groups for a government to follow Machado's. As the crisis grew, parts of the army revolted and demanded his resignation, and on the afternoon of 12 August 1933 Machado flew to the Bahamas. A provisional government headed by Carlos Manuel de Céspedes y Quesada took power on 13 August amid a general strike in Havana. Machado went into exile in Miami Beach and died there of colon cancer in 1939.
gerhard-iii-count-of-holstein-rendsburg: Gerhard belonged to the Schauenburg family and was the son of Henry I, Count of Holstein-Rendsburg, who died on 5 August 1304. He inherited his share of Holstein as a boy and, as a young man, enlarged it by outmanoeuvring his relatives and conquering other parts of the county, which made him a powerful local prince. He also fought as a paid condottiere for neighbouring kings, among them King Eric VI of Denmark, often together with his cousin John III, Count of Holstein-Plön. He married Sophia of Werle, a granddaughter of Eric V of Denmark, and their children included Henry II and Nicholas, later counts of Holstein-Rendsburg.

In 1325 Gerhard became guardian of his young nephew, Duke Valdemar of Schleswig, which made him a natural ally of the discontented Danish magnates. In 1326 he and the rebels deposed Christopher II, placed Valdemar on the Danish throne and made Gerhard regent. Through the Constitutio Valdemariana he secured the separation of Schleswig from Denmark, the basis of lasting German influence in South Jutland. When rebellions and a quarrel with Count Johan followed, he restored Christopher as a puppet king in 1329, and after Christopher's death in 1332 he ruled Jutland and Funen, leaving the rest of the country to Johan.

His hold was insecure. Creditors who had paid for his armies could press him, the Danish gentry that had once backed him turned against foreign rule, peasant risings and lawlessness at sea spread, and neighbouring German states supported Christopher's son, the future Valdemar IV. Gerhard seems to have been ready to compromise if his debts were settled, but in spring 1340 he set out against rebels in North Jutland. On 1 April 1340, at Randers, Niels Ebbesen and some of his men entered his bedroom and killed him.

His death ended Holstein rule in Denmark. His sons gave up his Danish titles, and Valdemar IV took the throne. In Denmark Gerhard has traditionally been seen as a German tyrant, and his killing as a high point of the nation's history that still inspired poets and writers during the German occupation of 1940–1945. He is also remembered unfavourably in Dithmarschen, which he ravaged, while in Holstein he has been regarded as a national hero. Contemporary sources show him as energetic, a brutal warrior and deeply religious.
gerhard-von-scharnhorst: Gerhard Johann David von Scharnhorst was born on 12 November 1755 at Bordenau near Hanover, into a minor landowning family. He educated himself and gained admission to the military academy of William, Count of Schaumburg-Lippe, at the Wilhelmstein fortress. He received a Hanoverian commission in 1778, moved to the artillery in 1783 and taught at the new artillery school in Hanover.

He founded a military journal that lasted until 1805 and wrote handbooks for officers, since writing was his chief income. His first campaign was in the Netherlands in 1793, where he served under the Duke of York at the defence of Menen. In 1801 he accepted a Prussian offer at twice his Hanoverian pay, on condition that he keep his seniority and receive a pension and a patent of nobility.

In Prussia he taught at the military academy, where Clausewitz was among his pupils, and founded the Berlin Military Society. In 1806 he was chief of staff to the Duke of Brunswick, was lightly wounded at Auerstedt on 14 October, and went into captivity with Blücher at Ratekau on 7 November before being quickly exchanged. He helped lead L'Estocq's corps beside the Russians and received the order Pour le Mérite for Eylau in February 1807.

He became a major-general soon after the Peace of Tilsit and headed a reform commission with Gneisenau, Grolman and Boyen, joined by Stein. The commission converted the professional long-service army wrecked at Jena into a national one. Foreign enlistment was abolished, corporal punishment was limited to flagrant insubordination, promotion for merit was established, and the Landwehr reserves were begun. Napoleon grew suspicious and Frederick William III repeatedly suspended the reforms, and universal service had not been secured by Scharnhorst's death.

In 1811 and 1812, when France forced Prussia into an alliance against Russia, Scharnhorst left Berlin on unlimited leave and wrote a work on firearms. After the retreat from Moscow he returned to the king's headquarters as chief of staff to Blücher. He was wounded in the foot at Lützen on 2 May 1813, and the wound, worsened by the retreat to Dresden, proved fatal at Prague on 28 June 1813, where he had gone to negotiate Austria's intervention.

He had just been promoted lieutenant-general. Frederick William III had a statue of him by Christian Daniel Rauch put up in Berlin, and he was buried at the Invalidenfriedhof. The German armoured cruiser of 1906, the battleship of 1936 and the East German Scharnhorst Order bear his name.
german-busch: Busch was the fifth of six children of Pablo Busch Wiesener, a physician and German immigrant, and Raquel Becerra Villavicencio. Historians dispute whether he was born in San Javier, in Santa Cruz, or in El Carmen de Iténez, in the Beni, and he was raised in Trinidad. He entered the Military College of the Army in La Paz on 16 January 1922. In 1928 he married Matilde Carmona Rodó, with special permission, since officers below captain were not then allowed to marry.

In 1931 President Daniel Salamanca sent him with thirty men to find the lost Jesuit mission of San Ignacio de Zamucos, to support Bolivia's claim to the Chaco Boreal; the search earned him the Order of the Condor of the Andes. He served with distinction in the Chaco War against Paraguay, which began on 9 September 1932, and joined the officers who ousted Salamanca in 1934.

After the defeat of 1935 he founded the Legion of Veterans. During the great strikes of May 1936 he promised the labour leader Waldó Álvarez that the army would not act against the strikers, and on 17 May he forced President José Luis Tejada Sorzano to resign, serving briefly as provisional president before his mentor David Toro took over on 22 May. Within Toro's junta he championed military socialism, but grew impatient with its compromises, and on 10 July 1937 the veterans named him their Supreme Leader shortly before the coup of 13 July.

Busch's first cabinet gave the finance ministry to the conservative Federico Gutiérrez Granier. The convention of 1938 elected him president, and on 21 July 1938 the Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Boundaries signed in Buenos Aires ended the Chaco War, leaving roughly 75 per cent of the Chaco Boreal to Paraguay. On 24 September he created the Pando Department. On 24 April 1939 he suspended the assembly, cancelled elections and began to rule by decree, nationalising railways, industries and the Central Bank.

Weeks earlier he had asked the German minister Ernst Wendler for advisers; the German government declined on 22 April. Attacked in the press and grieving his mother, he was shot in his home after his wife's birthday celebration in August 1939. Whether it was suicide or assassination is still disputed. General Carlos Quintanilla seized the Palacio Quemado and ended the era of military socialism.
german-cruiser-blucher: Blücher was the second of five Admiral Hipper-class heavy cruisers of the Kriegsmarine, built after the Nazi Party came to power in 1933 and repudiated the disarmament clauses of the Treaty of Versailles. The Anglo-German Naval Agreement of 1935 allowed Germany five cruisers of 10,000 long tons, a limit the Hippers nominally met but greatly exceeded, at over 16,000 long tons. The ship was named for Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher, the Prussian victor of Waterloo, and was laid down at Kiel on 15 August 1935, launched on 8 June 1937 and commissioned on 20 September 1939. She was armed with eight 20.3 cm guns in four twin turrets.

Blücher was declared ready for service on 5 April 1940 and assigned to the invasion of Norway. Rear Admiral Oskar Kummetz boarded as commander of Group 5, whose task was to seize Oslo, together with 800 troops. The group left port on 8 April and was seen at night by the Norwegian patrol boat Pol III, whose radio alarm warned the defences.

At 04:21 the old 28 cm guns of Oscarsborg Fortress opened fire at very close range in the Battle of Drøbak Sound and hit Blücher twice; the second shell started a fire that detonated explosives carried for the infantry. At 04:34 two torpedoes from a concealed battery struck the boiler and turbine rooms. A fire later reached a 10.5 cm magazine, which exploded, and Blücher capsized and sank at 07:30. Estimates of the dead vary: Henrik Lunde gives 600 to 1,000 soldiers and sailors, while Jürgen Rohwer gives 125 seamen and 195 soldiers.

The loss of Blücher and damage to the cruiser Lützow made the German force withdraw. Troops landed on the eastern side of the fjord and took Oscarsborg by 09:00 on 10 April, and Oslo was in German hands by 14:00 that day, but the delay allowed the Norwegian government and royal family to escape the city. The wreck lies at a depth of 64 metres in the Drøbak Narrows. Leaking oil led to an operation in October 1994 that removed 1,000 tonnes and recovered one of her Arado 196 seaplanes. The wreck was protected as a war memorial and war grave on 16 June 2016 to protect it from looters.
german-east-africa: The colony began when Carl Peters, founder of the Society for German Colonization, signed treaties with chieftains on the mainland opposite Zanzibar. An imperial charter for his company was announced on 3 March 1885, signed by Chancellor Otto von Bismarck. The Sultan of Zanzibar protested, and Bismarck sent five warships, which arrived on 7 August 1885 and trained their guns on the Sultan's palace. He had to accept German claims on the mainland outside a 16-kilometre coastal strip. The Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty of 1890 with Britain gave Heligoland to Germany and fixed the border with British East Africa.

German expansion relied on military groups such as the Wissmann Truppe, African soldiers under German commanders, which committed widespread atrocities. The Hehe under Chief Mkwawa resisted from 1891 to 1894, and Mkwawa killed himself in 1898 after years of guerrilla warfare. The Maji Maji rebellion of 1905 was put down by Governor Gustav Adolf von Götzen, who ordered measures to create a famine, and it may have cost as many as 300,000 lives.

German administrators relied heavily on local chiefs to keep order and collect taxes. Sisal, the largest cash crop, covered over 40,000 hectares, and coffee, rubber and cotton were also grown. Local officials often colluded with planters in forcing Africans to work, though Berlin had banned forced labour. The Central Railway linking Dar es Salaam and Kigoma was completed in July 1914. New enslavement and the commercial slave trade were banned in 1901, but private sales were not. The colony had more than 7.5 million inhabitants and about 10,000 Europeans on the eve of the First World War.

In the First World War General Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck led German forces of 3,500 Europeans and 12,000 African askaris and porters, and won at Tanga on 3 to 5 November 1914. Dwindling supplies and attacks from the Belgian Congo made him abandon the colony, and he agreed a ceasefire in Northern Rhodesia after the armistice. The Paris Peace Conference awarded the colony to Britain in May 1919, and Britain ceded Ruanda and Urundi to Belgium. The Kionga Triangle went to Portugal. The transfer took effect on 10 January 1920, and the British territory was named Tanganyika.
german-east-africa-company: The company grew out of the Gesellschaft für deutsche Kolonisation, the Society for German Colonisation, founded in 1884 to trade in Africa. Its backers saw colonies as sources of raw materials and consumers for an industrialising Germany. Carl Peters, born in Hanover in 1856 and trained in history, philosophy and law, persuaded local rulers in East Africa to sign over control of their land, impressing them with gunfire, dress and flags. The German protectorate of Wituland, in modern Kenya, began as a separate German sphere in 1885. The company's flag showed a stylised Southern Cross.

The company leased the coastal strip opposite Zanzibar from Sultan Khalifa bin Said for 50 years. Its attempt to take over the administration set off a general revolt along the coast of what is now Tanzania, and it held Dar es Salaam and Bagamoyo only with the help of the German navy before asking the German government in 1889 to put the rising down. Hermann von Wissmann, an army officer who had come to Africa with an explorer, led the military operations that restored German control.

Peters became administrator of the region but was dismissed for his brutal treatment of Africans, who called him mkono wa damu, the man with blood on his hands. He was put on trial and found guilty, a verdict the German press criticised. In 1891, when it was clear that the company could not govern its territory, it sold out to the German government, which then ruled German East Africa directly.

For a time the company kept running its mines, plantations, railways, banking and minting before handing them to the colonial administration and other bodies, and it then worked as a land company within the colony. German East Africa eventually covered modern Tanzania, Burundi and Rwanda. Britain occupied it during the First World War, when both sides pressed thousands of Africans into service as porters and labourers and destroyed countless villages. Many streets once named after Peters have since been renamed.
german-emperor: In the revolutions of 1848 the Frankfurt Parliament offered King Friedrich Wilhelm IV of Prussia the title Emperor of the Germans in 1849. He declined, holding that it was not the Parliament's to give and that only the German princes could make such an offer, as in the tradition of the Holy Roman Empire.

The later title was chosen with care by Otto von Bismarck, Minister President of Prussia and Chancellor of the North German Confederation. Wilhelm I accepted it grudgingly on 18 January 1871, at Versailles during the Siege of Paris. He had preferred Emperor of Germany, but that would have claimed territorial sovereignty unacceptable to the South German monarchs and a claim to lands such as Austria and Switzerland. He rejected Emperor of the Germans because he believed he ruled by divine right, not by the will of the people, and he disliked a crown created by a constitution, fearing it would overshadow the Prussian one.

The constitution of 1 January 1871 turned the North German Confederation into the German Empire, a federal monarchy. The emperor was head of state and president of the federated monarchs, among them the kings of Bavaria, Württemberg and Saxony and the free cities of Hamburg, Lübeck and Bremen. The presidency was permanently held by the king of Prussia, so the imperial crown was tied directly to the Prussian crown. Since 1867 the presidency of the Confederation had already been hereditary in the Prussian kings. The emperors also bore a long list of titles reflecting the lands of the House of Hohenzollern, among them Margrave of Brandenburg, Burgrave of Nuremberg and Count of Hohenzollern.

Wilhelm II discovered the link between the two crowns in 1918. He wrongly believed he ruled the empire in personal union with Prussia and thought he could keep the Prussian crown. His last chancellor, Prince Max of Baden, knew this was legally impossible and on 9 November announced the abdication of both thrones. That night Wilhelm went into exile in the Netherlands, and on 28 November he formally gave up all claims. After the revolution the head of state was the president of the Reich, beginning with Friedrich Ebert.
german-empire: The German Confederation had been created by the Congress of Vienna on 8 June 1815. After the liberal Revolutions of 1848 were crushed, Otto von Bismarck's pragmatic Realpolitik took their place. He sought to extend Hohenzollern hegemony across the German states, which meant excluding Prussia's main German rival, Austria. The Second Schleswig War against Denmark in 1864, the Austro-Prussian War in 1866 and the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–1871 fed a growing pan-German ideal and brought victory for the Kleindeutsche Lösung, the Lesser German solution.

The empire was founded on 18 January 1871, when the south German states, except for Austria, Switzerland and Liechtenstein, joined the North German Confederation. Wilhelm I, King of Prussia, became German Emperor, Berlin remained the capital, and Bismarck became chancellor. It was a federal constitutional monarchy of 25 states, and Prussia held about two thirds of its population and territory.

Bismarck served as chancellor from 1871 to 1890. His tenure began with relatively liberal measures and shifted toward conservatism, marked by the Kulturkampf against the Catholic Church. He enacted universal male suffrage in 1871 and created pioneering social programmes in the 1880s. In 1879 he concluded the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary, which became the Triple Alliance with Italy in 1882. In the 1880s the empire entered the colonial race, acquiring territories in Africa, the Pacific and China.

Wilhelm I died on 9 March 1888. His son Frederick, who had incurable cancer of the larynx, died on 15 June 1888 after 99 days, and Wilhelm II became emperor. Wishing to rule in his own right, he came into conflict with Bismarck, who resigned in March 1890. Wilhelm II then pursued Weltpolitik, a more aggressive course that abandoned Bismarck's alliance system and left Germany increasingly isolated.

After the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the Kaiser gave Austria-Hungary full support against Serbia, a blank check in the term of the historian Fritz Fischer. The German plan to take Paris quickly failed, and the Western Front became a stalemate. In October 1918 the armies were in retreat and the allies had collapsed. The empire fell in the November revolution of 1918 with the abdication of Wilhelm II.

The Treaty of Versailles imposed reparations of 132 billion gold marks and limited the army to 100,000 men. The economic devastation that followed, and the humiliation felt by the German population, are considered leading factors in the rise of Adolf Hitler and Nazism. Many historians have stressed a German Sonderweg, or special path, as a root of the catastrophe of the 20th century. Large parts of the empire now belong to Poland, Russia and France.
german-general-staff: Before the 19th century Prussian victories depended largely on the sovereign's own skill, and after Frederick the Great generalship declined, though a Quartermaster General Staff of adjutants and engineers survived him. In the last years of the 18th century reformers such as Gerhard von Scharnhorst and August von Gneisenau had military experts assigned to assist the generals. The staff existed unofficially from 1806 and was established by law in 1814. On 15 October 1810 Scharnhorst opened the General War School in Berlin, where Carl von Clausewitz was among the first directors; his syllabus, drawn from the Napoleonic Wars, became the staff's central doctrine.

Officers were chosen for intelligence and proven merit rather than patronage or wealth, and their long training aimed to give a body of experts a common method, so that any of them could take over another's work. They alternated between line and staff duties but remained members for life. The staff itself was small, often fifty officers and rarely more than a hundred. The chief of staff of a formation in the field could record his disagreement with his commander in writing and appeal to the next higher command. For this reason Prussian victories were often credited to the chief of staff rather than the nominal commander.

Helmuth von Moltke the Elder, chief from 1857, each year trained the twelve best graduates of the Kriegsakademie himself through war games, map exercises and staff rides, and called them the nervous system of the army. Against Austria and France he issued brief directives and left subordinate staffs to work out the details. After unification in 1871 it became the Imperial German General Staff, with officers from Saxony, Württemberg and Bavaria. In August 1914 most of its officers joined the field armies, and the rest formed the General Staff of the Field Army within the Supreme Army Command.

The Treaty of Versailles ordered the Great General Staff dissolved, but Hans von Seeckt disguised it as the Truppenamt and kept training staff officers in the military districts, and the former chief of staff Paul von Hindenburg was elected Reichspräsident in 1925. In the Second World War its influence declined, as Hermann Göring's Luftwaffe gained weight and Hitler used the Armed Forces High Command as a rival planning staff. The Bundeswehr opened a new Army Academy in 1957.
german-labour-front: As early as March 1933, two months after Adolf Hitler became Chancellor, the Sturmabteilung began to attack trade union offices without legal consequences. Offices were occupied, furnishings destroyed, documents stolen or burned, and union members beaten, thrown out of windows and in some cases killed, while the police declared themselves without jurisdiction. The Nazi Party leadership adopted a general policy only in May. On 2 May 1933 union headquarters throughout Germany were occupied, their funds confiscated and the unions abolished, and their leaders were beaten and arrested.

Many were sent to concentration camps. The German Labour Front, the Deutsche Arbeitsfront, was created in May 1933 to take over the seized assets, and Hitler appointed Robert Ley, who had no previous experience of labour relations, to lead it.

Three weeks later Hitler issued a decree banning collective bargaining and appointing labour trustees to regulate labour contracts, which in effect outlawed strikes. Ley promised to restore absolute leadership in a factory to the employer. Unlike the unions, the Front also included employers and members of the professions, and its founding law said its aim was not to protect workers but to create a social and productive community of all Germans.

The trustees followed the wishes of employers, and Hitler wanted wages kept low. In February 1935 a workbook system was introduced: the employer kept each worker's book and could refuse to release it, which prevented the worker from being legally employed elsewhere.

To offset these restrictions the Front offered leisure through Strength Through Joy, which provided concerts, adult education, subsidised theatre and opera tickets and cheap holidays, especially cruises. The number of people taking holiday cruises rose from 2.3 million in 1934 to 10.3 million in 1938. At Prora on Rügen it began a seaside complex 4.5 kilometres long, planned for 20,000 beds, which was never finished. It also subsidised a car factory, partly from payroll deductions, but none of the 340,000 workers paying for a Volkswagen received one, since the factory was turned to war production after the invasion of Poland.

Membership was in theory voluntary, but workers found it hard to get a job without it, and many unemployed people were drafted into the Front, given uniforms and tools and put to work. By 1939 it had over 35,000 full-time employees. It ran the Bank of German Labour and programmes of medical screening, occupational training and legal assistance, and the Beauty of Labour organisation, which aimed to improve workplaces with renovations and new canteens. It also organised the Reichsberufswettkampf, a national vocational competition.
german-peasants-war: In the sixteenth century the Holy Roman Empire was a decentralised body of hundreds of largely independent territories, with Charles V as emperor. Princes tried to force freer peasants into serfdom by raising taxes and introducing Roman civil law, which brought land into their personal ownership. Nobles had defeated the cities and peasants in the Cities Wars of 1440–60 and then raised rents, tightened serfdom and restricted access to the commons.

In the course of the war local groups presented lists of demands, and a study of hundreds of them found that 90 percent attacked serfdom, 81 percent restrictions on the commons and 72 percent demanded lower rents. Historians still disagree about whether the revolt arose chiefly from economic grievances, from the religious controversy around Martin Luther, or from resistance to a centralising state.

The revolt began in the harvest of 1524 at Stühlingen, south of the Black Forest, when the Countess of Lupfen ordered serfs to gather snail shells for use as thread spools. Within days 1,200 peasants had gathered and drawn up a list of grievances, and within weeks most of south-western Germany was in revolt.

On 15 and 20 March 1525 peasants of Upper Swabia meeting at Memmingen adopted the Twelve Articles, which were printed over 25,000 times in two months. Peasants in the Odenwald and Neckar valley, led by Jakob Rohrbach, took Weinsberg and forced the Count of Helfenstein and about 70 nobles to run the gauntlet of pikes.

The princes' armies, among them that of the Swabian League under Georg, Truchsess von Waldburg, then won a series of battles. At Böblingen on 12 May the Württemberg band lost approximately 3,000 peasants, with estimates from 2,000 to 9,000, while the League lost no more than 40. On 15 May the troops of Philip I of Hesse and Duke George of Saxony defeated Thomas Müntzer's force near Frankenhausen. Peasants at Königshofen on 2 June and near Würzburg were also beaten. By September 1525 all fighting and punitive action had ended.

Up to 100,000 of about 300,000 poorly armed peasants were killed. The rebels lacked a command structure, artillery and cavalry, and the separate bands were cut off from one another by territorial divisions. Luther condemned the revolt in Against the Murderous, Thieving Hordes of Peasants, which contributed to its defeat. Surviving peasants were fined and achieved few of their goals, and the war reduced their rights and freedoms and pushed them out of political life, although in some upper Swabian territories they kept seats on territorial assemblies. Charles V and Pope Clement VII thanked the Swabian League for its intervention. In 1850 Friedrich Engels wrote The Peasant War in Germany, reading the events as prefiguring the revolutions of 1848.
german-reunification: After the unconditional surrender of 1945, Germany was occupied and divided by the four Allied powers, and no peace treaty followed. The American, British and French zones formed the Federal Republic of Germany on 23 May 1949, and the Soviet zone formed the German Democratic Republic in October of the same year. West Germany joined NATO in 1955, and in 1952 the Western Allies and West Germany rejected the Soviet idea of a neutral reunified Germany.

For decades reunification seemed unlikely. In the 1980s many left-wing parties in West Germany, especially the SPD and the Greens, favoured lasting coexistence. East Germany began to falter on 2 May 1989, when Hungary removed its border fence with Austria and thousands of East Germans fled west through Hungary.

The Peaceful Revolution, a series of protests by East German citizens, led to the fall of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989. On 28 November, Chancellor Helmut Kohl announced a ten-point programme for closer cooperation towards eventual reunification. East Germany held its first free elections on 18 March 1990. A treaty on monetary, economic and social union took effect on 1 July, when the West German Deutsche Mark replaced the East German mark.

On 23 August 1990 the East German parliament, the Volkskammer, declared the accession of the German Democratic Republic to the Federal Republic under Article 23 of the West German Basic Law, effective 3 October. On 12 September the two German states and the four Allies signed the Two Plus Four Treaty in Moscow. A treaty with Poland on 14 November confirmed the Oder–Neisse line as the permanent eastern frontier.

The reunited state was not a new one but an enlarged continuation of the Federal Republic, which kept West Germany's seats in the European Economic Community, NATO and the United Nations.
