The Two Plus Four Treaty entered into force on 15 March 1991 and ended the remaining limits on German sovereignty, and the last Russian occupation troops left on 31 August 1994.

The official term is Deutsche Einheit, German unity, and 3 October became the national holiday, German Unity Day; 9 November, the day the Wall fell, was thought unsuitable because it was also the anniversary of the Nazi pogroms of 1938. Not everyone welcomed unification: Margaret Thatcher told Mikhail Gorbachev that the United Kingdom did not want it. The economic restructuring of the east was costly.
german-revolution-of-1918-1919: The First World War exposed weaknesses in the German Empire's social and political structures. The Allied blockade from 1914 to 1919 cut off imported food and led to widespread hunger as early as the Turnip Winter of 1916 and 1917, while profiteering, inflation and class antagonism rose. The initial enthusiasm for the war waned. After the Russian Revolution of October 1917, the moderate Social Democratic Party leadership drew a line between itself and the Bolsheviks, and fear of civil war on the Russian model shaped its choices. When the request for a ceasefire came, the war-weary population wanted only peace, and Wilson's Fourteen Points fed the belief that a democratic Germany would get a just peace.

The revolution began on 29 October 1918, when sailors at Kiel mutinied against an unauthorized naval order to sail against the British Royal Navy. By 7 November it controlled all the large coastal cities and had spread to Cologne and Munich, where Kurt Eisner proclaimed the People's State of Bavaria on 8 November. By the end of the month the dynastic rulers of the other German states had abdicated without bloodshed. On 9 November Chancellor Prince Max of Baden announced that the Emperor had renounced the throne and handed the chancellorship to Friedrich Ebert, and a republic was proclaimed. Wilhelm II fled to Holland the next day.

On 10 November the Council of the People's Deputies was formed as a provisional government of the two main socialist parties under Ebert, who kept most of the imperial officer corps and administration in place. The split between moderate and radical socialists turned violent. The Spartacist uprising of January 1919 failed and led to the murders of Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht by members of the Freikorps. Local soviet republics appeared in Bavaria, Bremen and Würzburg and were put down.

On 19 January 1919 Germans voted for a constituent national assembly, in an election that included women for the first time. It met at Weimar from 6 February and accepted the Treaty of Versailles on 16 June. The revolution is generally said to end on 11 August 1919, when the Weimar Constitution was adopted. It ended the monarchies of the Empire and the states, abolished hereditary titles of nobility and introduced equal suffrage, creating a representative democracy new to Germany.

It left much of the military hierarchy and imperial civil service, including the judiciary, untouched, and many who stayed were monarchists. Far-right extremists used the stab-in-the-back myth to blame communists, socialists and Jews for the defeat. The Kapp Putsch of March 1920 collapsed within days under a general strike, and the Nazi Beer Hall Putsch of 9 November 1923 was stopped in Munich. The Weimar Republic eventually ended with the ascent of Hitler.
german-south-west-africa: European contact began in January 1486, when the Portuguese explorer Diogo Cão landed at Cape Cross, but settlement stayed limited and temporary for centuries. The London Missionary Society founded a small mission at Blydeverwacht in February 1805, and in 1840 it handed its work to the German Rhenish Missionary Society, whose missionaries, among them Franz Heinrich Kleinschmidt and Carl Hugo Hahn, founded churches across the territory. Merchants and farmers set up outposts at the same time.

In 1882 the Bremen merchant Adolf Lüderitz asked Chancellor Otto von Bismarck for protection for a station at Angra Pequena, later named Lüderitz. The German flag was raised on 7 August 1884, and German claims were confirmed at the Conference of Berlin. A law of 17 April 1886 created a dual legal system, with one set of laws for Europeans and another for Africans. By 1913 the colony had 213,000 people, of whom 14,830 were white. Mixed-race marriages were banned in 1905, and Africans were confined to reservations and forced to carry identity documents.

Uprisings against German rule began with the Nama under Hendrik Witbooi in 1893 and 1894. In 1904 the Herero rose, and about 150 German settlers were killed. Lieutenant General Lothar von Trotha, with 14,000 more troops, defeated them at the Battle of Waterberg. He ordered the Herero to leave the country or be killed, and they were driven into the waterless Omaheke, where many died of thirst. The Nama fought on under Witbooi and Jakobus Morenga until 1907 and 1908. Between 25,000 and 100,000 Herero, more than 10,000 Nama and 1,749 Germans died.

Survivors were held in camps and used as forced labour, and many were later dispossessed and segregated. The First World War ended German rule: South African troops attacked in September 1914, and the last Schutztruppe commander, Victor Franke, capitulated near Khorab on 9 July 1915.

After the war the territory passed to the Union of South Africa as South West Africa under a League of Nations mandate, and it became independent as Namibia on 21 March 1990. The genocide was recognised by the United Nations and by the Federal Republic of Germany. Many German names, buildings and businesses remain, about 30,000 people of German descent live in Namibia, and German is still widely used. Lutheranism is the predominant Christian denomination.
germania: Roman geographers placed Germania roughly between the Rhine in the west and the Vistula in the east, from the upper Danube northwards along the North and Baltic seas to the known parts of southern Scandinavia. The free lands are also called Magna Germania, and by modern scholars Germania Libera or the Germanic Barbaricum. The origin of the name Germani is uncertain. Tacitus wrote that the name had once belonged only to the Tungri, west of the Rhine, and was later extended to supposedly related peoples beyond it.

The country held many peoples with little unity among them, and river names suggest that another Indo-European group lived there, probably under Germanic domination. Archaeologically it corresponds, from the 1st to the 4th century CE, to the Roman Iron Age: largely agrarian, without cities or coinage of its own. Amber was a primary export, and Roman luxury goods were imported on a large scale and have been found as far away as Scandinavia and western Russia.

Julius Caesar met peoples from beyond the Rhine during the Gallic Wars and called their homeland Germania, a name the Romans appear to have borrowed from the Gauls. Augustus later carried Roman arms as far as the Elbe and in 7 BCE created a short-lived province, Germania Antiqua, before the victory of Arminius ended the attempt. The Rhine became the frontier. Germani such as the Ubii and Sicambri were settled on the Roman bank, which was heavily affected by the Revolt of the Batavi under Gaius Julius Civilis in 69–70 CE.

Under the Flavian dynasty the two provinces were organised, Germania Inferior with its headquarters at Colonia, the modern Cologne, and Germania Superior at Mogontiacum. The Romans also occupied the land between the Rhine, Main and Danube, known as the Agri Decumates. In the 3rd century confederations such as the Alemanni and Franks emerged and raided the provinces, and around 280 CE the Agri Decumates were evacuated and taken by the Alemanni. In 406 a large number of people fleeing the Huns crossed the Rhine, and Roman rule there eventually collapsed.

Much of Germania, including all the former Roman provinces, was eventually incorporated into the Frankish Empire and later East Francia. The name survived in learned use: it is attested in Old English translations of Bede and Orosius, and since the 17th century the usual English name of Germany has been derived from it, as are the names of that country in many other languages.
germania-inferior: Germania Inferior, Lower Germany, lay on the west bank of the Rhine and bordered the North Sea. The adjective refers to its position downstream of the Rhine relative to Germania Superior. According to Ptolemy it included the Rhine from its mouth up to the mouth of the Obringa, a river identified with either the Aar or the Moselle. Its territory included present-day Luxembourg, the southern Netherlands, part of Belgium and part of North Rhine-Westphalia west of the Rhine.

Its principal settlements included Castra Vetera and Colonia Ulpia Traiana near Xanten, Coriovallum (Heerlen), Lugdunum Batavorum (Katwijk), Forum Hadriani (Voorburg), Ulpia Noviomagus Batavorum (Nijmegen), Traiectum (Utrecht), Atuatuca Tungrorum (Tongeren), Bona (Bonn) and the provincial capital, Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium, now Cologne.

Roman settlement began around 50 BCE, within the province of Gallia Belgica. Julius Caesar invaded the region in 57 BCE and in the next three years annihilated several tribes, among them the Eburones and the Menapii, probably Celtic or mixed Celtic and Germanic peoples, though Caesar called them Germanic. Germanic influence, mainly through the Tungri, grew in Roman times and led to the assimilation of the Celtic peoples.

The area was largely occupied from the reign of Augustus but became a province only under Domitian, about 85 CE, after his campaigns against the Chatti of 83 to 85. Germania Inferior and Germania Superior were then split from Gallia Belgica. The army of Germania Inferior included several legions at different times, of which Legio I Minervia and Legio XXX Ulpia Victrix were the most permanent. The Classis Germanica, the fleet that patrolled the Rhine and the North Sea coast, was based at Castra Vetera and later at Cologne.

In the 4th century the province was renamed Germania Secunda, as the Notitia Dignitatum, an early 5th-century document, attests. It was governed by a consularis and belonged to the Diocese of Gaul. It remained heavily garrisoned until the end of Roman control and was inhabited by Romans and Ripuarian Franks in the 5th century. Cologne became the seat of a Christian bishopric whose ecclesiastical province survived the fall of the Western Roman Empire, and the former province became the core of the Frankish Kingdom.
germanic-peoples: The Germanic peoples were tribal groups who lived in Northern Europe during Classical antiquity and the Early Middle Ages. Scholars generally agree that Germanic languages can be spoken of from about 500 BCE. Archaeologists usually associate the earliest clearly identifiable Germanic-speaking peoples with the Jastorf culture of central and northern Germany and southern Denmark from the 6th to 1st centuries BCE. Some scholars call for the term's abandonment as a modern construct, since it implies a common identity for which there is little evidence, while others defend it on the ground of a common language. The name Germani, whose etymology is unknown, was first used for a large category of peoples distinct from the Gauls and Scythians by Julius Caesar, around 55 BCE.

The Cimbri, Teutones and Ambrones, whom Caesar later classified as Germanic, migrated late in the 2nd century BCE and defeated several Roman armies in the Cimbrian War of 113-101 BCE before being defeated. Under Augustus the Romans tried to conquer Germania between the Rhine and the Elbe but withdrew after the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in 9 CE, and thereafter they managed the frontier with the fortified Limes Germanicus. After the Marcomannic Wars of 166 to 180, new groupings appear, such as the Franks, Goths, Saxons and Alemanni.

In the Migration Period, traditionally dated from 375 to 568, Germanic peoples entered the Roman Empire and established kingdoms within the Western Roman Empire. The Franks became the most powerful, and Merovingian Frankia was divided into Austrasia, Neustria and Burgundy. Pepin the Short became king in 751 and founded the Carolingian dynasty, and his son Charlemagne conquered the Lombards, Saxons and Bavarians and was crowned Roman emperor in 800.

Roman sources portrayed Germanic life as more primitive than archaeology shows: it has revealed a complex society and economy. Agriculture was organised around villages rather than the large villae rusticae of the Roman provinces, and only about 30 percent of Germania was covered in forest. Despite Tacitus's claim that the Germani had little iron, smiths were skilful. Roman sources report decisions made in a popular assembly, the thing, alongside kings and war leaders.

The peoples shared a native script, the runes, whose earliest form has 24 characters, and a common poetic tradition. Most continental Germanic peoples and the Anglo-Saxons converted to Christianity during Late Antiquity, the Saxons and Scandinavians much later.
germanicus: Germanicus was born in Rome on 24 May 15 BCE to Nero Claudius Drusus and Antonia the Younger, and his younger siblings were Livilla and the future emperor Claudius. His grandparents included the triumvir Mark Antony and Octavia Minor on his mother's side. His father's victories in Germania earned the name Germanicus, which was awarded to the father after his death in 9 BCE. In 4 CE his uncle Tiberius adopted him, and he entered the gens Julia as Germanicus Julius Caesar. He married Agrippina the Elder, a granddaughter of Augustus, and was the father of Caligula and the maternal grandfather of Nero.

He became quaestor in 7 CE, five years before the legal age, and was sent to Illyricum to help Tiberius suppress the Pannonian and Dalmatian rebellion, where he defeated the Mazaei. In 12 CE he was consul, and in 13 CE Augustus appointed him commander on the Rhine, with eight legions, about one third of the Roman army. When Augustus died in 14 CE the legions of the Lower Rhine mutinied over unpaid bonuses, and Germanicus dealt with them. Their attempt to proclaim him emperor failed, since he stayed loyal and led them against the German tribes instead.

He campaigned in Germania from 14 to 16 CE, avenged the defeat in the Teutoburg Forest and recovered two of the three legionary eagles lost there. On 26 May 17 he held a triumph in which Thusnelda, the wife of Arminius, and her three-year-old son were led among the captives, although Arminius himself was never taken. In 18 CE he was given command in the east with imperium maius, reorganized the provinces of Asia Minor and incorporated Cappadocia and Commagene.

In the east he quarrelled with Gnaeus Calpurnius Piso, the governor of Syria whom Tiberius had appointed. Germanicus fell ill at Antioch, became convinced that Piso was poisoning him, and renounced their friendship. He died on 10 October 19. Several sources blamed Piso, acting on the orders of Tiberius, but this was never proven. Piso died before his trial in the Senate ended, ostensibly by suicide, and Tacitus supposes that Tiberius may have had him killed.

Tacitus described Germanicus as a fine general, kind and temperate. The historian Anthony A. Barrett accepts that he was an able general. Ancient writers often contrasted him as a tragic hero with Tiberius as a tyrant. In 4 CE Germanicus also wrote a Latin version of Aratus's Phainomena, which survives.
germanisation: Germanisation covers different forms and degrees of the expansion of the German language and of elements of German culture. There are cases of complete assimilation, as with the pagan Slavs in the Diocese of Bamberg in the 11th century, and of voluntary adoption, as in the law of Imperial and present-day Japan, which follows the German model. It took place through cultural contact, by the political decision of the adopting party, or by force. In linguistics the word also describes non-German languages taking in many German words. In Slavic countries it is often understood as the acculturation of Slavic and Baltic speakers after conquest by or contact with Germans.

Early Germanisation went with the Ostsiedlung in the Middle Ages, in lands formerly inhabited by Slavic tribes such as the Obotrites, Veleti and Sorbs. Historians note that this settlement did not include deliberate Germanisation. In East Prussia the Teutonic Order decimated and resettled the Old Prussians, and their language became extinct in the 17th century. After the 1620 Battle of White Mountain the Bohemian lands saw two centuries of recatholicisation and growing influence of German-speaking elites. Emperor Joseph II decreed that German would replace Latin as the official language of government.

In the 19th century Prussia and, to a lesser degree, Austria imposed German culture and language on non-German peoples, Slavs in particular. After 1815 Prussia's king promised Poles in Posen the use of their language, and policy eased in 1815–30. About 350,000 Poles moved to the Ruhr in the late 19th century, where they were watched by the authorities and many changed their names to Germanised forms. Under the Nazis the policy had an ethnic and racial meaning, and plans assumed that up to 50 per cent of Czechs could be Germanised while 80 to 85 per cent of Poles were to be deported to western Siberia.

In occupied Poland an estimated 50,000 to 200,000 children judged racially acceptable were taken from their families to be raised as Germans, and at least 10,000 of them are estimated to have been murdered after being judged unfit. Only 10 to 15 per cent returned to their families after the war. The pressure of Germanisation provoked national movements among Czechs, Poles, Slovene speakers and others in the 19th century. Josef Dobrovský's first modern grammar of Czech, from 1809, was published in German because Czech was not used in academic writing.
germantown-philadelphia: Germantown lies about six miles north-west of the centre of Philadelphia and stretches for about two miles along Germantown Avenue. It was founded as an independent borough and incorporated in 1689, separated from the rural Germantown Township by Washington Lane; its north-western border moved several times before the Act of Consolidation absorbed it into the City of Philadelphia in 1854. The former borough now makes up two neighbourhoods, Germantown and East Germantown, bordered by Mount Airy, Logan, Nicetown–Tioga and East Falls.

The first thirteen families, who arrived on 6 October 1683, were nearly all Dutch, with some Swiss; they had moved to Krefeld and Monsheim to escape persecution for their Mennonite beliefs before emigrating. Their leader, the German Franz Pastorius, named the town and became its first bailiff. The town stayed largely Dutch-speaking until 1709, when German immigration grew. In 1688 Pastorius, Gerret Hendericks and the brothers Derick and Abraham op den Graeff wrote their petition against slavery at the house of Thones Kunders, which began the process that ended slavery among the Society of Friends in 1776 and in Pennsylvania in 1780.

In 1723 the first congregation of Schwarzenau Brethren in the New World formed there. During the British occupation of Philadelphia, British units were quartered in Germantown, and in the battle of 4 October 1777 the Continental Army attacked them and withdrew after its troops fired on one another in the confusion. George Washington and his family later lodged at the Deshler-Morris House to escape the yellow fever epidemic of 1793. In 1832 the Philadelphia, Germantown and Norristown Railroad, the city's first, linked the town to Center City.

Italians began to settle in 1880. In the 20th century the Great Migration brought African Americans to the city, and from 1954 to 1956 an influx of lower-income African Americans was followed by white flight to the suburbs, which a former president of the Germantown Historical Society attributes to blockbusting.

Colonial Germantown and Rittenhousetown are National Historic Landmark Districts, and Cliveden, the estate of Benjamin Chew, the John Johnson House, a stop on the Underground Railroad, and Wyck House are among its landmarks open to the public. La Salle University's west campus stands on the grounds of the old Germantown Hospital.
germanus-of-auxerre: The main source for Germanus's life is the Vita Germani written by Constantius of Lyon around 480. According to it he was the son of Rusticus and Germanilla, of one of the noblest families of Gaul, studied at Arles and Lyon and then eloquence and civil law in Rome, and married Eustachia. The emperor made him one of the six dukes governing the Gallic provinces, with his residence at Auxerre. After a quarrel over hunting trophies hung on a tree once used for pagan worship, Bishop Amator tonsured him against his will and made him a deacon; Germanus succeeded him and was consecrated on 7 July 418.

Around 429 an assembly of Gaulish bishops sent Germanus and Lupus, Bishop of Troyes, to Britain, where Pelagianism was said to be spreading among the clergy under a bishop's son named Agricola. On the way, at Nanterre, he met the girl who became St. Geneviève of Paris. In Britain he defeated the Pelagians in a public debate and then gave thanks at the grave of Saint Alban, who, he said, revealed the story of his martyrdom to him in a dream; the Passio Albani may have come from his circle at Auxerre. Tradition places the Alleluia victory near Mold in North Wales.

Constantius also tells of a second visit with Severus, Bishop of Trier, though some scholars think it a doublet of the first. The Historia Brittonum of about 829 adds a legend that Germanus condemned and cursed Vortigern, a story that appears to have no historical basis.

Germanus confronted Goar, king of the Alans, and died at Ravenna while pleading with the imperial government for leniency towards the people of Armorica, against whom Aëtius had sent the Alans. His tomb is venerated in the Abbey of Saint-Germain d'Auxerre, and the church of Saint-Germain l'Auxerrois in Paris bears his name. In Britain he is the patron of Selby Abbey and of churches at St Germans in Cornwall and elsewhere, and medieval tradition often confused him with the Welsh Saint Garmon. Saunders Lewis made his visit the subject of the radio play Buchedd Garmon in 1936.
germany: Ancient humans were present in what is now Germany at least 600,000 years ago. Germanic peoples expanded from southern Scandinavia and northern Germany, and the Celtic-speaking peoples of the south were later assimilated by them. Under Augustus, the Roman Empire created a short-lived province of Germania between the Rhine and Elbe rivers, and in 9 CE Arminius defeated three Roman legions in the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest, an outcome that dissuaded the Romans from conquering Germania. After the invasion of the Huns in 375 and the decline of Rome from 395, the Franks established the Frankish Kingdom.

Charlemagne founded the Carolingian Empire in 800, and after its division in 843 the Kingdom of Germany and the Holy Roman Empire emerged from the eastern successor kingdom of East Francia. Northern German regions became the centre of the Protestant Reformation in the 16th century. After the Holy Roman Empire's dissolution in 1806 the German Confederation was formed in 1815, and Prussia led unification into the German Empire in 1871. The Weimar Republic replaced the Empire after World War I. The Nazi rise to power in 1933 led to a totalitarian dictatorship under Adolf Hitler, which resulted in World War II and the Holocaust.

In 1949, after the war and Allied occupation, Germany was organised into two polities with limited sovereignty: the Federal Republic of Germany, or West Germany, and the German Democratic Republic, or East Germany. The first was a founding member of the European Economic Community, while the second was a communist Eastern Bloc state and a founding member of the Warsaw Pact. The former East German states joined the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990, and Germany regained its full sovereignty on 15 March 1991.

Germany covers 357,022 square kilometres between the Baltic Sea and the North Sea in the north and the Alps in the south, and its highest point is the Zugspitze at 2,963 metres. It is a federal parliamentary republic of sixteen Länder under the Basic Law of 1949, and Berlin is the capital and most populous city. The census of 2023 recorded a population of 84.7 million. Four national minorities live in the country: a Danish minority, the Sorbs, the Roma and Sinti, and the Frisians.
gero-the-great: Gero was the son of Count Thietmar, tutor of Henry the Fowler. In 937 Otto I is thought to have made him count and margrave on the lower Saale in succession to his brother Siegfried. The appointment angered Thankmar, the king's half-brother, who rebelled in 938 with Eberhard of Franconia and Wichmann the Elder; Thankmar died within a year and Gero kept his march. Thietmar of Merseburg later called him Margrave of the East, and historians long spoke of a March of Gero, though some charters describing it are now considered forgeries.

His early war against the Slavs went badly, as they refused tribute. After an Obodrite attack in 939, Gero invited thirty Slav chieftains to a banquet and killed all but one. When the Stodorani revolted he restored German control, and he bribed the baptised prince Tugumir to deliver his people; the Obodrites and Wilzes then submitted. In 954 he put down a revolt of the Ukrani with Conrad the Red, and in 955 he fought with the king and Liudolf, Duke of Swabia, against a Slav alliance that was defeated on the Drosa.

While Otto was in Italy in 962–963, Gero forced Mieszko I of the Polans to pay tribute and recognise German sovereignty, and Widukind of Corvey wrote that Lusatia was reduced to the last degree of servitude. Gero subjected the Liutizi and Milzini and extended German rule over the land between the Elbe and the Bober, where the Slav population was reduced to serfdom.

After the death of his eldest son Siegfried, Otto's godson, Gero went on pilgrimage to Rome in 959 and in 960 founded the collegiate church of St Cyriakus and the convent of Gernrode, which received much of his wealth. He died on 20 May 965, when his march reached the Neisse. Unpopular with the Saxon nobility for his low birth and moral strictness, he was remembered in the Nibelungenlied as the marcgrâve Gêre. His territory was split into several marches, among them the Northern March, the March of Meissen and the March of Merseburg, and his tomb at Gernrode bears a painting of about 1350 showing him over a vanquished Wend.
gerousia: Sparta's political power was divided between three bodies, the Gerousia, the Ephorate and the Assembly. Scholars debate their relative power, but the Gerousia was apparently the most prestigious. Its earliest mention is the Great Rhetra, dated perhaps to about 700 BCE and quoted by Plutarch, which fixed its membership at thirty, including the two kings. The Spartans held that the lawgiver Lycurgus had created it, and Plato said it tempered the feverish government of kings with the moderating influence of old age. Scholars assume it descended from a group of advisers to the kings, like the noble councillors of Homeric epic.

The twenty-eight gerontes had to be at least sixty, the age at which Spartans stopped army service. They were elected by acclamation: candidates passed before the Assembly, and a jury shut in a windowless building judged whose shouts were loudest. Plutarch says a newly elected geron crowned himself with a wreath, visited the temples and was feted at banquets. Aristotle called the procedure childish and the selection dynastic. The gerontes were probably drawn from a few families that held a de facto monopoly. The kings sat by birth and, entering before sixty, usually served far longer, and a king who was absent could have his closest relative in the Gerousia vote for him.

The Gerousia was Sparta's highest court and tried capital cases, even those of kings. Pausanias says that in 403 BCE it joined the ephors and the other king in the trial of king Pausanias, who was acquitted. It also prepared motions for the Assembly, a power of preliminary deliberation, and guarded the law. In 243 BCE, according to Plutarch, it rejected the reforms of Agis IV by one vote.

In 227 BCE Cleomenes III, after abolishing the Ephorate, reduced the Gerousia's power and probably made election to it annual. Pausanias says he destroyed its power and set up a new magistrate, the patronomos. The Gerousia is still mentioned in the exile of twenty-four leading Spartans in 149 BCE. By the reign of Augustus its members numbered twenty-three, and the minimum age had probably dropped to perhaps forty. Inscriptions list the gerontes of each year, but the body had lost much of its authority and prestige.
gers: The Gers is a department in the region of Occitania, in south-western France. It is bordered by the departments of Hautes-Pyrénées and Pyrénées-Atlantiques to the south, Haute-Garonne and Tarn-et-Garonne to the east, Lot-et-Garonne to the north and Landes to the west. Its inhabitants are called Gersois and Gersoises, after the Gers River. The landscape is one of sleepy bastide villages and rolling hills, with the Pyrenees visible to the south. Annual rainfall varies from more than 900 mm in the south-west to less than 700 mm in the north-east, around Auch, Condom and Lectoure. Winters are mild and summers hot and dry.

The Gers is one of the original 83 departments created during the French Revolution, on 4 March 1790. It was formed from parts of the former provinces of Guyenne and Gascony. In 1808 it lost Lavit, on its north-eastern side, to the newly created department of Tarn-et-Garonne.

The culture is largely agricultural, with weight placed on local food and drink: Armagnac brandy, Côtes de Gascogne wine, Floc de Gascogne, foie gras and wild mushrooms. Maize, colza, sunflowers and grain are the main crops. Gascon, a dialect of Occitan, is spoken only by a minority. The department is among the most thinly peopled and most rural areas in Western Europe, with about 31 people per square kilometre and a population of 192,645 in 2023.

Alexandre Dumas, père, made the Gersois d'Artagnan the fourth musketeer of The Three Musketeers, and a museum to d'Artagnan stands in the village of Lupiac. A horse race at the Auteuil Hippodrome is named after André Boingnères, a local race-horse owner and mayor of Termes-d'Armagnac from 1951 to 1976.
gertrude-of-merania: Gertrude was the daughter of the Bavarian Count Berthold IV of Andechs, Margrave of Carniola and Istria, and of Agnes of the Saxon House of Wettin. Her elder sister Agnes of Merania married King Philip II of France, and her younger sister, Saint Hedwig of Silesia, married the Piast duke Henry I the Bearded. Among her brothers, Otto inherited the title of Duke of Merania, Henry took over Carniola and Istria, and Berthold became Archbishop of Kalocsa and a close adviser to her. Her parents arranged political marriages for their daughters, and Gertrude married the Árpád prince Andrew II, younger son of King Béla III of Hungary, before 1204.

Andrew's marriage drew him into the conflict over the German throne: he joined his father-in-law in backing Duke Philip of Swabia, while his elder brother King Emeric of Hungary supported King Otto IV. Gertrude exerted much political influence over her husband, and it was probably she who persuaded him to conspire again against Emeric. Emeric went unarmed to Andrew's camp near Varasd and Andrew surrendered, was arrested and soon escaped, and Gertrude was sent back to her father for a time. Andrew took over the government on Emeric's death in 1204, officially as regent for his nephew Ladislaus III, who died in exile a year later.

As queen from 1205 she was regent during her husband's frequent absences, and the chronicler Dietrich of Apolda says she ran the kingdom like a man. Medieval chroniclers say she gave Hungarian land to her favourites, as much as a third of the country, which the magnates recovered after her death. Her brother Berthold was made Archbishop of Kalocsa in 1206 and Voivode of Transylvania in 1212. She and Andrew had five children, among them King Béla IV and Saint Elizabeth of Hungary.

While Andrew was campaigning in Galicia, a Hungarian noble, Peter, son of Töre, assassinated the queen in 1213, during a hunt in the Pilis Mountains with Berthold and their guest Duke Leopold VI of Austria. Her body was torn to pieces, while her brother and Leopold narrowly escaped. Recent research suggests the killer may have acted alone with a personal motive, and that Andrew, on learning of it, had him impaled. Decades later Béla IV used the killing for political purposes. Andrew then married Yolanda de Courtenay.

Gertrude is the villain of József Katona's play Bánk bán (1819) and Ferenc Erkel's opera of 1861, retellings in which Hungarian nobles conspire against her. They are strongly fictionalised: there are no reliable sources on the assassination, and no proof that she was an exploitative regent.
gessius-florus: Gessius Florus was born in Clazomenae. According to Josephus, Emperor Nero appointed him seventh procurator of Judea, in place of Lucceius Albinus, because his wife Cleopatra was a friend of Nero's wife Poppaea. Josephus, the main source for his term, treats him as the chief cause of the First Jewish–Roman War and stresses his hostility to the Jewish population of the province.

Governing from Caesarea, Florus favoured the city's Greek population over its Jewish one, and the Greek population took advantage of it. In one provocation, while Jews were worshipping in their synagogue, a Hellenist sacrificed birds on a chamber pot at its entrance, which made the building ritually unclean. The Jews sent men to seek redress; Florus accepted eight talents to hear them, then refused to listen and had the petitioners imprisoned.

He then had seventeen talents taken from the treasury of the Temple in Jerusalem, saying the money was for the emperor. The city fell into unrest, and some Jews mocked him by passing round a basket to collect coins as if he were poor. The next day Florus sent soldiers into Jerusalem to raid the city and arrest a number of its leaders, who were whipped and crucified, though many of them were Roman citizens. After the war broke out he was replaced as procurator by Marcus Antonius Julianus.
gesta-hungarorum: The Gesta Hungarorum, or The Deeds of the Hungarians, is the earliest Hungarian chronicle to survive. It was written in Latin by an unidentified author, called Anonymus in scholarship since the first Hungarian translation of 1790. In the opening sentence he describes himself as 'P who is called magister, and sometime notary of the most glorious Béla, king of Hungary of fond memory'. Four Hungarian kings bore the name, and most historians identify him as Béla III, who died in 1196.

Its sources included the Bible, Isidore of Seville's Etymologiae, the Exordia Scythica, Regino of Prüm's Chronicon and early medieval romances of Alexander the Great. He also used folk songs and ballads, and knew a version of the late 11th-century Hungarian Chronicle. The work survives in one manuscript of 24 folios in Gothic minuscule, made in the middle or second half of the 13th century. It is now in the Széchényi National Library in Budapest.

The Gesta has a prologue and 57 chapters. Its main subject is the conquest of the Carpathian Basin at the turn of the 9th and 10th centuries. The first seven chapters describe the Hungarians' supposed homeland, called Scythia or Dentumoger, and trace their ancestors to the Scythians and Huns.

The next chapters follow the Hungarians past Kiev and describe their fights with the Rus' and the Cumans. Anonymus names opponents of the Hungarians that no other source mentions, including Glad, Menumorut and Gelou, and does not name those known from sources written around 900. One theory holds that he took these names from place names.

The single manuscript suggests the chronicle was not much read in its own time or later. Later chronicles did not use it, which Gyula Kristó takes to mean that contemporaries knew Anonymus had invented most details of his account of the conquest. Scholars at Halle and Göttingen soon doubted it, pointing to its anachronistic account of the Rus' principalities, and in the 1780s Juraj Sklenár dismissed it because it never mentions Great Moravia.

Romanian historians have presented Gelou, Glad and Menumorut as Romanian rulers, taking them as proof of Romanian polities at the time of the conquest. Modern views are mixed. Alexandru Madgearu judges the work generally credible despite chronological mistakes, while Macartney called it the most misleading of the early Hungarian texts. Dennis Deletant concludes that the case for and against Gelou and the Vlachs cannot be proven.
gestapo: After Adolf Hitler became Chancellor, Hermann Goring was named Interior Minister of Prussia, which gave him command of the largest police force in Germany. He detached the political and intelligence sections of the police, filled their ranks with Nazis, and on 26 April 1933 merged them as the Geheime Staatspolizei. A post office clerk abbreviated the name to Gestapo for a franking stamp. Goring had wanted to call it the Geheimes Polizeiamt, but its initials looked too like those of the Soviet GPU.

On 20 April 1934 Heinrich Himmler, head of the SS, took over its oversight, and it became a national agency within the Security Police. From 27 September 1939 it was administered by the Reich Security Main Office as its Amt 4.

Its first targets were political opponents such as members of the Communist Party of Germany. On 2 May 1933, a day after Hitler addressed 1.5 million people at the Tempelhofer Feld, Gestapo officers who had been shadowing some 58 trade union leaders arrested them, and the German Labour Front replaced the unions on 12 May. The Nuremberg Laws of September 1935 widened the range of denunciable behaviour, including expressions of sympathy toward Jews. The Gestapo also monitored church organisations and arrested the leaders of the White Rose student group in 1943, several of whom were executed. It operated throughout occupied Europe, where it took part in deporting workers, torturing and executing civilians and murdering Jews, and it held a vital part in the Holocaust.

The Gestapo was smaller than its reputation. By March 1937 it employed an estimated 6,500 people in fifty-four regional offices, and in 1939 only 3,000 of 20,000 men held SS ranks, mostly honorary. Most officers came from the Weimar Republic's police forces. Local offices were thin: Stettin and Frankfurt am Main had 41 men between them in 1939, and in Lower Franconia twenty-two officers oversaw 840,000 or more inhabitants. It therefore relied on ordinary citizens who denounced others, rather than on full-time informers. Torture was a routine method of extracting confessions.

The Gestapo was declared a criminal organisation by the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg, together with the SS. Its chief Heinrich Muller was never tried, having disappeared at the end of the war. In 1997 Cologne turned the former regional Gestapo headquarters, the EL-DE Haus, into a museum documenting its actions.
getulio-vargas: Getúlio Dornelles Vargas was born on 19 April 1882 in São Borja, Rio Grande do Sul, near the border with Argentina, into a powerful local family. He joined the army in 1898 and studied at the military college at Rio Pardo until 1901, when he and twenty other cadets were forced out after a protest over a lack of water. After law school he became state attorney of Rio Grande do Sul through his party and his father, and in 1911 he married Darci Lima Sarmanho. He was a state deputy, took part in the state's 1923 civil war, and became a national deputy that year. He was finance minister under Washington Luís and in 1928 became president of Rio Grande do Sul.

In the First Republic an alliance of São Paulo and Minas Gerais held power. When President Luís named another paulista, Júlio Prestes, as his successor, he broke that arrangement, and Prestes was declared winner of the 1930 election amid claims of fraud on both sides. After the assassination of Vargas's running mate João Pessoa the opposition took up arms. Vargas's provisional presidency began on 3 November 1930. He governed by decree, imprisoned opponents and created a Ministry of Labor, brought unions under state control, and introduced the secret vote and women's suffrage. He survived the Constitutionalist Revolution of 1932 and was elected president in 1934.

Citing a possible communist insurrection, Vargas seized powers in 1937 and began the Estado Novo. Opponents were arrested or exiled and the press censored. In May 1938 armed Integralists attacked the presidential palace and besieged him for hours. The Estado Novo's chief social reforms were a minimum-wage law and a single labor code. Brazil declared war on Italy and Germany on 21 August 1942 after attacks on its ships. As discontent grew, Vargas abolished censorship in 1945, but the military feared he would seize absolute power and forced him from office on 29 October.

Vargas ran in 1950 as candidate of the Brazilian Labor Party and took office on 31 January 1951. He pursued a nationalist economic policy and founded Petrobras. A crisis followed the murder of an Air Force officer outside the home of his adversary Carlos Lacerda, which implicated the chief of Vargas's personal guard. Generals demanded his resignation, and on 24 August 1954 he shot himself in the chest at Catete Palace. Many historians regard him as the most influential Brazilian politician of the twentieth century, and he was nicknamed the Father of the Poor.
geum-river: The Geum rises at Jangsu-eup in North Jeolla Province and runs north before turning south-west near Greater Daejeon. It is the third longest river in South Korea, and its basin covers 9,859 square kilometres. The upper river winds slowly through part of the Noryeongsanmaek Mountains in many meanders, while the middle and lower courses bend more gently. Its tributaries include the Gap-cheon, Yugu-cheon, Miho-cheon, Unsan-cheon, Seokseong-cheon and Nonsan-cheon, and the river and these streams have built several small alluvial plains, among them the Honam and Nonsan Plains.

From prehistoric times, through the Mumun Pottery Period and into the Three Kingdoms of Korea, the river and its tributaries served as a route from the west coast deep into the interior of the peninsula. A bronze culture flourished in the area from about 850 BCE to 100 CE, and some of the first complex societies in southern Korea briefly flourished in the valleys of its tributaries. The basin held the chiefdoms of Mahan, and later Ungjin, capital of Baekje from 475 to 525, and Sabi, its capital from 525 to 660.

Around Buyeo County the river is called the Baengmagang, the White Horse River, and many legends link Baekje with it. It is the subject of the sin minyo song Kkumkkuneun Baengmagang, Dreaming Baengmagang. The river's Korean name, Silk River, sounds like the word for diamond, and it is not to be confused with the Diamond Mountain in North Korea.

The Daecheong Dam and the Yongdam Dam on the middle and upper river supply water for farming and industry. Greater Daejeon and the farms and industries of South Chungcheong Province depend heavily on the Geum and its tributaries, and its alluvial plains are important farmland.
geumwa: Hae Geumwa's story is told in the Samguk sagi, the Samguk yusa and the Book of King Dongmyeong, which make him the second ruler of Dongbuyeo and date his reign to 48 to 7 BCE. According to the Samguk yusa, Hae Buru, old and without an heir, found a gold-coloured child like a frog, or in another reading a snail, under a large rock near Lake Gonyeon. He named the child Geumwa, golden frog, and made him crown prince. Hae Buru had founded Dongbuyeo by moving his capital east to Gaseopwon by the East Sea.

After Hae Buru's death Geumwa became king. At the Ubal river, south of Mount Taebaek, he met Lady Yuhwa, the disowned daughter of Habaek, god of the Amnok River, or in another interpretation of the sun god Haebak, and brought her to his palace. She was made pregnant by sunlight and bore Chumong. Geumwa's two sons resented the boy, as did Geumwa himself, who tried many times to destroy him before giving up. Chumong fled to Jolbon, the former Bukbuyeo, and there founded Goguryeo.

When Yuhwa died, Geumwa buried her as a queen mother, although she had never been a queen. Chumong sent him many gifts in thanks for caring for his mother, and peace seemed to return between the two kingdoms.

Geumwa was succeeded by his eldest son, Daeso, who attacked Goguryeo in the reign of its second ruler, King Yuri. Goguryeo's third ruler, King Daemusin, invaded Dongbuyeo and killed Daeso, and after internal strife Dongbuyeo fell and its lands were absorbed into Goguryeo.
geunchogo-of-baekje: Geunchogo, also called Chogo II, was the fourth son of Baekje's 11th king, Biryu, and came to the throne as its 13th king on the death of King Gye. His accession seems to have settled the long rivalry between two royal lines: the descendants of the 5th king, Chogo, whose name he took, gained a lasting hold on the throne over those of the 8th king, Goi, and the alternating kingship ended. The Samguk sagi describes him as robust in body and broad in knowledge.

Geunchogo strengthened the crown against the aristocracy and set up local government under regional heads appointed by the court. He took a queen from the Jin clan, a precedent his successors followed. The last Mahan tribes were annexed in 369, giving Baekje all of present-day Jeolla, and Gaya states west of the Nakdong River became its dependencies. In 366 he allied with Silla to the east.

When King Sayu, Gogugwon of Goguryeo, came to Chiyang in 369 with 20,000 men, Crown Prince Geungusu routed them and, by the Samguk sagi, took more than 5,000 prisoners. In 371 the king and the crown prince led 30,000 troops against the fortress of Pyongyang, where the Goguryeo king was killed by a stray arrow. Baekje then held all of Gyeonggi, Chungcheong and Jeolla and parts of Gangwon and Hwanghae. In 375 Goguryeo took the fortress of Sugok, and a drought stopped the planned revenge; the king died in the 11th month of that year.

In 372 Baekje sent a mission to the Jin court, which named Geunchogo General Stabilizing the East and Administrator-General of Lelang. Baekje became a centre of trade between China, Korea and Japan. Its ties with the Wa of Yamato Japan are shown by the Seven-Branched Sword he gave to the Yamato ruler, and the Nihon Shoki says he sent the scholars Wang In and Ajiki to teach Confucianism and Chinese characters. In his reign the scholar Go Heung compiled Seogi, a history of Baekje of which no copy survives.
gevaudan: After the conquest of Gaul the Romans kept the capital of the Gabali, Anderitum, but renamed it Gabalum, the present Javols. In the Gallo-Roman period the region was known as the Pagus Gabalicus. It later belonged to the Kingdom of the Franks and then to the Kingdom of Aquitaine, and came under the rule of the Count of Toulouse. By the beginning of the 10th century Mende had replaced Javols as its religious and administrative capital, while the western part of the region formed the Viscounty of Grèzes.

In 1096 the Count of Toulouse, leaving for the Crusade, passed his rights over eastern Gévaudan to the Bishop of Mende, and in 1166 the region was inherited by Alfonso II of Aragon. In the 12th century Bishop Adalbert of Mende used the indifference of its nominal rulers to increase his own power, and Louis VII of France granted him temporal power over the region by the Golden Bull of Gévaudan. Gévaudan thus became the first Occitan-speaking land to acknowledge the suzerainty of the king of France. Its eight baronies were in constant rebellion against the bishop.

Under the peerage of 1307 the bishop received the title of Count of Gévaudan, with the right to mint coins and dispense lower justice. Although nominally part of Languedoc, Gévaudan kept its own States General until 1789, and it lay at a crossroads of pilgrimage routes. It was very wealthy at the beginning of the 16th century, but the French Wars of Religion ruined it; Huguenots had settled there around 1550.

Gévaudan ceased to exist after the French Revolution, on 4 March 1790, when the department of Lozère was created from the former county. Its name survives above all through the Beast of Gévaudan, which has been the subject of many works of fiction.
geza-grand-prince-of-the-hungarians: Géza was the elder son of Grand Prince Taksony. His mother, according to the Gesta Hungarorum, came from the land of the Cumans, which suggests she was of Khazar, Pecheneg or Volga Bulgarian origin. The Byzantine emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus did not list him among Árpád's descendants about 950, and Gyula Kristó wrote that Géza, born about 940, was ignored because of his youth. His father arranged his marriage with Sarolt, daughter of the chieftain Gyula, who ruled Transylvania independently of the grand prince and had converted to Christianity in Constantinople. Bruno of Querfurt described her Christianity as languid and muddled.

Géza succeeded his father about 972 and adopted a centralising policy. Sources close to his time agree that he was merciless, and the longer Life of his son says his hands were 'defiled with blood'. Pál Engel wrote that he carried out a large-scale purge of his relatives, which would explain why no other members of the Árpád dynasty are mentioned from about 972, except Koppány, who kept the south of Transdanubia.

A marriage alliance between the German and Byzantine dynasties brought the two powers near Hungary closer in 972, and Géza made peace with the Holy Roman Empire. A monk named Bruno, sent by Otto I, arrived about 972, and Hungarian legates were at a conference held by the emperor at Quedlinburg in 973. Thietmar of Merseburg confirms that conversion began under Géza, who was baptised as Stephen, though he went on performing pagan rites.

After Emperor Otto II's death, Géza took advantage of conflict in the empire to invade Bavaria and take the fortress of Melk in 983. In 991 the Bavarians counter-attacked, and in a peace treaty of 996 with Henry IV of Bavaria he gave up the lands east of the Leitha. He arranged the marriage of his son Stephen to Henry's sister Giselle.

Earlier he had summoned the Hungarian leaders to an assembly and forced them to swear to his son's right to succeed. Historians such as Kristó say the first Catholic diocese in Hungary, at Veszprém, was set up in his reign, though not all accept this, and a charter of his son's reign names Géza as founder of Pannonhalma Archabbey. Stephen was crowned the first King of Hungary in 1000 or 1001.
geza-i-of-hungary: Géza was the eldest son of the future King Béla I of Hungary and a daughter of King Mieszko II of Poland. He was born in about 1040, in Poland according to the Illuminated Chronicle, and his baptismal name was Magnus. In about 1048 his father returned to Hungary and received one third of the kingdom as a duchy from his brother, King Andrew I. Béla became king on 6 December 1060 and died on 11 September 1063, as German troops entered Hungary to restore Solomon.

Géza offered to accept Solomon's rule in return for his father's duchy. Solomon refused, and Géza and his brothers went to Poland. They returned with Polish reinforcements, and a treaty signed at Győr on 20 January 1064 gave them the duchy. Silver half-denars were minted for Géza as DUX MAGNUS.

Géza and Solomon worked closely until a quarrel at the siege of the Byzantine fortress of Belgrade in 1071. Solomon's adviser Count Vid pushed the king towards war, and the royal army routed Géza at Kemej on 26 February 1074. Géza won the decisive battle of Mogyoród on 14 March 1074 with his brother Ladislaus and Duke Otto I of Olomouc, who brought Czech reinforcements. Solomon withdrew to Moson, and Géza took almost the whole kingdom. He was not crowned at once because the royal jewels remained with Solomon. In mid-1074 the German monarch Henry IV led an expedition as far as Vác, but Géza used scorched earth tactics and bribed German commanders to persuade him to retreat.

Géza approached Pope Gregory VII for recognition, but the pope tried to win acknowledgement of papal suzerainty and Géza did not obey. He asked Emperor Michael VII Doukas for a crown instead. The emperor sent a gold and enamel diadem inscribed Géza, the faithful king of Hungary, which by the end of the 12th century formed the lower part of the Holy Crown of Hungary. Géza was crowned with it in early 1075.

Solomon still held Moson and Pressburg, and royal troops under Ladislaus failed to take Pressburg in 1076. According to the Illuminated Chronicle, Géza considered giving up the crown to Solomon from the end of that year and opened peace talks, which came to nothing. He died on 25 April 1077 and was buried in the cathedral of Vác, which he had built in honour of the Holy Virgin. His sons were children, so his brother Ladislaus succeeded him. He had married twice, first Sophia and then Synadene, a niece of Nikephoros Botaneiates; his sons Coloman and Álmos were born around 1070.
geza-ii-of-hungary: Géza was born in 1130, the eldest son of Béla the Blind and Helena of Serbia. His father had been blinded in the 1110s, together with his own father Álmos, on the orders of King Coloman. Béla became king in 1131, and Queen Helena took Géza and his younger brother Ladislaus to an assembly at Arad, where she ordered the killing of sixty-eight noblemen who had counselled the blinding, according to the Illuminated Chronicle. Béla died on 13 February 1141, and Géza, aged eleven, was crowned on 16 February. His mother and her brother Beloš ruled as regents in the first years.

In early 1146 the pretender Boris Kalamanos, with German mercenaries recruited with the consent of Conrad III, took the fortress of Pressburg. The royal forces blockaded it and the mercenaries surrendered. Géza, sixteen and girded with a sword as a sign of coming of age, led an army across the Leitha and routed Henry Jasomirgott, Margrave of Austria, in the Battle of the Fischa on 11 September. He married Euphrosyne, sister of Grand Prince Iziaslav II of Kiev, in the second half of that year. In 1147 he paid money to the Germans and the German crusaders crossed Hungary without major incident. Louis VII of France refused to hand Boris over but took him out of Hungary.

Between 1148 and 1155 Géza intervened at least six times in the struggle for Kiev on behalf of Iziaslav II, sending reinforcements or leading troops himself. He sided with Roger II of Sicily against Conrad III and Emperor Manuel I Komnenos and supported Serbia in wars with the Byzantines, who restored their suzerainty over Serbia. Peace treaties with Manuel were signed in about 1150 and 1151, at Sardica in 1153 and again in 1155. He invited Western European knights, primarily German, to settle, and the Diploma Andreanum of 1224 says the ancestors of the Transylvanian Saxons were invited by him. He also employed Muslim soldiers recruited from the peoples of the steppes.

Géza's brothers Stephen and Ladislaus fell out with him and fled to the court of Manuel in Constantinople. From 1158 to 1160 Géza sent archers to help Frederick I against the Lombards. He first recognised Victor IV as pope in 1160, then changed sides to Alexander III after most European monarchs had done so, and in 1161 signed a concordat with Alexander. Shortly before his death he granted Dalmatia, Croatia and other lands to his younger son Béla as an appanage duchy. He died on 31 May 1162 and was buried at Székesfehérvár. His eldest son Stephen succeeded him, and Béla later inherited the kingdom after Stephen's death in 1172.
ghadames: Ghadames, also written Ghadamis, stands in an oasis in the Nalut District of the Tripolitania region, roughly 462 kilometres southwest of Tripoli, near the borders with Algeria and Tunisia. It is known as the pearl of the desert and is one of the oldest pre-Saharan cities. The oasis has a population of around 10,000, mainly Berbers. Its domestic architecture divides functions vertically: the ground floor stored supplies, the first floor was for the family, overhanging covered alleys that form an almost underground network of passageways, and open-air terraces at the top were reserved for the women. The climate is hot desert, with an average annual precipitation of only 73.1 millimetres.

Archaeological evidence suggests the area has been settled since the 4th millennium BCE. The first written records come from the Roman period, when the settlement was called Cydamus. In the 1st century BCE the Roman proconsul Lucius Cornelius Balbus invaded it during the reign of Augustus, and a permanent garrison was established under Septimius Severus, who may have visited around 202 CE. The Romans withdrew a few decades later during the Crisis of the Third Century. The name Ghadames is believed to descend from the Berber tribe of the Tidamensi, from Fezzan, whose name the Romans corrupted into Cydamus.

In the 6th century a bishop lived in the oasis, after Byzantine missionaries had converted its people to Christianity, and it became a stronghold of the Donatist heresy until Muslim Arabs conquered it in the late 7th century. The population quickly converted to Islam, and Ghadames served as a base for the trans-Saharan trade until the 19th century. It was also an important town in the trans-Saharan slave trade, and in the 12th century the geographer Abu Hamid al-Gharnati counted it among the countries of Sudan.

Italian soldiers occupied Ghadames in October 1911, soon after the Italo-Turkish War broke out; they withdrew to Tripoli in June 1915 after a general rising in Libya and restored control in December 1918. In 1943 Free French forces occupied it, and it was the capital of the Military Territory of Fezzan-Ghadames until Libyan independence in 1951.

The old town, surrounded by a city wall, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1986. Each of the seven clans that once lived there had its own district with a public place for festivals. In the 1970s new houses were built outside the old town, though many inhabitants return to it in summer, as its architecture protects better against the heat.
ghana: Ghana lies on the Gulf of Guinea, a few degrees north of the Equator, and covers 239,567 square kilometres with an Atlantic coastline of about 560 kilometres. It borders Ivory Coast, Burkina Faso and Togo. The land consists of low coastal plains, forested hills in the centre, and savanna in the north. The Prime Meridian passes through Tema, near Accra. Lake Volta, formed by the Akosombo Dam completed in 1965, is the largest reservoir in the world by surface area. The highest point is Mount Afadja, at 885 metres, in the Akwapim-Togo Range.

The earliest kingdoms to emerge were Bonoman in the south, existing in the 11th century, and the Kingdom of Dagbon in the north. From the 17th century Akan states, mainly based on gold trading, emerged from what is believed to have been the Bonoman area; they included Adansi, Asante, Denkyira, Akyem and Akwamu. By the 19th century the south was included in the Asante Kingdom, whose government grew from a loose network into a centralised kingdom with a specialised bureaucracy centred on Kumasi.

The Portuguese came to the Gold Coast in the 15th century to trade, and in 1481 King John II of Portugal commissioned Diogo de Azambuja to build Elmina Castle. The Dutch joined the gold trade by 1598 and captured Elmina in 1617. The British eventually controlled the coast by the 19th century. The modern borders took shape after more than a century of colonial resistance and joined four British territories: the Gold Coast, Ashanti, the Northern Territories and British Togoland.

On 6 March 1957 Ghana became the first colony in Sub-Saharan Africa to achieve sovereignty. Under President Kwame Nkrumah it became influential in decolonisation and the Pan-African movement. Ghana alternated between civilian and military governments until January 1993, when the Fourth Republic began after elections in late 1992.

The name comes from Wagadu, an empire of west Africa from the 3rd to 12th centuries that Arab traders called Ghana; it is thought to derive from the title Kaya Maghan, meaning ruler of gold. According to Jack Goody, the idea that the Akan descended from the medieval empire lacked linguistic and historical evidence, yet became influential among nationalist intellectuals. The name was adopted as a symbol of precolonial prestige before independence. English is the official language.
ghana-empire: It is uncertain among historians when Ghana's ruling dynasty began. The first identifiable mention is by al-Khwārizmī in 830, and the 11th-century Cordoban scholar al-Bakri gave further information. Ghana meant warrior or war chief and was the title of the rulers, who were also called Kaya Maghan, king of gold. Soninke oral tradition names Dinga as the ancestor, who killed a serpent deity, Bida, and whose son Dyabe founded Wagadu. Medieval Arabic chronicles proposed Soninke, Wangara or Sanhaja Berber origins for the rulers, while archaeology since the mid 20th century has led scholars to favour a local origin: the Dhar Tichitt site shows a complex culture there by 1600 BCE.

Towards the end of the 3rd century CE a wet period in the Sahel opened new land, and the introduction of the camel turned irregular trade routes into a network between North Africa and the Niger. Wagadu made its profits from a monopoly on gold heading north and salt heading south, though it did not control the goldfields.

In 734 the Umayyad Caliphate sent an expedition against the Sous and the Sudan, and al-Bakri noted that descendants of its troops still lived in Ghana and followed the native religion. When Muslim merchants first crossed the desert, Ghana was the most powerful state in the Sahel. As the Sahel dried, the centres of trade moved south to the Niger and west to the Senegal, which strengthened Ghana's vassals and weakened its core. Awdaghost, then a seat of the king, fell to the Almoravids in 1054, and the country converted to Islam around 1076. In 1083 it asked the Almoravids to help it attack Tadmekka.

By 1203 the Sosso had risen against their masters and conquered Ghana, creating a short-lived empire. Ibn Khaldun wrote that the people of Mali vanquished the Susu and acquired both their kingdom and that of Ghana. Maurice Delafosse assigned the date 1235 to this event, but it is arbitrary.

Kingship was matrilineal and traditionally passed to the son of the king's sister. Al-Bakri described a capital of two towns about 10 km apart, so built up between that they might be said to have merged. The royal town, El-Ghaba, had a stone wall, a sacred grove where priests lived and the king's palace, and the other town was almost entirely Muslim, with twelve mosques, scholars and jurists. The usual identification is Koumbi Saleh, excavated by French teams from the 1920s, but scholars increasingly dispute it. Contemporary sources suggest an army reliant on infantry with swords, spears and bows.
ghardaia: Ghardaïa lies in the Sahara in northern-central Algeria, on the left bank of the Wadi Mzab, which is dry through most of the year. The M'Zab valley is a limestone plateau about 600 kilometres south of Algiers, where five fortified towns stand on rocky outcrops: Ghardaïa, Melika, Beni Isguen, Bou Noura and El Atteuf. The climate is hot desert, with extremely hot summers and large differences between day and night. The Mozabites developed a system of tunnels to harvest the rain of the valley's brief floods and divert it equitably to the gardens, and wells reach water in the Albian groundwater below.

The Ibadis, a branch of Berber Muslims whose cultural identity is traced to the Maghreb, had their capital at Tahert. They were forced to leave after a devastating fire in 909, which is reported to have been caused by the founder of the Shi'ite Fatimid dynasty. They moved first to Sedrata and finally to the M'Zab valley, where the original architecture is dated to the early 11th century. Each of the five towns was planned on the same principles, as a miniature citadel with its own mosque and minaret serving as a watchtower, houses built round the mosque in concentric circles, and a high wall. The mosque also stored grain and arms for defence. In summer inhabitants moved to a palm grove outside the walls.

Ghardaïa's founders, a small group under a sheikh, chose a hill south of the wadi for defence and created a palm grove farther west. The town did not reach its present form at one time, and its heritage agency counts four phases of growth until the French army annexed it in 1882. Together with Melika it housed not only Ibadi Berbers but also Maliki Arabs and a Jewish community until Algerian independence. The deaf Jews of Ghardaïa developed a village sign language, which they took with them when the community left for France and Israel.

Ghardaïa is the capital of Ghardaïa Province and the traditional heart of the Ibadi religious sect in Algeria, which differs from the Maliki practice of most Algerians in its way of prayer and its mosque design. The town is a centre of date production, with nearly 60,000 palm trees, and of rug and cloth making. The M'Zab was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1982 for the influence of its settlements on urban planning, its Ibadi cultural values and a settlement culture that has lasted to the present century. In her 1963 book La Force des choses, Simone de Beauvoir described Ghardaïa as a Cubist painting beautifully constructed.
ghat: Ghat is the capital of the Ghat District in the Fezzan region of south-western Libya, just east of the Algerian border. It lies in the Sahara and has a hot desert climate, with summer highs above 40 °C and about 8 millimetres of rain a year, which makes it one of the driest places on Earth. Prehistoric rock paintings and engravings survive in the neighbouring Tadrart Acacus and Tassili N'Ajjer mountains.

In historical times Ghat was an important terminal point of a trans-Saharan trade route and a major administrative centre of the Fezzan. It was a stronghold of the Kel Ajjer Tuareg federation, whose territory covered most of south-western Libya, including Ubari, Sabha and Ghadames, and south-eastern Algeria. From the 5th century BCE to the 5th century CE the Fezzan was the home of the Garamantian Empire, which ran the trade routes between the Carthaginians and later the Roman Empire and the Sahelian states.

Portions of the Fezzan were part of the Kanem Empire in the 13th and 14th centuries, and the Ottoman rulers of North Africa asserted control there in the 17th century. The English traveller James Richardson described Ghat and its people in detail on his journeys of 1845 and 1846.

From 1911 Italy occupied Ghat and the Fezzan. Berber and Arab followers of the Sanusiya, a militant Sufi order, resisted early Italian attempts at conquest, and Italian control remained precarious until at least 1923. To defend their position the Italians built the Fortress of Ghat on the hill of Koukemen. France occupied Ghat in 1943 during the Second World War. On 21 November 1949 the United Nations General Assembly resolved that Libya should become independent before 1 January 1952, and Fezzan Province was then absorbed into the Kingdom of Libya.

The Fortress of Ghat still dominates the town from Koukemen hill and is its main attraction. Ghat is a destination for visitors to the rock art and desert landscapes of the nearby mountains, and has its own airport.
ghazan-khan: Mahmud Ghazan was born on 5 November 1271 near present-day Bandar Torkaman, the son of Arghun and a great-grandson of Hulegu Khan. He was raised an Eastern Christian and educated by a Chinese Buddhist monk, who taught him Buddhism and the Mongolian and Uighur scripts. When his father was enthroned as Ilkhan in 1284, the eleven-year-old Ghazan became viceroy in Khorasan, and he spent about ten years defending its frontier against the Chagatai Khanate.

After Arghun's death in 1291 he could not press his claim, being occupied by the raids of the emir Nawruz and by famine and revolt in Khorasan. In 1295 Taghachar and his fellow conspirators had Gaykhatu killed and set Baydu on the throne. Ghazan marched on Baydu, who was executed outside Tabriz on 4 October 1295.

Ghazan converted to Islam on taking the throne in 1295. Nawruz, made chief of state, issued an edict against other religions, and his followers persecuted Buddhists and Christians so severely that Buddhism in Iran never recovered; churches were destroyed in Tabriz and Hamadan. Ghazan later issued an edict exempting Christians from the jizya and in 1296 re-established the Patriarch Mar Yaballaha III. He also purged nobles who had served earlier rulers, many of them executed.

He appointed Rashid-al-Din Hamadani vizier, a post he held until 1318, and commissioned from him the Jami' al-Tawarikh, a history of the Mongols that grew into a history of the world. Ghazan ordered a census to set fiscal policy, unified measures, coinage and weights, brought abandoned land back under cultivation, improved the postal relay, built hostels, hospitals and schools, and banned lending at interest. He took Damascus on 30 December 1299 in a war with the Mamluks and, like his father, sought a Franco-Mongol alliance.

Ghazan was said to have been depressed after the death of his wife Karamun in January 1304. He named his brother Öljaitü as heir, having no son, and died on 11 May 1304 near Qazvin. He may have been initiated as a Sufi. Considered the most prominent of the Ilkhans, he spoke Mongolian, Chinese, Arabic and probably Latin, and a Byzantine historian praised his skill in making saddles and helmets. His conversion marked a turning point for the dominant religion of the Mongols in West Asia.
ghazi-muhammad: Ghazi Muhammad was born in Gimry, in the Koysubu confederation of Avar villages, to a learned craftsman from Gidatl and a mother from Gimry, and as the son of migrants he was thought rootless by the villagers. At ten he went to Karanay to study Arabic and the Quran, and later studied under scholars such as Sayyid al-Harakani. In 1825 he joined the Naqshbandi order at Gazi-Kumukh under Jamal al-Din al-Ghazi-Ghumuqi and completed his training with Muhammad al-Yaraghi, whose daughter he married in 1831. He introduced his friend Shamil to his teacher.

As mullah and qadi of Gimry he called on Muslims to abandon customary law (adat) for sharia, and in 1826 or 1827 Gimry did so, followed by the other villages of Koysubu and Salatau. The historian Michael Kemper writes that this probably meant corporal punishment for adultery and drinking and bans on dancing, music and usury. In his treatise The clear evidence of the heresy of the elders who administer customary law in Dagestan he called followers of adat unbelievers. His campaign set him against village elders and mullahs whose authority rested on adat.

Proclaimed imam at Gimry in late 1829, he declared holy war, and during his rule some 30 nobles he saw as false believers and Russian collaborators were executed. He gathered 8,000 to 10,000 followers, appointed na'ibs and set up a treasury. After failing to take Khunzakh, the Avar capital, in 1830 he withdrew to pray and fast, then extended his power into Chechnya. In 1831 he took Tarki, besieged Vnezapnaya and for eight days Derbent, and on 1 November sacked Kizlyar, taking 168 prisoners, mostly women, whom he ransomed. That year his authority covered most of Chechnya and Dagestan.

On 13 December 1831 the Russians stormed Aghach Qala, killing most of its 600 defenders, and in 1832 his siege of Nazran failed and the mountain communities fell away. On 29 October 1832 Russian troops trapped him in a fortified house at Gimry, and he is said to have leapt onto their bayonets; only the wounded Shamil and one other escaped. His body was displayed at Tarki and buried near Burnaya, later carried back to Gimry, where his shrine became a place of pilgrimage. His deputy Hamzat Bek succeeded him, and the Imamate fought on until 1859.
ghaznavid-empire: The Ghaznavids were a culturally Persianate, Sunni Muslim dynasty of Turkic Karluk origin. They arose from the Turkic slave-guards of the Samanid Empire. After the death of Abd al-Malik I in 961 the Samanid generals Alp Tigin and Abu al-Hasan Simjuri competed for control by placing on the throne emirs they could dominate. A court party of civilian ministers rejected Alp Tigin, who retired south of the Hindu Kush and captured Ghazna. His slave and son-in-law Sabuktigin, a former mamluk, became governor there and founded the dynasty. He received further governorships for helping the Samanids in Khurasan, and he did not regard his dynasty as independent.

Sabuktigin's son Mahmud defeated his brother Ismail at the Battle of Ghazni in 998 and took the governorship. His reign, to 1030, is described as the height of the empire. He led seventeen expeditions through northern India, defeating the Hindu Shahis at Peshawar in 1001, sacking Mathura in 1018 and plundering the Somnath Temple in 1026, and he brought home enormous wealth. His authority reached from Rey to Samarkand and from the Caspian Sea to the Yamuna.

Mahmud's son Mas'ud blinded his brother Mohammed to take the throne, and after the defeat at Dandanaqan in 1040 lost all Ghaznavid lands in Persia and Central Asia to the Seljuks. Ibrahim, who became king in 1058, made peace with the Seljuks and re-established a smaller empire that was sustained by raids on northern India. In 1151 Ala al-Din Husayn of the Ghurids took and burned Ghazni. The Ghaznavids withdrew to Lahore, which Muhammad of Ghor conquered in 1186, deposing Khusrau Malik.

Though Turkic in origin, the dynasty was thoroughly Persianised in language, culture and administration, which it took over from the Samanids; Persian bureaucrats ran the state. The army rested on Turkish soldiers and Afghans trained south of the Hindu Kush, later with Hindu troops under their own commander. The Ghaznavids are said to have been the first Muslim army to use armoured war elephants in battle.

Mahmud made Ghazni a centre of learning, inviting Ferdowsi and al-Biruni, and hundreds of poets gathered at his court. The historian Abu'l-Fadl Bayhaqi wrote his Tarikh-e Beyhaqi in Persian in the later 11th century. Lahore became a major Persian cultural centre, and Ghaznavid marble panels at Ghazni carry geometric, vegetal and Kufic designs.

The Ghaznavids are generally credited with spreading Islam into the Indian subcontinent. Their conquests opened the way for the Turko-Afghan period in India, which the Ghurids continued until the Delhi Sultanate was established.
ghazni: Ghazni stands on a plateau about 2,219 m above sea level, on the Kabul–Kandahar Highway, which follows paths that have served for thousands of years as the main roads between Kabul, Kandahar and Gardez. In antiquity it was a small market town. It was conquered by Cyrus II in the 6th century BCE and by Alexander the Great in 329 BCE, when it was called Alexandria in Opiana.

After the fall of the Greco-Bactrian kingdoms the region became the heart of Zabulistan, a kingdom that controlled the trade routes between India, Iran and Central Asia. From the 5th to the 7th centuries it was ruled by the Nezak Huns, and the area was a major centre of Buddhism, and also of Zoroastrianism and Hinduism. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang visited in 644 and described a city he called Jaguda. Arab armies brought Islam to the region in 683. The Saffarids later conquered it from the Zunbils, but the non-Muslim Lawik dynasty remained in Ghazni until the Samanid slave commander Alp-Tegin besieged the citadel in 962 and took the city from Abu Bakr Lawik.

From 977 to 1163 Ghazni was the capital of the Ghaznavid Empire, which covered much of present-day Afghanistan, Turkmenistan, Pakistan, eastern Iran and Rajasthan. The Ghaznavids carried Islam into Hindustan and returned with riches looted from temples. Under Sultan Mahmud, who reigned from 998 to 1030, Ghazni was in the early 11th century the most important centre of Persian literature, since he gathered scholars, philosophers and poets at his court to support his claim to royal status in Iran.

The Ghurids sacked Ghazni, but in 1173 it became their secondary capital and flourished again. It was ruled by the Khwarazmian Empire between 1215 and 1221. When Ibn Battuta visited in 1333 he found most of the town in ruins. It stayed under Mughal control until Nader Shah invaded in 1738, and then became part of the Durrani Empire. British forces partly demolished its fortifications on 23 July 1839 in the First Anglo-Afghan War.

Ghazni is the capital of Ghazni Province in southeastern Afghanistan, about 150 km south-west of Kabul. Its monuments include the Ghazni Citadel, the mausoleum of Sultan Mahmud, the tomb of al-Biruni and the Palace of Sultan Mas'ud III. The two Ghazni Minarets, built on a stellar plan and decorated with geometric patterns, date from the middle of the 12th century and are the surviving elements of the mosque of Bahramshah.
ghent: Ghent lies at the confluence of the Scheldt and the Leie, in the East Flanders province of the Flemish Region of Belgium. Archaeological evidence shows human presence there from the Stone Age and Iron Age. Most historians derive the older name, Ganda, from a Celtic word meaning confluence or river mouth, while other sources connect it with an obscure deity named Gontia. The rivers flowed through land that flooded periodically, and these water-meadows were well suited to grazing sheep, whose wool fed the city's cloth trade.

Around 650 Saint Amand founded two abbeys in Ghent, St. Peter's and St. Bavo's, and around 800 Louis the Pious appointed Einhard, the biographer of Charlemagne, abbot of both. The city grew from the abbeys and a commercial centre, and Vikings plundered it in 851 and 879. Under the protection of the County of Flanders it flourished from the 11th century as a small city-state. By the 13th century it was the biggest city in Europe north of the Alps after Paris, with up to 65,000 people within its walls, and the leading centre of woollen cloth manufacture; by the middle of that century the industry employed 4,000 weavers and 1,200 fullers.

In 1453 Ghent suffered a heavy defeat at the Battle of Gavere at the hands of Philip the Good, after high taxes had led to rebellion. Afterwards the political and social centre of the Low Countries began to shift from Flanders towards Brabant. After the Revolt of Ghent in 1539, Charles V, a native of the city, made its nobles walk before him barefoot with a noose around the neck, so that its people have since been called Stroppendragers, or noose bearers. St. Bavo's Abbey was torn down and replaced with a fortress for Spanish troops. The Eighty Years' War ended Ghent's role as a centre of international importance.

Ghent's textile industry flourished again in the 18th and 19th centuries, and in 1800 Lieven Bauwens introduced the first mechanical weaving machine on the European continent after smuggling plans out of England. The Treaty of Ghent, adopted on Christmas Eve 1814, formally ended the War of 1812 between Great Britain and the United States.
