The city was occupied by the Germans in both world wars but escaped severe destruction, and was liberated on 6 September 1944.

Ghent is the capital and largest city of its province and the third largest city in Belgium, a port and university city. Much of its medieval architecture survives, including St. Bavo's Cathedral with the Ghent Altarpiece, the belfry, the Gravensteen castle and the buildings along the old Graslei harbour. UNESCO recognised its béguinages as World Heritage Sites in 1998, and the belfry and adjacent cloth hall in 1999.
ghent-altarpiece: The altarpiece was commissioned by Jodocus Vijd, a wealthy merchant and one of the most powerful citizens of Ghent, and his wife Lysbette Borluut, as part of a larger project for a chapel of the Saint Bavo Cathedral. The couple died childless, and the gift was meant to secure a legacy and their position in the hereafter, and to show Vijd's prestige.

Art historians generally agree that Hubert van Eyck designed the structure in the early 1420s and that his younger brother Jan painted most of the panels between 1430 and 1432, although no convincing separation of their hands has been made. A lost inscription on the frame called Hubert greater than anyone and Jan second best in the art. Its installation took place on 6 May 1432.

Twelve panels in two registers, with folding wings, show different scenes according to whether the altarpiece is open or closed. It was opened on feast days. Opened, the upper register holds a Deësis of the Virgin Mary, John the Baptist and a central enthroned figure, who may be Christ or God the Father, with singing angels and Adam and Eve at the sides. The lower register is a continuous landscape with streams of people, including warriors, judges, hermits and pilgrims, approaching the Lamb of God on an altar. Closed, the altarpiece shows prophets and sibyls, the Annunciation, grisaille figures of the two Saints John painted to look like sculpture, and the donors kneeling at the outer edges. It measures 375 by 260 centimetres closed.

Light is one of its main innovations: figures cast short diagonal shadows, and the Annunciation is lit as though by daylight from the chapel where it stands. Plants are painted with an almost scientific accuracy, and the surfaces of armour, jewels and water show new handling of oil paint and glazes.

The altarpiece was restored in 1550 by Lancelot Blondeel and Jan van Scorel, and during the Reformation it was moved to keep it from the iconoclasts. The French took it to the Louvre after the Revolution, and it returned in 1815.

That year the diocese pawned the wings, which were sold in 1816 and then in 1821 to King Frederick William III of Prussia for £16,000, and hung in Berlin. The panels left in Ghent were damaged by fire in 1822. The art historian Noah Charney counts 13 crimes against it, seven of them thefts. A restoration from 2012 found that about 70 per cent of the outer panels had been overpainted in the 16th century, and the five lower panels returned to the cathedral in January 2020.
gheorghe-gheorghiu-dej: Gheorghe Gheorghiu-Dej was born in Bârlad on 8 November 1901, the son of a poor worker. Poverty made him leave school and begin work at 11. He settled as an electrician and joined the workers' union at a factory in Comănești. In 1930 he joined the Communist Party of Romania and was sent to organise agitation in the railway workshops of Moldavia. A punitive transfer in 1931 took him to Dej in Transylvania, and the secret police later gave him the name Gheorghiu-Dej to tell him apart from other union activists called Gheorghiu. With Constantin Doncea he led the Grivița railway strike of 1933 in Bucharest and was arrested that February.

Sentenced by a military court, he served in Doftana and other prisons and became leader of the prison faction of the party, as distinct from the Muscovite faction in exile. He was held in the Târgu Jiu camp during Ion Antonescu's regime and escaped on 10 August 1944. He became general secretary in 1944 but did not consolidate his power until 1952, when he purged Ana Pauker and her comrades of the Muscovite faction. On 30 December 1947 he and Prime Minister Petru Groza forced King Michael I to abdicate, and Parliament abolished the monarchy and declared a People's Republic. Gheorghiu-Dej was prime minister from 1952 to 1955 and head of state from 1961.

He did not amend repressive policies after Stalin's death, such as the penal labour used on the Danube–Black Sea Canal, and he carried out forced collectivisation of land. In the late 1950s he built heavy industry, including the Galați steel plant, against Soviet plans that had made Romania a granary of the bloc. The Red Army withdrew its last troops in 1958, and trade with the West grew to 25 percent of the total by 1957. At the same time the Securitate remained his instrument. Many political prisoners were released in 1964, and he established diplomatic relations with Western states.

Gheorghiu-Dej died of lung cancer in Bucharest on 19 March 1965. Prime Minister Ion Gheorghe Maurer, hostile to Gheorghe Apostol, rallied the party leadership round Nicolae Ceaușescu instead, who had met Gheorghiu-Dej in prison and who succeeded him. His funeral was attended by 33 foreign delegations. He was buried in a mausoleum in what is now Carol Park, and in 1991 his body was exhumed and reburied at Bellu Cemetery. The city of Onești was once named after him.
ghezo: Ghezo was born Gakpe, a son of King Agonglo and younger brother of Adandozan. Around 1818 Adandozan imprisoned the Afro-Brazilian slave trader Francisco Félix de Sousa, who had demanded repayment of a loan. De Sousa escaped to Grand-Popo and from exile sent Ghezo gifts and money with which to build support. Tradition says that at the Annual Customs of 1818 Ghezo appeared holding the palace war drum, and the Migan and Mehu took the royal sandals from Adandozan and named him king; the struggle was probably more violent than this story suggests.

When Ghezo refused tribute, Oyo sent an ambassador, whom he killed, and then a force of 4,000 men with cavalry, which he routed in a night raid that killed its leader Ajanaku. Early defeats by the Mahi and the sale of Dahomey's own people made him unpopular, but after the mid-1820s he expanded against the Mahi and the Gbe. Abeokuta, founded as a refuge from slave raiding, became his chief enemy. He made the Mino, the women's palace guard, into a fighting force, giving them uniforms and weapons.

Under British pressure in the 1840s, Ghezo called the slave trade the ruling principle of his people and proposed palm oil exports instead, though these too relied on domestic slavery. His attack on Abeokuta in March 1851 failed against the Egba and their British allies. Facing a British blockade, he signed an agreement in January 1852 to end the trade from Dahomey, while letting captives leave through other ports. He also said he had reduced human sacrifice at the Annual Customs. A faction led by the Migan and the Yovogan pressed him to resume the trade in 1857.

Ghezo died soon after the renewed campaign against Abeokuta, which he had resisted. Accounts give poison, smallpox or death in battle, but he was most likely shot by a sniper hired from Abeokuta. His heir Glele partly undid his reforms. A Benin Armed Forces base in Cotonou, Camp Ghezo, bears his name, and he appears in novels by George MacDonald Fraser and Maryse Condé and in the film The Woman King.
ghilman: Ghilman, from an Arabic word meaning boys or servants, were slave soldiers or mercenaries in armies across the Islamic world. They were taken as prisoners of war from conquered or frontier regions, especially among the Turkic peoples of Central Asia and the peoples of the Caucasus. There is no evidence that the Prophet Muhammad or the Rashidun Caliphs organised slave armies, although individuals of slave origin may have fought. Under the Umayyads some Slavs and Berbers served in military roles, but large-scale recruitment became a defining feature of Islamic military systems only by the mid-9th century, under the Abbasids. The first Muslim ruler to form an army of slave soldiers seems to have been Ibrahim I ibn al-Aghlab of Ifriqiya.

Ghilman came to the Abbasid Caliphate under al-Mu'tasim (r. 833–842), who relied on them for his personal guard. Native Arab opposition led to riots against them in Baghdad in 836 and forced al-Mu'tasim to move his capital to Samarra. Under the weak rulers who followed, the ghilman became kingmakers: they revolted several times during the Anarchy at Samarra in the 860s and killed four caliphs. Starting with Ahmad ibn Tulun in Egypt, some became autonomous rulers, leading to the dissolution of the Abbasid Caliphate by the mid-10th century.

The Buyids, the Saffarids, the Samanids and the Ghaznavid dynasty, which originated from a Samanid slave soldier, all built armies of slave soldiers, as did the Seljuks, the Ghurids, the Turkic Khwarazmian dynasty and the Delhi Sultanate. The Mongols did not adopt the institution, but it returned under the Qara Qoyunlu and Aq Qoyunlu, and the Safavid, Afsharid and Qajar dynasties drew soldiers from Georgians, Circassians and Armenians. From the 10th century masters gave ghilman iqta land grants to support them.

A ghulam was trained and educated at his master's expense and could earn his freedom through service, joining the elite corps as a mounted warrior after the formative training. Ghilman were required to marry Turkic slave women chosen by their masters, and some seem to have lived celibate lives. The lack of family life was possibly one reason they generally failed to found dynasties, with exceptions such as the Ghaznavid dynasty. They were expected to be loyal because they had no ties to the rest of society, though they often were not. In the Abbasid army they fought chiefly as a mounted strike force, armed with a lance, a round shield and a sword worn at the belt.
ghilzai: The Ghilji, also spelled Ghilzai, Khilji and Khalji, are one of the largest Pashtun tribes. Their traditional homeland is Ghazni and Qalati Ghilji in Afghanistan, and they make up around 20–25% of Afghanistan's population. According to the historian C. E. Bosworth the name derives from that of the Khalaj, a people usually referred to as Turks who, he thinks, formed the core of the tribe. A popular folk etymology instead derives it from Gharzay, meaning born of the mountain. Another account holds that the Ghilji descend from the Hephthalites. The 17th-century courtier Nimat Allah al-Harawi gave a mythical genealogy tracing them to Shah Hussain Ghori.

Geographers of the 9th and 10th centuries, Ibn Khordadbeh and Istakhri, wrote that the Khalaj had crossed the Amu Darya and settled around Ghazni; the Hudud al-'Alam described them as sheep-grazing nomads. Al-Utbi wrote that when Sabuktigin defeated the Hindu Shahi ruler Jayapala in 988, the Pashtuns and Khalaj between Laghman and Peshawar agreed to serve him, and that Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni recruited them in large numbers. In 1221 Khalaj and other tribesmen in the army of Jalal al-Din Mangburni helped defeat the Mongols at the Battle of Parwan, then left over the booty.

In April 1709 Mirwais Hotak, of the Hotak tribe of the Ghilji, led a revolution against the Safavids and founded the Hotak dynasty at Kandahar, declaring southern Afghanistan independent. His son Mahmud Hotak conquered Iran in 1722, and Isfahan remained the dynasty's capital for six years. The dynasty ended in 1738, when Nader Shah Afshar defeated its last ruler, Hussain Hotak, at the Battle of Kandahar. Azad Khan Afghan, of the Andar tribe, rose to power in western Iran between 1752 and 1757.

During the First Anglo-Afghan War (1839–1842), a Ghilji force attacked the British Indian garrison retreating from Kabul on 6 January 1842. On 12 January the last survivors were killed or captured near Gandamak, and only the surgeon William Brydon reached Jalalabad, on 13 January. After the Ghilji rebelled in 1886, Emir Abdur Rahman Khan forced many of them to migrate to northern Afghanistan.

The Ghilji of the central region speak Central Pashto, a dialect transitional between the southern and northern varieties. In Afghanistan they live chiefly between the Durand Line, a line from Kandahar through Ghazni to Kabul, and Jalalabad. The modern nomadic Kochi are predominantly Ghilji, and before the 1947 partition of India some Ghilji wintered there as nomadic merchants, carrying goods by camel caravan to sell or barter in Afghanistan. Their subtribes include the Ahmadzai, Hotak, Andar, Kharoti, Tokhi and Sulaimankhel.
ghirlandina: The tower was originally called the Torre di San Geminiano. It was built along with the cathedral to a design by Lanfranco and had four storeys on a square base. Since it was incomplete and lacked a bell tower, builders from Campione were commissioned to finish it in 1167. By 1179 they had added a fifth storey, and from 1261 a sixth, also on a square base.

In the following century, partly because of rivalry with Bologna, the characteristic octagonal spire was added, based on a design by Arrigo da Campione, who adapted the style of the cathedral and tower to the new northern Gothic manner. The tower was crowned with a golden sphere in 1319. A marble balustrade runs around the base of the octagonal roof, with pinnacle-like finials at the corners. Each is decorated on two sides with cascading garlands, which gave the tower its present name.

The Ghirlandina is the campanile of the Cathedral of Modena in Emilia-Romagna, Italy, and the symbol of the city. The cathedral, the bell tower and the Piazza Grande were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997. The storeys decrease in height towards the top and are marked by cornices, but they do not match the internal structure.

The Sala della Secchia rapita, at about the level of the first outer string course, served from the 14th century as a kind of treasury and archive for the municipality, where documents and relics of saints from the cathedral were kept. Its name, the Hall of the Stolen Bucket, refers to a bucket from a fountain in Bologna that was taken at the Battle of Zappolino in 1325, in the War of the Bucket. It was kept as a war trophy and put into verse by Alessandro Tassoni in 1622. Higher up the tower is largely open, with a staircase running along the walls, and on about the fifth floor is the Stanza dei Torresani, whose Romanesque capitals are noteworthy.

On the north side, facing the small Piazza Torre, three plaques show photographs of Modena partisans who fell fighting against Italian fascism. In front stands a monument to Tassoni, made by the sculptor Alessandro Cavazza and erected in 1860. A restoration began in December 2007 and lasted until September 2011, longer than first announced. The scaffolding was hidden behind a screen painted by the sculptor Mimmo Paladino, a choice that caused perplexity in the town because of its cost.
ghiyath-al-din-muhammad: Ghiyath was the son of Baha al-Din Sam I, who reigned briefly over the Ghurids in 1149. According to the Tabaqat-i-Nasiri of Minhaj al-Siraj his birth name, like his younger brother's, was Muhammad; his mother called him Habshi for his dark complexion, and as a prince he bore the title Shamsuddin. He and his brother were imprisoned by their uncle Ala al-Din Husayn and released by his son Sayf al-Din Muhammad. When Sayf died in 1163, the Ghurid nobles raised Ghiyath to the throne.

With his brother's help Ghiyath killed a rival chief, Abu'l Abbas, and defeated his uncle Fakhr al-Din Masud and the Seljuq governor Yildiz at Ragh-i Zar, then conquered Zamindawar, Badghis, Gharchistan and Guzgan. He spared his uncle and restored him at Bamiyan. In 1173 he took Ghazni from the Oghuz Turks and installed Mu'izz al-Din there, and two years later he seized Herat and Pushang. The rulers of Sistan and the Oghuz of Kirman acknowledged his sovereignty.

In 1186 the brothers captured Lahore and ended the Ghaznavid dynasty, executing its last ruler, Khusrau-Malik. In 1190 Ghiyath defeated the Khwarazmian prince Sultan Shah at Marw al-Rudh and annexed most of his lands in Khorasan, then beat off Tekish at Herat and the Kara-Khitans in Guzgan. After Tekish died in 1200 the brothers took Nishapur, but Mu'izz al-Din's undisciplined advance towards Ray led to their only reported quarrel.

Ghiyath died in Herat on 13 March 1203. Mu'izz al-Din hurried back from India, won the support of the nobles and was crowned sultan at Firuzkuh. Under the two brothers the Ghurids became one of the great powers of the eastern Islamic world. Ghiyath was buried in the Great Mosque of Herat, in a mausoleum at its northern gate, which was destroyed when the mosque was renovated in the 1950s.
ghiyath-al-din-tughluq: Tughluq belonged to the Qara'unas, a Mongol tribe from Central Asia, although sources differ in detail on his ancestry. Ibn Battuta and Shams-i Siraj Afif describe him as a Turk or Mongol. His father served under Balban and his mother belonged to the Hindu Jat community of the Punjab, so Firishta gives him a mixed Turk and Jat lineage. Tughluq was his personal name, not a dynastic name. Amir Khusrau's Tughluq Nama says that he described himself as an unimportant man early in his career, and he began as a menial servant of a merchant before entering Khalji service.

According to Khusrau, he joined the imperial guard of Jalaluddin Khalji and first distinguished himself in the early 1290s at the Siege of Ranthambore. He rose to prominence under Alauddin Khalji, leading the vanguard against the Mongol invasion of 1306 and becoming governor of Multan and then of Dipalpur, frontier provinces that held the routes used by Mongol invaders. His armies consisted mainly of Jat tribesmen from Dipalpur. Khusrau says that he defeated the Mongols 18 times and Ziauddin Barani says 20.

In July 1320 Mubarak Shah was murdered in a conspiracy by his general Khusrau Khan, who became ruler of Delhi. Tughluq was one of the governors who refused to recognise him. His son Fakhruddin Jauna, later Muhammad bin Tughluq, asked for his help, and Tughluq declared that he would fight for the glory of Islam, out of loyalty to Alauddin's family and to punish the criminals in Delhi. His army defeated Khusrau Khan at the Battle of Saraswati and the Battle of Lahrawat, Khusrau Khan was captured and killed a few days later, and Tughluq was proclaimed ruler on 6 September 1320.

His policy towards the Mongols was harsh: he killed envoys of the Ilkhan Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan and punished Mongol prisoners severely. In 1323 he sent Fakhruddin Jauna against the Kakatiya capital Warangal, and the Siege of Warangal ended in the annexation of Warangal and the end of the Kakatiya dynasty. In the same year he named Muhammad bin Tughluq his heir and took a written promise from the ministers and nobles. He also began construction of Tughlaqabad Fort.

In 1324 Tughluq turned to Bengal, then in civil war. After his victory he placed Nasiruddin on the throne of West Bengal as a vassal and annexed East Bengal, and on his way back he defeated the Raja of Tirhut and annexed his territory. At Kara-Manikpur in February 1325 the wooden pavilion built for his reception collapsed, killing him and his second son Prince Mahmud Khan. Ibn Battuta claimed it was a conspiracy by the vizier Jauna Khan. Muhammad bin Tughluq succeeded him.
ghor: Ghor occupies the end of the Hindu Kush mountains in central Afghanistan, towards the north-west. It lies about 2,500 metres above sea level, and heavy snowfalls often block many of its rugged passes from November to April. In summer the area is prone to drought. Its historical name was Mandesh, and medieval writers also called it Ghoristan, the mountainous country between Herat and Ghazni. Agriculture and animal husbandry are the main economic activities.

Remains of the oldest settlements, found by Lithuanian archaeologists in 2007 and 2008, date back to about 5000 BCE. Before the 12th century the region was home to Buddhists, Zoroastrians, Hindus and a small number of Jews, and a Buddhist monastery was carved by hand into a bluff above the Hari Rud. In 725 the Umayyad governor Asad b. 'Abdallah al-Qasri raided Ghur without success. The geographers Istakhri and Ibn Haukal describe it as a rugged country of unbelievers, bounded by Muslim districts, whose people spoke a language different from that of Khurasan. Minhaj al-Siraj records constant strife between non-Muslims and Muslims there, and names the Shansbani Amir Suri as the head of its chiefs.

Mahmud of Ghazni defeated the Buddhist prince Ibn-i Suri in a hard-fought engagement, and in 1011, 1015 and 1020 Mahmud and Mas'ud I led expeditions into Ghur to establish Islam in place of the indigenous paganism. Ghur then became a vassal of the Ghaznavid Empire, although it later gained autonomy.

Its rise to power in the 12th century, in a small and isolated area between the Ghaznavid Empire and the Seljukids, was unusual and unexpected. Some accounts hold that a form of Mahayana Buddhism persisted there until the end of that century. Ghor was the centre of the Ghurid dynasty in the 12th and 13th centuries, and the Mongols sacked and destroyed its capital Firozkoh in 1222.

Ghor is one of the 34 provinces of Afghanistan, with eleven districts and a population of 764,472. Its capital is Firuzkoh. Western Ghor is predominantly Tajik and eastern Ghor mostly Hazara. The remains of Firozkoh include the Minaret of Jam, which is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
gia-long: Gia Long was born Nguyễn Phúc Ánh on 8 February 1762 in Phú Xuân, now Huế, the third son of Nguyễn Phúc Luân and a grandson of the lord Nguyễn Phúc Khoát. He was a minor member of the family, without support among court powerbrokers, when in 1777 his family was slain in the Tây Sơn revolt and he, aged 15, went into hiding. His loyalists regained and lost Saigon several times. He befriended the French Catholic bishop Pierre Pigneau de Behaine, whom he sent to Pondicherry in 1785 to seek French aid. The French authorities there refused to intervene, but Pigneau returned in 1789 with two ships that stayed in Nguyễn service.

From 1789 Nguyễn Phúc Ánh gained the upper hand. In the Saigon region, called Gia Định, he re-established a civil service, created a Council of High Officials in 1788 and in 1790 had French officers build a European-style citadel with a perimeter of 4,176 metres. He settled soldiers on fallow land to raise grain, and built up a navy in which European ships served beside traditional galleys. The death of the Tây Sơn leader Nguyễn Huệ in 1792 let him march north, and by 1802 he had reunited Vietnam, reaching the Qing border.

As emperor he moved the capital from Hanoi to Huế, built fortresses and a palace there, and restored the Confucian education and civil service examinations that the Tây Sơn had abolished. He founded the National Academy in 1803 and opened the first Nguyễn examinations in 1807. He asked the Qing Jiaqing Emperor to name the country Nam Việt, and Jiaqing agreed instead to Việt Nam. He abolished large landholdings by princes and nobles and ended the practice of rewarding nobles with a share of village taxes. Under him Vietnam forced Siam out of Cambodia in 1813 and kept a garrison in Phnom Penh. He tolerated Catholic missionaries in gratitude to the French but refused European trading overtures, among them a British one in 1804.

Gia Long died on 3 February 1820. His line, the Nguyễn dynasty, was the last of Vietnam and ruled the unified territory until 1945. His successors, beginning with his son Nguyễn Phúc Đảm, restricted the missionaries he had tolerated. He had many wives and almost 100 concubines, daughters of mandarins, whom he took to secure the loyalty of his circle.
giacomo-da-lentini: Giacomo, known by the appellative Il Notaro, wrote in literary Sicilian, but his poems survive only in Tuscan copies. Some scholars see his poetry of courtly love as an adaptation of the Provençal poetry of the troubadours. The critic William Baer argues instead that the first eight lines of the earliest Sicilian sonnets, rhymed ABABABAB, match the eight-line Sicilian folk stanza called the strambotto, so that the inventor of the form, Giacomo or another, added two tercets to it to make a poem of fourteen lines.

Like other poets of his time he circulated his poems in manuscript and commented on those of others; one of his main correspondents was Pier della Vigna. Some of his sonnets belong to a tenzone, an exchange in which one poet wrote a sonnet and another answered with one, and he took part in such an exchange with the Abbot of Tivoli.

Among his best-known poems is the canzone Meravigliosa-mente. Its speaker, too timid to show his love, says he carries the lady's image painted in his heart and has made a picture of her to look at when she is absent. The poem ends by sending the song to her with a request to give her love to the notary born in Lentini.

In the twenty-fourth canto of the Purgatorio, Virgil and Dante Alighieri meet the soul of the poet. In the nineteenth century Dante Gabriel Rossetti translated his poems, with those of Emperor Frederick and other poets of the Sicilian School, in The Early Italian Poets. Jorge Luis Borges made him the unnamed subject of his sonnet Un Poeta del Siglo XIII, A Poet of the 13th Century.
giacomo-matteotti: Giacomo Matteotti was born on 22 May 1885 into a wealthy family in Fratta Polesine, near Rovigo, and he joined the youth wing of the Italian Socialist Party in 1898. He graduated in law at the University of Bologna in 1907 with a thesis on recidivism, for which he travelled through several countries. He followed Filippo Turati, leader of the gradualist wing of the party. He was elected mayor of Villamarzana in 1912. Because he opposed the First World War, he was interned in Sicily. Elected to the Chamber of Deputies in 1919, he was re-elected in 1921 and 1924, and earned the nickname Tempesta, Storm, for his combative character.

In 1921 Matteotti published a pamphlet on the violence of the Fascist action squads, and he was himself attacked during that election campaign. At the party congress of 1922 the gradualist wing led by Turati was expelled from the Socialist Party, and Matteotti followed Turati in founding the Unitary Socialist Party, whose secretary he became. He rejected the violence he saw in Bolshevik communism, and in 1924 refused a proposal from the Communists for a united front, wanting an anti-fascist bloc of the Socialist Party, the Italian People's Party and the Unitary Socialists.

In the general election of 6 April 1924, held amid intimidation and violence by the squads, the government list won all 356 of its candidates. On 30 May Matteotti addressed the Chamber of Deputies to contest the result and denounced the violence, illegalities and abuses of the Fascists. Fascist deputies interrupted him with threats and at the end cheered Mussolini.

On 10 June 1924, at about four in the afternoon, five men bundled Matteotti into a black Lancia on the Lungotevere as he walked to Parliament. They acted as members of Mussolini's secret political police, under Amerigo Dumini, and stabbed him in the car. The news spread quickly and the foreign press strongly criticised Mussolini, which caused a diplomatic crisis.

Historians have debated whether the murder came on Mussolini's orders, but the murder and Mussolini's later speech assuming responsibility are generally seen as the start of his dictatorship. The deputies who left Parliament in the Aventine Secession in protest were later dismissed, and by 1926 the Fascistissime laws had made Italy a one-party state. Only Dumini, Albino Volpi and Amleto Poveromo were convicted, in 1926, and they were soon released under an amnesty. In the Italian Republic Matteotti is regarded as a martyr.
giacomo-puccini: Giacomo Puccini was born in Lucca, then in the Grand Duchy of Tuscany, the sixth of nine children of Michele Puccini and Albina Magi. His great-great-grandfather, also named Giacomo, had made the family a local musical dynasty as maestro di cappella of the Cattedrale di San Martino, a post passed down through his son Antonio, his grandson Domenico and Michele. Each studied music at Bologna and composed church music, and Domenico and Michele also wrote operas. Michele's funeral was an occasion of public mourning.

At the Milan Conservatory, Puccini studied under Ponchielli and Bazzini. His thesis piece, the Capriccio sinfonico, was performed on 14 July 1883 and favourably reviewed. His first opera, Le Villi, was entered for a competition run by the publisher Sonzogno but was disqualified because its manuscript was illegible. The publisher Giulio Ricordi then commissioned Edgar, which premiered at La Scala on 21 April 1889 to a lukewarm response and never became popular. Ricordi kept Puccini on and continued his allowance. Manon Lescaut was completed with the librettists Luigi Illica and Giuseppe Giacosa.

La bohème, based on Henri Murger's La Vie de Bohème, premiered in Turin in 1896 under Arturo Toscanini and was soon performed in leading opera houses in Europe and the United States. Tosca followed in 1900, arguably his first venture into verismo, the realistic depiction of life including violence. Madama Butterfly, first given at La Scala on 17 February 1904, was greeted with hostility, probably owing to inadequate rehearsals; Puccini withdrew it and revised it, and a fifth version of 1907 became the standard one.

La fanciulla del West, from a play by David Belasco, premiered at the Metropolitan Opera in New York on 10 December 1910, the first world premiere of an opera there. La rondine was first given at Monte Carlo on 27 March 1917, and Il trittico, three one-act operas, in New York in 1918. Puccini left Turandot unfinished; Franco Alfano completed the last two scenes from his sketches.

In 1903 Puccini was seriously injured in a car crash on the road from Lucca to Torre del Lago, where he had a villa on the lake from about 1900, and he was found to have a form of diabetes. Late in 1923 he began to complain of a sore throat, and doctors diagnosed throat cancer and recommended an experimental radiation treatment in Brussels. He died there on 29 November 1924, aged 65, of complications after the treatment. News reached Rome during a performance of La bohème, which was stopped while the orchestra played Chopin's Funeral March. He is buried in a chapel at the Villa Puccini.
giambattista-bodoni: Giambattista Bodoni was born on 16 February 1740 in Saluzzo, then in the Kingdom of Sardinia and now in Piedmont, the seventh child and fourth son of the printer Francesco Agostino Bodoni and Paola Margherita Giolitti. His grandfather was also a printer, and his boyhood toys were his grandfather's leftover punches and matrices.

At 17 he left for Rome, on 8 February 1758, and found work as an assistant compositor at the press of the Propaganda Fide under Cardinal Giuseppe Spinelli and Costantino Ruggieri. He sorted punches in Middle Eastern and Asian languages, studied Hebrew and Arabic at La Sapienza, became the press's compositor of foreign languages and began cutting his own punches. After eight years he set out for England but fell ill with malaria and returned to Saluzzo.

In February 1768 Bodoni went to Parma, where Duke Ferdinand and his prime minister, Guillaume du Tillot, were setting up a royal press. At first he ordered type from Pierre Simon Fournier and imitated it, gradually developing his own style. His first major publication there was the Descrizione delle Feste, celebrating the duke's wedding to Archduchess Maria Amalia of Austria. His first specimen book, Fregi e majuscule, appeared in 1771.

When the Spanish ambassador José Nicolás de Azara tried to draw him to Rome, the duke in 1791 gave him a private press of his own. That year Bodoni married Margherita Dall'Aglio at the age of 51 and stayed in Parma for life. After 1791 he produced much of his finest work, including Horace, Virgil, Tasso and Homer. Napoleon, pleased with the gift of the Iliad, made him a Chevalier of the Order of the Reunion and gave him a pension for life. In 1806 he presented Pope Pius VII with an Oratio Dominica in 155 languages.

Bodoni died on 30 November 1813, with Racine's Théatre Complet on the press for Joachim Murat. His widow completed the series and in 1818 published the two-volume Manuale tipografico, over 600 pages. With Firmin Didot he evolved the Modern style, in which letters have strong contrast between thick and thin parts. Admirers praised his refinement, while William Morris thought his near-mechanical perfection cold. The Museo Bodoniano opened in Parma in 1963, in the Palazzo della Pilotta, and several revivals of his typefaces, all called Bodoni, are used as display faces.
giambattista-vico: Giambattista Vico was born on 23 June 1668 to a bookseller in Naples. Ill health and dissatisfaction with the scholasticism of the Jesuits led to his being educated at home by tutors. He graduated from the University of Naples in 1694 as Doctor of Civil and Canon Law. In 1699 he married Teresa Caterina Destito and accepted a chair in rhetoric at the University of Naples, which he held until he retired through ill health in 1741. In 1734 Charles III, King of Naples, appointed him historiographer royal at a salary greater than he had earned as a professor.

On returning to Naples Vico found the physics of Descartes at the height of its renown, and studies of rhetoric and civic discourse met with growing disdain. He answered that the realms of verifiable truth and of human concern overlap only slightly, and that reason is needed in both. He did not hold the Cartesian method irrelevant, only unfit for the civic sphere, where practical wisdom and the arts of persuasion are also needed.

His best-known principle, verum factum, was first formulated in 1710 in that book. It states that truth is verified through creation or invention rather than, as for Descartes, through observation: the criterion of the true is to have made it. Vico later argued that civil life, like mathematics, is wholly constructed. His main work, the New Science of 1725, tries to organise the humanities as a single science that records and explains the historical cycles by which societies rise and fall. In it the Age of Men, a time of equal rights, would in his view lead to chaos and collapse, which is why he saw a need for religion and divine providence to keep order.

Vico died on 23 January 1744. He was relatively unknown in the 18th century and read only in Naples, but French Romantic historians began in the 19th century to use his works as models. Karl Marx mentioned him in Capital, and Georges Sorel drew on his principle to treat social science as the study of how human groups produce institutions and cultures. He is regarded as having inaugurated the modern philosophy of history.
gian-galeazzo-visconti: Gian Galeazzo Visconti was born on 16 October 1351, the son of Galeazzo II Visconti, who held the signoria of Pavia, and Bianca of Savoy. His first marriage was to Isabelle of Valois, who brought him the title of comte de Vertus in Champagne, rendered in Italian as Conte di Virtù, the name by which he was known early in his career. After she died in childbirth in 1372, he married his cousin Caterina Visconti, daughter of Bernabò, on 2 October 1380. His daughter Valentina, by Isabelle, married Louis I, Duke of Orléans, on 17 August 1389.

In 1385 Gian Galeazzo gained control of Milan from his uncle Bernabò, with whom he had ruled Lombardy jointly. According to the account given, he faked a religious conversion and ambushed him during a procession. Bernabò was imprisoned and soon died, supposedly poisoned on Gian Galeazzo's orders. He then took Verona, Vicenza and Padua, and controlled almost the whole Po Valley, including Piacenza, though Padua reverted to Francesco Novello da Carrara in 1390. In 1395 King Wenceslaus of the Romans gave him the title Duke of Milan for 100,000 florins.

He spent 300,000 gold florins trying to turn the Mincio and the Brenta from their courses to leave Mantua and Padua helpless. In 1400 he appointed clerks and departments for public health and, with his chancellor Francesco Barbavara, is credited with an efficient and innovative bureaucracy. He completed the Visconti Castle at Pavia, begun by his father, founded the Certosa di Pavia and furthered work on Milan's Duomo.

Gian Galeazzo angered France by seeking to keep Genoa from French sovereignty, and when Queen Isabeau's faction spread rumours about Valentina and she was exiled from Paris in 1396, he threatened war. After the French-led crusade met disaster at Nicopolis, he was strongly suspected of having told the Turks its strength and plans.

He dreamed of uniting northern Italy as a revived Lombard empire, and in 1402 he attacked Bologna and Florence, which had joined the League of Bologna; he won a victory over the Bolognese at Casalecchio on 26–27 June 1402. He fell ill at the castle of Melegnano and died on 3 September 1402. His lands were divided among his legitimate and illegitimate children, who fought each other, and the territories he had ruled broke apart.
gian-gastone-de-medici: Gian Gastone was born in Florence in May 1671, the second son of Grand Duke Cosimo III and Marguerite Louise d'Orléans, who returned to France when he was four. Tutored by Cardinal Henry Noris, he became an antiquarian, a botanist and an amateur scientist who spoke several languages. These tastes earned him the disdain of his father and his elder brother, Grand Prince Ferdinando, and a scant allowance.

In 1697 his sister, the Electress Palatine Anna Maria Luisa, arranged his marriage to the wealthy widow Anna Maria Franziska of Saxe-Lauenburg, and they married at Düsseldorf on 2 July 1697. The couple despised each other and had no children. He found life at her Bohemian residences intolerable and drank heavily, and Cosimo recalled him to Florence in 1708. He never saw his wife again.

Ferdinando died on 30 October 1713, which caused a succession crisis. On 4 April 1718 Great Britain, France and the Dutch Republic, and later Austria, named Charles of Spain as heir, disregarding Cosimo's plan to make the Electress Palatine heiress. Gian Gastone succeeded on 31 October 1723, finding an army of under 3,000 men, empty coffers and a city full of beggars. He began by releasing prisoners and abolishing exorbitant taxes and public executions, repealed penal laws restricting Jews, and reversed Cosimo's ban on teaching new ideas at the University of Pisa.

He delegated most public duties to his sister-in-law Violante Beatrice of Bavaria and spent most of his time in bed, remaining bedridden after a sprained ankle in July 1729. To secure his sister's inheritance he separated the Medici's private property from that of the state. The Treaty of Vienna of 1731 confirmed Charles of Spain as his heir, and later peace terms of 1735 transferred the claim to Francis of Lorraine; neither the grand duke nor Francis was consulted.

Gian Gastone ordered a statue of Galileo Galilei for the Basilica of Santa Croce, and died on 9 July 1737, the last Medici grand duke, ending almost three centuries of Medici rule over Florence. Anna Maria Luisa inherited the family's allodial possessions, while Francis of Lorraine received the title of grand duke. His people mourned him sincerely; Charles de Brosses wrote in 1739 that the Tuscans would give two-thirds of their property to have the Medici back. He is buried in the Basilica of San Lorenzo.
gian-lorenzo-bernini: Gian Lorenzo Bernini was born on 7 December 1598 in Naples, the sixth of thirteen children of Angelica Galante and the Mannerist sculptor Pietro Bernini, who came from Florence. He was recognised as a prodigy at eight, and Pope Paul V is said to have remarked that the child would be the Michelangelo of his age. In 1606 his father received a papal commission and moved the family to Rome, where he continued his son's training. Under the patronage of the wealthy Cardinal Scipione Borghese the young Bernini rose rapidly as a sculptor.

Pope Gregory XV gave Bernini the rank of Cavaliere in 1621. From 1623 to 1644 he enjoyed a near monopoly of patronage from Urban VIII and the Barberini family, who first set him to architecture. His first fountain, the Barcaccia at the foot of the Spanish Steps, commissioned in 1627, was a low-lying boat that made the most of Rome's weak water pressure. After Urban's death Innocent X, an enemy of the Barberini, left him in eclipse for four years, partly because of the failed bell towers of St. Peter's, which Bernini had designed.

Under Alexander VII, who planned to make Rome a world capital, Bernini was chief collaborator, and St. Peter's Square was built from 1656 to 1667. In 1665 political pressure sent him to Paris to work for Louis XIV on the Louvre, and he stayed from April to October. Later he refurbished the Ponte Sant'Angelo under Clement IX, and in 1674 he made the statue of the Blessed Ludovica Albertoni in six months.

Bernini was first and foremost a sculptor, and the latest catalogue of his sculpture lists 143 entries, from 1610 to a marble Salvator Mundi bust of 1679. He also designed tomb monuments, among them those of Urban VIII and Alexander VII in St. Peter's, painted perhaps 150 canvases of which 35 to 40 survive, and wrote, directed and acted in plays, mostly Carnival satires. The art historian Irving Lavin called his ability to combine sculpture, painting and architecture into one whole the unity of the visual arts.

He worked until two weeks before his death, from a stroke, on 28 November 1680. Few artists have so shaped the appearance of a city as he did Rome, and sculptors and architects studied his work for decades afterwards.
gianfrancesco-i-gonzaga: Gianfrancesco was the son of Francesco I Gonzaga and Margherita Malatesta. He inherited the rule of Mantua in 1407 at the age of 12 and in his first years was under the patronage of his uncle Carlo Malatesta and, indirectly, of the Republic of Venice. In 1409 he married Paola Malatesta, daughter of Malatesta IV Malatesta of Pesaro. They had eight children, among them Ludovico, who succeeded him, Carlo, Margherita and Cecilia.

Gianfrancesco ruled as Captain of the People until Emperor Sigismund granted him the title of marquis on 22 September 1433, making him the first of the Gonzaga to bear it; he held it until his death, and was also a condottiere. As a soldier he fought for the Papal States in 1412 and for the Malatestas in 1417, and from 1434 he was capitano generale, commander-in-chief, of the Venetian armies. He later broke with Venice and entered the service of the Visconti of Milan, beginning an unsuccessful war against Venice in which Mantua lost several of its territories.

His court drew artists such as Pisanello as well as Vittorino da Feltre, beginning Mantua's role as a capital of the Italian Renaissance, and he founded the first workshop in Italy for making tapestries. His daughter Cecilia Gonzaga, taught by Vittorino, became a humanist scholar and a nun. Gianfrancesco had sought to marry her to Oddantonio da Montefeltro, the first Duke of Urbino, but gave up the plan when the duke proved a cruel ruler. He died on 23 September 1444.
giardini-naxos: Giardini Naxos, literally Naxos Gardens and called I Jardina in Sicilian, is a comune in the Metropolitan City of Messina. It lies on the coast of the Ionian Sea, on a bay between Cape Taormina and Cape Schisò, with the town of Taormina in the hills above it that can easily be reached by car and bus.

Naxos was founded in 734 BCE by Thucles the Chalcidian, in the part of southern Italy and Sicily known as Magna Graecia. It was never a powerful city, but its temple of Apollo Archegetes, the protecting deity of all the Greek colonies, gave it prominence in religious affairs. Leontini and Catania were both colonised from Naxos. Hippocrates, tyrant of Gela, captured the city in 494 BCE. Its opposition to Syracuse led in the end to its capture and destruction in 403 BCE by the tyrant Dionysius, after it had supported Athens in that city's disastrous Sicilian Expedition. The site continued to be inhabited, but most activity shifted to the neighbouring Tauromenium.

In 1544, after raids by the corsair Kheir-ed-Din, several military buildings were constructed to protect Cape Schisò from the Barbary pirates, who continued to attack and plunder the coastal villages. They were Schisò Castle, rebuilt from an earlier castle of the 13th century, Schisò fort and Vignazza Tower. The tower is a quadrangular watchtower that patrolled the coast south of Port Schisò, and observers inside it could alert the villagers and neighbouring watchtowers with smoke signals if pirate boats were sighted.

Until the early 1970s Giardini Naxos was a quiet fishing village. It is now a seaside resort and a stop for cruise ships, with beaches, a small fishing port, a larger port for the cruise ships, several churches and an archaeological park. Many Italians own summer homes there, and every Ferragosto people spend the night camping and celebrating on the beaches.
gibeah: Gibeah is a Hebrew word meaning hill, and the Hebrew Bible names three places so called, in the tribes of Benjamin, Judah and Ephraim. Gibeah of Benjamin, also called Gibeah of Saul, is the most often mentioned. It is generally identified with Tell el-Fūl, a hill 3 miles (4.8 km) north of ancient Jerusalem on the watershed ridge, 2,754 feet (839 m) above sea level; Josephus placed Gabaothsaul about 30 stadia north of Jerusalem, which roughly fits. Edward Robinson and C. Umhau Wolf preferred Jaba', and Israel Finkelstein also challenged the identification, but Jaba' is now widely identified with biblical Geba.

In the Book of Judges, Gibeah is the setting of the rape of the Levite's concubine and the resulting Battle of Gibeah (Judges 19–21). In the Book of Samuel it is the first capital of the united Kingdom of Israel under Saul, who reigned there 22 years (1 Samuel 8–31). Josephus wrote that the 10th Roman Legion under Titus camped in the Valley of Thorns near Gabaothsaul before the siege of Jerusalem in 70 CE. Jerome, in the late fourth and early fifth centuries, called Gibeah of Saul a town destroyed to the ground.

Charles Warren excavated Tell el-Fūl in 1868, William F. Albright in 1922–1923, and P. W. Lapp in 1964. Kenneth Kitchen reports an Iron I occupation replaced after an interval by a fortress, later refurbished and then abandoned. The oldest level may reflect the Gibeah of Judges 19–20, and Albright's work favoured Saul having built the first fortress, quadrangular with a rectangular corner tower. The site was inhabited again around the start of the Hellenistic period, its citadel was repaired in the second century BCE, and it was abandoned at that century's end.

Tell el-Fūl lies in northern Jerusalem, on the outskirts of the Pisgat Ze'ev and Shuafat neighbourhoods. King Hussein of Jordan began building a royal palace there, but work stopped when the Six-Day War broke out, and only the skeleton of the building remains. The modern neighbourhood of Givat Shaul bears the name of Gibeah of Saul but stands elsewhere. Gibeah of Judah (Joshua 15:57) is identified by C. R. Conder with Jab'a, and Gibeah of Ephraim (Joshua 24:33), where Eleazar was buried, is possibly Awarta.
gibraltar: Gibraltar lies near the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula, on the Bay of Gibraltar, close to where the Mediterranean Sea meets the Atlantic Ocean at the Strait of Gibraltar. Its territory covers 6.8 square kilometres and shares a land border of 1.2 kilometres with Spain. The Rock of Gibraltar dominates the landscape, and the town stands at its foot. The name comes from the Arabic Jabal Ṭāriq, the Mount of Tariq, after the eighth-century North African commander Tariq ibn Ziyad, who began the Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula across the strait in 711.

Neanderthals lived in Gorham's Cave about 50,000 years ago, and Homo sapiens went on using the caves of Gibraltar from about 40,000 years ago to about 5,000 years ago. Neolithic pottery found in the caves is mostly of the Almerian culture of Andalusia. There is little evidence of habitation in the Bronze Age, when people had largely stopped living in caves.

The Almohads founded Gibraltar as a permanent watchtower in 1160. In the Late Middle Ages control passed between the Nasrids, Castilians and Marinids, and the place gained strategic weight with the destruction of nearby Algeciras around 1375. It became part of the Crown of Castile again in 1462. Anglo-Dutch forces captured it from Spain in 1704, during the War of the Spanish Succession, and it was ceded to Great Britain in perpetuity by the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713.

Its control of the narrow entrance to the Mediterranean made it an important base for the Royal Navy, particularly during the Napoleonic Wars and the Second World War. Gibraltar was declared a crown colony on 25 June 1830. Water was a constant concern: with no rivers or streams, the town relied on wells, cisterns and rainwater, and in the late nineteenth century a Sanitary Commission introduced large-scale desalination and giant catchments after cholera and yellow fever had spread. In 1969 Francisco Franco closed the land frontier with Spain, and it reopened in 1982.

Gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory with almost complete internal self-government through an elected parliament, while the United Kingdom remains responsible for defence and foreign policy. Spain asserts a claim to the territory; Gibraltarians overwhelmingly rejected Spanish sovereignty in a referendum in 1967 and shared sovereignty in 2002. English is the language of government, commerce and education, and many Gibraltarians also speak Spanish and a local dialect called Llanito. About 38,000 people live there, and their ancestry includes Genoese, Maltese, Portuguese, Sephardic Jewish and Moroccan as well as Spanish and British.
giengen-an-der-brenz: Giengen lies in the district of Heidenheim at the eastern edge of the Swabian Alb, on the Brenz River about 30 kilometres north-east of Ulm, near the border with Bavaria. It stands on the Nuremberg, Ulm and Constance route, one of the main feeder routes of the Way of St. James, and walking pilgrims on their way to Santiago de Compostela pass through it. It is the home of the toy company founded by Margarete Steiff, who lived from 1847 to 1909.

The first record of the town is a monastery chronicle of Peterhausen reporting the death in battle in 1078 of Margrave Diepold II von Vohburg, lord of Giengen. In 1147 Adele, daughter of Diepold III, married Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa; the marriage ended in divorce after a few years because it was childless. Barbarossa probably granted market rights and the unicorn coat of arms during a stay in 1171. Described as a village in 1216, Giengen seems to have been a city by 1252.

Successive emperors pawned the city more than once, and the counts of Württemberg and of Oettingen vied for control. Only in 1395 did all recognise Giengen as a free imperial city. In 1481 it was exempted from the jurisdiction of any outside court, and it joined the Swabian League in 1488. In the imperial register of 1521 it owed two horsemen, 13 foot soldiers and 60 gulden, near the bottom of the list of 85 free imperial cities. The Reformation transformed it. The first Protestant preacher, Kaspar Pfeiffelmann, preached at the hospital church in 1528, the council hired the reformer Martin Rauber in 1531, and the city officially adopted Lutheran doctrine in 1537. Catholic services were prohibited in 1556.

The Thirty Years' War brought repeated looting and ransoms by Swedish, imperial and French troops, and a fire in 1634 destroyed much of the city. The population fell from close to 2,000 in 1618 to 1,200 in 1651. The 18th century was quiet; Goethe stayed two nights at the Goldenen Gans inn in June 1788. In 1802 Duke Frederick II of Württemberg wrote that Giengen should be incorporated, and the city, with 1,695 inhabitants, lost its independence.
giessen: Giessen stands on the Lahn river, which divides the town into a western and an eastern part, roughly 50 kilometres north of Frankfurt am Main. The name comes from Giezzen, as the place was first referred to in 1197, and it describes the position of the town between several rivers, lakes and streams. It is the capital of both the district and the administrative region of Giessen.

Giessen began as a moated castle built in 1152 by Count Wilhelm von Gleiberg, although the community in the north-east, in today's suburb of Wieseck, dates back to 775. The town became part of Hesse-Marburg in 1567 and passed to Hesse-Darmstadt in 1604. The university was founded in 1607, and the botanical garden of 1609 is the oldest in Germany still at its original location. The town was included in the Grand Duchy of Hesse created in 1806 during the Napoleonic Wars and, after the First World War, in the People's State of Hesse. The physicist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was professor of physics at the university from 1879 until 1888.

In the Second World War a subcamp of the Buchenwald concentration camp stood at the Heil- und Pflegeanstalt Licher Straße. Heavy bombing in 1944 destroyed about 75 percent of the town, including most of its historic buildings.

American units reached Giessen in early April 1945, and the airfield was converted into the Giessen Army Depot, the central United States army depot for all of Europe, which was returned to German authorities on 28 September 2007. In 1977 Giessen was merged with Wetzlar to form a new city of Lahn, but the merger was reversed in 1979 because both populations disliked it. The administrative region of Giessen was founded on 1 January 1981.

Giessen has about 90,000 inhabitants, of whom roughly 37,000 are university students. The university is officially named Justus Liebig University after the chemist, and the Liebig Museum, founded in 1920, honours him. The Old Cemetery holds the graves of Röntgen and his wife Anna Bertha. The Mathematikum, opened in 2002, offers hands-on mathematical exhibits. A dialect called Manisch, a variety of rotwelsch, was spoken in poorer neighbourhoods of the town, and it is now nearly extinct in terms of fluent speakers.
gifu: Gifu is the capital of Gifu Prefecture, on the northern edge of the Nōbi Plain. The Nagara River cuts the city in half, and its alluvial plain is fertile but prone to flooding in typhoons, so dykes and levees have been built. Mount Kinka, 329 metres high beside the river, is one of the city's main symbols and carries Gifu Castle. Traditional industries include Mino washi paper and agriculture, and the city is part of the Chūkyō metropolitan area centred on Nagoya.

Two sites in the city, Ryomonji and Kotozuka, have produced large burial mounds of the late Yayoi period. In the Sengoku period it was said that whoever controls Gifu controls Japan, since its central location suited those seeking to unify the country. The Toki clan held Mino Province for over 200 years until Saitō Dōsan, a Toki vassal, rebelled and took control in 1542, building Inabayama Castle on Mount Inaba. Oda Nobunaga, who followed Dōsan in the castle, gave the castle and the surrounding town the name Gifu. The castle was first built by the Nikaidō clan in the Kamakura period and has been rebuilt many times, the present one in 1956.

In the Edo period the nearby post towns of Kanō-juku and Gōdo-juku on the Nakasendō provided traffic and were later absorbed by Gifu, which became a city in 1889. Its first major industry was textiles, and for a long time it rivaled Tokyo and Osaka as a centre of Japanese fashion. In the Pacific War, Gifu was an industrial centre, and the air raid of 9 July 1945 caused 1,383 casualties, 863 of them deaths, and affected 20,426 buildings. It merged with Yanaizu in 2006.

Cormorant fishing on the Nagara River is the city's best-known attraction and is said to date back more than 1,300 years. Six fishing masters work the river together from 11 May to 15 October, catching ayu sweetfish. Temples tied to Saitō Dōsan and Oda Nobunaga include Jōzai-ji, where Dōsan's remains are interred, and Sōfuku-ji, with its Blood Ceiling.
gifu-castle: Gifu Castle stands on Mount Kinka, northeast of the centre of Gifu, facing the Nagara River, and it is one of the main symbols of the city. Before a severe flood in 1586 the Kiso River ran north of its present bed and much closer to the castle, so two large rivers protected it. It also commanded the main route into Mino Province from the Tokaido highway, which connected Kyoto with the eastern provinces. It was designated a National Historic Site in 2011.

The Nikaido clan built the first castle between 1201 and 1204, in the Kamakura period, as little more than a small fort. In the Muromachi period Saito Toshinaga rebuilt it on a much larger scale. The Saito clan was later supplanted by the Toki, and its fortunes were restored by an adventurer from Kyoto who took the name Saito Dosan, the Viper of Mino. He expelled the Toki clan and defeated an invasion from Owari led by Oda Nobuhide. His own son Saito Yoshitatsu killed him in a revolt, and Yoshitatsu died at the age of 34, leaving Inabayama Castle to his son Saito Tatsuoki.

In 1567 Oda Nobunaga attacked Mino from Sunomata Castle, crossed the Kiso River and began a siege on 13 September. It lasted about two weeks. Near the end his retainer Kinoshita Tokichiro led a small party up the steep cliffs, entered from the unguarded rear and opened the front gates. Nobunaga renamed the stronghold Gifu Castle after an ancient Chinese practice, built a tenshu on the summit and brought in huge stones for the ramparts. He lived there for about ten years, until Azuchi Castle was finished in 1579.

Nobunaga's son Oda Nobutada held it until he was killed with his father at the Honno-ji Incident in 1582. Toyotomi Hideyoshi then gave it to Oda Nobutaka, who sided with Shibata Katsuie against Hideyoshi and was forced to commit seppuku there. Oda Hidenobu later joined Ishida Mitsunari against Tokugawa Ieyasu, and the castle fell after a one-day siege in 1600, a prelude to Sekigahara. Okudaira Nobumasa, Ieyasu's son-in-law, found it in poor repair, abolished it and built Kano Castle at the foot of the mountain in 1603, moving some structures there.

The main keep was rebuilt in the 1910s, using wood from the old bridge over the Nagara, and burnt down in an accident in 1943. The present keep is a concrete and steel structure based on the original drawings and plans, with some changes. It holds a museum on three floors and an observation deck with a view of the Nagara River and Nagoya. A ropeway runs from Gifu Park to the summit.
gihon-spring: The Gihon Spring, also called the Fountain of the Virgin or Saint Mary's Pool, rises in a cave in the Kidron Valley and was the main source of water for the Pool of Siloam and the City of David. It is one of the major intermittent springs of the world. Before the water table declined through modern overpumping, it flowed three to five times a day in winter, twice daily in summer and once daily in autumn, a pattern explained by an outlet shaped like a siphon. Its output, about 600,000 cubic metres a year, is the largest in the area. Because it flowed only at intervals, the Pool of Siloam was excavated to store water for the town.

The spring supplied drinking water and also irrigated gardens in the Kidron Valley, which fed the ancient settlement. Three systems brought its water under cover. The Middle Bronze Age Siloam Channel was cut about 20 feet into the ground and covered with slabs, leading to the oldest or Upper Pool of Siloam. The Warren's Shaft system, of slightly later date, was a set of tunnels from the Well Gate on the Ophel down to the spring, by which people collected water. The Iron Age Siloam Tunnel, a winding rock-cut aqueduct to the Pool of Siloam, replaced the older channel, and the Siloam inscription was found carved into its wall.

The name Gihon is thought to come from the Hebrew word giha, meaning gushing forth, and is also the name of one of the four rivers of Eden in Genesis. The name Fountain of the Virgin comes from a legend that Mary washed the swaddling clothes of Jesus there.

In the mid-19th century James Turner Barclay tried to explore a passage leading from the spring, but stones and debris blocked it. In 1997, while a visitor centre was being built, archaeologists unexpectedly uncovered two monumental towers fortifying the spring, one protecting the base of Warren's Shaft and the other the spring itself. Their dating has been debated. A 2017 study by the Weizmann Institute of Science used radiocarbon dates and considered both Middle Bronze Age and Iron Age II construction. Israel Finkelstein suggested the tower could be Bronze Age but restored in the Iron Age, while Ronny Reich in 2018 defended the original Middle Bronze Age dating. The spring is controlled today by the Ir David Foundation.
gijon: Gijón lies on the coast of central Asturias, about 24 km north-east of Oviedo and 26 km from Avilés. The peninsula of Cimavilla, the original settlement, separates the beach of San Lorenzo to the east from the beaches of Poniente and Arbeyal, the shipyards, the recreational port and the Port of El Musel to the west. The ground rises from sea level to 513 m at Picu Samartín and 672 m at Peña de los Cuatro Jueces. The name may come from Gigia, a medieval form tied to the Roman wall on the Cimavilla peninsula, called the Gegionem, or from a hypothetical Roman name Sessio that became Xixón; the second theory is now thought the more acceptable.

The earliest evidence of human presence is a series of tumuli on Monte Deva and Neolithic dolmens on Monte Areo, supposedly built around 5000 BCE. The first settlement, Noega at Campa Torres, began between the 6th and 5th centuries BCE, was populated by Astures and later Romanized, and was gradually abandoned once the Roman wall on Cimavilla was built. The region submitted to the Visigoth king Sisebut in the 7th century. Gijón was the capital of the Muslim territories on the Cantabrian Sea under Munuza for a short period between 713 and 718 or 722. In 722 the Asturians led by Pelagius, the first king of the Kingdom of Asturias, won the Battle of Covadonga, regarded as the beginning of the Reconquista.

Until 1270 there are no reliable references to Gijón as a settlement. That year Alfonso X of Castile gave it the status of puebla. In the 14th century the war between Alfonso Enríquez, Count of Gijón and Noreña, and Henry III of Castile ended with the village burned and destroyed. It re-emerged in the 15th and 16th centuries, when a new dock added fishing and commerce, and in the 17th and 18th centuries it developed rapidly through the commercial links of its port with the American colonies. The Oviedo–Gijón road and the recognition of the port as the best in Asturias started industrial activity late in the 18th century.

The 19th century brought the coal trade, the Gijón–León road and the Langreo–Gijón railway, and in 1893 a new port, El Musel, was built as the first coal port of the peninsula. New neighbourhoods such as Natahoyo, La Calzada, Tremañes and El Humedal housed the workers the industry drew. Iron manufacture was the main industry from the last years of the 19th century until the last decades of the 20th. In the Spanish Civil War the city supported the Republican side, and the resistance was eliminated in August 1936. It was then the capital of the Sovereign Council of Asturias and León until General Franco's troops occupied it in October 1937.
gil-alvarez-carrillo-de-albornoz: Albornoz was born in Carrascosa del Campo, in Cuenca. His father, Garcialuarez Albornoz, fourth lord of Albornoz, was a tutor to the future King Alfonso XI of Castile, and his mother, Doña Teresa de Luna, was a sister of Jimeno de Luna, archbishop of Toledo. He was raised and educated in Zaragoza with his mother's brother and studied law at Toulouse. The cathedral chapter of Toledo elected him to succeed his uncle as archbishop, and Pope Benedict XII confirmed the election on 13 May 1338.

As archbishop he held two reform synods, at Toledo in May 1339 and at Alcalá in April 1347. He fought against a Marinid invasion from Morocco at the Battle of Río Salado in 1340 and led the armed levy of his archbishopric at the taking of Algeciras in 1344. He left Spain on the death of Alfonso XI in March 1350 and never returned; the claim that he fled for fear of Pedro of Castile rests on no contemporary evidence. In December 1350 Pope Clement VI made him cardinal-priest of San Clemente, and he resigned Toledo.

Sent to Italy as legate in 1353 at the head of a small mercenary army, he defeated Giovanni di Vico, lord of Viterbo, at the battle of Viterbo on 10 March 1354. In the Marche and Romagna the Malatesta of Rimini, the Montefeltro of Urbino and the da Polenta of Ravenna submitted. After a recall to Avignon he returned to face Francesco II Ordelaffi of Forlì, who had hired Konrad von Landau's Grand Company, and Ordelaffi surrendered on 4 July 1359. When Innocent VI died, Albornoz refused the papal tiara and Urban V was elected.

The decade of war did not pacify Italy. Mercenary companies still roamed the peninsula, Rome fought Velletri from 1361 to 1367, and Campagna rose in a general rebellion, while papal forces executed the whole population of Cesena, a town loyal to the papacy. In 1364 Albornoz founded the College of Saint Clement at Bologna for Castilian, Aragonese and Portuguese students. Urban V made him legate at Bologna in 1367, but he died at Viterbo the same year. At his wish his remains were carried to Toledo, where Henry of Castile had them entombed with almost royal honours.
gil-gonzalez-davila: Gil González Dávila first appears in the records in 1508, with a royal commission to examine the accounts and tax records of estates, and in 1511 he was made contador, accountant, of Hispaniola. He came to hold an estate with over 200 Indian slaves, and in 1518 he sent Charles V a report highly critical of the colony's management. At Ávila the pilot Andrés Niño approached him with a plan to explore the Pacific coast, and with the help of Bishop Juan Rodriguez de Fonseca, president of the Council of the Indies, they won the king's consent in June 1519.

In Panama the governor, Pedrarias, blocked his inspection of the colony's taxes and hindered his search for ships, so González and Niño built four brigantines in the Pearl Islands. They sailed on 26 January 1522, but leaking ships forced González to march west by land while Niño followed the coast. According to the treasurer Andrés de Cereceda, the people of Nicoya offered no resistance and more than 6000 were baptised. González reached the lakes later named Nicaragua and Managua before attacks forced him back to his ships, and in June 1523 he returned to Panama with three leaking ships, 100 exhausted men and much gold.

Escaping Pedrarias's attempt to arrest him, he went to Santo Domingo and fitted out a new expedition. In 1524 a storm drove him to the Caribbean coast of Honduras, where he named Puerto Caballos and founded San Gil de Buenavista. Marching south, he found that Francisco Hernández de Córdoba, sent by Pedrarias, held his territory; he captured a force under Hernando de Soto by a trick but released it. Cristóbal de Olid, sent by Hernán Cortés, then took him prisoner at Naco, until Olid's own men turned on Olid, who was tried and beheaded.

González and Francisco de las Casas declared their loyalty to Cortés and went to Mexico, where Salazar de la Pedrada, in charge for Cortés, had them arrested and prosecuted for Olid's death. He meant to execute them but was forced to send them to Spain as prisoners. What happened to González there is unknown; his patron Fonseca had died in 1524. He died in Ávila on 21 April 1526, leaving a son of the same name.
gilaks: The Gilaks are an Iranian people native to the south of the Caspian Sea, and one of the main ethnic groups of northern Iran. With the closely related Mazandarani they form part of the Caspian people of the southern and south-western coast. It has been suggested that their ancestors came from the Caucasus, perhaps displacing an earlier group. Linguistic evidence supports this, since Gilaki and Mazandarani, unlike other Iranian languages, share certain typological features with Caucasian languages. A study of mitochondrial DNA and Y chromosomes found that the Gilaks resemble Iranian groups in the first and South Caucasus groups in the second. One proposed explanation is a south Caucasian origin followed by the arrival of local Iranian women, which would have replaced the ancestral language.

The mountainous country on the south-western Caspian coast, now the south-eastern half of Gilan Province, was also called Daylam, and its inhabitants were the Daylamites. The Ziyarid and Buyid dynasties arose in Gilan in the mid-10th century. The Turkish invasions of the 10th and 11th centuries, which brought the Ghaznavid and Seljuk dynasties, ended Daylamite rule. From the 11th century until the rise of the Safavids, local rulers such as the Eshaqvand dynasty and the Ispahbads of Gilan paid tribute to the dominant power south of the Alborz range but ruled independently.

Some scholars suggest a link between the Gilaks and the Zazas, who call themselves Dimli, a name derived from Daylam. During the Safavid, Afsharid and Qajar eras large numbers of Georgians, Circassians, Armenians and other peoples of the Caucasus settled in Gilan, and their descendants still live there.

The Gilaks live along the Alborz mountains and in the surrounding plains. Those on the northern side of the mountains tend to raise livestock, while those on the plains farm. They supply a large share of the region's rice, grains, tobacco and tea, and fishing, caviar exports and silk are other major industries. Their number was estimated at between 3 and 4 million in 2006, and they make up about 70% of the population of Gilan Province. They speak Gilaki, a north-western Iranian language with eastern and western dialects, divided by the Safidrud River, and shading eastward into Mazandarani. Because Persian is the language of education, Gilaki is taught to children at home.
gilan: Gilan Province lies in the north-west of Iran, along the south-western Caspian Sea, west of Mazandaran, east of Ardabil and north of Zanjan and Qazvin; in the north it borders Azerbaijan. Its capital is Rasht, and its main port is Bandar-e Anzali, formerly Bandar-e Pahlavi. The climate is humid subtropical, with the heaviest rainfall in Iran, generally around 1,400 mm a year. Large parts of the province are mountainous and forested, and the coastal plain is used mainly for rice paddies. Gilaks and Talysh form the majority of the population; the Gilaki language belongs to the north-western Iranian branch.

The Gelae, or Gilites, seem to have entered the region south of the Caspian coast in the second or first century BCE; Pliny identified them with the Cadusii, though they were more likely a separate people from the Dagestan region. Gilan was the home of the Ziyarid and Buyid dynasties in the mid-10th century. Its Deylamite warriors resisted the Arabs, who never conquered the region, and under the Buyid ruler Mu'izz al-Dawla the Deylamites took Baghdad in 945. After the Turkish invasions ended the Deylamite states, local rulers governed independently until the Mongol Ilkhan Öljeitü conquered the region in 1307.

Silk made Gilan wealthy from the 15th century, and it was the major exporter of silk in Asia from the 16th century until the mid 19th century. Shah Abbas I ended the rule of Khan Ahmad Khan, the last semi-independent ruler, and annexed the province, and Georgians, Circassians and Armenians settled there under the Safavids. Russia held Gilan for about ten years after the war of 1722 to 1723, and Russian influence lasted until 1946. A disease of silkworms in the mid 19th century caused hardship and a turn to rice and tea.

In the late 1910s Mirza Kuchik Khan led the Jangal movement, and in 1920, in alliance with the Bolsheviks against British forces, the Jangalis helped found the Persian Socialist Soviet Republic, which lasted from June 1920 until September 1921. After the Soviets withdrew support, the Jangalis were defeated and control returned to Tehran. Gilan is one of the 31 provinces of Iran. Rasht is known as the City of Rain, and the coast draws domestic and international visitors.
gilbert-de-clare-1st-earl-of-pembroke: Gilbert de Clare was born at Tonbridge, the second son of Gilbert Fitz Richard de Clare and Alice de Claremont. As his elder brother took the family properties, he inherited no substantial land, though he belonged to the powerful House of de Clare. He later inherited the estates of his paternal uncles Roger and Walter: the baronies and castles of Bienfaite and Orbec in Normandy and, in the Welsh March, the castle of Striguil, later Chepstow, with the lordship of Nether Gwent.

Before 1130 he married Isabel de Beaumont, daughter of Robert de Beaumont, Earl of Leicester and Count of Meulan, and Elizabeth de Vermandois; Isabel had earlier been the mistress of King Henry I of England. Their children included Richard de Clare, 2nd Earl of Pembroke, and Basilia de Clare, who married Raymond FitzGerald and then Geoffrey FitzRobert.

In 1136 Gilbert led an expedition against Exmes and burned parts of the town, including the church of Notre Dame, but forces of William III, Count of Ponthieu, caught him and he escaped only after heavy losses. In Wales, Owain Gwynedd's defeat of the Norman settlers near Cardigan in 1136 had shaken Norman power, but the disorder after the death of Gruffydd ap Rhys in 1137 let the Normans partly recover. When King Stephen made him Earl of Pembroke in 1138, he also gave him the rape and castle of Pevensey in Sussex.

Gilbert fought for Stephen at the Battle of Lincoln on 2 February 1141, but after the king's defeat he rallied to Empress Matilda when she recovered London in June. He joined Geoffrey's plot against Stephen and, when it collapsed, returned to the king, serving at the siege of Oxford late in 1142. In 1147 he rebelled when Stephen refused him the castles surrendered by his nephew Gilbert, 1st Earl of Hertford, and the king nearly captured him at his nearest castle. He seems to have made peace with Stephen before he died on 6 January 1148.
gilbert-elliot-1st-earl-of-minto: Gilbert Elliot was born in Edinburgh on 23 April 1751, the eldest son of Sir Gilbert Elliot, 3rd Baronet, and of Agnes, daughter of Hugh Dalrymple-Murray-Kynynmound. His uncles included John Elliott, Governor of Newfoundland, and Andrew Elliot, colonial governor of New York, and the poet Jean Elliot was his aunt. Around 1763 he and his younger brother Hugh Elliot were sent to Paris, where the Scottish philosopher David Hume supervised their studies and where they became close to Honoré Mirabeau.

After two winters at the University of Edinburgh, in 1766 and 1767, he went up to Christ Church, Oxford, and on leaving the university was called to the bar. In 1777 he married Anna Maria Amyand, daughter of Sir George Amyand, 1st Baronet, and sister-in-law of Lord Malmesbury. They had several children, among them Gilbert, later 2nd Earl of Minto, and Admiral Sir George Elliot.

In 1776 Elliot entered the House of Commons as an independent Whig member for Morpeth. He became a friend of Edmund Burke, helped him in the attack on Warren Hastings and Sir Elijah Impey, and stood twice without success for the office of Speaker, in January and June 1789. In 1793 he was named Civil Commissioner for Dunkirk, then besieged by the Coalition forces, but the siege failed and the post remained on paper; a similar appointment for Toulon came to nothing as well.

He was sworn of the Privy Council in 1794. In 1797 he took the additional names of Murray and Kynynmound and was created Baron Minto. From 1799 to 1801 he was Envoy-Extraordinary to Austria, and after a few months as President of the Board of Control he was appointed governor-general at the end of 1806. In India he secured in 1810 the release of the navigator Matthew Flinders, held for six years on the Isle de France (Mauritius), and during the Napoleonic Wars extended British power to the Moluccas, Java and other Dutch possessions in the East Indies.

On his return he was created Viscount Melgund and Earl of Minto. He died at Stevenage, Hertfordshire, on 21 June 1814, aged 63, and was buried in Westminster Abbey with his brother Hugh. His eldest son Gilbert succeeded to his titles. The district of Minto in New South Wales, now a suburb of Sydney, was named after him in 1809.
gilbert-islands: The Gilbert Islands, called Tungaru in Gilbertese and formerly the Kingsmill Islands, lie about halfway between Papua New Guinea and Hawaii and form the eastern-most part of Micronesia. They run in a rough north to south line, with the northernmost island, Makin, about 780 kilometres from the southernmost, Arorae. They are grouped as the Northern, Central and Southern Gilberts. In the north, a chief living on Butaritari ruled Butaritari and Makin with full authority, while in the south power was held collectively by the unimwane, the old men of the island. The north has more rainfall, which allows a wider range of crops. Tembinok', the last king of Abemama, Kuria and Aranuka in the central group, died in the early part of the 20th century.

The islands had been inhabited by Oceanians for at least 2,000 years and probably 3,000. In 1606 the Portuguese navigator Pedro Fernandes de Queirós sighted Butaritari and Makin. Vice-Admiral John Byron passed through in 1765. In 1820 Adam Johann von Krusenstern named them after Captain Thomas Gilbert, who had crossed the archipelago in 1788, and the French captain Louis Duperrey was the first to map the whole group. Whaling ships called in numbers from 1825 until the 1860s, and ships of the United States Exploring Expedition charted reefs and anchorages.

An Anglo-German agreement of 1886 placed the islands in the British sphere of influence, and Captain Edward Davis of HMS Royalist proclaimed a British protectorate on 27 May 1892. The conduct of the second resident commissioner, William Telfer Campbell, including allegations of forced labour, was the subject of Arthur Mahaffy's report of 1909. The Gilbert and Ellice Islands were later proclaimed a colony. In the early and middle 20th century islanders earned income mainly from phosphate production on Banaba, and the missions ran the village schools.

The Japanese invaded the islands on the day of the attack on Pearl Harbor and occupied three of them by 9 December 1941. On 17 August 1942, 221 US Marines raided Makin; the raid is believed to have alerted the Japanese to the islands' importance and led to their fortification. US forces landed on Makin and Tarawa on 20 November 1943, and the Japanese were defeated.

The Gilbert and Ellice Islands became autonomous in 1971. The Ellice Islands were separated from 1975, and Tuvalu became independent in 1978. In 1979 the Gilberts became the independent state of Kiribati, whose name is the Gilbertese rendering of Gilberts. They make up the main part of the country.
gildas: Gildas was a 6th-century British monk, known also as Gildas Badonicus and Gildas Sapiens, and called Gweltaz in Breton. The Life of Saint Gildas, in versions that agree on this point, says he was born at Arecluta, named for the River Clut, which was long taken to mean the Clyde in what is now Scotland.
