Some historians think his origins lay farther south, because his writing shows little familiarity with Strathclyde and a knowledge of classical Latin texts more likely acquired within former Roman Britain; Chester and Arclid in Cheshire have been suggested. He states that he was born in the year of the Battle of Mount Badon.

The First Life, written in the 11th century by a monk of the monastery he founded, makes him the son of Caunus, king of Alt Clud, and says he studied under Saint Illtud in Glamorgan. A second Life, by Caradoc of Llancarfan, is an entirely fictional account that links him to Glastonbury Abbey and King Arthur.

Gildas is best known for De Excidio et Conquestu Britanniae, a sermon in three parts and the only substantial source for the history of its period by a near-contemporary, though it is not meant as an objective chronicle. The first part explains his purpose and gives a short narrative of Roman Britain, including the Groans of the Britons, their last appeal for Roman aid.

It praises Ambrosius Aurelianus, whom Gildas is the first to describe as a leader of resistance to the Saxons, and mentions the victory at Mons Badonicus without naming its leader. Part two condemns five British kings, Constantine, Aurelius Conanus, Vortiporius, Cuneglasus and Maelgwn, and part three attacks the clergy. The work was usually dated to the 540s, though some historians place it earlier. Gildas says he was 44 when he wrote it.

According to the traditions, Gildas later settled in Brittany, where he founded the monastery now called Saint-Gildas-de-Rhuys, and he is thought to have died at Rhuys and been buried there. His relics were venerated in the abbey until the 10th century, when they were removed to Berry; they have since been returned to Saint-Gildas-de-Rhuys, where a reliquary head, an arm reliquary and a femur are kept. He is patron of several churches and monasteries in Brittany, and his feast day is 29 January. A hymn called the Lorica is credited to him, and David Dumville suggests he taught Finnian of Moville.
gildo: Gildo was probably born in the 340s in Mauretania Caesariensis, a Romanised Berber by birth and a son of King Nubel, described as a regulus or kinglet of the Jubaleni. Besides Firmus and Mascezel, his brothers were Mazuca, Sammac and Dius, and he had a sister named Cyria. Following a hypothesis of Stéphane Gsell, later developed by Gabriel Camps, Nubel may be the Flavius Nuvel who commanded the cavalry unit of the equites Armigeri junior and, with his wife Nonnica, built a basilica housing a relic of the True Cross. The name Gildo may come from the Berber root GLD, meaning chief or king.

When Firmus revolted against Emperor Valentinian I in 375, Gildo stayed loyal and fought alongside the general Theodosius the Elder; after the revolt was put down he was rewarded with the immense patrimony confiscated from his brother. In 386 Emperor Theodosius I appointed him Comes Africae and Magister utriusque militiae per Africam, and he ruled the province with some independence, holding the rank of vir spectabilis before 393.

After Theodosius died and his sons Arcadius and Honorius came to the throne, Africa took over from Egypt the task of supplying grain to the city of Rome, which raised Gildo's importance. Incited by the eunuch Eutropius, he considered pledging allegiance to Arcadius and the Eastern Roman Empire. The threat to Rome's granary caused unrest in the city, and on an appeal by Stilicho the Roman Senate declared Gildo an enemy of the state.

Gildo had quarrelled with Mascezel, who fled to the court of Honorius, and took revenge by killing his brother's two sons. Stilicho gave Mascezel command of a chosen body of Gallic veterans who had served under Eugenius, and Gildo's larger army melted before their discipline. Gildo fled in a small boat towards the East, but unfavourable winds drove it back to the harbour of Tabraca, where the inhabitants threw him into the dungeons. Taken over by Mascezel's forces, he died on 31 July 398, executed or forced to kill himself.

His estates were confiscated and became imperial property, so vast that a new office, the Count of Gildo's Patrimony (comes Gildoniaci patrimonii), was created to manage them. Through his daughter Salvina, who married Nebridius, a nephew of Flaccilla, first wife of Theodosius I, his family was linked by marriage to the imperial house.
gilead: Gilead is the ancient and biblical name of the mountainous northern part of the region of Transjordan. It is bounded in the west by the Jordan River, in the north by the deep ravine of the river Yarmouk and the region of Bashan, and in the southwest by the plains of Moab, with no definite boundary to the east. It corresponds roughly to the Irbid, Ajloun, Jerash and Balqa Governorates of Jordan. The Hebrew Bible explains the name as derived from galʿêḏ, from gal, a heap or hill, and ʿêḏ, witness, so that it means a heap of stones of testimony.

The name first appears in the biblical account of the last meeting of Jacob and Laban, in the Book of Genesis, where Laban's entourage camped on Gilead. It was also called by the Aramaic name Yegar-Sahadutha, with the same meaning. According to the biblical account of the Exodus, half of Gilead was held by Sihon and the other half, across the river Jabbok, by Og, king of Bashan; after the two Amorite kings were defeated, Moses allotted the region to the tribes of Gad, Reuben and the eastern half of Manasseh.

In the Book of Judges the thirty sons of the judge Jair controlled thirty towns of Gilead, and the judge Jephthah defeated the Ammonites who tried to retake it. Ammon and Moab sometimes expanded to include southern Gilead. King David fled to Mahanaim in Gilead during the rebellion of Absalom, and the prophet Elijah is later named as coming from it. About 733 BCE King Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria established the province of Gal'azu, the Assyrian form of Gilead.

In Arabic the name is Jalʿād, used for the mountainous land north and south of the Jabbok and, more generally, for the whole region east of the Jordan River. It corresponds today to the northwestern part of the Kingdom of Jordan. The region appears in ancient Safaitic inscriptions.
gilgamesh: Most historians agree that Gilgamesh was a historical king of the Sumerian city-state of Uruk, who ruled early in the Early Dynastic Period. Stephanie Dalley states that precise dates cannot be given, but that they are generally agreed to lie between 2800 and 2500 BCE. The Tummal Inscription, written during the reign of Ishbi-Erra, credits him with building the walls of Uruk and names his son Ur-lugal.

Andrew George holds that there was probably once a King Bilgames in Uruk, as there may have been a real King Arthur in Britain, but that the Gilgamesh of the epic traditions is a literary character to whom many separate traditions have attached. The Greek writer Aelian, in the 2nd century CE, tells of his birth: his grandfather kept his mother under guard because an oracle said her son would overthrow him, and when the child was thrown from a tower an eagle caught him and set him down in an orchard, where a gardener raised him.

In the later Early Dynastic Period Gilgamesh was worshipped as a god at various places in Sumer. King Utu-hengal of Uruk adopted him as patron deity in the 21st century BCE, and the kings of the Third Dynasty of Ur called him their divine brother and friend. King Shulgi declared himself the son of Lugalbanda and Ninsun and brother of Gilgamesh. Prayers on clay tablets address him as a judge of the dead in the Underworld.
Five Sumerian poems tell of his exploits. Gilgamesh and Aga describes his revolt against his overlord Aga of Kish, and others recount his defeat of the giant Huwawa and the Bull of Heaven.

The standard Akkadian Epic of Gilgamesh, composed by a scribe named Sin-leqi-unninni, introduces him as two thirds divine and one third mortal, an oppressive ruler for whom the god Anu creates the wild man Enkidu. When Enkidu dies, Gilgamesh visits Utnapishtim, survivor of the Great Flood, seeking immortality, fails the trials set before him and returns to Uruk.

Fragments of an epic found at Tell Haddad relate that at his death Gilgamesh was buried under the river bed, the workmen of Uruk having diverted the Euphrates for the purpose. The Epic of Gilgamesh was rediscovered in 1849 in the Library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh by Austen Henry Layard. George Smith's translation of the early 1870s caused controversy because of its similarities to the Hebrew Bible. Most scholars hold that the epic influenced the Iliad and the Odyssey.
gilgit: Gilgit lies in the broad Gilgit Valley near the confluence of the Gilgit and Hunza rivers, southwest of the Karakoram range. It has a cold desert climate with little rainfall, and its irrigation comes from rivers fed by melting snow. The economy has mainly rested on agriculture, with wheat, maize and barley the main crops. The earliest known mention of the name is the Hatun Rock Inscription of the 7th century CE, which gives it as Giligitta, and al-Biruni recorded it in Arabic as klkt in the 11th century.

Gilgit was an important city on the Silk Road, along which Buddhism spread, and the Chinese pilgrims Faxian and Xuanzang passed through it. In the 600s and 700s, according to Chinese records, a Buddhist dynasty called Little Balur governed it, believed to be the Patola Shahis. China held suzerainty in the mid-600s, and the Tibetan Empire took the region in the late 600s and held it until the late 800s. Later the Trakhan dynasty ruled until the death of Raja Abbas about 1810, its best known ruler being Queen Dadi Jawari in the 17th century, who built irrigation canals.

In 1846 Gilgit was transferred from the Sikhs to the British and sold to Gulab Singh of Jammu under the Treaty of Amritsar, and Dogra troops took over. The people drove them out in 1852, but Dogra forces from Ranbir Singh retook the town in 1860. In 1877 the British India Government established the Gilgit Agency to guard against the advance of Russia. On 1 November 1947 Major William Brown of the Gilgit Scouts mutinied and overthrew the governor, Ghansara Singh. A provisional government lasted 16 days, and Pakistan's political agent took over the administration on 16 November.

Gilgit is the capital and most populous city of the Pakistani-administered territory of Gilgit-Baltistan, renamed from the Northern Areas in 2009. It lies about 10 kilometres from the Karakoram Highway, which links it to Kashgar in China and to Chitral, Skardu, Peshawar and Islamabad, and it is a hub for trekking and mountaineering in the Karakoram.
gilgit-baltistan: Gilgit-Baltistan is the northern portion of the larger Kashmir region, a territory disputed between India and Pakistan since 1947 and between India and China since 1959, and it is administered by Pakistan. It borders Azad Kashmir, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the Wakhan District of Afghanistan and the Xinjiang region of China. It covers about 72,496 square kilometres, over two thirds of it glaciers, mountains and lakes. The Karakoram, the Hindu Kush and the western Himalayas meet there, and it contains five of the fourteen eight-thousanders, among them K2. Gilgit is the capital and largest city.

Rock carvings, notably at Passu in Hunza, suggest human presence since about 2000 BCE, and the petroglyphs along the Karakoram Highway include some of 5000 to 1000 BCE. Tibetic peoples preceded the Balti of Baltistan, while Indo-Aryan peoples, sometimes called Dards, settled the western areas and speak Shina, Khowar and, in Hunza, the isolate Burushaski. The people followed the Bon religion in the 1st century and practised Buddhism in the 2nd. After the decline of the Tibetan Empire the region broke into small principalities. In the 14th century Sufi preachers from Persia and Central Asia introduced Islam to Baltistan, and in the Gilgit valley it entered through the Trakhān dynasty.

In the early 19th century Ahmad Shah of Skardu unified much of Baltistan, and Gohar Aman of Yasin conquered Gilgit in 1842. The Dogra dynasty of Jammu and Kashmir conquered much of the region in the following decades. After 1947 the residents expressed a desire to join Pakistan, which declined to merge the region because of its link to Jammu and Kashmir. In 1949 Azad Kashmir handed its administration to the federal government under the Karachi Agreement. Until 1972 it was governed under the Frontier Crimes Regulations without a democratic set-up.

The territory became a single unit as the Northern Areas in 1972 and was renamed Gilgit-Baltistan in 2009, when it received an elected assembly. It is neither a province nor a state of Pakistan, and its present arrangements rest on the Order of 2018. It had 1.7 million people at the 2023 census, speaking Shina, Balti, Burushaski, Khowar, Wakhi and other languages, with Urdu as the lingua franca. The Karakoram Highway, built in 1978, runs from Hasan Abdal to the Khunjerab Pass. Polo is the most popular sport, and the Shandur Polo Festival is a major event.
gillo-pontecorvo: Gillo Pontecorvo was born in Pisa on 19 November 1919 into a wealthy secular Italian Jewish family. His brothers included Bruno, a nuclear physicist who defected to the Soviet Union in 1950, and Guido, a geneticist who settled in Britain. He studied chemistry at the University of Pisa but dropped out after passing two exams, and there he first met leftist students and professors. In 1938, faced with growing antisemitism, he followed Bruno to Paris, where he worked in journalism and as a tennis instructor and began making short documentaries. He assisted the directors Joris Ivens and Yves Allégret and met Pablo Picasso, Igor Stravinsky and Jean-Paul Sartre.

In 1941 Pontecorvo joined the Italian Communist Party. He went to northern Italy to help organise anti-fascist partisans and, under the pseudonym Barnaba, led the Resistance in Milan from 1943 until 1945. From 1948 to 1950 he co-edited the communist weekly Pattuglia. He broke with the party in 1956 after the Soviet intervention against the Hungarian uprising, though he did not renounce Marxism.

The catalyst for his turn to film was Roberto Rossellini's Paisà (1946). He bought a 16mm camera and made documentaries, beginning with Missione Timiriazev in 1953. His first full-length film, La grande strada azzurra (1957), about a fisherman off the coast of Sardinia, won a prize at the Karlovy Vary International Film Festival. Kapò (1960), a drama set in a Nazi death camp, was nominated for an Oscar for Best Foreign-Language Film. He spent months, sometimes years, researching the social situations he portrayed.

The Battle of Algiers (1966) portrays the Algerian resistance in the Algerian War in a neorealist style, with newsreel-style footage and almost entirely non-professional actors; the part of Djafar was played by the FLN leader Yacef Saadi. It won the Golden Lion at the 27th Venice Film Festival and earned Pontecorvo Oscar nominations for direction and screenplay. It has been used as a training video by revolutionary groups and by military dictatorships facing guerrilla resistance. Burn! (1969), with Marlon Brando, concerns a fictional slave revolt in the Lesser Antilles, and Ogro (1979) concerns Basque separatists in Spain under Franco. He directed the Venice Film Festival from 1992 to 1994.

Pontecorvo died of congestive heart failure in Rome on 12 October 2006, aged 86. He is associated with the political cinema of the 1960s and 1970s, and the semi-documentary style of The Battle of Algiers influenced later filmmakers. It remains popular in Algeria as a memory of the struggle for independence from France.
gimry: Gimry is a rural locality in the Untsukulsky District of the Republic of Dagestan, Russia, known in Avar as Genub. Its population was 3,362 at the 2002 census and 4,654 at the 2010 census. It lies on the east bank of the north-flowing Avar Koysu river at the bottom of a canyon 5,000 feet deep. Four kilometres north the Avar Koysu joins the Andi Koysu to form the Sulak River. In the nineteenth century the only approaches from the east were from the village of Karanai and along the sides of the Sulak and Avar Koysu canyons.

Gimry belonged to a group of villages called Koysubu or Hindal and was a centre of resistance to Russia during the Caucasian War (1829–1859). Both Ghazi Muhammad and Shamil, who resisted Russian expansion as imams, were born there in the 1790s. In 1830 the Russian commander Baron Rosen tried unsuccessfully to attack the village, and Ghazi Muhammad died there during the Battle of Gimry in 1832. Lanskoy attacked it in 1834. In 1837 the Russians were defeated just to the north at the battle of the Ashitla bridge. Gimry stayed neutral during the Siege of Akhoulgo in 1839 and was attacked by Klugenau in 1840, after which the centre of resistance moved northwest to the forests of Chechnya.

During the Dagestan Uprising of 1920, ninety percent of the buildings were destroyed by artillery, and the surrender of the village in late February 1921 was almost the end of the uprising. In 2014 Russian soldiers tried to capture Magomed Suleymanov, a native of Gimry proclaimed emir of the Caucasus Emirate, and the village was for a time blocked to all but its residents.
ginevra-de-benci: Leonardo painted the portrait in Florence between 1474 and 1478. The sitter, Ginevra de' Benci, a well-known young Florentine woman born around 1458, is universally considered to be the subject. The picture may commemorate her marriage at sixteen to Luigi di Bernardo Niccolini, but an engagement is more likely: wedding portraits of women were usually made in pairs, with the woman on the right facing left, and this one faces right.

Ginevra was also the subject of ten poems by members of the Medici circle, Cristoforo Landino and Alessandro Braccesi, and of two sonnets by Lorenzo de' Medici. Her brother Giovanni, born in 1456, was a friend of Leonardo.

A juniper bush surrounds Ginevra's head and fills much of the background. In Renaissance Italy the juniper was regarded as a symbol of female virtue, and the Italian word for it, ginepro, plays on her name. The reverse of the panel carries a juniper sprig encircled by a wreath of laurel and palm, with the Latin motto Virtvtem Forma Decorat, meaning Beauty adorns virtue.

The laurel and palm form part of the personal emblem of Bernardo Bembo, a Venetian ambassador to Florence, whose platonic relationship with Ginevra is revealed in poems they exchanged. Infrared examination has shown Bembo's motto, Virtue and Honor, beneath the juniper, making it likely that he was involved in the commission. The sitter is beautiful but austere, with no hint of a smile and a gaze that seems indifferent to the viewer. The bottom of the panel was cut away at some point, presumably after damage, and her arms and hands are thought to be lost.

The painting was acquired by the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C., from Franz Joseph II, Prince of Liechtenstein, in February 1967, for a record price for a painting of between 5 and 6 million dollars. It is the only painting by Leonardo on public view in the Americas, and one of the highlights of the National Gallery, admired for its portrayal of the sitter's temperament.
gingee: Gingee, originally called Singapuri, lies between three hills with a perimeter of three kilometres, west of the Sankaraparani River, at an average elevation of 92 metres. The nearest railway stations are at Tindivanam, Viluppuram and Thiruvannamalai, and the town is 147 kilometres from Chennai and 64 from Pondicherry. The earliest mention of the hill fort is an inscription of the reign of Vikrama Chola, in which a Kadava feudatory calls himself lord of Senji of the strong embattled fort.

From the Hoysalas the area passed to the Vijayanagara Empire, which divided the Tamil country among the Nayaks of Madurai, Tanjore and Gingee; the Nayaks strengthened the forts and enlarged the town. The last Nayak surrendered to the Bijapur Sultanate, which took booty said to be worth 20 crore rupees. In 1677 Shivaji conquered the fort, and the Marathas greatly strengthened it. The Mughals took it from Rajaram I early in 1698 after a siege of seven years under Zulfikar Khan.

Aurangzeb later gave the fort to his Bundela Rajput servant Raja Swarup Singh. When his son Desingh refused to pay the arrears demanded by Sadatullah Khan, Nawab of Arcot, he was killed in battle on 3 October 1714, aged 22, against a far larger army, and ballads about him are still sung locally. Daud Khan had already moved the provincial headquarters to Arcot, and Gingee declined. The French under the Marquis de Bussy took it on 11 September 1750 and held it until after the fall of Pondicherry; Hyder Ali carried it by assault in November 1780, and the English recovered it from Tipu Sultan in 1799.

Gingee is a panchayat town in Viluppuram district, with a population of 27,045 at the 2011 census, and its fort draws visitors. A Shiva temple below the fort dates from the time of Raja Desingh, and the nearby Mel Sithamur Jain Math is the main religious centre of the Tamil Jain community.
ginkaku-ji: Ginkaku-ji, officially named Jishō-ji, 'Temple of Shining Mercy', is a Zen temple in the Sakyo ward of Kyoto and one of the constructions that represent the Higashiyama culture of the Muromachi period. Ashikaga Yoshimasa planned a retirement villa and gardens as early as 1460, a pleasure villa where the shoguns could rest from their administrative duties. Work on its main structure, the two-storied Kannon-den, or Kannon hall, began on 21 February 1482. Yoshimasa wanted it to emulate the golden Kinkaku-ji, commissioned by his grandfather Ashikaga Yoshimitsu. Like Kinkaku-ji, it was built as a place of rest and solitude for the shogun.

The Kannon-den is popularly known as Ginkaku, the Silver Pavilion, because of the initial plans to cover its exterior in silver foil. That nickname dates only from the Edo period (1600 to 1868). Construction was halted during the Ōnin War, and the silver overlay was delayed so long that it was never applied before Yoshimasa's death. The present appearance of the building is understood to be the same as when Yoshimasa last saw it, and this unfinished look is taken to illustrate the quality of wabi-sabi.

According to Ichito Ishida and Delmer M. Brown, the building was planned in relation to its surroundings: openings in the south-east corner of the ground floor look across a pond to where the moon rises between the peaks of Higashiyama, and the north-east room was planned as a library because a lake reflected enough light to read by.

The property has wooded grounds covered with a variety of mosses. The garden was supposedly designed by the landscape artist Sōami. Its sand garden is particularly well known, and a carefully formed pile of sand, said to symbolise Mount Fuji, is an essential element. Because the garden was financed by the shogunate as a retreat for aesthetic enjoyment, rather than designed by and for monks practising zazen, it does not represent Zen culture entirely.

Yoshimasa inspired a new outpouring of traditional culture, known as Higashiyama Bunka, the culture of the Eastern Mountain. It is said that, having retired to the villa, he sat in the pavilion contemplating the gardens while the Ōnin War worsened and Kyoto burned. In 1485 he became a Zen Buddhist monk, and after his death on 27 January 1490 the villa became a Buddhist temple complex, renamed Jishō-ji after his Buddhist name.

The temple is associated with the Shōkoku-ji branch of Rinzai Zen. After extensive restoration begun in February 2008 the garden and temple complex are open to the public. No silver foil has been used, and it was decided not to refinish the lacquer to its original state; the lacquer was the source of the original silver appearance, through the reflection of the pond on its surface.
giorgio-vasari: Giorgio Vasari was born prematurely on 30 July 1511 in Arezzo. Recommended early by his cousin Luca Signorelli, he became a pupil of the glass painter Guglielmo da Marsiglia. At sixteen he was sent to Florence by Cardinal Silvio Passerini and joined the circle of Andrea del Sarto and his pupils Rosso Fiorentino and Jacopo Pontormo, where his humanist education was encouraged. He befriended Michelangelo, whose style influenced his own.

He married Niccolosa Bacci of Arezzo, was made a Knight of the Golden Spur by the Pope, and rose to gonfaloniere in his native town. In 1563 he helped found the Florentine Accademia e Compagnia delle Arti del Disegno, with Cosimo I de' Medici and Michelangelo as its heads. He died in Florence on 27 June 1574.

Vasari visited Rome in 1529 to study Raphael and other masters of the High Renaissance, and in 1547 he painted the Sala dei Cento Giorni in the Palazzo della Cancelleria. He worked for the Medici in Florence and Rome. His chief paintings are on the wall and ceiling of the Sala di Cosimo I in the Palazzo Vecchio, where he and his assistants worked from 1555. His last major commission was a vast Last Judgement for the cupola of Florence Cathedral, begun in 1572 and finished after his death by Federico Zuccari.

As an architect he designed the Uffizi and the Vasari Corridor, which joins the Uffizi to the Palazzo Pitti across the Arno, passing over the Ponte Vecchio. He remodelled the churches of Santa Maria Novella and Santa Croce, and in 1562 built the octagonal dome of the Basilica of Our Lady of Humility in Pistoia.

Vasari's Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects, dedicated to Cosimo I, was first published in 1550 and partly rewritten in 1568 with woodcut portraits added. It created the genre of the encyclopedia of artistic biographies and presented art as a history of heroic individuals. He used the word rinascita, rebirth, for the change in style begun by Giotto, and the term lies behind the later word Renaissance.

The work is openly biased towards Florentines, and Venetian art is largely ignored in the first edition. Vasari made errors, for example claiming that Andrea del Castagno killed Domenico Veneziano, who in fact outlived him, and his hostile life of Il Sodoma is judged unfair. Some anecdotes are plainly fiction. He did consult archives for dates, and his accounts of his contemporaries are considered the more reliable.
giorgione: Little is known of Giorgione's life beyond what Giorgio Vasari records in his Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects. He came from Castelfranco Veneto, about 40 km inland from Venice, and the name Giorgione may be translated as Big George. Stylistic evidence supports Carlo Ridolfi's statement that he trained in Venice under Giovanni Bellini. In 1500 he was chosen to paint portraits of the Doge Agostino Barbarigo and the condottiere Consalvo Ferrante, and in 1504 he was commissioned to paint an altarpiece in the cathedral of Castelfranco. In 1507 and 1508 he worked on the exterior frescoes of the rebuilt Fondaco dei Tedeschi, having already decorated the exteriors of several Venetian palaces; very little of this work survives.

Apart from the altarpiece and the frescoes, his surviving works are small paintings made for wealthy collectors to keep at home, mostly under 60 cm in either dimension. He was the first major Italian painter to concentrate on this market. In the Castelfranco Madonna the landscape background gains an importance that was new in Venetian art. He painted pictures that told no story, embodying moods of lyrical or romantic feeling, and used the soft modelling called sfumato at about the time Leonardo da Vinci did.

The Tempest has been called the first landscape in Western painting. Its subject is unclear, and radiography shows the man at the left was once a seated female nude. The Sleeping Venus in Dresden was left unfinished, and Titian is generally agreed to have painted its landscape. None of his paintings is signed and only the portrait of Laura bears a reliable date, 1 June 1506. Attributions are therefore disputed: the Pastoral Concert in the Louvre is now widely given to Titian. Charles Hope wrote in 2012 that only three paintings have clear early evidence of his authorship, though he is generally credited with between twenty and forty.

Giorgione died of the plague on 17 September 1510. He was usually thought to have died on the island of Poveglia in the Venetian lagoon, but an archival document published in 2011 places his death on Lazzareto Nuovo. Isabella d'Este asked in October 1510 for a painting by him, and the reply a month later said it was not to be had at any price. Titian finished some of his paintings, though which ones remains controversial. Giorgione influenced Titian, Sebastiano del Piombo and Palma il Vecchio, and he was among the first Italians to paint landscapes with figures as independent pictures with no devotional, allegorical or historical purpose.
giosafat-barbaro: Giosafat Barbaro was born into the patrician Barbaro family in a palazzo on the Campo di Santa Maria Formosa in Castello, Venice. His father, Antonio Barbaro, died while serving as Count and Captain of Scutari when Giosafat was young; his mother, Franceschina, was the daughter of the wealthy silk merchant Nicolo Quartari. Presented to the Balla d'Oro in 1431, he became eligible for the Venetian Senate, and in 1434 he married Cenone (Nona) Duodo, daughter of Arsenio Duodo.

From 1436 to 1452 Barbaro traded at Tana, which linked the Danube, Polish and Persian routes with the road from Astrakhan to China. He sailed there in July 1436 on one of two galleys sent by the Senate, with his father-in-law, who had been elected consul at Tana. In Venice he held a series of offices: advocate at the court of foreigners in 1434, member of the Council of Forty in 1446 and of the Merchants Council in 1447, and in 1448 Provveditore of the colonies of Modon and Corone in the Peloponnese.

In 1455 he found two Tatars held illegally as slaves by a Venetian wine merchant, one of them a man he knew from Tana; after the court freed them he housed both for two months until he could send them home. Chosen in 1473 as an additional ambassador to Uzun Hasan for his experience and his Turkish and Persian, he left Venice in February with an escort, galleys of artillery and gunners and gifts for the ruler, but was held up in Cyprus for a year before reaching Persia.

Recalled in 1477, he found the Crimean Khanate too disordered to cross and went back to Tabriz. He was the last Venetian ambassador to leave Persia, escaping with an Armenian guide through Erzerum, Malatya and Aleppo to Beirut and reaching Venice in 1479. He then sat on the Council of Ten and in 1482-1484 governed Rovigo and the Polesine, lately ravaged in the War of Ferrara, where he reduced taxes and forgave debts.

Barbaro wrote the account of his travels in 1487. Its first part describes the peoples around Tana, above all the Tatars, their farming, the differences between nomadic and settled life and the trade of Genoese and Venetian merchants; its second covers Uzun Hasan's court, his wars, trade routes and cities from Tabriz to Hormuz, and the ruins of Persepolis. Much of what it reports about the Kipchak Khanate, Persia and Georgia appears in no other source.
giotto: Almost every aspect of Giotto's life is subject to controversy: his birth date, birthplace, apprenticeship and the order of his works. Tradition places his birth in a farmhouse near Colle di Romagnano, but recent research has presented documentary evidence that he was born in Florence, the son of a blacksmith named Bondone. Giorgio Vasari tells that the painter Cimabue found him as a shepherd boy drawing his sheep on a rock and took him as an apprentice. Many scholars today consider this a legend and cite earlier sources suggesting he was not Cimabue's pupil. Around 1290 he married Ricevuta di Lapo del Pela, and they had four daughters and four sons, one of whom, Francesco, became a painter.

Giotto worked in Rome in 1297-1300. By 1301 he owned a house in Florence, and documents of 1301 and 1304 show large estates there; he probably led a large workshop with commissions from across Italy. Around 1305 he painted the interior frescoes of the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua, commissioned by Enrico degli Scrovegni. Its 37 scenes follow the lives of Joachim and Anne, the Virgin and Christ in three tiers, with the Last Judgement on the west wall and monochrome figures of the virtues and vices below. His figures are solidly three-dimensional, with faces and gestures based on close observation and garments that hang naturally, unlike the stylized figures of Cimabue and Duccio.

Whether he painted the Life of St Francis in the Upper Church at Assisi is among the most disputed questions in art history; technical comparisons in 2002 gave strong evidence that he did not. He painted frescoes in the Lower Church there between 1306 and 1311. In Florence he painted the Ognissanti Madonna, the only panel painting universally accepted as his, and the Bardi and Peruzzi chapels in Santa Croce, whose dates are disputed. The Peruzzi cycle was especially admired in Renaissance times, and Masaccio and Michelangelo are known to have studied it. King Robert of Anjou called him to Naples, where he stayed until 1333.

In 1334 the Commune of Florence appointed Giotto chief architect of Florence Cathedral, and he designed the bell tower, begun on 18 July 1334. After his death in January 1337 Andrea Pisano and then Francesco Talenti completed it in 1359, not entirely to his design. His contemporaries Dante and Giovanni Villani praised him, and Vasari credited him with breaking from the Byzantine style. Vasari says he was buried in Florence Cathedral. Bones found in the 1970s beneath Santa Reparata were examined in 2000 and judged by Italian researchers to be his, while others, among them Franklin Toker, are sceptical.
giovanni-battista-aleotti: Aleotti was born in Argenta and moved to Ferrara while young. There he learned from technicians such as Marco Antonio Pasi, Cornelio Bentivoglio, Galasso Alghisi and Silvio Belli, in a city whose cultural life included Francesco Patrizi, Antonio Montecatini, Cesare Cremonini and Torquato Tasso. He began as an apprentice in art and engineering, and in 1571 he entered the service of Alfonso II d'Este.

In Ferrara he designed the façade of the University with Alessandro Balbi in 1610 and helped design the façades of the Palazzi Bentivoglio and Bevilacqua-Costabili. He also gave a new façade to the Rocca of Scandiano, home of the Boiardo family. In Parma, besides the Teatro Farnese, he designed the hexagonal church of Santa Maria del Quartiere, built from 1604 to 1619 with the help of his pupil Giovanni Battista Magnani.

With Biagio Rossetti he is counted as the architect who most shaped the city and territory of Ferrara. He built churches such as San Carlo and the Stimmate, theatres for the Intrepidi and in the hall of the Palazzo Pubblico, both since lost, and fortifications for the city. In the countryside he worked on the cut of Porto Viro, the regulation of the river Reno and the Este and Bentivoglio land reclamations.

Aleotti translated the Pneumatics of Hero of Alexandria as Gli artifitiosi et curiosi moti spiritali, published in Ferrara by Baldini in 1589, and added four theorems of his own describing mechanical and hydraulic devices. The translation was reprinted at Bologna in 1647 and at Paris in 1693. Much of his writing as a theorist remains unpublished; it drew on a wide knowledge of scientific and technical literature, as his private library shows. He died on 12 December 1636.
giovanni-battista-tiepolo: Born in Venice, Giovanni Battista Tiepolo was the youngest of six children of Domenico Tiepolo, a small shipping merchant, and Orsetta Tiepolo. His family bore the patrician name without claiming noble descent. In 1710 he became a pupil of Gregorio Lazzarini, but he was at least as strongly influenced by Sebastiano Ricci, Giovanni Battista Piazzetta, Tintoretto and Veronese. His earliest known works are apostles painted in 1715 and 1716 at Santa Maria dei Derelitti in Venice, and he painted his first fresco in 1716 on a church ceiling at Biadene, near Treviso. In 1719 he married Maria Cecilia Guardi, sister of the painters Francesco and Giovanni Antonio Guardi. They had nine children, and two sons, Giovanni Domenico and Lorenzo, worked as his assistants.

In about 1719-20 he painted the Triumph of Aurora and the Myth of Phaethon for the villa of Giambattista Baglione at Massanzago, a fluid spatial illusion that became a recurring theme. Commissions from the Dolfin family followed, including cycles for the archbishop's palace at Udine, completed in 1726 to 1728, and ten large canvases of Roman history for Ca' Dolfin in Venice. He used a cooler palette than earlier Venetian painters to give a convincing effect of daylight. Later works include the ceiling of the Gesuati in Venice and the story of Cleopatra at the Palazzo Labia, painted from 1745 to 1750. He also produced two sets of etchings, the Capricci and the Scherzi di fantasia.

In November 1750 he arrived in Würzburg at the invitation of Prince-Bishop Karl Philipp von Greifenclau. He frescoed the Kaisersaal with his sons, then painted the ceiling over Balthasar Neumann's staircase, finished in November 1753. This Allegory of the Planets and Continents covers 677 square metres and includes portraits of Tiepolo, his son Giandomenico and Neumann.

After returning to Venice in 1753 he was elected President of the Academy of Padua and painted villas such as the Villa Valmarana and the Villa Pisani at Stra. King Charles III of Spain commissioned him to decorate the throne room of the Royal Palace of Madrid with the Apotheosis of Spain. In Spain he met the opposition of Anton Raphael Mengs, the champion of Neoclassicism, and his canvases for the church of San Pascual at Aranjuez were replaced by works by Mengs.

Tiepolo died in Madrid on 27 March 1770 and is buried in Madonna dell'Orto in Venice. The rise of Neoclassicism slowly ended the Rococo style associated with him but did not damage his reputation. In 1878 Mark Twain wrote in his diary, Tiepolo is my artist.
giovanni-bellini: Giovanni Bellini was born in Venice and raised in the household of the painter Jacopo Bellini, long considered his father. The art historian Daniel Wallace Maze claims instead that Jacopo was his much elder half-brother and that Gentile Bellini was his nephew rather than his brother. Gentile was more highly regarded than Giovanni during their lifetimes. His brother-in-law was the painter Andrea Mantegna, to whose work his early paintings are often linked, and those early works are all in the old tempera method. In 1470 he received his first commission, to work with Gentile and others in the Scuola di San Marco.

After 1479 or 1480 much of his time went to his duties as conservator of the paintings in the great hall of the Doge's Palace, for which he received a fixed annual pension of eighty ducats. He repaired the work of predecessors and painted new subjects on Venice's part in the wars of Frederick Barbarossa and the pope. None of these survived the fire of 1577, and much of his public work is lost.

His religious works survive in greater number. He gradually mastered the oil medium that Antonello da Messina brought to Venice about 1473, using it for blended colour and atmospheric gradation of tone. The San Giobbe Altarpiece and the San Zaccaria Altarpiece are both of the Holy Conversation type, with the Madonna enthroned beneath a golden half dome recalling St Mark's. In the later work the light is soft and diffuse, and the altarpiece, dated 1505, is considered perhaps the most imposing of his altarpieces. Later altarpieces include those at San Francesco della Vigna in 1507 and San Giovanni Crisostomo in 1513.

In his last years he was besieged with more commissions than he could complete. Isabella Gonzaga of Mantua had difficulty obtaining a painting for which she had paid in part in advance. Albrecht Dürer, visiting Venice in 1506, called him very old but still the best in painting. In 1514 he undertook The Feast of the Gods for Duke Alfonso I of Ferrara.

Bellini died in 1516 and was buried in the Basilica di San Giovanni e Paolo. He outlived the Vivarini rivals and his brother Gentile, who died in 1507. His pupils included Giorgione and Titian, and also Vittore Belliniano, Rocco Marconi and Andrea Previtali. His Coronation of the Virgin is credited with introducing single-panel altarpieces, the pala, to Venice, and he joined oil painting's realism to Venetian and Byzantine traditions of colour and iconography. His most important contribution is thought to lie in his experiments with colour and atmosphere in oil.
giovanni-boccaccio: Boccaccio was the son of the Florentine merchant Boccaccino di Chellino and an unknown woman, and was probably born out of wedlock. He grew up in Florence, where his father worked for the Compagnia dei Bardi, and may have been tutored by Giovanni Mazzuoli, who gave him an early introduction to the works of Dante. In 1326 his father was appointed head of a bank and the family moved to Naples. Boccaccio disliked banking and studied canon law at the Studium for six years, while pursuing scientific and literary studies and meeting scholars and the Neapolitan nobility.

In Naples Boccaccio began what he considered his true vocation, poetry. Il Filostrato and the Teseida of this period were the sources for Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde and The Knight's Tale. He returned to Florence in early 1341, after tensions between the Angevin king and Florence, and his father, who had gone bankrupt, died in 1349. He began the Decameron around 1349; the choice of a hundred tales and the frame story of three men and seven women dates from this time. It was largely complete by 1352 and revised in 1370-1371.

From 1350 he was closely involved with humanism and with the Florentine government, which sent him on missions to Romagna, Brandenburg, Milan and Avignon. He housed Leontius Pilatus and encouraged his tentative translations of Homer, Euripides and Aristotle. In October 1350 he welcomed Francesco Petrarch to Florence, and Petrarch became his teacher and friend. Their discussions fed the Genealogia deorum gentilium, completed in 1360, a reference work on classical mythology that defended the study of ancient literature against clerical intellectuals who wished to limit it. In 1360 he began De mulieribus claris, biographies of 106 women, completed in 1374, and in 1373 he lectured on Dante, which produced his Esposizioni sopra la Commedia di Dante.

Illness troubled Boccaccio's last years. He died on 21 December 1375 in Certaldo, where he is buried, and his library passed to the monastery of Santo Spirito in Florence. He is counted with Dante and Petrarch as one of the Three Crowns of Italian literature. Pietro Bembo made his style a model of Italian prose in the sixteenth century, and he influenced Chaucer, Miguel de Cervantes and Lope de Vega.
giovanni-gentile: Giovanni Gentile was born on 29 May 1875 in Castelvetrano. He won a competition to become one of four exceptional students at the Scuola Normale Superiore in Pisa and graduated in letters and philosophy in 1898. He drew on the Risorgimento thinkers Mazzini, Rosmini, Gioberti and Spaventa, and on Hegel and Fichte. He became professor of the history of philosophy at Palermo in 1910, of theoretical philosophy at Pisa in 1914 and of the history of philosophy at Rome in 1917. He and Benedetto Croce, who edited the journal La Critica together from 1903 to 1922, were the leading figures of Italian idealism.

Before the First World War Gentile saw himself as a conservative liberal in the tradition of Cavour and wrote mostly on education. The war drew him into politics, and he saw it as a chance to complete the Risorgimento. In 1922, on Croce's recommendation, he became Minister for Public Education in Benito Mussolini's government, and he joined the National Fascist Party in 1923.

His Gentile Reform of that year was the first major legislation of the Fascist regime, and Mussolini called it the most Fascist reform. It made religious instruction mandatory in junior schools, gave private and state schools equal standing, tried to limit the number of women teachers, and made Italian the only language of public schools, which hit the non-Italian speaking minorities of Alto Adige and the Julian March. In 1925 Gentile wrote the Manifesto of the Fascist Intellectuals, and Croce answered with a manifesto against fascism that ended their friendship. He was the first editor of the Enciclopedia Italiana and wrote part of The Doctrine of Fascism of 1932.

Gentile remained a Fascist after the armistice of 1943 and followed Mussolini into the Italian Social Republic. On 15 April 1944 Bruno Fanciullacci and Antonio Ignesti, communist partisans of the Gruppi di Azione Patriottica, approached his parked car, and he was shot dead. The killing divided the anti-fascist front. He was buried in the church of Santa Croce in Florence.

His system, which he called actual idealism, was set out in works such as the Theory of the Pure Act of 1903. It held that the subject is concrete and the object an abstraction, and from it he derived a rejection of individualism and a state as the final authority. Patrick Romanell wrote that he held the honour of being the most rigorous neo-Hegelian in Western philosophy and the dishonour of being its official philosopher of fascism.
giovanni-giustiniani-longo: Giustiniani, born in 1418, belonged to the House of Giustiniani and was probably a native of Chios. That he lived as a mercenary suggests he was not the first-born son of his family. He left no testimony of his reasons for going to Constantinople. Reportedly Emperor Constantine XI promised him sovereignty over the island of Lemnos in case of victory.

Constantine XI gave him the rank of protostrator. Why he in particular was chosen is unclear; one explanation offered is that the emperor distrusted the city's large and discontented Venetian population and preferred a Genoese. Giustiniani trained the recruits, strengthened the fortifications and brought back men who had fled to monasteries to escape military duty. Drawing on the siege of 1422, he concentrated the defence on the outer walls. Some 8,000 to 9,000 people were available to defend the city, and his own post was at the lowest-lying section of the walls, between the gates of St. Romanos and Charisius.

After Sultan Mehmed II arrived on 6 April, Giustiniani led sorties that destroyed Ottoman troops, siege works and artillery, until their cost in lives caused them to be given up. Against the Ottoman guns, which included a cannon 6 metres long, he had the walls covered with soft surfaces and the breaches filled with debris, into which the cannonballs sank. On 18 April his men repelled the first assault, by Janissaries and archers at a narrow breach, after four hours.

In the final assault of 29 May two waves were beaten back before the Janissaries attacked a line held by no more than 3,000 exhausted troops. The accounts differ on his wound: a cannon shot or a crossbow bolt struck his arm, chest or leg. He was taken to his ship and sailed away with his men when the fall of the city became known. He died on 1 June and was buried in the church of San Domenico in the Castle of Chios. The tomb is lost, possibly destroyed in the earthquake of 1881, though descriptions of its inscription survive.

Sources hostile to the Genoese, above all the Venetian eyewitness Nicolò Barbaro, claim that he was lightly wounded or not at all and left his post out of fear. The charges of cowardice and treason spread so widely that the Republic of Genoa denied them in letters to the chanceries of England, France, the Duchy of Burgundy and others. The historians Marios Philippides and Walter Hanak rebut Barbaro, citing several other sources that record an injury.
giovanni-ii-bentivoglio: Giovanni was born in Bologna on 12 February 1443, the son of Annibale I Bentivoglio, chief magistrate of the commune, and Donnina Visconti. He was a small child when his father was murdered by his rival Battista Canneschi in June 1445. Bologna was then ruled by Sante I Bentivoglio, once an apprentice of the wool guild of Florence and said to be a son of Annibale's cousin Ercole. Machiavelli, in The Prince, tells how the Bolognese, out of goodwill toward the family, fetched Sante from Florence and let him govern until Giovanni came of age.

When Sante died in 1463, Giovanni made himself lord of the commune, though it was nominally a fief of the Church under a papal legate. On 2 May 1464 he married Sante's widow, Ginevra Sforza, who bore him sixteen children and acted as his counsellor, and Pope Paul II made him perpetual head of the Senate. He fought as a condottiero, and in the War of Ferrara in 1482 helped Ercole d'Este against Pope Sixtus IV and Venice. In 1488 his daughter Francesca poisoned her husband, Galeotto Manfredi of Faenza; Giovanni was captured trying to put down the revolt that followed and was freed through Lorenzo de' Medici.

The same year he crushed a plot by the Malvezzi family, almost all of whom were hanged or exiled, and in 1501 the Marescotti met the same fate. He withstood Cesare Borgia, but on 7 October 1506 Pope Julius II deposed and excommunicated him. As papal troops and a contingent sent by Louis XII of France advanced he fled, and Julius entered the city on 10 November.

An attempt by his sons Annibale II and Ermes to retake Bologna in 1507 failed, and the Bolognese destroyed his palace. He died a prisoner of Louis XII in the Castello Sforzesco in Milan on 15 February 1508. He kept a splendid court and improved the city's waterways, while the poor lived in misery. He commissioned the frescoes of Saint Cecilia's life in the Oratorio di Santa Cecilia by Francesco Francia, Lorenzo Costa the Elder and Amico Aspertini, and Costa's Bentivoglio Altarpiece in San Giacomo Maggiore.
giovanni-paolo-lascaris: Giovanni Paolo Lascaris di Ventimiglia e Castellar was born on 28 June 1560, the second son of Giannetto Lascaris and Franceschetta di Agostino Lascaris, of the old family of the Counts of Ventimiglia, related to the Lascaris emperors of Nicaea. He entered the Order of St. John of Jerusalem in 1584 and lived for over thirty years in a priory. He was put in charge of the order's grain supplies and in 1615 of its furnaces, became master of the St Anthony prison and in 1632 was sent as ambassador to Spain.

At the election after the death of Grand Master Antoine de Paule, attended by the inquisitor Fabio Chigi, later Pope Alexander VII, Martin de Redin could not win enough votes and urged his supporters to back Lascaris, who was elected on 16 June 1636. The following year he commissioned the Lascaris towers around Malta, designed by the papal military architect Vincenzo Maculani. In 1639 he banned women from wearing masks or attending masked balls at carnival; crowds blamed his Jesuit confessor, a Jesuit college was ransacked, and he banished the Jesuits for a short time.

The same year Pope Urban VIII asked for the order's ships against the Dukes of Parma in the First War of Castro. Lascaris sent warships while assuring the dukes that they were only a show of force, and his men fired no shot. In 1651 the Knights bought Saint-Christophe with Saint Croix, Saint Barthélemy and Saint Martin from the Compagnie des Îles de l'Amérique; a treaty with France two years later left the king sovereign but gave the order full jurisdiction there. In 1652 he obtained the reopening of a monastery on Gozo closed by Pope Innocent X.

Lascaris died on 14 August 1657 at the age of 97, still Grand Master, and Martin de Redin succeeded him and added further towers. His carnival ban is remembered in Malta as Lascaris' ban, and the Maltese idiom wiċċ Laskri, face of Lascaris, describes a sad or frustrated person. Lascaris Battery is named after him.
giovanni-pico-della-mirandola: Giovanni Pico was born at Mirandola, near Modena, the youngest son of Gianfrancesco I Pico, Lord of Mirandola and Count of Concordia. His mother, Giulia, intended him for the Church, and he was named a papal protonotary, probably an honorary post, at the age of 10. In 1477 he went to Bologna to study canon law. After his mother died he turned to philosophy at Ferrara, and from 1480 to 1482 he studied at Padua, a major centre of Aristotelianism, where Elia del Medigo taught him Hebrew and Arabic and translated Jewish manuscripts for him. In 1485 he went to Paris, where he probably began the 900 Theses.

Pico settled for a time in Florence in November 1484, where he met Lorenzo de' Medici and Marsilio Ficino, and Lorenzo protected him until his death in 1492. On his way to Rome, a love affair in Arezzo led to his being wounded and imprisoned until Lorenzo intervened.

In Perugia he came to know the Kabbalah and the Hermetic writings, and Rabbi Johannan Alemanno was among his tutors. The most original of his theses concerned the Kabbalah, and he is regarded as the founder of the tradition of Christian Kabbalah. He published the Conclusiones in December 1486 and offered to pay the expenses of scholars who came to Rome to debate them.

In February 1487 Pope Innocent VIII halted the debate and appointed a commission, which condemned thirteen theses. Eventually all 900 were condemned, and the book was the first printed book banned by the Church. Pico fled to France in 1488 and was imprisoned at Vincennes until King Charles VIII released him. He lived near Fiesole under Lorenzo's protection, and his censures were lifted only in 1493. There he wrote the Heptaplus and De Ente et Uno, and the Disputationes against astrology, which was published after his death.

After Lorenzo's death Pico became a follower of Girolamo Savonarola, and he planned to become a monk. He died in 1494 at the age of 31, on the day Charles VIII entered Florence. A rumour held that his secretary had poisoned him, and Savonarola delivered the funeral oration. When the bodies of Pico and the poet Angelo Poliziano were exhumed in 2007, forensic tests suggested that both had died of arsenic poisoning. Later investigation found that Pico may have died of acute arsenic poisoning, accidental or deliberate, but that the evidence for Poliziano was weaker. Pico's Oration on the Dignity of Man has been called the Manifesto of the Renaissance.
giovanni-pierluigi-da-palestrina: Palestrina was born in the town of Palestrina, east of Rome, to Neapolitan parents, Santo and Palma Pierluigi. In 1540 he moved to Rome and studied in the school of the Huguenot Claude Goudimel. He came of age under the influence of the northern European polyphony that Guillaume Du Fay and Josquin des Prez had established in Italy, and Orlando di Lasso, who accompanied him in his early years, advised him on his style. From 1544 to 1551 he was organist of the Cathedral of St. Agapito in his native town.

In 1551 Pope Julius III appointed him maestro di cappella of the Cappella Giulia at St. Peter's Basilica. His first published work, a book of masses dedicated to Julius III in 1554, was the first book of masses by a native composer, since most composers of sacred music in the Italian states came from the Low Countries, France or Spain. In 1555 Pope Paul IV ordered that all papal choristers be clerics, and Palestrina, who had married young and had four children, could not stay. He held posts at St. John Lateran and Santa Maria Maggiore, and returned to the Cappella Giulia in 1571.

In the 1570s he lost his brother, two sons and his wife, Lucrezia Gori, to plague. He married a wealthy widow, Virginia Dormoli, whose money gave him independence, and he composed prolifically until his death in Rome of pleurisy on 2 February 1594.

He left 105 masses, 68 offertories, at least 140 madrigals, more than 300 motets, 35 magnificats and many hymns. His early work was strongly influenced by the Franco-Flemish school; he then simplified polyphony, favouring clarity of text, while remaining faithful to Gregorian chant. The tale that the Missa Papae Marcelli persuaded the Council of Trent not to ban polyphony is contradicted by recent scholarship, which shows the mass was composed earlier and that the council never banned any church music.

His influence rests less on individual works than on the Palestrinian style, codified by Johann Joseph Fux in Gradus ad Parnassum of 1725 and widely used in the teaching of counterpoint. Johann Sebastian Bach studied his Missa sine nomine.
giovanni-pisano: Giovanni Pisano was born in Pisa, the son of the sculptor Nicola Pisano, and trained in his father's workshop. From 1265 to 1268 he worked with Nicola on the pulpit of Siena Cathedral. Their next major work was the Fontana Maggiore in Perugia, completed in 1278. These early works were made in Nicola's style, and it is hard to separate the contributions of the two artists, although a Madonna and Child can be attributed to Giovanni with certainty because of its new way of expressing intimacy between mother and child. Nicola is thought to have died either around 1278 or in 1284, when Giovanni took up residence in Siena.

Giovanni then carved the statues in the two rows of traceried gables on the exterior of the Baptistry, made between 1277 and 1284. Their vivacity shows that he had left his father's serene style behind. Between 1287 and 1296 he was capomaestro, or chief architect, of Siena Cathedral, and the design and sculptures of its façade blend Gothic art with reminders of Roman art.

Memmo di Filippuccio continued the work after his death with still more Gothic elaboration. In 1296 he returned to Pisa as capomaestro of the cathedral there. He began the pulpit of Sant' Andrea in Pistoia in 1297 and completed it in 1301. It has five reliefs, among them the Massacre of the Innocents, the Crucifixion and the Last Judgement.

His work of 1302 to 1310 on the new pulpit for Pisa Cathedral shows a preference for animation that moved his father's style further away. The pulpit, which has become his masterwork, has nine scenes from the New Testament in white marble with a chiaroscuro effect, and it includes a bold, naturalistic naked Hercules. It was packed away after the fire of 1595 and re-erected only in 1926. Around 1313 he made a monument to Margaret of Brabant, who had died in 1311, at the request of her husband the emperor Henry VII.

He is best known for sculpture that combines French Gothic with ancient Roman art, and Henry Moore, speaking of the statues for the façade of Siena Cathedral, called him the first modern sculptor. His pupils included Giovanni di Balduccio, Tino di Camaino and the architect and sculptor Agostino da Siena, and he influenced the painter Pietro Lorenzetti. Giorgio Vasari included a biography of him in his Lives.
giovanni-pontano: Pontano was born at Cerreto in the Duchy of Spoleto, where his father was murdered in one of the civic brawls common in Italian towns of the time. His mother fled with him to Perugia, where he received his first teaching in languages and literature. Unable to recover his inheritance, he left Umbria and at about twenty-two settled in Naples, which remained his home. There he became a close friend of the scholar Antonio Beccadelli, through whom he entered the royal chancery of Alfonso the Magnanimous.

The king made him tutor to his sons, among them the younger Alfonso, who would reign for a single year and whose energies between 1485 and 1495 brought the Renaissance to Naples in poetry, villas, portrait sculpture and fortifications. Pontano served the Aragonese dynasty as political adviser, military secretary and chancellor, was crowned laureate by Pope Innocent VIII on 8 January 1486, and was enrolled among the nobles of the realm. He took part in the Barons' War, the wars with the Papacy and the expulsion and restoration of the dynasty. His welcome to Charles VIII of France when the king entered Naples in 1495 is the most questioned act of his career, as a desertion of the princes who had made his fortune.

In 1461 he married Adriana Sassone, who bore him a son, Lucio, and three daughters before her death in 1491. He then married a young woman of Ferrara known only as Stella, whose one child, Lucilio, lived fifty days. Having lost both sons, he spent his last years alone and died in Naples in 1503. His tomb in the church of Monte Oliveto has painted, life-sized terracotta figures showing him with Alfonso and Jacopo Sannazaro before the dead Christ.

Pontano wrote dissertations on the liberality of princes and on magnificence, arguing that architecture and great monuments marked a great ruler; his prose treatises are valued as evidence of the social customs of his day. He was known above all as a Latin poet. His hexameter poem Urania sets out the astronomy of the period, and De hortis Hesperidum treats the growing of orange trees. His personal poems include De conjugali amore, Eridanus, Tumuli, Naeniae and Baiae. Aldus Manutius printed his works in Venice.
giovanni-sforza: Giovanni Sforza was born on 5 July 1466, the illegitimate son of Costanzo I Sforza, of the Pesaro and Gradara line of the House of Sforza, while another branch held the Duchy of Milan. When his father died in 1483 he inherited Pesaro and Gradara at seventeen, and his father's widow Camilla d'Aragona at first ruled as regent. In 1489 he married Maddalena Gonzaga, daughter of Federico I of Mantua, who died the next year. As a link to Milan he then became valuable to the Borgia family.

With the help of his cousin Cardinal Ascanio Sforza, the marriage with the twelve-year-old Lucrezia Borgia was agreed in February 1492, with a dowry of 31,000 ducats and a proxy wedding on 12 June. The couple spent two years in Pesaro, where Lucrezia never settled, and Giovanni's value to the Borgias faded as they turned to Naples; Pope Alexander VI found that he was spying for Milan. Back in Rome by Christmas 1495, he left on campaign and in February 1497 fled the city in disguise.

Pressed by the pope and by Ascanio Sforza, he at first refused the annulment, which would have cost him the dowry and required him to declare himself impotent. He answered with the charge that Lucrezia had committed incest with her father and later her brothers, a claim that has shadowed the family ever since though it cannot be verified. When his own family threatened to withdraw its protection, he accepted terms that let him keep the dowry but still declared his impotence.

He was excommunicated in 1500, survived an attempt on his life by the citizens of one of his towns, and appealed in vain to France and the Holy Roman Empire against Cesare Borgia. After the death of Alexander VI and Cesare's illness in 1503 he went back, and the following year Pope Julius II confirmed him as vicar of Pesaro. With his second wife, Ginevra Tiepolo, he had two sons, Ascanio, who died in infancy, and Costanzo II, who succeeded him. Giovanni died in Pesaro on 27 July 1510, aged 44.
gipuzkoa: Gipuzkoa lies at the easternmost extreme of the Cantabric Sea, in the Bay of Biscay, and has 66 km of coastline. It borders Labourd in the French Basque Country to the northeast, Navarre to the east, Biscay to the west and Álava to the southwest. The province is hilly and green, with the mountains and the sea close together and many towns spread across the territory. Several mountains, among them Aiako Harria, Hernio, Txindoki, Aizkorri and Izarraitz, have an emblematic place in local tradition, and their summits carry crosses, memorials and mountaineers' postboxes.

The rivers rise in the hills of the Basque interior, flow from south to north through narrow valleys and reach the sea after a short, steep course. From west to east they are the Deba, Urola, Oria, Urumea, Oiartzun and Bidasoa. The climate is oceanic, with cool summers, moderate winters and rain throughout the year, between 1,200 and 1,700 mm a year.

The first recorded name of the province, Ipuscoa, appears in a document of 1025, and several similar forms follow in later documents. The full etymology has not been ascertained. The name may be linked to the Basque root ip-, related to words for north, and could then mean something in the north. The inland route of the Way of St James entered the province at Irun and turned south-west along the Oria towards the tunnel of San Adrian. It stayed in use until 1765, when the Royal Road moved to the Deba valley.

The province gave Spain many explorers and conquistadors. Among its natives were Juan Sebastián Elcano, the first to sail round the world, in 1522, the navigator Andrés de Urdaneta and Miguel López de Legazpi, governor of the Captaincy General of the Philippines. Ignatius of Loyola, the founder of the Society of Jesus, was born in the neighbourhood of Loyola in Azpeitia, and he is a patron saint of the province together with Our Lady of Arantzazu.

Gipuzkoa is a province of Spain in the Basque Autonomous Community and the smallest in the country, with an area of 1,981 km2 and its capital at San Sebastián. Its assembly is the Juntas Generales. The Basque form Gipuzkoa is the spelling recommended by the Royal Academy of the Basque Language, while Guipúzcoa is the Spanish form. Gipuzkera, the local dialect of Basque, is vigorous, and the traditions of the province include bertsolaritza, trikiti and txistu music and the farmhouses called baserris.
giralda: The Great Mosque of Seville was commissioned in 1171 by the caliph Abu Ya'qub Yusuf to replace the smaller 9th-century Mosque of Ibn 'Addabas, which could no longer hold the congregation. The Sevillian architect Ahmad Ibn Baso designed it, and craftsmen came from across al-Andalus and the Maghreb. By 1176 it was complete except for the minaret, though Friday prayer was held there only from 1182. The caliph ordered the minaret in 1184 but the work halted that year with the deaths of the architect and, six weeks later, the caliph at the Siege of Santarém. His son Abu Yusuf Yaqub al-Mansur ordered it continued, and work restarted in 1188.

Ibn Baso had begun the base in cut stone. 'Ali al-Ghumari, a Maghrebi Berber architect, built the main body in brick, and the Sicilian architect Abu Layth al-Siqilli built the small secondary shaft on top. Local brick was used with recycled marble from old Umayyad monuments. On 10 March 1198 the tower was finished with a finial of four metal spheres, to commemorate al-Mansur's victory over Alfonso VIII of Castile four years earlier.

The base is a square of 13.6 metres on each side. The main shaft is 50.51 metres tall, and the smaller second shaft above it is 14.39 metres. Inside, 35 ramps wind around seven vaulted chambers and were wide enough, one chronicler wrote, for beasts of burden, people and custodians. The facades are divided into three vertical zones: windows in the middle zone, with horseshoe or multifoil arches, and large panels of sebka decoration in the other two, above blind arcades of polylobed arches. Leopoldo Torres Balbás counted 92 reused Umayyad capitals in the tower.

After Seville was taken by the Christians in 1248 the mosque was converted into a cathedral, and the minaret became a bell tower. The earthquake of 1356 badly damaged the mosque and brought down the metal spheres, which a cross and bell replaced in 1400. The first public striking clock in Spain was added about then.

Between 1558 and 1568 Hernán Ruiz the Younger built the Renaissance belfry, bringing the tower to about 95 or 96 metres, and in 1568 the bronze weather vane known as the Giraldillo was set on top. It is 4 metres tall and weighs 1,500 kilograms, and gave the tower its name. The cathedral, with the Alcázar and the General Archive of the Indies, was registered as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987. Other towers, among them those at Lebrija and Carmona, copy the Giralda and are called Giraldillas.
giray-dynasty: The House of Giray, in Crimean Tatar the Geraylar, was a Genghisid Turkic dynasty. In Ottoman Turkish it was called Âl-i Cengiz, 'the Genghisids'. Its members traced their descent from Jochi, the eldest son of Genghis Khan. Their early ancestor was Togay Timur, a younger son of Jochi, and the story of the Girays begins with his son Öreng Timur, who received Crimea from Mengu-Timur. Apart from the royal Girays there was a lateral branch, the Choban Girays. Young Girays were brought up before reaching the age of majority in one of the Circassian tribes, where they were instructed in the arts of war.

The Giray khans were elected by other Crimean Tatar dynasts, called myrzas, who also elected an heir apparent, the qalgha sultan. In the 15th century the dynasty sought sanctuary in Lithuania before establishing itself on the Crimean peninsula. In later centuries the Ottoman sultan obtained the right to install and depose khans at will.

The house reigned in the Khanate of Crimea from its formation until its downfall in 1783, and supplied several khans of Kazan and Astrakhan between 1521 and 1550. Under Ottoman suzerainty the Giray khan ranked, in the 15th and early 16th centuries, second only to the Ottoman sultan and so above the grand vizier in protocol.

After the disobedience and removal of Mehmed II Giray in 1584, the sultan demoted the khan to the level of the grand vizier. The khans remained sovereigns of their own realm: they could mint coins, make law by decree and had their own tughras. Some scholars, among them S. S. Montefiore, hold that the Girays were regarded as the second family of the Ottoman Empire, the likely heirs if the Ottoman house became extinct.

The khanate allied with the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth and with the Zaporizhian Sich. The help of İslâm III Giray in 1648, during the Khmelnytsky Uprising, contributed greatly to the first military successes of the Cossacks.

After Imperial Russia annexed the khanate in 1783, the last khan, Şahin Giray, remained nominally in power until 1787. He then took refuge in the Ottoman Empire and was executed on Rhodes. Qattı Giray, a young son of Selim III, was converted to Protestantism by missionaries and married a Scottish heiress, Anne Neilson. After Şahin Giray's execution under Abdul Hamid I, his family lived on Burgazada, near Istanbul. Genetic studies carried out since 2017 suggest that the Girays most likely carry the R1a-Z93 haplogroup, common among Turkic peoples, though further research is needed.
giresun: Giresun lies on the Black Sea coast of north-eastern Turkey, about 175 kilometres west of Trabzon. The older parts of the city stand on a peninsula crowned by a ruined Byzantine fortress, which shelters a small natural harbour. The ancient Greeks called the place Kerasous, and the modern name is derived from it.

The name is probably from a pre-Greek word for the cherry, and Pliny says Lucullus first exported the cherry from Kerasous to Europe in Roman times. Another theory derives it from the Greek keras, horn, because of the horn-shaped peninsula. The Turks made it Giresun after they gained permanent control of the region in the late 14th century.

Pharnaces I of Pontus renamed the city Pharnacia after himself, and it was called that as late as the 2nd century CE. According to A. H. M. Jones, it officially reverted to Kerasous in 64 CE. Xenophon names Kerasous in the Anabasis.

In late antiquity it became a Christian bishopric, and the bishops Gregorius at the Council of Ephesus in 431 and Gratianus at the Council of Chalcedon in 451 are among those recorded. It remained a metropolitanate until 1703, when its church was placed under Trebizond. In the Empire of Trebizond it was the second city. Alexios II Megas Komnenos defeated the Turkoman Koustoganes there in September 1302 and built a fortress overlooking the sea.

From 1244 the Seljuk Turks moved into the area, at times pursued by the Mongols. The Emirate of Chalybia held the city briefly from 1398 to 1400. By the 15th century most of the coast belonged to the Ottoman Empire under Mehmed II. Local tradition says that Kerasous held out for many months after the fall of Trebizond in 1461 and then surrendered on terms that let the Christian inhabitants keep their arms.

The Greeks of the island of Aretias held out against the Ottomans for seven years. Early in the 20th century the city had 14,000 residents, of whom 1,200 families were Greek, 1,000 Turkish and 300 Armenian. After the Pontic Greek genocide the surviving Greeks were expelled to Greece in the 1923 population exchange.

Giresun is the seat of Giresun Province and has a population of 125,682. The surrounding region grows most of Turkey's hazelnuts, as well as walnuts and cherries, and the port has long handled these products. A well-preserved castle stands in the city centre. Giresun Island, called Aretias in antiquity, is the place where, according to Apollonius of Rhodes, the Argonauts met the Amazons, who had dedicated a temple to Ares. A fertility festival is held there each May. The old Ottoman houses of the Zeytinlik district survive.
girnar: Girnar is a hill in Junagadh, Gujarat, administered by the Junagadh Municipal Corporation. Geologically it is a major igneous plutonic complex that intruded into the basalts towards the close of the Deccan Trap period, with rocks that include gabbros, diorites, lamprophyres, alkali-syenites and rhyolites. For Jains it is a Mahatirth, a great pilgrimage site, where Neminatha, the 22nd Tirthankara, is believed to have attained omniscience and later nirvana at the highest peak, Neminath Shikhar, together with five hundred and thirty-three other enlightened sages, according to the Kalpa Sutra of Acharya Bhadrabahu.

Fourteen of Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts, dated to about 250 BCE, are cut on a large boulder outside the town of Junagadh, in Brahmi script and a language similar to Pali; they mark the beginning of the written history of Junagadh. On the same rock the Western Satrap ruler Rudradaman I added a Sanskrit inscription around 150 CE, which tells of Sudarshan Lake and the storm that broke it. Another, from about 450 CE, refers to the Gupta emperor Skandagupta. The Nawab Rasool Khan of Junagadh built a protective building around the rock in 1900.

Jain texts record Girnar as an ancient pilgrimage site from which countless monks attained liberation. Acharya Dharasena practised penance in the Candragumpha cave and taught Pushpadanta and Bhutabali, who wrote the Shatkhandagama between 86 CE and 156 CE. In the 7th century the Chinese traveller Hsuan-tsang mentioned Girnar as a place of supernatural monks. Inscriptions at the temples record gifts and pilgrimages from the 12th century onward. One of 1232 CE states that Vastupala built four temples with his own money, and those of 1230 CE on the Vastupala and Tejahpala temple praise Neminatha, Vastupala and Svetambara monks.

Girnar holds a group of Svetambara Jain temples and one Digambara temple. The first peak carries the black granite temple of Neminatha, with carved pillars and coloured mosaics. The second peak has the temple of the goddess Ambika, and the third and fourth hold the foot idols of Muni Samba Kumar and Pradyumna Kumar. The fifth, reached by a climb of 10,000 steps, holds the foot idol of Neminatha.

Tradition says the present idol of Neminatha was installed in the 10th century by Ratnasar of Kashmir, who is said to have received it from Ambika, and that Sajjana, a minister of Jaysimha Siddharaja, renovated the temple in the 12th century. A ropeway 2,320 metres long, opened on 24 October 2020, takes passengers to the Ambika temple in ten minutes. The main Hindu event is the Maha Shivaratri fair, held every year in the month of Magha.
girolamo-riario: Girolamo was born in Savona in 1443, the son of Paolo Riario and Bianca della Rovere. His uncle, Pope Sixtus IV, appointed him Captain General of the Church in 1471 and in 1473 granted him the lordship of Imola as the dowry for his marriage with Caterina Sforza, daughter of Galeazzo Maria Sforza, Duke of Milan. The couple had six children, among them Ottaviano, later lord of Imola and Forlì, and Cesare, later Archbishop of Pisa.

Girolamo was one of the plotters of the Pazzi conspiracy of 1478, which was to kill Lorenzo and Giuliano de' Medici and would have made him lord of Florence; only Giuliano was killed. In 1480 the pope made him Count of Forlì, confiscating the lordship from the Ordelaffi. There he built the fortress of Rocca di Ravaldino, one of the most important strongholds of the Romagna, and in Imola he tore down decayed houses and rebuilt much of the town.

He lived mostly in Rome with his wife. In 1484 he began a feud with the Colonna family, whose lands Sixtus wished to take, and had the papal protonotary Lorenzo Colonna arrested and tortured to death. When Sixtus died, Caterina occupied the Castel Sant' Angelo with troops to sway the conclave, and after ten days of chaos Girolamo agreed to withdraw in return for 7,000 ducats.

Girolamo promoted further plots against the Medici, none successful. On 14 April 1488 Checco and Ludovico Orsi of Forlì, supposedly over a financial dispute, entered the government palace with seven others and cut him down despite his guards; his body was thrown into a piazza and the palace looted. The Medici gave the assassins no written support, opinion turned to Caterina, and the Orsi fled while mobs destroyed their remaining property. His body, recovered by a friar, lay in state for three days in the church of San Francesco.
girolamo-savonarola: Girolamo Savonarola was born on 21 September 1452 in Ferrara. His grandfather Michele Savonarola, a successful physician, oversaw his education, and he earned an arts degree at the University of Ferrara before giving up the idea of studying medicine. His early poems show his concern with the state of the Church. On 25 April 1475 he went to Bologna and asked to be admitted to the Dominican friary of San Domenico.

In 1482 he was sent to teach in the Convent of San Marco in Florence, where his preaching met little success: Florentines disliked his Ferrarese speech, his strident voice and his unpolished style. In 1490 he returned to San Marco at the initiative of the humanist Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, who persuaded Lorenzo de' Medici to bring him back.

Back in Florence, Savonarola preached on the Book of Revelation to crowds so large that he moved to the cathedral. He attacked tyrants who took the people's freedom and the rich who exploited the poor,. His followers were called Piagnoni, the Weepers. When Charles VIII of France crossed the Alps in September 1494, many saw the invasion as the fulfilment of his prophecies. He led a delegation to the king's camp in November, the Florentines expelled Piero de' Medici.

Savonarola, who as a cleric could not hold office, guided the new republic. Its constitution enfranchised the artisan class and created a Great Council. He declared that Florence would be the New Jerusalem, and had laws passed against sodomy, adultery and public drunkenness. He staged processions and bonfires of the vanities. In 1495 Pope Alexander VI summoned him to Rome and, when he refused, banned him from preaching. Savonarola resumed preaching, and the pope excommunicated him on 12 May 1497.

In April 1498 a rival Franciscan preacher proposed a trial by fire to test Savonarola's mission, and when rain cancelled it the crowd blamed him. Savonarola and two fellow friars, Domenico da Pescia and Silvestro Maruffi, were arrested. Under torture he confessed to inventing his prophecies, then retracted and confessed again. On 23 May 1498 the three were condemned as heretics and schismatics, hanged in the main square and burned.
