The Piagnoni kept his cause alive until the Medici returned in 1512. Martin Luther praised him as a martyr and forerunner, though Savonarola never abandoned Catholic doctrine, and Paul IV declared in 1558 that he was not a heretic. Niccolò Machiavelli, in The Prince, cited him as a prophet who failed because he was unarmed.
girona: Girona stands where the Ter, Onyar, Galligants and Güell rivers meet, in a strategic natural corridor between the Empordà plain and the Catalan Coastal Depression, a defile cut by the Ter. It links Barcelona and southern Catalonia with the Costa Brava and France. The Onyar crosses the city from south to north, and catastrophic floods have shaped its development since early times. The old town stands on the steep hill of the Caputxins east of the Onyar, the newer part on the plain to the west.

The first inhabitants were Iberians, and Girona is the ancient Gerunda, a city of the Ausetani, where the Romans built a citadel. The Visigoths ruled until the Moors conquered it in 715. Charlemagne reconquered it in 785 and made it one of the fourteen original counties of Catalonia. The Moors sacked it in 827, 842, 845, 935 and 982, and in 878 Wilfred the Hairy incorporated it into the County of Barcelona. In 1414 King Ferdinand I gave his first-born son, Alfonso, the title of Prince of Girona.

A Jewish community is documented from about 885. In the 12th century it had one of the most important Kabbalistic schools in Europe, and its rabbi Moshe ben Nahman Gerondi, known as Nahmanides, became Great Rabbi of Catalonia. The community, centred on the Call, ended in 1492, when the Catholic Monarchs outlawed Judaism throughout Spain and Jews had to choose conversion or exile.

Girona has undergone twenty-five sieges. In the Peninsular War it was besieged from May to December 1809 by about 35,000 French troops. Under heavy bombardment it held out under Álvarez de Castro until disease and famine forced it to capitulate on 12 December. The French held it until 1813.

Girona is the capital of its province, 99 km north-east of Barcelona, and much of its old quarter is preserved. The Gothic cathedral, approached by ninety steps, has a nave vault of 22.98 m. Between 1983 and 2003 the missing eastern parts of the city walls were rebuilt.
gironde-estuary: The Gironde estuary is a navigable estuary, though often called a river, formed where the Dordogne and the Garonne meet just downstream from the centre of Bordeaux. It covers around 635 square kilometres, is about 75 kilometres long and 3 to 12 kilometres wide, and is the largest estuary in Western Europe. It gives its name to the French département of Gironde. Strong tidal currents mean that boats of any size or type need great care when navigating it.

A series of small islands lies between the Pointe de Grave at the seaward end and the Bec d'Ambès. Île de Patiras, of 200 hectares, has a lighthouse and grows vines and maize. Île Sans-Pain and Île Bouchaud have almost joined through silting as Île Nouvelle. The Île Verte, Île du Nord and Île Cazeau are left natural and serve migrating birds, and Île Margaux, of 25 hectares, lies in the Médoc wine region.

Between 1685 and 1693 a fort was built on Île Paté as part of the national fortification programme planned by Vauban. Oval in shape and about 12 metres high, it was equipped with about 30 cannons. Together with Fort Médoc on the left bank and the old citadel of Blaye on the right bank, it defended the estuary and Bordeaux. During the French Revolution the fort served as a prison for priests.

In December 1942 the estuary was the setting of Operation Frankton, a raid on ships moored at the docks of Bordeaux. Six canoes were carried to the estuary by submarine, and twelve Royal Marines of the Boom Patrol Detachment, led by Herbert Hasler, paddled by night to the port. They attached limpet mines, sank one ship and badly damaged four others, and only two of the men returned alive to the UK. Their raid disrupted the use of the harbour for months. The prototypes of the Char B1 ter heavy tank were lost in the Gironde after German bombing in 1940.

The estuary lies within the Gironde estuary and Pertuis sea Marine Nature Park, created in 2015. The Conservatoire du Littoral owns Île Nouvelle, and Île Paté is protected from development as a sensitive natural area.
gisela-of-bavaria: Gisela was a daughter of Henry II, Duke of Bavaria, and Gisela of Burgundy, and is also known as Gisela of Hungary. She received a solid Catholic education, most likely with Bishop Wolfgang of Regensburg as her teacher. In 996 she married King Stephen I of Hungary as part of Hungary's policy of opening up to the West. The wedding marked a turning point in Hungarian history. The couple had a son, Saint Emeric, who died on 2 September 1031 while hunting boar.

As queen, Gisela played a fundamental role in spreading the Christian faith and Western culture in Hungary. She also took part in the dynastic affairs of the wider region. When Edmund Ironside of England died and was succeeded by Cnut, Edmund's infant sons were sent abroad and ended up under the protection of King Stephen. One of the twins died young, but the other, Edward Atheling, was brought up as a protégé of Queen Gisela, and was regarded at that foreign court as heir to the Anglo-Saxon throne. Gisela also commissioned a jewelled cross for the tomb of her mother, who died in 1006 and was buried in the Niedermünster in Regensburg.

Stephen died in 1038. In 1046 Gisela, her attendants and a number of Bavarian settlers left Hungary to return to Bavaria, where she joined the Niedernburg convent in Passau and became its abbess. She died there. Her grave is well known and regarded as a holy place.

An attempt to canonise her in the 18th century failed, and she was beatified in 1975. Her memorial days are 7 May and 1 February. On 4 May 1996 a bone from her arm was brought to Veszprém, where she once lived, together with the preserved right hand of King Stephen for a mass marking the thousandth anniversary of their wedding.
gita-govinda: The Gita Govinda is organised into twelve chapters, each divided into one or more prabandhas, twenty-four in all. The prabandhas contain couplets grouped into eights, called ashtapadis. The chapters are named for moods of Krishna, from the Exuberant Krishna of the first to the Exultant Krishna of the last. The work describes the love of Krishna for Radha, the milkmaid, his faithlessness and his return to her. It is taken as symbolical of the human soul's straying from its true allegiance and returning at length to the God that created it. The text also elaborates the eight moods of the heroine, the Ashta Nayika, which has inspired many compositions and choreographic works in Indian classical dance.

The Gita Govinda is one of the earliest musical texts in which the author names the raga and tala in which each song is to be sung. Most of those indicated continue in practice in the tradition of Odissi music, and Jayadeva mentions several unique to Odisha, such as the ashtatali. Every night during the Badasinghara, the last ritual of the Jagannatha temple at Puri, it is sung to Odissi ragas and talas such as Mangala Gujjari, in a tradition said to have continued unbroken since Jayadeva himself sang in the temple.

After his time the singing became a mandatory service at the temple, performed by the Maharis or Devadasis and recorded in inscriptions and the Madala Panji. Musicians of Kerala adapted the ashtapadis into a form performed in temples called sopana sangeetham, and Jayadeva's hymns are included in the Guru Granth Sahib.

Many commentaries were written. Thomas Donaldson notes that the poem was known at Puri not long after its composition, since the earliest commentary, the Bhavavibhavini Tika of Udayanacharya, was written in Odisha around 1190. Gaudiya Vaishnava scholars also wrote commentaries, among them Prabhodananda Sarasvati and Chaitanyadasa.

The poem has been translated into most modern Indian languages and many European ones. Sir William Jones published the first English translation in 1792, and Edwin Arnold's The Indian Song of Songs followed in 1875. Friedrich Rückert began a German verse translation in 1829, and Goethe read a German rendering by F. H. van Dalberg based on Jones's. Miniature paintings of the poem are held by museums such as the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Guimet Museum.
giuliano-de-medici: Giuliano de' Medici was born on 28 October 1453, the second son of Piero de' Medici, called the Gouty, and Lucrezia Tornabuoni. As co-ruler of the Florentine Republic with his brother Lorenzo de' Medici, he complemented Lorenzo's image as patron of the arts with his own as the handsome, sporting golden boy. At fifteen he stood beside Lorenzo at the head of the Florentine Signoria. Despite his passion for art and culture there were occasional frictions between the brothers because of their differing characters, but Lorenzo wanted him at his side in governing Florence.

On 29 January 1475 Giuliano took part in the tournament in Piazza Santa Croce, one of the main occasions of his public visibility. He rode a steed brought from the court of Naples, and horse and rider were decked in adornments and jewels worth more than 60,000 florins. Angelo Poliziano wrote of the joust in verse in his Stanze. Several marriages were proposed for him, with the Correr family of Venice, the Borromeo and a niece of Girolamo Riario, but none came about.

In 1477 he agreed to marry Semiramide Appiani, on condition that the settlement included a lease of the iron mines of Elba to the Medici brothers. He died before the wedding. With his mistress Fioretta Gorini he had a son, Giulio, later Pope Clement VII.

The Pazzi conspirators first tried to lure the brothers away from Florence, on the road to Piombino, in Rome and at a banquet at Fiesole, but Giuliano claimed to be ill. The killing was moved to high mass at the last minute, because the soldier chosen as assassin would not kill in a church. On 26 April 1478, at the sounding of the Elevation, Francesco de' Pazzi and Bernardo Baroncelli attacked him in the Duomo, giving him a fatal wound to the head and stabbing him 19 times. Lorenzo escaped to the Medici palace and did not learn of the death for hours. Giuliano was buried on 30 April in his father's tomb in San Lorenzo, and later reinterred with Lorenzo in the Medici Chapel.
giulio-alberoni: Alberoni was born near Piacenza in the Duchy of Parma, probably at Fiorenzuola d'Arda. His father, a gardener, died when he was ten, and he first served the church as bellringer and verger in the cathedral of Piacenza. He followed the banished judge Ignazio Gardini to Ravenna, where he met Giorgio Barni, who became bishop of Piacenza in 1688 and made him chamberlain of his household. Ordained priest, he later became a canon of the cathedral of Parma.

In the War of the Spanish Succession the Duke of Parma sent him to Louis-Joseph, duc de Vendôme, commander of the French forces in Italy. He went with Vendôme to Paris in 1706, where Louis XIV received him well, and to Spain as his secretary, promoting the cause of Philip V.

After Vendôme's death in 1713 Alberoni became Parma's agent at Philip's court. When the queen, Maria Luisa of Savoy, died in 1714, he and the princesse des Ursins arranged the king's marriage to Elisabetta Farnese, daughter of the Duke of Parma, who then allied with Alberoni and banished the princess. By the end of 1715 he was a grandee, Bishop of Málaga and chief minister, and in July 1717 Pope Clement XI made him a cardinal.

Copying the reforms of Colbert, he abolished internal customs houses, promoted trade with the Americas, set up a regular mail service to the colonies and reorganised state finances. Spain occupied Sardinia in 1717 and landed 38,000 troops on Sicily in 1718, but the Quadruple Alliance formed against it, the Royal Navy destroyed a Spanish fleet off Cape Passaro, and his backing of a Jacobite landing and of the Cellamare conspiracy against the French regent failed. After France invaded and a British force took Vigo, he was dismissed on 5 December 1719.

Pursued by a commission of cardinals, Alberoni found refuge in Austrian Lombardy, took part in the conclave of 1721 and was briefly confined in a monastery before being cleared. Under Clement XII he served as legate at Ravenna, where he built the Porta Alberoni. At Piacenza he replaced the decayed leper hospital of San Lazzaro with a seminary for seventy poor boys, the Collegio Alberoni, and on his death on 26 June 1752 left 600,000 ducats to endow it. The college still holds his collections of Flemish tapestries and paintings, among them Antonello da Messina's Ecce Homo.
giulio-romano: Giulio Pippi was born in Rome and began his career there as a young assistant to Raphael. He became an important member of Raphael's large team working on the frescoes in the Raphael Rooms and the Vatican loggias, and painted a group of figures in the Fire in the Borgo. He also collaborated on the ceiling of the Villa Farnesina. After Raphael's death in 1520 he took a leading role in completing the Vatican commissions, designing the frescoes of the life of Constantine and finishing Raphael's Coronation of the Virgin and Transfiguration. Michelangelo tried to take over the Raphael Rooms, but Giulio and Perino del Vaga kept the work because they held the drawings.

In Rome he decorated the Villa Madama for Cardinal Giuliano de' Medici, later Clement VII, and designed the Villa Lante al Gianicolo and the Palazzo Maccarani Stati. From 1522 Federico Gonzaga, ruler of Mantua, courted him, apparently attracted above all by his skill as an architect. According to Giorgio Vasari, Baldassare Castiglione was sent to secure him. In late 1524 Giulio moved to Mantua, where he stayed for the rest of his life, and so avoided the Sack of Rome in 1527.

His chief work there is the Palazzo del Te, a suburban palace of leisure begun around 1524 and finished about a decade later, with illusionistic frescoes of c. 1525–1535. He also helped rebuild the ducal palace, reconstructed the cathedral and designed the church of San Benedetto Po. Vasari records that when Charles V came to Mantua, Giulio made arches, scenery for comedies and costumes for jousts and tournaments. He also designed tapestries.

Giulio Romano was more influential as an architect than as a painter. His works had a large effect on Italian Mannerist architecture, and at the Villa Lante he already treated the classical orders as visually independent of their structural purposes. His drawings have long been treasured, and prints of them by Marcantonio Raimondi helped to spread the Italian style of the sixteenth century across Europe. His studio in Mantua became a popular school of art. He is the only Renaissance artist William Shakespeare names, in The Winter's Tale, where Hermione's statue is ascribed to Julio Romano. He died in Mantua in 1546.
giuseppe-garibaldi: Garibaldi was born and christened Joseph-Marie Garibaldi on 4 July 1807 in Nice, to a Ligurian family of coastal traders, which drew him to a life at sea. He lived in the Pera district of Istanbul from 1828 to 1832, teaching Italian, French and mathematics. In April 1833, in the port of Taganrog in the Russian Empire, he met Giovanni Battista Cuneo, a member of Giuseppe Mazzini's Young Italy movement, which sought Italian unification as a liberal republic. After taking part in an uprising in Piedmont he was sentenced to death, escaped and sailed to South America, where he spent 14 years in exile.

In Brazil he joined the rebels known as the Ragamuffins in the war of 1835, taking up their cause of an independent Riograndense Republic and later a Catarinense Republic. There he met Ana Maria de Jesus Ribeiro da Silva, known as Anita, who joined him aboard his ship in 1839 and fought beside him. He also became involved in the Uruguayan Civil War, raising an Italian force that wore red shirts.

He returned to Italy in 1848, offered his services to Charles Albert of Sardinia, who treated him with distrust, and then helped the provisional government of Milan. In 1849 he took command of the defence of the Roman Republic against a French force. Forced to emigrate again, he spent the next years in Tangier, New York and, in 1854, on Tyneside, where working men welcomed him.

In 1859 he led the Hunters of the Alps to victories over the Austrians at Varese and Como. On 5 May 1860 he left Quarto, near Genoa, with the volunteers known as the Thousand or the Redshirts, on two ships, and landed at Marsala in Sicily on 11 May. The expedition ended with the annexation of Sicily, southern Italy, the Marche and Umbria to the Kingdom of Sardinia before the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed on 17 March 1861. In 1866 he led some 40,000 men into the Trentino and defeated the Austrians at Bezzecca; ordered to halt, he telegraphed the reply Obbedisco, meaning I obey. His last campaign was with the Army of the Vosges in the Franco-Prussian War.

Ill with arthritis, Garibaldi died on 2 June 1882. He had asked for a simple funeral and cremation, which were not respected, and he was buried on his farm on the island of Caprera. His popularity, skill in rousing the common people and military exploits are credited with making Italian unification possible; to achieve it he gave up his ambition of a republic. Abraham Lincoln, Victor Hugo, Charles Dickens and Friedrich Engels were among his admirers, and a bust of him stands outside the old Supreme Court Chamber in the United States Capitol.
giuseppe-mazzini: Mazzini was born in Genoa, which had recently been annexed by the First French Empire. His father Giacomo was a university professor who had adhered to Jacobin ideology, and his mother Maria Drago was known for her Jansenist religious fervour. He entered university at 14 and graduated in law in 1826, practising at first as a poor man's lawyer, while hoping to become a historical novelist or dramatist. In 1827 he travelled to Tuscany and joined the Carbonari. He was arrested at Genoa on 31 October 1830, and on his release in early 1831 he chose exile in Geneva rather than confinement in a small hamlet.

In exile he founded Young Italy, a secret society with the aim of One, free, independent, republican nation and the motto God and the People. It counted about 60,000 adherents in 1833. The insurrection he planned that year was discovered before it began; twelve participants were executed, his friend Jacopo Ruffini killed himself, and Mazzini was sentenced to death in absentia. A second attempt in 1834 was crushed by Piedmontese troops. That year he also helped found Young Europe, hoping that free nations might one day form a loosely federal Europe. He settled in London in January 1837, in very poor circumstances.

On 7 April 1848 he reached Milan, but he had never been popular there because he wanted Lombardy to become a republic rather than join Piedmont, and he left after the failure of the First Italian War of Independence. A republic was declared in Rome on 9 February 1849, and Mazzini arrived the same day. On 29 March he became one of its triumvirate with Carlo Armellini and Aurelio Saffi, and soon its true leader. French troops called by the Pope defeated the republican troops under Giuseppe Garibaldi, and he left on 12 July 1849. Failed risings in Mantua in 1852 and Milan in 1853 damaged his movement's prestige.

In 1860 he published Doveri dell'uomo, Duties of Man, which argued that individual rights are won through work, sacrifice and virtue and called for recognition of women's rights. He joined faith to politics, describing himself as a Christian and a deist, and he held that thought must be followed by action. He opposed Marxism and class struggle. Critics have argued that his refusal to compromise with the monarchy made his goals harder to reach. He refused a seat in the Italian Chamber of Deputies in 1867 and died of pleurisy in Pisa on 10 March 1872, aged 66. About 100,000 people took part in his funeral in Genoa.
giuseppe-verdi: Verdi was the first child of Carlo Giuseppe Verdi and Luigia Uttini, an innkeeper and a spinner according to the baptismal register of 11 October 1813. He was born at Le Roncole, near Busseto, then in the Taro department of the First French Empire, and from the age of four had private lessons in Latin and Italian. He learned the organ and showed so much interest in music that his parents gave him a spinet. With the help of a local patron, Antonio Barezzi, he received a musical education. In 1835 he became director of the Busseto school, and the La Scala impresario Bartolomeo Merelli agreed to stage his first opera, Oberto, in November 1839.

Nabucco, in 1842, made his reputation, and I Lombardi alla prima crociata followed in 1843. Verdi then wrote twenty operas over sixteen years, a period he later called sixteen years in the galleys. Rigoletto, based on Victor Hugo's Le roi s'amuse, was written for Venice in 1851, and with Il trovatore and La traviata it cemented his fame. Censors objected to Stiffelio and Rigoletto, and Verdi refused to compromise on the hunchbacked hero of the latter.

After La traviata he wrote only six new stage works in eighteen years, up to Aida, and he returned happily to his estate at Sant'Agata. In 1859 he began to take an active interest in Italian politics, and he served briefly as an elected politician. After the success of Otello in 1887 he said that having massacred so many heroes and heroines he had the right to laugh a little, and with a libretto by Boito he wrote the comedy Falstaff, of 1893.

Critics divide Verdi's work into early, middle and late periods. Macbeth of 1847 has been called his first masterpiece, and his late masterpieces are the Requiem of 1874 and the operas Otello and Falstaff. He was influenced by Rossini, Bellini and Donizetti and by the French Grand opera of Meyerbeer and Spontini.

Historians debate how political his operas were. The chorus Va, pensiero from Nabucco became an anthem of Italian patriots, and from 1859 the slogan Viva VERDI was used as an acronym for Viva Vittorio Emanuele Re D'Italia. The music historian Philip Gossett notes that myths exaggerating his early nationalism circulated in the nineteenth century: the audience is said to have demanded an encore of Va, pensiero at its Milan premiere, but the piece encored was in fact the hymn Immenso Jehova.
gjergj-arianiti: Gjergj Arianiti was the eldest of three sons of Komnen Arianiti, whose domains lay near Durrës; his brothers were Muzakë and Vladan. His mother was a daughter of Nicolò Sevati according to Franz Babinger and Lindsay L. Brook, of Nikollë Zaharia according to Dhimitër Shuteriqi. Marriage to Maria Muzaka brought him lands from Mallakastër to south of Vlorë, and the centre of his domains lay between Librazhd and Elbasan. After 1423 he fell under Ottoman influence and probably lived at the sultan's palace as a hostage, returning in 1427 to govern his lands.

Ottoman reforms in southern Albania took away much of his power, though he kept his lands as a vassal of the sultan. In the spring of 1432, after Andrea Thopia defeated a small Ottoman unit, Arianiti became one of the main leaders of a revolt that spread across much of Albania. In the winter of 1432–33 his men ambushed and routed an army of 10,000 under Ali Beg in the valleys of the Shkumbin, and the Byzantine chronicler Chalcondyles wrote of his glorious victory. When the campaigns of Ali Beg and Turakhan Beg in 1435 and 1436 forced a partial submission, he withdrew to Skrapari and Tomorica, and Sultan Murad II tacitly left him the lands between the Shkumbin and the Vjosa under a truce.

Arianiti rose again in August 1443, leading an army deep into Macedonia, and joined Skanderbeg in the League of Lezhë. The historian Robert Elsie stresses that he was often Skanderbeg's rival. He allied with the Kingdom of Naples in 1446 and with Venice in 1456, supported the recapture of Svetigrad with 4,000 men, losing a brother there, and in 1451 signed a treaty with King Alfonso V like the one Skanderbeg made at Gaeta.

Between 1460 and 1462 he gathered a last resistance force. An Ottoman attempt to encircle him failed and his fortress of Sopot held, but in his absence it was taken through bribery and treachery and its entire population was massacred. He fought on until his death in 1462. He was the only Albanian leader with two capitals, Kanina near the coast and Sopot near the eastern mountains. Of his many children, Donika married Skanderbeg, Angjelina married Stefan Branković and is venerated as a saint by the Orthodox Church, and Constantine was regent of Montferrat from 1495 to 1499.
gjin-bua-shpata: Gjin Bua Shpata was born in Epirus in the first half of the 14th century, the son of Pjetër Bua, an Albanian noble. His name is often rendered John Spata; spata, Albanian shpatë, means sword, so the historian Hammond takes it as John the Sword. In 1358 Albanian commanders overran Epirus, Acarnania and Aetolia and set up two principalities under Shpata and Pjetër Losha. After the Battle of Achelous, Simeon Uroš, who ruled in Thessaly as a self-proclaimed emperor, chose in 1360 to leave Arta and Aetolia to them and recognised Shpata as Despot.

When Pjetër Losha died of the plague in 1374, Shpata took Arta and, not bound by Losha's agreement with Thomas Preljubović, Despot of Ioannina, besieged Ioannina and ravaged its countryside. Thomas made peace the next year by betrothing his sister Helena to him. The Achaean Knights Hospitallers of Juan Fernández de Heredia then invaded, taking Nafpaktos and, in April 1378, Vonitsa, but Shpata defeated them and took Heredia hostage, and he was again master of Nafpaktos by 1380.

Thomas was killed by his bodyguards in 1384. Shpata attacked Ioannina but could not break the defence of Esau de' Buondelmonti, who gained Ottoman help in 1386. After the Battle of Kosovo in 1389 the Ottomans could no longer help Esau, and the Albanians raided around Ioannina and confined him within the city. In January 1396 the archons of Ioannina made peace by having Esau marry Shpata's daughter Irene.

Shpata died on 29 October 1399, under the continuing pressure of Tocco, and his son became despot of Arta and Angelokastron for the next decade. His family's genealogy is poorly documented: the scholar G. Schiró, working from the Chronicle of Ioannina, the Chronicle of Tocco and the Venetian archives, judged earlier reconstructions by Karl Hopf inaccurate. A poem about Shpata and the battle of Arta in 1378 survives among Albanian epic songs.
gjirokaster: The earliest recorded inhabitants of the area were the Chaonians, a Greek tribe, and the ancient urban centre stood at Antigonia, about 5 kilometres from the modern town on the opposite bank of the Drino. Gjirokastër itself grew on the hill of its castle in the Middle Ages. The first fortification dates to the 5th and 6th centuries and was expanded in the 9th and 10th; urban settlement around it dates to the 13th and 14th. The town appears in the record as Argyrokastron, silver castle, in the account of John VI Kantakouzenos of 1336, when it stayed loyal to the Byzantine emperor during a local rebellion in Epirus. It was later contested between the Despotate of Epirus and the Albanian clan of the Zenebishi.

Under the Ottomans the town became the seat of the Sanjak of Albania and grew quickly. The traveller Evliya Çelebi, who visited in 1670, counted about 2,000 houses, eight mosques and 280 shops, and called it the city of wailing after hearing a professional mourner's lament. From the 16th century to the early 19th a mainly Christian town became one with a large Muslim population, and it became a centre of Bektashi Sufism. In 1811 it passed to the pashalik of Ali Pasha of Ioannina, and in the 19th century it was a major centre of the Albanian National Awakening.

Gjirokastër lies about 300 metres above sea level in a valley between the Gjerë mountains and the Drino, in southern Albania. It was taken by the Hellenic Army in the Balkan Wars and joined the newly independent Albania in 1913; the local Greek population rebelled in 1914 and proclaimed the short-lived Autonomous Republic of Northern Epirus, with the town as its capital. Under communist rule it was designated a museum city, together with Berat.

Most of the buildings date from the 17th and 18th centuries. A typical house is a tall stone block of up to five storeys, with a cistern and stable below, and many have roofs of flat dressed stones, which earned the town the nickname City of Stone. The writer Ismail Kadare set his novel Chronicle in Stone here, and the old town is a World Heritage Site.
gjon-kastrioti: The Kastrioti family came from a region of northern Albania between Mat, Dibër and Has, and used the name Mazreku, horse breeder, to mark their tribal affiliation. Gjon's father is called Georgius Castriotus, lord of Aemathia and Castoria, by Giovanni Andrea Angelo Flavio Comneno, and Paulo Castrioto by Gjon Muzaka, who says he ruled no more than two villages. That claim is disputed, since noble families built their influence over several generations. The Kastrioti first appear in archival records in Gjon's time, at the end of the 14th century.

Gjon commanded some 2,000 horsemen and governed the land between the Cape of Rodon and Dibër. In 1402 he led his retinue for Sultan Bayezid I at the Battle of Ankara, and in the vacuum after the Ottoman defeat he strengthened his position towards the coast. He gave merchants safe passage, made no claim on Venetian territory and became a citizen of Venice with his heirs in 1413. Customs from Ragusan traders, grain exports and salt were his main income; in 1424 Venice forced him to destroy the salt pans he had built to escape its monopoly.

From 1419 to 1426 he was an ally of the Serbian Despot Stefan Lazarević, and Albanians led by one of his sons joined the despot's war on Venice in Zeta, though in 1423 he left Lazarević's ranks and refused Venetian money to fight him. After an Ottoman vassalage begun between 1415 and 1417, Venice encouraged him to rebel in 1428. In April 1430 the Ottomans under Isak-Beg, sanjakbey of Skopje, took most of his land, leaving him only a small part, and he was defeated again after joining the uprising of Gjergj Arianiti of 1432–36.

Gjon is said to have changed faith with his alliances: Catholic as Venice's ally, Orthodox as Lazarević's, Muslim from 1431, and a saying of southern Albania, where the sword is, there lies religion, is believed to come from him. In 1426 he gave the taxes of two villages to the Serbian monastery of Hilandar on Mount Athos, where his son Reposh died in 1431, and its Saint George Tower became known as the Albanian Tower. The Ottomans listed his former territory as Yuvan-ili, from the Turkish form of his name.
gla: The fortress stands on a flat-topped limestone outcrop that jutted into Lake Kopais or formed an island in it. The outcrop rises up to 38 m above the plain and measures about 900 by 575 m at its widest. The site's ancient name is unknown: it has not been identified with any place in the Iliad, and a proposed link with Arne in the Catalogue of Ships has been disputed by George Mylonas among others. Local people call it Palaiokastro, ancient fortress, and the name Gla comes from the Arvanitic goulas, from the Turkish kulle, tower.

The Cyclopean walls, about 3 m thick and 2.8 km long, often rise straight from the cliffs and enclose nearly 20 hectares, about ten times the citadels of Athens or Tiryns. There were four gates, an unusually large number, reached by built ramps. Permanent buildings cover less than a quarter of the interior. In the north stands a large L-shaped building of three wings on an artificial terrace, often called a palace, though it lacks a throne room, a circular hearth and a bathroom. Two parallel complexes to the south may have been barracks, stores or workshops; one held large amounts of carbonised grain.

Archaeologists think the empty ground sheltered the farmers of the Kopais in times of attack. The lake was drained at about the time the fortress was built, by a system of dams and canals: two large canals, together more than 50 km long, met about 1 km north of Gla and carried the waters of the Boeotian Cephissus and the Melas toward outlets to the sea, creating a fertile plain that may have been a bread basket of the Mycenaean world. The works collapsed at or after the end of the Mycenaean civilisation, and in Classical antiquity the lake had returned.

Lake Kopais was drained a second time in the 19th century. The fortification walls were always visible, and excavation has revealed the buildings inside them. Finds of fired pan and cover tiles suggest that some Mycenaean buildings already had pitched, tiled roofs. The site has also yielded Neolithic and Byzantine pottery, but it seems not to have been occupied in the Archaic, Classical or Roman periods.
glaphyra: Glaphyra was a princess of Greek, Armenian and Persian descent. Her father, Archelaus of Cappadocia, was a Roman ally king; her only full sibling was her younger brother Archelaus of Cilicia, and she was named after her paternal grandmother, the hetaera Glaphyra. Her mother was an Armenian princess whose name is unknown, possibly a daughter of King Artavasdes II of Armenia. In 25 BCE Augustus gave her father more lands, among them the port of Elaiussa Sebaste, where the family settled and Archelaus built a palace on an island in the harbour.

Herod the Great wanted a foreign princess for his son Alexander, and in 18 or 17 BCE Glaphyra married him at Herod's court in Jerusalem. The marriage is described as happy, and she adopted Judaism. They had two sons, Tigranes and Alexander, and a daughter whose name is not recorded. At court she boasted of descent from the kings of Macedonia and the rulers of Persia and taunted Salome and Herod's wives for their low birth, and Salome spread a rumour that Herod was in love with her. The hostility helped persuade Herod that Alexander and his brother Aristobulus IV were plotting against him.

After the executions Herod questioned Glaphyra, sent her home to Cappadocia and kept her children, who joined her after his death in 4 BCE and gave up Judaism. Juba II of Mauretania met her while touring the eastern Mediterranean with Augustus's grandson Gaius Caesar, and she became his queen. The marriage seems to have been brief: her name appears in no North African inscription, though the council and people of Athens honoured her as Queen Glaphyra, wife of King Juba.

Glaphyra met Herod Archelaus again and the two decided to marry; she divorced Juba, and he divorced his cousin Mariamne. The marriage of a widow to her former brother-in-law broke Jewish law on such unions; it was considered immoral and caused a major religious scandal in Judaea. According to the account of her end, she dreamed soon after the wedding that Alexander stood beside her, reproached her and said he would reclaim her, and she died two days later. Around that time Augustus deposed Archelaus for cruelty and banished him to Vienne in Gaul.
glarentza: The town stood on a small plateau at the northern tip of a headland, known since antiquity as the best anchorage in Elis and probably the site of the ancient city of Cyllene. It was founded in the mid-13th century by William II of Villehardouin as the harbour of the princely capital at Andravida, some 13 kilometres inland, and with Andravida and the fortress of Clermont or Chlemoutsi it formed the administrative heart of the principality. Its name, Clarence in French and Chiarenza in Italian, shows its Frankish foundation.

As the main port between the Morea and Italy, Glarentza grew prosperous and cosmopolitan, frequented by Venetian merchants, soldiers and emissaries; it had a hospital, banks and a Franciscan monastery, and a list of fiefs of 1391 counts about 300 hearths. Its mint struck denier tournois coins until 1353, and parliaments met there, among them the oath of allegiance to Isabella of Villehardouin and Florent of Hainaut in 1289. In June 1315 Ferdinand of Majorca took the town, but he was killed at the Battle of Manolada on 5 July 1316.

Decline came in the early 15th century. Leonardo II Tocco seized the town in 1407, the adventurer Olivier Franco in 1418, and he sold it in 1421 to Carlo I Tocco. In 1428 it was handed over as part of the dowry of Carlo's niece Maddalena on her marriage to the Despot Constantine Palaiologos, who destroyed its walls after a Catalan fleet captured it in 1429. It was the residence of Thomas Palaiologos until 1432 and fell to the Ottomans in 1460 with the rest of the Byzantine Peloponnese.

By the 16th century the town was abandoned and half-ruined, and during the German occupation of Greece in World War II, the German Army demolished many of its remains. Traces of the city wall, its gates, a monumental staircase, a large church and the silted-up harbour survive, managed by the 6th Ephorate of Byzantine Antiquities. The old claim that the English title Duke of Clarence came from Glarentza was rejected in 1846 by William Martin Leake, who traced it to Clare in Suffolk.
glasgow: Glasgow lies on the banks of the River Clyde in west central Scotland, with the Kelvin as an important tributary. The name is Brittonic in origin, from glas, meaning grey-green or grey-blue, and a second element meaning hollow, giving a sense of green hollow; it is often said to mean dear green place, and the dear green place remains an affectionate name for the city. The area around Glasgow has hosted communities for millennia and the Romans built outposts there and the Antonine Wall.

Glasgow grew from a small rural settlement near its cathedral into a medieval bishopric and burgh, and was raised to the status of Royal Burgh in 1611. Its early trade was in agriculture, brewing and fishing, and from 1668 the magistrates created a deep water port at Port Glasgow, down the Clyde, because the river was then too shallow for seagoing merchant ships.

After the Acts of Union in 1707 Glasgow became prominent as a hub of trade with the Americas, in sugar, tobacco, cotton and manufactured goods. The city prospered from the triangular trade and the Atlantic slave trade on which it depended, and its merchants dealt in slave-produced crops. From 1717 to 1766 Scottish slave ships, mainly sailing from Greenock and Port Glasgow, carried approximately 3,000 enslaved Africans to the Americas. By the late 18th century more than half of the British tobacco trade was concentrated on the Clyde. The city became a major centre of the Scottish Enlightenment.

As the population grew, about 4,000 people died in an outbreak of cholera in 1848–1849, which led to the Loch Katrine aqueduct, 26 miles long, opened by Queen Victoria in 1859. The population reached 1,034,174 in 1921 and peaked at 1,127,825 in 1938, and boundary extensions between 1912 and 1936 tripled the city's area. In the First World War approximately 18,000 Glaswegian soldiers were lost. Clearance of poor inner-city areas such as the Gorbals and resettlement in new towns including Cumbernauld and East Kilbride reduced the population from the 1960s.

Glasgow is the most populous city in Scotland and one of its 32 unitary council areas, administered by Glasgow City Council. Its cultural institutions include the Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, the Hunterian Museum and Art Gallery, the Burrell Collection, Scottish Opera and Scottish Ballet, and it was European Capital of Culture in 1990. St. Mungo's Cathedral, of the 13th century, and Provand's Lordship, of the 15th, are the two main landmarks of the medieval city.
glassblowing: Glassblowing exploited a property of glass previously unknown to glassworkers: inflation, the expansion of a molten blob of glass by introducing a little air. Molten glass is viscous enough to be blown and hardens gradually as it loses heat. A worker who blows glass is a glassblower, and the head of a workshop is a gaffer. The glass is gathered on the end of a blowpipe, rolled on a marver to form a cool skin, then inflated. The two main methods are free-blowing and mould-blowing. In free-blowing the worker blows short puffs of air into the gather and shapes it by rotating and swinging the pipe.

Phoenician and Syrian craftsmen developed the technique in the 1st century BCE, and it quickly eclipsed casting and core-forming. Its invention coincided with the establishment of the Roman Empire, which helped it spread. The first large workshops stood in what is now Lebanon and Israel and in Cyprus, where Ennion was among the most prominent glassworkers, known for complex multi-panelled mould-blown vessels. Mould-blowing, in which glass is inflated into a carved wooden or metal mould, came in the first part of the second quarter of the 1st century CE and allowed objects to be made quickly in large numbers.

Phoenician glassworkers set up workshops in Italy by the middle of the 1st century CE, in Rome and in Campania, Morgantina and Aquileia, producing perfume containers, tableware and window glass. Craftsmen who had been forbidden to travel carried the technique north of the Alps. Rhineland workshops at Cologne made mould-blown flagons and bottles, and fragments of clay blowpipes survive from Avenches in Switzerland.

After the Roman Empire the tradition continued. The Franks made drinking vessels shaped like animal horns in the Rhine and Meuse valleys, Byzantine workers made mould-blown glass with Christian and Jewish symbols in Jerusalem, and mould-blown vessels were found at Samarra. Venetian glassworkers from Murano produced the fine glassware known as cristallo in the Renaissance, and by the late 17th century blowing with the cylinder and crown methods made window panes. Free-blowing kept its leading position until the late 19th century and is still widely used for artistic purposes.

The studio glass movement began in 1962, when Harvey Littleton and Dominick Labino held two workshops at the Toledo Museum of Art, experimenting with a small furnace. Artists such as Dale Chihuly followed.
glastonbury-abbey: Excavations have shown Roman and Saxon occupation of the site, and the abbey was founded by Britons. Saxons under Cenwalh of Wessex took Somerset as far as the River Parrett after the Battle of Peonnum in 658 and let the British abbot Bregored stay in power. King Ine of Wessex enriched the community and is reputed to have ordered a stone church in 712. In the 10th century Dunstan enlarged the church, built the cloisters and instituted the Benedictine Rule. Kings Edmund I and Edmund Ironside were buried there. After the Norman Conquest the abbey was the richest monastery in the country when the Domesday Book was commissioned in 1086.

A great fire in 1184 destroyed the monastic buildings, and the Lady Chapel was consecrated in 1186. In 1191 the monks reported finding the tomb of King Arthur and Queen Guinevere. Giraldus Cambrensis wrote that a hollowed oak trunk with two skeletons lay about 16 feet down, beneath a lead cross naming Arthur on the Isle of Avalon. Historians today generally dismiss the find as a publicity stunt to raise funds for rebuilding. In the 14th century only Westminster Abbey was more richly endowed. The abbey also helped to drain the Somerset Levels, reclaiming 722 acres near Westonzoyland in 1234.

The abbey controlled large tracts of land and a water-borne transport network that grew from a canal of the mid-10th century to the River Brue. Stone came from its quarries at Doulting, and tithe barns held crops at Doulting, Mells and Pilton. Fish were an important product, as the abbey needed them on Fridays, fast days and in Lent, and a Fish House built at Meare in the 14th century survives. Its library held unique early histories, and around 40 manuscripts are known to have survived the Dissolution.

In September 1539 Richard Layton, Richard Pollard and Thomas Moyle arrived without warning on Thomas Cromwell's orders. The abbey was stripped of its valuables, and the last abbot, Richard Whiting, who had signed the Act of Supremacy, resisted and was hanged, drawn and quartered as a traitor on Glastonbury Tor on 15 November 1539. Stone and lead were later taken from the ruins, and the Abbot's Kitchen is the only building to survive intact. The Ancient Monuments Protection Act 1882 stopped further damage.

The Bath and Wells Diocesan Trust bought the ruins in 1908. The great church and the Lady Chapel are grade I listed, and services in Anglican, Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox traditions are held there.
glele: Glele was born Badohou and took Glele as his throne name. Counting kings without Adandozan, he was the tenth king of the Aja kingdom of Dahomey, in what is now Benin. He carried on his father's war campaigns, in part to avenge Ghezo's death and in part to capture slaves, and under him Dahomey remained a centre of the palm oil and slave trades. His symbols were the lion and the ritual knife of the adepts of Gu, the Vodou of fire, iron, war and cutting edges.

Although the Europeans had banned the slave trade, Glele kept slavery as an institution at home: slaves worked most of his fields and were a main source of the sacrificial victims, the messengers to the ancestors, of the court's ceremonies. In 1860 he met William Foster, captain of the Clotilda, the last ship to carry slaves illegally to the United States, presumably to approve the sale.

Glele signed treaties with the French, who already held a concession at Porto-Novo from its king, and granted them a customs and commerce concession at Cotonou. He resisted British approaches, distrusting their manners and their more active opposition to the slave trade: from 1840 the British navy raided slavers along the West African coast. Among his wives were his favourite, Visesegan, and Miagbe, a Yoruba-speaking high official who bore him three sets of twins and was given a household, land and servants of her own.

Late in the reign Cotonou's growing commercial weight and differing readings of the extent and terms of the concession soured relations with France. Glele died suddenly on 29 December 1889, possibly by suicide, just before French negotiators arrived. His son Prince Kondo, who had handled the talks with the French, succeeded him under the name Béhanzin.
glendalough: Glendalough, from the Irish Gleann Dá Loch, meaning valley of two lakes, lies in County Wicklow. The valley was formed during the last ice age by a glacier that left a moraine across its mouth. The Poulanass River, which plunges into the valley from the south, built a delta that eventually divided the original lake in two. The massif of Conavalla, 734 metres high, dominates the head of the valley. Semi-natural oak woodland surrounds the lakes, much of it formerly coppiced for wood, charcoal and bark.

Kevin, a descendant of one of the ruling families of Leinster, studied as a boy under three holy men, Eoghan, Lochan and Eanna, and went to Glendalough during this time. He later returned with a small group of monks to found a monastery where two rivers meet. His fame as a holy man attracted numerous followers. He died in about 618, traditionally on 3 June. For the next six centuries the settlement flourished, and the Irish Annals record the deaths of abbots, among them Minndenach in 800, and raids on the site.

Around 1042 oak timber from Glendalough was used to build a Viking longship about 30 metres long. At the Synod of Rath Breasail in 1111 the place was designated one of the two dioceses of North Leinster, and the Book of Glendalough was written there about 1131. Laurence O'Toole, born in 1128, became abbot and later Archbishop of Dublin. The dioceses of Glendalough and Dublin were united in 1214, after which the cultural and ecclesiastical standing of the place diminished. English forces destroyed the settlement in 1398, leaving a ruin that remained a church of local importance and a place of pilgrimage.

At its height the monastery included workshops, areas for writing and copying manuscripts, guest houses, an infirmary, farm buildings and dwellings for monks and a large lay population. The buildings that survive probably date from between the 10th and 12th centuries.

The round tower, built of mica-slate interspersed with granite, stands about 30 metres high, with its entrance 3.5 metres above the ground; its conical roof was rebuilt in 1876 from the original stones. Beside it stand the cathedral of St Peter and St Paul, the largest of the buildings, and the stone-roofed St Kevin's Church, known as the Kitchen. The head of the valley was also the site of a galena lead mine from 1825 to 1957, and the valley is now a recreational area with marked walking trails.
gliwice: Gliwice lies in the Silesian Highlands on the Kłodnica river, a tributary of the Oder, in Upper Silesia. Its name comes from a Slavic root, gliw or gliv, suggesting loamy or wet ground. The town stood on a trade route between Kraków and Wrocław, and the Gliwice Canal now links its harbour to the Oder.

Gliwice was first mentioned as a town in 1276, though Duke Władysław Opolski of the Piast dynasty had granted it town rights earlier. It belonged to several Piast duchies and was the capital of its own Duchy of Gliwice from 1322 to 1342. In 1335 it came under the suzerainty of the Bohemian Crown, which passed to the Habsburgs in 1526, and in 1532 it was incorporated into the Habsburg monarchy as Gleiwitz. In the Silesian Wars of the mid-18th century Prussia took it. The first coke-fired blast furnace on the European continent was built there in 1796 under John Baildon, and industry turned it into a major city.

After the First World War a plebiscite on 20 March 1921 gave Gleiwitz 32,029 votes for remaining in Germany and 8,558 for Poland, and the League of Nations left it in Germany, near the new Polish border. On 31 August 1939 German secret police staged the Gleiwitz incident, a false-flag attack on the radio station, which Nazi Germany used as a pretext to invade Poland. During the war the Germans ran prisoner-of-war and forced-labour camps in the city, including four subcamps of Auschwitz from July 1944. Its New Synagogue had been destroyed in 1938.

The Red Army occupied the city on 24 January 1945, and Soviet troops murdered over 1,000 civilians. Gliwice was incorporated into Poland on 18 March 1945, after almost three centuries outside Polish rule. The German population was expelled and replaced by Poles, many of them displaced from the east, among them academics from Lwów who founded the Silesian University of Technology.

Gliwice is a city of 175,102 permanent residents in 2021 and an industrial and university centre that moved from steelworks and coal mining towards automotive and machine industries after the 1990s. Its Old Town keeps medieval walls and churches, Piast Castle and the Market Square. The Radio Tower, 118 metres high, is the last remaining wooden radio tower in the world and is a Historic Monument of Poland.
glogow: Głogów was founded as a stronghold by the Dziadoszanie, a West Slavic tribe, and in the 10th century passed to the emerging Polish state under Mieszko I. Its first known record is in the chronicle of Thietmar of Merseburg, who also tells how forces of King Henry II of Germany besieged it on 9 August 1017 without success. In 1157 it fell to Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa. Duke Konrad I established the Duchy of Głogów in 1251 and two years later granted the town Magdeburg rights. Trade, brewing and clothmaking then made it prosper. In 1331 the duchy came under the overlordship of King John of Bohemia.

The Głogów line of the Silesian Piasts ended with Jan II the Mad, whom the troops of King Matthias Corvinus expelled in 1488. From 1491 to 1506 the duchy was held by John Albert and Sigismund the Old, both later kings of Poland, and in 1506 it was incorporated into the Kingdom of Bohemia. It passed to the Habsburgs in 1526 and was fortified during the Thirty Years' War, changing hands several times before returning to the Habsburgs in 1648. In the First Silesian War it was captured in a night attack by the Prussian army under Prince Leopold II of Anhalt-Dessau and became part of the Kingdom of Prussia under Frederick II, under the German name Groß-Glogau.

During the Napoleonic Wars the French took Glogau after the Battle of Jena in 1806, and its garrison of 9,000 French troops was besieged in 1813 and 1814; when it surrendered on 10 April 1814 only 1,800 defenders remained. Its fortress status held back growth until the fortifications were pulled down in 1902. In 1945 the Germans made it a stronghold again, and a six-week siege by the Soviet Red Army left 98 percent of its buildings completely destroyed. Its German population was expelled under the Potsdam Agreement and replaced by Polish settlers, and the town began to grow again in 1957 after a copper foundry was built.

Głogów, with about 65,400 people, lies in Lower Silesian Voivodeship and is one of four cities of the Copper Basin. The ducal castle, rebuilt between 1971 and 1983, houses a museum of history and archaeology. The surviving landmarks include the Gothic Collegiate Church of the Assumption, parts of the medieval walls and a monument to the Polish defence of 1109.
gloria-in-excelsis-deo: The hymn is an example of the psalmi idiotici, private psalms composed by individuals in imitation of the biblical Psalter, which were popular in the 2nd and 3rd centuries. The Te Deum and the Phos Hilaron are other surviving examples. In the 4th century it became part of morning prayers, and it is still recited in the Byzantine Rite Orthros service. The Latin translation is traditionally attributed to Hilary of Poitiers, who may have learned it in the East in 359–360.

In Latin the hymn renders the Greek hypsístois of Luke 2:14 as excelsis, not altissimis, the word Jerome preferred in his translation. The Vulgate was commissioned only in 382. The Latin text praises God in a series of verbs (we praise you, we bless you, we adore you, we glorify you), addresses Jesus Christ as the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world, and closes with the words that he alone is the Holy One, the Lord and the Most High.

In the Byzantine Rite it is the Greater Doxology, always sung, at Orthros on Sundays and feast days. The priest exclaims "Glory to Thee, Who hast shown us the Light", the choir begins, and all the lamps and candles are lit. In the Coptic Orthodox Church it is a congregational prayer, called the Praise of the Angels, said at the Morning Raising of Incense. The Syriac Orthodox Church knows it as Teshbuhto d'malakhe.

In the Roman Rite it is sung or said at Mass after the Kyrie on Sundays outside Lent and Advent, and on solemnities and feasts. A tradition recorded in the Liber Pontificalis ascribes its use at the Christmas Mass to Pope Telesphorus and its use on Sundays and martyrs' feasts, by bishops only, to Pope Symmachus (498–514). Priests were allowed it at first only at Easter and on their ordination day, but by the end of the 11th century they used it on Sundays and feasts. In the Church of England's 1549 Book of Common Prayer it stood in the Roman position, but it was later moved to the end of the service.

The Gloria has been sung to a wide variety of melodies, and modern scholars have catalogued well over two hundred used in the medieval church. Almost all polyphonic settings of the Mass include it, and there are settings of the Gloria alone by J. S. Bach (BWV 191), Antonio Vivaldi (RV 589 and RV 588), Francis Poulenc and others. The German paraphrase Allein Gott in der Höh sei Ehr was an early Lutheran hymn, and the Christmas carol Angels We Have Heard on High uses its beginning as a refrain.
glorious-revolution: James II became king in February 1685 with wide backing in all three kingdoms, although he was a Roman Catholic, and Protestant uprisings were quickly crushed. His supporters accepted his personal faith so long as he kept the primacy of the Protestant Church of England and Church of Scotland. They opposed his policy of toleration for Catholics, and Parliament refused to repeal the Test Acts of 1678 and 1681. He suspended Parliament in November 1685 and ruled by decree, dismissing judges who disagreed. Historians generally accept that he wished to promote Catholicism rather than set up an absolute monarchy, but his inflexible response to opposition had the same result.

The birth of his son James Francis Edward Stuart on 10 June 1688 raised the prospect of a Catholic dynasty. Opponents then issued the Invitation to William, written by Henry Sydney, to his daughter Mary's Protestant husband, William III of Orange, stadtholder of the Dutch Republic. William wished to bring England into an alliance against France. His expedition of over 400 ships carrying 40,000 men was the largest fleet assembled in European waters up to that date, and he landed in Devon on 5 November 1688.

James had thought himself safe from invasion. He panicked and offered concessions, but his overwhelmingly Protestant army disintegrated, and he went into exile in France on 23 December. William took control of the provisional government on 28 December. On 6 February 1689 a Convention Parliament declared that in choosing exile James had abdicated, and it offered the crown jointly to William and Mary. A separate settlement was made in Scotland in June 1689.

James landed in Ireland on 12 March 1689 with 6,000 French troops, supported by the Catholic majority, and a Jacobite rising followed in Scotland. The revolution formally established constitutional monarchy as the British form of government and the primacy of parliamentary sovereignty. Britain and the Dutch Republic became allies against French expansion for much of the 18th century. Between 1688 and 1720 world trade dominance shifted from the Dutch Republic to Great Britain. Protestant preachers gave the name Glorious two decades later. Thomas Macaulay presented the revolution as a largely consensual and bloodless triumph, but its assessment among historians remains disputed.
glorious-revolution-spain: By the 1860s the reign of Queen Isabella II had become deeply unpopular. Her government was plagued by corruption, economic crises and political repression. She had alienated liberals and progressives and become more dependent on conservative and clerical factions, and her troubled marriage and other scandals further eroded public confidence. Earlier attempts to overthrow her had failed, most notably in 1854 and 1861. An 1866 rebellion led by General Juan Prim and a revolt of the sergeants at the San Gil barracks in Madrid showed liberals and republicans that there was serious unrest to be harnessed.

Exiles made agreements at Ostend in 1866 and Brussels in 1867. The death of Leopoldo O'Donnell in 1867 caused the Unión Liberal to unravel, and many of its supporters joined the movement against Isabella.

In September 1868 naval forces under Admiral Juan Bautista Topete mutinied in Cádiz, the city where Rafael del Riego had launched his coup against Isabella's father, Ferdinand VII, half a century earlier. When Generals Prim and Francisco Serrano denounced the government, much of the army defected to them as they arrived in Spain. The queen made a brief show of force at the Battle of Alcolea, where her loyal generals under Manuel Pavía were defeated by Serrano. Isabella crossed into France and retired from Spanish politics. She lived in exile at the Palacio Castilla in Paris until her death in 1904.

The coalition of liberals, moderates and republicans lacked direction. Control passed to Serrano, who was named regent while a monarch was sought. In 1869 the Cortes promulgated a liberal constitution, the first in Spain since 1812, and Prim was also named regent that year. Candidates for the throne included the elderly Espartero, who rejected the idea but still received eight votes, Isabella's son Alfonso and Ferdinand of Saxe-Coburg. Politicians feared that offering the crown to Prince Leopold of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen would trigger a Franco-Prussian War. In August 1870 the Cortes chose Amadeo of Savoy, a younger son of Victor Emmanuel II of Italy, who was elected King on 3 November 1870.

Amadeo landed at Cartagena on 27 December, the day Prim was assassinated as he left the Cortes. He reigned two years, after which the parties formed the first Spanish Republic, which also lasted two years. In 1875 the Cortes proclaimed Isabella's son King Alfonso XII.
glory-to-hong-kong: The song was written by a composer and Cantonese lyricist using the pseudonym Thomas dgx yhl, who first posted an instrumental version and lyrics on LIHKG, an online forum of pro-democracy Hongkongers. Forum users suggested changes, among them the protest motto "Liberate Hong Kong; revolution of our times", which was worked into the last of its four Cantonese stanzas. The composer said the song was meant to boost protesters' morale and unite people; a pop rock artist by his own account, he took two months over the melody, citing models such as God Save the King and The Star-Spangled Banner.

A music video of protest scenes appeared on YouTube on 31 August 2019 and spread within days, and an orchestral version with chorus followed on 11 September. German, Japanese, French, Catalan and Taiwanese versions appeared that autumn.

In September 2019 the song was sung at a sit-in at Prince Edward station, by crowds in more than a dozen shopping malls at 8:31 in the evening, by students forming human chains and by football supporters at a World Cup qualifier against Iran. Some protesters wanted it to replace March of the Volunteers as the anthem of Hong Kong, though the composer insisted it could only be a protest song. The state-owned Wen Wei Po called it an anthem for independence whose lyrics idealised violence.

Because web searches for the anthem of Hong Kong often returned the song, it was played by mistake at international events, among them a rugby match in Incheon in November 2022. Chief Executive John Lee said it was closely connected to the 2019 violence and to advocacy of independence.

After the national security law of 2020, the government declared some of its phrases separatist and subversive and told schools not to allow it, and people who played it in public faced prosecution on other charges. In June 2023 the government sought an injunction against the song; the Court of First Instance refused, citing the chilling effect on free expression, but on 8 May 2024 the Court of Appeal granted it, with exceptions for academic and journalistic use. YouTube blocked 32 videos in Hong Kong, saying it shared human rights groups' concerns, and after weeks of removal and reuploading the song was restored to streaming platforms abroad.
gloucester: Gloucester lies on the River Severn between the Cotswolds to the east and the Forest of Dean to the west, at the traditional lowest bridging point of the river. The Roman settlement stood at an important crossing of the Severn near the Fosse Way, the early front line after the Roman invasion of Britain. The Roman name Glevum came from a Brythonic word meaning bright, and the Welsh name Caerloyw, attested from the 8th century, means bright fort.

Glevum was founded around 48 as a fort at Kingsholm. Twenty years later a larger legionary fortress was built on slightly higher ground, centred on the present Gloucester Cross, and a civilian settlement grew around it. Legio XX Valeria Victrix was probably based there until 66, and Legio II Augusta after it, as Roman forces prepared to invade Wales. In 97, in the reign of Nerva, Glevum became a colonia, and it was probably the provincial capital of Britannia Prima.

After the Roman withdrawal about 410, leading families of the Dobunni may have regained power. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle shows Gloucester as part of Wessex from the Battle of Deorham in 577. It later belonged to the minor kingdom of the Hwicce, which became a sub-kingdom of Mercia after the Battle of Cirencester in 628 and lost its separate standing from about 780. Mercia submitted to Alfred the Great's Wessex in about 877–883.

After the Norman Conquest, William Rufus made Robert Fitzhamon the first baron of Gloucester, linking the city's history closely with Cardiff. Henry II granted the first known borough charter in 1155, and in 1216 Henry III, aged nine, was crowned with a gilded iron ring in the Chapter House of the cathedral. The city withstood a Royalist siege in 1643 in the First English Civil War. John Hooper, Bishop of Gloucester, was burned there in 1555, and Elizabeth I made Gloucester a port in 1580.

Gloucester is a cathedral city and the county town of Gloucestershire, with a population of around 132,000 including suburban areas. Gloucester Cathedral grew from an abbey dedicated to Saint Peter and holds the tomb of Edward II. The Gloucester and Sharpness Canal links the docks to the Severn Estuary. In 1780 Robert Raikes founded the first Sunday school in England there. The city has a long history in aircraft making, and the Gloster E.28/39, the first British jet aircraft, powered by Frank Whittle's turbojet, first flew at the company's airfield at Brockworth.
gloucestershire: Gloucestershire is a ceremonial county of South West England covering about 3,150 square kilometres and bordered by Herefordshire, Worcestershire, Warwickshire, Oxfordshire, Wiltshire, Bristol, Somerset and the Welsh county of Monmouthshire. It is bisected by the River Severn, which forms a wide valley down its centre before broadening into a tidal estuary. The east and south contain most of the Cotswolds, and the uplands of the west belong to the Forest of Dean and the Wye Valley. Besides Gloucester, the towns include Cheltenham, Tewkesbury, Cirencester, Stroud and Yate.

The county was likely established in the tenth century, when it is mentioned in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, and reached roughly its present borders in the eleventh, as Winchcombe and the Forest of Dean were added only in the late 11th century. In the late Middle Ages it was relatively settled and held wealthy monasteries at Tewkesbury, Gloucester, Hailes and Cirencester, while the Forest of Dean was a major iron-producing region. Hailes Abbey was founded by Richard, Earl of Cornwall, in 1246.

Bristol, once a small town within the county, became a county in its own right in 1373, when it was the third-largest city in England. Gloucestershire was not heavily industrialised during the Industrial Revolution, but the Port of Gloucester was expanded with new docks and the small Forest of Dean coalfield was worked. Some northern parishes passed to Warwickshire in 1931. From 1974 to 1996 the area north of Bristol belonged to the county of Avon, and after Avon was abolished it became the unitary authority of South Gloucestershire, which lies within the ceremonial county.

The county is predominantly rural and had a usual resident population of 935,500 at the 2021 census. Its antiquities include Roman remains such as Chedworth Roman Villa and the Eastgate Viewing Chamber in Gloucester, the cathedral of Gloucester, and the abbey church of Tewkesbury, which has the tallest Norman tower in England. Berkeley Castle is over 800 years old. Sudeley Castle contains the burial place of Catherine Parr, sixth wife of Henry VIII, and Thornbury Castle was built by Edward Stafford, Duke of Buckingham, who was beheaded in 1521. The Gloucestershire Old Spots pig takes its name from the county.
gluckstadt: Glückstadt (Danish: Lykstad) lies in the Steinburg district of Schleswig-Holstein, on the right bank of the Lower Elbe at the confluence of the small Rhin river, about 45 km north-west of Altona. It stands on marsh land along the river, which is why levees were needed from the start. The town belongs to the Hamburg Metropolitan Region. Its name translates literally as Luck City or Fortune City.

King Christian IV of Denmark, as Duke of Holstein, founded the town in 1617 and had levees, fortifications and a ducal residence built. He promised settlers tax exemption and freedom of religion, and Glückstadt soon became an important trading centre intended to compete with the Imperial city of Hamburg upstream. Calvinists, Remonstrants and Mennonites from the Netherlands settled there, as did Sephardic Jews and Catholics. After the king intervened in the Thirty Years' War, imperial and Catholic troops under Albrecht von Wallenstein and Count Tilly besieged the town for fifteen weeks in 1627/28, without success.

In 1649 King Frederik III of Denmark moved the seat of the Holstein administration to Glückstadt, and the duchy became known as Holstein-Glückstadt. In 1773 the town became the capital of all Holstein lands, once the lands of the Holstein-Gottorp line were incorporated. In 1814, during the War of the Sixth Coalition, the allies blockaded it; it capitulated and its fortifications were demolished. It was made a free port in 1830. Holstein-Glückstadt stayed under the Danish Crown until Denmark's defeat in the Second Schleswig War of 1864. Austria occupied it, and after the Austro-Prussian War of 1866 it was incorporated into the Prussian Province of Schleswig-Holstein.

The Marsh Railway reached Glückstadt in 1845 from Elmshorn and was extended to Itzehoe in 1857. Trains now run from Hamburg-Altona to Westerland on Sylt, and a ferry crosses the Elbe to Wischhafen in Lower Saxony. The town lies on the Deutsche Fährstraße theme road and the Elbe Cycle Route.
glyptothek: Crown Prince Ludwig of Bavaria, later Ludwig I, commissioned the Glyptothek as a monument to ancient Greece. He envisioned a German Athens in which Greek culture would be remembered, and had it built in front of the gates of Munich. It stands beside the Königsplatz and the building that houses the State Collection of Greek and Roman Antiquities, and it is the oldest public museum in Munich. The architects Karl von Fischer and Leo von Klenze laid out the Königsplatz in 1815, and Klenze arranged it like a forum, with the Glyptothek on its north side.

Between 1806 and the opening in 1830 Ludwig built up a notable collection through his agents. It came to include the Medusa Rondanini, the Barberini Faun and, in 1813, the figures from the temple of Aphaea on Aegina. Frescoes and stuccos by Peter von Cornelius, Clemens von Zimmermann and Wilhelm von Kaulbach once adorned the walls.

The building is neoclassical. Twelve Ionic columns form the portico, and thirteen rooms are arranged around a courtyard. The gable carries a group by Johann Martin von Wagner showing Athena as protector of the plastic arts.

The collection runs from the Archaic age, about 650 BCE, to the Roman era, about 550 CE. Archaic works include the Munich Kouros and the temple figures from Aegina. Classical pieces include the portrait of Homer, the Medusa Rondanini and the Alexander Rondanini, and the Hellenistic period is represented above all by the Barberini Faun. The Roman galleries hold busts of Augustus, Nero and Septimius Severus. A bust of Caligula excavated in Córdoba in 1937 was acquired in 2017, so the museum owns portraits of all five Julio-Claudian emperors.

The Second World War did not destroy much of the sculpture, but the frescoes did not survive, and when the museum reopened in 1972 only lightly plastered bricks were visible. Klenze's Assyrian Hall of 1864 was not rebuilt, and the Assyrian reliefs from the palace of Ashur-nasir-pal II and a lion from the Ishtar Gate of Babylon went to the Staatliche Sammlung für Ägyptische Kunst. It is now part of the Kunstareal, and its sculptures are complemented by the terracotta and bronze collections of the Antikensammlung opposite.
gnaeus-cornelius-scipio-calvus: Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus belonged to the patrician family of the Cornelii Scipiones. His father was Lucius Cornelius Scipio, consul of 259 BCE, and his grandfather the censor of 280 BCE, Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus. His younger brother Publius Cornelius Scipio, consul of 218 BCE, was the father of Scipio Africanus. The nickname Calvus, meaning the bald, distinguished him from his uncle, Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Asina, who had been consul twice during the First Punic War.

Elected consul for 222 BCE with Marcus Claudius Marcellus, he led an army against the Insubres of Cisalpine Gaul. While Marcellus fought them at Clastidium, Scipio besieged Acerrae. After it fell he marched on Mediolanum, drew the Gauls out and routed them, then took the city, which forced the tribe to submit to the Romans.

In 218 BCE Scipio served as a legate in the consular army of his brother Publius, which sailed to the allied Greek city of Massilia. When Publius learned that Hannibal was three days ahead, he sent the army on to the Iberian peninsula under Gnaeus and returned to northern Italy to organise its defence. Gnaeus landed at Emporion with 20,000 infantry, 2,200 cavalry and 60 quinqueremes. Emporion and Tarraco welcomed the Romans, and he began to win over the Iberian tribes north of the Ebro.

Hanno, left by Hannibal to hold that territory, attacked the Romans near Cissa and was defeated, losing 6,000 men in the battle. The Romans took his camp, 2,000 soldiers, Hanno himself and the Iberian chieftain Indibilis. In spring 217 BCE Scipio commanded 55 warships in a surprise attack near the mouth of the Ebro, where the Carthaginians lost 29 of their 40 ships and the control of the seas around the peninsula. In early 215 BCE the brothers jointly fought Hasdrubal Barca at Dertosa; his attempt to envelop the Roman army failed, and the reinforcements meant for Hannibal in Italy were diverted to him.

In 212 BCE the brothers captured Castulo, a mining town and the home of Hannibal's wife Imilce. They then hired about 20,000 Celt-Iberian mercenaries and divided their forces. Publius was defeated and killed near Castulo. Gnaeus, facing Hasdrubal Barca, saw the mercenaries bribed to desert him. He withdrew by night towards the Ebro, was caught by Numidian cavalry and took position on a hilltop near Ilorca. The Carthaginians overran his improvised defences of baggage and saddles, and he died in the fighting.

His death did not end the war in Iberia, which his nephew Publius Cornelius Scipio later carried to its conclusion. His sons were Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica, consul in 191 BCE, and Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Hispallus, consul in 176 BCE.
gnaeus-julius-agricola: Agricola was born on 13 June 40 at the colonia of Forum Julii in Gallia Narbonensis, now Fréjus in France. Both his grandfathers had served as imperial governors. His father, Lucius Julius Graecinus, a senator noted for his interest in philosophy, was put to death on the order of the emperor Caligula for refusing to prosecute the emperor's second cousin Marcus Junius Silanus. His mother was Julia Procilla, whom Tacitus describes as a lady of singular virtue. Agricola was educated at Massilia (Marseille).

He served as a military tribune in Britain under Gaius Suetonius Paulinus from 58 to 62 and almost certainly took part in the suppression of the Boudican uprising in 61. He was quaestor in the province of Asia in 64, tribune of the plebs in 66 and praetor in 68. In the Year of the Four Emperors he gave his support to Vespasian, and was given command of the Legio XX Valeria Victrix in Britain, where he reimposed discipline and fought the Brigantes under Quintus Petillius Cerialis. He then governed Gallia Aquitania for almost three years and in 76 or 77 was made suffect consul.

Returning to Britain as governor in the summer of 77, he found that the Ordovices had virtually destroyed the Roman cavalry in their territory, and defeated them before subduing Anglesey. In 79 he pushed his armies to the estuary of the river Taus, usually taken to be the Firth of Tay. He reformed the corn levy and encouraged the building of towns on the Roman model, and had the sons of native nobles given a Roman education, which Tacitus calls a means of pacifying the tribes. In 83 he faced the Caledonians under Calgacus at Mons Graupius. Tacitus puts their numbers above 30,000 and their losses at about 10,000 against 360 Roman dead, and two thirds of their army escaped into the Highlands.

Agricola was recalled after an unusually long tenure. Tacitus claims that the emperor Domitian ordered this because Agricola's successes outshone his own modest victories in Germany. He was awarded triumphal decorations and a statue but never held another civil or military post, and he declined the governorship of Africa, from ill health or, as Tacitus claims, because of Domitian's machinations. He died on 23 August 93 on his family estates in Gallia Narbonensis, aged fifty-three. Rumours of poisoning by Domitian circulated, but no evidence for them was ever produced. His career is known mainly from the biography by Tacitus, his son-in-law, and from archaeological evidence in northern Britain.
gnaeus-marcius-coriolanus: Later ancient historians generally accepted Coriolanus as a real person, and Livy, Plutarch and Dionysius of Halicarnassus retold a consensus story of his life. His first name is traditionally given as Gnaeus, the form used by Livy, while Dionysius calls him Gaius, as Plutarch followed. According to the tradition he came to fame as a young man in the army of the consul Postumus Cominius in 493 BCE, during the siege of the Volscian town of Corioli. When a Volscian force from Antium attacked the Romans and the garrison made a sally, Marcius gathered a small force, repelled them and charged through the town gates, setting fire to houses by the wall. The town was captured, and he gained the cognomen Coriolanus.

In 491 BCE, after a grain shortage, a large quantity of grain was imported from Sicily, and the senate debated how to distribute it to the commoners. Coriolanus advocated providing it only if the pro-plebeian reforms arising from the first secessio plebis of 494 BCE were reversed. The senate thought this too harsh, the populace was incensed and the tribunes put him on trial. He refused to attend and was convicted.

He fled to the Volsci and lived with their leader Attius Tullus Aufidius. In Plutarch's account he entered Aufidius's home in disguise as a supplicant. The two persuaded the Volsci to break their truce and invade, and led the army against Roman towns and colonies, then besieged Rome from a camp at the Cluilian trench, five miles from the city. Coriolanus directed the Volsci to ravage plebeian properties and spare those of the patricians. Ambassadors and then priests sent by the Romans achieved nothing.

His mother Veturia, his wife Volumnia and his two sons, with the matrons of Rome, then went to the Volscian camp and implored him to stop. He was overcome by their pleas and withdrew, and Rome honoured the women with a temple of Fortuna. His fate afterwards is unclear. One version says he retired to Antium, where Aufidius had him put on trial by the Volsci and assassinated before the trial ended.

Some modern scholars question the story, since accounts of it first appear in works of the 3rd century BCE, about two hundred years later, and few authoritative records exist from before the Gallic sack of Rome in 390 BCE. The story is the basis of Shakespeare's Coriolanus, which draws on Thomas North's translation of Plutarch, and of Beethoven's Coriolan Overture, written for Heinrich Joseph von Collin's play of 1804.
gnaeus-pompeius-strabo: Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo was born around 135 BCE into a noble family of Picenum in central Italy. The cognomen Strabo means cross-eyed. His mother, Lucilia, came from Suessa Aurunca and was a sister of the satirical poet Gaius Lucilius, and his father was Sextus Pompeius.
