The Pompeii had become the richest and most prominent family of the region, with a large clientele and influence in Picenum and Rome, which the Senate could not ignore despite its prejudice against rural families. After military service, probably as a tribune, Strabo rose through the offices and governed Sicily as promagistrate in 93 BCE.

In the Social War he commanded against the Italian rebels in the north. In 90 BCE a large force of Picentes, Vestini and Marsi attacked his marching legions, and he was blockaded in Picenum. In the autumn he launched two sorties that caught his enemies in a pincer, and the survivors fell back on Asculum, which he set out to starve. The success made him popular and he was elected consul for 89 BCE with Lucius Porcius Cato. He defeated a rebel column marching into Etruria, killing 5,000 men, and another 5,000 died trying to recross the Apennines.

Cato was killed attacking the enemy camp near the Fucine Lake, which left Strabo sole consul. He defeated an Italian relief army of 60,000 near Asculum. After the city fell he had the rebel leaders whipped and executed and auctioned off their goods, keeping the proceeds, which may explain his reputation for greed.

He triumphed on 27 December 89 BCE. When his consulship ended he kept his army in the field, and the Senate transferred it to the consul Quintus Pompeius Rufus, whom Strabo's soldiers murdered. He stayed out of events when Sulla took Rome in 88 BCE. In 87 BCE he answered the Senate's request for help against Gaius Marius and Lucius Cornelius Cinna, but he played the sides against each other, and Publius Rutilius Rufus called him the vilest man alive.

In 87 BCE Strabo camped outside the Colline Gate, where disease broke out among his troops. He caught dysentery and died within days. His avarice and cruelty had made his soldiers hate him so much that they dragged his corpse from the bier and through the streets. Plutarch told another story, that he was struck by lightning. His son Pompey the Great took the legions back to Picenum and used them to support Sulla a few years later. Strabo also had a daughter, Pompeia, and the cities of Alba Pompeia and Laus Pompeia were named in his honour.
gniezno: Gniezno lies about 50 km east of Poznań and was founded, like Rome, on seven hills. At the beginning of the 10th century the site held several places sacred to the Slavic religion. A ducal stronghold was founded on Lech Hill just before 940. According to the Polish version of a legend, the name comes from gniazdo, a nest: the hunter Lech, one of three brothers, settled where he found a white eagle guarding its nest.

Around 940 Gniezno, an important pagan cult centre, became one of the main fortresses of the early Piast rulers. After Mieszko I of Poland adopted Christianity, his son Bolesław I the Brave deposited the remains of Saint Adalbert in a church newly built on the hill, to underline the city's importance as the religious centre and capital of his realm. At the Congress of Gniezno in the year 1000 Bolesław received the Holy Roman Emperor Otto III, and they marked the founding of the Polish ecclesiastical province with an archbishopric at Gniezno. New bishoprics were set up at Kołobrzeg, Wrocław and Kraków beside the older one at Poznań.

The cathedral saw the coronations of Bolesław I in 1024 and of his son Mieszko II Lambert in 1025. In 1038 the Bohemian duke Bretislav I captured and destroyed Gniezno and Poznań, which led later Polish rulers to move the capital to Kraków. Bolesław II the Generous was crowned in the rebuilt cathedral in 1076, and Gniezno was again the coronation site in 1295 and 1300. The Teutonic Knights destroyed the city in 1331, and in 1419 its status as the capital of Christianity in Poland was confirmed when the archbishops received the title of Primate of Poland.

Prussia annexed Gniezno in the Second Partition of Poland in 1793 and renamed it Gnesen. After the Greater Poland Uprising of 1918–1919 and the Treaty of Versailles it became part of the Second Polish Republic. In the Second World War German troops took it on 11 September 1939 and annexed it to Germany.

Gniezno is the seat of Gniezno County in the Greater Poland Voivodeship and of the oldest archdiocese in Poland, whose archbishop is the Primate of Poland. Gniezno Cathedral is a designated Historic Monument of Poland. It holds the Romanesque Gniezno Doors and the coffin of Saint Adalbert.
goa: Goa lies on the southwestern coast of India, in the Konkan region, separated from the Deccan highlands by the Western Ghats. It covers 3,702 square kilometres, and its highest point, Sonsogor, rises to 1,167 metres. The climate is tropical monsoon, with over 90 per cent of the rain falling from June to September. Rock engravings at Usgalimal and Kajur are among the earliest known traces of human life in India.

In the 3rd century BCE Goa belonged to the Maurya Empire under Ashoka. Between the 2nd century BCE and the 6th century CE it was ruled by the Bhojas of Goa, then by the Chalukyas of Badami from 578 to 753 and the Rashtrakutas from 753 to 963. The Kadambas, who followed as feudatories of the Chalukyas of Kalyani, patronised Jainism.

In 1510 the Portuguese defeated the Bijapur sultan Yusuf Adil Shah with the help of a local ally, Thimmayya or Timoji, and set up a permanent settlement at Old Goa. Under Afonso de Albuquerque the city became capital of the Estado da Índia. The Goa Inquisition was established in 1560 and abolished in 1812, and the first printing press in India produced its first books in 1556. Old Goa was abandoned in the 19th century after outbreaks of disease. On 19 December 1961 the Indian Army invaded in Operation Vijay and annexed Goa, and on 30 May 1987 it became India's twenty-fifth state.

Goa is a state of India with Panaji as its capital and Vasco da Gama as its largest city. Konkani is its sole official language, with Marathi also permitted for official purposes. The census of 2011 counted 1,458,545 people, 66.1 per cent of them Hindu and 25.1 per cent Christian. The Bom Jesus Basilica and the churches and convents of Old Goa form its World Heritage Site; the basilica holds the remains of Saint Francis Xavier. Goan cooking, based on rice, fish and coconut, is heavily influenced by Portuguese cuisine.
goa-gajah: Goa Gajah, the Elephant Cave, lies in Gianyar on the island of Bali near Ubud, in Indonesia, and served as a sanctuary. The exact origins of the cave are uncertain, but it is believed to have been made as a place for spiritual meditation. One folk tale says it was created by the fingernail of the giant Kebo Iwa. From its style, the sanctuary probably dates from the 11th century, in the time of the Bali Kingdom. The site is mentioned in the Javanese poem Desawarnana, written in 1365.

The complex holds both Hindu and Buddhist imagery. The cave contains a lingam and yoni, symbols of Shiva, and an image of Ganesha, while by the river there are carved stupas and chattra, imagery of Buddhism. Menacing faces are carved into the stone, and their purpose is assumed to be warding off evil spirits. The main figure was once thought to be an elephant, which gave the site its nickname, though other sources say it is named after the stone statue of the elephant-headed god Ganesha inside the temple.

The entrance is reached only by walking down a long flight of stairs, and the small interior is usually filled with trails of white smoke from burning incense. The complex also has seven statues of women holding water pitchers, one of them destroyed by an earthquake, which depict seven holy rivers of India: the Ganga, Sarasvati, Yamuna, Godavari, Sindhu, Kaveri and Narmada.

Dutch archaeologists rediscovered the cave in 1923, but the fountains and bathing pool were not found until 1954, and the extensive bathing place was not excavated until the 1950s. The site was added to the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List on 19 October 1995 in the Cultural category, and was withdrawn in 2015 along with eleven other sites.
gobelins-manufactory: The Gobelins were a family of dyers who settled in the middle of the 15th century in the Faubourg Saint-Marcel in Paris, on the banks of the Bièvre. In 1602 Henry IV of France rented space from them for his Flemish tapestry makers, Marc de Comans and François de la Planche. Their sons Charles de Comans and Raphaël de la Planche took over the workshops in 1629, but their partnership ended around 1650 and the works were split in two. Tapestries from this early Flemish period are sometimes called pre-gobelins.

After the purchase of 1662 the works became a general upholstery factory, where tapestries and furniture of every kind were made under Charles Le Brun, director and chief designer from 1663 to 1690. Workshops there also served as foundries for most of the bronze statues in the park of Versailles. Louis XIV's financial problems closed the establishment in 1694, but it reopened in 1697 to weave tapestry, chiefly for royal use, and rivalled the Beauvais works until the French Revolution suspended its work.

The factory was revived under the Bourbon Restoration, and in 1826 the making of carpets was added to that of tapestry. In 1871 the building was partly burned during the Paris Commune, and Jean-Camille Formigé built a new one on the avenue des Gobelins in 1912. A branch was set up in London, probably early in the 18th century, in what is now Fulham High Street; around 1753 the priest and adventurer Pierre Parisot appears to have taken it over, but it closed a few years later.

The manufactory stands at 42 avenue des Gobelins in the 13th arrondissement of Paris and is run by the administration of the Mobilier National and the national carpet and tapestry manufactories of the French Ministry of Culture. Its four irregular 17th-century buildings hold Le Brun's residence and looms that still weave tapestries by 17th-century techniques, now in limited numbers and with contemporary subjects for French government buildings. The Galerie des Gobelins, built in the gardens by Auguste Perret in 1937, holds temporary exhibitions and reopened on 12 May 2007.
gobi-desert: The Gobi is a large, cold desert and grassland region in southern Mongolia and North China. It measures about 1,600 km from southwest to northeast and 800 km from north to south, and covers approximately 1,295,000 square kilometres. The name comes from the Mongolian word Gov', meaning dryland, used for all waterless regions of the Mongolian Plateau; the Chinese term gēbì refers to rocky semi-deserts rather than sandy ones, and much of the Gobi is bare rock rather than sand.

It lies on a plateau roughly 910 to 1,520 m above sea level, with frost and occasional snow on its dunes, and an average of about 194 mm of rain a year. Its climate is one of great extremes, with changes of as much as 35 °C in 24 hours. Geographers divide it into five dry ecoregions, among them the Eastern Gobi desert steppe, the Alashan Plateau semi-desert and the Dzungarian Basin semi-desert; some regard the Tarim basin in the west as a separate Taklamakan Desert.

Little is known about early habitation. Lisa Janz has proposed three phases: Oasis I, the Mesolithic from 13500 to 8000 calibrated years before the present, when people began to use oases and made microblades, small milling stones and plain, low-fired pottery; Oasis II, the Neolithic from 8000 to 5000, when oases were used extensively; and Oasis III, the Bronze Age from 5000 to 3000.

A warm wet phase began around 8000 years ago, and lakes in the western Gobi peaked by 7500. Bronze Age herder burials, Karasuk bronze knives and Mongolian deer stones have been found. A period of desertification followed between 5000 and 4500 years ago, and increasing aridity between 3500 and 3000 led to a decline in habitation. The region was later inhabited mostly by nomadic Mongols, Uyghurs and Kazakhs.

The Gobi is a source of important fossil finds. The first dinosaur eggs, twenty-six averaging 23 cm in length, were uncovered there in 1923, and the Nemegt Basin in Mongolia is noted for early mammals, dinosaur eggs and stone implements some 100,000 years old. It supports black-tailed gazelles, wild Bactrian camels and the Mongolian wild ass, and large reserves include Gobi Gurvansaikhan National Park. The desert is expanding, mostly on its southern edge into China, which loses about 3,600 km2 of grassland a year, and China's Three-North Shelter Forest Program, begun in 1978, is meant to run through 2050 to slow it.
gobir: Gobir was one of the seven original kingdoms of Hausaland and the northernmost of them, relied on to shield its sister states from northern enemies, above all the Tuareg. Broader Hausa tradition names its founder as Duma, a grandson of Bayajidda, but the records of the ruling house trace its descent from Copts of Arabia led by a first king, Bana Turmi. The historians S. J. Hogben and A. H. M. Kirk-Greene noted that some think this claim was invented by Bawa Jan Gwarzo (r. 1777–1795) to avoid paying tribute to Bornu.

In the 15th century Leo Africanus described Gobir's many herding villages and its weavers and artisans, whose textiles and shoes reached Timbuktu and Gao. Constant Tuareg pressure pushed the Gobirawa south from Asben to Maigali, then Goran Rami and, in the early 18th century, Birnin Lalle. Sarkin Gobir Soba besieged Zabarma for three years, raided as far as Ilorin and was finally killed fighting Agadez. His successor Uban Iche was murdered by his son Babari (1742–1770), who sacked Birnin Zamfara and built a new walled capital, Alkalawa, on the Gulbin Rima River.

Sarki Bawa appears to have invited Usman dan Fodio to Gobir in 1774, and dan Fodio settled at Degel and preached against the abuses of the Hausa elite. Later rulers turned against him, and Yunfa, after failing to have him killed, exiled him and his followers. Resistance to the jihad went on in the north-east, and in 1836 Sarki Mayaki built a new capital at Tibiri, 10 km north of Maradi, but Sultan Muhammed Bello crushed a Gobir revolt that year at the Battle of Gawakuke. In 1975 a reunited traditional sultanate took up residence in Sabon Birni, Nigeria.

Gobir followed the sarauta system of kingship. The sarki was chosen by an electoral college called the Taran Gobir, the Gobir nine, whose members had to agree unanimously and also served as his council. After the sarki the highest titleholder was the ubandawaki, commander of the cavalry. Officials at court represented the guilds of blacksmiths, weavers, dyers and other crafts, the indigenous groups and the immigrant communities, such as the Tuareg and the Fulbe, together with the mallamai, the Islamic scholars. The Inna, usually the sarki's sister, was high priestess of the Bori cult and served the dynastic goddess Inna Baka.
gochang-hwasun-and-ganghwa-dolmen-sites: Dolmens in East Asia are generally classed in two types: the table or northern type, in which four stones form the walls of a box capped by a stone laid on top, and the go-board or southern type, with underground burial and stones supporting the capstone. The Gochang site, known as the Jungnim-ri dolmens and centred on Maesan village in North Jeolla province, holds the largest and most varied group. Its dolmens stand at the foot of hills at altitudes of 15 to 50 metres, with capstones of 1 to 5.8 metres that may weigh up to 225 tons, and 442 have been documented. The group is believed to date from around the seventh century BCE.

The Hwasun site lies in the valleys around the Jiseokgang River and is marked by 596 dolmens in a small area, among them the largest in Korea at Daesin-ri, 7.3 metres long and 280 tons in weight. The Ganghwa dolmens stand on the slopes of mountains on Ganghwa Island, higher than the others. They are believed to be the earliest, since the groups at Bugeun-ri and Gocheon-ri resemble early dolmens, though this has not been conclusively proved. The notable Ganghwa dolmen is a table-type stone measuring 2.6 by 7.1 by 5.5 metres, resting on only two supporting stones.

Three theories exist for the origin of Korean dolmens: transmission by sea from Southeast Asia along with rice culture, transmission from Neolithic peoples in Manchuria and southern Siberia, and a local Korean origin. The second is weakened because dolmens there are much less concentrated than in Korea. Whether the dolmens were only tombs has been debated. Complete human bones found at the Hwangseok-ri dolmen in Jecheon in 1967 confirmed their use for burial, but some argue that table dolmens also served as altars, and unusually large ones may have displayed the authority of the group that built them. Excavation at the sites began in 1965.

Dolmens in South Korea are concentrated in South Jeolla Province, which has 10,068, with 1,597 in North Jeolla. Many in the Seoul area were lost to urban development, including those at Wonji-dong found with artefacts in 1984. The Gochang dolmen site is listed as Historic Site No. 391, the Hwasun site as No. 410 and the Ganghwa dolmen as No. 137. The three sites were registered together as a UNESCO World Heritage Site at the 24th session of the World Heritage Committee in Cairns, Australia, in late 2000, and the Korean government has carried out a programme of inventory and preservation.
god-defend-new-zealand: The competition of 1876 was won by John Joseph Woods of Lawrence, Otago, who was Vandemonian-born and composed the melody in a single sitting on the evening after he learned of it. The song was first performed at the Queen's Theatre in Princes Street, Dunedin, on Christmas Day 1876, and sheet music was published in February 1878. In 1878 Thomas Henry Smith of Auckland, a judge in the Native Land Court, made a Māori version at the request of Premier George Edward Grey. The anthem has five verses in each language, and the Māori is not a direct translation of the English. Its structure is a prayer to God, with the refrain God defend New Zealand.

In 1897 Premier Richard Seddon presented a copy of the words and music to Queen Victoria. In 1940 the government bought the copyright and made the song the national hymn in time for the centennial celebrations. It was used at the British Empire Games from 1950, and at the Olympics in 1952, when it and God Save the King were played after Yvette Williams won the long jump. A campaign for its adoption as the anthem began after the 1972 Munich Games. With the consent of Queen Elizabeth II, the government of Robert Muldoon gazetted it as a second national anthem on 21 November 1977, on equal standing with the royal anthem.

Until the 1990s only the first English verse was commonly sung. After Hinewehi Mohi sang only the first Māori verse at a 1999 Rugby World Cup match between the All Blacks and England, it became usual to sing the first verse in Māori and then in English.

Some of the words, such as thy, thee, ramparts and assail, have been criticised as antiquated or obscure, and the melody as hard to sing at its original pitch, but no widely acceptable replacement has been found. The phrase Pacific's triple star has no official explanation; unofficial readings include New Zealand's three main islands and the three stars on the flag of Te Kooti, a 19th-century Māori leader. In 2013 the original score and lyrics were added to the UNESCO Memory of the World Aotearoa New Zealand register; the documents are kept at the Auckland Central City Library.
god-rest-ye-merry-gentlemen: The carol is in the Roxburghe Collection and is number 394 in the Roud Folk Song Index. The manuscript of the 1650s opens Sit yow merry Gentlemen. Some sources date the carol as far back as the 16th century, others to the 18th or early 19th. Its popularity owes most to the English solicitor and antiquarian William Sandys, who included it in Christmas Carols Ancient and Modern (London, 1833), a collection of carols he had gathered and apparently also improvised. A variant text printed in 1775 in The Beauties of the Magazines was taken from a song-sheet bought from a caroller in the street.

The opening phrase God rest you merry meant may God grant you peace and happiness; the Oxford English Dictionary records it from 1534, and it appears in Shakespeare's As You Like It, while rest you merry is in Romeo and Juliet. Today merry is often misread as an adjective describing the gentlemen, so the line is often punctuated God rest you, merry gentlemen, as already in the 1775 variant. The form ye is a pseudo-archaism, since ye was only ever a subject pronoun.

The better-known minor-key melody first appears in print in a rondo for fortepiano by Samuel Wesley, reviewed in 1815, and had been linked with the carol since at least the mid-18th century, when James Nares wrote it down as The old Christmas Carol; the full current melody was published by Chappell in 1855. A second tune, Cornish, is seldom heard today.

In March 1824 The Gentleman's Magazine complained that in London no carols were heard except some croaking ballad-singer bawling out this one. Charles Dickens referred to it in A Christmas Carol (1843), replacing rest with bless, and George Eliot quoted it in Silas Marner (1861). Gustav Holst included it in his choral fantasy Christmas Day (1910), and the third movement of Victor Hely-Hutchinson's Carol Symphony (1927) is a scherzo on its tune. Bing Crosby recorded it on 8 June 1942, and it has since been recorded by many popular musicians.
god-save-the-king: The author of the song is unknown, and it may originate as a plainchant, although an attribution to the composer John Bull has sometimes been made. In The Oxford Companion to Music, Percy Scholes notes similarities to an early plainsong melody, though the rhythm is distinctly that of a galliard. He quotes a keyboard piece by John Bull dated 1619 with some similarities to the modern tune, and a piece by Henry Purcell that sets the words God Save the King to its opening notes. Nineteenth-century writers mention a widespread belief that an old Scots carol, Remember O Thou Man, was its source.

The phrase itself is much older than the song. A text based on 1 Kings 1:38–40 has been sung and proclaimed at every coronation since that of King Edgar in 973, and by 1545 it was a watchword of the Royal Navy.

In the United Kingdom the song derives its official status from custom and use, not from a royal proclamation or act of Parliament. Beyond its consistent first verse it has many versions, and usually only one verse is sung. King George V considered himself an expert on how it should be played, and in 1933 an Army Order laid down its tempo and orchestration.

It spread with the British Empire, serving as the national anthem of each country, and declined in use in most states that became independent. In New Zealand it was the sole national anthem until 1977, when God Defend New Zealand was introduced as a second. In South Africa it was a co-national anthem from 1938 until 1957. In Australia it was declared the royal anthem on 19 April 1984.

The melody has served elsewhere with new words. It was the anthem of Prussia, Heil dir im Siegerkranz, from 1795 until 1918, the imperial anthem of Russia from 1816 to 1833, and the anthem of Switzerland from the 1840s until 1961. It remains the national anthem of Liechtenstein and the royal anthem of Norway, and it is the basis of the American song My Country, 'Tis of Thee. About 140 composers have used the tune, among them Beethoven, who wrote seven piano variations on it in 1802–1803.

In 1796 the philosopher Jeremy Bentham praised the melody for its beauty and simplicity. In 1951 the song became the first music played on a computer, programmed by Christopher Strachey at Manchester.
god-save-the-tsar: The anthem was chosen in a competition held in 1833 and first performed on 18 December 1833. The music was written by the violinist Alexei Lvov and the words by the court poet Vasily Zhukovsky. It served as the national anthem of the Russian Empire until the February Revolution of 1917. The Worker's Marseillaise was then adopted as the new anthem, and remained so until the Bolsheviks overthrew the Russian Provisional Government in the October Revolution of the same year.

The tune was also used as the royal anthem of the Principality of Bulgaria, where it had been imposed by the temporary Russian government and the Russian army commanders. Bulgaria gave up its use after the declaration of independence in 1908.

Many composers used the theme. Tchaikovsky quoted it in the 1812 Overture, the Marche Slave, his overture on the Danish national anthem and the Festival Coronation March. In the Soviet era the authorities altered such works, replacing the theme with other patriotic melodies, such as the Glory chorus from Mikhail Glinka's opera A Life for the Tsar. Charles Gounod used it in his Fantaisie sur l'Hymne National Russe, and later film scores, among them William Walton's for Three Sisters in 1970 and Maurice Jarre's for Doctor Zhivago in 1965, are built on it.

In 1842 the English author Henry Chorley wrote the words God, the Omnipotent! for Lvov's tune, and as the Russian Hymn it appeared in 19th- and 20th-century hymnals and still appears in several others. The melody also carries the words of many college and school songs. The Royal Scots Dragoon Guards still play the anthem at formal events as a tribute to Nicholas II, former colonel-in-chief of their predecessor regiment, the Scots Greys. In 1998 the rock artist Alexander Gradsky proposed reviving the theme as the Russian national anthem, with substantially different lyrics.
godfrey-binaisa: Godfrey Lukongwa Binaisa was born in Kampala on 30 May 1920. He was educated at King's College Budo and Makerere College, took an LLB at King's College London in 1955 and was called to the Bar at Lincoln's Inn in 1956. He became a Queen's counsel and had a private law practice in Kampala. In the 1950s he belonged to the Uganda National Congress and the United Congress Party, and he later joined the Uganda People's Congress, which formed Uganda's first post-independence government in 1962. He was Attorney General from 1962 until 1968, when he resigned over disagreements with President Milton Obote about constitutional matters, particularly the president's powers of detention.

Binaisa returned to private practice in 1969. After Idi Amin took power in 1971 he went into exile, first in London, where he worked for the maritime law firm Graham & James, then in San Francisco. He joined the Uganda Freedom Union, one of several anti-Amin groups in exile. After Amin was overthrown in 1979 Binaisa returned to Uganda. Yusuf Lule had served as interim president for 68 days, and on 20 June 1979 the National Consultative Commission, then the supreme body of the Uganda National Liberation Front, appointed Binaisa president.

He called his ideology Umbrella and used it to consolidate his position, seeking to unite all Ugandans in one political fold. The Movement system later used under Yoweri Museveni has often been attributed to him.

When Binaisa dismissed the army chief of staff, Brigadier Oyite Ojok, the UNLF's Military Commission, headed by Paulo Muwanga and with Museveni as deputy, removed him on 12 May 1980. A Presidential Commission that included Muwanga, Museveni, Ojok and Tito Okello governed until the general elections of December 1980. Obote's Uganda People's Congress won them, but the results were disputed, and Museveni launched a guerrilla rebellion that led to his gaining the presidency in 1986.

After his presidency Binaisa returned to London for a time and then practised law in Mount Vernon, New York. He later returned to Uganda and lived quietly in retirement; he was the only former president supported by the state under the Constitution. He died in his sleep on 5 August 2010, aged 90, after a stroke or heart attack earlier that year, and was given a state funeral.
godfrey-i-of-louvain: Godfrey, also called the Courageous or the Great, was born about 1060, the son of Henry II and Adela of Orthen, a daughter of Count Everard of Orthen. In 1095 he succeeded his brother Henry III, who died wounded in a tournament and left only young daughters. He became Landgrave of Brabant and Count of Brussels and Leuven, and from 1106 he was also Margrave of Antwerp. Early in his rule he came into conflict with Otbert, Bishop of Liège, over the county of Brunengeruz, which Emperor Henry IV allotted to the bishop in 1099.

Godfrey was in favour with the emperor and defended his interests in Lorraine. In 1102 he stopped Count Robert II of Flanders from invading the Cambraisis. After Henry IV died in 1106, his son Henry V, who had been in rebellion, imprisoned the loyal Duke Henry of Lower Lorraine and gave the duchy to Godfrey. The deposed duke escaped and captured Aachen but failed to retake the duchy. In 1114, during a rift between the emperor and Pope Paschal II, Godfrey led a revolt in Germany, and in 1118 he and the emperor were reconciled.

By marrying his daughter Adeliza to Henry I of England, who was also the father-in-law of the emperor, he greatly increased his prestige. After Henry V died in 1125, Godfrey supported Conrad of Hohenstaufen against Lothair of Supplinburg, who was elected. Lothair withdrew Lower Lorraine and granted it to Waleran of Limburg, whom Godfrey fought at the Battle of Wilderen, where Godfrey was defeated. He kept the margraviate of Antwerp and the ducal title, which in 1183 became that of duke of Brabant. After the assassination of Charles the Good in 1127 he intervened in Flanders on behalf of Theodoric of Alsace, who prevailed against William Clito.

Godfrey spent his last years in the abbey of Affligem, died of old age on 25 January 1139 and was buried in the left aisle of the abbey church; a death date of 1140 is an error. He married Ida, a daughter of Count Otto II of Chiny, and had several children, among them Godfrey II of Louvain, who succeeded him, and Adeliza, who after Henry I's death married William d'Aubigny, 1st Earl of Arundel. His second wife, Clementia, widow of Robert II of Flanders, bore him no children. By an unknown mistress he had a son, Joscelin of Louvain, who married Agnes de Percy.
godfrey-iii-count-of-louvain: Godfrey was the son of Count Godfrey II of Louvain and Luitgarde of Sulzbach. Because he succeeded as an infant he was called dux in cunis, the duke in the cradle, and some Brabantian vassals tried to use his minority to make themselves independent of the duke, in what became the Wars of Grimbergen of 1141 to 1159. On 30 March 1147 he was present at Aachen at the coronation of Henry Berengar, son of Conrad III of Germany. When Conrad left on crusade the war began again in 1148, and peace was elusive until the election of Frederick Barbarossa.

In 1158 Godfrey married Margaret of Limburg, daughter of Henry II, Duke of Limburg, uniting two powerful and antagonistic houses of the region. The war with the Berthout ended in 1159 when he burned their castle at Grimbergen. In 1171 he fought Hainaut and was defeated. In 1172 he bought the County of Aarschot from its count, Godfried III, a purchase from which the later dukes of Aarschot descend. In 1179 he married his son Henry to a niece of Philip of Alsace, Count of Flanders.

Between 1182 and 1184 Godfrey went on a campaign to Jerusalem, and in the meantime Barbarossa granted Henry the title of duke of Brabant. By Margaret he had Henry I, Duke of Brabant, and Albert of Louvain, who was elected bishop in 1191 and assassinated at Reims in 1192. His second wife, Imagina of Loon, daughter of Louis I, Count of Loon, bore him William of Louvain, lord of Perwez, and a younger Godfrey, who went to England in 1196 and became seneschal of the Honour of Eye.

Godfrey died in August 1190; the sources give the 10th or the 21st of the month. He left his lands larger than he had received them and had built the fortress of Nedelaer, near Vilvoorde. The ducal title passed to his son Henry at the Diet of Schwäbisch Hall in September 1190.
godfrey-of-bouillon: Godfrey was the second son of Eustace II, Count of Boulogne. His uncle, Godfrey the Hunchback, was murdered on 22 February 1076 without issue, having designated him as heir, and Godfrey became Lord of Bouillon through an inheritance from his mother's family. His claim was challenged by several rivals, among them his aunt Matilda of Tuscany, Albert III of Namur and Count Theoderic of Veluwe. Emperor Henry IV first gave the duchy of Lower Lorraine to his own infant son Conrad. Godfrey supported Henry during the Investiture Controversy and gained Lower Lorraine in 1087.

In 1096 Godfrey joined the First Crusade with his brothers Eustace and Baldwin of Boulogne. He either sold or mortgaged most of his estates to the bishops of Liège and Verdun to raise an army, reportedly 40,000 strong, which set out in August 1096. He reached Constantinople in November and, like most of the crusaders, agreed to a modified oath to Emperor Alexios I Komnenos promising to restore some lands. He took part at Nicaea, Dorylaeum and the Siege of Antioch.

The crusaders reached Jerusalem in June 1099, and the major attack took place on 14 and 15 July. Godfrey and some of his knights were among the first to take the walls. On 22 July a council met in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and after Raymond IV of Toulouse refused the crown, Godfrey agreed to rule, preferring the title Advocate of the Holy Sepulchre to that of king. Its meaning is disputed, since early chroniclers used the term princeps or his old rank of duke, while later ones wrote rex.

Godfrey defeated the Fatimids at the Battle of Ascalon in August 1099 and in 1100 made Acre, Ascalon, Arsuf, Jaffa and Caesarea tributaries. Godfrey died on 18 July 1100. The Arab chronicler Ibn al-Qalanisi reports that an arrow killed him at Acre, but Christian chroniclers say he fell ill at Caesarea, and a disease like typhoid is thought more likely than poison. His supporters seized Jerusalem and his brother Baldwin succeeded him; Dagobert crowned Baldwin as first Latin king on 25 December 1100.

Later accounts idealized him as the crusade's military leader and as a legislator of the assizes of Jerusalem, and in the early 14th century he was chosen as one of the Nine Worthies. In reality he was one of several leaders, and the assizes developed gradually. He was the hero of Torquato Tasso's epic Jerusalem Delivered.
godin-tepe: Godin Tepe lies in the Luristan region, in Kermanshah province, on the left bank of the Gamas Āb river, and its importance may have come from its role as a trading outpost in the early Mesopotamian networks. It was found in a survey in 1961 and excavated from 1965 to 1973 by a Canadian expedition under T. Cuyler Young Jr., sponsored by the Royal Ontario Museum. Because its layers lie so deep, the nearby site of Seh Gabi, 6 km to the northeast, was dug to study the earliest periods.

The site was inhabited by about 5200 BCE. In Level VIII, about 4200–4000 BCE, it lay within growing trade networks in metals and stones such as lapis lazuli from Badakshan. In the late fourth millennium the pottery of Level VI.I shows Uruk influence, with parallels at Susa, Uruk and Nippur, and merchants from Susa may have kept a trading post there. Thirteen seal impressions, two cylinder seals and 38 numerical tablets, mostly accounts, were found. A large Oval Enclosure was burnt about 3000 BCE, its debris full of sling bullets, though one researcher has argued that the enclosure did not exist.

Level IV, about 3000–2650 BCE, probably marks the arrival of people of the Kura–Araxes culture from the north. Level III, from about 2600 BCE, has links with Susa and much of Luristan and may have belonged to the Elamite confederacy. Near 1400 BCE the site was abandoned, and it stayed empty until about 750 BCE.

The new settlers built a fortification wall three metres thick with arrow slits and a hall of 30 wooden columns, 24 by 28 metres inside, which the excavators took for the palace or manor house of a powerful local figure. Its pottery matches Iron Age sites such as Bābā Jān Tepe, Tepe Nush-i Jan and Pasargadae. Godin was abandoned again in the 6th century BCE, perhaps in the face of the expansion of Cyrus the Great, and its last building was an Islamic shrine of about the 15th century.

The mound covers about 15 hectares and rises 30 metres above the plain, its northern end eroded to a cliff. It is divided into a low Outer Town to the south, an Upper Citadel and a Citadel, and has been damaged by gullies, by digging for brick earth and farm soil, by an Islamic cemetery and by a modern road.
godomar-ii: Godomar II, also spelled Gundomar, was a son of King Gundobad of Burgundy and a younger brother of Sigismund. According to Gregory of Tours, Sigismund married a daughter of the Ostrogoth King Theodoric and had a son, Sigeric. After Sigismund remarried, his second wife maltreated and insulted her stepson and persuaded the king that Sigeric planned to kill his father and seize the throne. Sigismund ordered the young man to be taken while drunk and drowned in a well.

The murder of Sigeric in 523 caused tension between the Ostrogoths and the Burgundians, and the sons of Clovis took advantage of it to attack the Burgundian kingdom, which now stood alone. Sigismund and Godomar led the defence but lost. Sigismund, his wife and his two sons were captured through treachery by Clovis's eldest son, Chlodomer, king at Orléans, and executed. Godomar is suspected of having sided with the Franks in this battle. He fled, then rallied the Burgundian army and regained his territory.

Chlodomer, with his brother Theuderic I, king at Metz, marched on Burgundy in 524. On 25 June 524 Godomar led the Burgundians to victory over the Franks at the Battle of Vézeronce, where Chlodomer himself fell. The Franks retreated and gave up the fight for Burgundy for the time being. Three years after Sigismund's death Godomar had his body recovered and buried in the Chapel of St John in the Abbey of Saint-Maurice d'Agaune, the monastery Sigismund had founded.

When the Franks tried again in 532, Godomar could not repel them. The Battle of Autun ended his reign and the kingdom, which the Merovingians incorporated into their realm and divided among themselves in 534. His further fate is not known.
gods-wife-of-amun: A shorter title, God's Wife, was already in use under the Twelfth Dynasty, when it was held by the non-royal women Iy-meret-nebes and Neferu, and as early as the First Intermediate Period there is mention of a Wife of the God in connection with the god Min. The full title of God's Wife of Amun appears only from the Eighteenth Dynasty, whose kings came from Thebes, drove the Hyksos out of Egypt and believed that their local god Amun had guided them to victory.

The first royal woman to hold the new title was Queen Ahmose-Nefertari, wife of Ahmose I, as a stele in the temple of Amun at Karnak records. She passed it to her daughter Ahmose-Meritamun, who handed it to Hatshepsut before Hatshepsut took the throne as pharaoh. Both Ahmose-Nefertari and Hatshepsut sometimes used it in place of the title King's Principal Wife, and Hatshepsut passed it on to her own daughter Neferure.

The title referred to the myth of the king's divine birth, in which his mother was made pregnant by Amun. In practice the pharaoh used the office to secure royal authority over the Theban region and the powerful priesthood of Amun. Scenes in Hatshepsut's Chapelle Rouge show the God's Wife and a male priest in a rite that seems aimed at destroying the names of enemies, and other scenes show her worshipping the gods, being purified in the sacred lake and following the king into the sanctuary, though they say little about her duties.

Under Thutmose III the title passed among his mother, lesser wives and a daughter, and Amenhotep II greatly reduced the power and prestige of the role. It fell out of favour when Amenhotep IV, renamed Akhenaten, raised the Aten above the other gods and suppressed the worship of Amun. Horemheb, the last ruler of the dynasty, restored the priesthood of Amun but appointed its priests from the high ranks of his army. Ramesses VI of the Twentieth Dynasty revived the office for his daughter Iset, adding the title Divine Adoratrice of Amun.

The office reached the height of its political power in the late Third Intermediate Period, when Shepenupet I, daughter of Osorkon III, held it at Thebes. The Nubian king Kashta had his daughter Amenirdis appointed as her successor, and her tomb at Medinet Habu shows the standing of the post. The office lasted until 525 BCE under Ankhnesneferibre, successor of Nitocris, when the Persian Empire overthrew Psamtik III, the last Saite ruler, and enslaved his daughter. It was not recreated when Egypt later regained its independence from Persia.
godwin-earl-of-wessex: Godwin's father was probably Wulfnoth Cild, a thegn of Sussex whose origin is unknown. In 1009 Wulfnoth was accused of unknown crimes at a muster of the fleet of Æthelred the Unready and fled with twenty ships; the ships sent to pursue him were destroyed in a storm. Godwin was probably an adherent of Æthelred's eldest son Æthelstan, who left him an estate at Compton, Sussex. After Cnut seized the throne in 1016, Godwin's rise was rapid. By 1018 he was an earl, probably of eastern Wessex, and by about 1020 of all Wessex. He accompanied Cnut on an expedition to Denmark between 1019 and 1023, distinguished himself there, and married Gytha, sister of the Danish earl Ulf.

When Cnut died in 1035, England was disputed between Harold Harefoot and Harthacnut, and Godwin supported Harthacnut. In 1036 Alfred Ætheling, younger son of Emma of Normandy and Æthelred, attempted an invasion of England; Godwin intercepted him and handed him to Harold Harefoot. Alfred was blinded and died soon afterwards. Godwin's responsibility was disputed, but the affair left a stain that affected his future. He almost certainly supported Harold's recognition as king in 1037, backed Harthacnut's accession in 1040 and, after 1042, supported Edward the Confessor.

Soon after Edward became king he extended Godwin's jurisdiction to include Kent, and in January 1045 Godwin secured his daughter Edith's marriage to the king. Godwin led opposition as Edward drew advisers from a Normano-French circle. After a violent clash between the people of Dover and Eustace II, Count of Boulogne, Godwin refused the king's order to punish Dover. Edward and Godwin raised armies, and an agreement was reached to bring the case before a court in London. Losing support, Godwin and his family fled, he himself to Flanders and his sons Leofwine and Harold to Dublin. They returned in spring 1052 with armed forces and the support of the navy, burghers and peasants, which compelled Edward to restore the earldom.

Godwin died on 15 April 1053, days after collapsing at a royal banquet at Winchester; contemporary accounts suggest a sudden illness, possibly a stroke. A later story by Aelred of Rievaulx, which appears to be Norman propaganda, has him choking on a crust after swearing he was innocent of Alfred's death. His son Harold succeeded him as Earl of Wessex, and Godwin's other sons held the earldoms of Northumbria, East Anglia and Kent. Harold became king in 1066 but was overthrown and killed in the Norman Conquest.
goguryeo-sui-war: The Sui dynasty reunited China in 589 by defeating the Chen dynasty and then claimed to be overlord of its neighbours. King Pyeongwon of Goguryeo and his successor, Yeongyang, insisted on an equal relationship, and Goguryeo kept raiding the Sui frontier. In 596, after Sui envoys saw Goguryeo diplomats in the yurt of the Eastern Turkic Khaganate, Emperor Wen of Sui demanded that Goguryeo give up any alliance with the Turks, stop its raids and accept Sui as overlord. In 597 Yeongyang answered with a pre-emptive attack, together with the Malgal, on the border in present-day Hebei.

In 598 Emperor Wen sent his youngest son, Yang Liang, and Admiral Zhou Luohou with 300,000 men by land and sea. Heavy rain, disease and constant attacks wore down the army, and the fleet lost many ships to rough seas and to Goguryeo raids whenever it anchored.

Emperor Yang, who had built the Grand Canal after taking the throne in 604, assembled a far larger army; the Book of Sui counts 1,133,800 troops, though Tang historians may have exaggerated its size and losses. In 612 it crossed the Liao River on extended bridges, but Yodong and the other fortresses held, partly because the emperor required his generals to refer every decision, even a surrender, to him. A naval force under Lai Huni was ambushed by 500 Goguryeo troops while looting an outer castle of Pyongyang, and its 40,000 men were reduced to a few thousand.

The land army under Yu Zhongwen and Yuwen Shu ran short of food. The Goguryeo commander Ŭlchi Mundŏk drew it south with feigned retreats to within about 20 km of the capital, then offered terms. As it withdrew he attacked it at the Salsu, thought to be the Chongchon River, and of the 305,000 men who had crossed the Liao only 2,700 returned. A campaign in 613 was broken off when Yang Xuangan rebelled, and in 614 Emperor Yang accepted Yeongyang's offer of peace and the return of the fugitive Husi Zheng.

Yeongyang never came to swear allegiance, and Emperor Yang was dissuaded only with difficulty from another invasion. The losses in men and resources cost the dynasty the trust of its people, and peasants, soldiers, aristocrats and officers rose against it. Yang moved his capital south to Yangzhou, where Yuwen Huaji, a son of Yuwen Shu, led a coup and killed him, and the Duke of Tang proclaimed a new dynasty.
goi-of-baekje: Goi is recorded as the second son of the fourth king, Gaeru, and the younger brother of the fifth, Chogo. When the sixth king, Gusu, died, his eldest son Saban took the throne but proved too young to rule, and Goi dethroned him. Because of the gaps in time, the recorded descent is disputed, and many believe his father was a collateral relative of Gaeru. Some scholars place him in the Utae–Biryu lineage rather than among the descendants of Onjo, and some identify him with Gutae, whom the Chinese Book of Zhou and Book of Sui name as the founder of Baekje.

On taking the throne Goi set up a central military office to curb the independence of the regional clans. In 260, according to the Samguk sagi, he created six ministers called jwapyeong, among them a Minister of the Interior, to which he appointed his younger brother Usu, and ruled that the first six ranks wear purple with silver flowers on their crowns. In 262 he decreed that officials who took bribes or stole must repay three times the amount and be imprisoned for life. He also ordered rice fields to be made from the marshes south of the capital.

Under Goi, Baekje extended its control of the Han River region and gained lasting ascendancy over the remaining states of the Mahan confederacy. In 246, by both the Samguk sagi and the Chinese Sanguozhi, Baekje attacked the commanderies of Daifang and Lelang during a war of Cao Wei against Goguryeo, and Daifang's governor Gong Zun was killed; fearing a counterattack, Goi returned his captives and sued for peace. He also attacked Silla repeatedly, in 266 at Bongsan Fortress, where its master Jikseon routed his troops, and again in 272 and 278.

In the spring of 286 Goi sent envoys to Silla to sue for peace, and he died in the eleventh month of that winter. He was succeeded by his eldest son, Chaekgye, the ninth king. His queen is recorded as a daughter of Gongsun Du, commander of Daifang Commandery. Historians generally credit him with centralising the kingdom and concentrating royal power, though the full system of offices may have been completed after his reign.
goiania: Goiania lies in the cerrado, a landscape of savanna crossed by gallery forests and stream valleys, on mostly flat land along the Meia Ponte River. It covers about 739 square kilometres and lies about 200 kilometres from Brasilia. The climate is tropical wet and dry, with a wet season from October to April and a dry one from May to September, and annual rainfall of around 1,300 millimetres.

The first state capital, Vila Boa, today the City of Goias, was chosen when the economy rested on gold. When cattle-raising and agriculture came to dominate, it was considered remote. Plans to move the capital were put forward in 1753 by Marcos de Noronha, who favoured Pirenopolis, and in 1863 by Jose Vieira Couto de Magalhaes, who proposed the Araguaia river. In 1891 the constitutional delegates included a transfer in the constitution, which was ratified in 1898 and again in 1918.

The idea became reality under Pedro Ludovico, appointed governor after the military revolt of 1930. A commission created in 1932 chose the municipality of Campinas, whose mayor Andrelino Rodrigues de Moraes donated about 242 acres of land. The city was founded on 24 October 1933 and planned for 50,000 people, with streets radiating like spokes from the Praca Civica, where the state and municipal governments were to sit. A local newspaper held a contest for the name in 1933, and Ludovico first used Goiania in 1935 in the decree creating the municipality. A decree of 1937 transferred the capital from the City of Goias, and the official inauguration took place in 1942 with the president of the republic present.

The first buildings, designed by Attilio Correia Lima, were inspired by art deco, and 22 of them are listed as National Heritage. On 13 September 1987 a radiotherapy source containing caesium-137 was stolen from an abandoned hospital. People attracted by its bluish glow took grains of the salt home, and four people died, with many more suffering radiation poisoning. Several city blocks had to be demolished.

Goiania is the capital and largest city of Goias, with 1,536,097 inhabitants and a metropolitan area of 2,890,418. It is the second most populous city of the Central-West Region after Brasilia. Its economy grew from agriculture in and around the city, and it is also a regional centre of industry and medicine. It has many parks, among them the Bosque dos Buritis and the Vaca Brava Park,. Goias is regarded as the cradle of sertanejo, a country music genre.
gojong-of-korea: Gojong was born into a distant branch of the royal House of Yi, a descendant of Grand Prince Inpyeong, the third son of King Injo. When King Cheoljong died without a son, the influential Andong Kim clan nominated him as the next king, and he was crowned on 13 December 1863. Queen Sinjeong acted as regent, assisted by his father, Heungseon Daewongun, who remained the dominant figure at court. The Daewongun was the chief proponent of isolationism and persecuted native and foreign Catholics, a policy that led to French and United States expeditions to Korea in 1866 and 1871. Gojong announced his direct rule in 1873, and after the Daewongun's retirement in November 1874 Queen Min and the Yeoheung Min clan controlled the court.

The Treaty of Ganghwa of 1876 was the first unequal treaty Korea signed with a foreign country. It gave Japanese citizens extraterritorial rights and opened the ports of Busan, Chemulpo (Incheon) and Wonsan to trade. In the Imo Incident of 1882, soldiers of the old army, unpaid for 13 months, rioted, and Queen Min asked the Qing Empire for help; about 3,000 Qing soldiers came to Seoul. The Kapsin Coup of December 1884 failed after three days. In 1895 Japanese agents, in a plot organised by the Japanese minister Miura Gorō, killed Queen Min in Gyeongbokgung. In February 1896 Gojong fled to the Russian legation in Seoul and governed from there for about a year.

On 13 October 1897 he proclaimed himself emperor of the Great Korean Empire at the altar of Hwangudan, with the era name Gwangmu, a gesture marking the end of Qing suzerainty. The constitution of 17 August 1899 granted him absolute power. His reforms improved the military, industry and education to some degree, and in 1898 he abolished the Independence Club. After Japan's victory in the Russo-Japanese War, Korea lost its diplomatic sovereignty in the Japan–Korea Treaty of 1905. Gojong refused to sign it and appealed to other powers, including a letter to President Theodore Roosevelt, but without result.

Gojong was forced to abdicate on 20 July 1907, and his son Sunjong replaced him. He was confined to Deoksugung and made several attempts to escape, in 1910, 1915 and 1918, all unsuccessful. Korea was formally annexed by Japan on 22 August 1910, and Gojong received the title King Emeritus Yi of Deoksu. He died suddenly at Deoksugung on 21 January 1919, aged 66. The official cause was a cerebral haemorrhage, but suspicion that Japan had poisoned him arose around the time of his death and persists. His death and funeral were a catalyst for the March First Movement. He is buried with his wife at Hongneung in Namyangju, part of the Royal Tombs of the Joseon dynasty, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
gokstad-ship: The mound at Gokstad farm had long been called Gokstadhaugen or Kongshaugen, the king's mound, a name dismissed as folklore because other sites in Norway bear similar names. In 1880 the sons of the farm's owner, who knew the legends, dug into the still frozen ground and uncovered the bow of a boat. Nicolay Nicolaysen, president of the Society for the Preservation of Ancient Norwegian Monuments, reached the site in February 1880, had the digging stopped, and later excavated the mound from the side. Though ploughing had lowered it to 5 metres, it still measured 50 by 43 metres.

The ship is clinker-built, mostly of oak, and was meant for war, trade and carrying people and cargo. Each side has 16 tapered planks fixed with iron rivets above the waterline, while the lowest nine are thinner and tied to the frames with withies, which made the bottom light and flexible. The stem is carved from a single curved oak log, and a quarter rudder fastened to a block on the hull could be raised quickly in shallow water.

Its square sail of about 110 square metres may have driven it at over 12 knots, and the mast could be lowered. Tree-ring dating puts the felling of its timber around 890, at the height of Norse expansion in Dublin and York and in the reign of King Harald Fairhair.

A timber burial chamber held the skeleton of a man of forty to fifty years, strongly built and 181 to 183 cm tall, on a bed. Twelve horses, six dogs and a peacock lay around him, and the grave also held three small boats, a tent, a sledge and riding equipment. No gold, silver or weapons were found, as the grave had probably been plundered in ancient times. In the 1920s Professor Anton Willem Brogger of the University of Oslo identified the man as King Olaf Gudrodson of Vestfold, but this has not been proven.

The ship, the rebuilt chamber, two of the small boats and other surviving finds are shown in the Viking Ship Museum on the Bygdøy peninsula in Oslo. The replica Viking, which sailed from Bergen to the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, was reported by its captain, Magnus Andersen, to reach about 10 or 11 knots. Later copies include the Gaia, sailed to North America in 1991.
gol-gumbaz: Mohammed Adil Shah came to the throne of Bijapur in 1627, succeeding his father Ibrahim Adil Shah II, who had commissioned the Ibrahim Rauza. Mohammed intended his own tomb to surpass his father's in size and scale. He brought architects and engineers from different regions of the subcontinent and hired local labourers for the decoration. The building went up in three stages: the foundation and a raised platform, then the four basalt walls joined by octagonal corner towers, and finally the brick and lime-mortar dome.

No contemporary inscription names the chief architect, though historians have speculated that Malik Yaqut, an Abyssinian slave architect, played a significant part. Soil from the shrine of Husayn ibn Ali at Karbala was placed in the central vault. Building continued until the sultan's death in 1656, when the inner walls were still being plastered.

The name means Round Dome. The mausoleum is built of dark grey basalt and decorated plaster, and combines Persian, Mughal and local features. Its plan is simple: a cube 62 metres wide including the corner towers, each of seven floors and capped by a small dome. The great hall inside is a single chamber about 41 metres across and 54 metres high.

The dome measures 44 metres outside and about 38 metres inside. Unlike the domes of the Pantheon or St Paul's Cathedral it uses no metal tension rings, resting instead on pendentives formed by eight intersecting arches, a system generally traced to Central Asia. Six cenotaphs stand on a platform in the hall, for the sultan, two wives, a mistress, a daughter and a grandson, above the real tombs in a crypt. A gallery round the dome's base carries a whisper to the opposite side, and in 1945 S. S. Reuben recorded a handclap giving up to 14 echoes.

After the Mughal conquest of Bijapur in 1686 the complex was largely abandoned. In 1891 the archaeologist Henry Cousens surveyed it and described the dome as among the largest the world has seen. A museum opened in the old drum house in 1892, and the Archaeological Survey of India took charge of the site in 1962. Since 2014 the monument has been part of a group of Deccan Sultanate sites on UNESCO's tentative list.
golan-heights: The Golan is a basaltic plateau at the south-western corner of Syria, generally bounded by the Jordan Valley on the west, the Yarmouk River on the south and the Sa'ar stream on the north, with its eastern limit at the Ruqqad or the Allan river. It is about 65 km long and 12 to 25 km wide and overlooks the Jordan Rift Valley and the Sea of Galilee. Volcanic eruptions that began about 4 million years ago formed it, and dormant volcanoes and cinder cones are scattered across it. The snow of Mount Hermon, 2,814 m high, feeds springs and rivers in the Jordan watershed.

The earliest evidence of habitation dates to the Upper Paleolithic, and settlement grew from the 2nd millennium BCE. After the Late Bronze Age collapse the kingdom of Geshur emerged; the Hebrew Bible describes David's marriage to Maacha, daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur, as a dynastic alliance. By the mid-9th century BCE Aram-Damascus had absorbed Geshur, and the Assyrians conquered the region in the 8th century BCE. Gaulanitis, the Greek name for the region, appears after Alexander the Great's conquest, under Ptolemaic and then Seleucid rule. In the middle of the 2nd century BCE the Itureans moved in, and the Roman and Byzantine periods left Diocletianic boundary stones and 25 ancient synagogues.

After the Battle of Yarmouk the Golan came under Muawiyah I, the future first Umayyad caliph, and then passed from the Abbasids to the Fatimids and the Seljuk Turks. Crusader forces held Banias in 1128–32 and 1140–64, and the Ayyubids under Saladin later ruled the area. The Mongols swept through in 1259 and were driven off by Qutuz at Ain Jalut in 1260. In the 1560s the Ottoman official Mustafa Lala Pasha made al-Qunaytira a regional centre.

When the French mandate ended in 1946 the Golan became part of the independent Syrian Arab Republic. Israeli forces captured the plateau on 9–10 June 1967 in the Six-Day War, and an estimated 80,000 to 130,000 people fled or were driven out. After the 1973 war a third of the plateau returned to Syrian administration. In 1981 the Knesset passed the Golan Heights Law applying Israeli law there, which the UN Security Council condemned in Resolution 497.
golasecca-culture: The Golasecca culture grew by cultural continuity out of the earlier Canegrate culture, which emerged around the 13th century BCE with strong links to the Central European Urnfield tradition, and it is seen as an early western example of the wider Hallstatt movement. Its remains are spread over about 20,000 km2 south of the Alps, between the rivers Po, Serio and Sesia, in western Lombardy, eastern Piedmont, Canton Ticino and Val Mesolcina.

The first finds were made from 1822 by the abbot Giovanni Battista Giani, who took the graves for remains of the Battle of Ticinus of 218 BCE. In 1865 Gabriel de Mortillet assigned them to a pre-Roman culture of the early Iron Age, and the Archaeological Congress of Stockholm in 1874 divided it into three periods. Modern study rests on A. Mira Bonomi's excavations at Monsorino in 1965–69.

Early houses were circular wooden buildings along the edge of the river floodplain, each on a low stone base around a central hearth, with floors of river pebbles set in clay. People kept goats, sheep, pigs, cattle and horses, grew some legumes and cereals and gathered nuts and fruit. Pottery was shaped by hand without a wheel. Unlike the Este and Villanova cultures, Golasecca had a large warrior class, shown by the chariots and weapons in the tombs of leaders at Sesto Calende and the four-wheeled wagon at Ca' Morta near Como.

The culture is best known for its burials. An apparent ancestor cult kept the cemeteries untouched by farming; burials were by direct inhumation or in lidded cists, and cremation, with ashes and bones placed in terracotta jars, persisted into the second period. Urns were painted, and the bronzes buried with the dead are mostly pins, fibulas, armbands and necklaces. A tomb at Pombia holds the oldest known remains of beer made with hops.

The site of Golasecca, where the Ticino leaves Lake Maggiore, was well placed for long-distance exchange, and its people acted as intermediaries between the Etruscans and the Hallstatt culture of Austria in the salt trade. The trade later reached the Greek world, bringing oil, wine, Attic pottery, incense and coral, and the north, source of tin and Baltic amber. The culture flourished most in its second period, from the 6th to the early 5th century BCE; its third period shows growing Celtic influence until the Gallic conquests of the 4th century BCE, after which it was finally absorbed into the hegemony of the Roman Republic.
golconda-fort: Golconda, also called Muhammadnagar, is a fortified citadel and ruined city on the western outskirts of Hyderabad in Telangana. The name is thought to come from the Telugu Gollakonda, meaning Shepherd's hill. Its fortifications include four distinct forts within an outer wall with 87 semicircular bastions, eight gateways and four drawbridges, with royal apartments, halls, temples, mosques, magazines and stables inside. The outermost enclosure is entered by the Fateh Darwaza, the Victory gate, so called because Aurangzeb's army marched in through it. A hand clap beneath the dome there can be heard at the Bala Hisar pavilion, the highest point, almost a kilometre away.

The fort began as a small mud fort that tradition ascribes to the Kakatiya ruler Pratāparudra, and it is also thought that the Kakatiya ruler Ganapati built a stone hilltop outpost there to defend the western region. It was made over to the Bahmani Kingdom by sanad from the Rajah of Warangal, and under the Bahmani Kingdom it slowly rose to prominence. Quli Qutb Shah, sent by the Bahmanids as governor, made the city his seat around 1501 and formally became independent in 1518, founding the Sultanate of Golconda. Over 62 years the first three Qutb Shahi sultans turned the mud fort into a massive granite fortification. It remained the dynasty's capital until 1590, when the capital moved to Hyderabad.

Golconda flourished as a trade centre of large diamonds from the nearby mines, especially the Kollur Mine, and the diamonds believed to have come from its mines include the Koh-i-Noor and the Hope Diamond. In the early seventeenth century it also had a strong cotton-weaving industry, exporting muslin and calico to Persia and Europe and printed cloth to Java and Sumatra. In January 1687 Aurangzeb besieged the fort. After eight months it fell, the Qutb Shahi reign ended and the last king, Abul Hasan Qutb Shah, was taken captive.

The fort is listed by the Archaeological Survey of India. Inside stand the Jagdamba temple, visited by many Hindu devotees during the Bonalu festival, and the Taramati mosque. About a kilometre north of the outer wall are the Qutb Shahi tombs, in Indo-Islamic style within gardens. The fort, the Charminar and the tombs were submitted to UNESCO in 2010 and are on India's tentative list. The Golconda Artillery Centre of the Indian Army, raised in 1962, lies in and around the fort. In the Renaissance and early modern periods the name Golconda became a byword for vast wealth.
golden-bull-of-1222: The Golden Bull was issued at the diet of Fehérvár in the spring of 1222, one of several charters of the 13th century that sought to constrain royal power. Peter II of Aragon had planned concessions in 1205, Simon de Montfort issued the Statute of Pamiers in 1212 and King John of England granted Magna Carta in 1215. Historian James Clarke Holt holds that there is no need to assume the authors borrowed from each other, since such charters embodied the natural reaction of feudal societies to monarchical importunity.

Andrew II, king from 1205, gave large royal domains in the central regions to his supporters, a policy known as novae institutiones, the new arrangements. They cut the revenues of the ispans of the counties and of the crown, and he introduced new taxes. A group of dignitaries tried to dethrone him in 1209, and the discontented gathered at the court of his son Béla. The circumstances of 1222 are uncertain because few sources survive, but discontented noblemen seem to have staged a coup that spring.

The Bull was drafted by Cletus Bél, royal chancellor and provost of Eger. More than a third of its articles dealt with the grievances of the royal servants. It limited the judicial power of the ispans on their estates and exempted them from following the king on military expeditions abroad. Nobles were exempted from taxes unless their courts agreed, and if a nobleman died without a male heir, his daughter received a quarter of his possessions. Nobles need not go to war outside the kingdom unless paid, but all had to serve against an invading army.

Foreigners could not receive honours and offices without the Royal Council's approval, and no title or public office could be inherited. Treasury officials, collectors of the salt tax and toll-keepers had to be noblemen of the kingdom, neither Ismaelite nor Jews. The final clause gave the bishops, retainers and nobles the right to resist and speak against the king and his successors, without the taint of infidelity, should they break the settlement.

Seven copies were made, each sealed with the golden seal: for the Pope, the Knights of Saint John, the Knights Templar, the king, the Archbishop of Esztergom, the Archbishop of Kalocsa and the palatine. The Bull is regarded as one of the first constitutional limits placed on a European monarch and as the first constitutional document of Hungary, and it is often compared to Magna Carta. In a bull of 15 December 1222 Pope Honorius III described a king confused by the demands of an unruly crowd.
golden-bull-of-1356: The Golden Bull was a decree of the Imperial Diet at Nuremberg and Metz, headed by Emperor Charles IV, which fixed important parts of the constitution of the Holy Roman Empire for more than four hundred years. It was named for the golden seal it carried. The election of the King of the Romans by the chief ecclesiastical and secular princes was already established, but disputes over the process and papal involvement had caused controversy, most recently in 1314, when Louis of Bavaria and Frederick of Austria were elected by opposing sets of electors. Louis had tried to clarify matters in the Declaration of Rhense of 1338, which renounced papal involvement and limited the choice of a king to the prince-electors.

The Bull named the seven prince-electors and set out their largely ceremonial court offices. For the first time in the Empire it stated the principle of majority voting: four of seven votes sufficed to elect a king. The electoral principalities were declared indivisible and their succession regulated, and the electors received a number of privileges. The Bull also regulated the election in detail. It was to be held in Frankfurt, the coronation in Aachen and the first diet of a reign in Nuremberg, and electors who had not agreed within thirty days of taking their oath were to live on bread and water. Chapter 15 outlawed conspiracies and confederations, which meant the city leagues, and most of them were dissolved.

The Bull fixed the electoral vote on the Palatinate branch of the Wittelsbachs rather than on Bavaria, partly because Louis IV was of that branch, and Louis's sons protested. The Habsburgs, rivals of the House of Luxembourg, were left out altogether, and Duke Rudolf IV of Austria had the Privilegium Maius forged in retaliation. The Habsburgs held no electoral vote until they gained Bohemia in 1526. The Bull made no mention of papal confirmation of an election, and Pope Innocent VI did not protest because he needed Charles's support against the Visconti. It also helped the growth of largely independent states in the Empire, a process completed only centuries later. The Golden Bull was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in June 2013.
golden-bull-of-rimini: From 1209 the Piast duke Konrad I of Masovia campaigned against the pagan Old Prussians, and in 1217 Pope Honorius III allowed Bishop Christian of Oliva to treat these conquests as the Prussian Crusade. Konrad's attempt in 1222/23 to subdue the Culmer Land east of the Vistula, backed by his cousins Leszek I the White and Henry I the Bearded, met relentless Prussian counter-attacks, and the Order of Dobrzyń, founded by Bishop Christian, was too weak to hold them. When the Prussians attacked his residence at Płock Castle, Konrad opened talks with the Teutonic Order in 1226.

The Order, under Grand Master Herman of Salza, had served in the Burzenland of Transylvania since 1211, until King Andrew II of Hungary expelled it in 1225 for trying to set up an autonomous principality. Salza would now go to Prussia only once the emperor had confirmed the Order's claims.

The decree recounts that Konrad, Duke of Masovia and of Kujawy, had promised the Master and his brethren the Chełmno Land and land between his border and the Prussians, so that they might undertake the invasion of Prussia. Declaring the land to be under the sole rule of the Empire, Frederick II granted the land of Prussia to the Master, the forces of his order and all who joined the invasion. Many princes signed it, among them the dukes of Saxony and Spoleto. The historian Tomasz Jasiński holds that it was backdated and in fact issued in 1235.

The bull is the first of three documents behind the Order's claims. By the Treaty of Kruszwica, said to have been signed on 16 June 1230 and known only from later references, Konrad ceded the Chełmno Land and all conquests in Prussia; the historian Max Perlbach held that the Order forged it. In 1234 Pope Gregory IX's Golden Bull of Rieti confirmed the earlier agreements and the Order's absolute ownership of the Chełmno Land and its Prussian conquests, which were to be no one's fief. Pope Alexander IV confirmed it again in 1257.
golden-bull-of-sicily: Bohemian rulers had been made kings before, but not for good. Emperor Henry IV raised the Přemyslid duke Vratislaus II to kingship at the diet of Mainz in 1085, but after his death in 1092 his brother Conrad I ruled again as duke. Emperor Frederick Barbarossa gave the title in 1158 to Vladislaus II, who had joined his Italian campaign against Milan, but Vladislaus could not secure the succession of his eldest son, Frederick.

In 1198 Frederick's half-brother Ottokar I exploited the rivalry between the two men elected King of the Romans, Otto IV of the House of Welf and the Hohenstaufen Philip of Swabia. Philip gave him a hereditary royal title for his support, and Ottokar won recognition from Otto IV and Pope Innocent III as well. After Philip's assassination and the papal ban on Otto IV in 1210, Ottokar changed sides again: in 1211 he and several princes met at Nuremberg and elected the young Frederick II as alium imperatorem, the other emperor. On his way to Germany Frederick issued the bull at Basel on 26 September 1212.

The bull made Bohemia and Moravia an autonomous and indivisible part of the Holy Roman Empire. The Bohemian king was no longer appointed by the emperor and had to attend only those imperial diets held near the Bohemian border. He was to be the premier prince-elector of the Empire and to provide every future emperor with a bodyguard of 300 knights for his journey to Rome to be crowned. Frederick also declared that he and the Empire would grant the investiture of Bohemia only to a ruler approved by the people of the country.

The kingship gave Bohemia an exceptional place within the Empire. When Charles IV held both Bohemia and Germany in 1346, he established the Crown of Bohemia, whose lands remained outside the Empire's suzerainty and were not counted as Imperial States. For the 800th anniversary of its signing, the document was shown to the public at the National Archive for four days in September 2012.
golden-gate-kyiv: The Golden Gate was the main gate in the 11th-century fortifications of Kyiv, the capital of the Kievan Rus', and one of three built by Yaroslav the Wise, at about the time of the Saint Sophia Cathedral. It was first called the Southern Gate, one of three main entrances to the walled city beside the Ladski and Zhydivski gates, which have not survived. The stone fortifications ran for only 3.5 kilometres. The name was probably given in imitation of the Golden Gate of Constantinople.

Once the Church of the Annunciation, or Blahovist Church, was built beside it, its golden domes were a landmark seen from outside the city, and the gate took the name Golden. Its passage was about 12 metres high and 6 metres wide.

For almost five hundred years the gate served as Kyiv's triumphal arch and a symbol of the city. A church over the passage, mentioned in the chronicle and in Metropolitan Ilarion's Word of Law and Grace, was meant to give the city heavenly protection and was also a place of worship. In 1240 Batu Khan's Golden Horde partly destroyed the gate, which remained in use for ceremonies into the 18th century while gradually falling into ruin. A gate in Vladimir, where Andrei I Bogolyubsky founded his own state, was later given a similar name. In 1832 Metropolitan Eugenius had the ruins excavated and surveyed, and works in the 1970s added a pavilion housing a museum.

Only two wall segments of the original, 24 and 13 metres long, of Roman brick and stone, survive. No images of the original gate survive either. The Soviet authorities rebuilt it completely in 1982, for the 1500th anniversary of Kyiv, a decision that has been intensely controversial because many competing reconstructions had been proposed.

Some art historians called for the reconstruction to be demolished so that the ruins could be seen. The medieval sections are protected as a monument of national significance, while the reconstructed outer parts are not listed. Inside is a branch of the museum Sophia of Kyiv, and a monument to Yaroslav the Wise stands beside it since 1997.
golden-horn: The Golden Horn, Altın Boynuz or Haliç in Turkish, is the estuary of the Alibey and Kağıthane Creeks. It is 7.5 kilometres long and 750 metres across at its widest, and about 35 metres deep where it flows into the Bosphorus. Its waters mark the northern boundary of the peninsula of old Istanbul, the ancient Byzantium and Constantinople, and separate the historic centre from the rest of the city. Its name is understood to refer to its horn-shaped outline. Historians think that the word golden refers either to the riches brought in through its harbour or to the yellow light on the water at sunset. The Turkish name means estuary and derives from the Arabic khaleej, a gulf.

Archaeological finds show a significant urban presence around the Golden Horn from at least the 7th century BCE, with smaller settlements back to 6700 BCE, from ancient ports and ships found during construction of the Yenikapı subway station and the Marmaray tunnel. The deep harbour was an economic and military asset, and Constantine I founded Nova Roma, later Constantinople, on the existing city of Byzantium for the same reason. The Eastern Roman Empire kept its naval headquarters there, and walls were built along the shore against attack from the sea.

A large chain was drawn across the entrance from Constantinople to the old tower of Galata, called the Megàlos Pyrgos by the Byzantines. It was broken or circumvented three times. In the 10th century the Kievan Rus' dragged their longships around Galata and relaunched them in the Horn, and the Byzantines defeated them with Greek fire. In 1204, during the Fourth Crusade, Venetian ships broke the chain with a ram, and the Latin Crusaders largely destroyed the tower. In 1453 Sultan Mehmed II, having failed to break the chain by force, towed his ships over greased logs past Galata into the estuary. The Genoese built a new tower in 1348, now the Galata Tower.

After the conquest of 1453 Mehmed II resettled Greeks in the Phanar, today's Fener. Balat had been inhabited by Jews in the Byzantine age, and Bayezid II invited the Jews expelled from Spain to settle there. In 1502 Leonardo da Vinci drew a single-span bridge of 240 metres over the Horn for Bayezid II, which was never built. Mehmed II founded the Haliç Shipyard in 1455, which worked into the 1960s.

Both shores of the Golden Horn are now settled, with parks, museums, university campuses, naval facilities and Muslim, Jewish and Christian cemeteries. The inlet is crossed by bridges including the Galata Bridge and the Atatürk Bridge, and ferries link its suburbs. Industrial waste polluted it until the 1980s, and it was later cleaned in two phases.
golden-madonna-of-essen: The statue is 74 cm high and 27 cm wide at the base. Mary sits on a stool, holding up a globe with her thumb and two fingers and supporting on her lap an oversized Christ child in a pontifical gown, who presses a book to his chest. The gold leaves, less than 0.25 mm thick, are held by tiny golden bolts, and the eyes are of cloisonné enamel. The child's silver hand was added in the 14th century. Its maker is unknown, but the folds of the gown resemble those of the Cross of Otto and Mathilde of 982, which points to Cologne rather than Hildesheim.

Scholars read the orb as an apple of salvation, making Mary the New Eve, or as a sign of power over the world held for her son. In the second reading the statue may reflect the regency of Theophanu for the young Otto III after Otto II died in 983, and Theophanu may have given it to the abbey.

The statue was probably kept out of sight in the treasury and brought out for processions. The Liber Ordinarius of 1370, its first documented mention, describes a liturgy built around it. On the Purification of the Virgin the youngest canon carried it under his cloak to St Gertrude's church, and the next morning it was borne back to the cathedral, unveiled and crowned with Otto III's child's crown. These processions ended in 1561, when the Reformation reached the town. Cardinal Franz Hengsbach, Essen's first bishop, revived the crowning in 1978, but it stopped in 2000 on the restorers' advice.

In the Thirty Years' War Abbess Maria Clara von Spaur took the treasure to Cologne in 1634, and in 1794 the statue was hidden at Steele from the French revolutionary army.
