After unrest in the Ruhr in 1920 an Aachen goldsmith hid it somewhere in the Diocese of Hildesheim until 1925, and in the Second World War American troops found it in a shelter at Siegen.

Restorations in 1905, after the Second World War and in 2004 dealt with woodworm and loosened gold leaves. Pope John XXIII named the image Our Lady of Good Counsel and patroness of the Diocese of Essen on 8 July 1959, and since then it has stood in a climate-controlled case in the cathedral's northern side chapel.
golden-stool: Its full name is Sika Dwa Kofi, the Golden Stool born on a Friday. In tradition Okomfo Anokye, high priest and one of the two chief founders of the Asante Confederacy, made it descend from the sky onto the lap of the first king, Osei Tutu. Stools were customary signs of a chief's leadership, and the Golden Stool is held to house the spirit of the Asante nation, living, dead and yet to be born.

It is a curved seat 46 cm high, with a platform 61 cm wide and 30 cm deep. Like other Asante stools it is carved from a single block of Alstonia boonei, a tall forest tree with numinous associations, and its whole surface is inlaid with gold and hung with bells to warn the king of danger. Few have seen it, and only the king, the queen and trusted advisers know where it is kept.

A stool is understood as the seat of its owner's soul. The Golden Stool must never touch the ground and rests on a blanket. It is carried to the king on a pillow, since only the Asantehene may handle it, and at his inauguration a new king is raised and lowered over it without touching it. On solemn occasions it stands at the king's left on a throne of its own, the hwedom dwa. Replicas made for chiefs are blackened with animal blood at their funerals.

Many wars have been fought over the throne. In 1896 Asantehene Prempeh I accepted deportation rather than risk losing both a war and the stool. Sir Frederick Hodgson, Governor of the Gold Coast, demanded the right to sit on it and ordered a search, and the war that followed ended with the annexation of Ashanti to the British Empire but left the stool untouched.

In 1921 African road workers found it and stripped some of its gold ornaments; tried by local custom, they were sentenced to death, but the British intervened and they were banished instead. After a British assurance of non-interference the stool came out of hiding, and in 1935 it was used to crown Osei Tutu Agyeman Prempeh II.
golden-temple: The Golden Temple, or Harmandir Sahib, stands in Amritsar and is the pre-eminent spiritual site of Sikhism. Guru Ram Das acquired the land for the site, by one account buying it from the village of Tung, by another receiving it as a gift from Emperor Akbar. The pool on the site was completed by Ram Das in 1577, and Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, finished the construction. In 1604 Arjan placed a copy of the Adi Granth in the temple.

The early history is hard to reconstruct for lack of records. The few Persian sources are biased, and the Sikh sources are reverential. Guru Arjan was arrested on the orders of the Mughal emperor Jahangir and executed in 1606. The shrine was repeatedly destroyed by Mughal and Afghan armies and rebuilt by the Sikhs.

The complex centres on the sanctum and the Amrit Sarovar, the pool of nectar, which is about 150 metres square, with the shrine in its middle reached by a causeway. The plan is square with four entrances, which Sikhs take to symbolise the welcome of people of all castes and ethnicities. It is entered by descending rather than ascending. Its architecture shows both Hindu and Islamic influences.

Ranjit Singh took Amritsar in 1802 and announced that he would rebuild the temple in marble and gold; he added marble flooring and the gilding. This is the origin of the name Golden Temple. In front of the sanctum stands the Akal Takht, founded by Guru Hargobind after his father's death, the chief of the five Sikh seats of authority. A langar, a free kitchen, serves vegetarian meals to visitors of every faith.

The complex is understood as the principal shrine and headquarters of Sikhism, and an exception is made to Sikhism's disapproval of pilgrimage because hymns are sung there constantly. Reformers of the Singh Sabha movement removed idols and images from the temple in 1905. After the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 1919, the British transferred management to the elected Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee. The Punjabi Suba movement, which led to the state borders of 1966, centred on the complex.

From 1 to 8 June 1984 the Indian Army carried out Operation Blue Star to remove Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale and his followers, who had taken refuge in the buildings. Thousands of soldiers, militants and civilians died, and the Akal Takht was destroyed. The complex was rebuilt afterwards.
golestan-palace: The royal citadel of Tehran was built in the reign of Tahmasp I (r. 1524–1576) of the Safavid dynasty. Abbas the Great laid out a large garden in the northern part of its enclosure, later surrounded by a high wall, with a royal residence inside. The palace was later renovated by Karim Khan of the Zand dynasty (r. 1750–1779). Agha Mohammad Khan, founder of the Qajar dynasty, chose Tehran as his capital, and the citadel became the seat of the Qajars (1794–1925), with the palace of Golestan as their official residence. It was rebuilt to its present form in 1865 by Haji Ab ol Hasan Mimar Navai.

The complex is a group of royal buildings within a wall, most of them dating from the 19th century, and it holds Iranian and European crafts and gifts from the 18th to the 20th century. Its halls include the Marble Throne terrace, built in 1747–1751, the Mirror Hall, the Salam Hall and the Ivory Hall, a dining room decorated with gifts to Naser ed-Din Shah from European monarchs. The Edifice of the Sun, begun in 1865, carries a clock given by Queen Victoria. The Abyaz Palace, completed in 1883 to show Ottoman gifts, is neo-baroque and was designed by the shah himself. A photographic archive was created on the shah's order.

In the Pahlavi era (1925–1979) the palace was used for formal receptions. The coronation of Reza Shah in 1926 and that of Mohammad Reza Shah and Shahbanu Farah in 1967 took place in the Salam Hall. Between 1925 and 1945 a large part of the complex was destroyed on Reza Shah's order, because he believed historic Qajar palaces should not hinder the growth of a modern city, and commercial buildings were put up in their place. UNESCO proclaimed the palace a World Heritage Site on 23 June 2013 at a meeting in Phnom Penh.
goliath: Goliath is attested in the Biblical narratives of 1 and 2 Samuel. The Dead Sea Scrolls text of Samuel, Josephus and the Septuagint give his height as four cubits and a span, about 2.06 metres, while the Masoretic Text has six cubits and a span, about 2.97 metres. Many scholars think the smaller number grew in transmission. The name Goliath is not Semitic and has been linked with that of the Lydian king Alyattes. Tell es-Safi, the biblical Gath, was one of the largest Philistine cities until its destruction in the 9th century BCE. A potsherd found there, dated between the 10th and mid-9th centuries BCE, bears the names ʾLWT and WLT, which are etymologically related to Goliath.

In 1 Samuel 17 Saul and the Israelites face the Philistines in the Valley of Elah. For forty days Goliath comes out between the lines each morning and evening and challenges the Israelites to send a champion to decide the matter in single combat. Saul is afraid. David, a young shepherd, accepts, declines Saul's armour and takes his staff, sling and five stones from a brook.

Goliath curses him by his gods, and David answers that the battle is the Lord's. David's stone strikes Goliath in the forehead and David cuts off his head with Goliath's own sword. The Philistines flee, pursued as far as Gath and the gates of Ekron. Many scholars see the purpose of the story as showing that Saul, a head taller than anyone in Israel yet unwilling to take the challenge, was unfit to be king.

Another verse, 2 Samuel 21:19, says that Elhanan, son of Jaare-oregim, the Bethlehemite, killed Goliath the Gittite. Most scholars regard this as the older account, which the authors of the Deuteronomistic history reworked to credit David.

The armour described in 1 Samuel 17 resembles Greek armour of the 6th century BCE, and a similar story appears in the Iliad, where Nestor recalls conquering the giant Ereuthalion. Other scholars hold that the description fits a Philistine warrior of the 10th century BCE. The Babylonian Talmud makes Goliath a son of Orpah, the sister-in-law of Ruth. The phrase David and Goliath has come to describe a smaller, weaker opponent facing a much stronger one.
golkar: In 1959 President Sukarno introduced Guided Democracy, in which so-called functional groups would play a role in government in place of political parties. The Indonesian National Armed Forces supported them because they believed the groups would balance the growing strength of the Communist Party of Indonesia. In 1960 Sukarno gave sectoral groups such as teachers, the armed forces and police, workers and artists seats in the Mutual Cooperation House of Representatives. The armed forces then founded an anti-communist trade union, Soksi, and used it as the core of the Joint Secretariat of Functional Groups, or Sekber Golkar. Its members included the Trikarya organisations and professional groups, and during the New Order it was formally divided into main organisation groups.

General Suharto was elected the second president of Indonesia in March 1968. Having no party of his own, he settled on Golkar in order to distance himself from the old regime, and ordered his associate Ali Murtopo to turn it from a federation of organisations into an electoral machine. It presented itself as non-ideological, promising economic development and stability, and encouraged civil servants to vote for it as a sign of loyalty. Murtopo sometimes used the military and gangs of young men to eliminate political competition.

Golkar won 62 per cent in 1971 and then 62 per cent in 1977, 64 in 1982, 73 in 1987, 68 in 1992 and 74 in 1997. After 1973 Suharto banned all parties except the Indonesian Democratic Party and the United Development Party. Five of six New Order chairmen were military officers.

After Suharto fell in May 1998, Akbar Tandjung became chairman in July by beating Army General Edi Sudrajat, the first time a chairman was elected rather than appointed. In 1999 Golkar lost its first democratic election to Megawati Sukarnoputri's PDI-P, with 20 per cent of the vote, and then supported Abdurrahman Wahid for president. It won the 2004 legislative election with 21 per cent, and its member Jusuf Kalla became vice president that year.

Jusuf Kalla became chairman in December 2004, and Aburizal Bakrie in 2009. Several former members founded rival parties, among them Hanura under Wiranto and Gerindra under Prabowo Subianto. A dispute between camps led by Bakrie and Agung Laksono ended on 17 May 2016 when Setya Novanto was elected chairman, and the party then backed President Joko Widodo. Airlangga Hartarto later became chairman, and in 2024 Golkar won 102 seats in the House of Representatives. Its stated ideology has been described as centrist, centre-right or catch-all by observers.
gollub-war: The First Peace of Thorn of 1411 had not fixed the border between Samogitia and Prussia, and Poland also contested Pomerelia and the Chełmno Land. After the brief Hunger War of 1414 the parties took their dispute to the Council of Constance, which created a Samogitian diocese at Varniai but settled nothing by its end in 1418. Talks at Gniewków in 1419 also failed, and the matter passed to Emperor Sigismund.

On 6 January 1420 at Wrocław Sigismund declared the Peace of Thorn valid: Samogitia would belong to Lithuania only for the lifetimes of Vytautas the Great and King Jogaila of Poland and then return to the Order. The emperor, who probably hoped for the help of the Teutonic Knights against the Hussites, whom Vytautas supported, gave the Order more than it had asked. Vytautas and Jogaila refused the ruling, and Jogaila appealed in vain to Pope Martin V.

In July 1422, while Sigismund and the Order were taken up with the Hussite raids on Germany, Vytautas and Jogaila attacked Prussia. Grand Master Michael Küchmeister von Sternberg had been forced to resign in March, and his successor Paul von Rusdorf had released most of the hired mercenaries, leaving the Order with very few soldiers. The Polish and Lithuanian forces marched north to Osterode while the Knights fell back to Löbau. Without siege engines, Jogaila advanced towards Marienburg, took Riesenburg and plundered the villages around it, then turned south, took Golub and failed before Schönsee.

Jogaila sought a quick end before the reinforcements Rusdorf had asked of the Empire could arrive. A truce was signed on 17 September 1422, and the war ended ten days later with the Treaty of Melno, which closed the territorial disputes between Lithuania and the Knights that had lasted since 1398. Poland fought the Order again in 1431–1435, when the Knights backed Švitrigaila rather than the Polish candidate Sigismund Kęstutaitis as Vytautas's successor.
gommateshwara-statue: The statue is carved from a single block of granite and stands on an open lotus. It shows the prolonged meditation of Bahubali, standing still in the kayotsarga posture for so long that climbing vines have grown around his legs. The nude figure has curly ringlets of hair and large ears; the eyes are half open, the gaze resting on the nose to show his detachment from the world, and a faint smile touches the corners of the lips. The shoulders are broad, the arms stretch straight down, and from the thighs upwards the figure has no support.

Behind it rises an anthill, a sign of his incessant penance, from which a snake and a creeper emerge and twine around the legs and arms, ending in clusters of flowers and berries. On either side stand two richly ornamented chauri bearers, a yaksha and a yakshini. A trough carved on the rear of the anthill collects the water and other ingredients used for the ritual bath.

The statue symbolises the Jain precepts of peace, non-violence, sacrifice of worldly affairs and simple living, and it is one of the holiest sites in Jainism. Vindhyagiri, also known as Indra-giri, is one of the two hills of Shravanabelagola, and neighbouring areas hold Jain temples known as basadis. The other hill, Chandragiri, with Jain centres much older than the statue, is dedicated to Bharat, the brother of Bahubali and son of the first Tirthankara, Rishabhnath.

At the Mahamastakabhisheka the statue is bathed in milk, saffron, ghee, sugarcane juice and other liquids, and the German Indologist Heinrich Zimmer saw in this anointing the reason for its freshness. According to legend, the first such bathing, organised by Chavundaraya once the statue was finished, failed because the liquids would not flow below the navel, until Kushmandini, disguised as a poor old woman, poured milk from the shell of half a Gullikayi fruit over it from head to toe.

Krishna-Rajendra Wodeyar attended the festival in 1910, and Narendra Modi and Ramnath Kovind in 2018. J. L. Jaini, introducing his English translation of the Gommatsāra, wrote that English missionaries he met on his visit in 1910 took off their shoes out of respect for the image. The Archaeological Survey of India lists the statue in a group of monuments in Shravanabelagola known as the Adarsh Smarak Monument.
gomti-river: The Gomti, also written Gumti or Gomati, flows entirely within the Indian state of Uttar Pradesh and is a tributary of the Ganges. Fed by monsoons and groundwater, it begins at the Gomat Taal, near Madhotanda in Pilibhit district, and meets the smaller Gaihaaee about 20 kilometres from its source.

It stays a narrow stream until Mohammadi Kheri, in Lakhimpur Kheri district, about 68 kilometres from its origin, where tributaries including the Sukheta, Choha and Andhra Choha join it. The Kathina joins it at Mailani and the Sarayan in Sitapur district, and a major tributary, the Sai River, joins it near Jaunpur. The Markandey Mahadeo temple stands at the confluence of the Gomti and the Ganges.

After flowing 190 kilometres the Gomti enters Lucknow, meandering through the city for about 30 kilometres and supplying its water; at the downstream end of the city a barrage turns the river into a lake. Besides Lucknow, Gola Gokaran Nath, Misrikh, Neemsar, Lakhimpur Kheri, Sultanpur Kerakat, Jaunpur and Zafarabad are the most prominent of the 20 towns in its catchment, and the river cuts the Sultanpur district and Jaunpur in half. High embankments were built around the river after a major flood in the 1970s, which altered its natural floodplain.

Its natural drains, which once carried surplus water into the river in the monsoon and recharged the water table, came to carry residential and industrial sewage, and the floodplain was covered by districts such as Gomti Nagar and Triveni Nagar. The river rises 10 to 12 metres in the monsoon, and a major flood was reported in 2008. Around 2012 a riverfront scheme modelled on Ahmedabad's Sabarmati was studied with the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee; the study warned that narrowing the river to under 250 metres would speed its flow and raise flood levels, and environmentalists opposed the plan.

According to Hindu belief, the Gomti is the daughter of the sage Vashishtha, and bathing in it on Ekadashi, the eleventh day of each lunar fortnight, is thought to wash away sins. The Bhagavata Purana names it as one of the five transcendental rivers of India. The rare Gomti Chakra is found in it.
gonaives: Gonaïves lies on a flood plain, below mountains that are largely unforested. Even among Haiti's port cities it has long been vulnerable to hurricanes for this reason. The Gulf of Gonâve takes its name from the town, which is also called Les Gonaïves, and in Haitian Creole Gonayiv.

The city was founded around 1422 by a group of Taíno, who named it Gonaibo, a locality of the cacicat of the Jaragua. In 1802 the Battle of Ravine-à-Couleuvres, an important engagement of the Haitian Revolution, was fought near it.

Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared Haiti independent from France on 1 January 1804 by reading the Act of Independence, drafted by Boisrond Tonnerre, on the Place d'Armes of the town. His wife, Marie-Claire Heureuse Félicité, died in Gonaïves in August 1858.

In the early 2000s the city saw substantial rioting and violence, motivated mainly by opposition to President Jean-Bertrand Aristide. On 5 February 2004 a group calling itself the Revolutionary Artibonite Resistance Front seized control of the city, which began the 2004 Haitian rebellion.

Storms struck the city twice in four years. In September 2004 Hurricane Jeanne caused major flooding and mudslides. Four years later Hurricane Hanna devastated it again and killed 529 people, mostly in the flooded parts of Gonaïves, where the destruction was described as catastrophic. At least 48,000 people from the Gonaïves area were forced into shelters, according to the mayor, Stephen Moise.

Gonaïves is a commune of Haiti and the capital of the Artibonite department. Its population was 356,324 at the 2015 census. The city has a public university, the Université Publique de l'Artibonite aux Gonaïves, as well as a law and economics school and La Providence Hospital. Its association football clubs include Eclair AC and Racing FC.
gondar: Gondar lies in the North Gondar Zone of the Amhara Region, north of Lake Tana on the Lesser Angereb River and south-west of the Simien Mountains. The name is first recorded under Amda Seyon I as that of a regiment stationed, probably in Wegera, to guard trade routes and control a restive population. In 1636 Emperor Fasilides chose the place as his katama, or royal camp, in the midst of Kémant country. It stood where caravans from Sudan and the Red Sea converged, which brought trading benefits to the court.

Fasilides ordered the building of Fasil Ghebbi, or Fasilides Castle, and founded five other churches. In 1648 a Yemeni ambassador, Hassan ibn Ahmad al-Haymi, described the palace as a great house of stone and lime. By Fasilides' death in 1667 the city was so well established that his successor Yohannes I did not seek a new capital. In 1669-1670 Yohannes ordered Muslims and Jews to live apart from Christians in quarters of their own. Iyasu I (1682-1706) added a castle and several churches, and under him the population was estimated to exceed 60,000. The French physician Charles Poncet was the first European observer to describe the city.

After the death of Iyasu I in 1706 the city declined. Oromo influence grew, and the warlord Ras Mikael Sehul became master of Gondar, killing Emperor Iyoas I in May 1767. The empire then entered the period of weak central rule known as the Zemene Mesafint. Early in the 19th century soldiers plundered the city repeatedly, and in 1864 Emperor Tewodros II ordered it violently sacked, calling it a town of priests who did not love him. Mahdist forces from Sudan burned its churches in January 1888 and attacked again the following June. The population, over 60,000 in the 18th century, was said to have shrunk to 8,000 in the 1870s.

Italian forces occupied Gondar without a fight on 1 April 1936, during the Second Italo-Ethiopian War. They laid out a piazza, new roads and buildings in the modernist style of the 1930s, and about 2,000 Europeans settled there within two years. British and Italian forces fought in the city from 13 to 17 November 1941.

Gondar has about 44 churches, more than any other Ethiopian settlement for many years, and is a centre of learning of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. Its region is the homeland of most Ethiopian Jews. Fasil Ghebbi holds Fasilides' castle, Iyasu's palace, Dawit's Hall, Empress Mentewab's castle and three churches. Nearby are Fasilides' Bath, blessed each year in a ceremony, and the Debre Berhan Selassie Church. The University of Gondar includes Ethiopia's main faculty of medicine.
gondophares: Gondophares, also Guduvhara, is known only from silver and copper coins bearing his portrait. His name was not a personal name but an epithet, from the Old Iranian Vindafarnâ, meaning may he find glory. Ernst Herzfeld maintained that his dynasty represented the House of Suren, a family of Arsacid Iran with the hereditary right to lead the royal military and to crown the Parthian king. Around 129 BCE the Saka and the Yuezhi invaded Drangiana, which became Sakastan, and the Parthian king Mithridates II later defeated the Saka there and installed satraps. Gondophares probably belonged to a line of local princes who governed the province, and the Surenids may have repelled the Indo-Scythians and then seized their lands in Arachosia and the Punjab.

Gondophares ascended the throne in about 19 or 20 CE, quickly declared independence from the Parthian Empire and minted coins in Drangiana, where he took the Greek title autokrator, one who rules by himself. He took the Kabul Valley, the Punjab and Sindh from the Scythian king Azes, though a number of vassal rulers seem simply to have switched allegiance. His empire was vast but a loose framework that fragmented soon after his death. His capital was Taxila, and his coins bear an Iranian royal name with other legends in Greek and Kharoṣṭhī. He was succeeded in Drangiana and Arachosia by Orthagnes, and in Gandhara by his nephew Abdagases I.

The apocryphal Acts of Thomas mentions a king Gudnaphar, long associated with Gondophares, and the Apostle Thomas is said to have been brought before him at Taxila. A. D. H. Bivar found the dates of a Gondophares in the Takht-i-Bahi inscription consistent with the dates given in the apocryphal text for the Apostle's voyage to India. It has also been suggested that these mentions concern a successor of the same name, and R. C. Senior's numismatic work favours Gondophares-Sases, the fourth king to use the title. Through the Armenian Gastaphar his name may lie behind Gaspar, one of the Magi of Christian tradition.
gondwana-india: Gondwana, also called Gondaranya, has no clear boundary, since the Gond people are spread widely across central India; its core is the Vidarbha region of Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh, and it reaches into northern Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and southern Uttar Pradesh. It lies on the northern Deccan plateau at about 600–700 metres, on rugged, hilly ground of mostly Precambrian rock, overlain in the west by the Deccan Traps. The climate is hot and semi-arid, with large dry monsoon forests. The supercontinent Gondwanaland was named after the region for its fossil-bearing rocks.

The first Gond kingdom recorded is that of Narsingh Rai, King of Kherla, said in 1398 to have ruled all the hills of Gondwana, until Hoshang Shah, king of Malwa, overthrew and killed him. Of the later kingdoms, Garha-Mandla held the upper Narmada valley, Deogarh-Nagpur the Kanhan and upper Wainganga valleys, and Chanda-Sirpur the present Chandrapur, Gadchiroli and eastern Adilabad districts. They were nominally subject to the Mughal emperors, who set governors at Paunar and Kherla after annexing Berar in 1595, but the Gond kings kept their independence within their lands.

In the 17th century the Bundela ruler Chhatar Sal took part of the Mandla principality. The Marathas won Bundelkhand in 1733 and Saugor by 1735; from 1742, when the Peshwa advanced to Mandla, Garha-Mandla was practically a Maratha dependency until its Gond dynasty was overthrown in 1781. Raghoji Bhonsle of Berar settled at Nagpur in 1743 and by 1751 had conquered Deogarh, Chanda and Chhattisgarh. British rule brought permanent settlement in the 19th century, and several rebellions followed, some of them in defence of forests against commercial logging.

Gondwana has a relatively high share of people of the Gond tribes, who are recognised as scheduled tribes. Its forests hold several national parks with tigers. Many forts of the Gond kingdoms carry the emblem of a lion triumphing over an elephant on their gateways.
gonghe-regency: According to the sources, King Li of Zhou raised taxes to pay for his pleasures, barred commoners from profiting from communal forests and lakes, and made speaking against him punishable by death. His rule drove peasants and soldiers across Zhou China into revolt in what was called the Compatriots Rebellion. Li was sent into exile at a place called Zhi near modern Linfen, and his son was taken by one of his ministers and hidden.

To keep order in the resulting vacuum of power, He, Earl of Gong, took control. He had been born in the State of Wei and was later enfeoffed in Gong, where he formed a state of his own. The Lüshi Chunqiu records that the Zhou turned to He of their own accord. When King Li died in exile, power passed to his son, King Xuan of Zhou, which ended the regency, and He returned to his home state.

The Han historian Sima Qian read gonghe as joint harmony in his Records of the Grand Historian and concluded that two dukes, Duke Ding of Zhou and Duke Mu of Shao, had shared power. The Bamboo Annals, a text found in antiquity but after Sima Qian's time, names a single ruler, He, Earl of Gong, and an independent unearthed text, the Xinian, supports that reading. Han sources often saw the events as a usurpation, while present-day scholars tend to follow the Lüshi Chunqiu in calling them a popular uprising.

Sima Qian was able to build a year-by-year chronology back to the first year of the regency, but found his sources for earlier dates unreliable and contradictory and did not adopt them. The Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project, sponsored by the government of the People's Republic of China, later sought better estimates for earlier dates, but its draft report of 2000 has been criticised by various scholars.

The name also passed into modern political language. Meeting the Western word republic, the Japanese drew a parallel with the regency and coined kyouwakoku, a shared harmony country. The term was borrowed back into Chinese as gònghéguó and from Chinese into Vietnamese as cộng hòa quốc.
gongmin-of-goryeo: Gongmin, also known by his Mongolian name Bayan Temür, was the 31st ruler of Goryeo and the second son of King Chungsuk. Goryeo had been a semi-autonomous vassal of the Mongol Yuan dynasty since the Mongol invasions of the 13th century. Starting with King Chungnyeol, prospective rulers married Mongolian princesses and were customarily sent to the Yuan court, in effect as hostages. Following this custom Gongmin was sent there in 1341 and spent many years at the court before ascending the throne, and he married a Mongolian princess who became Queen Indeok. The Yuan began to crumble in the mid-14th century and was replaced by the Ming dynasty in 1368.

As Yuan power fell apart, Gongmin began efforts to reform the Goryeo government, first removing pro-Mongol aristocrats and military officers. The deposed men formed a faction that plotted an unsuccessful coup, and a rebellion by the high official Cho Il-sin was put down by General Ch'oe Yŏng. In 1356 the Goryeo army retook the northern provinces that the Mongols had annexed as the Ssangseong and Dongnyeong Prefectures, helped by the defection of Yi Cha-ch'un and his son Yi Sŏng-gye. His land reform met opposition from officials who were landowners themselves. He also faced Japanese pirates, the Wokou, and Red Turban troops who invaded in 1359 and 1361 and briefly occupied Kaesong. The diplomat Mun Ikchŏm introduced cotton cultivation by smuggling seeds from China.

Queen Indeok, Princess Noguk, died in childbirth in 1365. Gongmin then became indifferent to politics and entrusted the state to the monk Pyeonjo, renamed Sin Ton, who tried to reform Goryeo society. Sin Ton lost his position after six years, and the king had him executed in 1371.

The Goryeo bureaucracy never forgave his reforms and saw his ties with Ming China as a threat to its status.The Goryeosa, written to legitimise the succeeding dynasty and so possibly colouring its account, is the only record of his death. It says that on the night of the twenty-first day of the ninth lunar month of 1374 several men entered his chamber at the palace in Songdo and killed him with swords, while guards and servants did not move. The eunuch Ch'oe Man-saeng and five members of the Jajewi, a guard of young men Gongmin had formed in 1372, were executed. The official Yi In-im then enthroned the eleven-year-old King U. Gongmin was also a skilled painter and calligrapher.
gongyang-of-goryeo: Gongyang was born on 9 March 1345 with the personal name Wang Yo, the second and youngest son of Wang Kyun, a sixth-generation descendant of King Sinjong through his youngest son, Duke Yangyang. His mother, Princess Boknyeong, was a great-granddaughter of King Chungnyeol, so that he was of the Goryeo royal blood on both sides. As a young man he was honoured as Prince Jeongchang and married the daughter of No Ch'aek of the Gyoha No clan. His niece, Lady Kang, became the second wife of Yi Sŏnggye.

Although he did everything to show that he had no political ambitions, the faction of Yi Sŏnggye used him as a tool. In 1389 Yi's supporters forced King Chang from the throne and set Wang Yo in his place as the 34th and last ruler of the dynasty. The same faction directed the events of his short reign, which included the killings of the former kings U and Chang.

After the murder of Chŏng Mong-ju, the last major supporter of the Goryeo kings, Yi Sŏnggye, his son Yi Pangwŏn, Chŏng Tojŏn and others deposed the king in 1392, bringing the Goryeo dynasty to an end, and Yi went on to establish the new kingdom of Joseon.

After his deposition the former king was sent into exile at Wonju with the title of Prince Gongyang, and later moved to Samcheok. There, in 1394, he was strangled together with his son, Crown Prince Wang Sŏk. His consort, Royal Consort Sun of the Gyoha No clan, had borne him at least two sons and three daughters. In 1416 King Taejong of Joseon honoured him with the title King Gongyang and sent an envoy to inspect his tomb. The last Goryeo king has since appeared as a character in many television dramas about the founding of Joseon, among them Tears of the Dragon and Six Flying Dragons.
gongyang-zhuan: The commentary covers the Annals from Duke Yin of Lu to Duke Ai of Lu. Its starting assumption is that Confucius wrote the Spring and Autumn Annals to criticise the politics of his time and to set a guide for later ages: a sage who should have received the Mandate of Heaven and become king, he instead passed judgement on the events and people of the Spring and Autumn period. Unlike the Zuo Zhuan, with its vivid narrative, it explains little historical context and looks for deeper meaning in the wording of the Annals, which led the scholar Jiang Qing to call it the political theory wing of Confucianism.

Among the themes later readers drew from it are three stages of human history, from chaos through restored order to great harmony, the unity of cosmic and political order, limits on the ruler's power, the distinction between Chinese and non-Chinese cultures, and just retribution.

According to the Book of Han, the oral commentary was written down in the early Han dynasty by Gongyang Shou, a descendant of Gongyang Gao, with Humu Sheng, who became an erudite of the Han court. When Emperor Wu of Han adopted the proposal of Dong Zhongshu, its leading authority, to make Confucianism the state ideology, the Gongyang school gained great influence. Dong's Luxuriant Dew of the Spring and Autumn Annals gave it a mystical reading, while officials cited the work in policy debates as a source of precedents for government.

Late in the Western Han dynasty, Liu Xin's proposal to establish chairs for the Zuo Zhuan and the Guliang Zhuan ended the school's monopoly. In the later Han, He Xiu defended it and spent seventeen years on a commentary that largely survives and became the main basis for later study. Study of the work declined under the Tang, though in Japan Hayashi Gahō published an annotated edition in 1688. Under the Qing it was taken up by the Changzhou school, including Zhuang Cunyu, Liu Fenglu, Gong Zizhen and Wei Yuan, and Kang Youwei's reading prepared an audience for the reformist ideas of the Hundred Days' Reform.
gongyi: Gongyi lies in the middle of Henan province, on the northern side of Mount Song. The Yellow River runs through the northern part of the city. Zhengzhou lies 82 km (51 mi) to the east and Luoyang 76 km (47 mi) to the west. The city has an area of 1,041 km2 (402 sq mi) and was formerly called Gong County.

The city was once known as Zhenxun and was reputedly the capital of China during part of the Xia dynasty. According to the Bamboo Annals, Houyi occupied Zhenxun with his forces while the Xia king Taikang was off hunting beyond the Luo River. Houyi was then usurped by his lieutenant Han Zhuo and his son, before the Xia were eventually restored.

The Song tombs lie scattered through the towns of Xicun, Zhitian and Huiguo. They are the resting place of seven emperors of the Northern Song dynasty and of the father of the dynasty's founder. There are also graves of loyal Song ministers. After the founding of the People's Republic of China, Gongyi was placed under the jurisdiction of Zhengzhou, came under the control of Kaifeng in January 1955 and reverted to Zhengzhou in August 1983. In 1991 it became a county-level city under Zhengzhou. It is thought to be the birthplace of the Tang dynasty poet Du Fu.

Gongyi is a county-level city of Henan province, administered by the prefecture-level city of Zhengzhou. Its population is about 790,000. Its administrative divisions include five subdistricts, one of them named for Du Fu, and fifteen towns.
gonur-depe: Gonur Depe covers about 55 hectares in the delta of the Murghab River, where more than 150 ancient settlements have been found and where it is among the largest ruins. Archaeologists divide it into three sectors. Gonur North, an almost elliptical fortified area of about 330 by 460 metres, was occupied from about 2400 to 1900 BCE. At its centre stood the Monumental Palace, about 150 by 140 metres, inside a double wall, with two large courtyards, an axial corridor, storerooms and rooms that may have been a throne room and audience halls; water sources fed by ceramic pipes lay near its entrance.

About 200 metres west lies the Large Necropolis, some 10 hectares in extent. Only adults and young people over eight were buried there; children were buried near houses or in abandoned buildings. Gonur South, a smaller square complex of about 1.5 hectares, was lived in from about 1900 to 1600 BCE and was fortified by two rings of massive walls with round towers.

Scholars think the Oxus culture may have begun at sites such as Anau on the northern slopes of the Kopet-Dag, and that settlers moved from there to places like Gonur as the climate changed. Genetic study of people buried at Gonur finds that most of their ancestry resembles that of Neolithic farmers of the Iranian Plateau; some outliers had South Asian-related ancestry, possibly through contact with the Indus Valley Civilisation. Ivory objects in the last phase of the Royal Necropolis are contemporary with late layers at Altyn Depe and Mohenjo-daro. Camps of the Andronovo culture appeared at the site more often between 1800 and 1500 BCE.

Viktor Sarianidi first collected pottery sherds from the surface in 1972. He described a walled shrine in Gonur South, the Temenos, as a precinct of the Soma cult and reported a vessel for preparing the drink with traces of cannabis, poppy and ephedra. Mosaics of the late third millennium BCE that decorated walls and wooden chests in the Necropolis have close parallels at Mari in Syria and in the Royal Cemetery at Ur. Archaeologist Julio Bendezu-Sarmiento holds that the foal and wagon burial predates similar Sintashta burials by about a century and a half. Stratigraphic studies from 2014 to 2018 by Robert M. Sataev, Nadezhda A. Dubova and others identified five building periods.
gonzalo-fernandez-de-cordoba: Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba was born on 1 September 1453 at Montilla, the younger son of Pedro Fernández de Córdoba, Count of Aguilar, and Elvira de Herrera. His father died when he was two, and his older brother Alonso inherited the family estates, leaving Gonzalo to seek his own fortune. In 1467 he entered the household of Alfonso, Prince of Asturias, and after Alfonso's death in 1468 he attached himself to Alfonso's sister Isabella of Castile. He fought for Isabella in the civil war after 1474 and in 1479 led 120 lancers in the final battle against the Portuguese.

From 1481 he took part in the ten-year campaign against Granada, distinguishing himself in the sieges of Loja, Tajara, Illora and Montefrío, where he was reported to be the first attacker over the walls. Because he knew Arabic and Boabdil, he was one of the officers chosen to arrange the surrender in 1492. In 1495 he landed in Naples with about 5,000 infantry and 600 light cavalry against the French of Charles VIII, was defeated at Seminara on 28 June 1495, and then retrained his army, used guerrilla tactics and won at Atella.

On his return to Spain he introduced an infantry formation armed with pikes and the arquebus, with sections assigned to specific roles. In the Second Italian War he held out at Barletta until reinforced, then won at Cerignola on 28 April 1503, where 6,000 Spanish troops faced 10,000 French and the Duke of Nemours was killed. On the night of 29 December 1503 he bridged the Garigliano and surprised the French. The French were forced to sign the Treaty of Blois in 1505, giving up Naples.

Made Duke of Terranova and Viceroy of Naples in 1504, he lost his chief supporter when Isabella died that year. Ferdinand II of Aragon suspected his loyalty and thought he spent too freely, and in 1507 travelled to Naples, removed him and promised him the mastership of the Order of Santiago, which never came. Gonzalo, retired to a country estate and died of malaria on 2 December 1515 near Granada.

His combined use of pikes, firearms, fortifications and siegecraft is credited with laying the foundations of the tercios. Bernard Montgomery credited him with raising the infantryman to the most important fighting man on the battlefield for the next 400 years. His tomb in the Monastery of San Jerónimo in Granada, hung with some 700 captured banners, was desecrated by Napoleonic troops in 1810.
gonzalo-guerrero: Little is known of Guerrero's life before 1511, when the caravel Santa María de la Barca, carrying him and 20 to 30 passengers, was wrecked in a tropical storm between the Yucatán Peninsula and Cuba. The survivors drifted in rowing skiffs for thirteen days before sighting the eastern coast of Yucatán, by which time only ten were still alive. On landing they were seized by the Maya militia of Waymil; some were ritually sacrificed and the rest were forced into slavery under provincial aristocrats.

In about 1514 Guerrero entered the service of Nachan Can, the halach uinich or governor of Chetumal, while his crew-mate Gerónimo de Aguilar remained a slave of the batab of Xamanha. Guerrero is thought to have earned the rank of nakom, or commanding officer, and to have served Chetumal or its allies against the expeditions of Hernández de Córdoba in 1517 and Juan de Grijalva in 1518. He converted to Maya polytheism and married a Maya woman believed to be the governor's daughter, and their children are counted among the first mestizos of the Americas.

When Hernán Cortés landed on Cozumel on 6 March 1519 he invited both Spaniards to join him. According to the conquistador Bernal Díaz, Guerrero told Aguilar that he had three children, that the Maya looked on him as a lord and a captain in war, and that his face was tattooed and his ears pierced. His wife, Zazil Há, angrily told Aguilar to leave them alone.

Guerrero went on to lead the Maya against the Spanish. He is thought to have been central to the failure of Francisco de Montejo's entrada of 1527–1528: Chetumal sent his awaited reinforcements off course with false scouts, and Montejo sailed away in 1528 without fighting. Guerrero is also thought to have fought Alonso de Avila's entrada of 1531–1533, which took the provincial capital but in the end failed.

Late in 1535 Guerrero is thought to have led fifty canoes across the Bay of Honduras to support the cacique Cicumba against the Spanish villa of Buena Esperanza in the Sula Valley. In 1536 Pedro de Alvarado stormed Cicumba's fortified camp on the Ulua River. Andrés de Cereceda, writing to the king on 14 August 1536, reported that the tattooed body of a Spaniard killed by an arquebus shot was found after the battle; he named the man Gonzalo Aroca, but historians identify him as Guerrero.

No writing by Guerrero is known to survive. Reviled by the sixteenth-century chroniclers, he was later recast in Mexico as the father of the mestizos, above all in Eugenio Aguirre's novel Gonzalo Guerrero of 1980.
gonzalo-jimenez-de-quesada: Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada was an Andalusian lawyer, trained in Granada. His father, Luis Jiménez de Quesada, was a hidalgo, and he had two distant cousins among the conquistadors, Hernán Cortés and Francisco Pizarro. In 1535 he was appointed chief magistrate and second in command of an expedition to present-day Colombia led by Pedro Fernández de Lugo, who had bought the governorship of Santa Marta. Quesada was then out of favour at home, having lost an important court case. The fleet carried over a thousand men, but Santa Marta proved a settlement of hovels and diseased colonists.

In 1536 Fernández de Lugo chose Quesada to lead an expedition into the interior. A land party went south from Santa Marta to the Magdalena River while a fleet carrying about 900 men sailed up it. From La Tora the party climbed the Opón River into the cordillera. Only 180 of 800 men survived the journey, reduced to eating snakes, lizards and the leather of their harnesses.

The Muisca had two rulers, one at Muyquytá and one at Hunza. Taking advantage of a war between them, Quesada's force subdued Muyquytá and then attacked Hunza successfully. Quesada took possession of the land in the name of Charles V. At the end of 1538 Sebastián de Belalcázar arrived from Quito and Nikolaus Federmann from Venezuela, and all three claimed the territory. Quesada persuaded them to take the dispute to the crown, and in July 1539 they sailed from Cartagena. None obtained the governorship.

Quesada returned to New Granada in 1550 and lived there for nearly thirty years as its most influential settler. He was governor of Cartagena from 1556 to 1557. In 1569, aged 63, he was commissioned to conquer the Llanos east of the cordillera. The expedition lost most of its livestock to a grass fire, reached the confluence of the Guaviare and the Orinoco in December 1571 and returned to Bogotá in December 1572 with 25 Spaniards. Suffering from leprosy and owing more than 60 thousand ducats, he died aged 70 in Mariquita, and his remains were moved to Bogotá in 1597. He wrote the Memoria de los descubridores (1567).
gonzalo-pizarro: Gonzalo Pizarro was born in Trujillo, Spain, the illegitimate son of the infantry colonel Gonzalo Pizarro y Rodríguez de Aguilar, who had served under Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba in the Italian Wars. He was the younger paternal half-brother of Francisco Pizarro and Hernando Pizarro and the older full brother of Juan Pizarro. In 1530 he accompanied Francisco on his third expedition to Peru. After the capture of the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca and his execution, the Pizarro brothers took Cuzco on 15 November 1533, and Gonzalo and Juan were made regidores of the city on 24 March 1534.

Gonzalo and Juan ruled Cuzco while Francisco founded Lima in 1535. Their treatment of the Inca ruler Manco Inca Yupanqui, including, by one account, Gonzalo's rape of his queen Cura Ocllo, helped provoke a large rebellion, and the Incas temporarily took Cuzco on 6 May 1536. Diego de Almagro imprisoned Gonzalo and Hernando on 8 April 1537, but Gonzalo escaped, and the brothers later defeated Almagro at Las Salinas.

In November 1539 Francisco made Gonzalo vice-governor of Quito and sent him to look for El Dorado and the Land of Cinnamon. He left Quito in February 1541 with Spaniards and thousands of Native Americans, and Francisco de Orellana followed. The expedition ran out of food and many died. Gonzalo turned back with about 80 men, while Orellana went on to explore the length of the Amazon River.

Almagristas killed Francisco Pizarro on 26 June 1541. In 1544 Emperor Charles V sent Blasco Núñez Vela as the first viceroy of Peru with the New Laws, framed by Bartolomé de las Casas to protect Indigenous peoples. Conquistadors who would lose their hold on native labour backed Gonzalo and Francisco de Carvajal in the Great Encomendero Rebellion, and their army defeated Núñez at Añaquito, near Quito, in 1546.

Carvajal urged Gonzalo to proclaim himself King of Peru, but he refused. Pedro de la Gasca then arrived with pardons and the repeal of the New Laws, and most of Gonzalo's army deserted him before Jaquijahuana, near Cuzco. He surrendered and was beheaded on 10 April 1548. Werner Herzog's film Aguirre, the Wrath of God of 1972 reimagines his expeditions.
good-friday-agreement: When the Irish Free State was established in 1922, six northern counties of the island remained in the United Kingdom. In the decades that followed there were tensions, sometimes violent, between unionists who wished to remain with Britain and nationalists who wanted unification with the Free State, later the Republic of Ireland. From the late 1960s the conflict, known as the Troubles, became more intense, and over 3,500 deaths were attributed to it in more than thirty years.

Serious political efforts to end it began in the late 1980s, and ceasefires were declared and later broken. The talks that produced the Agreement were chaired by the United States special envoy George J. Mitchell, with Tony Blair and Bertie Ahern as the British and Irish leaders and Mo Mowlam as Secretary of State for Northern Ireland.

The Agreement consists of two documents agreed in Belfast on 10 April 1998: the Multi-Party Agreement between most Northern Ireland parties and the two governments, and the British–Irish Agreement between the governments. Among the eight parties were the Ulster Unionist Party, the Social Democratic and Labour Party, Sinn Féin and the Alliance Party. The Democratic Unionist Party was the only major group to oppose it.

It acknowledged as legitimate both the wish of a majority in Northern Ireland to remain in the United Kingdom and the wish of many to see a united Ireland. Northern Ireland would stay in the United Kingdom until majorities in both Northern Ireland and the Republic wished otherwise. Strand 1 set up an Assembly and a power-sharing Executive, Strand 2 the North/South Ministerial Council, and Strand 3 the British–Irish Council. Participants committed to decommissioning of paramilitary arms, police reform and the early release of prisoners from groups keeping a ceasefire. A total of 428 were released by 28 July 2000.

Both parts of Ireland voted on 22 May 1998. In Northern Ireland turnout was 81% and 71% of votes were in favour, and in the Republic 56% voted and 94% supported the constitutional amendment, which removed the territorial claim in Articles 2 and 3. The British–Irish Agreement came into force on 2 December 1999, when power was devolved to the Assembly and direct rule from Westminster ended.

The Assembly has been suspended several times, sometimes for years, and parts of the rights provisions, such as a Bill of Rights for Northern Ireland, have not been fully implemented. Because it binds the British government on points of law, the Agreement has become part of the constitution of the United Kingdom.
gooty: Gooty is a town in Anantapur district of Andhra Pradesh, India, 52 kilometres from Anantapur, at an average elevation of 345 metres. It is the mandal headquarters of Gooty mandal in Ananthapuramu revenue division. The town is known for the Gooty hill fort.

Eight inscriptions have been found on the rocks close to the Narasimha temple within the fort. They are badly damaged but appear to date from the reign of the Western Chalukya king Vikramaditya VI (r. c. 1076–1126). The earliest surviving fortifications and structures can be dated to the late Chalukya period. The fort later came under the control of the Vijayanagara Empire, which lost it to the Qutb Shahi dynasty during the reign of Venkata II (r. c. 1584–1614). The Mughals appear to have controlled it after conquering the Qutb Shahi capital of Golconda.

Around 1746 the Maratha general Murari Rao captured the fort, and eight years later he made it his permanent residence. He repaired the fort and commissioned the stucco ornament of the small gateways. In 1775 the Mysore ruler Hyder Ali attacked and besieged it, and after two months Murari Rao was forced to surrender because he had run out of water. The fort later came under the East India Company, whose administrator Thomas Munro was buried in the cemetery at the foot of the hill.

The town had a population of 48,658 at the 2011 census. It was constituted a third-grade municipality on 3 September 2011. Gooty Junction railway station lies on the Guntakal–Chennai Egmore section of the Mumbai–Chennai route and has a diesel locomotive shed, and the town is on the Bangalore–Hyderabad highway.
gopal-krishna-gokhale: Gopal Krishna Gokhale was born on 9 May 1866 in Kotluk village in Ratnagiri district, then part of the Bombay Presidency. His family was relatively poor, but it made sure he received an English education, and he belonged to one of the first generations of Indians to attend a university. He studied at Rajaram College in Kolhapur and graduated from Elphinstone College in 1884. He became an admirer of Western political thinkers such as John Stuart Mill and Edmund Burke, and was deeply influenced by the social work of Justice Mahadev Govind Ranade.

Gokhale joined the Indian National Congress in 1889. He was a moderate who sought to petition the British authorities and win greater respect for Indian rights through dialogue. He later became joint secretary of Congress with Bal Gangadhar Tilak, whose early career had run parallel to his own, though they differed over methods: Tilak favoured protest, boycott and agitation. Their disagreement over the Age of Consent Bill of 1891–92, which Gokhale supported, and over control of the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha led Gokhale to found the Deccan Sabha in 1896.

He sat on the Bombay Legislative Council from 1899 and on the Imperial Council of the Governor-General from 1901. His statements before the Welby Commission and his budget speeches, rich in statistics, won praise, and he played a leading part in the Morley-Minto Reforms. At the Surat session of 1907, when rival camps backed different presidential candidates, the Congress split amid scuffles; Gokhale stood beside Tilak to protect him.

In 1905, as Congress president, he founded the Servants of India Society to promote Indian education. He also campaigned against indentured labour, and in 1910 his resolution in the Imperial Legislative Council helped end indentured migration to Natal.

Gokhale visited South Africa in 1912 at Mahatma Gandhi's invitation, and Gandhi's autobiography calls him his mentor and guide. Gandhi nonetheless rejected his faith in Western institutions and did not join the Servants of India Society. Gokhale, deeply concerned about the split of the Congress, hoped to see it reunited. He died on 19 February 1915, and Tilak paid tribute to him in an editorial in Kesari.
goppingen: Göppingen is part of the Stuttgart Region of Baden-Württemberg and the capital of the district of Göppingen. It lies at the foot of the Hohenstaufen mountain, in the valley of the river Fils. Its districts are Bartenbach, Bezgenriet, Faurndau, Hohenstaufen, Holzheim, Jebenhausen and Maitis, besides Göppingen itself.

Tradition holds that the town was founded by an Alemannic leader called Geppo in the 3rd or 4th century. A fire on 25 August 1782 destroyed most of it, and it was rebuilt at once. Industrialisation in the 19th century made the area a centre of industry, and companies such as Märklin and Schuler show its importance still.

Göppingen and the nearby village of Jebenhausen had a Jewish community from 1777 until the Holocaust. In that year the Baron von Liebenstein issued a letter of protection allowing Elias Gutmann and other Jews to settle in Jebenhausen. The community peaked in the middle of the 19th century, when its centre shifted from Jebenhausen to Göppingen, and many families emigrated to America by the late 19th century. The synagogue built in 1881 was destroyed in the Kristallnacht of 9 and 10 November 1938. Rabbi Aron Tänzer, who served the community from 1907 to 1937, collected detailed records and published a history of the Jews of Jebenhausen and Göppingen in 1927. The Jewish Museum in Jebenhausen opened in 1992.

A civilian airfield built north of the town in 1930 was taken over by the Luftwaffe in 1935 and expanded into a barracks. From 1945 to 1949 it housed displaced persons and refugees. It was renamed Cooke Barracks in 1949, and from late 1950 United States Army units were stationed there, among them divisions that used it as headquarters. The barracks were returned to the German government in 1992 and later returned to civilian use.

Göppingen is the home of the toy company Märklin and the headquarters of TeamViewer. The local handball club Frisch Auf Göppingen plays in the men's top division of the Handball-Bundesliga. The town has its own daily newspaper, the Neue Württembergische Zeitung, and its twin towns are Foggia in Italy, Klosterneuburg in Austria, Pessac in France and Sonneberg in Germany. Among its natives are the mathematician and astronomer Michael Maestlin, the mentor of Johannes Kepler, and the pietist theologian Friedrich Christoph Oetinger.
gorani-language: Gorani, also called Gurani, and known by the name of its main dialect, Hawrami, is a Northwestern Iranian language, or a group of similar dialects, spoken in small pockets in north-eastern Iraq and north-western Iran. Its name in Kurdish means song. Its linguistic homeland is believed to lie somewhere around the Caspian Sea, and it is suggested that its speakers migrated together from that region to their present settlements at an unknown early date.

Classification is disputed. Ethnologue places it with Zaza in a Zaza-Gorani subgroup, though significant differences between the two have been found, and Glottolog places it in an Adharic subgroup. Broader classifications include it among the Kurdish languages. The Hawrami linguist Mihemed Emîn Hewramanî argued that Hawrami is a dialect within the unified tree of Kurdish. The great majority of its speakers consider their language to be Kurdish, though some emphasise an identity distinct from the Kurds.

Gorani comprises dialects including Bajelani, Hawrami, Sarli and Shabaki, and most lack gender and case, except Hawrami. Hawrami, regarded as the most archaic, is spoken mainly in the Hawraman region, on both sides of the Iran–Iraq border, by around 23,000 people, and UNESCO classed it as definitely endangered in 2010. Bajelani has about 59,000 speakers, mostly around Mosul, and Sarli fewer than 20,000.

Gorani had an estimated 180,000 speakers in Iran and 120,000 in Iraq in 2007. Many speakers in Iran also speak Sorani, Persian and Southern Kurdish, and most in Iraq also speak Sorani, while some speak Mesopotamian Arabic.

Under the independent rulers of Ardalan, with their capital latterly at Sanandaj, Gorani became the vehicle of a considerable corpus of poetry. Hawrami was the traditional literary language and koiné of Kurds in the historical Ardalan region of the Zagros Mountains, but was later supplanted by Central Kurdish and Southern Kurdish. Gorani remains the first language of the scriptures of the Ahl-e Haqq, or Yarsani, sect. The names of forty classical poets are known, but most of their lives are undated. Perhaps the earliest is Mele Perîşan, who is reported to have lived about 1356–1431.

Gorani verse consists almost entirely of stanzas of two rhyming half-verses of ten syllables each. Poets include Khana Qubadi, who wrote Shirin and Khosrow in 1740. Long masnavis, mostly translated from Persian literature, include Layla and Majnun and Khosrow and Shirin, and manuscripts are kept in Berlin, London and Paris.
gordian-i: Gordian I's cognomen suggests that his family came from Anatolia, more specifically Galatia or Cappadocia, and his name Marcus Antonius suggests ancestors who received Roman citizenship under Mark Antony. The Historia Augusta, an unreliable source, names his mother as Ulpia Gordiana and his father as the senator Maecius Marullus; many modern historians dismiss the father's name as false. His career began relatively late in life. He commanded the Legio IV Scythica when it was stationed in Syria, governed Roman Britain in 216 and was a suffect consul during the reign of Elagabalus. Inscriptions in Britain bearing his name were partly erased, which may show imperial displeasure.

He gained great popularity through the games and shows he produced as aedile, and his retired life did not arouse the suspicion of Caracalla, in whose honour he wrote a long epic poem, the Antoninias. He kept his wealth and political influence through the chaotic years of the Severan dynasty, which suggests a dislike of intrigue. Philostratus dedicated his Lives of the Sophists to either him or his son. Under Alexander Severus he drew lots for the proconsular governorship of Africa Proconsularis and took it up in 237, by which time he was in his late sixties.

Maximinus Thrax had killed Alexander Severus at Mogontiacum and become emperor, and his oppressive rule bred discontent. In 238 a revolt broke out in Africa after Maximinus' fiscal curator was murdered in a riot. The people demanded that Gordian accept the throne, and he yielded to the clamour and took the cognomen Africanus; Herodian puts his age at about eighty. Because of his age he insisted that his son be associated with him. He entered Carthage with the support of the population and local leaders, and an embassy under Publius Licinius Valerianus won the Senate's confirmation, and many provinces sided with him.

Opposition came from Numidia, where the governor Capelianus, a loyal supporter of Maximinus, invaded the African province with the Legio III Augusta and veteran units. Gordian II, leading an untrained militia, lost the Battle of Carthage and was killed. Gordian I hanged himself with his belt. The two had reigned only 22 days, the shortest reign of any Roman emperor, and Gordian I was the first emperor to commit suicide since Otho in 69.

His reputation rests on his reportedly amiable character and his fondness for literature, though neither he nor his son had the skills or resources of capable rulers. The Senate, having embraced his cause, had to continue the revolt and appointed Pupienus and Balbinus as joint emperors, and by the end of 238 the recognised emperor was Gordian III, his grandson.
gordian-ii: Gordian II, in Latin Marcus Antonius Gordianus Sempronianus Romanus, was the only known son of Gordian I, who was said to be related to prominent senators. His first two names suggest that his paternal ancestors received Roman citizenship under Mark Antony or one of his daughters, and his cognomen Gordianus suggests family origins in Anatolia, especially Galatia and Cappadocia. His younger sister Maecia Faustina was the mother of the later emperor Gordian III.

The only surviving account of his early career is the Historia Augusta, a source that cannot be taken as reliable. It has him serve as quaestor under Elagabalus and as praetor and consul suffect under Severus Alexander, and it names his mother as Fabia Orestilla, a descendant of Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius, a claim modern historians dismiss. Some evidence suggests that his mother may instead have been a granddaughter of the Greek sophist Herodes Atticus. In 237 or 238 he went to the province of Africa Proconsularis as legate under his father, the proconsular governor.

Early in 235 mutinous troops at Moguntiacum, now Mainz, killed Emperor Severus Alexander and his mother Julia Avita Mamaea, and their leader Maximinus Thrax became emperor despite the disapproval of the Senate. In 238, probably at the end of March, a local elite that had just killed Maximinus's procurator forced Gordian I into a full-scale revolt. Because of his father's age, the younger Gordian, said to be 46, was joined to the throne and acclaimed augustus, and like his father received the cognomen Africanus. Because Maximinus was unpopular, the Senate and most of the other provinces ratified their claim.

Opposition came from the neighbouring province of Numidia. Its governor Capelianus, a loyal supporter of Maximinus who held a grudge against Gordian, invaded Africa with the legion III Augusta, the only legion stationed in the region, and other veteran units. Gordian II led a militia of untrained soldiers, lost the Battle of Carthage and was killed. According to the Historia Augusta his body was never recovered. On hearing the news his father killed himself.

Gordian II died in April 238, and because he died before his father his reign of about 22 days is the shortest recorded of any Roman emperor. The rebellion failed, but by the end of 238 his nephew Gordian III was recognised as emperor by the whole Roman world. Edward Gibbon, in The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, wrote that twenty-two acknowledged concubines and a library of sixty-two thousand volumes attested to the variety of his inclinations.
gordian-iii: Gordian III was born on 20 January 225, the son of Maecia Faustina, daughter of Emperor Gordian I and sister of Emperor Gordian II, and her husband Junius Balbus, who died before 238. Their names come from the unreliable Historia Augusta, and very little is known of his early life before his acclamation. In 238 a rebellion in the province of Africa proclaimed his grandfather and uncle joint emperors against Maximinus Thrax, but it was suppressed within a month by Cappellianus, the governor of Numidia and a loyal supporter of Maximinus.

The Senate, hostile to Maximinus, elected Pupienus and Balbinus as joint emperors. As these senators were not popular, it raised Gordian to the rank of Caesar. Maximinus' march met difficulties in an Alpine winter, and at Aquileia, short of supplies, he besieged the city; after four weeks his demoralized army mutinied and the Legio II Parthica murdered him. Pupienus and Balbinus then faced popular riots, military discontent and an enormous fire in Rome, and the Praetorian Guard killed them. Gordian was proclaimed sole emperor, probably around August, at the age of 13. Because of his youth, the imperial government passed to the aristocratic families who controlled Rome through the Senate.

In 240 Sabinianus revolted in Africa but was quickly defeated. In 241 Gordian married Furia Sabinia Tranquillina, daughter of the newly appointed praetorian prefect Timesitheus, who as father-in-law and chief of the Guard became the de facto ruler of the empire. Severe earthquakes in his reign led him to consult the Sibylline Books.

When the Sasanians under Shapur I invaded Mesopotamia, Gordian opened the doors of the Temple of Janus for the last time in Roman history and sent a large army east. The Sasanians were driven back over the Euphrates and defeated at the Battle of Resaena in 243. Timesitheus then died in unclear circumstances, and Gaius Julius Priscus and later his brother Marcus Julius Philippus, Philip the Arab, became the Praetorian Prefects. Around February 244 the Sasanians fought hard to halt the Roman advance to Ctesiphon.

The accounts of Gordian's fate differ. An inscription of Shapur I claims a major Sasanian victory near modern Fallujah and Gordian's death. Roman sources say the soldiers proclaimed Philip emperor, that he made a shameful peace, and that Gordian died as the army left; Zonaras says he fell from his horse in battle. One view holds that he was murdered by his frustrated army at Zaitha, and scholars regard the Sasanian version as better than the Roman one. Accounts of his burial also differ: David S. Potter says Philip brought the body to Rome and arranged his deification, while Edwell, Dodgeon and Lieu say it was buried at Zaitha.
gordion: Gordion lies at the site of modern Yassıhüyük, 70 to 80 kilometres south-west of Ankara, where the Sakarya and Porsuk rivers meet. The ancient road between Lydia and Assyria and Babylonia crossed the Sangarius river here. People lived on the site from the Early Bronze Age, about 2300 BCE, until the 4th century CE, and again in the 13th and 14th centuries. The Citadel Mound covers about 13.5 hectares, and at its largest the settlement spread over about 100 hectares.

In the Late Bronze Age Gordion belonged to the Hittite Empire, at the western edge of its heartland. A circuit wall and the East Citadel Gate were built in the Early Phrygian period of the 10th and 9th centuries BCE, and the gate still stands ten metres high, the best preserved in Anatolia. Tumulus W, about 850 BCE, is the first known tumulus burial in Anatolia. The megaron halls on the citadel include some of the earliest known pebble-mosaic floors. A fire about 800 BCE sealed this level. It was once blamed on a Cimmerian attack around 700 BCE, but radiocarbon dating and tree-ring analysis show it was about a century earlier and probably accidental.

After the fire the citadel was rebuilt on a similar plan, and the city grew into the capital of a kingdom controlling much of Asia Minor west of the Halys. Midas was probably on the throne by about 740 BCE, and Assyrian sources of about 718 to 709 BCE call him Mit-ta-a. Tumulus MM, over fifty metres high and about three hundred metres across, was built about 740 BCE. Excavated in 1957, it held a royal burial on purple and golden textiles in a log coffin, with bronze vessels and well-preserved carved wooden furniture. It is generally assumed to be the tomb of Midas' father Gordias.

Cyrus the Great's forces besieged Gordion in 546 BCE, and it passed to the Achaemenid Empire. Alexander the Great came in 333 BCE, and by tradition cut the Gordian Knot, which tied the yoke to the pole of a wagon on the acropolis; a prophecy said that whoever loosened it would rule Asia. Galatians settled there from the mid-3rd century BCE. The site was abandoned in the 1st century BCE and refounded under Rome.

Gustav and Alfred Körte excavated the site in 1900, and the University of Pennsylvania Museum worked there from 1950 under Rodney S. Young. Finds are displayed in the Museum of Anatolian Civilizations in Ankara, the Istanbul Archaeological Museums and the Gordion Museum in Yassıhöyük. Gordion was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.
gorgan: The present city of Gorgan is the capital of Golestan province and lies about 400 km north-east of Tehran and some 30 km from the Caspian Sea. North of it stretches the wide Dasht-e Gorgan, the Plain of Gorgan. The city has hot, humid summers and cool, wet winters, with about 584 millimetres of rain a year, while the Gorgan valley has a semi-arid climate. Some 150 km to the east is the Golestan National Park.

More than 50 archaeological sites lie on the Gorgan Plain, among them Tureng Tepe and Shah Tepe, with remains from the Neolithic and Chalcolithic periods. According to the Greek historian Arrian, Zadracarta was the largest city of Hyrcania and the site of its royal palace. Hyrcania became part of the Achaemenid Empire under Cyrus the Great or his successor Cambyses. The Great Wall of Gorgan was built in the Parthian and Sasanian periods, and under the Sasanians the name Gurgan was used for a city, a provincial capital and a province.

The region kept its independence as a Zoroastrian state even after the Arab conquest of Persia in the 7th century. In 1210 the city was invaded and sacked by the army of the Kingdom of Georgia under the Mkhargrdzeli brothers. Old Gorgan was destroyed during the Mongol invasion of the 13th century, and the centre of the region moved to Astarabad, which is the city now called Gorgan. Astarabad was an important political and religious city in the Qajar era.

The census of 2016 counted 350,676 people in the city, against 269,226 in 2006. It has several universities, among them Golestan University and Gorgan University. Among the people the city counts as its own are the 11th-century poet Fakhroddin Asaad Gorgani, composer of Vis and Ramin, the 11th-century grammarian Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani, and Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar, Shah of Iran from 1789 to 1797.
gorgias: Gorgias was born about 483 BCE in Leontinoi, a Chalcidian colony in eastern Sicily allied with Athens. His brother Herodicus was a physician who sometimes travelled with him. Several ancient writers report that he studied under the philosopher Empedocles of Acragas, though it is not known when or for how long. In 427 BCE, when he was about sixty, his fellow citizens sent him to Athens as head of an embassy to ask for protection against Syracusan aggression.

After 427 BCE he seems to have settled in mainland Greece, living in several cities including Athens and Larisa. He was an itinerant teacher who gave public displays at Olympia and Delphi and charged fees. According to Aristotle his pupils included Isocrates, and he is thought to have influenced Thucydides and the tragic poet Agathon.

Gorgias is credited with bringing rhetoric from Sicily to Attica and with spreading the Attic dialect as the language of literary prose. He is held to be the first orator known to develop and teach a distinctive style, and he introduced paradoxical expression, called paradoxologia. His surviving rhetorical works are the Encomium of Helen, the Defense of Palamedes, On Non-Existence and the Epitaphios, which come to us through a rhetorical manual called the Technai; only the first two are believed to survive complete.

In the Encomium he argues that Helen should not be blamed for going to Troy, whether the gods, force, love or speech led her, and he compares the effect of speech on the soul to that of drugs on the body. The lost On Non-Existence is known only from paraphrases by Sextus Empiricus and the author of On Melissus, Xenophanes, and Gorgias. It argued that nothing exists, that if it did it could not be known, and that if known it could not be communicated. Because of it he has been called a nihilist, a label that most recent scholars reject.

Gorgias is reputed to have lived past a hundred. A gold statue of him was set up in the temple of Apollo at Delphi after his Pythian Oration. He died at Larisa in Thessaly. In antiquity Plato named a dialogue after him and portrayed him as a shallow orator, and Aristotle called him a sophist who aimed at profit. For most of western history he was a marginal figure, until writers in the nineteenth century, among them Hegel and George Grote, began to rehabilitate the sophists.
gorgon: According to Hesiod and Apollodorus, the Gorgons were daughters of the sea-god Phorcys and the sea-monster Ceto, and sisters of the Graeae. Hyginus makes them daughters of a single Gorgon, offspring of Typhon and Echidna. In Euripides' Ion the Gorgon is a child of Gaia, born to help the Giants against the Olympian gods. The name is associated with the Greek adjective gorgós, meaning grim, fierce or awesome when said of an eye or look. Where the Gorgons lived varies in the sources: Hesiod puts them far to the west beyond Oceanus, and Aeschylus in the far east on the plains of Cisthene.

Stheno and Euryale were immortal, but Medusa was mortal. In Apollodorus' version Polydectes ordered Perseus to bring back Medusa's head. Guided by Hermes and Athena, Perseus took the one eye and one tooth the Graeae shared and so learned the way to the nymphs, who gave him winged sandals and the cap of Hades. Hermes gave him an adamantine sickle. Perseus found the Gorgons asleep and beheaded Medusa while looking at her reflection in his bronze shield. Pegasus and Chrysaor sprang from her neck. He gave the head to Athena, who set it on her aegis.

Homer and Hesiod, around 700 to 650 BCE, give the earliest literary accounts. In the Iliad the Gorgon is a dread monster whose head on the aegis is grim and glaring. Apollodorus describes Gorgons with dragon scales, tusks like a swine's, brazen hands and golden wings. By the 5th century BCE Pindar could call Medusa beautiful, and Ovid says she was once a beautiful maiden whom Minerva punished by turning her hair into snakes.

Gorgons were a popular subject in Greek, Etruscan and Roman art, with over six hundred representations catalogued. The earliest, of the mid-7th century BCE, are a Boeotian relief pithos and the Eleusis Amphora. Archaic Gorgons have snaky hair, menacing eyes, wide mouths with lolling tongues and tusks, and the head always faces the viewer.

The gorgoneion, the face alone, is the most frequent of Greek demon images. It is thought to have protected the object that bore it, and it appears on temple pediments, antefixes, shields, coins and the bases of cups. From the 5th century BCE Gorgons were increasingly shown as beautiful young women, and after the 4th century BCE full-bodied Gorgons were no longer made.
goris: Goris lies in the valley of the Goris, or Vararak, River, surrounded by the Zangezur Mountains, at an average elevation of 1,385 metres. It is 254 kilometres from Yerevan and 67 kilometres from Kapan, the provincial capital. The mountains to the south and east are known for medieval cave dwellings carved from the soft rock. The place has been called Kores and Gorayk, and one explanation derives the name from Indo-European prelanguage words for rock and to be, meaning a rocky place.

The area has been settled since the Stone Age. A cuneiform inscription of King Rusa I of Urartu, who reigned from 735 to 713 BCE, names Guria or Goriaya among 23 countries he conquered, and some scholars connect it with Goris. In the Middle Ages the settlement, called Kores, stood on the left bank of the river and appears in Stepanos Orbelian's 13th-century History of the Province of Syunik. In the early 16th century the region became part of Safavid Persia, and in 1813 the Treaty of Gulistan gave it to the Russian Empire.

The Russians founded the town in 1870 as the centre of the Zangezur uezd, and the new town was completed in 1876 near old Kores to a plan by a German architect. After the fall of the First Republic of Armenia in 1920, a congress at Tatev declared the Republic of Mountainous Armenia on 26 April 1921, with Goris as its de facto capital and Garegin Nzhdeh as leader. It capitulated on 13 July 1921 after Red Army operations, on Soviet promises to keep Zangezur in Soviet Armenia. Under Soviet rule the town was a regional centre, and its economy grew with hydroelectric plants and new industry.

Goris is a town in Syunik Province and the seat of the Diocese of Syunik of the Armenian Apostolic Church. The Cathedral of Saint Gregory the Illuminator was built between 1897 and 1904, and in February 1921 Nzhdeh was announced there as commander of the forces of the coming republic. The stone pyramids of Old Kores and the 4th-century basilica of Saint Hripsime stand in the old town. The archaeological museum opened in 1948, and a house museum of the writer Axel Bakunts has operated since 1970.
gorizia: Gorizia stands at the foot of the Julian Alps and the confluence of the Isonzo and Vipava valleys, on the border with Slovenia. Its name comes from the Slovene word gorica, little mountain. The place began as a watchtower or castle controlling the fords of the Isonzo. Sheltered from the cold bora wind, the town has a mild climate, and in the 19th century it was a summer resort of the Austrian nobility.

The name Goriza was first recorded on 28 April 1001, when Emperor Otto III gave the castle and village to the Patriarch of Aquileia and Count Verihen of Friuli. Count Meinhard is mentioned in 1107 and by 1127 styled himself Count of Gorizia. Between the 12th century and the early 16th, the town was the centre of the essentially independent County of Gorizia, whose lands at their height reached from Friuli and Istria to western Carinthia and East Tyrol.

The dynasty of the counts died out in 1500 and the county passed to Habsburg rule, after a short Venetian occupation in 1508 and 1509. Friulian, German and Slovene were all spoken in the town. The Archdiocese of Gorizia was established in 1751 after the suppression of the Patriarchate of Aquileia. Before the First World War the town had around 31,000 inhabitants, of whom about 48 percent spoke Italian or Friulian and 35 percent Slovene.

Italy entered the war in May 1915, and the hills west of the town became a scene of fierce battles on the Isonzo front. Italian forces took Gorizia in August 1916, and Austro-Hungarian forces regained it after Caporetto in 1917. It became part of Italy in 1920, and under the Fascist regime Slovene organisations were dissolved and the public use of Slovene was prohibited.
