A provincial governor could take over the whole government in a breakdown, and at the centre defence, foreign affairs, the army and India's financial obligations stayed under British control. Unlike the 1919 act, it had no preamble promising responsible government, and it contained no bill of rights.

No significant group in India accepted the federal part. Jawaharlal Nehru called it "a machine with strong brakes but no engine", and Jinnah "thoroughly rotten, fundamentally bad and totally unacceptable". In Britain Winston Churchill, who had campaigned against Indian self-government since 1929, denounced the bill in the House of Commons.

The federation required half the princely states by weight to join; they did not, and it was postponed indefinitely when the Second World War began. The viceroy Lord Linlithgow brought in provincial autonomy after the 1937 elections, but when he declared India at war with Germany in September 1939 without consulting its elected representatives, the Congress provincial ministries resigned and the governors ruled those provinces directly through the war. Modified by the Indian Independence Act 1947, the act served as the interim constitution of India and Pakistan.
government-of-ireland-act-1920: Earlier attempts at Irish home rule had failed: the First Home Rule Bill of 1886 was defeated in the Commons and the Second, of 1893, was vetoed by the House of Lords. The Third, introduced in 1912, received royal assent a few weeks after Britain entered the First World War, but the Suspensory Act 1914 put off its implementation for the war's duration. Meanwhile the Easter Rising of 1916 and the Conscription Crisis of 1918 helped make Sinn Féin the dominant voice of Irish nationalism.

Sinn Féin won 73 of the 105 Irish seats in the 1918 general election, refused to sit at Westminster and set up Dáil Éireann, which declared independence as the Irish Republic. From September 1919 a cabinet committee under Walter Long, a former leader of the Irish Unionist Alliance, proposed two home rule entities with separate parliaments. The bill passed its third reading on 11 November 1920 by 183 votes to 52; all the Ulster Unionist MPs voted against it, preferring that Ulster remain fully within the United Kingdom.

Northern Ireland was defined as the parliamentary counties of Antrim, Armagh, Down, Fermanagh, Londonderry and Tyrone and the boroughs of Belfast and Londonderry, seen as the largest area in which Unionists could expect a safe majority, although Fermanagh and Tyrone had nationalist majorities in 1918. Each territory was to govern itself except in matters reserved to Westminster, chief among them the Crown, defence, foreign affairs, international trade and currency. A Lord Lieutenant would represent the monarch in both and appoint a cabinet; no provision existed for a prime minister.

The act came into force on 3 May 1921, the date taken as the founding of Northern Ireland, whose parliament first met in Belfast City Hall in June 1921, when King George V appealed for reconciliation. In the south all 128 members were returned unopposed in May 1921, and the 124 of Sinn Féin assembled as the Second Dáil; the Parliament of Southern Ireland, attended by four unionist members and fifteen senators, was suspended. The Irish Free State came into being on 6 December 1922, and Northern Ireland opted out of it the next day.

The Council of Ireland, of 20 members from each parliament, which Britain intended to grow into a single Irish parliament, never met. Northern Ireland's institutions under the act worked until the British parliament suspended them in 1972 during the Troubles, and the last provisions in force were repealed under the Northern Ireland Act 1998, after the Good Friday Agreement.
gozo: Gozo, in Maltese Għawdex, was known in antiquity as Gaulos and later as Gaudos, from which the Arabic name derives. It is the second-largest island of the Maltese archipelago and is rural in character, less developed than the island of Malta.

Gozo has been inhabited since 5000 BCE, when farmers from nearby Sicily crossed the sea. Similar pottery of the Għar Dalam phase has led to the suggestion that the first colonists came from the area of Agrigento, but where in Sicily they came from is not known. During the Neolithic period the Ġgantija temples were built, which are among the oldest free-standing structures and the oldest religious structures in the world. The name means belonging to the giants, because Maltese and Gozitan folklore says that giants built them. Native tradition and some ancient Greek writers, notably Euhemerus and Callimachus, hold that Gozo is the island Homer described as Ogygia, home of the nymph Calypso.

The Carthaginians occupied Gozo and built a temple to Astarte. Local coins with a Greek inscription suggest that it fell to the Greeks at some time, and it was probably annexed by Rome about 218 BCE. In the 1st century BCE it minted its own bronze coins bearing the head of Astarte and the legend Gaulitōn.

In 1530 the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V gave Gozo, with Malta, to the Knights Hospitalier. In July 1551 an Ottoman force under Sinan Pasha and Dragut invaded and ravaged the island, enslaving most of its 5,000 inhabitants and taking them to Libya. Mainland Maltese repopulated the island between 1565 and 1580 under the Knights. Gozo has generally been governed with Malta. The exception came after the French garrison surrendered to the British under Captain Alexander Ball on 28 October 1798, when Gozo was briefly independent until the French garrison in Valletta surrendered on 4 September 1800. Malta and Gozo then became a British protectorate and in 1813 a Crown colony.

Gozo is part of the Republic of Malta and had about 39,287 inhabitants in 2021, called Gozitans. It has its own Roman Catholic bishopric, the only suffragan of the Archbishop of Malta. The main town is Victoria, and ferries link the port of Mġarr to Ċirkewwa on Malta.
graaff-reinet: Graaff-Reinet lies in the Eastern Cape, 750 metres above sea level, on the banks of the Sundays River, which rises a little further north on the southern slopes of the Sneeuberge and splits into several channels at the town. It is the oldest town in the province and the sixth oldest in South Africa, after Cape Town, Stellenbosch, Simon's Town, Paarl and Swellendam. It is known for its mohair industry and for sheep and ostrich farming.

The Dutch East India Company established the town in 1786. It is named after the then governor of the Cape Colony, Cornelis Jacob van de Graaff, and his wife. In 1795 its burghers proclaimed themselves the independent Colony of Graaff-Reinet and asked the government of the Netherlands for guardianship, and the burghers of Swellendam took similar action. The authorities at Cape Town had to capitulate to the British, who invaded and occupied the Cape before they could act against the rebels.

In January 1799 Marthinus Prinsloo, a leader of the 1795 movement, rebelled again but surrendered that April. He and another commandant were sentenced to death after trial, but the sentences were not carried out, and the prisoners were released in March 1803 when the Cape returned to the Netherlands. Another revolt in 1801 ended through the measures of General Francis Dundas. The town sent groups of Voortrekkers on the Great Trek under Gerrit Maritz and Piet Retief and supplied many Voortrekkers in 1835–1842.

A railway to Port Elizabeth, begun in 1877, was officially opened on 26 August 1879. In the Second Boer War the town was the centre of British military operations for the Eastern Cape. In 1901 captured Boer rebels were tried there, and eight of nine death sentences were carried out by firing squad on its outskirts. A monument commemorates them.

Graaff-Reinet has more national monuments than any other town or city in South Africa. Its sights include the Dutch Reformed church, a stone building seating 1,500 whose architecture is influenced by Salisbury Cathedral, the Reinet House Museum, a Cape Dutch building that was formerly the church parsonage, the Valley of Desolation and Camdeboo National Park.
gracanica-monastery: Gračanica was built to replace an older cathedral of the Holy Virgin of the 13th century, which stood on the same spot in the centre of the Eparchy of Lipljan. A founder's inscription on the southern wall, in the words of King Stefan Milutin, says that he saw the ruins of the temple and built it from the ground. After the Serbian Archbishopric became a Patriarchate in 1346, the bishops of Lipljan were called metropolitans of Lipljan or Gračanica.

The narthex and tower were added a few decades later to protect the frescoes of the west facade. The Ottomans damaged the narthex several times between 1379 and 1383, when the tower was burned and a fire destroyed a rich collection of manuscripts; it was rebuilt in 1383. Under Ottoman rule the monastery kept some of its lands. Metropolitan Nikanor, in office from 1528 to 1555, had icons painted for the altarpiece and in 1538-1539 set up a Cyrillic printing press, which published the Gračanica Octoechos. Patriarch Makarije Sokolović had new frescoes completed in 1570. Of the former compound only the church survives, and nuns renewed it as a convent after the Second World War.

The church has the form of a double inscribed cross, one inside the other, which lifts the central dome on a graded arrangement of masses. The dome rests on four free-standing pillars, with four smaller domes above the spaces between the arms of the cross. The walls are built in alternate courses of brick and stone. It is regarded as the culmination of medieval Serbian building in the Serbo-Byzantine tradition.

The frescoes of the nave were painted in 1321-1322 and show the earthly life of Jesus and the church calendar. In the narthex are portraits of the founders, King Milutin and Queen Simonida, with Queen Helen, the king's mother, as a nun, and Milutin as a monk. It also holds the earliest painted genealogy of the Nemanjić dynasty, from Stefan Nemanja to Milutin, and a large Last Judgment.

The paintings rank highest among the achievements of Milutin's period and show the influence of the Byzantine style known as the Paleologan Renaissance. The Church of Saint Sava in Belgrade takes Gračanica and Hagia Sophia as models, and a detailed replica, the New Gračanica church in Chicago, was consecrated in 1984. In 2006 the monastery was placed on UNESCO's World Heritage List, as an extension of the Visoki Dečani site, under the name Medieval Monuments in Kosovo.
gracchi: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus was born about 163 BCE and his younger brother Gaius about 154 BCE. Their father, also Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, had been consul in 177 and 163 BCE and censor in 169 BCE. Their mother Cornelia was the daughter of Scipio Africanus, and their sister Sempronia married Scipio Aemilianus. Tiberius began his military career in 147 BCE under Scipio Aemilianus at Carthage, where he was among the first to scale the walls.

In 137 BCE, as quaestor under the consul Gaius Hostilius Mancinus in Hispania Citerior, he negotiated a treaty of surrender after a failed campaign in the Numantine War. The senate rejected it humiliatingly. Cicero later attributed his reforms to an attempt to win back standing after that episode, while favourable sources credit spirited advocacy for the poor.

Tiberius' land law as tribune in 133 BCE had three aims: a commission to survey the public land, a limit of about 500 jugera for any one possessor, and distribution of the remainder to poor Roman citizens, with Italians excluded. It was meant to stimulate population growth and enlarge the number of men qualified for army service. The commission distributed more than 3,268 square kilometres in its first few years. Tiberius was killed in 133 BCE, and the consular commission of 132 BCE passed sentences of exile on his supporters.

Gaius, elected tribune in the elections of 124 BCE, presented himself as the heir of his brother's programme, but most of his proposals did not concern land. He extended the right of provocatio to the sentences passed on Tiberius' supporters, and his lex repetundarum created an equestrian jury to try senatorial governors for provincial corruption. Both brothers were killed during or shortly after their tribunician terms.

The death of Tiberius is widely viewed as the start of the late republic. Jürgen von Ungern-Sternberg writes that his assassination made 133 BCE a turning point and the beginning of the crisis of the Republic, since the use of violence against political enemies then became acceptable. Modern historians stress that archaeology does not support the ancient picture of a collapsing Italian peasantry, and that most of the brothers' legislation was not repealed.

Ancient sources are late and mostly follow the narrative of Gaius and his supporters, so what is known of Tiberius is filtered through his brother. Later ages saw them as martyrs or demagogues. The revolutionary François-Noël Babeuf took the name Gracchus in the French Revolution, though modern scholars regard comparisons with socialism as unapt.
grace-omalley: Grace O'Malley was born in Ireland around 1530, the only child of Eoghan Dubhdara Ó Máille, Chief of the Name of Clan Ó Máille and Lord of Umhaill, based at Clew Bay in County Mayo. The Uí Mháille were a seafaring clan of Connacht with a row of castles facing the sea, and they demanded black rent from those who fished off their coasts, even fishermen from England. They recognised the Mac William Íochtar branch of the Bourkes as nominal overlords.

Local oral tradition says that as a girl she cut off most of her hair to shame her father into taking her on a trading voyage to Spain, which earned her the nickname Gráinne Mhaol. She was married in 1546 to Dónal an Chogaidh Ó Flaithbheartaigh, heir to the Chief of the Name of Clan Ó Flaithbheartaigh, and bore three children.

Dónal was killed in an ambush in 1565. When the Joyces moved against Hen's Castle on Lough Corrib, thinking she would not resist, she fought them off, and she then returned to her own lands and made Clare Island her principal residence. By 1566 she had married Risdeárd an Iarainn Bourke, the Mac William Íochtar, so called for his ironworks at Burrishoole.

In 1576 she took part in the surrender and regrant process with the Lord Deputy Sir Henry Sidney. Sir Richard Bingham, Lord President of Connacht, called her in 1593 nurse to all rebellions in the province for forty years. An expedition from Galway attacked her castle on Clare Island in March 1579 but was put to flight.

In 1593 Bingham captured her son Tibbot Bourke and her half-brother Dónal an Phíopa, and O'Malley petitioned Elizabeth I and travelled to England. Tradition, but not the written sources, places a meeting at Greenwich Palace, and many tales have grown around it. The Queen ordered the release of the prisoners and asked that provision be made for O'Malley from her sons' estates. Bingham at first resisted. He later quartered soldiers on her ships and property, which impoverished her. During the Nine Years' War she supported her son Tibbot in fighting for the Crown against Tyrone's confederation.

She most likely died at Rockfleet Castle around 1603, the year of Elizabeth's death, though the year and place are disputed. Her family's usual burial place was Clare Island Abbey. She is not mentioned in the Irish annals, so most evidence comes from English sources such as State Papers and the eighteen Articles of Interrogatory put to her on the Queen's behalf. No contemporary image of her survives. The historian Anne Chambers, her biographer, describes her as a fearless leader by land and sea and a shrewd negotiator. The Browne family of Westport House, Marquesses of Sligo, descend from her.
gracias-a-la-vida: Gracias a la vida, Oh Life, Thank You, is one of Violeta Parra's best-known songs and one of the most covered Latin American songs. The Chilean music journalist Marisol García called it a humanist hymn, and in 2013 it entered the Latin Grammy Hall of Fame. In 2009 Michelle Bachelet expressed her affection and admiration for the song and for Mercedes Sosa, calling it a song of Chile's own but also a universal one.

Sosa's version of 1971, on her album Homenaje a Violeta Parra, made the song popular across the Spanish-speaking world. Joan Baez introduced it to the United States on her album of the same title in 1974 and kept it in her concerts, and the Italian singer-songwriter Gabriella Ferri made it popular in Italy on her album Remedios the same year. Later recordings include those of Cote de Pablo for the 2015 film The 33 and Kacey Musgraves on her album Star-Crossed in 2021, as well as versions by the cellist Yo-Yo Ma, the mezzo-soprano Elīna Garanča and the Cuban singer Omara Portuondo.

After the Chilean earthquake of 2010, Beto Cuevas, former singer of the group La Ley, brought together the supergroup Voces Unidas por Chile to record the song for the victims. Produced by the Chilean Humberto Gatica and released on 4 May 2010, it featured among others the Colombians Shakira and Juanes, the Dominican Juan Luis Guerra, the Mexican Fernando Olvera, the Spanish singers Alejandro Sanz and Miguel Bosé, the Italian Laura Pausini and the Canadian Michael Bublé.

Warner Music released it internationally on disc and as a download, and the profits went to Habitat for Humanity, which provides housing for families in need in several countries, Chile among them. Pausini compared Chile's loss with the earthquake her own country had suffered in the Abruzzo region the year before.
grameen-bank: Muhammad Yunus, a professor at the University of Chittagong, was inspired by the Bangladesh famine of 1974 to lend a total of 27 US dollars to 42 people, mostly makers of bamboo stools, as start-up money free of predatory interest. He began a research project with the university and Janata Bank to test a way of giving credit to the rural poor, and in 1976 the village of Jobra became the first to be served. The project reached the Tangail District in 1979 and then more districts.

An ordinance dated 2 October 1983 turned it into the Grameen Bank, whose name means village bank in Bengali. The bankers Ron Grzywinski and Mary Houghton of ShoreBank, a community development bank in Chicago, helped Yunus incorporate it under a grant from the Ford Foundation.

The bank rests on the principle that loans are better than charity for reducing hardship. It lends to groups usually without access to formal finance, such as the poor, women and the illiterate, on terms of group lending and weekly instalments. No written contract is made with borrowers, and the system works on trust. Repayment rests on the individual, and no formal joint liability exists, though members often cover a defaulter's debt, since the bank gives no further credit to a group in which a member defaults. About 97 per cent of its members are women.

Borrowers recite the Sixteen Decisions, which encourage habits such as sending children to school. Funding came at first from donor agencies, from the mid-1990s chiefly from the central bank of Bangladesh, and since 1995, 90 per cent of its loans have been financed by interest income and customer deposits. The bank also runs a Village Phone programme for women entrepreneurs in rural areas.

The bank's Low-cost Housing Program won a World Habitat Award in 1998, and the bank and Yunus were jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006. Its success has inspired similar projects in more than 64 countries, including a World Bank initiative to finance Grameen-type lending systems. In 2013 the Bangladesh parliament passed the Grameen Bank Act, replacing the ordinance of 1983.
gran-chaco: The Gran Chaco, also called the Chaco or Chaco Plain, covers about one million square kilometres across eastern Bolivia, western Paraguay, northern Argentina and parts of Brazil, and forms part of the Río de la Plata basin. It lies west of the Paraguay River and east of the Andes and is mostly an alluvial plain. The name comes from the Quechua word chaqu, meaning hunting land.

The region has historically been divided into three parts: the Chaco Austral south of the Bermejo River, the Chaco Central between the Bermejo and the Pilcomayo, both now in Argentina, and the Chaco Boreal north of the Pilcomayo as far as the Brazilian Pantanal, in Paraguay and partly Bolivia. The west is dry and sparsely vegetated, while the east has a seasonally flooded plain with palm savanna and quebracho trees, the source of timber and tannin. Jaguars, peccaries, armadillos and tapirs live there; the Chacoan peccary was thought extinct until 1975.

Nomadic peoples, notably the Guaycuru groups, occupied the Chaco and resisted Spanish control, often successfully, from the 16th until the early 20th century. Other peoples of the region include the Wichí, Qom, Pilagá, Guaraní and Ayoreo. The Spaniards treated the whole area as a colonial region called Chiquitos before independence.

The Chaco was disputed territory from 1810. Argentina claimed land north of the Bermejo River until Paraguay's defeat in the War of the Triple Alliance fixed its present border with Argentina. Over the following decades Bolivia pushed the indigenous peoples out and settled in the Chaco, while Paraguay paid little attention. After losing its Pacific coast in the War of the Pacific, Bolivia sought the Paraguay River as an outlet, and the conflict over the Chaco Boreal, and supposed oil there, led to the Chaco War of 1932–1935 between Paraguay and Bolivia.

The Argentine foreign minister Carlos Saavedra Lamas mediated a ceasefire and a treaty signed in 1938, which gave Paraguay three quarters of the Chaco Boreal and gave Bolivia a corridor to the Paraguay River with use of Puerto Casado.

Mennonites came to the Paraguayan Chaco from Canada in the 1920s, and more arrived from the the USSR in the 1930s and after the Second World War; they founded some of the region's largest and most prosperous municipalities. In the 1960s Paraguay built the Trans-Chaco Highway, and Argentina built National Routes 16 and 81, each running about 700 km from east to west. Kaa-Iya del Gran Chaco National Park in Bolivia was established in September 1995 and is administered by indigenous peoples, among them the Izoceño Guaraní, the Ayoreode and the Chiquitano.
gran-colombia-peru-war: The war was the first international conflict of Peru, independent since 1821. Colonial borders between the Viceroyalty of Peru and the Royal Audience of Quito, part of the Viceroyalty of New Granada from 1717, had never been clear, and a royal decree of 1802 moved the military and church administration of Maynas to Peru without settling whether the land went with it. Simón Bolívar's principle of uti possidetis juris, borders as they stood in 1809, left much of present-day Ecuador open to claims by both sides. Early in 1828 Peru forced the Colombians out of Bolivia, and Bolívar resolved on war.

Both presidents, José de La Mar and Simón Bolívar, ordered mobilisation on 3 July 1828, and Sucre, who had resigned the presidency of Bolivia under duress, took command of the Gran Colombian army. At sea the Peruvian corvette Libertad won the battle of Malpelo on 31 August. The Peruvian squadron under Admiral Martin George Guisse attacked Guayaquil from 22 to 24 November; Guisse was mortally wounded, but his first lieutenant, José Boterín, kept up the siege, and the city surrendered on 19 January 1829 and stayed occupied until 21 July.

On land the Peruvians took Loja after a surprise attack on Saraguro on 13 February 1829 and occupied Cuenca, La Mar's birthplace. Sucre and General Juan José Flores then met them near Cuenca at Portete de Tarqui on 26 and 27 February. La Mar and Sucre signed the La Mar-Sucre Convention on 28 February, but La Mar refused to give back Guayaquil and strengthened his army at Piura while Bolívar prepared to take command.

The Armistice of Piura of 10 July 1829 returned Guayaquil to Gran Colombia and recognised Tumbes, Jaén and Maynas as Peruvian. A peace treaty signed on 22 September 1829 affirmed uti possidetis, allowed small concessions for a more natural border and set up a joint commission to fix it. Because the old viceregal borders had never been well defined, later disputes were almost certain. Ecuador came to rest its claims against Peru on the Pedemonte-Mosquera Protocol, said to have been signed in Lima on 11 August 1830; Peru disputes that it ever existed, since no original has been produced.
gran-sasso: Gran Sasso d'Italia, meaning the Great Rock of Italy, is a massif of the Apennine Mountains. Its highest summit, Corno Grande, at 2,912 metres, is the highest in the Apennines and the second highest in Italy outside the Alps. The other main summits are Corno Piccolo and Pizzo d'Intermesoli, which a deep valley, Val Maone, separates from the other two. The ash colour of Corno Grande and Corno Piccolo comes from their limestone and dolomite, and their rough vertical walls attract rock climbers. Corno Piccolo is known as the Sleeping Giant for its profile of a reclined face.

The mid and lower slopes are grazed in spring, summer and autumn by sheep, cattle and semi-wild horses. The park is home to the Apennine wolf, the Marsican bear, the European wildcat and the Abruzzo chamois, as well as golden eagles and peregrine falcons. East of Corno Grande and Corno Piccolo lies Campo Imperatore, a high plain 27 kilometres long and 8 wide at about 2,000 metres.

The Hotel Campo Imperatore was Benito Mussolini's prison until September 1943, when Nazi commandos freed him in the Gran Sasso raid. On the southern edge of the plain lie three medieval hill towns once ruled by the Medici: Calascio, below the ruined fortress of Rocca di Calascio, Santo Stefano di Sessanio and Castel del Monte. Pope John Paul II visited the Gran Sasso several times, and in 2005 a peak of 2,424 metres once called the Gendarme was renamed John Paul II Peak.

A ten-kilometre motorway tunnel for the A24 was bored through the massif in 1984, with a second tunnel completed in 1995. Its construction included the Gran Sasso National Laboratory at Assergi, an underground physics laboratory beneath 1,400 metres of rock whose first large experiments began in 1989. Opposition to the tunnel and laboratory from Italian and international environmental groups is credited by some with spurring the Italian environmental movement and the creation of the Gran Sasso and Monti della Laga National Park in 1991.

The massif lies within the Gran Sasso and Monti della Laga National Park. Its low background radiation makes the laboratory a site for work on neutrinos, cosmic rays, dark matter and nuclear decay. Campo Imperatore has Italy's oldest continuously operating commercial ski area, reached by cable car from Fonte Cerreto, and a station of the Rome Observatory. The Alpine Botanical Garden of Campo Imperatore and Lake Pietranzoni are among its points of interest.
granada: Granada lies in Andalusia at the foot of the Sierra Nevada, at the confluence of four rivers, the Darro, the Genil, the Monachil and the Beiro. It sits on the Vega de Granada, at an average elevation of 738 m and about 50 km from the Mediterranean coast. The pomegranate, granada in Spanish, is its heraldic device. The meaning of its Arabic name, Ġarnāṭa, is uncertain and debated.

The area has been populated since at least 5500 BCE. The oldest ruins belong to an oppidum called Ilturir, founded by the Iberian Bastetani around 650 BCE, later known as Iliberri or Iliberis, which became a Roman colony in 44 BCE. After the Umayyad conquest from 711 CE, the main settlement in the area was Madīnat Ilbīra (Elvira), while a smaller fortified settlement, Ġarnāṭa, with a mainly Jewish population, stood on the Albaicín site. Granada became a major city of al-Andalus in the 11th century under the Zirid Taifa of Granada.

As Almohad rule collapsed after 1228, Castile took Córdoba in 1236 and Seville in 1248. Ibn al-Ahmar (Muhammad I) established the Nasrid dynasty, the last and longest reigning Muslim dynasty in the peninsula, ruling the Emirate of Granada. He became a vassal of Ferdinand III of Castile in 1246, and Granada thereafter was a tributary state of Castile, though wars often interrupted this. On 2 January 1492 Emir Muhammad XI, called Boabdil by the Spanish, surrendered the emirate to the Catholic Monarchs, Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile. The city was progressively made a Christian city during the 16th century, and the University of Granada was founded in 1531 by Charles V.

Granada is the capital of the province of Granada, with a population of 233,532 in 2024. The Alhambra, a fortified palace complex on the Sabika hill and one of the best-preserved palaces of the historic Islamic world, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1984. The Albaicín and other medieval monuments preserve Islamic-period influence, and the 16th century brought Mudéjar and Renaissance architecture. The Sacromonte, with cave houses dug into the hillside, has a reputation as a centre of flamenco.
granada-war: The Emirate of Granada had been the last Muslim state in Iberia for more than two centuries. After the death of Emir Yusuf III in 1417 it lived in almost constant low-level civil war, with clan loyalties stronger than allegiance to the emir. Its economy declined, ordinary Granadans paid triple the taxes of Castilians, and tribute to Castile bled it further. The frontier with Andalusia was in constant flux, with raids and truces. The War of the Castilian Succession from 1475 to 1479 ended with the victory of Isabella, who had married Ferdinand of Aragon in 1469, so that Castile and Aragon stood united.

Granada launched a surprise attack on Zahara on 26 December 1481, and the town's population was enslaved. The Christian seizure of Alhama, endorsed by the Crown, is usually said to mark the formal beginning of the war, and Ferdinand took command there on 14 May 1482. The campaigns were seasonal, launched in spring and broken off in winter. Abu Abdallah, called Boabdil, rebelled against his father, and after Christians captured him at Lucena Ferdinand freed him in 1483 to divide Granada further. In 1485 the Marquis of Cádiz took Ronda after fifteen days, and Marbella followed.

Málaga, Granada's chief port, fell on 18 August 1487 after a siege begun on 7 May, and Ferdinand punished almost all its inhabitants with slavery. Baza surrendered in 1489 after a six-month siege, on generous terms. Boabdil, holding only the city of Granada and the Alpujarras, then rebelled against the Catholic Monarchs, and an eight-month siege of Granada began in April 1491. Artillery shortened the sieges: the historian Weston F. Cook Jr. wrote that gunpowder firepower won the war. The Treaty of Granada was signed on 25 November 1491, and the city capitulated on 2 January 1492.

The treaty's terms were generous. For three years Muslims could emigrate and return freely, and no one was to be forced to change religion. Boabdil was offered money and a small principality in the Alpujarras, but he left for Morocco in October 1493. Castile began to revoke the tolerant terms under Archbishop Cisneros, who ordered mass conversions, and a revolt followed in which many Muslims had to choose between baptism, exile or execution. In 1492 Jews were forced to convert or be exiled, and by 1501 all of Granada's Muslims were obliged to convert, be enslaved or leave. Castile annexed Granada, and the war was later regarded in Spanish historiography as the final war of the Reconquista.
grand-bahama: Grand Bahama is the northernmost of the islands of the Bahamas and the third largest in a chain of approximately 700 islands and 2,400 cays. It covers roughly 1,400 square kilometres and is about 153 kilometres long from west to east and 24 kilometres wide at its widest point. Its westernmost town, West End, lies 104 kilometres east of Palm Beach, Florida. Administratively it consists of the Freeport Bonded Area and the districts of East Grand Bahama and West Grand Bahama. The climate has a hot, rainy season from May to October and a warm, dry season from November to April.

The Lucayan people called the island Bahama, meaning large upper middle island. For almost two centuries its fate was largely governed by the coral reefs around it, which repelled its Spanish claimants, who largely left it alone apart from stops for provisions, and attracted pirates, who lured ships onto the reefs and plundered them. The Spaniards took little interest in the island after enslaving the Lucayan inhabitants. In 1670 Charles II of England granted the Bahamas to the eight Lords Proprietors of the Carolinas, and by 1828 Grand Bahama was almost unpopulated.

During Prohibition in the United States, West End and Bimini served as waystations for illicit liquor imports. In the late 1940s the British firm Butlin's built a resort for 1,000 guests and West End Airport at West End, and ran it for a single season, in 1950, before running out of money.

By the mid-20th century the population was around 500. In 1955 the Virginian financier Wallace Groves began redevelopment with the Bahamian government under the Hawksbill Creek Agreement, creating the Grand Bahama Port Authority and the city of Freeport. Edward St. George, with the financial help of Sir Jack Hayward, added a harbour, an airport and the tourist centre of Port Lucaya in 1962. Grand Bahama became the second most populous island of the Bahamas.

Freeport is the main city, with the commercial harbour and the main airport, and Lucaya is the tourist district. Tourism is the mainstay of the economy, and the island also has an oil storage and transshipment terminal, a container port, quarrying and a shipyard. On 1 September 2019 Hurricane Dorian struck as a Category 5 hurricane and caused catastrophic destruction, damaging or destroying nearly half of the island's homes.
grand-banks-of-newfoundland: The Grand Banks are relatively shallow, ranging from 15 to 91 metres in depth, and the mixing of the cold Labrador Current with the warm waters of the Gulf Stream often causes extreme fog. The mixing of these waters and the shape of the ocean bottom lifts nutrients to the surface, creating one of the richest fishing grounds in the world. Fish include Atlantic cod, swordfish, haddock and capelin, and shellfish include scallop and lobster. The area also supports large colonies of seabirds, such as northern gannets and shearwaters, and sea mammals such as seals, dolphins and whales.

During the Last Glacial Maximum the area was glaciated. By approximately 13,000 years ago most of the ice had melted, leaving the Grand Banks exposed as several islands extending for hundreds of kilometres, which rising seas are believed to have submerged around 8,000 years ago.

No archaeological evidence of a European presence survives from between the Norse settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows in 1000 CE and John Cabot's crossing in 1497, though some evidence suggests voyagers from the Basque Region and Bristol preceded Cabot. Some 15th-century texts refer to a land called Bacalao, the land of the codfish, possibly Newfoundland. Ships from France and Portugal pioneered fishing there, followed by Spain, and ships from England were scarce at first. This changed after Bernard Drake's Newfoundland Expedition in 1585, which virtually wiped out the Spanish and Portuguese fishing industries in the area.

On 18 November 1929 an earthquake struck the south-western Grand Banks, causing an underwater landslide that damaged transatlantic cables and generated a rare Atlantic tsunami. It struck the south coast of Newfoundland and killed 29 people on the Burin Peninsula. From around 1990 large factory ships, sonar and disputes over territorial sea and exclusive economic zone boundaries led to overfishing and a serious decline in fish stocks, particularly of cod.

Canada's exclusive economic zone covers most of the Grand Banks, except the nose, near the Flemish Cap, and the tail. The 1783 Treaty of Paris gave the United States shared fishing rights there, but that section is no longer in force. The French territory of Saint Pierre and Miquelon has its own zone at the western edge. Oil fields such as Hibernia, Terra Nova and White Rose have been developed, and the harsh environment also led to the Ocean Ranger disaster.
grand-bassam: Grand-Bassam lies in south-eastern Ivory Coast, east of Abidjan, and is the seat of Grand-Bassam Department. The Ébrié Lagoon divides it in two. Ancien Bassam, the former French settlement, faces the Gulf of Guinea and holds the grander colonial buildings, some of them restored, as well as a cathedral and the Ivory Coast National Museum of Costume, housed in the former Governor's Palace. Nouveau Bassam lies across a bridge on the inland side of the lagoon; it grew from the African servants' quarters and is now the main commercial centre of the town. The name Bassam may come from an ancient African word for the mouth of the Comoé River.

The Nzema people have lived in the area since the 15th century, and the place grew into a fishing village and trading centre. In 1843, after signing a treaty with the African ruler of the region, the French built Fort Memours on the banks of the river. It became their main trading point in the region and, after the Berlin Conference of 1885, a base for the exploration of West Africa. Grand-Bassam was the capital of the French Colonie de Côte d'Ivoire from 1893. A devastating outbreak of yellow fever that decimated its population led the colonial administration to move to the nearby town of Bingerville.

The town remained a key seaport until Abidjan grew in the 1930s. At independence in 1960 the remaining administrative offices moved to Abidjan, and for many years the town was inhabited only by squatters. From the late 1970s it began to revive as a tourist destination and craft centre.

The historic centre of Grand-Bassam was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012 for its outstanding colonial architecture and town planning and for the juxtaposition of the colonial town with a traditional Nzema village. Large sections of the old town were abandoned for decades, which gave it the aura of a ghost town. It is the seat of a Roman Catholic diocese, whose cathedral is the Cathédrale Sacré Cœur.
grand-cayman: Grand Cayman is the largest of the three Cayman Islands and the site of the territory's capital, George Town. It lies about 75 miles (121 km) south-west of Little Cayman and 90 miles (145 km) south-west of Cayman Brac. It holds 76 per cent of the territory's land. The island is about 22 miles (35 km) long and 8 miles (13 km) wide at its widest, and unlike many Caribbean islands it is mostly flat, rising from sea level at the beaches to 60 feet (18 m) on the Mastic Trail on the North Side. The Central Mangrove Wetland occupies roughly 17.8 per cent of the island.

Grand Cayman includes five of the six districts of the Cayman Islands: Bodden Town, East End, George Town, North Side and West Bay. Bodden Town was founded in the 1700s and was the original capital of the Cayman Islands. West Bay has the Cayman Turtle Farm, which raises green sea turtles for their meat and to release into the wild, and between 1980 and 2006 released about 30,600 turtles. Wildlife includes the blue iguana, Grand Cayman amazon parrots and four endemic snake species, the most common being the Grand Cayman racer; the Grand Cayman thrush is extinct.

Grand Cayman contains about 97 per cent of the territory's population, which the 2021 census recorded at 71,105 for the Cayman Islands as a whole, of whom 39,047 were Caymanians. Expatriates come mostly from Jamaica, the Philippines, the United States, the United Kingdom and India. George Town is a centre of offshore banking, investment and insurance, which drive the island's economy, and tourism is the other mainstay.

Seven Mile Beach has the largest concentration of visitors, and attractions include the blow holes of the East End, Hell in West Bay, the Queen Elizabeth II Botanic Park and the coral reefs, sea walls and shipwrecks popular with divers. Owen Roberts International Airport serves the island and the Port of George Town is its harbour.
grand-council-of-fascism: The Grand Council of Fascism was the main body of Mussolini's government in the Kingdom of Italy, and it held great power over the institutions of government. It was created in 1922 as a body of the National Fascist Party and became a state body on 9 December 1928. Its composition was revised by a law of 14 December 1929, and its members were chosen from the party's leading figures, among them the quadrumvirs, members of parliament, ministers, the secretary of the party and the heads of the corporations. It usually met at the Palazzo Venezia in Rome, which was also the seat of the head of the government.

The council elected the party's deputies, nominated the party secretary and other leaders, approved the party statutes and set party policy. It also held powers over the royal succession, including the choice of the heir to the throne, over possible successors to the Prime Minister, and over the membership of the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies, later the Chamber of Fasces and Corporations. Meetings were convened by the Prime Minister himself, and decrees and laws became valid only with his approval. Unlike the Führerprinzip in Nazi Germany, the council kept the power to recommend that the King remove the Prime Minister. Since the other institutions had been subordinated to the party, it was the only check on Mussolini's power.

The Allies invaded Sicily in July 1943, and the council member Dino Grandi proposed a vote of no confidence in Mussolini. The vote was held on the night of 24 to 25 July 1943 and passed with 19 votes for, 8 against and one abstention. Among those voting for it were Mussolini's son-in-law Galeazzo Ciano and Marshal Emilio De Bono. The next day King Victor Emmanuel told Mussolini that General Pietro Badoglio would lead Italy, and Mussolini was arrested.

In September 1943 German commandos freed him, and he regained power in northern Italy. He had those who voted against him tried for treason at the Verona trial, and all were found guilty. Only six were present, among them Ciano, De Bono and Giovanni Marinelli, and all but Tullio Cianetti were shot on the morning of 11 January 1944. The council ceased to exist after these events.
grand-council-qing: In the early Qing dynasty power lay with the Council of Princes and High Officials, set up in 1637, whose decisions took precedence over those of the Grand Secretariat; under rules set by Nurhaci it could even depose the emperor. It was abolished in 1717. From 1677 the Kangxi Emperor also drew counsel from the Southern Study, where members of the Hanlin Academy chosen for literary merit were posted close to him.

In 1729 the Yongzheng Emperor launched an offensive against the Dzungar Khanate, and because the Grand Secretariat met outside the Gate of Supreme Harmony, there were fears for military secrets. A new office, the Junjichu, was therefore set up in the Inner Court of the Forbidden City and staffed with trusted members of the cabinet. Its streamlined working pleased the emperor, and in 1732 the temporary office became a Grand Council that soon outstripped both older bodies.

Shortly before his death in 1735 the Yongzheng Emperor set up an interim council to assist his son, the Qianlong Emperor; it was disbanded in 1738 and the Grand Council reconstituted. Under Qianlong the council drafted edicts and advised on policy while also handling paperwork, court entertainments and the emperor's travel. After 1799 the Jiaqing Emperor purged his father's favourite Heshen, a councillor since 1776, reduced the number of grand councillors and made them liable to administrative punishment.

During the regencies of the empress dowagers Ci'an and Cixi from 1861, papers passed through Prince Gong and the council, which drafted orders for the dowagers' approval; after an audience in 1869 Zeng Guofan remarked that the power of the grand councillors surpassed that of the imperial master. In May 1911 the regent Prince Chun abolished the council in favour of an Imperial Cabinet, and the dynasty fell not long after.

The council remained an informal body of the inner court whose members held other posts at the same time. It usually had five members, two Manchus, two Han Chinese and a Prince of the First Rank as president, though the number varied from three to ten. At first most were Manchus; Zhang Tingyu was one of the earliest Han Chinese to serve. Its offices stood in a modest building west of the gate to the Palace of Heavenly Purity.
grand-duchy-of-lithuania: The name of Lithuania was first mentioned in 1009 in the Annals of Quedlinburg. Between 1180 and 1183 the Lithuanians began sustained military raids on Slavic provinces, including Polotsk and Pskov, which marked the consolidation of the Lithuanian lands in Aukštaitija. Mindaugas, duke of southern Lithuania, had by the mid-1230s acquired supreme power in the whole country. He was baptised in 1252 and crowned in 1253, and Lithuania was recognised as a Christian state until 1260, when he supported an uprising in Courland and, according to the German order, renounced Christianity. The pagan state was the target of crusades by the Teutonic Knights and the Livonian Order but survived.

Under Grand Duke Gediminas the state grew quickly. In 1320 most of the principalities of western Rus' were vassalised or annexed, and in 1321 he captured Kiev. He established the permanent capital at Vilnius, probably in 1323. His sons Algirdas and Kęstutis then ruled together, and the state continued to expand.

Algirdas's son Jogaila signed the Union of Krewo in 1386, which made a dynastic union between the grand duchy and the Kingdom of Poland and led to the conversion of Europe's last pagan state, which took place in 1387. The reign of Vytautas the Great, son of Kęstutis, brought the widest territorial expansion and the defeat of the Teutonic Knights at the Battle of Grunwald in 1410. By 1440 the state was the largest in Europe, reaching from the Baltic Sea to the Black Sea. It was multi-ethnic and multiconfessional: Ruthenians, ancestors of modern Belarusians and Ukrainians, spoke Ruthenian, the language of most official documents.

Wars with the Teutonic Order and the loss of land to Moscow forced a closer alliance with Poland, and the Union of Lublin of 1569 created the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. The grand duchy kept its own ministries, laws, army and treasury. The Constitution of 3 May 1791 was meant to unite the two states, but Russia invaded in 1792, and the partition of 1795, after the Kościuszko Uprising, divided the territory among Russia, Prussia and Austria.

Historians from Lithuania, Belarus and Ukraine still debate whether the state was essentially Lithuanian or Ruthenian-Lithuanian. The Lithuanian annexation of much of southern and western Ruthenia is held to have led to the lasting division between Ukrainians, Belarusians and Russians.
grand-duchy-of-moscow: Moscow is first mentioned in chronicles under the year 1147, as part of the principality of Rostov-Suzdal, and was made a fortified stronghold in the 1150s. It was sacked during the Mongol invasions of 1237 to 1238. It became a separate principality when Daniel, the youngest son of Alexander Nevsky, received the city and its surroundings as an appanage, and his reign is dated 1263 to 1303.

By the end of the 13th century Moscow was one of the leading principalities within the Grand Principality of Vladimir, alongside Tver. Daniel's son Yury contested the title of grand prince with Mikhail of Tver, and the khan of the Golden Horde, who held suzerainty over the princes, made Yury grand prince in 1318.

Ivan I, who ruled from 1325 to 1340, regained the title and collected tribute for the khan from the other Russian princes, which increased Moscow's wealth. The seat of the Russian Orthodox Church moved from Vladimir to Moscow in his time. Dmitry, who ruled from 1359 to 1389, permanently united the thrones of Vladimir and Moscow and defeated the Tatars in 1380. Vasily I took advantage of the strife in the Golden Horde to expand the realm, but he had to resume paying tribute after Tatar raids, and in 1408 Edigu besieged Moscow. The city survived on payment of a large indemnity.

Vasily II, who ruled from 1425 to 1462, won a civil war against his uncle Yury of Galich, and the Russian Church declared autocephaly in 1448. Ivan III, who ruled from 1462 to 1505, absorbed nearly all of the Russian states. Novgorod surrendered in 1478, and Ivan abolished its system of government. His defeat of the Tatars in 1480 traditionally marks the end of Tatar suzerainty. Vasily III completed the annexation of the remaining appanages, including Pskov in 1510 and Ryazan in 1521, and captured Smolensk from Lithuania in 1514. Ivan IV was crowned as the first Russian tsar in 1547.

The unification gave the grand prince dominance, and he treated the country as his personal patrimony. The historian Sergey Platonov wrote that the prince was not only the ruler of the country but also its owner. The veche and other traditional institutions were abolished, and appanage princes became part of the boyar class. Ivan III and Vasily III created a small bureaucracy of state secretaries known as dyaki.

The great majority of the population were peasants, whose primary allegiance was to the commune, and its members were collectively responsible for paying taxes. Monasticism spread between the 14th and 16th centuries, and one estimate suggests about 250 cenobitic monasteries and convents were founded. Andrei Rublev led a distinct Moscow school of icon painting, and his Trinity dates from the early 15th century.
grand-duke-konstantin-pavlovich-of-russi: Konstantin was born at Tsarskoye Selo in 1779, the second son of Paul Petrovich and Maria Fyodorovna. His grandmother, Catherine the Great, named him after Constantine the Great, and a medal struck for his birth bore the inscription Back to Byzantium, alluding to her Greek Plan. She directed his upbringing, and Cesar La Harpe was his tutor-in-chief from 1783 to 1795. On 26 February 1796 he married Juliane of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld, who left him in 1799 after his violent treatment of her. The marriage was annulled on 20 March 1820, and on 27 May he married the Polish Countess Joanna Grudzińska, who became Princess of Łowicz.

In the campaign led by Suvorov he lost the battle of Bassignana by his own fault but distinguished himself at Novi, and Paul gave him the title tsesarevich. In 1805 he commanded the Imperial Guards and shared responsibility for the defeat at Austerlitz, though he captured the first French Imperial Eagle of the coalition's wars. After the peace of Tilsit he admired Napoleon and in 1812 pressed for a quick peace. Barclay de Tolly twice sent him away from the army for disorderly conduct. At La Fère-Champenoise in March 1814 he was praised for his bravery.

Alexander I installed him in Congress Poland as de facto viceroy and commander-in-chief, adding in 1819 the command of the Lithuanian troops. After Alexander suspended the Sejm for five years and authorised him to keep order, Konstantin strengthened the secret police, replaced Poles with Russians in the administration and army, and often insulted and assaulted subordinates. Yet he supported Polish musicians such as Maria Agata Szymanowska and Frédéric Chopin.

When Alexander I died on 1 December 1825, Nicholas had Konstantin proclaimed emperor in Saint Petersburg; when the news reached Warsaw, Konstantin formally abdicated. The confusion over the succession gave the Decembrist conspirators their opening. After an assassination attempt in November 1830 and the outbreak of the November Uprising, he refused to use Russian troops, saying that the Poles had started the disturbance and Poles must stop it. On 3 December he withdrew towards Russia. He died of cholera at Vitebsk on 27 June 1831. Russians remembered his stands against the imperial family as brave, while in Poland he was viewed as a tyrant and appears in literature as a cruel despot.
grand-duke-of-tuscany: The title of grand duke was created on 27 August 1569 by a papal bull of Pope Pius V for Cosimo I de' Medici, and Pius crowned him in Rome on 5 March 1570. The Medici had ruled the Florentine Republic since 1434, first as lords of Florence and then as dukes. The title of Duke of the Florentine Republic, created by Pope Clement VII in 1532, was the first papal recognition of this kind, and the grand ducal title was the second.

The residence of the grand dukes was the Palazzo Pitti in Florence, which the Medici bought in 1549. Before that, margraves had ruled in the 9th century, when the region was part of the Margraviate of Tuscany, and from the 11th century it was divided among independent cities such as Pisa, Florence, Siena, Lucca and Arezzo.

The grand duchy was the first period after centuries of political division in which most of the region was under a single ruler. Its territory covered almost all of present-day Tuscany, except the Republic of Lucca, the Principality of Piombino, the Duchy of Massa and Carrara and the State of the Presidi. The Medici held the title from 1569 to 1737, when it passed to the house of Habsburg-Lorraine.

Napoleon replaced the grand duchy in 1801 with the Kingdom of Etruria, ruled by the Bourbon-Parma until 1807, when France annexed Tuscany. In 1809 his sister Elisa Bonaparte received the title of Grand Duchess of Tuscany, de jure sovereign but de facto honorary. The Habsburg-Lorraine returned in 1814.

Leopoldo II was driven out by revolution from 21 February to 12 April 1849 and again on 27 April 1859, and he abdicated in favour of his son Ferdinando IV, who was never recognised in Tuscany and was deposed by the provisional government on 16 August 1859. Piedmont-Sardinia annexed Tuscany on 22 March 1860. Habsburg-Lorraine claimants to the title continue to be listed.
grand-embassy-of-peter-the-great: The mission left on 9 March 1697. Its main aim was to strengthen and widen the Holy League, Russia's alliance with European states against the Ottoman Empire in its struggle for the northern coast of the Black Sea; Peter also wanted to hire foreign specialists and buy weapons. A third grand ambassador, Prokopy Voznitsyn, served beside Franz Lefort and Fedor Golovin. Peter's disguise was thin: at 2.03 metres he was one of the tallest men in Europe.

On the way Peter negotiated with Friedrich Casimir Kettler, Duke of Courland, and concluded an alliance with Frederick I of Prussia. He reached the Dutch Republic in mid-August 1697 and from 1 September worked incognito as a shipbuilder. In Amsterdam he learned to draw ships and to etch from the seascape painters Adam Silo and Ludolf Bakhuysen, studied anatomy with Frederik Ruysch and met Jan van der Heyden, inventor of the fire hose; Antonie van Leeuwenhoek visited him in October. The States General refused support against the Ottoman Empire, and Peter also met William III, who ruled both the Netherlands and England.

At William's invitation Peter went on to England, where he stayed until 21 April 1698. He visited the Royal Observatory, the Royal Mint, the Royal Society, the University of Oxford, shipyards and Woolwich Arsenal, learning shipbuilding in the royal dockyards at Deptford, where English practice was written down as Dutch practice was not. Peregrine Osborne, Marquess of Carmarthen, designed him a yacht, the Royal Transport. He met William Penn and other Quakers. His party did such damage to Sayes Court, John Evelyn's house, that Sir Christopher Wren assessed the bill at £305 9s 6d. Reports put the British subjects who entered Russian service at between 60 and 500.

Talks in Vienna failed to stop Austria making a separate peace with Turkey, and a planned visit to Venice was cancelled when news came of the Streltsy uprising in Moscow. The embassy did not reach its main goal, but it showed that the coming War of the Spanish Succession ruled out a stronger anti-Ottoman coalition. On the way home Peter met Augustus II of Poland-Lithuania at Rava-Ruska, and their talks laid the basis of the alliance against Sweden in the Great Northern War. The mission ended on 25 August 1698.
grand-national-assembly-of-turkey: Turkey had parliamentary experience before 1920. The Ottoman First Constitutional Era lasted two years: the assembly was dissolved on 28 June 1877 after criticism of the Russo-Turkish War, and the second assembly was dissolved by Sultan Abdul Hamid II on 14 February 1878, which suspended the Ottoman constitution of 1876. The Second Constitutional Era began on 23 July 1908 with the Young Turk Revolution. In both eras the General Assembly of the Ottoman Empire was bicameral, with a Senate chosen by the sultan and an elected Chamber of Deputies.

After the First World War the Allied Powers planned to dismember the Ottoman Empire through the Treaty of Sèvres. In a speech of 19 March 1920 Mustafa Kemal announced that an assembly with extraordinary powers would gather in Ankara, and he said that members of the dispersed Ottoman Chamber of Deputies could also take part. Elections followed in the style of the earlier Chamber, and the new body held its first session on 23 April 1920. Until 1923 the provisional government was known as the Government of the Grand National Assembly.

Multi-party politics began unsteadily. The Progressive Republican Party, founded in 1924 at Mustafa Kemal's request, was closed after several months, and the Liberal Party of Ali Fethi Okyar, founded in 1930, was dissolved on 17 November 1930 after disorders. No further attempt was made until 1945. The Democrat Party, established the year after the National Development Party of 1945, won the general elections of 1950, and Celal Bayar became President and Adnan Menderes Prime Minister.

A military coup on 27 May 1960 arrested Menderes, Bayar, the ministers and the members of the Assembly and closed it. A Constituent Assembly drafted the 1961 Constitution, accepted in a referendum on 9 July 1961 by 61.17 percent of voters, which made parliament bicameral. After the coup of 12 September 1980 the 1982 Constitution, accepted by 91.37 percent on 7 November 1982, made it unicameral with 550 members and introduced a 10 percent electoral threshold. After the referendum of 2017 Turkey adopted a presidential system, and the number of deputies rose from 550 to 600.

The 600 deputies are elected for five years by the D'Hondt method of party-list proportional representation, from 87 electoral districts that represent the 81 provinces. Parties with at least 20 deputies may form a parliamentary group, and the work is divided among specialised committees. The Assembly has met in three buildings. The first was converted from the Ankara headquarters of the Committee of Union and Progress, designed by Hasip Bey, and is now the War of Independence Museum. The second, by Vedat Tek, served from 1924 to 1960 and is now the Republic Museum. The present building in the Bakanlıklar neighbourhood of Ankara was designed by Clemens Holzmeister.
grand-palace: Construction of the Grand Palace began on 6 May 1782 at the order of King Phutthayotfa Chulalok, Rama I, who had seized the crown from King Taksin of Thonburi and meant to build a capital for his new Chakri dynasty. He moved the seat of power from Thonburi, on the west side of the Chao Phraya River, to the east side at Bangkok, where canals dug along the east side made the new capital an artificial island, named Rattanakosin. The old royal palace at Thonburi was small and sandwiched between two temples, Wat Arun and Wat Tai Talat, which prevented its expansion.

The new palace was built on a rectangular plot on the western edge of the island, between Wat Pho to the south and Wat Mahathat to the north, with the river on the west. The land had been occupied by a Chinese community, which Rama I ordered to move to an area south of the city walls, now Bangkok's Chinatown. The castellated walls were built in 1782 and extended southwards under Rama II.

The palace is a rectangle of about 218,400 square metres, surrounded by four walls with twelve gates and seventeen small forts, on the banks of the river. It is not a single building but numerous halls and pavilions set round lawns, gardens and courtyards, and its asymmetry and mixed styles come from two centuries of additions and rebuilding by successive kings, especially Chulalongkorn, Rama V.

It is divided into the Temple of the Emerald Buddha, the Outer Court with public buildings, the Middle Court with the main throne halls, the Inner Court and the Siwalai Gardens. The Temple of the Emerald Buddha, Wat Phra Kaew, built in 1783, is a royal chapel rather than a temple, as it has no living quarters for monks, and follows the tradition of the royal chapels at Sukhothai and Ayutthaya. In the Phra Maha Prasat group Rama I built a copy of an Ayutthaya throne hall, where he held his full coronation; lightning burned it down in 1789.

The king, his court and his government were based in the palace until 1925. The Outer Court, historically called Fai Na, held ministerial offices, a theatre, elephant stables, barracks, the royal mint and an arsenal. The Inner Court, Fai Nai, was reserved for the king and his queens and consorts, their children and a multitude of ladies-in-waiting and servants, and was a town within itself with its own shops, government and schools. Royal polygamy ended in practice under Rama VI and was outlawed by Rama VII. After the abolition of absolute monarchy in 1932 all government agencies left the palace. It is now partly open as a museum, and royal ceremonies and state functions are still held within its walls.
grand-trunk-road: The road follows an ancient route called the Uttarapatha, the Northern Road, which Buddhist literature mentions before the Maurya Empire and which Pāṇini also names. Its precursor was built on the orders of the emperor Chandragupta Maurya and was inspired by the eastern stretch of the Persian Royal Road, the Great Khurasan Road. In Mauryan times overland trade between India, Western Asia and Bactria passed through the north-western cities of Takshashila and Purushapura. The Greek diplomat Megasthenes, who spent fifteen years at the Mauryan court, records that Chandragupta had a department of officials to maintain it.

The road is said to have been built in eight stages linking Purushapura, Takshashila, Hastinapura, Kanyakubja, Prayag, Patliputra and Tamralipta, a distance of around 2,600 kilometres. The emperor Ashoka recorded in an edict that he had trees planted, wells dug at every half kos and rest-houses built along the route.

In the 16th century Sher Shah Suri of the Sur Empire repaired the road, rerouted it at Sonargaon and Rohtas and widened it. He added caravanserais, kos minars and baolis, and gardens beside some sections. His son Islam Shah Suri built an additional sarai between each of his father's on the way to Bengal, and the Mughals built more. Jahangir decreed that all sarais be of burnt brick and stone, planted broad-leaved trees between Lahore and Agra and bridged the water on the route. Sher Shah's road was called Sadak-e-Azam, and the Mughals called it Badshahi Sadak. Over the centuries it served as a major trade route and carried both travellers and the post.

The Afghan end was rebuilt under Mahmud Shah Durrani. In the 1830s the East India Company began a programme of metalled roads for commerce and administration, and the road from Calcutta through Delhi to Kabul was rebuilt at a cost of £1,000 a mile; the rebuilding ran between 1833 and 1860. It appears in the writing of Rudyard Kipling, who in Kim described the Brahmins, bankers, tinkers and pilgrims, all the world going and coming, on a road bearing India's traffic like a river of life.

Today the Indian sections coincide with parts of the National Highways NH 19, NH 112 and NH 44, and in Pakistan the road coincides with the N-5. India submitted the historic sites along it to the tentative list of UNESCO World Heritage Sites in 2015.
grand-turk-island: Grand Turk is the largest island of the Turks Islands, the smaller of the two archipelagos that make up the Turks and Caicos Islands, a British Overseas Territory in the Lucayan Archipelago. It covers 18 square kilometres (6.9 sq mi). The territory's capital, Cockburn Town, and the JAGS McCartney International Airport are on the island. The name comes from the Turk's cap cactus, Melocactus intortus, whose cap recalls an Ottoman fez.

The Lucayan people, the indigenous inhabitants, called the island Abawana, the First Small Land, and the Spanish later called it Amuana. Bermudians first colonised it in 1681 and set up the salt industry. In 1754 HMS Jamaica and HMS Shoreham found no French inhabitants but did find marks of possession bearing the arms of the French king; the British cut them down and left a declaration. In 1764 HMS Jamaica and HMS Venus found a brick column 60 feet high, inscribed Phare de Choiseul. Believing it a mark of possession, they undermined and destroyed it, and learned later that it had been built for the preservation of shipping.

In 1766 the island became the capital. In September 1836 Britain declared it a free port for the warehousing of goods, and a lighthouse designed by Alexander Gordon and built by Chance Brothers was completed on 1 October 1852. Many ships were lost on its reef, among them RMS Medina in 1842. From 1954 until 1980 a U.S. Naval Facility operated on the island, part of an undersea surveillance system, and Grand Turk was the first down-range station of the Eastern Range to have a Missile Impact Location System. John Glenn's Friendship 7 spacecraft landed near it in 1962.

Some argue that Grand Turk, not San Salvador Island or Samana Cay in the Bahamas, was the Guanahani of Christopher Columbus's first landfall in 1492, citing his journals' descriptions and the distance from Hispaniola. The historian Gregory McIntosh concluded instead that it was Babueca, an island found separately by Martín Alonso Pinzón in 1492.

Grand Turk is the administrative, historic, cultural and financial centre of the territory. Its population was approximately 4,831 in 2012. Tourism has been promoted since the 1950s, and in 2004 Carnival Cruise Line announced a cruise port on the island.
grand-vizier: The title Grand Vizier, in Ottoman Turkish Vezir-i Azam or Sadrazam, comes from Classical Persian, while its components derive from Arabic. The word vizier comes from wazīr, from a root meaning to bear a burden, which reflects the official's role in carrying the burdens of the state for the sovereign. The rank was formally established as a state office in the Abbasid Caliphate, where the term was used in the 8th century. The Ottomans took the office from the Seljuks of Anatolia in the early 14th century, and in the first phase of the state vizier was the only title in use.

The first Ottoman vizier to be called Grand Vizier was Çandarlı Halil Pasha the Elder, in the reign of Murad I. The title distinguished the holder of the sultan's seal from other viziers. He was the first holder with a military background, and the first of a political family that rivalled the Ottoman dynasty itself. His grandson Çandarlı Halil Pasha the Younger opposed the siege of Constantinople and was executed two days after Mehmed II won it. After this the post went almost exclusively to men of the kul system and the devshirme, who were easier for the sultan to control.

Power was centralised in the office in the Köprülü era. Köprülü Mehmed Pasha, appointed in 1656 under Mehmed IV, sent the sultan away from the city on hunting trips, removed officers suspected of corruption and executed those who stayed. On his deathbed five years later he persuaded the sultan to appoint his son Köprülü Fazıl Ahmed Pasha. After the Tanzimat of the 19th century, Grand Viziers came to resemble the prime ministers of Western monarchies.

The Grand Vizier held the imperial seal and could convene all other viziers. In conference they were called the Kubbealtı viziers, after the Kubbealtı in Topkapı Palace, and the Grand Vizier's offices stood at the Sublime Porte. In Ottoman legal theory the sultan was supposed to conduct state affairs only through him, but the arrangement was often circumvented. As the Ottomanist Colin Imber writes, the sultan often had closer contact with the pages of the privy chamber and other courtiers than with the Grand Vizier.

Elsewhere the office had its own course. In the Mughal Empire holders included Bairam Khan, who led the forces of Akbar to victory at the Second Battle of Panipat. In Qajar Iran the chief minister was styled sadr-e aʿzam, a title adopted in the Ottoman manner.
grande-armee: The Grande Armée was formed in 1804 from the Armée des côtes de l'Océan, also called the Armée d'Angleterre, the field army of over 100,000 men that Napoleon had assembled at the port of Boulogne for a planned invasion of the United Kingdom. When the Third Coalition formed against France after his coronation as Emperor of the French, the army turned east in 1805. At its formation it consisted of six corps led by Napoleon's marshals and senior generals.

In 1805 rapid marches surrounded General Karl von Mack's Austrian army at Ulm, which yielded 60,000 prisoners for the loss of some 2,000 French soldiers. On 2 December 1805 the Grande Armée defeated a combined Russian and Austrian army at the Battle of Austerlitz, and the Treaty of Pressburg followed on 26 December. After the stalemate at Eylau, victory at the Battle of Friedland on 14 June 1807 brought the Treaties of Tilsit. The army was dissolved in October 1808 and its parts formed into the Army of Spain and the Army of the Rhine.

In 1812 Napoleon assembled the largest field army he had ever commanded to invade Russia. After the capture of Smolensk and the battle of Borodino, the French reached Moscow on 14 September 1812, but disease, desertion, exhaustion and long supply lines had already reduced the army. On the retreat, cold, starvation, disease and harassment by Cossacks and partisans destroyed it as a fighting force, though its pontoon builders saved it from complete annihilation at the Berezina River. Later armies fought on in 1813, notably at the Battle of the Nations at Leipzig, and the Hundred Days of 1815 ended its campaigns.

The army was divided into corps, usually five to seven, each of between 10,000 and 50,000 men, commonly 20,000 to 30,000. Each corps was a self-contained army of combined arms, commanded by a marshal or a general, and the corps marched on separate routes within a day's march of one another. They were small enough to live by foraging, so fewer supplies had to be carried. The Imperial Guard formed a single corps of its own and served as a reserve.

Soldiers could rise through the ranks regardless of class, wealth or national origin. More than one-third of the troops who marched into Russia were not French and came from 20 countries. Each soldier carried four days' provisions, and Napoleon encouraged his men to live off the land. Every regiment included women called cantinières, married to soldiers, who sold food and drink and fed the troops when other arrangements broke down.
grantha-script: Grantha is a classical South Indian Brahmic script found particularly in Tamil Nadu and Kerala. In Sanskrit grantha means a knot, a word used for books and for the script they were written in, from the practice of binding inscribed palm leaves with a thread held by knots. The script emerged from the Pallava script in the 4th century CE. This early Pallava Grantha was used until the 7th century to write Sanskrit texts and inscriptions on copper plates and on the stones of Hindu temples and monasteries. Middle Grantha first appears in the Kuram copper plates of about 675 CE, and Grantha in its present form dates from the 14th century.

The scholar Francis distinguishes Grantha and Tamil as two closely related writing systems used for Sanskrit and Tamil respectively, while noting that the match was not absolute: Sanskrit loanwords could be written with Grantha letters within Tamil inscriptions. Grantha was also used for Manipravalam, a blend of Tamil and Sanskrit; by the 15th century a Sanskrit root was written in Grantha and any Tamil suffix in the Tamil script, even within one word, a convention kept in printed editions until the middle of the 20th century. Today Tamil-speaking Hindus use it in religious settings, such as writing a child's name at the naming ceremony, and it is used to chant hymns in traditional Vedic schools.

The modern Malayalam script is a direct descendant of Grantha, and Thai, Javanese and Sinhalese are derived from, or closely related to, Grantha through the early Pallava script. The Tamil purist movement of the colonial era sought to purge Grantha from use, which Kailasapathy saw as part of Tamil nationalism and a regional ethnic chauvinism. A later proposal to unify Grantha and Tamil caused discontent, and it was decided that the two should not be unified, except for the numerals. Grantha was added to the Unicode Standard in June 2014.
granville-sharp: Sharp was born in Durham, the son of Thomas Sharp, Archdeacon of Northumberland, and Judith Wheler, and a grandson of John Sharp, Archbishop of York. The family's funds for education were nearly spent, so he was taught mainly at home, and at fifteen he was apprenticed to a London linen-draper. To argue with his fellow apprentices he taught himself Greek and Hebrew. In 1757 he became a clerk in the Ordnance Office at the Tower of London, a post that left him time for study.

In 1765, at his brother William's surgery, Sharp met Jonathan Strong, a young enslaved man from Barbados whom his master, the lawyer David Lisle, had beaten close to blindness and cast into the street. The brothers paid for his treatment at Barts Hospital. In 1767 Lisle sold Strong to a Jamaica planter, James Kerr, and had him seized, but Sharp took the case to the Lord Mayor, who freed him. In 1769 Sharp published the first tract in England attacking slavery.

In 1783 Olaudah Equiano told him of the Zong, whose crew had thrown an estimated 132 enslaved people overboard so that the owners could claim insurance; the court refused the claim, but Sharp's attempt to bring a prosecution for murder never got off the ground. In 1787 he was unanimously chosen chairman of the new Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade, though he never took the chair at meetings and failed to persuade the committee to target slavery itself.

Sharp sympathised with the American colonists and resigned from the Ordnance Office in 1776 rather than supply the war against them. He also championed parliamentary reform, the legislative independence of Ireland and an end to the impressment of sailors. A classicist and biblical scholar, he set out the Granville Sharp Rule on the Greek article and was a founder of the British and Foreign Bible Society.

Sharp lived to see the Slave Trade Act receive royal assent on 25 March 1807 and died on 6 July 1813. He was buried at All Saints' Church, Fulham, and is commemorated in Westminster Abbey, on the Clarkson Memorial in Wisbech and in the names of Granville Town in Sierra Leone and the free village of Granville in Jamaica. In 2007 Royal Mail put him on a stamp marking the 200th anniversary of the abolition of the slave trade.
graubunden: The canton lies in the Alps and, unlike any other Swiss canton, extends fully on both sides of the main Alpine barrier, from the northern plains at Maienfeld to the southern plains at Roveredo. Much of it belongs to neither side: the Engadin is a large inner Alpine valley that drains through the Inn to the Danube. Parts of the canton lie in four of the country's five drainage basins, drained by the Rhine, the Po, the Adige and the Inn. Its heraldic symbol is the Alpine ibex.

The deep valleys were first settled by the Raetians. Archaeological evidence of settlement at Chur goes back to the Pfyn culture, 3900 to 3500 BCE. Most of the land became part of the Roman province of Raetia, established in 15 BCE, with Chur as Curia, and later lay in the territory of the diocese of Chur.

In the late Middle Ages three leagues formed. The League of God's House was founded in 1367 to resist the rising power of the Bishop of Chur. The Grey League followed in 1395 in the Upper Rhine valley, named for the homespun grey clothes of its people, and that name was used exclusively after 16 March 1424. In 1436 the people of ten bailiwicks of the former Toggenburg countship, whose dynasty had died out, formed the League of the Ten Jurisdictions. An alliance of 1471 produced the Three Leagues, which before the end of the 15th century became an ally of the Old Swiss Confederacy. The Grey League's name gave the canton its German name, meaning the Grey Leagues.

Chur is the capital and the only sizable city; most people live in mountain valleys, and the canton has 200,096 inhabitants. Romansh has official status here and has been a national language of Switzerland since 1938; in 1996 it was declared an official language of the Confederation. It consists of five dialect groups, with a common written form, Rumantsch Grischun. Since the late Middle Ages it has lost more than half its original territory, which included Liechtenstein and parts of western Austria.

Three World Heritage Sites lie in the canton: the Benedictine Convent of Saint John, the Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona and the Rhaetian Railway in the Albula and Bernina landscapes. The church of Zillis holds a Romanesque painted ceiling added about 1130, and the canton has many medieval castles, among them Tarasp in the Engadin.
graz: Graz lies on both sides of the river Mur in southeast Austria, about 150 kilometres southwest of Vienna and some 50 kilometres north of Maribor in Slovenia. It is in the Graz Basin on the eastern edge of the Alps, with the city centre at 353 metres, and the Schlossberg, or Castle Hill, 475 metres high, dominates the old town. Because the basin is open only to the south, the climate is warmer than expected at that latitude.

The oldest settlement on the site dates to the Copper Age, but there is no continuity of settlement before the Middle Ages. The name most likely derives from the Slavic gradec, small castle, though the city itself was founded by Bavarian settlers who arrived shortly after the Slavs and intermixed with them. They called it Bayrischgraz, Bavarian Graz, to distinguish it from the older Windischgraz, Slovenian Graz, which it soon eclipsed. The name first appears in records in 1128, and the earliest documented mention dates from the 12th century, when Graz developed as a fortified settlement under the Babenbergs.

In the Late Middle Ages Graz became a commercial and administrative centre and the residence of the Inner Austrian branch of the Habsburg dynasty, from which come many of its Renaissance and Baroque buildings. It was also a stronghold against the Ottoman Empire, through the fortifications on the Schlossberg. As capital of the multiethnic Duchy of Styria it was a centre of Slovene culture from the founding of the University of Graz in 1586 until the University of Ljubljana was established in 1919. Industrialisation in the 19th and 20th centuries made it a major industrial and cultural centre of southern Austria.
