Graz is the capital of the Austrian state of Styria and the second-largest city in Austria after Vienna, with 307,912 residents with a primary residence. Its historic centre, with over 1,000 buildings from the Gothic to the contemporary, was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1999, and Eggenberg Palace on the western edge of the city in 2010. Graz was European Capital of Culture in 2003, and the Clock Tower on the Schlossberg is its symbol.
great-council-of-venice: Tradition dates the Great Council to 1172, but it probably grew out of a Council of Wise Men, attested in 1141, which limited the power of the Doge, and it replaced the people's assembly, the Concio. With 300–400 members already in the 13th century, it was too large to govern, and real decisions fell to smaller bodies such as the Council of Forty, whose three heads, with the six ducal councillors and the Doge, formed the Signoria. A few electors, chosen partly by lot and partly by rotation, named one hundred men for the next year's council, and with no other slate all were elected.

Rising wealth brought more families seeking a seat, while the old patrician families of the Rialto resisted newcomers. Reform proposals of October 1286 failed. In 1289, after the death of Doge Giovanni Dandolo, a crowd demanded the admiral Giacomo Tiepolo as Doge, but he refused and the council elected Pietro Gradenigo, who then pushed through the Serrata. Among the families admitted under it were about a dozen that had fled the fall of Acre in 1291. A commoner, Marin Bocconio, was hanged in 1300 for plotting to kill Gradenigo.

Traditional historiography lamented the Serrata as the birth of a closed oligarchy. Others judge its effects broadly beneficial: members were guaranteed a share in power and so harder to manipulate than the old assembly, and the large number of families taking part kept rivalries in check, sparing Venice the factional strife of other Italian cities.

The Concio was formally abolished in 1423. Over the 15th and 16th centuries the Senate took over most functions of government and became the real legislature, while the Great Council kept its judicial power and the election of officials. From 1498 nobles who followed an ecclesiastical career were barred, and the records of noble births and marriages set up in 1506 and 1526 formed the Golden Book; the council then reached its largest size, 2746 members. From about 1420 it met in a new hall of the Doge's Palace, which burned on 20 December 1577.

Wealthy families were admitted for gifts during the War of Chioggia and the War of Candia, and poor nobles, the Barnabites, kept their seats, which opened the way to vote buying. In 1797, upon the Napoleonic invasion, the council accepted the abdication of the last Doge, Ludovico Manin, by 512 votes to 30, although the quorum of 600 was lacking.
great-depression: The Depression was preceded by a period of industrial growth known as the Roaring Twenties. Much of the profit generated by the boom was invested in speculation, such as in the stock market, which contributed to growing wealth inequality, and banks were subject to minimal regulation, which meant loose lending and widespread debt. Share values continued to rise until the crash of October 1929, when the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped from 381 to 198 over two months. The causes of the Depression are disputed: some historians stress non-monetary causes, while others ascribe its severity and length to failures of monetary policy and the lack of an adequate response to the bank failures that followed.

The decline of the United States economy triggered downturns in most other countries through falling trade, capital movements and business confidence. In June 1930 the United States Congress passed the Smoot–Hawley Tariff Act, which most economists hold made things worse. The gold standard was the main transmission mechanism: countries that devalued early, such as Britain, Argentina and Brazil, returned to growth faster than those that kept to it, such as France and Belgium.

By 1933 United States unemployment had risen to 25 per cent, about one-third of farmers had lost their land and 9,000 of its 25,000 banks had failed. In Germany, which depended heavily on American loans, the collapse of the Credit Anstalt in Vienna in May 1931 deepened the crisis, and unemployment rose to nearly 30 per cent. World gross domestic product fell by an estimated 15 per cent between 1929 and 1932, and international trade by more than half. Chile was labelled the country hardest hit by the League of Nations, since 80 per cent of its government revenue came from copper and nitrates.

In most countries recovery began in 1933. In the United States, where Franklin D. Roosevelt had defeated Herbert Hoover in 1932 and began the New Deal programmes of relief and job creation, output did not return to the 1929 level for over a decade. The outbreak of the Second World War in 1939 ended the Depression, as it stimulated factory production.

Most countries underwent some political upheaval, pushing them to the right, and many democracies in Europe and Latin America were overthrown, notably in Germany in 1933, where the crisis paved the way for Adolf Hitler's Nazi Party to rise to power. The term Great Depression is most often attributed to the British economist Lionel Robbins, whose 1934 book of that name formalised it.
great-exhibition: The exhibition was organised by Prince Albert, Henry Cole and other members of the Royal Society for the Encouragement of Arts, Manufactures and Commerce, which had received its royal charter only in 1847. It was in part a response to the highly effective French Industrial Exposition of 1844, and its prime motive was for Britain to make clear to the world its role as industrial leader. The government was persuaded to form the Royal Commission for the Exhibition of 1851, and subscription committees across the United Kingdom took donations from ordinary citizens.

The royal family was at first hesitant about bringing crowds from Europe into London in a revolutionary period. Some conservatives feared that the visitors might become a revolutionary mob, and Ernest Augustus, King of Hanover, wrote shortly before his death that the Queen's consent to this trumpery was folly.

The building was designed by Joseph Paxton, who drew on his experience of greenhouses for the sixth Duke of Devonshire, with the engineer Charles Fox, and went from organisation to opening in nine months. It was a huge glasshouse of 1,848 by 454 feet, about 563 by 138 metres, made of cast-iron frames and glass produced almost wholly in Birmingham and Smethwick. The exhibition ran from 1 May to 15 October 1851. The catalogue lists exhibitors from Britain, its colonies and dependencies and 44 foreign states, with 13,000 exhibits in all. They included a Jacquard loom, a reaping machine sent from the United States and the Koh-i-Noor diamond, one of the most popular attractions of the India exhibit.

About six million people visited, equal to a third of the population of England and Wales at the time, and most were commoners who paid an entrance fee. Average daily attendance was 42,831, with a peak of 109,915 on 7 October. Railways offered cheap tickets, and Thomas Cook arranged travel for 150,000 people. The first modern public flush toilets, invented by George Jennings, were installed, and 827,280 visitors paid the penny fee. Queen Victoria visited three times with her family and 34 times on her own.

The exhibition made a surplus of £186,000. It was used to found the Victoria and Albert Museum, the Science Museum and the Natural History Museum in the area to the south, nicknamed Albertopolis, and to set up an educational trust for grants and scholarships for industrial research. The Crystal Palace was moved and re-erected in enlarged form in 1854 at Sydenham Hill in south London, and was destroyed by fire on 30 November 1936. The Great Exhibition was the first in a series of world's fairs, and it has become a symbol of the Victorian age. Its catalogue, illustrated with steel engravings, is a primary source for High Victorian design.
great-famine-ireland: Ireland was incorporated into the United Kingdom in January 1801. Under the middleman system, landlords' agents leased large tracts on fixed rents and sublet them in ever smaller parcels, which encouraged harsh exploitation of tenants. The population grew from about 2 million in 1700 to 8 million by the time of the famine, and by 1845 24 per cent of tenant farms were of 0.4 to 2 hectares and 40 per cent of 2 to 6 hectares. Only potatoes could feed a family from such plots. The crop was unreliable: the Census Commissioners recorded 24 failures going back to 1728.

Crop failures from the blight Phytophthora infestans began in 1845, and the worst year, 1847, became known as Black '47. Prime Minister Robert Peel secretly bought £100,000 of maize and cornmeal from America, but the meal was unfamiliar and hard to mill and cook. His Whig successor, Lord John Russell, influenced by laissez-faire doctrine, assumed that the market would supply food. The government refused to interfere with the movement of food to England and ended the earlier relief works. A new programme of public works employed a third to half a million people by December 1846 but proved impossible to administer.

Charity added perhaps £1.5 million, of which £856,500 came from outside Ireland. Landlords were liable for the rates of tenants paying £4 or less, and many cleared their small tenants. The great mass of evictions came in 1847, and police counted almost 250,000 people evicted between 1849 and 1854. The workhouse system was overwhelmed by the scale and duration of the famine. John Mitchel, an Irish nationalist, wrote that the Almighty sent the potato blight but the English created the Famine.

The number of the dead is not known exactly, and more died of disease than of starvation. The 1841 census recorded 8,175,124 people and that of 1851 counted 6,552,385. Estimates of excess deaths run from 775,000 to 1.5 million. About a million long-distance emigrants left between 1846 and 1851, mainly for North America, with 200,000 or more going to Britain. As many as a third of Irishmen and a quarter of Irishwomen never married in the decades after.

The famine became part of folk memory and strengthened nationalism and republicanism among the Irish at home and abroad. Historians such as Christine Kinealy hold that it was neither inevitable nor unavoidable, and most historians reject the claim that the British response was a genocide. Ireland's National Famine Memorial stands at Murrisk, County Mayo.
great-fish-river: The Great Fish River runs 644 kilometres through the Eastern Cape. It is called great to distinguish it from the Fish River of Namibia, and the name is a misnomer: it translates the Dutch Groot Visch Rivier, the name of a tributary near Cradock, which at its confluence with the Little Fish forms what is properly called the Eastern Cape Fish River. The river was first named Rio do Infante, after João Infante, captain of one of the caravels of Bartolomeu Dias, who visited it in the late 1480s. The coastal area between Port Elizabeth and the river mouth is known as the Sunshine Coast.

The river rises east of Graaff-Reinet and runs through Cradock. The Tarka River joins its left bank, and after a zig-zag to Cookhouse it meanders down the escarpment east of Grahamstown before a near-straight run to its estuary, 8 kilometres northeast of Seafield, on the Indian Ocean. Although its headwaters rise in an arid region it generally has water all year, and it is tidal for roughly 20 kilometres. In the 1970s a tunnel from the Gariep Dam at Oviston brought Orange River water into it for agricultural and industrial use, and much of its ecosystem is now taken over by Orange River flora and fauna.

In the 19th century the river formed the border of the Cape Colony and was contested during the Xhosa Wars, dated 1779 to 1878, between the Xhosa nation on one side and Afrikaner colonists and the British Empire on the other. In 1835 the Fingo people were permitted to settle on its banks. During apartheid its lower reaches formed the western boundary of the nominally independent Ciskei homeland.

In 1846 and 1847, during the War of the Axe, the river mouth area was busy with activity. A ferry linked the Cape Colony on the western side with Waterloo Bay, a landing place for soldiers and supplies. The main military camp stood on the eastern bank of the Old Woman's River and was called Cape Maitland, after Sir Peregrine Maitland, Governor of the Cape Colony, and later Fort Albert; it was abandoned at the end of the war. Several ships were wrecked off the coast in these years, among them the Catherine and the Justina.

A lighthouse at Great Fish Point, built in 1898 near the mouth about 25 kilometres from Port Alfred, stands 76 metres above sea level. Fishing along the lower reaches is mainly recreational, and the Fish River Canoe Marathon runs over two days from Grassridge Dam to Cradock. Divers visit the wrecks near the mouth.
great-heathen-army: The Great Heathen Army, also called the Great Danish Army and the Viking Great Army, was a coalition of Scandinavian warriors mainly from Denmark. Viking raids on England began in the late 8th century, chiefly on wealthy monasteries; the first monastery raided was Lindisfarne in 793. By the 860s the Vikings changed tactics from raiding to invasion, in part because in 862 the West Frankish king fortified his towns and defended his rivers, making raiding in Francia harder. The name comes from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. The force probably contained men from Denmark, Norway, Sweden and Ireland as well as veterans of Francia, and legend names its leaders as three sons of Ragnar Lodbrok: Halfdan Ragnarsson, Ivar the Boneless and Ubba.

The army landed in East Anglia in 865, where King Edmund provided horses in return for peace, and wintered at Thetford before capturing York. In 867 it marched into Mercia and took Nottingham, and the Mercians paid it off. In 869 it returned to East Anglia, defeated Edmund, who was captured, possibly tortured, and killed, and later came to be known as Edmund the Martyr. In 871 it attacked Wessex, where Alfred, brother of King Æthelred, defeated it at the Battle of Ashdown on 8 January 871. Æthelred died soon after and Alfred, now king, bought the Vikings off. The army then wintered in London, returned to Northumbria and wintered at Torksey and at Repton.

In 874 the army drove the Mercian king into exile and conquered Mercia, replacing him with Ceolwulf, and then split in two. Halfdan led one band north to Northumbria, where in 876, according to Asser, he shared out land among his men, who ploughed it and supported themselves. Guthrum, Oscetel and Anwend led the other band to Cambridge and then Wareham. In May 878 Alfred the Great defeated the Vikings at the Battle of Edington. Guthrum agreed to be baptised and to leave Wessex, and the Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum set the boundaries between their territories, leaving the Vikings in control of much of northern and eastern England, later known as the Danelaw.

Guthrum withdrew to Cirencester and then, probably in late 879, to East Anglia, where he reigned as king until his death in 890. Much of the rest of the army settled in Northumbria and York. Two Viking cemeteries in Derbyshire, at Repton and Heath Wood, are believed to be connected with it. At Repton the remains of at least 249 people, at least 80 per cent of them male, were found in a mass grave. Another Viking army returned in 892 and disbanded in 896. Alfred reorganised his defence with a navy, a standing army and a system of fortified towns called burhs, recorded in the Burghal Hidage.
great-hymn-to-the-aten: The hymn belongs to the religious art of the Amarna period, which produced literature, new temples and a whole new city, Akhet-Aten, at the site of present-day Amarna, built as the capital of Egypt. Pharaoh Akhenaten forbade the worship of other gods, a radical departure from centuries of Egyptian religious practice. His reforms were later regarded as heretical and reversed under his successor Tutankhamun, and some scholars have called them monotheistic, while others consider them henotheistic. Courtiers' rock tombs at Amarna carry similar prayers to the Aten or to the Aten and Akhenaten jointly. One, found in almost identical form in five tombs, is known as the Short Hymn to the Aten.

The long version was found in the tomb of the courtier, and later pharaoh, Ay, and its first part is damaged and unreadable. The surviving text addresses the Aten as the sole god, like whom there is no other, who created the world alone. It names the countries of Syria, Nubia and Egypt, says that the god settles every man in his place and supplies his needs, and notes that tongues, natures and skins differ among peoples.

In the last part, translated by Miriam Lichtheim, the speaker says that no one knows the god except his son Neferkheprure, Sole-one-of-Re, that is Akhenaten, whom the god has taught his ways, and the text closes with praise of the king and of Queen Nefertiti. The Egyptologist John Darnell asserts that the hymn was sung.

The hymn resembles Psalm 104. James Henry Breasted thought the psalm was inspired by it, and Arthur Weigall asked whether both derived from a common Syrian source or the psalm from the pharaoh's poem. Lichtheim held that the likeness more probably reflects the generic similarity between Egyptian hymns and biblical psalms, and Mark S. Smith notes that enthusiasm for influence has cooled, although Jan Assmann and Donald Redford still argue for Egyptian influence.

Dominic Montserrat calls such texts formal eulogies of Aten and the royal couple rather than outpourings of emotion, and argues that they redefine the relation of god and king to Akhenaten's advantage. Redford finds little evidence that Akhenaten originated the monotheism of the Bible. Philip Glass set the hymn to music in his 1984 opera Akhnaten.
great-illyrian-revolt: Rome's hold on Illyricum had been won piecemeal. From 35 to 33 BCE Octavian campaigned against the Iapydes, seized Segesta in southern Pannonia and took Dalmatian strongholds, and a series of risings in southern Pannonia and northern Dalmatia from 14 to 10 BCE, the Bellum Pannonicum, was finally put down by Tiberius. In 6 CE Tiberius was about to launch a second campaign against the Marcomanni in Germania, and Marcus Valerius Messalla Messallinus, governor of Illyricum, ordered the local tribes to supply auxiliary contingents. When these troops gathered, they rebelled under Bato the Daesitiate and defeated a Roman force sent against them.

The Breuci of southern Pannonia, under another Bato, marched on Sirmium, while other rebels invaded Macedonia, massacring Roman civilians and veterans. Augustus ordered a general levy, recalled veterans and required rich families to supply freedmen, a measure not taken since the aftermath of the Battle of Cannae, and warned that the rebels could reach Rome in ten days. Velleius Paterculus, who served in the war, put the rebel population at more than 800,000, a figure modern scholars treat with caution. Trained in Roman auxiliary units, the rebels avoided pitched battles and relied on guerrilla tactics.

Tiberius answered with a war of attrition and scorched earth. In 7 CE Augustus, suspecting delay, sent Germanicus, while legions from Moesia and Asia under Aulus Caecina Severus and Marcus Plautius Silvanus fought their way into Illyricum. In 8 CE, worn down by famine and disease, many Pannonians broke with the rebels after Bato the Breucian overthrew their king Pinnes and was himself executed by Bato the Daesitiate; Silvanus conquered the Breuci, and the Pannonians laid down their arms at the River Bathinus. In 9 CE the war was confined to Dalmatia, where Germanicus took Splonum and Raetinum.

When Bato surrendered, Tiberius asked him why his people had rebelled; in Cassius Dio's account he answered that the Romans sent as guardians of their flocks not dogs or shepherds but wolves. Suetonius called the war the most serious of Rome's foreign wars since those with Carthage, though his figure of fifteen legions is known to be wrong. Afterwards the Romans regrouped the tribes: the civitates of the Osseriates, Colapiani and Varciani were probably formed from the Breuci, and other tribespeople were probably sold as slaves or deported.
great-khan: Khagan, also written Qaghan, is a title of imperial rank in Mongolic, Turkic and some other languages, equal to emperor and borne by the ruler of a khaganate. The usual Western rendering Great Khan, in the case of the Mongol Empire, translates Yekhe Khagan, Great Emperor, and the title may also be taken as Khan of Khans. Its origin is unknown. It may be a loanword from the Rouran language, and scholars have proposed Xiongnu, Turkic, Mongolic and Iranian roots. The title is first seen in a speech between 283 and 289, in which a general addressed the Xianbei chief Tuyuhun as kehan. The Rouran Khaganate, from 330 to 555, was the first people to use khagan and khan for its emperors.

The Avar Khaganate, from 567 to 804, also used the title, and the Avars ruled the Carpathian region for over a century. Among the Turks it became associated with the Ashina clan of the Göktürks and their successors, such as the Khazars. Emperor Taizong of Tang was crowned Tian Kehan, Heavenly Khagan, after defeating the Göktürks. The Rus' used kagan in the early 10th century.

In the Secret History of the Mongols only Genghis Khan and his ruling descendants are called Khagan, while other rulers are called Khan. The early khagans were Genghis Khan from 1206 to 1227, Ögedei Khan from 1229 to 1241, Güyük Khan from 1246 to 1248 and Möngke Khan from 1251 to 1259. The empire began to split with the Toluid Civil War of 1260 to 1264 and the death of Kublai Khan in 1294. The emperors of the Yuan dynasty, which lasted from 1271 to 1368, kept the title of Ikh Khagan. Only the Ilkhanate truly recognised the Yuan's overlordship, though it was in effect autonomous. The Yuan were the nominal suzerains of the western khanates for a few decades, until their collapse in 1368.

After the Yuan fell the title continued with the Northern Yuan. Dayan Khan revived the authority of the emperor on the Mongolian Plateau, but he divided his realm among his sons and relatives, which again led to decentralised rule. The last khagan of the Chahars, Ligdan Khan, died in 1634 while fighting the Jurchen-led Later Jin dynasty. Hakan, the Turkish form, was among the titles of the Ottoman sultans, and Khagan was the second title of the Safavid and Qajar shahs of Iran. Kağan, Hakan and Kaan remain common Turkish names.
great-lakes: The Great Lakes are a series of interconnected freshwater lakes spanning the Canada-United States border: Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario. Hydrologically, Michigan and Huron are a single body of water joined at the Straits of Mackinac. Water flows from Superior to Huron and Michigan, south to Erie and finally north to Lake Ontario, and leaves by the Saint Lawrence River to the Atlantic. The lakes hold more than 20 per cent of the world's surface fresh water, and because of their rolling waves and distant horizons they have long been called inland seas.
The lakes began to form at the end of the Last Glacial Period around 14,000 years ago, as retreating ice sheets exposed the basins they had carved and meltwater filled them.

Indigenous peoples, called Paleo-indians, inhabited the region around 10,000 BCE. From around 1000 CE the peoples of the region traded copper nuggets, which were fashioned into ornaments and weapons found in the mounds of southern Ohio. Several lake names come from Indigenous languages: Erie from an Iroquoian word for long tail, Michigan from the Ojibwe mishi-gami, great water, and Ontario from the Wendat ontarí'io, lake of shining waters. The first French explorers named Lake Huron for the Wendat.

After the War of 1812 the Rush-Bagot Treaty of 1818, and later the Treaty of Washington, eventually led to a complete disarmament of naval vessels on the lakes. Storms and reefs have sunk hundreds of ships, and the Lake Superior shipwreck coast from Grand Marais, Michigan, to Whitefish Point became known as the Graveyard of the Great Lakes.

The Great Lakes Waterway connects all five lakes, and the Saint Lawrence Seaway links them to the Atlantic. Most trade is in bulk goods such as iron ore, grain and potash, and large sections of the lakes freeze in winter. Major cities of the region include Chicago, Detroit, Cleveland, Buffalo and Milwaukee on the American side and Toronto, Mississauga and Hamilton on the Canadian side.
great-lakes-twa: The Great Lakes Twa, also called Batwa (singular Mutwa), Abatwa or Ge-Sera, are a Bantu-speaking group native to the African Great Lakes region on the border of Central and East Africa. As an indigenous pygmy people they are generally assumed to be the oldest surviving population of the region. They live in Rwanda, Burundi, Uganda and the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and in 2000 numbered about 80,000 people. They speak distinct dialects of Rundi, Kiga and Tembo. When the Hutu arrived in the region they subjugated hunter-gatherers they called Abatwa, generally assumed to be the ancestors of the Twa, though the Twa may have arrived alongside the Hutu or have mixed ancestry.

Traditionally the Twa have been semi-nomadic hunter-gatherers of the mountain forests, living in association with agricultural villages. Unusually for pygmy peoples, who generally trade meat for agricultural products, iron and pottery, the Twa are potters themselves. For several hundred years they have been a small minority, about 1 per cent in Rwanda and Burundi, with little political role, though some Twa served in the government of the Tutsi king and others held a privileged position at the royal court as entertainers or executioners. Their custom of eating sheep, taboo to Tutsi and Hutu, was among the reasons they were looked on unfavourably.

About 30 per cent of the Twa population of Rwanda died in the genocide of 1994, though the Twa are often omitted from discussions of the conflict between Hutu and Tutsi. Clearing of forests for agriculture and logging, development projects and conservation areas has forced the Twa out of the mountain forests. In Uganda they were expelled from the Bwindi Impenetrable Forest when it became a World Heritage Site, and in 1975 about 6,000 Batwa were displaced when Kahuzi-Biega National Park in the Congo was expanded. Their ancestral land rights have not been recognised, and many are landless. The Batwa still make pottery for its cultural and social meaning, though it is no longer profitable.
great-lavra: The Monastery of Great Lavra, in Greek Moní Megístis Lávras, stands at the south-eastern foot of Mount Athos on the Athos peninsula in geographical Macedonia, at an elevation of 160 metres. It was the first monastery built on Mount Athos, and its founding in 963 by Athanasius the Athonite marks the beginning of organised monastic life there. On the site there had been one of the ancient cities of the peninsula, perhaps Akrothooi; the sarcophagi kept in the monastery's oil storage house come from it.

Athanasius began the buildings in 963 at the wish of his friend, the Byzantine emperor Nikephoros II Phokas, who funded the project. Nikephoros had promised to become a monk of Great Lavra, but circumstances and his death cancelled those plans. A permanent imperial grant, doubled by John I Tzimiskes, allowed the buildings to be completed. The emperors also gave lands, among them the island of Saint Eustratius and the Monastery of Saint Andreas in Thessaloniki, and the number of monks grew from 80 to 120.

According to the 11th-century biography of Athanasius, work began with the protective wall and continued with the church and cells. After his death the monastery carried on normally, favoured by the emperors. In the 11th century it had 700 monks, and smaller monasteries had been ceded to it. In the 14th century it suffered, like the other monasteries of Mount Athos, from pirates, among them Spaniards from the crown of Aragon. The resulting crisis produced the Idiorrhythmic Way of monasticism, despite the objections of the Church and the emperors.

In 1574 the Patriarch of Alexandria, Sylvester, helped it return to cenobitic life, but the idiorrhythmic way soon came back. In 1655 Patriarch Dionysios III donated his personal fortune for a return to cenobitic life, and further attempts in 1914 failed. The monastery has been cenobitic since 1980. Its archives have been kept almost intact, so its history is the most complete among the Athos monasteries.

The main church, the Katholikon, was founded by Athanasius, who died with six other workers when a dome fell during construction. Its frescoes were painted in 1535 by the painter Theophanis. The trapeza, shaped like a cross, is the largest on Mount Athos. The library holds 2,116 Greek manuscripts, 165 codices and over 20,000 printed books, and is one of the richest collections of Greek manuscripts in the world. The vestry keeps a gospel manuscript with a golden cover given by Nikephoros II Phokas and about 2,500 icons.
great-leap-forward: The campaign grew out of Mao Zedong's push for rapid development through mass mobilization and a reaction against the Soviet development strategy. Its core goal was to raise industrial and agricultural output by increasing labour inputs and so overcome China's lack of material, technological and monetary resources. Before 1949 peasants had farmed small plots of their own, and it was recognized that a state monopoly on agriculture to finance industry would be unpopular, so peasants were to be brought under Party control in agricultural collectives.

Mao unveiled the campaign at a meeting in Nanjing in January 1958. An experimental commune at Chayashan in Henan in April 1958 abolished private plots and introduced communal kitchens, and in August the Politburo decided that people's communes would be the new form of organization throughout rural China. By the end of the year about 25,000 communes had been set up, averaging 5,000 households each, with work points replacing wages and money. Steel production was to double within the year, mostly through backyard furnaces; the 1958 effort reached its target of 10.7 million tons, but more than 3 million tons of it was unusable.

On the communes, innovations based on the ideas of the Soviet agronomist Trofim Lysenko included close cropping and deep ploughing, which generally lowered grain production. Famine worsened when procurement quotas were set using false reports from the countryside. At the Lushan Conference of July and August 1959 the only senior leader to speak out openly was Marshal Peng Dehuai. Mao dismissed him and launched a campaign against rightist opportunism, in which over 3 million Party members were purged or penalized, and misreporting and coercive collection intensified.

Much of the harvest was left to rot in some areas because labour had been diverted to steel and construction, and a locust swarm followed the killing of natural predators in the Four Pests Campaign. Not all deaths were from starvation: people were beaten or killed for reporting real harvest figures, refusing to hand over food or trying to flee. Armed rebellions occurred in several provinces, though they never seriously threatened the central government.

The Party studied the damage at conferences from 1960 to 1962, notably the Seven Thousand Cadres Conference in 1962, where Mao ceded day-to-day leadership to moderates such as Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping. Mao acknowledged mistakes while holding that the three red flags could not be challenged, and in 1966 he launched the Cultural Revolution. The campaign failed to industrialize China rapidly, though it left substantial capital construction in iron, steel, mining and textiles, and a gradual de-collectivization followed in the 1960s.
great-man-made-river: In 1953 a search for oil in southern Libya led to the discovery of large quantities of drinkable fossil water underground. The Great Man-Made River was conceived in the late 1960s. On 3 October 1983 the General People's Congress held an extraordinary session that decided to fund and carry out the project, and on 28 August 1984 Muammar Gaddafi laid the foundation stone in the Sarir area. Construction was divided into five phases, and the first required 85 million cubic metres of excavation. The Libyan government paid for it, without loans from world banks, and the cost was projected at more than 25 billion US dollars.

The project is a network of pipes that carries water from the Nubian Sandstone Aquifer System in southern Libya to cities on the northern coast, including Tripoli and Benghazi, over distances of up to 1,600 kilometres. According to the project's website it has 2,820 kilometres of pipes and aqueducts and more than 1,300 wells, most of them over 500 metres deep, and supplies 6,500,000 cubic metres of water a day to cities including Tripoli, Benghazi and Sirte. The first phase's water reached the Ajdabiya reservoir on 11 September 1989, and water reached Tripoli in 1996.

The aquifer accumulated during the last ice age and is not being replenished. One estimate held that at the rates of 2007 the water could last a thousand years, while others suggested it could be exhausted in 60 to 100 years. Analysts say the groundwater system costs about a tenth as much as desalination.

The pipes were made at plants at Brega and Sarir, inaugurated on 28 August 1986, from pre-stressed concrete cylinders wound with steel wire largely made in Italy. A South Korean firm, the Dong Ah Consortium, was the primary contractor for the first phases, and goods from Korea and Europe, mainly Italy, arrived by sea at Brega on the Gulf of Sidra. UNESCO has provided training to its engineers and technicians since 1990. Gaddafi described the project as the Eighth Wonder of the World. On 22 July 2011, during the First Libyan Civil War, a NATO air strike hit the Brega pipe plant.
great-morava: The Great Morava begins at the confluence of the South Morava and the West Morava near the village of Stalać and ends at the Danube northeast of Smederevo, after 185 kilometres. With the West Morava, its longer branch, it is 493 kilometres long, and the Ibar–West Morava–Great Morava system, 550 kilometres, is the longest waterway in the Balkan Peninsula. The river drains a basin of 6,126 square kilometres, and the whole Morava system drains 38,207 square kilometres, 42 percent of the area of Serbia. It flows through the most fertile and densely populated area of central Serbia, called the Morava valley or Pomoravlje.

The Romans called the river Margus, and the West and South Morava Brongus and Angrus. The present city of Ćuprija existed in Roman times as Horreum Margi, the Granary of Margus. According to Predrag Komatina of the Institute for Byzantine Studies in Belgrade, the river is named after the Merehani, an early Slavic tribe that was still unconquered by the Bulgars in the time of the Bavarian Geographer. After 845 the Bulgars added these Slavs to their societas, and they are last mentioned in 853.

In the past the river could be navigated as far as Ćuprija, for about three quarters of its length. It was notorious for flooding, and it changed its course many times, leaving old bends as small lakes called moravište. Silt brought by the South Morava raised the bed and made floods more frequent. Disastrous floods kept people from settling on the banks, so that the valley's towns, among them Paraćin, Jagodina, Velika Plana, Požarevac and Smederevo, stand a little way from the river. Works begun in 1966 built reservoirs on the tributaries and cut through meanders, shortening the Great Morava from 245 to 185 kilometres.

The Great Morava is a textbook example of a meandering river, and before regulation its meandering ratio of 118 to 245 was one of the highest in Europe. It is navigable today for only 3 kilometres from its mouth. Before it meets the Danube it splits and sends a 47-kilometre arm, the Jezava, into the Danube separately at Smederevo. The valley has long been the most populous part of Serbia, and Serbian songs celebrate the Morava and its fertility while also telling of the damage done by its floods. Among them are Oj Moravo and Moravo, tija reko.
great-mosque-of-al-nuri-mosul: Tradition holds that Nur ad-Din Zangi, a Turkoman atabeg of the Zengid dynasty, built the mosque in 1172-1173, shortly before his death. According to the chronicle of Ibn al-Athir, after taking control of Mosul he ordered his nephew Fakhr al-Din to build it. Nur ad-Din rode to the site, ordered that neighbouring houses and shops be added to the land but that nothing be taken without the willing agreement of the owners, and put Sheikh Umar al-Malla in charge. The properties were bought at substantial prices, and the building was completed in the year 568 of the Islamic calendar, or 1172-1173. The mosque underwent many renovations over the years.

The Great Mosque of al-Nuri is a Sunni mosque in Mosul, in the Nineveh Governorate of Iraq, known for its leaning minaret, al-Hadba, 'the hunchback', which gave the city its nickname. The cylindrical minaret stood 45 metres high, with seven bands of decorative brickwork in geometric patterns. By the time Ibn Battuta visited in the 14th century it was already listing and had its nickname. Its design follows a form developed in Iran and Central Asia and resembles minarets in Mardin, Sinjar and Arbil. According to local tradition the minaret bowed in reverence when Muhammad passed overhead on his ascent to heaven, while local Christian tradition says it bows towards the tomb of the Virgin Mary.

The mosque, its madrasa and its tomb were dismantled and reassembled in 1942 in a restoration programme of the Iraqi government. Attempts to stabilise the minaret were made in 1981, and bombing of Mosul in the Iran-Iraq War worsened the lean. After the Islamic State occupied Mosul on 10 June 2014, Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi appeared at Friday prayer in the mosque on 4 July 2014 to declare a new caliphate. On 21 June 2017, during the Battle of Mosul, Iraqi government forces reported that the mosque had been blown up; the Islamic State's Amaq agency claimed a United States airstrike, a claim not substantiated, and an Iraqi video showed charges exploding inside the structure.

On 23 April 2018 the United Arab Emirates pledged US$50.4 million for reconstruction with UNESCO, Iraq's culture ministry and ICCROM, and a foundation stone was laid on 17 December 2018. In April 2021 a group of eight Egyptian architects won a competition among 123 entries; the design was criticised as resembling Gulf architecture more than that of Mosul. On 13 November 2024 workers fitted an Iraqi flag on top of the new minaret, marking the end of reconstruction, and an official opening was held on 1 September 2025.
great-mosque-of-kairouan: The mosque was established by the Arab general Uqba ibn Nafi at the founding of Kairouan in 670, at the centre of the city near the governor's headquarters. Around 690 it was destroyed during the Berber occupation of Kairouan led by Kusaila, and the Ghassanid general Hasan ibn al-Nu'man rebuilt it in 703. Between about 724 and 728 the Umayyad governor Bishr ibn Safwan, acting for Caliph Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik, pulled it down and rebuilt it except for the mihrab; the construction of the minaret began then. A further reconstruction followed in 774 under the Abbasid governor Yazid ibn Hatim.

Under the Aghlabids, Kairouan was at its height. In 836 Emir Ziyadat Allah I rebuilt the mosque, which then acquired its present appearance, and the mihrab's ribbed dome was raised on squinches. Around 862-863 Emir Abu Ibrahim added three bays to the north and the cupola over the portico before the prayer hall, and in 875 Emir Ibrahim II added three more bays, reducing the courtyard.

The mosque covers some 9,000 square metres in a slightly irregular quadrilateral. From outside it resembles a fortress, with ochre walls 1.90 metres thick and buttressed corner towers. A marble-paved courtyard lies to the north, with the square minaret at the middle of its north side. The hypostyle prayer hall to the south has 17 aisles of eight bays, the central nave being higher and wider, and it meets the wider bay along the qibla wall in a T shape before the mihrab. The Hafsid gate Bab Lalla Rihana was added in 1293.

Between the ninth and eleventh centuries Kairouan was one of the great centres of Islamic civilisation, and the mosque served both as a place of prayer and as a teaching centre for the Maliki school, with courses in mathematics, astronomy, medicine and botany. Its role has been compared to that of the University of Paris in the Middle Ages. Scholars there included the jurists Sahnun ibn Sa'id and Asad ibn al-Furat. After the Hilalian invasions of 1057 the city declined, and intellectual life moved to the University of Ez-Zitouna in Tunis.

The mosque's library held a collection of manuscripts, the oldest dating from the second half of the ninth century, including the oldest surviving Maliki legal literature and the pages of the Blue Qur'an, with gold kufic script on indigo-dyed vellum. Many are now in the Raqqada National Museum of Islamic Art. The mosque is a model for later mosques in the Maghreb, and the town of Kairouan is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
great-mosque-of-tlemcen: Yusuf ibn Tashfin founded the mosque in 1082, when he established the city of Tagrart, the core of present-day Tlemcen, beside the older Idrisid-era city of Agadir. An inscription below the dome before the mihrab dates his son's renovation to 1136, though the emir's name has been erased from it, possibly by the Almohads who ruled the city after the Almoravids. The Almoravid palace, the Qasr al-Qadima, is believed to have adjoined the mosque on its northwestern side, which is why that corner of the building is cut off.

In 1236 the minaret was added, the courtyard was reshaped and the building was extended northwards, so that the original, probably larger rectangular courtyard became a square one no longer aligned with the mosque's middle axis. An Islamic court and university once stood beside it. Under French rule the mosque was declared a Historic Monument in 1875, and French architects carried out its first modern restorations and studies.

The mosque measures about 50 by 60 metres and, like most North African mosques, has a hypostyle prayer hall and an inner courtyard. Twelve rows of horseshoe arches running perpendicular to the qibla wall divide the hall into 13 aisles, the central one wider than the rest. The ribbed dome before the mihrab is purely ornamental: its intersecting arches form a twelve-pointed star, and pierced arabesque screens between the ribs let in light. A carved wooden screen dated 1138, which once enclosed the maqsura below it, is now in the Museum of Art and History in Tlemcen.

The brick minaret is 6.3 metres square and 29.15 metres high with its lantern, its faces carved with sebka panels. A large chandelier hung from the central dome; the archaeologist Lucien Golvin suggested it came from the Marinid mosque of al-Mansura. Its remains are in a local museum, and a replacement was made in the 20th century by the Tlemcen metalworker Mohammed ben Kalfate.

Antonio Almagro has argued that the mosque's first plan resembled the great mosques of Al-Andalus, a likeness later alterations obscured. Its dome descends from the 10th-century ribbed domes of the Great Mosque of Cordoba and in turn inspired those of the Great Mosque of Fes el-Jdid and the Great Mosque of Taza in the Marinid period. Jonathan Bloom notes that so few Almoravid mosques survive that its features may have been less exceptional in their own time.
great-northern-war: Between 1560 and 1658 Sweden created a Baltic empire centred on the Gulf of Finland, with the provinces of Karelia, Ingria, Estonia and Livonia, and during the Thirty Years' War it gained territory in Germany, including Western Pomerania, Wismar and the duchies of Bremen and Verden. These gains rested on a well-trained, professional army and on a modernised administration. When Charles XII succeeded in 1697, aged 14, he took over the empire as an absolute monarch. Sensing an opportunity under a young king, Denmark–Norway, Saxony and Russia formed a coalition against Sweden, and the plans to attack were made at a meeting of Augustus II the Strong and Peter the Great at Rawa Ruska in September 1698.

The war began in 1700. Denmark invaded Sweden's ally Holstein-Gottorp, while Saxony and Russia attacked Swedish Livonia and Ingria. Charles XII forced Denmark–Norway out of the war in August 1700 by the Peace of Travendal, after the Swedish navy and an Anglo-Dutch fleet bombarded Copenhagen. He then turned on Augustus II, defeating the Saxon-Polish forces at Kliszów in 1702 and Pultusk in 1703, replacing Augustus with Stanisław Leszczyński in 1704 and compelling Augustus to accept defeat in the Treaty of Altranstädt in October 1706.

Meanwhile Peter the Great recovered from Narva. In 1703 he took Nyen at the mouth of the Neva and built Saint Petersburg nearby, which cemented Russian access to the Baltic Sea. Charles then marched into Russia, and the campaign ended in 1709 with the destruction of his main army at the Battle of Poltava. Charles fled to the Ottoman town of Bender. The anti-Swedish coalition revived, and Hanover, Prussia and later Britain joined it. By 1710 the Swedes had been evicted from Tallinn, and by 1714 Russia held Finland.

Charles returned and led two campaigns against Norway, in 1716 and 1718. He was shot dead while besieging Fredriksten on 30 November 1718, and his sister Ulrika Eleonora succeeded him. Sweden still refused peace on Peter's terms, and in July 1719 a Russian fleet landed raiders with nearly 30,000 men on the Swedish east coast, burning towns such as Norrtälje, Södertälje, Nyköping and Norrköping.

The war ended Swedish supremacy in northern, central and eastern Europe, which a coalition led by Russia had successfully contested. Russia, which had founded Saint Petersburg in 1703 and held secure access to the Baltic Sea, stood in a stronger position at its end in 1721. The Swedish empire built since 1560 did not recover its supremacy.
great-peace-of-montreal: The treaty ended the Beaver Wars, fought for control of the fur trade after Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec City in 1608. The Hurons and Algonquins, backed by the French, faced the Haudenosaunee of the League of Five Nations, backed first by New Netherland and later by the English. In 1666 the Carignan-Salières Regiment devastated Mohawk communities, but the Haudenosaunee went on expanding westward. After their raid on Lachine in 1689, Governor Frontenac sent raids against the English frontier, and the border war formally ended with the Treaty of Ryswick in 1697, which left Haudenosaunee sovereignty unresolved.

French allies in the upper Great Lakes kept raiding deep into Haudenosaunee territory, and the English could not protect them. Weakened by war and epidemics, and with the fur trade collapsing as prices fell, the Haudenosaunee pursued peace. Talks in 1698 and 1699 were hampered by the English, but a first conference was held at Onondaga in March 1700, and in September a preliminary treaty was signed in Montreal with the five Haudenosaunee nations.

All the nations of the Great Lakes were then invited to Montreal for the summer of 1701, and delegations arrived after long journeys. Talks with Governor Callière dragged on as both sides bargained. The document was signed on a field prepared outside the city, each nation's representatives placing their clan's symbol, such as a turtle, wolf or bear, at its foot. A banquet followed, at which the chiefs shared a peace pipe.

Negotiated according to First Nations diplomatic custom, the treaty put negotiation in place of direct conflict, with the French as arbiters between the signatory nations, and for those nations it established the Tree of Peace among all the Great Lakes peoples. Trade and exploration resumed, and Antoine Laumet de La Mothe, Sieur de Cadillac, left Montreal to found Fort Pontchartrain du Détroit, now Detroit. The peace was fragile: within three years the Odawa attacked a Haudenosaunee village near a French fort at present-day Kingston, Ontario.

The treaty is still considered valid by the Indigenous nations involved. A square in Old Montreal was renamed Place de la Grande-Paix-de-Montréal for its 300th anniversary, and the Kondiaronk Belvedere honours the Petun leader Kondiaronk, one of its architects.
great-peacemaker: In Haudenosaunee oral tradition the Peacemaker's name, Deganawida, means Two River Currents Flowing Together. The many legends about him conflict. Some accounts say his mother was a virgin, making his birth miraculous; others say he was born an Onondaga and later adopted by the Mohawk. The Onondaga name his mother as Gahę·déhsųk, his maternal grandmother as Gahę·dóʼkthaʼ and his birthplace as Gaha·ná·yęʼ, Forks Lying, a place that is not known.

Tradition holds that he travelled between the settlements speaking only of peace, friendship and unity. In some legends his first ally was Jigonhsasee, later called the Mother of Nations, who lent her home for meetings of the rival leaders. When the Mohawk at first rejected him, he climbed a tree above Cohoes Falls and had the warriors cut it down; he vanished into the rapids, was found the next morning by a campfire, and the Mohawk became the founding nation of the confederacy. The Great Peace he taught had three parts, the Good Word, Health and Power.

The Onondaga, ruled by the evil sorcerer Tadodaho, at first refused the Great Law. With Jigonhsasee and Hiawatha, the Peacemaker freed Tadodaho of the evil that tormented him and named him Chief of Chiefs of the Grand Council. The five nations gathered at Onondaga Lake, planted a Tree of Peace and buried their weapons beneath it. Hereditary chiefs held their places through their mothers' lines, and clan mothers judged their fitness and could depose them.

The dates of his life and of the founding have not been fixed with certainty. A Seneca account tells of fighting that stopped when the sun darkened, and since William Canfield's suggestion of 1902 many scholars have read it as a solar eclipse: most favour 1451, some 1142, and in 1982 the archaeologist Dean Snow found no support for an eclipse before 1350. The Haudenosaunee revere him as a founding father, and in 1988 Concurrent Resolution 331 of the U.S. Congress recognised the confederacy's influence on the United States Constitution.
great-purge: A power vacuum opened in the Communist Party after Vladimir Lenin's death in 1924. Joseph Stalin, the party's general secretary, triumphed over his opponents by 1928 and gained control of the party. His main adversary, Leon Trotsky, was forced into exile in 1929. In the early 1930s party officials began to lose faith in Stalin's leadership, largely because of the human cost of the first five-year plan and the collectivization of agriculture, including the Holodomor famine in Ukraine.

Between 1936 and 1938 three large Moscow trials of former senior party leaders were held. The defendants were accused of conspiring with fascist and capitalist powers to assassinate Stalin, dismember the Soviet Union and restore capitalism, and forced confessions helped to obtain convictions. Trotsky was tried in absentia and sentenced to death for treason; historians have found no evidence to support the charge. The third trial, in March 1938, tried 21 defendants including Nikolai Bukharin, Alexei Rykov and the recently disgraced NKVD head Genrikh Yagoda.

The purge reached beyond the party. On 2 July 1937 Stalin ordered regional party and NKVD chiefs to estimate the number of kulaks and criminals in their districts, who were to be arrested and shot or sent to the Gulag. Mass operations against nationalities followed in 1937 and 1938; the Polish Operation was the largest, with 143,810 arrests and 111,091 executions. In the army and navy the purge removed three of five marshals, 13 of 15 army commanders and eight of nine admirals. Similar purges took place in Mongolia, where about 18,000 Buddhist lamas were killed, and in Xinjiang.

In the summer of 1938 Nikolai Yezhov was relieved as head of the NKVD and was eventually tried and executed, and Lavrentiy Beria succeeded him. A decree of 17 November 1938 cancelled most orders of systematic repression and suspended the carrying out of death sentences. Official figures put verifiable executions in 1937 and 1938 at 681,692, and estimates of total deaths range up to 1.2 million. Historians with archive access have confirmed Stalin's close involvement: he signed 357 lists in those two years authorizing about 40,000 executions.

Nikita Khrushchev denounced the purges in his secret speech to the 20th party congress in February 1956, acknowledging that many victims were innocent and convicted on confessions obtained by torture. Historians have since disagreed over how to explain the terror: the totalitarian school stressed fear as an instrument of control, while revisionists emphasized rival factions exploiting Stalin's paranoia.
great-pyramid-of-cholula: The Great Pyramid of Cholula, called Tlachihualtepetl, Nahuatl for constructed mountain, stands in the city of Cholula, 6.4 km (4 mi) west of Puebla. It is a temple that has traditionally been viewed as dedicated to the god Quetzalcoatl. Over about a thousand years before the Spanish invasion, successive building phases made it the largest pyramid in Mexico by volume. Its architecture was closely linked with that of Teotihuacan, with influence from the Gulf Coast, especially El Tajín, and its earliest phase has the talud-tablero style associated with Teotihuacan. At its peak Cholula had an estimated 100,000 inhabitants, the second largest population in Mexico. The name Cholula comes from the Nahuatl Cholollan, place of refuge.

The adobe brick pyramid stands 25 metres (82 ft) above the plain, far lower than the Great Pyramid of Giza at 146.6 metres, but much wider: 300 by 315 metres (984 by 1,033 ft) in its final form. Its volume is estimated at over 4.45 million cubic metres, against about 2.5 million for the Giza pyramid, and its base of 94,500 square metres is the largest of any pyramid in the Americas. It was enlarged by building over earlier structures, and the last stage has stairs on the west side leading to a temple that faced Iztaccíhuatl. The pyramid is only a small part of the archaeological zone of Cholula, estimated at 154 hectares.

In the 12th century Toltec-Chichimecas conquered the city and pushed the Olmeca-Xicallanca to the south. Religious focus shifted to a new temple of Quetzalcoatl, though people kept burying their dead around the pyramid. By the time the Spanish arrived it was overgrown. They built the Church of Our Lady of Remedies on its summit in 1594, and the pyramid still looks at first like a natural hill. The church is a major pilgrimage destination, and the site is also used for native rites.

The Swiss-born American archaeologist Adolph Bandelier arrived at Cholula in 1881 and published his findings in 1884, taking the first precise measurements and making the earliest plan of the site. The architect Ignacio Marquina began exploring the substructures by tunnelling in 1931, and the excavations ended officially in 1970 with the reports of Proyecto Cholula. About eight kilometres of tunnels were dug, of which about 800 metres are open to visitors. Altars, floors, walls and burials have been found. There are two well-known murals, the Chapulines, showing grasshoppers, and the Bebedores, showing figures drinking pulque. Because of the church, the pyramid as a whole has not been excavated and restored.
great-pyramid-of-giza: The Great Pyramid is the largest of the Egyptian pyramids and the chief monument of the Giza pyramid complex. It served as the tomb of Khufu, called Cheops by the Greeks, who ruled during the Fourth Dynasty of the Old Kingdom, and it still contains his granite sarcophagus. It was built over a period of about 26 years. Like other tombs of Egyptian elites it housed and protected the body, showed the status of the dead man and his family, kept his place in society and gave a place for offerings.

The pyramid was 280 royal cubits high, with a base length of 440 cubits, or about 230.3 metres a side. Most of its smooth white limestone casing was later removed, which lowered the height from 146.6 to 138.5 metres. The structure is about 2.6 million cubic metres in volume and includes an internal hillock. Hemiunu, Khufu's vizier, is believed by some to have been the architect.

An estimated 2.3 million blocks were quarried, with about 5.5 million tonnes of limestone, 8,000 tonnes of granite and 500,000 tonnes of mortar. Most stone came from the Giza Plateau. White limestone for the casing was brought by boat on the Nile from Tura, and granite blocks weighing up to 80 tonnes for the King's Chamber came from Aswan. The ancient Greeks believed that slave labour was used, but discoveries at nearby workers' camps suggest that thousands of conscript labourers built it. Graffiti shows that haulers were divided into groups of 40 men, each with overseers of ten.

Around the pyramid stood a funerary complex of two mortuary temples joined by a causeway, tombs for Khufu's family and court, including three smaller pyramids for his wives, a satellite pyramid and five buried solar barques. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Memphis and its Necropolis.

The attribution to Khufu rests first on classical authors, above all Herodotus and Diodorus Siculus. Herodotus wrote more than 2,000 years after the pyramid was built, drawing on priests, officials, local Egyptians and interpreters, and his account mixes description with error and legend.

Flinders Petrie made the first precise measurements in 1880 to 1882. Radiocarbon dating of 46 samples of ash in the mortar, taken in 1984 and 1995, was calibrated to 2871 to 2604 BCE, a range thought to run 100 to 300 years early because old wood was burned. A reanalysis placed completion between 2620 and 2484 BCE. By both methods the pyramid is about 4,600 years old.
great-sioux-war-of-1876: The Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868, signed after Red Cloud's War, set aside the western half of present-day South Dakota, Black Hills included, as the Great Sioux Reservation, with the Powder River Country as unceded hunting grounds closed to white settlers. Custer's expedition of 1874 reported gold in the Black Hills, and thousands of miners followed in breach of the treaty. In May 1875 Spotted Tail, Red Cloud and Lone Horn went to Washington to ask President Ulysses S. Grant to keep the treaty, but refused an offer of $25,000 and removal to Indian Territory.

In November 1875 Grant, Lieutenant General Philip Sheridan and Brigadier General George Crook agreed that the army would stop evicting miners. The bands outside the reservation were told to report to the agencies by 31 January 1876, in the depth of winter, and on 8 February Sheridan ordered the campaigns to begin. On 17 March Colonel Joseph J. Reynolds burned a village, Northern Cheyenne rather than the Crazy Horse camp the army believed it was, but withdrew under fire.

In the summer three columns under Crook, General Alfred Terry and Colonel John Gibbon converged on the hunting grounds. Crook was checked at the Rosebud on 17 June, and on 25 June nearly 270 men of the Seventh Cavalry, Custer among them, were killed at the Little Bighorn.

The army then changed its tactics. In August Congress cut off the rations of the Sioux until they ceded the Black Hills, and in October troops surrounded the villages of Red Cloud and Red Leaf at the agencies. Colonel Ranald S. Mackenzie destroyed a Northern Cheyenne village in the Dull Knife Fight on 25 November 1876, and Colonel Nelson A. Miles campaigned through the winter from the Tongue River, fighting Crazy Horse at Wolf Mountain in January 1877. Peace missions led by George Sword, Spotted Tail and Red Cloud persuaded band after band to come in.

The Agreement of 1877, enacted on 28 February, took the Sioux land. Dull Knife's and Standing Elk's Northern Cheyenne surrendered on 21 April 1877 and were sent to Indian Territory; many who broke out of Fort Robinson in January 1878 were killed. Crazy Horse surrendered at Red Cloud on 5 May and was fatally bayoneted at Camp Robinson in September 1877. Most of the Lakota who had gone to Canada surrendered in 1880 and 1881. Nearly two-thirds of the Lakota had stayed at the agencies, and the divisions of the war shaped their politics for decades.
great-st-bernard-pass: The pass lies near the western end of the Valais Alps, on the main watershed that separates the basin of the Rhône from that of the Po. It is the lowest pass on the ridge between the two highest mountains of the Alps, Mont Blanc and Monte Rosa. The road joins Martigny on the upper Rhône to Aosta, climbing through the Val d'Entremont. The summit is well above the tree line, and snow in winter may be as much as 10 metres deep. The Great St Bernard Tunnel, opened in 1964, has reduced the old road's commercial importance, and the road over the pass is passable only from June to September.

The pass is one of the most ancient in the western Alps, with evidence of use from the Bronze Age. It first appears in history as the route of the Celtic Boii and Lingones in their invasion of Italy in 390 BCE. In 57 BCE Julius Caesar sent Servius Galba to seize it, but Galba judged he could not take it and withdrew. Augustus succeeded, founding the colony of Augusta Praetoria Salassorum, now Aosta, below it. By 43 CE, under Claudius, a good Roman road crossed the pass, with a temple to Jupiter Poeninus, from which came the later name Mons Jovis.

In May 1800 Napoleon Bonaparte, First Consul of the French Republic, led an army over the pass to strike the rear of an Austrian army of 140,000 that was besieging French-occupied Genoa. He crossed with 40,000 men and a third of their heavy artillery, sending 20,000 more over three other passes as a diversion. The guns were disassembled and dragged over the snow in hollowed pine half-logs. The Austrians were defeated at Montebello and at Marengo in June 1800.

A hospice for travellers was founded on the pass in 1049 by Saint Bernard of Menthon, and the hospice and pass took his name in the 16th century. Buildings had probably stood there since Roman times but were destroyed several times in an insecure region, and its first concern was to clear the region of bandits. The hospice became known for its St Bernard dogs, bred to cross deep snow and find lost people by scent; the first evidence of their use is two paintings of 1690 by Salvator Rosa. A handful of monks live there permanently, and it serves as a spiritual centre for those on retreat.
great-stand-on-the-ugra-river: The main Russian defence line ran along the Oka River from Kaluga east towards Nizhny Novgorod, and was extended westward along the Ugra. The land west and south of Kaluga was claimed by Lithuania. Ivan III was uniting the lands north of the Oka while the Golden Horde broke up and its steppe remnant came to be called the Great Horde.

Casimir IV Jagiellon of Poland-Lithuania was allied with the Great Horde, and Muscovy with the Crimean Khanate. Akhmat raided the Oka at Aleksin in 1472 and was driven off, and in 1476 Russia officially stopped paying tribute to the Tatars. A quarrel in late 1479 between Ivan and his brothers Andrey Bolshoy and Boris of Volotsk may have influenced Akhmat's decision to attack.

News of the invasion reached Moscow in late May 1480. One faction wanted to flee north but was overruled. Ivan sent troops to the Oka, to Serpukhov, Tarusa and Kolomna, and later moved them west towards Kaluga. Around 30 September he returned to Moscow to consult his bishops and boyars, settled the quarrel with his brothers, and moved the treasury and royal family north to Beloozero.

Akhmat camped at Vorotynsk and waited for Casimir, who never came because he was tied down fighting the Crimeans in Podolia. On 6 to 8 October Akhmat moved up to the Ugra, and fighting lasted almost four days. His attempts to cross failed, largely because of Russian missiles, and the river was wide enough to make Tatar arrows ineffective. Talks led nowhere but gave Ivan time to bring up more troops.

On 26 October Ivan began to pull back from the Ugra to Kremenets and Borovsk, where he had a good position to protect Moscow. On 8 November Akhmat began to withdraw, and news reached Ivan on 11 November. Akhmat raided twelve Lithuanian towns on the way. Ivan returned to Moscow on 28 November. Reasons for Akhmat's withdrawal are guesswork: Casimir's absence, the end of Ivan's quarrel with his brothers, the coming winter, disease, and a Tatar preference for raids over attacking a concentrated army.

Akhmat was killed on 6 January 1481 in a clash with the Nogais under Ibak Khan. In 1502 Crimea destroyed the Great Horde as an organisation, which led to Russo-Crimean wars that lasted until 1784. Russian historiography treats the stand as the end of the Tatar yoke. Some modern historians regard it as indecisive: Charles Halperin noted that Moscow had probably ceased paying tribute to the Great Horde in the 1470s, and Janet Martin called its significance embellished. After it, no Russian prince needed to ask a khan's permission to rule.
great-syrian-revolt: In 1918 Ottoman forces withdrew from Syria after defeat by the Allied Powers and their Hashemite Arab allies. The British had promised the Hashemites a united Arab state, even as the Allies made other plans in the 1916 Sykes–Picot Agreement. In March 1920 the Hashemites established the Kingdom of Syria under Faisal, with Damascus as capital, but it was short-lived. Under the French Mandate, administrators were placed at every level of government with the stated aim of training Syrians, but in practice they did the work themselves, which local notables resented. France also restricted the tribes, banning arms in settled areas and imposing lump taxes on livestock.

The spark was the treatment of the Druze. In 1923 the leaders of Jabal al-Druze reached an agreement with the French, hoping for the autonomy they had enjoyed under the Ottomans. After Selim al-Atrash resigned, the majlis chose a French officer, Captain Cabrillet, as governor, and his term was extended indefinitely.

When the Druze revolted in September 1925 the French had only 14,397 men and officers in the Mandate, with 5,902 Syrian auxiliaries, down from 70,000 in 1920. The Druze won a series of victories, annihilated a French relief column and captured the fort at al-Suwayda. The French withdrew for the winter, which the new high commissioner, Henry de Jouvenel, called a tactical error, since it encouraged a regional rebellion to take on national dimensions.

Sultan al-Atrash led the revolt from Jabal al-Druze. In Damascus, Hasan al-Kharrat led an assault in which he briefly captured the residence of the high commissioner, Maurice Sarrail, before withdrawing under heavy bombardment. On 4 October 1925 Fawzi al-Qawuqji led an uprising in Hama, and Mohammed al-Ayyash planned a front along the Euphrates at Deir ez-Zor.

The revolt was defeated and the Syrians failed in their main goal of independence and the removal of French forces. Damascus was bombed by air for 24 continuous hours, and some villages in Jabal al-Druze were emptied after being destroyed and burned. The death toll reached 4,213, of whom 2,064 died in Jabal al-Druze. France nevertheless reunified Syria, which it had divided into four states, removed its high commissioner and some officers, and held elections won by the national opposition led by Ibrahim Hananu and Hashim al-Atassi. The revolt increased Syrian nationalism and unity after earlier sectarian divisions. A memorial edifice in al-Qurayya, begun in 1987, opened in 2010.
great-trek: Britain occupied the Cape by force in the early 19th century and formally assumed permanent control around 1815. Relations between the Boer farmers and the new administration quickly soured. British authorities opposed the Boers' ownership of slaves and what they saw as harsh treatment of indigenous peoples, and insisted that the colony finance itself through taxation. In 1815 the Slachter's Nek Rebellion ended with five Boers executed for insurrection. In 1828 the governor gave all native inhabitants except slaves the rights of citizens, and English replaced Dutch in the courts.

The abolition of slavery in 1834 amplified the resentment. Some 35,000 registered slaves were to be freed, and compensation had to be collected in London, which few Boers could afford. Some considered leaving for the unmapped interior, and trekboers were frustrated that the British would not extend the colony's borders eastward. The Dutch Reformed Church refused to endorse the migration, and many Boers stayed.

In 1834–1835 a Kommissietrek led by Petrus Lafras Uys scouted Natal, and Jan Gerritze Bantjes's report on Natalia helped inspire the migration. The first wave, from 1835 to 1840, involved an estimated 6,000 people, and the first two parties, under Louis Tregardt and Hans van Rensburg, left in September 1835. In October 1836 an army of 4,600 Ndebele attacked Hendrik Potgieter's laager at Vegkop and was repulsed by thirty-five armed trekkers. Punitive raids then forced Mzilikazi and his followers to flee to what is now Zimbabwe.

In October 1837 Piet Retief met the Zulu king Dingane to negotiate for land, and Dingane had Retief and seventy followers killed. Zulu forces then attacked encampments at Blaauwkrans and Weenen, killing 532 people, including 282 Voortrekkers. On 16 December 1838 Andries Pretorius defeated a Zulu army at the Battle of Blood River. Dingane's half-brother Mpande allied with the trekkers to overthrow him, and the Voortrekkers proclaimed the Natalia Republic, which the British annexed in 1843.

The Great Trek led directly to the founding of autonomous Boer republics, the South African Republic, the Orange Free State and Natalia, and to conflicts that displaced the Northern Ndebele and contributed to the decline and collapse of the Zulu Kingdom. The trek broke down the earlier class hierarchy, and leaders relied on patriarchal family structure and military reputation to keep control, with lasting effects on Afrikaans culture.

The centenary of 1938 played a major role in the growth of Afrikaans nationalism. It included a re-enactment ending at the Voortrekker Monument in Pretoria, completed in 1949. 16 December, first called Dingane's Day and later the Day of the Vow, was a public holiday, renamed the Day of Reconciliation after apartheid.
great-turkish-war: The war grew out of earlier Ottoman conflicts with Poland-Lithuania. In August 1672 Sultan Mehmed IV attacked Kamenets Podolski, which surrendered, and by the Treaty of Buchach the Poles ceded Kamenets and Podolia and agreed to pay tribute. The General Sejm refused the tribute and raised an army under Sobieski, which won the Battle of Khotyn in 1673. Sobieski was elected king and fought the Ottomans without success until the Treaty of Żurawno of 17 October 1676, which left the Turks only Kamenets-Podolski.

The Ottoman main army laid siege to Vienna on 14 July 1683. On 6 September the Poles under Sobieski joined the Imperial troops and forces from Saxony, Bavaria, Baden, Franconia and Swabia, and around six in the evening the allies attacked, with Sobieski leading 3,000 Polish heavy lancers, the Winged Hussars. The Ottoman lines broke, and within three hours the Christian forces had won. A Holy League initiated by Pope Innocent XI, joined by the Holy Roman Empire, Poland-Lithuania and Venice in 1684 and Russia in 1686, then counterattacked.

Buda, held by the Ottomans since 1541, fell on 2 September 1686 after resisting for 78 days. The Second Battle of Mohács in 1687 was a crushing Ottoman defeat that led to a mutiny, the execution of the grand vizier and the deposition of Mehmed IV.

The Holy League took Belgrade by 1688, but when France besieged Philippsburg on 27 September 1688 and began the Nine Years' War, Imperial resources were drawn west and the Ottomans retook Belgrade in 1690. At the Battle of Slankamen in 1691 Louis of Baden defeated the Turks, securing Hungary and Transylvania. Prince Eugene of Savoy won a decisive victory at Zenta on 11 September 1697, killing over 30,000 Ottomans. In the Morean War Francesco Morosini took Koroni in 1685 and Nafplion in 1686, and by 1687 Venice held most of the Peloponnese.

The Treaty of Karlowitz of 1699 ended the war. The Ottomans ceded most of Hungary, Transylvania and Slavonia and parts of Croatia to the Habsburgs, Podolia returned to Poland, and most of Dalmatia passed to Venice along with the Morea, which the Ottomans regained in the Treaty of Passarowitz of 1718. The war was the first in which the Ottoman Empire lost substantial territory, and it was the first time Russia joined an alliance with Western Europe. Ottoman sources call it the Disaster Years. After further losses in 1716 to 1718, the Ottomans adopted a more defensive military policy in the following century.
great-wall-of-china: The Chinese were already familiar with wall-building by the Spring and Autumn period, between the 8th and 5th centuries BCE. During that time and the Warring States period that followed, states such as Zheng, Chu, Qin, Wei, Zhao, Qi and Yan built extensive fortifications to defend their own borders. These were made mostly of stone or of earth and gravel stamped between board frames.

After Qin emerged victorious in 221 BCE, its ruler, the First Emperor, ordered the destruction of the wall sections that divided his empire among the former states. To position the empire against the Xiongnu, however, he had new walls built to connect the remaining fortifications along the northern frontier. The guiding principle was Build and move on, implying that the walls were not a permanently fixed border. Later the Han, the Northern dynasties and the Sui repaired, rebuilt or expanded sections at great cost, while the Tang and Song undertook no significant effort in the region.

The Ming dynasty made the most substantial contributions after its defeat by the Oirats at the Battle of Tumu. Dynasties founded by non-Han peoples, among them the Northern Wei, the Liao, the Jin and the Western Xia, also built walls, further north than the Han ones. A survey reported in 2012 concluded that the walls and trenches of all periods span 21,196.18 km, of which the Ming wall measures 8,850 km.

Before the Ming the wall was mainly rammed earth, stone and wood. The Ming used bricks heavily, which were easier to work with and bore more weight, and cut stone for foundations and gateways. Sticky rice mortar, made of sticky rice soup and slaked lime, held the bricks together. Signal towers on hilltops allowed units to call reinforcements and warn garrisons.

The name Long Wall appears in Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian. Because of the wall's association with the First Emperor's supposed tyranny, later dynasties usually avoided that name for their own additions. Only in the Qing period did it become the general term. The belief that the wall can be seen from the Moon is a myth; an early reference to the claim is a letter of 1754 by the antiquary William Stukeley.
great-zab: The Great Zab, or Upper Zab, is a river of about 400 kilometres. It rises in Turkey near Lake Van, at about 3,000 metres, crosses the provinces of Van and Hakkâri, and flows through Iraq's Duhok and Erbil governorates to join the Tigris on its left bank south of Mosul. Its basin covers about 40,300 square kilometres by the highest estimate. In its upper reaches it runs through steep, rocky gorges. The river is fed by rainfall and snowmelt, so its discharge varies greatly, and medieval Arab geographers called it, with the Little Zab, demoniacally possessed because of its torrential nature. In Kurdish it is the Great Zê, or Badinan Zê.

People have lived in the Zagros since the Lower Palaeolithic. Neanderthals occupied Shanidar Cave in the Sapna Valley, known for its Neanderthal burials, and Erbil's citadel has been occupied since at least the sixth millennium BCE. The earliest historical reference to the region is from the Ur III dynasty, when King Shulgi mentioned Urbilum, the ancient name of Erbil. The Assyrian capitals of Assur, Nineveh, Nimrud and Dur-Sharrukin lay in the foothills where the Great Zab meets the Tigris, and Ashurnasirpal II built a canal that drew water from the river to irrigate the land around Nimrud, which Tiglath-Pileser III and Esarhaddon restored.

After the Assyrian empire fell, the area passed to the Medes, then to the Achaemenids in 550 BCE and to the Seleucids after Alexander's death. In 750 CE the Abbasid as-Saffah defeated the last Umayyad caliph, Marwan II, in the Battle of the Zab on the Khazir River, a tributary. Survivors of the Mongol sack of Erbil in the 13th century sought refuge in the river's inaccessible valleys. In the 19th century local Kurdish leaders controlled the area, and in the 19th and 20th centuries its tribes rose repeatedly for autonomy, the last uprising starting in 1974.

Plans for a dam at the Bekhme Gorge were first proposed in 1937, and work began in 1989, but it was interrupted by the Gulf War in 1990 and the dam remains unfinished. Turkey has built the small Bağışlı Hydroelectric Power Plant on the river.
great-zimbabwe: Great Zimbabwe stands in the south-eastern hills of the modern country of Zimbabwe, near Masvingo. The word great distinguishes it from the many smaller ruins known as zimbabwes, or houses of stone, of which more than 400 have been identified across southern Africa. The name is Shona and was first recorded in 1531 by Vicente Pegado, captain of the Portuguese garrison of Sofala, who wrote that the people called such buildings Symbaoe, meaning court. The stone city spans 7.22 square kilometres and is composed of the Hill Complex, the Valley Complex and the Great Enclosure.

Construction of the stone buildings began in the 11th century and continued for more than 300 years. The ancestors of the Shona people, among them the Karanga, built them. Cattle and agriculture were the basis of the society, and the ruling dynasty first used wealth to build houses of thick earthen daub and then stone walls to shield themselves from public view. The process advanced rapidly in the 13th century.

The Great Enclosure, with dry-stone walls 11 metres high built without mortar, dates to the 13th and 14th centuries and probably served as the royal residence. Great Zimbabwe replaced Mapungubwe as a centre of trade around 1300. It controlled routes from the goldfields of the Zimbabwean Plateau to the Swahili coast, and gold and ivory went to the Indian Ocean through ports such as Sofala. Chinese porcelain and glass beads found there show the reach of that trade.

The cause of its decline is unknown. Shona oral tradition blames a shortage of salt, which may be a figurative way of speaking of exhausted land or resources. Other suggestions are that the water supply ran out or became contaminated. The city was abandoned in the 16th or 17th century.
