Great Zimbabwe is recognised as a World Heritage Site by UNESCO, and the modern independent state is named after it. Among the objects recovered are eight soapstone birds, carved on the tops of monoliths, which are thought to represent the bateleur eagle, a messenger of god in Shona culture. The first European visits date from the 19th century, and between the 1890s and 1920s antiquarians looted the site.

European writers ascribed its building to Phoenicians, Arabs and others, and under the government of Rhodesia archaeologists were pressured to deny African construction. David Randall-MacIver in 1905 and Gertrude Caton Thompson in 1929 concluded from excavations that it was Bantu and medieval, and that origin became the consensus among scholars in the 1950s.
greater-and-lesser-tunbs: The two islands lie in the eastern Persian Gulf, about 12 kilometres apart and some 20 kilometres south of the Iranian island of Qeshm. Greater Tunb covers 10.3 square kilometres and is known for its red soil; accounts of its population differ, some giving a few dozen to a few hundred inhabitants and others no native civilian population at all. Lesser Tunb, of 2 square kilometres, holds only a small airfield, a harbour and an Iranian military unit. The name is in all likelihood Persian, from a local word for a hill or low elevation.

Ibn Balkhi's 12th-century Farsnameh and Hamdallah Mustawfi's 14th-century Nuzhat al-Qulub refer to Greater Tunb as an Iranian island. From about 1330 the islands belonged to the Kings of Hormuz, and they remained under the Hormuzi-Portuguese administration until the Portuguese were expelled from the Persian coast in 1622. In the 18th century the Qasimi, a clan from the Persian coast, became rulers of Ras al-Khaimah on the Arabian shore while also governing Bandar Lengeh on the Persian side, and the islands fell under Qasimi control for about a century, the origin of the present dispute.

British surveys and maps from 1786 to 1886 showed the Tunbs as part of Lengeh under the province of Fars, and Britain acknowledged Persian ownership until 1886. After Persia reorganised its Gulf ports in 1887 and dissolved the Qasimi governorship, Britain, suspecting German and Russian influence, changed its stance. On 14 June 1904 Persia withdrew from Abu Musa and Greater Tunb with reservations, an arrangement Iranian histories call the status quo agreement; the sheikh of Sharjah raised his flags there three days later.

Iranian forces met resistance from a small Arab police force when they took the islands in 1971, and four Iranian marines were killed. According to some sources about 120 Arab inhabitants of Greater Tunb were then deported to Ras al-Khaimah, while others hold that the island had been uninhabited for some time. Bilateral talks in 1992 failed, and Iran refused to take the dispute to the International Court of Justice. In September 2026 the UAE raised the matter at the UN General Assembly, and on 29 October 2026 Canada recognised the islands as Emirati territory, which Iran condemned.

Iran administers both islands as part of its Hormozgan province and has built naval bases on them to watch over the Strait of Hormuz. The United Arab Emirates claims them for the Emirate of Ras al-Khaimah and refers to them as occupied, a claim the Cooperation Council for the Arab States of the Gulf has repeatedly supported.
greater-caucasus: The Greater Caucasus runs from the Taman Peninsula on the Black Sea to the Absheron Peninsula on the Caspian, reaching from the Western Caucasus near Sochi almost to Baku. It is traditionally divided into three parts: the Western Caucasus between the Black Sea and Mount Elbrus, the Central Caucasus between Elbrus and Mount Kazbek, and the Eastern Caucasus between Kazbek and the Caspian. The wetter Western Caucasus is heavily forested, with deciduous forest up to 1,500 metres, conifers up to 2,500 metres and alpine meadows above the tree line, while the drier Eastern Caucasus is mostly treeless.

Mount Elbrus, at 5,642 metres, is the highest mountain in Europe. Other great summits include Dykh-Tau at 5,205 metres, Shkhara at 5,201, Janga at 5,051 and Kazbek, called Mkinvartsveri in Georgian, at 5,047. The Georgian Military Road through the Darial Gorge and the Trans-Caucasus Highway cross the range at altitudes of up to 3,000 metres. Among its passes are the Bogovatchosgele Pass at 2,968 metres, the Abano Pass at 2,864 and the Mamison Pass at 2,836.

Some regard the watershed of the Caucasus as the boundary between Eastern Europe and Western Asia. The European part to the north is known as Ciscaucasia and the part to the south as Transcaucasia, which is dominated by the Lesser Caucasus. The watershed was the border in 1801 between the Caucasia province of the Russian Empire and the Ottoman Empire and Persia. After the Russian victory in 1813 and the Treaty of Gulistan the border moved well into Transcaucasia. The present border between Georgia and Russia still follows the watershed almost exactly, with a few exceptions in the Georgian west, Kakheti and Mtskheta-Mtianeti.
greater-east-asia-co-prosperity-sphere: The idea of a unified Asia under Japanese leadership is traced to Toyotomi Hideyoshi in the 16th century, who proposed to make China, Korea and Japan one. On 3 November 1938 Prime Minister Fumimaro Konoe and Foreign Minister Hachirō Arita proposed the New Order in East Asia, limited to Japan, China and the puppet state of Manchukuo, with six stated purposes that included joint defence against communism and economic co-operation. On 29 June 1940 Arita renamed the union the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere in a radio address, and on 1 August Konoe extended its scope to Southeast Asia. Japan also explained its expansion in Asia as analogous to the Monroe Doctrine of the United States.

The proposed objectives were economic self-sufficiency and co-operation among its members and resistance to Western imperialism and Soviet communism. In reality, militarists and nationalists saw it as a propaganda tool for enforcing Japanese hegemony, and Japanese spokesmen openly described it as a device for the development of the Japanese race. A secret document completed in 1943, An Investigation of Global Policy with the Yamato Race as Nucleus, laid out that Japan would take the superior position. A Land Disposal Plan drawn up by the Ministry of War in December 1941, with the consent of Hideki Tōjō, envisaged both territories under direct Japanese administration and nominally independent vassal states on the model of Manchukuo.

The outbreak of war in Europe gave Japan the chance to conquer Southeast Asian territories for their raw materials, and after the United States embargo on steel and oil it attacked British and Dutch colonies in December 1941. Propaganda used phrases such as Asia for the Asiatics, and invading forces sometimes received warm welcomes, but the brutality that followed led many inhabitants to regard Japan as worse than their former rulers. Estimates put at about 100,000 the Burmese and Malay Indian labourers who died building the Burma-Siam Railway. Plans to use the Philippines for crops needed by Japanese industry failed, and Japan declared the Philippines an independent republic in October 1943.

The Greater East Asia Conference met in Tokyo on 5 and 6 November 1943, with Tōjō hosting the heads of state of Manchukuo, China, Burma, the Philippines and the Provisional Government of Free India and an envoy from Thailand. It was mainly propaganda, without practical plans for economic development or integration. The Sphere collapsed with Japan's surrender in September 1945. Ba Maw, wartime head of state of Burma, blamed the Japanese military for its failure, saying that it saw everything only from a Japanese perspective.
greco-bactrian-kingdom: Greeks lived in Bactria long before Alexander the Great. According to the account given, the Persian kings Darius I and Xerxes I deported Greek communities there, and Greek language and communities were common when Alexander conquered the region, crossing the Hindu Kush in 329 BCE. He founded cities, most of them named Alexandria, and settled Macedonians and other Greeks. After his death control passed to Seleucus I Nicator.

Diodotus, the Seleucid satrap of Bactria, seceded and became king Diodotus I. The sources are somewhat contradictory and the date is not settled. A high chronology places the secession around 255 BCE, which would explain why Antiochus II issued so few coins in Bactria, and a low one in the mid-240s BCE links it with the Third Syrian War. The historian Justin called the kingdom the extremely prosperous Bactrian empire of the thousand cities.

Euthydemus, an Ionian Greek from Magnesia according to Polybius, overthrew the dynasty of Diodotus II around 230 to 220 BCE. Around 210 BCE the Seleucid ruler Antiochus III attacked him and defeated him on the Arius, but Euthydemus withstood a three-year siege at Bactra, and Antiochus recognised him and offered a daughter to his son Demetrius. Before 180 BCE Demetrius invaded the Indian subcontinent, which created the Indo-Greek Kingdom, a successor state that lasted almost two centuries.

Around 170 BCE Eucratides overthrew the Euthydemids at home and founded a short-lived dynasty. He minted coins in many Indian mints, but he was attacked and defeated by the Parthian king Mithridates I, who took Bactrian territory west of the Arius, and Justin reports that his own son killed him. Meanwhile the Yuezhi, driven west by the Xiongnu, moved south to the Oxus and the Saka invaded Bactria and Parthia from about 140 BCE. Heliocles was the last Greek king to rule in Bactria, and the kingdom fell around 120 BCE.

The kingdom was highly urbanised. Ai-Khanoum in north-eastern Afghanistan had a Greek theatre, a gymnasium and houses with colonnaded courtyards, and was burnt around 145 BCE and never resettled. Greco-Bactrian coin portraits are among the finest of Greek numismatic art, and Eucratides struck the largest gold coin of the Hellenistic world. Strabo says the Greeks of Bactria extended their empire to the Seres, meaning the Chinese.

The Yuezhi settled in Bactria, became Hellenized and founded the Kushan Empire around 30 CE, adopting the Greek alphabet and adding Greek deities to their pantheon. The Bactrian language was written in Greek script until the 9th century CE, and Greek art spread by the Indo-Greeks helped produce Greco-Buddhist art.
greco-persian-wars: The conflict began when the Persian king Cyrus the Great conquered the Greek-inhabited region of Ionia in 547 BCE. In 499 BCE the tyrant Aristagoras of Miletus mounted a failed expedition against Naxos with Persian support and, sensing his dismissal, incited Ionia to revolt against King Darius the Great. With Athens and Eretria he captured and razed Sardis in 498 BCE, and Darius vowed revenge. The Persians won a decisive victory at the Battle of Lade in 494 BCE, and the revolt collapsed.

In 492 BCE Mardonius re-subjugated Thrace and made Macedon a fully subordinate client kingdom, but a storm wrecked his fleet off Mount Athos and he withdrew. In 490 BCE Datis and Artaphernes, the satrap's son, crossed the Aegean, took the Cyclades and razed Eretria, but the Athenians and Plataeans defeated them at the Battle of Marathon. Darius died in 486 BCE, and his son Xerxes I crushed a revolt in Egypt and prepared a full-scale invasion.

In 480 BCE Xerxes led one of the largest armies of the ancient world into Greece. Leonidas I of Sparta held the pass of Thermopylae with 300 of his bodyguard and allied contingents, but the Persians won, took Boeotia, and razed an evacuated Athens. The combined Greek fleet then defeated the Persian fleet at Salamis in September. In 479 BCE the Greeks routed the Persian army at the Battle of Plataea, and the victory at Mycale prompted a second revolt of the Greek cities of Asia Minor.

The Greeks then took the offensive. They besieged and took Sestos and Byzantium, which gave them command of the straits and access to the Black Sea trade. Under the Delian League, which the Athenians came to lead, and the Athenian politician Cimon, the Greeks cleared Persian garrisons from Thrace and the Aegean in the 470s, and at the Battle of the Eurymedon the Athenians destroyed a Persian fleet and routed its army ashore.

Thucydides mentions no peace after the Battle of Salamis-in-Cyprus, while Diodorus reports a Peace of Callias, which some fourth-century authors rejected. Athens did not release its allies from their duty to provide money or ships, and the Delian League became the Athenian Empire. The rivalry between Athens and Sparta later led to the Second Peloponnesian War.
greco-roman-world: The Greco-Roman world is the modern term for the regions that historically and culturally fell under the direct influence of the language, culture, government and religion of the ancient Greeks and Romans. The two cultures first blended significantly in the military sphere of the Roman Republic and then of the widening Roman Empire. Greek became the language of intellectual culture and commerce in the Eastern Mediterranean, and Latin that of public administration and law, especially in the West. They were never the native languages of most of the rural peasants, who formed the great majority of the Empire's population, but they became the languages of the urban elites and a lingua franca.

Its core was the Mediterranean coast: the Italian Peninsula, Greece, Cyprus, Iberia, Anatolia, Thrace, Gaul, the Syrian region, Egypt, Roman Africa and Mauretania. Its periphery included Illyricum, Moesia, Pannonia, Dacia, Nubia, Arabia Petraea and the Tauric Chersonesus. To the east lay the Persians, with whom there was constant interaction, from the Greco-Persian wars to Alexander the Great's conquest and Marcus Licinius Crassus's defeat.

Education in art, philosophy and rhetoric was transmitted throughout the lands of Greek and Roman rule. Several hundred papyrus volumes found in a Roman villa at Herculaneum are in Greek, Cicero and Julius Caesar frequented schools in Greece, and most educated Romans were probably bilingual. Augustus's Res Gestae was set up in both Greek and Latin. In architecture the temple was the most representative building, in the Doric, Ionic and Corinthian styles of Greece.

In politics, Plato, Aristotle and Polybius set out theories of mixed government and civic virtue. Polybius described the Roman Republic as a mixture of monarchy, aristocracy and democracy, and Cicero linked the Roman res publica to the Greek politeia. In 211 the Constitutio Antoniniana of Caracalla made all the empire's free men citizens, and the people who remained within the empire's lands, including Byzantium, continued to call themselves Rhomaioi.

Mythology is regarded as one of classical antiquity's major contributions to Western society, along with philosophy and political theory. Early Christianity was born in the Greco-Roman world, which had a massive influence on Christian culture. Enlightenment philosophers such as Voltaire drew on Cicero's works, and saw the Roman Republic as an ideal system because it had features like a separation of powers.
greco-turkish-war-1897: In 1878 the Ottoman Empire signed the Pact of Halepa, which was to give Crete wide autonomy under the organic law of 1868. Ottoman commissioners repeatedly ignored it, and rebellions followed in 1885, 1888 and 1889. In 1896 clashes between the Greek and Muslim communities of the island flared again, and in January 1897 inter-communal violence broke out, with the Christian district of Chania set on fire. Cretan revolutionaries declared a struggle for independence and union with Greece.

In Athens, demonstrations accused King George I and the government of Theodoros Deligiannis of betraying the Cretan cause, and the nationalist National Society pressed for confrontation. In February 1897 Colonel Timoleon Vassos landed two battalions at Platanias and proclaimed Crete's union with Greece, although six Great Powers had already sent warships to Cretan waters.

Greece fielded about 45,000 men in Thessaly under Crown Prince Constantine, with 16,000 in Epirus. The Ottoman army, trained by a German military mission under Colmar von der Goltz and largely made up of Albanian troops, had 58,000 men in Thessaly under Edhem Pasha, and was armed with Mauser repeating rifles while the Greeks had single-shot Gras rifles. War was declared on 18 April. After fighting at Tyrnavos on 21 and 22 April the Greek staff ordered a general withdrawal, and Larissa fell on 27 April.

Farsala was attacked on 5 May and Volos fell on 8 May. At Domokos the Greeks gathered 40,000 men, joined by Italian volunteers under Ricciotti Garibaldi and a Philhellenic Legion, but in mid-May an Ottoman assault broke through. The road to Athens lay open, but Tsar Nicholas II telegraphed the Sultan, the Ottoman advance stopped on 19 May and a ceasefire took effect on 20 May. In Epirus the Greeks were halted in fighting around Arta and Preveza.

A peace treaty was signed on 20 September. Greece ceded minor border areas and paid heavy reparations, and its economy came under the oversight of the International Financial Commission. The Cretan uprising went on until November 1898, when the Great Powers evicted Ottoman forces and an autonomous Cretan State under Ottoman suzerainty was founded, with Prince George of Greece and Denmark as High Commissioner. It lasted until Greece annexed the island in 1913.

In Greece the defeat exposed the country's unpreparedness and led to the Goudi coup of 1909 and then to the reforms of Eleftherios Venizelos, which preceded Greek victory in the Balkan Wars of 1912 and 1913. The war was also the first to be filmed, though the footage is lost.
greco-turkish-war-1919-1922: The war grew out of the partition of the Ottoman Empire after the First World War, in which the Treaty of Sèvres was signed on 10 August 1920. The western Allies, particularly the British prime minister David Lloyd George, had promised Greece territory at Ottoman expense if it joined their side, including Eastern Thrace and parts of western Anatolia around Smyrna. The Greek government also pointed to the Greek-speaking Orthodox population of Anatolia, which it said needed protection, and to the Megali Idea, the nationalist vision of a greater Greece on both sides of the Aegean. Historians have debated whether Greeks formed a majority in the lands claimed.

On 15 May 1919 twenty thousand Greek soldiers landed at Smyrna under cover of the Greek, French and British navies. In the Greek Summer Offensive of 1920 they took western and north-western Anatolia, including Manisa, Balıkesir, Aydın, Bursa and Uşak. In 1921, after the Battle of Kütahya–Eskişehir, Greek forces almost reached Ankara but were checked at the Battle of the Sakarya.

The Turkish counter-attack, the Great Offensive, began on 26 August 1922. On 30 August the Greek army was decisively defeated at the Battle of Dumlupınar, and the generals Nikolaos Trikoupis and Kimon Digenis were captured. The war effectively ended with the recapture of Smyrna and the great fire of Smyrna. The Armistice of Mudanya, concluded on 11 October 1922, came into force on 15 October.

Greece accepted the Turkish demands and returned to its earlier borders, leaving Eastern Thrace and western Anatolia to Turkey. The Allies abandoned the Treaty of Sèvres and negotiated the Treaty of Lausanne, which recognised the independence of the Republic of Turkey and its sovereignty over Anatolia, Istanbul and Eastern Thrace. A separate agreement provided for a population exchange: over one million Greek Orthodox Christians were displaced, in exchange for about 500,000 Muslims from Greece. Both sides committed atrocities against civilians, and by 1922 most Ottoman Greeks of Anatolia had become refugees or had died.
greece: Greece lies mostly on the Balkan peninsula, with thousands of islands, and has the longest coastline on the Mediterranean basin, 13,676 kilometres. It consists of a mountainous mainland that ends at the Peloponnese peninsula, which the canal of the Isthmus of Corinth separates from the mainland. About 80% of the country is mountains or hills. Mount Olympus, the mythical abode of the Greek gods ruled by Zeus, reaches 2,918 metres at Mytikas peak, and the Pindus range has historically been a significant barrier to east–west travel. Extensive plains lie in Thessaly, Central Macedonia and Thrace, and are among the few arable places.

Neolithic settlements in Greece, dating from the 7th millennium BCE, are the oldest in Europe. The Cycladic culture flourished on the Aegean islands from around 3200 BCE, and from c. 3100 BCE to 1100 BCE Crete was home to the Minoan civilisation, which wrote in the undeciphered scripts Linear A and Cretan hieroglyphs. On the mainland the Mycenaean civilisation developed around 1750 BCE and lasted until c. 1100 BCE.

Its people used Linear B to write the earliest attested form of Greek. After its collapse came the Greek Dark Ages, from which written records are absent, traditionally ended in 776 BCE, the year of the first Olympic Games. Many kingdoms and city-states emerged, and some founded colonies in Asia Minor, on the Black Sea shores and in southern Italy. In 508 BCE Cleisthenes instituted the first democratic system of government in Athens.

Philip II of Macedon united most of present-day Greece in the fourth century BCE, and the Hellenistic period followed his son Alexander the Great's conquests. Rome annexed Greece in the second century BCE, and it remained part of the Roman Empire and the Byzantine Empire. After the Fourth Crusade in 1204 Greek lands fragmented into Latin and Byzantine successor states, and most came under Ottoman control by the mid-15th century. A war of independence from 1821 produced a modern nation state in 1830. The Kingdom of Greece expanded in the Balkan Wars (1912–1913) and the First World War until its defeat in the Greco-Turkish War in 1922.

Greece endured military occupation in the Second World War, then the Greek Civil War and a military dictatorship from 1967 to 1974. The present constitution, enacted in 1975, makes it a parliamentary republic with a 300-member unicameral Parliament. Greece joined what is now the European Union in 1981 and adopted the euro in January 2001. The population was estimated at 10.6 million in 2022, and Athens and Thessaloniki are the two largest cities.
greek-civil-war: When Axis forces approached Athens in April 1941, King George II and his government escaped to Egypt, and the Germans set up a collaborationist government in Athens. The power vacuum was filled by resistance movements that ranged from monarchist to Communist. The largest was the National Liberation Front (EAM), founded on 27 September 1941 and controlled by the Communist Party of Greece (KKE); its military wing, ELAS, was founded in February 1942. From mid-1943 the animosity between ELAS and the other movements, such as EDES, erupted into armed conflict. In 1944 ELAS had more than 50,000 fighters, while EDES and EKKA had around 10,000 each.

On 1 December 1944 the government of Georgios Papandreou ordered the disarmament of all guerrilla forces by 10 December. EAM called a strike and a demonstration on 3 December, in which at least 200,000 people marched in Athens. Shooting began near the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, and more than 28 demonstrators were killed and 148 injured. This began the Dekemvriana, 37 days of full-scale fighting in Athens between EAM fighters and the forces of the British army and the government. The Treaty of Varkiza of February 1945 provided for ELAS to be demobilised, an amnesty for political offences, a referendum on the monarchy and a general election.

Fighting resumed in March 1946, when about 30 former ELAS members attacked a police station at Litochoro the night before the elections. The rebels organised as the Democratic Army of Greece (DSE), with Markos Vafiadis in command from a base in Yugoslavia; Yugoslavia and Albania supported them, while the Soviet Union remained ambivalent. About 30,000 children were forcibly taken by the DSE to Eastern Bloc countries, while the Communist leadership said they were evacuated at the request of parents. The royal government was funded by the United States through the Truman Doctrine of 1947 and the Marshall Plan of 1948.

The insurgents were demoralised by the split between Stalin and Tito in June 1948. Party secretary Nikolaos Zachariadis chose to follow the Soviet Union and replaced Vafiadis in January 1949, and in July 1949 Tito closed the Yugoslav border to the DSE. The Hellenic Army under Marshal Alexandros Papagos defeated the DSE in its final stages. At least 80,000 people died in the war, and thousands were imprisoned or exiled to the islands of Gyaros and Makronisos, while many others fled to Communist countries or emigrated.
The KKE remained banned until 1974, and the conflict was officially recognised as a civil war in 1989. The division it left in Greek society contributed to the polarisation of the 1960s.
greek-fire: Incendiary weapons were used for centuries before Greek fire. Thucydides mentions a long tube on wheels that blew flames forward with a large bellows at the siege of Delium in 424 BCE, and the defenders of Petra in 550-551 threw fire pots of sulphur, pitch and naphtha. Greek fire proper was developed about 672 and is ascribed by the chronicler Theophanes the Confessor to Kallinikos, a Jewish architect from Heliopolis in Syria who fled to the Romans. Theophanes also reports fire-carrying ships with nozzles a couple of years earlier, so Kallinikos may have improved an established weapon.

It came when the Byzantines, weakened by wars with Sassanid Persia, had lost Syria, Palestine and Egypt to the Arabs, who about 672 set out to take Constantinople. Greek fire was used with great effect against the Muslim fleets and helped to repel the first and second Arab sieges of the city.

The method that set Greek fire apart was its projection through a tube, the siphon, aboard ships or in sieges. It was a liquid that burned on water, and its discharge was accompanied by thunder and much smoke. According to sources, only sand, strong vinegar or old urine could put it out. Grenades, catapult-thrown jars and hand siphons, claimed by Emperor Leo VI as his invention, were also used. It was a system of ships, heating device, siphon and trained operators, each known to few. When the Bulgars took Mesembria and Debeltos in 814 they captured 36 siphons and some of the substance but could make no use of them.

Its range was limited and it worked only in a calm sea and a favourable wind, and the Muslim navies learned to keep out of range and to use felt or hides soaked in vinegar. Emperor Constantine Porphyrogennetos told his son never to reveal the secret, which he said an angel had shown to Constantine the Great.

The composition was a closely guarded secret and has been lost. Theories that its chief ingredient was saltpetre, quicklime or calcium phosphide have been rejected, since saltpetre was not used in warfare before the 13th century and experiments did not reproduce the effects described. Most modern scholars agree that it was based on crude or refined petroleum mixed with resins, comparable to napalm. In 2002 John Haldon built a full-scale device using crude oil and wood resins, which reached a flame temperature above 1,000 °C and an effective range of up to 15 metres.
greek-language: Greek has been spoken in the Balkan peninsula since around the 3rd millennium BCE, or possibly earlier. The earliest written evidence is a Linear B clay tablet found in Messenia, dating to between 1450 and 1350 BCE, which makes Greek the oldest recorded living language. Proto-Greek, the assumed last common ancestor, is unrecorded. Greek forms an independent branch of the Indo-European family, and current consensus regards the extinct Phrygian language as its closest relative.

The language is conventionally divided into Mycenaean Greek, recorded in Linear B from the 15th century BCE; Ancient Greek, in its various dialects; and later Koine, Medieval and Modern Greek. Such divisions are relatively arbitrary, since Ancient Greek has enjoyed high prestige in every period. The dative case fell out of use, and the pitch accent was replaced by a stress accent during the Hellenistic and Roman period.

Linear B, a syllabary, was the first script used for Greek and was deciphered in the 1950s by Michael Ventris and John Chadwick, building on the research of Alice Kober. The Greek alphabet has been in use since about the 9th century BCE and was made by modifying the Phoenician alphabet, with the innovation of letters for vowels.

During antiquity Greek was by far the most widely spoken lingua franca of the Mediterranean world, and it eventually became the official language of the Byzantine Empire. It fell into disuse in Western Europe in the Middle Ages and was reintroduced after the fall of Constantinople. It was also the language of government and religion in the Christian Nubian kingdoms for most of their history. Homer's epic poetry begins a literature of lasting importance, many foundational texts of science and philosophy were composed in Greek, and the New Testament was originally written in it. Words such as mathematics, democracy, philosophy and theatre are of Greek origin.
greek-peoples-liberation-army: After the German invasion of 1941 several hundred members of the Communist Party of Greece (KKE) went underground. Following the German attack on the Soviet Union, the party pursued a popular front, and on 27 September 1941 four left-wing parties founded the National Liberation Front (EAM), in which the KKE was dominant. On 16 February 1942 EAM founded ELAS, and in June 1942 Athanasios Klaras, known as Aris Velouchiotis, entered the village of Domnista in Evrytania with 10 to 15 guerrillas and proclaimed the war against the Axis and its collaborators.

From its General Headquarters down to the platoon, ELAS was led by three men: a captain elected by the fighters, a military specialist, usually a regular army officer, and a political leader, usually a KKE member. At the top these posts were held by Velouchiotis, Stefanos Sarafis and Andreas Tzimas. British estimates put its strength at some 50,000 partisans two years after its founding, EAM sources at as many as 85,000. Velouchiotis imposed hard discipline: 25 deserters were caught and executed at Sperhiada. A small naval arm, the Greek People's Liberation Navy, was founded in 1943.

On the night of 25 November 1942 about 150 ELAS fighters, 60 to 65 of the rival EDES and 12 British saboteurs under Brigadier Eddie Myers overcame the Italian garrison and blew up the Gorgopotamos bridge, cutting German supply routes to the Afrika Korps for several weeks. ELAS then spread across central Greece, Thessaly and Macedonia. On 10 March 1944 EAM-ELAS set up the Political Committee of National Liberation, the Mountain Government, in elections where women voted for the first time in Greece.

From October 1943 ELAS attacked EDES and other groups it accused of collaboration, beginning a civil war that lasted until the Plaka ceasefire of February 1944. ELAS then attacked the 5/42 Evzone Regiment, and Dimitrios Psarros, leader of the EKKA resistance group, was killed in circumstances still debated. By autumn 1944 ELAS held every major city except Athens. After the Dekemvriana it was disarmed under the Varkiza Agreement, and many of its fighters later joined the Democratic Army of Greece.
greek-war-of-independence: All Greek territory except the Ionian Islands came under Ottoman rule in the 15th century, and Orthodox Christians were granted some political rights but considered inferior subjects. In the 18th century Greek merchants and sailors grew affluent and paid for schools, libraries and study at Western European universities, where they met Enlightenment ideas and romantic nationalism. Adamantios Korais and other members of the diaspora spread these ideas in Greek books and pamphlets.

In 1814 Nikolaos Skoufas, Emmanuil Xanthos and Athanasios Tsakalov founded the secret Filiki Eteria in Odessa. Its basic aim was a revival of the Byzantine Empire with Constantinople as capital, not a national state. After Ioannis Kapodistrias declined to lead it, the society turned to Alexander Ypsilantis, a Phanariote serving as a general in the Russian army, who accepted.

The first revolt began in the Danubian Principalities, where Ypsilantis crossed the river Prut in February 1821, but the Ottomans soon put it down. On 17 March 1821 the Maniots in the Peloponnese were the first to declare war, and in September 1821 Theodoros Kolokotronis captured Tripolitsa. The First National Assembly met at Epidaurus in late December 1821 and drafted the first Greek constitution. Factional quarrels led to two civil wars among the Greeks.

The Ottoman Sultan called in Muhammad Ali of Egypt, whose son Ibrahim Pasha landed in the Peloponnese in February 1825 and brought most of it under Egyptian control that year. Russia, Britain and France then sent naval squadrons in 1827 and destroyed the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet at the Battle of Navarino. In 1828 the Egyptian army withdrew under pressure from a French expeditionary force, and the revolutionaries retook central Greece. Massacres of civilians were committed by both sides, and tens of thousands of Greek civilians were killed, left to die or taken into slavery.

Greece was recognized as an independent state under the London Protocol of February 1830. Further negotiations in 1832 produced the Treaty of Constantinople, which defined the borders and made Prince Otto of Bavaria the first king. The new state had a population of 800,000, under one-third of the 2.5 million Greeks of the Ottoman Empire, and for much of the next century it pursued the Megali Idea of uniting all Greeks in one country.

The war's slogan, Eleftheria i thanatos, Freedom or death, became Greece's national motto. Dionysios Solomos wrote the Hymn to Liberty in 1823, and its first two stanzas are now the national anthem. The revolution is commemorated on 25 March.
green-gang: The society had its roots in the Luojiao, a Buddhist sect founded by Luo Qing in the mid-Ming dynasty. In the early 18th century three sworn brothers, Weng Yan, Qian Jian and Pan Qing, brought the sect to the workers who carried grain along the Grand Canal, where Luoist groups mixed with the boatmen's societies and provided burials and hostels. In 1768 the Qianlong Emperor ordered their temples destroyed and proscribed the sect, which went underground on the grain fleets themselves.

The Taiping Rebellion and the change in the course of the Yellow River around 1855 ended grain shipment on the canal. The boatmen scattered into the Taiping and Nian rebellions or into salt smuggling on the coast, and in northern Jiangsu in the 1870s boatmen and smugglers formed the Anqing Daoyou, the direct precursor of the Green Gang.

Shanghai suited the gang. It had become a transshipment point for grain and, as a treaty port, a gateway for foreign trade, opium included; the separate jurisdictions of the International Settlement and the French Concession favoured organised crime, and immigrants depended on hometown and sworn-brother networks through which the gang worked. Under Du Yuesheng, introduced to the older leader Huang Jinrong because his mentor came from Suzhou like Huang, it controlled crime across the city.

The Kuomintang often hired the gang to break up union meetings and strikes. Its leader Ying Guixin was involved in Yuan Shikai's assassination of Song Jiaoren in 1913, and under the name of the Society for Common Progress the gang, with other criminal gangs, carried out the massacre of about 5,000 pro-Communist strikers in April 1927 ordered by Chiang Kai-shek, who later made Du Yuesheng a general. The gang shared its drug profits with the Kuomintang through the Opium Suppression Bureau.

After the Nationalist defeat on the mainland in 1949 the gang left Shanghai and in the early 1950s opened heroin refineries in Hong Kong, but it lost the struggle with local syndicates and had disappeared by the mid-1950s. Chaozhou syndicates from Swatow took over the market with the help of its chemists, and by the end of the 1960s Hong Kong chemists had set up the first laboratory for high-grade no. 4 heroin on the border between Thailand and Burma.
green-march: Spanish Sahara had been a Spanish possession since the last third of the 19th century. In 1958 the regime of Francisco Franco declared it the 53rd Spanish province, and in 1960 the United Nations listed it as a non-self-governing territory. Morocco, which claimed it as part of a Greater Morocco, faced a domestic crisis under Hassan II, who survived coup attempts in 1971 and 1972. The Polisario Front, an anti-colonial guerrilla movement backed by Algeria, was founded in 1973. In 1974 Spain agreed to prepare a census for a UN-sponsored referendum.

Morocco sought an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice. Delivered on 16 October 1975, it found that some, but only some, Sahrawi tribes had ties of allegiance to the Sultan of Morocco, but that no tie of territorial sovereignty existed with either Morocco or Mauritania, so self-determination still applied. Within hours Hassan II announced on television a peaceful march of 350,000 unarmed volunteers carrying Qur'ans and Moroccan flags to reunite the territory with Morocco.

More than 524,000 Moroccans registered in three days, and quotas selected 350,000, among them 50,000 women. They were carried south in 113 special trains and thousands of trucks and buses to a tent city of 22,000 tents at Tarfaya. From 31 October about 10,000 Moroccan troops also crossed the eastern frontier and clashed with Polisario forces. On 4 November the Spanish commander withdrew his troops 12 kilometres from the border behind minefields, with orders to avoid bloodshed while Franco lay dying.

On 6 November about 40,000 marchers cut the wire at Tah and advanced ten kilometres before halting at the Spanish minefields. The same day the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 380, which deplored the march and called for withdrawal. On 7 November a second column of 100,000 crossed from Abattekh. After talks at Agadir on 8 November, Hassan II announced on 9 November that the march had reached its objective, and the columns returned to Tarfaya from 10 November.

On 14 November 1975 Spain, Morocco and Mauritania signed the Madrid Accords. Spain gave up administration by 28 February 1976 but kept fishing rights and 35 per cent of the Bou Craa phosphate mines. Morocco took the northern two thirds and Mauritania the south. The Polisario Front proclaimed the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic on 27 February 1976, and the Western Sahara War followed. Mauritania renounced its claim in August 1979, and Morocco occupied its sector. A UN-brokered ceasefire took effect in 1991 with the MINURSO mission; the referendum has not been held.

Morocco holds that the march restored its territorial integrity on the basis of historical allegiance. The United Nations has never recognised the Madrid Accords, and General Assembly resolutions describe the Moroccan presence as occupation.
green-revolution: The term Green Revolution was first used by William S. Gaud, administrator of the American aid agency USAID, in a speech on 8 March 1968. He set it against the violent Red Revolution of the Soviets and the White Revolution of the Shah of Iran. Its genesis in Mexico was a lengthy visit in 1940 by the American Vice President-elect Henry A. Wallace, who was appalled at the small maize yields. He persuaded the Rockefeller Foundation to fund an agricultural station to hybridise maize and wheat, and hired a young Iowa agronomist, Norman Borlaug, to lead it. Borlaug received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970.

The basic approach was to breed high-yielding varieties of cereals, expand irrigation, modernise management, distribute hybridised seed and supply synthetic fertilisers and pesticides. Semi-dwarfing genes were bred in so that the plants could absorb more nitrogen without falling over before harvest. In 1960 the Philippines, with the Ford Foundation and the Rockefeller Foundation, established the International Rice Research Institute. A cross made there in 1962 produced the rice IR8 in 1966, nicknamed Miracle Rice.

In 1961 Borlaug was invited to India by M. S. Swaminathan, and Punjab was chosen as the first site. Brazil limed the acid soil of its cerrado region from the 1960s. China's own programme began separately from the American one, with state sponsorship of research and peasant knowledge. Attempts to carry the programmes to Africa have generally been less successful.

Cereal production more than doubled in developing nations between 1961 and 1985, and India's annual wheat production rose from 10 million tons in the 1960s to 73 million in 2006. Studies credit the revolution with averted hunger, raised incomes and lower infant mortality. The Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research was established on 19 May 1971 as a network of research centres.

Critics raise further concerns. The new crops need far more fertiliser and pesticide, so the energy used to grow them rose faster than the harvest. A 1989 estimate counted around a million pesticide poisonings a year, about 20,000 of them fatal. Opinions differ over its effect on wild biodiversity, and in the Philippines the credit scheme behind IR8 came by 1980 to serve mainly rich landowners.
green-standard-army: The first Green Standard troops were the soldiers of Ming commanders who surrendered to the Qing in 1644 and after. They enlisted voluntarily for long terms, usually came from the poor and stayed apart from Chinese society, partly because of a deep prejudice against soldiers in the late Ming and partly because their pay was too low and irregular to support a family. The Qing used them to govern northern China locally, calling in the Banners only where resistance lasted. In areas with many Hui people, Muslims served in their ranks.

In the Revolt of the Three Feudatories (1673–81) the Qing deployed four hundred thousand Green Standard soldiers beside the Banners. When the Banners fared poorly against Wu Sangui, the Kangxi Emperor made the Green Standard the main force, and in 1680 it retook Sichuan and southern Shaanxi under Wang Jinbao and Zhao Liangdong. Its decline showed as early as the White Lotus Rebellion of 1794–1804, and after the mid-19th-century rebellions the hired brave battalions became the dynasty's rapid response force. In 1907 a reform commission proposed discharging the worst units and turning the rest into provincial Patrol and Defence Forces, a change unfinished at the 1911 Revolution.

From the 18th century the Green Standard served mainly as a constabulary, though it also supplied most of the troops for major campaigns. It was split into thousands of posts, some of only twelve men, grouped in battalions under regional brigade generals and provincial commanders-in-chief, and command was divided so that no officer controlled a whole army; in peacetime one officer rarely led more than 5,000 men. Pay that did not keep pace with inflation, scattered posts, rare drill, unfilled places whose allowances officers kept, hired substitutes, gambling and opium all weakened it.
green-vault: In 1547 the Holy Roman elector Moritz of Saxony ordered an additional wing to be built onto Dresden Castle. Four of the new rooms on the first floor were given elaborate moulded plaster ceilings, and their column bases and capitals were painted a bluish green, which gave the rooms their name. Their official name was the Privy Repository (Geheime Verwahrung), and thick walls and iron shutters and doors protected them against fire and robbery. Through the seventeenth century the electors of Saxony used them as a private treasure chamber for important documents and jewellery.

From 1723 the elector Frederick Augustus I, known as Augustus the Strong, turned the private chambers into a museum. The architect Matthäus Daniel Pöppelmann planned a suite of eight interconnecting rooms in German Baroque style, in which the objects were arranged by material: silver, gold, amber, ivory and bronze. The Pretiosensaal and the Eckkabinett were recorded as finished in the inventory of 1725, and an extension followed in 1727. By the end of his reign in 1733 Augustus had opened his crown treasures to a select public, which was unusual in the Baroque period.

The rooms stayed unchanged for almost two centuries. The treasures were taken to the Königstein Fortress in 1938, as war approached. The bombing of Dresden on 13 February 1945 destroyed three of the eight rooms, and the Red Army took the collection to the Soviet Union that year. It came back to Dresden in 1958 and was shown in part at the Albertinum. The New Green Vault opened on the second floor of the rebuilt castle in 2004, and the reconstructed Historic Green Vault reopened in 2006.

The Historic Green Vault shows about 3,000 pieces in its nine rooms and entrance chamber, among them the Moor with Emerald Cluster, made probably in 1724 by the court goldsmith Johann Melchior Dinglinger with the sculptor Balthasar Permoser. The emerald cluster it presents came from a Colombian mine and was given to Elector Augustus by Emperor Rudolf II in 1581. The New Green Vault, with roughly 1,100 pieces, holds Dinglinger's Golden Coffee Service and his Royal Household at Delhi, made between 1701 and 1708 with 4,909 diamonds; the elector paid almost 60,000 talers for it. The Dresden Green Diamond, of 41 carats, was bought by Augustus III of Poland from a Dutch merchant at the Leipzig Fair in 1742.

On 25 November 2019 thieves broke into the museum and stole three sets of early eighteenth-century royal jewellery, each of 37 items. In December 2022 investigators found 31 of the stolen objects, and in May 2023 five men were found guilty of the theft.
greeneville-tennessee: Greeneville lies in the foothills of the Appalachian Mountains, in the Ridge-and-Valley Province, roughly halfway between Bays Mountain to the northwest and the Bald Mountains to the southeast. The valley is part of the watershed of the Nolichucky River, which passes a few miles south of the town. Hunters were camping in the Nolichucky Valley as early as the Paleo-Indian period, around 10,000 BCE, and a substantial Woodland village stood at the river's confluence with Big Limestone Creek. By the late 18th century the Cherokee claimed the valley as hunting grounds. The Great Indian Warpath passed just northwest of the modern town.

Permanent European settlement began in 1772, when the North Carolina merchant Jacob Brown leased land from the Cherokee. After voting irregularities in a local election, the settler Daniel Kennedy led a movement for a separate county, granted in 1783 and named for Nathanael Greene. Robert Kerr, at whose home the first court sessions were held, gave 50 acres for the county seat, and Greeneville was recognised as a town in 1786.

In 1784 North Carolina tried to settle its debts by giving its western lands to Congress. Delegates from Greene and neighbouring counties met and resolved to form an independent state, later called Franklin, with John Sevier as governor. Greeneville was named its capital in August 1785, and its first legislature met in December in a crude log courthouse. Congress did not admit the state, and North Carolina reasserted control the next spring.

The area had a strong abolitionist movement among Quakers and others. Benjamin Lundy moved his antislavery newspaper to Greeneville in 1822. In June 1861 delegates from thirty pro-Union counties met there, hoping for a separate state in East Tennessee, but Nashville rejected the request. Confederate general John Hunt Morgan was killed in Greeneville on 4 September 1864 during a Union raid.

Andrew Johnson arrived in 1826, bought the town's tailor shop and married Eliza McCardle in 1827. He was elected to the town council in 1829 and mayor in 1834, and went on to the state legislature and then national office. The Andrew Johnson National Historic Site, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1963, holds his tailor shop and house, and the Andrew Johnson National Cemetery.

Greeneville is the county seat of Greene County and the second oldest town in Tennessee. Its population was 15,479 at the 2020 census. The Greeneville Historic District was established in 1974, and the submarine USS Greeneville was named for the town. Magnavox ran its main facilities there from 1947 to 2005.
greenland: Greenland is the world's largest non-continental island, lying between latitudes 59° and 83°N, with over 80% of its land north of the Arctic Circle. Its area is 2,166,086 square kilometres, of which the ice sheet covers about 81%. The highest point is Gunnbjørn Fjeld, at 3,700 metres, but most of the island lies below 1,500 metres. Nearly all of its people live along the fjords of the south-west, where the climate is relatively mild.

The early Norse settlers gave the island its name. The sagas say that Erik the Red, exiled from Iceland, named the land Grœnland in the hope that a pleasant name would attract settlers. In the Greenlandic language it is Kalaallit Nunaat, land of the Kalaallit, the principal group of Greenlandic Inuit in the west.

Successive Palaeo-Inuit cultures, known mainly from archaeology, lived on the island. The first entry is thought to have been about 2500 BCE. The Saqqaq culture inhabited the south and west from about 2500 to 800 BCE, with most finds around Disko Bay, and the Independence I culture lived in the north from 2400 to 1300 BCE. About 800 BCE the Saqqaq culture disappeared, and the Early Dorset and Independence II cultures emerged. The Thule people entered later from the north.

From the late 10th century Icelanders and Norwegians settled the west coast, in a contingent of 14 boats led by Erik the Red. They formed the Eastern, Western and Middle Settlements on fjords near the south-western tip. The Norse Greenlanders submitted to the Kingdom of Norway in 1261. Settlements such as Brattahlíð lasted for centuries but vanished in the 15th century, perhaps at the onset of the Little Ice Age. Dano-Norwegian explorers returned in the 17th century, found the earlier settlement extinct and re-established a Scandinavian presence.

Greenland passed from the Norwegian to the Danish crown when Denmark and Norway separated in 1814. Denmark integrated it into the Danish Realm in 1952, ending its colonial status, and granted home rule in 1979. The Self-Government Act, passed after a referendum in 2008, transferred further areas of government to the Naalakkersuisut, the Greenlandic government, and made Greenlandic the sole official language in 2009.

Greenland is an autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark, with Nuuk as its capital and largest city. A population of 56,583 was counted in 2022, most of them Greenlandic Inuit, with a Danish minority. Its parliament is the Inatsisartut. Greenlandic culture blends Inuit and Scandinavian traditions, among them the carved ivory figures called tupilak.
greenpeace: In the late 1960s the United States planned its Cannikin underground nuclear test on Amchitka, a tectonically unstable island in Alaska, and there were concerns that it might trigger earthquakes and a tsunami. About 7,000 people blocked the Peace Arch border crossing between British Columbia and Washington, carrying signs reading Don't Make A Wave. The protests did not stop the detonation.

When the Amchitka tests were over, the young organisation turned to French atmospheric nuclear testing at Moruroa Atoll in French Polynesia. In 1972 David McTaggart, a former businessman living in New Zealand, renamed his 12.5-metre ketch Vega as Greenpeace III and sailed it into the exclusion zone, a voyage sponsored by the New Zealand branch of the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament. The French Navy tried to stop it and assaulted McTaggart; a crew member photographed the incident and made it public, and after the publicity France announced it would stop atmospheric tests.

Greenpeace evolved from a group of Canadian and American protesters into a less conservative group of environmentalists, reflecting the counterculture of the 1960s and 1970s. Seagoing ships have played a vital role in its campaigns. In 1978 it launched the first Rainbow Warrior, a 40-metre former fishing trawler first used to disrupt the Icelandic whaling fleet. Between 1978 and 1985 its crews also acted against the ocean dumping of toxic and radioactive waste, the grey seal hunt in Orkney and nuclear testing in the Pacific. In May 1985 it carried out Operation Exodus, evacuating about 300 Rongelap Atoll islanders whose home had been contaminated by fallout from a US nuclear test.

In the 1990s the organisation was influential in raising public awareness of global warming and, with the refrigerator industry, developed a CFC-free refrigerator technology called Greenfreeze; the United Nations Environment Programme gave it an award in 1997 for contributions to protecting the ozone layer. In 2007 six activists who climbed the smokestack of the Kingsnorth power station in Kent were acquitted after arguing that they had a lawful excuse to prevent greater damage from climate change.

Greenpeace is a campaigning network of 26 independent national and regional organisations, with a coordinating body, Greenpeace International, in Amsterdam. It does not accept funding from governments, corporations or political parties, relying on individual supporters and foundation grants. It is known for nonviolent direct action and has been criticised, among other things over its opposition to genetically modified organisms, which led 107 Nobel laureates to sign an open letter in June 2016, and over damage to rock near the Nazca Lines in Peru in December 2014.
greensleeves: The ballad was registered at the Stationers' Company in London by Richard Jones in September 1580 as A Newe Northen Dittye of ye Ladye Greene Sleves. Six related ballads followed in less than a year. One, Edward White's answer from the Lady to her friend Donkyn, was registered on the same day, 3 September 1580. Others came on 15 and 18 September, on 14 December, on 13 February 1581 and in August 1581, the last being White's third, which begins Greene Sleeves is worne awaie.

The song then appears in the surviving collection A Handful of Pleasant Delights of 1584 as A New Courtly Sonnet of the Lady Green Sleeves. The tune is found in several sources of the late 16th and early 17th centuries, including Ballet's manuscript lute book and Het Luitboek van Thysius.

The melody fits the chords of several ground bass progressions well known at the time, among them the romanesca, the passamezzo antico and the Andalusian progression. The romanesca originated in Spain and is a sequence of four chords over a simple bass line. A popular reading of the words takes Lady Green Sleeves to be a promiscuous young woman, since green could carry a sexual sense, as in the phrase a green gown.

Against this, the earliest such association of green dates only from 1675, paintings show saints and noblewomen in green, and the lady rejects the singer's advances. Nevill Coghill remarks that for Chaucer's age green was the colour of lightness in love.

In The Merry Wives of Windsor, written about 1597, Mistress Ford twice mentions the tune and Falstaff cries that it may thunder to the tune of Greensleeves. From as early as 1686 Christmas and New Year texts were set to it, and in 1865 William Chatterton Dix wrote What Child Is This? for the tune. The London Trained Bands used it as a slow march in the 16th and 17th centuries.

Ralph Vaughan Williams worked it into his opera Sir John in Love of 1928, and the Fantasia on Greensleeves was arranged from it in 1934. Gustav Holst combined it with another tune in his Second Suite in F. In the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand it is also traditionally played by ice cream vans.
gregoire-kayibanda: Kayibanda was born on 1 May 1924 in Tare, Rwanda. He attended primary school at Tare and then at Kabgayi, entered the Saint Léon Minor Seminary of Kabgayi in 1937, and after finishing there in 1943 studied for four years at the Major Seminary of Nyakibanda. The Hutu majority had long resented the power held by the Tutsi minority, and was encouraged by Hutu advocates in the Catholic Church and by Christian Belgians.

Kayibanda, an ethnic Hutu, led the Hutu emancipation movement. He founded the party Parmehutu, the Hutu Emancipation Movement Party, and the Bahutu Manifesto of 1957 belongs to the same movement. In 1959 Tutsis founded the UNAR party, which wanted immediate independence for Ruanda-Urundi under the existing monarchy, and skirmishes began between UNAR and Parmehutu groups.

In 1961 the monarchy was dissolved and a brief transitional administration under Dominique Mbonyumutwa preceded the First Rwandese Republic. Rwanda became independent at midnight on 1 July 1962. Kayibanda thanked the Belgians, Germans and United Nations for their work, saying that although the Belgians had made some mistakes the net result had been most positive. He was elected president on 26 October and led the first Rwandan delegation to the United Nations General Assembly. He worked closely with the Belgian colonial official Guy Logiest, and together they shaped a system that stressed racial distinctions between Hutu and Tutsi rather than class antagonisms.

By 1965 Parmehutu was the only legal party, and Kayibanda stood alone in the presidential elections of that year and of 1969. His foreign policy was pro-Western and anticommunist, and in economic matters he drew on Christian socialism. In 1973 a project extended the presidential term from four to five years and removed the age limit of 60. His regime was accused of dismissing political leaders of the north and concentrating power among people from his native prefecture, Gitarama.

On 5 July 1973 the defence minister, Major General Juvénal Habyarimana, overthrew Kayibanda in a military coup that began the Second Rwandese Republic. The coup was described as bloodless, yet an estimated 55 people, mostly officials, lawyers or businessmen close to the old regime, were reportedly executed, and their families were given sums of money for their silence. Kayibanda and his wife Vérédiana were held in a secret location, rumoured to be a house near Kabgayi, where they were reportedly starved to death. He died in 1976.
gregor-mendel: Mendel was born Johann Mendel on 20 July 1822 into a German-speaking family at Heinzendorf bei Odrau in Silesia, now Hynčice in the Czech Republic. His parents worked a farm that the family had owned for at least 130 years, and as a child he worked as a gardener and studied beekeeping. From 1840 to 1843 he studied philosophy and physics at the University of Olomouc, struggling to pay for it; his sister Theresia gave him her dowry. He became a monk partly because the Augustinian order let him obtain an education without paying for it, and he took the name Gregor on joining. In 1851 Abbot Cyril František Napp sent him to the University of Vienna, where Christian Doppler taught him physics.

Mendel failed the oral part of the teacher's certificate in 1850 and again in 1856, but he taught physics at the abbey from 1853. In the monastery's experimental garden he worked on pea plants between 1856 and 1863, cultivating some 28,000 plants. He studied seven traits, including seed shape, flower colour and plant height. When true-breeding yellow and green peas were crossed, the offspring were all yellow, and in the next generation green reappeared at a ratio of one to three. He coined the terms recessive and dominant.

He presented his paper on plant hybridisation to the Natural History Society of Brno in February and March 1865. It was ignored by scientists, seen as being about hybridisation rather than inheritance, and cited only about three times in the next thirty-five years. His correspondence with the botanist Carl Nägeli did not lead to understanding. Once he became abbot his scientific work largely ended, as he was burdened by a dispute with the civil government over taxes on religious institutions.

Mendel died in Brno on 6 January 1884 of chronic nephritis, and Leoš Janáček played the organ at his funeral. His successor as abbot burned his papers to end the tax dispute. In 1900 Hugo de Vries and Carl Correns, working independently, repeated his experiments and found his writings, and both acknowledged his priority. In 1936 Ronald Fisher judged his data too close to expectation, but Daniel Hartl and Daniel Fairbanks later rejected the charge of falsification.
gregorio-luperon: Luperón was born in Puerto Plata on 8 September 1839. His father, Pedro Castellanos, did not recognise him, and he took the surname of his mother, Nicolasa Duperron, later changing its form himself. He grew up poor, working as a water bearer, baker, fisherman and seller of sweets and fruits, but attended a school run by an English subject, and as a young merchant learned French to use a merchant's library. His revolutionary career began in 1857 in the Cibaeño Revolution against Buenaventura Báez. He later rose to the 33rd degree of Masonry.

After the Dominican Republic was annexed to Spain on 18 March 1861, exiles entered from Haiti in mid-August 1863, and Luperón joined the operations against Santiago and the council of chiefs that named Gaspar Polanco commander. As governor of La Vega he said the fight was against the regime of annexation, not against the Spanish, yet had a Spanish colonel shot as a spy. After Báez returned to power in 1868 the leaders of the Blue Party went into exile, and on 17 April 1869 the Haitian president Nissage Saget brought Luperón and his rivals together in a manifesto at Saint Marc.

On 6 October 1879 Luperón disowned the government of Cesáreo Guillermo, and forces under his lieutenant Ulises Heureaux won the country for him. His provisional government at Puerto Plata was organised on liberal principles and promoted secularism with the help of Eugenio María de Hostos. He urged the intellectual Pedro Francisco Bonó, then the priest Fernando Arturo de Meriño, to take the presidency, and later backed Heureaux despite the executions Heureaux ordered after Guillermo's expedition through Higüey. At the end of 1886 he withdrew that support, and the persecution of Heureaux's opponents sent him into exile.

In exile at Saint Thomas he fell gravely ill from an infection. He sailed for home on 15 December 1896; Heureaux visited him on board and provided a doctor, and Luperón died in his birthplace, Puerto Plata, in May 1897, his last words being that men like him should not die lying down. He left his wife of 32 years, Ana Luisa Tavares, and two children. He is often called the fourth founding father of the Dominican Republic, and the town of Luperón, the Gregorio Luperón International Airport and a metro station in Santo Domingo bear his name.
gregory-of-tours: Gregory was born Georgius Florentius at Clermont in the Auvergne, into the upper stratum of Gallo-Roman society. His father Florentius was a senator of Clermont, and relatives of his held the bishoprics of Tours, Lyon and Langres at the time of his birth. After his father's death he was raised by his uncle Gallus, bishop of Clermont, and by Gallus's successor Avitus, who ordained him deacon. A serious illness led him to visit the tomb of Saint Martin at Tours, and he recovered.

When the see of Tours fell vacant, the clergy and people chose Gregory as bishop. Deputies overtook him at the court of King Sigebert of Austrasia, and he was consecrated on 22 August 573, at the age of 34, though he accepted much against his will. He spent most of his career at Tours, on the Loire, where Frankish influence from the north met Gallo-Roman influence from the south. As the centre of the cult of Saint Martin it was a pilgrimage site and a political sanctuary. He dealt with four Frankish kings, Sigebert I, Chilperic I, Guntram and Childebert II. After rumours that he had slandered Chilperic's wife Fredegund, Chilperic had him arrested and tried for treason.

His main work, the Decem Libri Historiarum or Ten Books of Histories, known as the History of the Franks, begins with the Creation and moves quickly to the spread of Christianity into Gaul, the conversion of Clovis I and the history of the Frankish kings. Books V to X, covering the years from 575 to 591, rest largely on his own knowledge. He added an epilogue in 594. He wrote in Late Latin and apologised for his rough style. He opens with a statement of his Catholic orthodoxy against Arianism. Recent scholarship holds that his underlying purpose was to set the vanity of secular life against the miracles of the saints.

He also wrote the Life of the Fathers, twenty lives of holy men, and the Book of the Glories of the Martyrs, begun in 587, which tie saints and relics to local shrines in Gaul. Historians value the History of the Franks as the central source for the Franks' rise, and it is often compared with Herodotus.
gregory-the-illuminator: In the Armenian tradition the standard life of Gregory derives from a fifth-century hagiographic history attributed to Agathangelos. It makes him the son of the Parthian nobleman Anak, who at the urging of the Sasanian king Ardashir I assassinated the Arsacid king of Armenia, Khosrov. The Armenian nobles put Anak and his family to death, but Gregory escaped with the help of his nurse and was taken to Caesarea in Cappadocia, where he received a Christian upbringing. Some modern scholars distrust this account. Marie Louise Chaumont suggested he was probably a Greek from Cappadocia. According to Movses Khorenatsi, Gregory married Mariam and had two sons, Aristaces and Vrtanes.

Gregory entered the service of King Tiridates III, son of the murdered Khosrov. When he refused to sacrifice to the goddess Anahit, the king had him tortured, and on learning whose son he was, had him thrown into the deep pit of Khor Virap near Artaxata, where he stayed for thirteen or fifteen years. Agathangelos says he was brought out after the king's sister Khosrovidukht had a vision. He then healed the king, whom the history describes as driven into animal madness for his sins, and Tiridates and his court accepted Christianity.

Gregory raised shrines to the martyrs Gayane and Hripsime at Vagharshapat, later called Ejmiatsin, and destroyed pagan temples. He was consecrated bishop of Armenia at Caesarea by Leontius of Caesarea, and his successors went there to be confirmed until the death of Nerses I. He built churches in place of the temples, founded schools teaching in Greek and Syriac, and baptized the king, the army and the people in the Euphrates. The conversion is traditionally dated to 301, but modern scholarship considers a date near 314 more likely, and holds that the spread of Christianity was more gradual than Agathangelos depicts.

Gregory appointed his younger son Aristaces as his successor and lived as an ascetic in the cave of Manē in Upper Armenia. According to Khorenatsi he was last seen after Aristaces returned from the Council of Nicaea in 325, and he died in seclusion, buried by shepherds who did not know who he was. His descendants, the Gregorids, held the patriarchate of Armenia, with some interruptions, until the death of Patriarch Isaac in the fifth century. The Armenian Church is sometimes called lusavorchakan, "of the Illuminator", or Gregorian. The Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic churches commemorate him on 30 September.
gregory-the-patrician: Gregory, Flavius Gregorius in Latin, was related by blood to Emperor Heraclius and his grandson Constans II, and was possibly the son of Heraclius' cousin Niketas. He is first attested as exarch of Africa, a province covering modern Tunisia, eastern Algeria and western Libya, in July 645, though he may have been appointed already under Heraclius.

The exarchate was divided between a mainly Chalcedonian population and supporters of Monotheletism, the compromise between Chalcedonianism and Monophysitism that Heraclius had promoted in 638 and that in Africa was championed mostly by refugees from Egypt. In July 645 Gregory hosted a debate at Carthage between Maximus the Confessor and the Monothelite former patriarch Pyrrhus, who returned to the Chalcedonian position, and over the following months local synods condemned Monotheletism as heresy.

His revolt of 646 was also a response to the Muslim conquest of Egypt, which the government in Constantinople had failed to stop; the Arab chronicler al-Tabari instead blames a levy of 300 pounds of gold demanded by Constans. Maximus and Pope Theodore I appear to have encouraged him, and the revolt found broad support among the Romanized Africans and the Berbers of the interior. Arab sources say he minted coins with his own effigy, but none has been found.

In 647 the caliph Uthman sent Abdallah ibn Sa'ad into the exarchate with 20,000 men. Gregory met the Arabs at Sufetula, where, in the Arab accounts, an ambush party led by Abdullah ibn Zubayr killed him in his chariot and his army broke. Agapius of Hierapolis and some Syriac sources say he survived and was reconciled with Constans, but most modern scholars accept the Arab chroniclers' account. The Arabs sacked Sufetula, raided the province and left in return for a heavy tribute in gold.

Ties with Constantinople were restored, but Byzantine rule in Africa had been shaken to its roots. The Berber tribes shook off their allegiance to the empire, and most of southern Tunisia slipped outside the control of Carthage. The historian Charles Diehl saw the battle as the beginning of an inevitable end of Byzantine domination in Africa.
greifswald: Greifswald lies on the River Ryck, near its mouth into the Danish Wiek, a sub-bay of the Bay of Greifswald on the Baltic coast. The city stands roughly midway between the two largest Pomeranian islands, Rügen and Usedom,. Its name derives from the dukes of Pomerania, the House of Griffin, and means Griffin's Forest.

In the Middle Ages the site was unsettled woodland on the border between the Danish Principality of Rügen and the Pomeranian County of Gützkow. In 1199 the Rugian Prince Jaromar I allowed Danish Cistercian monks to build Hilda Abbey, later Eldena Abbey, at the mouth of the Ryck. The lands granted to the monks included a natural salt pond beside an important trade route, and the town grew there. In 1241 Prince Wizlaw I and Duke Wartislaw III both granted market rights, and in 1250 Wartislaw gave a charter under Lübeck law.

Eldena Abbey and the main buildings of the town were raised in North German Brick Gothic. By the end of the 13th century Greifswald was one of the earliest members of the Hanseatic League. In 1456 the mayor Heinrich Rubenow laid the foundations of the university.

The Reformation ended Eldena's life as a monastery, and the friaries within the walls were secularised. During the Thirty Years' War Imperial forces held the town from 1627 to 1631. Swedish troops besieged it on 12 June 1631, and it surrendered four days later. Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden came to supervise the siege and received the university's homage. After the war the town became part of Swedish Pomerania, which remained Swedish until 1815, when it passed to the Kingdom of Prussia. By 1630 the population had shrunk by two thirds.

The town expanded beyond its medieval walls for the first time about 1900. It survived the Second World War without much destruction: in April 1945 Colonel Rudolf Petershagen defied orders and surrendered it to the Red Army without a fight. From 1949 to 1990 it belonged to the German Democratic Republic, and its population peaked at about 68,000 in 1988.

Greifswald is the seat of the district of Western Pomerania-Greifswald in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The 2021 population was listed at 59,332, many of them students and staff of the University of Greifswald, which has about 12,000 students. The Pomeranian State Museum holds works by Caspar David Friedrich, who was born in the city and often painted the ruins of Eldena Abbey.
greiz: Greiz lies in eastern Thuringia, 100 kilometres east of the state capital Erfurt, on the White Elster river. It stands at the confluence of the White Elster and its tributary the Göltzsch, a position that helped the town grow fast. The place name, originally Grouts, is of Slavic origin and means gord, a fortified settlement.

The first documented mention of the settlement dates from 1209. From the 12th century it was governed by advocati, or Vögte, and in 1236 it came into the possession of Gera. It was recognised as a town in the 13th century. The House of Reuss, a ruling dynasty whose male members were all named Heinrich, later built two castles there, the Upper Castle and the Lower Castle, both by noted architects. Greiz became the capital of the Principality of Reuss-Greiz, which lasted until 1918. Fire destroyed the town entirely in 1494 and almost totally in 1802.

Between 1934 and 1943, 809 people were forcibly sterilised by the Nazis in the district hospital, and a local old people's home and care home sent 122 sick people to the Aktion T4 euthanasia programme. During World War II prisoners of war and people from occupied countries worked as forced labourers at Sorgwald and elsewhere, and at least 102 died; there is a memorial in the Old Cemetery. A monument honours the officer Kurt von Westernhagen, shot by the Gestapo in April 1945 for refusing to blow up the bridge and defend the town. Three of the five bridges were destroyed, but the town was not otherwise much damaged. Ulf Merbold, the first West German astronaut, was born there in 1941.

Greiz is the capital of the district of Greiz and has about 20,400 inhabitants. It has a large park, classified as an English garden, in its centre, the Fürstlich Greizer Park, and streets of Jugendstil houses. Its economy includes mechanical engineering, plastics, medical technology, printing and breweries. Like many towns in the former East Germany it has lost population.
gremi: Gremi lies south-west of the present village of the same name in the Kvareli district of Kakheti, 115 kilometers east of Tbilisi. The surviving complex stands on a hill: the Church of the Archangels Michael and Gabriel, a three-story castle, a bell tower and a wine cellar (marani), enclosed by a wall with embrasures, turrets and towers. Remains also survive of a secret tunnel leading to the Ints’obi River.

Gremi was the capital of the Kingdom of Kakheti in the 16th and 17th centuries, founded by King Levan of Kakheti, who reigned from 1520 to 1574. It was a lively trading town on the Silk Road and a royal residence, covering some 40 hectares in three parts: the church complex, the royal residence and the commercial quarter. After the armies of Shah Abbas I of Persia razed it, the town never regained its prosperity, and the kings of Kakheti moved their capital to Telavi in the mid-17th century.

Levan had the Church of the Archangels built in 1565, and it was frescoed by 1577. It is a cruciform domed church built chiefly of stone, marrying traditional Georgian masonry with a local interpretation of the Iranian taste of the time. It has entrances on the west, south and north, a façade divided into three arched sections, and a dome on an arcaded drum pierced by eight windows.

Systematic excavations were led by A. Mamulashvili in 1939–1949 and by P. Zak’araia in 1963–1967. The bell tower houses a museum of archaeological finds and a 16th-century cannon, and its walls carry portraits of the kings of Kakheti painted by Levan Chogoshvili in 1985. Since 2007 the monuments of Gremi have been proposed for inclusion among the UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
grenadines: The Grenadines are a chain of small islands lying on a line between the larger islands of Saint Vincent and Grenada in the Lesser Antilles. Neither Saint Vincent nor Grenada counts as one of them. Nine are inhabited and open to the public: Bequia, Mustique, Canouan, Union Island, Petit St Vincent, Palm Island and Mayreau, all in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, and Petite Martinique and Carriacou in Grenada. Several privately owned islands, such as Calivigny, are also inhabited.

The chain is divided between two island nations at the Martinique Channel. The northern two-thirds, about 32 islands and cays, belong to Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, and the southern third to Grenada. Carriacou is the largest and most populous of the Grenadines. Petit Nevis was formerly used by whalers.

The history of the Grenadines is not well studied, because of their relative lack of geopolitical importance and the scarcity of original documents. The Kalinago sparsely populated the islands, using them mainly for fishing and food gathering. When the French claimed Grenada in 1650 the Grenadines were included, while Saint Vincent to the north remained Kalinago country.

Their small size, dangerous reefs and lack of fresh water led the French to use them mainly for fishing, turtle catching and lime-making; smugglers and pirates also used them. Permanent settlement began about 1740. When the British took over in 1762 there were a fair number of French plantations on Bequia and Carriacou. In 1791 the islands were divided between Grenada and Saint Vincent.
grenoble: Grenoble lies where the river Drac flows into the Isère at the foot of the French Alps. It is surrounded by mountains, with the Chartreuse to the north, the Vercors to the south and west and the Belledonne range to the east, and it is regarded as the capital of the French Alps. The Bastille, a series of fortifications on the mountainside, overlooks the city from the north. It was begun in the Middle Ages and extended in later centuries, and it has been credited as the most extensive example of early 18th-century fortification in France, on what was then the Alpine frontier with the Kingdom of Sardinia.

The first references to the place date to 43 BCE, when Cularo was a village of the Allobroges, a Gallic tribe, near a bridge over the Isère. The Emperor Gratian visited it and made it a Roman city, and in 381 it was renamed Gratianopolis, the city of Gratian, which through regular sound shifts became Graignovol in the Middle Ages and then Grenoble.

After the fall of the Roman Empire the city became part of the first Burgundian kingdom in the 5th century and then of the Kingdom of Burgundy until 1032, when it was integrated into the Holy Roman Empire. Grenoble grew significantly in the 11th century, when the Counts of Albon chose it as the capital of their scattered territories, and when they took the title of Dauphins it became the capital of the State of Dauphiné. The Parlement of Dauphiné sat in a Renaissance palace built around 1500 until the French Revolution.

The revocation of the Edict of Nantes by Louis XIV caused 2,000 Protestants to leave Grenoble, which weakened the economy but also the glove industry of Grasse, and so left Grenoble's glove makers without competition. At the start of the 18th century 12 glovers made 180,000 gloves a year, and by 1787 there were 64 making 1,920,000.

Grenoble is the prefecture and largest city of the Isère department in the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region. The commune had 156,140 inhabitants in 2023 and its metropolitan area 727,380, the largest in the Alps. It is a significant European scientific centre, and its post-war boom was symbolised by the Olympic Winter Games of 1968.
