grenzer: The name comes from the German Grenzer, border guard or frontiersman; in Serbo-Croatian they were graničari or krajišnici. The Military Frontier was a buffer zone between Christian Europe and the Ottoman Empire, and its troops were first raised to defend their own homes. In Croatia and Slavonia they were Croats and Serbs, in Hungary Croats, Serbs serving as Hajduks, Martolos and Vlachs. The Vlachs of Croatia and the Hajduks of Hungary held territorial as well as personal privileges, and the Vlachs from the Balkans brought their customary law and cooperative households with them.

The Grenzers succeeded the irregular Pandurs, who were raised as a militia in the 18th century and used as skirmishers in the Seven Years' War. By the Napoleonic Wars they formed regular regiments, and at the start of those wars their 18 infantry regiments made up about a quarter of the Habsburg army. Many Austrian commanders thought them poorer line infantry than the regular regiments, and after a mutiny in 1800 their numbers were cut from 57,000 to 13,000. Yet they fought well, notably at Marengo and Austerlitz, and Napoleon thought them the most warlike troops of the Austrian army.

After the War of the Fifth Coalition the Treaty of Schönbrunn of 1809 made Austria cede part of the Frontier, and six Grenz regiments passed into French service until Napoleon's abdication in 1814. In the 19th century the Ottoman threat faded, and the high command, suspicious of South Slav nationalism, steadily reduced their numbers. Grenzers invited to the Russian Empire formed the frontier region of New Serbia in what is now Ukraine.

The Grenz troops included light cavalry, light horse artillery and light and line infantry. They were trained in skirmishing, reconnaissance, screening, marksmanship, artillery observation and the basics of linear tactics, and the Austrian generals placed them somewhere between light and line infantry. When there was no war with the Ottomans the regiments served in other theatres, but one battalion of each always stayed to guard the border. The regiments of 1764 were named after their districts and seats, such as the Liccaner at Gospić and the Szekler and Wallachian regiments of Transylvania.
gresik: The town of Gresik, about 25 kilometres north-west of Surabaya, is the administrative centre of Gresik Regency in East Java Province. The regency takes in much of the northern and western suburbs of Surabaya and also Bawean Island, some 125 kilometres north of Java and Madura, and almost a third of its area is coastal. Thomas Stamford Raffles, in The History of Java, derived the name from Giri Gisik, meaning mountain near the coast, after the hills of the town centre close to the shore.

Merchants from as far away as China, India and Arabia traded at the port of Gresik-Djaratan, and some of them helped spread Islam in the area. The ancient Islamic tombs of Sheikh Maulana Malik Ibrahim and Fatimah bint Maimun mark the region as the first point of entry for Islam in Java. From the 14th century Gresik was one of the main ports and trading cities of the archipelago and a haven for ships sailing between Maluku, Sumatra and mainland Asia, including India and Persia, a role it kept into the era of the VOC.

In 1487 Sunan Giri, also known as Sultan Ainul Yaqin, began to rule Gresik, and his descendants governed the area for the following two centuries. The Portuguese apothecary and traveller Tomé Pires, in his book Suma Oriental of 1515, called Gresik the jewel of Java in trading ports. The area long formed part of Surabaya Regency until a government regulation of 1 November 1974 moved its administration to Gresik town under the new name of Gresik Regency. In the same year it became part of Gerbangkertosusila, the official metropolitan region of Surabaya.

The regency had 1,311,215 inhabitants at the 2020 census and is divided into eighteen districts, two of which make up Bawean Island. Its largest works are Semen Gresik, a maker of Portland cement, and the fertiliser producer Petrokimia Gresik, while home industries make songkok caps and bags. The town is also known for its many coffee shops, called warkop, from warung kopi.
grianan-of-aileach: The fort stands on Greenan Mountain, 244 metres high, at Burt on the Inishowen Peninsula, 11.25 kilometres northwest of the church site of Derry, with which its history is closely linked. From the summit one sees much of the counties of Londonderry, Donegal and Tyrone. The stone cashel has a wall about 4.5 metres thick and 5 metres high, with three terraces linked by steps and two long passages inside it; buildings once stood within. Outside are the remains of a well and a tumulus that may date from the Neolithic, a sign that the hill was used long before the fort.

The cashel was most likely built in the second half of the first millennium CE, though the dates proposed differ. The historian Brian Lacy holds that after the Cenél nEógain won control of the northern Uí Néill at the battle of Cloítech in 789, their kings moved to the Grianán, building inside an older hillfort as a sign of their mastery of the land in view, and that the dynasty lived there until about 1050. Irish legend instead says the Dagda, king of the Tuatha Dé Danann, built it around the grave of his son Aedh.

According to Tony Nugent, the site later served as a Mass rock during the anti-Catholic persecution that lasted until Catholic Emancipation in 1829. In the 19th century Walter Bernard of Derry rebuilt it from a ruin whose best walls stood about 6 ft high, taking Staigue Fort in County Kerry as his model, so that the fort seen today follows his idea of a Kerry cashel rather than evidence from Ulster. The name is usually explained as the stone place, Aileach, of the sunny view or royal residence, Grianán.

The fort is a national monument owned by the Irish state and visited by tourists. Bernard's work was crude and was crumbling within 30 years of the state taking it over, and after a wall collapsed the Office of Public Works began further repairs in 2001, which have been publicly disputed: large sections of wall have been replaced, some upper parts cemented and an iron gate set into the entrance.
grigori-rasputin: Grigori Yefimovich Rasputin was born a peasant in the village of Pokrovskoye on the Tura River in the Tobolsk Governorate, on 21 January 1869 by official records. His father Yefim was a peasant farmer and church elder who also worked as a government courier. Like most Siberian peasants he was not formally educated and remained illiterate well into early adulthood. In 1897 he left on a pilgrimage, for reasons that are unclear: some sources say to escape punishment for horse theft, others that he had a vision. At the St Nicholas Monastery at Verkhoturye he was deeply humbled by an elder called Makary, and he returned a changed man, a vegetarian who abstained from alcohol. He then spent years as a strannik, a holy wanderer.

In 1904 or 1905 he gained a reputation in Kazan as a wise starets, and church leaders sent him to Saint Petersburg, where aristocrats curious about the occult welcomed him. He met Nicholas II and Empress Alexandra Feodorovna in November 1905. From late 1906 he acted as faith healer for their son Alexei, who had haemophilia. In 1912, when the boy lay close to death after a hemorrhage, Rasputin telegraphed that the Little One would not die, and the bleeding stopped within days. In 1907 clergy in Pokrovskoye denounced him as a heretic. His power was at its height in 1915, when Nicholas left Saint Petersburg to oversee the army.

A group of nobles led by Purishkevich, Grand Duke Dmitri Pavlovich and Prince Felix Yusupov decided that his influence over Alexandra threatened the empire. He was murdered early on 30 December 1916 at Yusupov's home, dying of three gunshot wounds, one at close range to the forehead. Little else is certain, and historian Douglas Smith writes that what really happened will never be known. Historians often suggest that his scandalous reputation helped discredit the tsarist government and precipitate the overthrow of the House of Romanov shortly after. Accounts of his life were often based on rumour.
grigory-potemkin: Grigory Potemkin was born on 11 October 1739 (30 September in the old style) in the village of Chizhovo near Smolensk, into a family of middle-income noble landowners. After his father's death in 1746 his mother, Daria Vasilievna Kondyreva, took charge of the family and moved to Moscow, where he studied at the gymnasium attached to the university. He enlisted in the army in 1750 at the age of eleven, as noble children customarily did, and won the university's gold medal in 1757. He later lost the sight of his left eye, under circumstances the sources tell differently.

Potemkin returned to court in January 1774, and by February had become Catherine's lover and favourite. The offices that followed included Governor-General of Novorossiya, General-in-Chief and Commander-in-Chief of the Cossacks. Their surviving letters show a relationship of laughter and mutual admiration. He pursued the Greek Project, which aimed at a new Byzantine Empire around Constantinople, and by July 1783 he had engineered the peaceful annexation of Crimea and Kuban. Catherine rewarded him with one hundred thousand roubles, which he used to build the Tauride Palace in Saint Petersburg.

He became a field marshal in 1784 and governed the southern provinces as Prince of Taurida. His firm dealing with the Cossacks, notably the breaking of the Zaporozhian host in 1775, defined his rule. He founded or developed cities: Kherson, begun in 1778 as a base for the Black Sea Fleet; Sevastopol; Simferopol; and Nikolayev, founded in 1789. His effort to build Yekaterinoslav, now Dnipro, was his biggest failure. When a second Russo-Turkish war began in August 1787 he was commander-in-chief, and his army besieged Ochakov.

Potemkin fell ill at Iași, where he oversaw peace talks, and died on 16 October 1791 (5 October in the old style) on the open steppe, 60 km from the town. Some historians have suggested poisoning, but Simon Sebag Montefiore proposes bronchial pneumonia. Catherine bought the Tauride Palace and his art collection and paid his debts. When Paul I succeeded in 1796 he tried to undo Potemkin's reforms. The Potemkin village, a ruse of painted façades to impress visiting officials, is associated with his rule but is probably mythical. The battleship Potemkin, named in his honour, took part in the Russian Revolution of 1905.
grigory-shelikhov: Grigory Ivanovich Shelikhov was born in 1747 in Rylsk, in the Belgorod Governorate, the son of Ivan Shelikhov. He had a sister, Agrofena, and a younger brother, Vasilii, who went to Siberia with him to help with the business. In 1775 he married Natalia Alexeyevna Kozhevina, whose family belonged to a prominent clan of Okhotsk navigators and mapmakers. At his death he had five surviving daughters and one son.

From 1775 Shelikhov organised voyages of merchant ships to the Kuril Islands and the Aleutian Islands for the fur trade. In 1783 he founded the Shelikhov-Golikov Company in partnership with Ivan Larionovich Golikov, and in 1783 to 1786 he led an expedition to the coast of the mainland, where his party founded the first permanent Russian settlements in North America. Back in Russia, he hired Alexandr Baranov in 1790 to manage his fur-trading enterprise in Russian America.

In April 1784 he arrived at the place he named Three Saints Bay, on Kodiak Island, with two ships, the Three Hierarchs and the St. Simon. The Koniaga, an Alutiiq people of Alaska, defended themselves at Refuge Rock on Sitkalidak Island. In what became known as the Awa'uq Massacre, Shelikhov's armed men, who had guns and cannons, killed hundreds of the Alutiiq, including women and children, and took hundreds of hostages, many of them children, to force other Alaska Natives to submit. Having established his authority on Kodiak, he founded the settlement at Three Saints Bay. Unalaska had been settled long before, but it was not regarded as a permanent Russian base until his time.

Shelikhov died on 31 July 1795 (20 July in the old style). In 1799 the assets of his company were merged with the Russian-American Company under its correspondent Nikolai Rezanov, who was Shelikhov's son-in-law, having married his fourteen-year-old daughter Anna in January 1795. A gulf in the Sea of Okhotsk, a strait between Alaska and Kodiak Island, a bay on Kruzof Island and a town in Irkutsk Oblast bear his name, and a statue of him stands in Rylsk.
grimoald-i-of-benevento: Grimoald was the youngest son of Duke Gisulf II of Friuli and the Bavarian princess Ramhilde, daughter of Duke Garibald I of Bavaria. When the Avars invaded Italy in 611, Gisulf's army was outnumbered and the duchy overrun, and Gisulf died in battle. Grimoald and his brother Radoald escaped to Beneventum, where they were adopted by Duke Arechis, a distant kinsman. From 641 to 642 the brothers served as regents to Arechis's son Duke Aiulf I, who was killed in 642 defending against Slavic invaders; Radoald succeeded him, and Grimoald later succeeded Radoald as Duke of Benevento. As duke he defended the Sanctuary of Monte Sant'Angelo on Mount Gargano against "Greeks", possibly from Naples, who had come to plunder.

In 661 Aripert I, King of the Lombards, was succeeded by his sons Perctarit, who governed from Milan, and Godepert, from Pavia. In 662 the brothers fell out, and Godepert sent Garipald, Duke of Turin, to persuade Grimoald to help in a war against Perctarit. With Garibald's connivance, Grimoald assassinated Godepert and forced Perctarit to flee. He took over as king, married Godepert's sister Theodota to associate himself with the dynasty of Theodelinda, and passed the dukedom of Benevento to his eldest son Romuald.

He led his armies against the Byzantines of Emperor Constans II at the siege of Benevento, while Romuald took Taranto and Brindisi. Grimoald took Forlì from the Greeks and razed Oderzo, where his brothers Tasso and Kakko had been murdered years before. When Duke Lupus of Friuli, left as regent in the north, rebelled, Lupus was killed and his duchy destroyed with the help of the Avars, and Grimoald defeated Lupus's son Arnefrit and his Slavic allies at Nimis. He also defeated the Franks, who invaded during the infancy of Chlothar III, and suppressed the autonomy of the duchies of Friuli and Spoleto.

Grimoald remained nominally Arian despite his marriage to a Catholic; according to the Vita Sancti Barbati he and Romuald still practised the ancient pagan rites. He distanced himself from the papacy and saw Saint Michael as the warrior-protector of the Lombard nation, replacing Wodan, and had San Michele Maggiore built over the site of the palace chapel in Pavia. He died in 671 after concluding a treaty with the Franks and was buried in the Basilica of St. Ambrose in Pavia. His son Garibald was elected to succeed him but was deposed within three months by the returning Perctarit. Grimoald was remembered as generous and merciful as well as ruthless in war.
griots: A griot is a West African historian, storyteller, praise singer, poet or musician, a master of communicating stories and history orally. The word may derive from the French guiriot, a transliteration of the Portuguese criado, 'servant', and its origin is hard to pin down, hence the many local terms, such as jeli or jali among the Manding and gewel among the Wolof. Jali comes from a root meaning blood. In the Epic of Sundiata, Naré Maghann Konaté offered his son Sundiata Keita, founder of the Mali Empire, a griot, Balla Fasséké, as adviser. Balla Fasséké is considered the founder of the Kouyaté line of griots, which exists to this day.

Historically griots form an endogamous, professionally specialised group, or caste, whose members mostly marry other griots and pass the tradition down the family line. A family of griots accompanied a family of kings or emperors, called jatigi; in traditional culture no griot can be without a jatigi and no jatigi without a griot, though a jatigi can lend his griot to another. Most villages also had their own griot. Griots sing and share family history at weddings, act as mediators in disputes, and could criticise those of higher status.

Children born into jeli families are raised from an early age in verbal art, music and genealogy, and learn by observation, repetition and taking part in performances rather than through a classroom. In many performances men narrate the historical framework of epics while women, griottes, sing praise songs, and at weddings griottes dress the bride and sing praises that affirm the bond between the families. Griots have not always been treated positively: Thomas A. Hale writes that an ancient tradition marked them as a separate people and, in the worst case, meant burial in trees rather than in the ground, to avoid polluting the earth.

During the French colonial period griots were increasingly regulated. Colonial authorities in Saint-Louis expelled them from the city, and in 1930 formalised rules for their participation in weddings that limited drumming, set payments and imposed heavy fines. As kings declined, many griots began to work with modern politicians, and after independence they performed in concert halls and recording studios, using microphones, amplifiers and instruments with pickups. Griots today live among the Mande peoples, the Fula, Hausa, Songhai, Wolof, Serer and many other groups. Some compare rappers to griots, a comparison that is controversial among academics and rappers themselves.
gripsholm-castle: Gripsholm Castle is in Mariefred, Södermanland, by Lake Mälaren in south central Sweden, in the municipality of Strängnäs and about 60 km west of Stockholm. Since Gustav I Vasa it has belonged to the Swedish royal family, which used it as one of its residences until the 18th century. It is now a museum, but is still considered a palace at the disposal of the King and is one of the Crown palaces of Sweden.

Bo Jonsson Grip built a fortress on the site in the 1370s. It was sold to Queen Margaret I in 1404 and stayed with the crown until the Regent Sten Sture the Elder acquired it in 1472 by an exchange of lands, making it hereditary family land. In 1498 Sten gave it for a Carthusian monastery, Mariefred Charterhouse, which lasted almost 30 years. King Gustav I dissolved the monastery in 1526 during the Swedish Reformation, tore down the monastic buildings and the old castle, and built a fortified castle with circular corner towers between 1537 and 1545. Of the medieval fortress only the façade of a wall remains.

The royal children were housed there during the Dacke War. Between 1563 and 1567 King Eric XIV imprisoned his brother John and John's consort Catherine Jagiellon in the castle, and John's son Sigismund III Vasa, later king of Poland and Sweden, was born there on 20 June 1566. After John deposed Eric, Eric was held there from 1571 to 1573.

Maria Eleonora of Brandenburg, widow of Gustavus Adolphus, lived there from 1636 to 1640, and Queen Hedvig Eleonora rebuilt and expanded it between 1654 and 1715. In the 18th century it was for a time a prison. Gustav III renovated it in 1773, added a theatre in one tower, and used it for the French Theater of 1781–1792. After the Coup of 1809 the deposed Gustav IV Adolf and his family were held there, and he signed his abdication document in the castle.

In 1822 the castle came to house the National Portrait Gallery, one of the oldest portrait collections in the world, which was placed under the Nationalmuseum in the 1860s. The architect Fredrik Lilljekvist carried out a heavy and controversial restoration between 1889 and 1894 that removed many 17th and 18th-century alterations and added a third floor. The castle is open to the public with paintings and works of art.
grobogan-regency: The regency was created on 4 March 1726 and covers 2,023.84 square kilometres, the second largest in Central Java. It is a flat valley between two ranges, the Pegunungan Kendeng to the south and the Pegunungan Kapur Utara to the north. Its two main rivers, the Kali Lusi and the Kali Serang, often flood in the rainy season and destroy harvests, but dams such as the Klambu, Sedadi and Kedung Ombo make it one of the main rice-growing areas of the province. The Kedung Ombo dam, backed by the World Bank, was debated nationally for its social cost.

Local tradition places an early centre of the Mataram kingdom here, at Medhang Kamulan, before its capital moved towards Prambanan, and the region is tied to the folklore of Ki Ageng Sela, Ki Ageng Tarub, Bondan Kejawan and Aji Saka. Under the Islamic Mataram kingdom it was an outer province, and during the wars of Prince Prangwedana, Raden Mas Said, and Prince Mangkubumi it was one of their bases. The Giyanti Agreement of 1755 placed it within the sultanate.

An agreement between the governor-general, Daendels, and the court at Yogyakarta, dated 10 January 1811, handed Grobogan, Wirosari and other districts to the Dutch government. During the Diponegoro War Grobogan, Purwodadi and Wirosari were caught up in the fighting against the Dutch. Famine then struck so hard that the population fell from 89,000 in 1848 to only 9,000 in 1850.

Grobogan had 1,453,526 inhabitants at the 2020 census and is divided into nineteen districts, the twelve westernmost lying within the Semarang Metropolitan Area. Its capital is the town of Purwodadi. Islam is the main religion, alongside Christianity, Buddhism, Hindu worship and the traditional beliefs of Kejawen. Lying between Demak and Surakarta, it shows the influence of both in arts such as wayang kulit shadow puppetry and kethoprak theatre, and it is known for swikee, a soup of frog legs.
grodno: Grodno stands on the Neman River, about 300 km from Minsk, 15 km from the Polish border and 30 km from the Lithuanian. Its name is considered Slavic, derived from the Ruthenian horod, fortress, and the town grew from a small fortress and fortified trading outpost kept by Rurikid princes on the border with the lands of the Baltic Yotvingians. Before East Slavs arrived in the 10th and 11th centuries the area was inhabited by Yotvingians.

Grodno became part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in the 13th century, and Lithuanians rebuilt the stronghold. In 1276 Duke Traidenis sheltered there Yotvingians fleeing a massacre by the Teutonic Knights, who attacked the town repeatedly between 1283 and 1377. The union of Lithuania with Poland in 1385 made it a town of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, which gave it a charter in 1441 and used it as a royal residence. Stefan Batory made the Old Castle his principal residence and died there in December 1586.

Jews began to settle in the city in the 14th century, a privilege said to have been granted by Vytautas in 1389, though the YIVO Encyclopedia describes that document as a forgery of the early 16th century. They were expelled in 1495 and allowed back in 1503. Russia annexed the city in the Third Partition of Poland in 1795, and on 25 November that year Stanisław August Poniatowski, the last Polish king and Lithuanian grand duke, abdicated in the New Castle.

Germany occupied Grodno on 3 September 1915. In September 1939 the Soviet invasion brought heavy fighting in the Battle of Grodno, after which the Soviets massacred over 300 captured Polish defenders. Since 1945 the city has been part of Belarus, and most of its Polish inhabitants were expelled or fled to Poland in 1944–1946 and 1955–1959.
grodziec-castle: Grodziec, in German Gröditzburg, is first named in a bull of Pope Adrian IV of 23 April 1155. In 1175 Prince Bolesław I the Tall issued a privilege for the Cistercians of Lubiąż there, and under his heir, Henryk I the Bearded, a brick castle replaced the wooden one; the foundation of its church is attributed to Saint Hedwig. In the 14th and part of the 15th century it belonged to the knightly Busewoy family, and during the Hussite Wars a Hussite detachment took and plundered it.

Friedrich I, Prince of Legnica, bought the castle back in 1470, and master builders from Wrocław and Görlitz gave it its present plan. His son Friedrich II completed the work, making it one of the finest Gothic-Renaissance residences in Silesia, and his wedding to Sophie von Hohenzollern was marked there by a feast and a tournament. In the Thirty Years' War the forces of Albrecht von Wallenstein captured and burned it, and attempts to rebuild it in the 17th and 18th centuries were left unfinished.

In the 19th century Hans Heinrich XV von Hochberg-Pless of Książ took up preservation work, and from the mid-1830s the ruin drew many tourists. The art dealer Martin Usteri's collection of 32 glass panes was installed there after 1829, and six stained glass windows from the Augustinerkloster in Zürich later passed from it to the Swiss National Museum. Willibald von Dirksen had the castle rebuilt to a design by the architect Bodo Ebhardt, and Emperor Wilhelm II attended its reopening in 1908.

Dirksen's son Herbert von Dirksen, a German diplomat who served as ambassador to the Soviet Union, Japan and Great Britain, inherited the castle, which burned at the end of World War II in 1945. It was later given to the Silesian Society of History and Antiquarianism Lovers for use as a museum, restaurant and shelter-home. Part of it remains in ruins, and it hosts medieval tournaments with jousting and sword fighting.
groningen: Groningen lies at the northernmost point of the Hondsrug area. The origin of its name is uncertain: a folk story tells of exiles from Troy led by a figure called Gruno, one modern theory takes it to mean among the people of Groni, from an old Frisian personal name, and another derives it from a word for green fields. The Dutch sometimes call it Martinistad, after the Martinitoren tower.

The oldest document referring to the city dates from 1040, though Saxons had occupied the area centuries earlier. It gained city rights de facto in 1245, but no written record of a formal grant survives. Isolated from the successive Dutch centres of power in Utrecht, The Hague and Brussels, it long relied on itself and nearby regions. As a Hanseatic city it belonged to the North German trade network and later became chiefly a regional market centre. In the 13th century its people built a city wall, and the Gronings dialect became common in the surrounding lands.

Its most influential period came at the end of the 15th century, when the province of Friesland was administered from Groningen and the Martinitoren was built. At the height of its power it could be considered an independent city-state. In 1536 it accepted Emperor Charles V as its ruler, which ended its autonomy. Dutch and English forces under Maurice of Nassau captured it in the Siege of Groningen of 1594, after which the city and the province joined the Dutch Republic. The University of Groningen was founded in 1614, and the city grew rapidly, with a new wall.

In the Siege of Groningen of 1672, during the Third Anglo-Dutch War, the bishop of Münster, Bernhard von Galen, failed to take the city, an event still marked on 28 August as Gronings Ontzet. In 1811 Napoleon I annexed it to the French Empire, until 1813. In April 1945, in the Battle of Groningen, the main square and the Grote Markt were largely destroyed, though the Martinitoren, the Goudkantoor and the city hall were undamaged.

Groningen is the capital of its province and the largest city of the northern Netherlands, with 244,807 inhabitants. The University of Groningen is the second oldest university in the country, and students make up about a quarter of the population.
grootfontein: Grootfontein, meaning large fountain, was known to the Herero as Otjivanda. In 1885 forty Boer families from the north-west of South Africa settled there. They were part of the Dorsland trekkers heading towards Angola, and when that territory fell under Portuguese control they turned back and established the Republic of Upingtonia at Grootfontein. The settlement was abandoned by 1887 and became the headquarters of the South West Africa Company in 1893. In 1908 the Roman Catholic Church established a mission in Grootfontein as the base for its eventually successful attempt to found missions in Kavango.

The town lies in the Otjozondjupa Region and is one of the three towns of the Otavi Triangle, on the B8 national road from Otavi to the Caprivi Strip. Carbonate deposits in the upper parts of the mines have yielded fossils of simian or pongoid creatures. The Berg Aukas and Abenab mines to the north-east, which produced zinc and vanadium, were for decades the economic mainspring of the area and have since closed. Twenty-four kilometres west lies the Hoba meteorite, which at more than 60 tons is the largest known meteorite and the largest naturally occurring mass of iron known on the planet's surface.

Grootfontein has 26,839 inhabitants and a municipal council of seven seats. It is a railhead on the national railway system, and has an airfield able to handle large transport aircraft. It is home to Namibia's main military base, which housed several units of the South African Defence Force, and since 1911 it has held an annual agricultural exhibition, the Grootfontein Show. An old German Schutztruppe fortress of 1896 houses a museum of local history.
gross-domestic-product: Sir William Petty devised a concept of gross domestic product to calculate the tax burden, and to argue that landlords were unfairly taxed during the warfare between the Dutch and the English between 1652 and 1674. Charles Davenant developed the method further in 1695. The economist Simon Kuznets, who developed the first comprehensive set of measures of national income, warned of the uses and abuses of such measurements in his second report to the United States Congress in 1937. The international standard for measuring GDP is the System of National Accounts, prepared by representatives of the International Monetary Fund, the European Union, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, the United Nations and the World Bank.

Gross domestic product is the total market value of all final goods and services produced during a specific period, usually a year, by a country or countries. It can be determined in three ways that should in theory give the same result: the production approach, which sums the value added at each stage of production, the income approach, which adds the incomes paid to the factors of production, and the expenditure approach, which sums consumption, investment, government expenditure and net exports. Nominal GDP does not account for inflation, so comparisons over time use real values, and comparisons between countries are often adjusted for differences in the cost of living. GDP defines its scope by location, whereas gross national income defines it by ownership.

GDP is widely used as a broad measure of economic progress, but it has been criticised for leaving out externalities such as environmental harm, unpaid domestic work, non-market transactions and economies where little money is used. It also does not account for how income is distributed. In the 1980s Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum developed the capability approach, which looks at what people are able to achieve rather than at aggregate output. A commission including Joseph Stiglitz, Amartya Sen and Jean-Paul Fitoussi proposed in 2009 a well-being framework to broaden the focus beyond GDP.
gross-national-happiness: Gross National Happiness, also called Gross Domestic Happiness, was conceived by the fourth king of Bhutan, Jigme Singye Wangchuck, building on the idea of Gaki Phuensum, peace and prosperity, and on the modernisation of Bhutan under the third king, Jigme Dorji Wangchuck. In 1972 the king declared the idea more important than Gross Domestic Product. It implies that sustainable development should take a holistic approach and give equal importance to non-economic aspects of wellbeing. In defining it the king drew on Bhutan's long tradition of compassion and non-violence toward all living beings, rooted in its 1,200-year Buddhist heritage.

According to the Bhutanese government, GNH has four pillars: sustainable and equitable socio-economic development, environmental conservation, preservation and promotion of culture, and good governance. These are measured through nine domains: psychological well-being, health, time use, education, cultural diversity and resilience, good governance, community vitality, ecological diversity and resilience, and living standards. Each domain combines survey-based and objective indicators, and individuals are classified as happy or not yet happy by their scores. The political scientist Kent Schroeder notes that the values underlying the pillars are distinctly Buddhist, and GNH is seen as part of the Buddhist Middle Way.

A Gross National Happiness Commission, chaired by the Prime Minister, implements it, drafts the five-year plan and screens policies and projects for their likely effect on GNH. The index was developed by the Centre for Bhutan Studies with Oxford University researchers, using the Alkire and Foster method. National surveys were held in 2008, 2010 and 2015 and covered all twenty districts.

In 2011 the UN General Assembly passed resolution 65/309, urging member nations to follow Bhutan's example and measure happiness and well-being. In 2012 Bhutan and the UN convened a high-level meeting at which the first World Happiness Report was issued, and the UN declared 20 March the International Day of Happiness. Versions of the survey were used in Victoria, Seattle and the state of Vermont, and Thailand launched its own GNH centre in 2016.

Critics have described GNH as a propaganda tool that distracted from human rights abuses. Human Rights Watch documented the expulsion of over 100,000 Bhutanese of Nepalese origin, about one sixth of the population, before 2008. Other researchers say the philosophy has evolved through the contributions of western and local scholars into a more open version than the one the king used.
grosseto: Grosseto stands in the centre of the Maremma, on the alluvial plain called the Piana Grossetana, where the Ombrone valley meets the Tyrrhenian Sea. The Metalliferous Hills lie to the north, Mount Argentario and the Uccellina Mountains to the south and Mount Amiata to the east. In the past most of the plain was occupied by Lake Prile, which has almost disappeared after land reclamation completed between the 18th and 20th centuries. The area has been inhabited since prehistoric times, as remains in the Fabbrica Cave and the Scoglietto Cave show.

In the Etruscan period the city did not exist; the area belonged to Rusellae, a few kilometres north, most splendid in the 6th century BCE. The Romans conquered it in 294 BCE, and under the empire it became a colonia with a forum, basilica, amphitheatre and baths. It became a Christian bishop's seat, first attested in 499. Rusellae declined from the 6th century, and a first nucleus of Grosseto formed in the early 7th century, after the Lombard conquest. It is first mentioned in 803 as a fief of the Aldobrandeschi counts.

Sienese rule ended in 1559, when Charles V handed the duchy to Cosimo I de Medici, first grand duke of Tuscany. In 1564-65 the Medicean walls were begun to the design of Baldassarre Lanci, as part of making Grosseto a stronghold on the southern border. Malaria spread in the swamps, and the population, estimated at 7 000 to 8 000 before the Black Death of 1348, fell to about 600 under Medici rule. Under the House of Lorraine the town flourished and became capital of the new Maremma province. At Italian unification it had about 4 700 inhabitants, and growth followed the land reclamation completed under the Fascist regime. The Allies heavily bombed it in 1943.

Grosseto is the capital of its province and the most populous city of the Maremma, with 82,284 inhabitants in its comune. Its economy rests on services, agriculture and seaside tourism. The Medicean walls are now a public park and walking area, and the Romanesque cathedral of St Lawrence, begun at the end of the 13th century by Sozzo Rustichini of Siena, is its main monument. Andrea da Grosseto, a 13th-century writer who translated Albertano of Brescia's moral treatises in 1268, was born in the city.
grossmunster: The Grossmünster stands near the banks of the Limmat in Zurich. Its core was built on the site of a Carolingian church that legend says Charlemagne commissioned. According to the legend, his horse fell to its knees over the tombs of Felix, Regula and Exuperantius, the patron saints of Zurich. The story supports the church's claim to seniority over the Fraumünster, which was founded by Louis the German, Charlemagne's grandson. Archaeological evidence confirms a Roman burial ground at the site. The two churches competed for precedence through the Middle Ages.

The Grossmünster is a Romanesque church and one of the four major churches of the city, with the Fraumünster, the Predigerkirche and St. Peterskirche. Building began around 1100 and the church was inaugurated around 1220, using Bollinger sandstone. It has a carved portal with medieval columns whose capitals bear grotesques, and a Romanesque crypt dating from the 11th and 13th centuries. The twin towers were first raised between 1487 and 1492. Their wooden steeples burned in 1763, and the present neo-Gothic tops were completed in 1787.

Richard Wagner is known to have mocked the towers as two pepper dispensers. Augusto Giacometti added modern stained-glass windows in 1932, and Otto Münch made the bronze doors of the north and south portals in 1935 and 1950.

Huldrych Zwingli began the Swiss-German Reformation from his pastoral office here. After he won a series of debates in 1523, the civil authorities sanctioned the break with the papacy. In 1524 the reformers removed the organ and the religious statuary, and Zwingli and his successor Heinrich Bullinger made further changes, among them a ban on church music. Their reforms account for the plain interior. The church holds the graves of Felix and Regula, of Conrad Gessner and of Peter Martyr Vermigli.

The late 12th-century cloister belonged to the canons' foundation, which was repealed in 1832. The church is owned by the Canton of Zurich. A Reformation museum stands in the cloister, and the theological faculty of the University of Zurich has leased the annex since 1976. Both are listed as cultural property of national importance.
grover-cleveland: Stephen Grover Cleveland was born on 18 March 1837 in Caldwell, New Jersey, the son of Richard Falley Cleveland, a Congregational and Presbyterian minister, and Ann Neal. After his father died in 1853 he left school to help support his family, and in 1855 he decided to move west. He started his own law practice in 1862, and in January 1863 he became assistant district attorney of Erie County, New York. A Democrat from the start, he was elected mayor of Buffalo in 1881, on a ticket meant to attract voters tired of corrupt party machines, and governor of New York in 1882.

In 1884 reform-minded Republicans called Mugwumps denounced the Republican nominee, James G. Blaine, as corrupt and supported Cleveland, whose slogan was 'A public office is a public trust'. As president he said he would not dismiss Republicans who did their work well, and he vetoed hundreds of private pension bills for Civil War veterans, 414 vetoes in his first term, more than four times as many as any earlier president.

He signed the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 and the Dawes Act, which led Native Americans to cede about 100 million acres between 1887 and 1934. On 2 June 1886 he married Frances Folsom in the White House, the only president to marry there. In 1888 he won the popular vote but lost the electoral college to Benjamin Harrison.

He defeated Harrison in 1892. The Panic of 1893 struck shortly before his second term, and he persuaded Congress to repeal the silver coinage provisions of the Sherman Silver Purchase Act, which alienated the agrarian wing of his party. In 1894 the Pullman Strike put 125,000 railroad workers on strike; Cleveland obtained an injunction and sent federal troops into Chicago and 20 other rail centres, and the use of troops hardened organised labour against him. An anti-imperialist, he opposed the annexation of Hawaii and investigated the 1893 coup against Queen Liliʻuokalani. By the end of his second term he was highly unpopular, even among Democrats.

After leaving the White House, Cleveland served as a trustee of Princeton University. He joined the American Anti-Imperialist League in protest at the Spanish-American War of 1898, and he died on 24 June 1908. He was the first Democrat elected president after the Civil War and the first president to serve non-consecutive terms.
gruffydd-ap-llywelyn: Gruffudd was the son of Llywelyn ap Seisyll, who had ruled both Gwynedd and Powys, and of Angharad, daughter of Maredudd ab Owain, King of Deheubarth; he was a great-great-grandson of Hywel Dda. After his father's death in 1023, Iago ab Idwal ap Meurig of the House of Aberffraw took Gwynedd. In 1039 Iago was killed, supposedly by his own men, his son Cynan fled to Dublin, and Gruffudd was made king.

Soon after, he surprised a Mercian army at Rhyd y Groes near Welshpool and killed Edwin, brother of Leofric, Earl of Mercia. He fought Hywel ab Edwin for the south, beating him at Pencader in 1041, carrying off his wife, and killing him in 1044 when Hywel returned with an Irish fleet. Gruffudd ap Rhydderch of Gwent drove him from Deheubarth in 1047. In 1052 he raided Herefordshire with 18 ships from Ireland and defeated Normans and Anglo-Saxons at Leominster.

In 1055 he killed Gruffudd ap Rhydderch in battle and took Deheubarth. Allied with Ælfgar, son of Leofric, who had lost the earldom of East Anglia, he defeated Ralph the Timid, Earl of Hereford, on 24 October 1055, then sacked and burned Hereford. Ælfgar was restored to his earldom and peace was made, and Gruffudd also took Morgannwg, Gwent and lands along the English border. The historian John Davies called him the only Welsh king ever to rule the whole of Wales, and the chronicle Brut y Tywysogion called him the head and shield of the Britons.

Ælfgar's death in 1062 left him exposed. Late that year Harold Godwinson surprised his court at Rhuddlan, and Gruffudd escaped by sea. In spring 1063 Harold's brother Tostig Godwinson invaded North Wales while Harold's fleet sailed round the coast. Gruffudd took refuge in Snowdonia and was killed there on 5 August 1063; his head was sent to Harold. An Irish chronicle names Cynan, son of Iago, as his killer. Harold married his widow Ealdgyth, and Wales split into its old kingdoms under his half-brothers Bleddyn and Rhiwallon. His sons Maredudd and Idwal died fighting them at Mechain in 1069.
grutte-pier: Pier Gerlofs Donia was born around 1480 in Kimswerd, near Harlingen, in Wonseradeel. His mother, Fokel, was the daughter of the Schieringer nobleman Sybrant Doytsesz Bonga of Bongastate, Kimswerd. He married Rintsje Syrtsema and they had a son, Gerlof, and a daughter, Wobbel, born around 1510. With his brother-in-law Ane Pijbes he farmed the estate of Meyllemastate in Kimswerd. His life is mostly shrouded in legend, and the nickname Grutte Pier, Big Pier, refers to his size, strength and bravery. A description attributed to his contemporary Petrus Thaborita pictures him as a broad-shouldered man with a long black beard and moustache.

The Black Band, a Landsknecht regiment in the service of George, Duke of Saxony, was quartered at Franeker, about 7 km from Kimswerd, to suppress the civil war between the Vetkopers, who opposed Burgundian and later Habsburg rule, and the Schieringers. When their pay fell short it extracted money from villagers.

On 29 January 1515 it plundered Pier's village, allegedly raped and killed his wife, and burned the church and his estate. Seeking revenge, Pier began a guerrilla war against the Habsburgs and allied himself with Charles of Egmond, Duke of Guelders. His band, the Arumer Zwarte Hoop, was mainly active as pirates against Hollanders and Burgundians, capturing many English and Dutch ships on the Zuiderzee. Erasmus criticised his exploits.

On 24 June 1517 some 4,000 soldiers from Frisia and Guelders sailed to West Frisia, landed near Wervershoof and took Medemblik, killing many inhabitants and taking others prisoner. The band also took Asperen and slaughtered nearly all its inhabitants. Holland answered by outfitting a war fleet under Anthonius van den Houte, but in 1518 Pier seized eleven Holland ships off Hoorn and defeated 300 Hollanders at Hindelopen. Unable to turn the Burgundian and Habsburg tide, he retired, disillusioned, in 1519, and Wijerd Jelckama took command.

Pier died peacefully in bed in Sneek on 28 October 1520 and is buried in the Groote Kerk there. His son Gerloff died unmarried, and he has descendants through his daughter Wobbel. 6 kilograms, is in the Fries Museum in Leeuwarden, and a helmet said to be his is kept in Sneek's town hall.

Legends credit him with bending coins between his fingers, lifting a horse and ploughing by pulling the plough himself. In 2020 a study by Omrop Fryslân found that 70 per cent of respondents in Friesland considered him one of the Frisian historical heroes.
gruyeres: The medieval town stands at the top of an isolated hill 82 metres high, overlooking the Saane Valley and the Lake of Gruyère, at 810 metres above sea level and 4.5 kilometres south-south-east of the district capital Bulle. It lies in the foothills of Mount Moléson, where the Saane, called the Sarine in French, leaves the Fribourg Alps. Graves of the Hallstatt and La Tène eras and traces of the Bronze Age have been found at Épagny, together with the remains of a Roman villa of the 2nd or 3rd century CE.

The origins of the House of Gruyères remain mysterious. According to a legend, the founder Gruerius captured a crane, in French grue, and chose it as his heraldic animal, which gave the town its name. The town grew up beneath the counts' castle. By the end of the 12th century it was a market town with a central street and walls, and in 1397 Count Rudolph IV confirmed an older town charter modelled on that of Moudon. On 22 June 1476 Gruyères took part in the Battle of Morat against Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, and with the Old Swiss Confederacy routed the Burgundian army.

Nineteen counts are recorded between the 11th and 16th centuries. The last, Michel, was in financial trouble nearly all his life and went bankrupt in 1554. His creditors, the cantons of Fribourg and Bern, divided his county between them. From 1555 to 1798 the castle was the residence of the bailiffs and then of the prefects sent by Fribourg. It was sold in 1849 to the Bovy and Balland families, who restored it with the help of painter friends, and the canton of Fribourg bought it back in 1938 and made it a museum.

Gruyères has always been a rural town. Cheese and animals were traded there, and agriculture still specialises in milk and cattle, supplying the Gruyère cheese that carries the town's name. Most people speak French. The whole village is part of the Inventory of Swiss Heritage Sites, and Gruyères Castle, Saint-Germain Castle and the town's fortifications are heritage sites of national significance. The castle holds a regional museum and an arts museum, and in 1998 the painter and sculptor H. R. Giger acquired Saint-Germain Castle, which now houses a museum of his work.
gu-kaizhi: Gu Kaizhi, with the courtesy name Changkang, was born in Wuxi, in modern Jiangsu. His father, Gu Yuezhi, served as an assistant in the imperial secretariat. At about nineteen he became an aide to the Grand Marshal Huan Wen, and he went on to hold a series of minor official posts under various leaders of the Eastern Jin court. He is said to have first painted at Nanjing in 364. In 366 he became an officer, the Assistant to the Minister of Defense, and he was later promoted to Gentleman in Waiting to the Emperor.

He was also a poet and calligrapher and wrote three books on painting theory: On Painting, a book on the paintings of the Wei and Jin dynasties and Painting Yuntai Mountain. In one passage he wrote that in figure paintings the clothes and appearances were not very important, and that the eyes were the spirit and the decisive factor. His art is known today only through copies of silk handscrolls attributed to him.

The Admonitions of the Instructress to the Court Ladies illustrates nine stories from a political satire on Empress Jia Nanfeng by Zhang Hua. The British Museum scroll is dated between the 6th and 8th centuries and is probably an early Tang copy. It lacks its first three scenes. A Song copy in the Palace Museum in Beijing is complete in twelve scenes. The figures are drawn with a thin, unmodulated brush-line, described as spring silkworms spitting silk.

The Nymph of the Luo River illustrates a poem by Cao Zhi and survives in five copies of the Song and Ming dynasties. Wise and Benevolent Women, a five-metre scroll in ten sections, survives in a 13th-century Song copy.

A story is told of Huan Xuan, an art collector who served as emperor. Gu Kaizhi left a sealed chest of his best works with him. Huan Xuan broke it open, took the paintings, then resealed it and returned it. When the artist found the loss he said that the marvellous works had partaken of divine power and vanished, like men ascending to join the immortals.
guadalajara-spain: Guadalajara lies in the centre of the Iberian Peninsula at about 685 metres above sea level, on the left bank of the Henares river, between the river and the moors of La Alcarria. The historic core stands on a small rise between two small watercourses, which gave an easily defended site. Control of the scarce water supply was fought over by the local nobility.

A Roman mansio called Arriaca is presumed to have stood in the region, though there is no archaeological proof. The town was founded in the Islamic period, in the 9th century, and was officially known as Madīnat al-Faraŷ, after a person named Faraŷ. It was later known as Wādī al-Ḥijāra, from which the present name comes. It belonged to the Middle March of Al-Andalus, governed by the Masmuda Berber clan of the Banū Sālim for the Umayyad rulers of Córdoba. A fortress, walls and the bridge over the Henares date from the Muslim period.

Alfonso VI of León and Castile annexed it in 1085 with the Taifa of Toledo, and the town surrendered without resistance, although tradition says a force led by Álvar Fáñez de Minaya seized it by night. Alfonso VII gave the first fuero in 1133. Henry IV granted city status in 1460. The Mendoza family, Dukes of El Infantado from 1475, dominated the city for generations and patronised the arts, so that it was called the Atenas alcarreña, Alcarria's Athens. A large Jewish community maintained four synagogues until the expulsion of 1492.

The 17th century was a time of crisis, made worse by the expulsion of the moriscos in 1610, which took 10 percent of the population, and the Mendozas left for good in 1657. In the War of the Spanish Succession the city was sacked and its population fell to about 2,200. The French took Guadalajara in 1808 during the Peninsular War, and it became a provincial capital in 1833.

Guadalajara is the capital of its province in Castilla–La Mancha, with 93,470 registered inhabitants, and has grown quickly since 1959, when it was included in plans to relieve the congestion of Madrid's industrial estates. The Palacio del Infantado, the bridge over the Henares, built on Roman foundations, and the Mudéjar co-cathedral of Saint Mary are among its monuments. In March 1937, in the Spanish Civil War, Republican forces defeated an Italian expeditionary force near the city.
guadalcanal-campaign: After the attack on Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941, Japanese forces captured the Philippines, Malaya, Singapore, Burma, the Dutch East Indies, Wake Island, the Gilbert Islands, New Britain and Guam. In summer 1942 the Allies decided to mount offensives in New Guinea and the Solomon Islands, to defend the sea lines to Australia and eventually to attack the major Japanese base at Rabaul. The campaign followed the Allied defensive successes at the Battle of the Coral Sea and the Battle of Midway in May and June 1942.

Allied forces were under Robert L. Ghormley, reporting to Chester W. Nimitz, and Major General Alexander Vandegrift's 1st Marine Division moved from the United States to New Zealand. The Japanese defence rested on the Combined Fleet under Isoroku Yamamoto and the Seventeenth Army under Harukichi Hyakutake.

On 7 August 1942 mainly U.S. Marines landed on Guadalcanal, Tulagi and Florida Island, taking the Japanese defenders by surprise. Within days a Japanese force of seven cruisers and one destroyer under Vice Admiral Gunichi Mikawa defeated Allied screening ships at the Battle of Savo Island. The Marines formed a perimeter around Lunga Point and finished the airfield, named Henderson Field on 12 August. Japanese attempts to retake it came in mid-September and in late October.

The Japanese brought troops by fast destroyers at night, the runs the Allies called the Tokyo Express, while American aircraft at Henderson Field controlled the daytime. Naval battles followed, including the Eastern Solomons, Cape Esperance and the Santa Cruz Islands, and the Allies won the Naval Battle of Guadalcanal in mid-November. Japanese troops were short of supplies by late November. On 12 December the Japanese Navy proposed abandoning Guadalcanal, and imperial headquarters agreed on 26 December. In January 1943 the U.S. XIV Corps under Alexander Patch took over operations, and the last Japanese forces were evacuated by 9 February 1943.

Guadalcanal was the first major Allied land offensive against Japan. With the battles at Milne Bay and Buna–Gona on New Guinea, it marked the Allies' change from defence to offence and passed the strategic initiative to them. Failure to win air superiority forced Japan to rely on barges, destroyers and submarines for reinforcement, and the campaign strained the resources of both sides.

Afterwards Guadalcanal and Tulagi became major Allied bases, with extra fighter and bomber airfields and large port facilities for the advance up the Solomons. The campaign drew many war correspondents, among them Richard Tregaskis, whose Guadalcanal Diary was a bestseller in 1943.
guadalquivir: The Guadalquivir drains an area of about 58,000 km2 and rises at about 1,350 m above sea level, at a place known as Cañada de las Fuentes in the Sierra de Cazorla. Near the mouth the marshy lowlands called Las Marismas border the Doñana National Park. It is the only major navigable river in Spain. The modern name comes from the Arabic al-wādī l-kabīr, the great river.

During much of the Holocene the western valley was occupied by an inland sea, the Tartessian Gulf. The Phoenicians established the first anchorages and dealt in precious metals. The Romans, who called the river the Baetis, settled at Hispalis, now Seville, in the 2nd century BCE and made it an important river port. By the 1st century BCE it was a walled city with shipyards building boats to carry wheat,. In Roman times the river was navigable as far inland as Córdoba. Under Arab rule between 712 and 1248 the Moors built a stone dock and the Torre del Oro to reinforce the port's defences.

In the 13th century Ferdinand III expanded the shipyards, and grain, oil, wine, wool and many other goods were exported throughout Europe from Seville. After the discovery of the Americas the city became the economic centre of the Spanish Empire, because its port, under the Casa de Contratación, held the monopoly of trans-oceanic trade. Navigation was already becoming harder, and by 1500 much heavy cargo was handled downstream at Sanlúcar de Barrameda. Seville finally lost its monopoly to Cádiz. In the 16th century silting, and weirs built to power water mills, halted barge traffic between Seville and Córdoba, which had given Córdoba cheap transport to the sea. The Corta de Merlina, a canal built in 1794, began the modernisation of the port of Seville.

The Guadalquivir is 657 km long and is the fifth-longest river in the Iberian Peninsula. It flows through Córdoba and Seville and reaches the Gulf of Cádiz at Sanlúcar de Barrameda. Seville is its main port, and a lock protects the port entrance from tides.
guadalupe-victoria: Guadalupe Victoria was born on 29 September 1786 at Tamazula, in the province of Nueva Vizcaya in New Spain, now the state of Durango. His parents died early in his childhood and he lived with his uncle, the parish priest. In 1807 he went to Mexico City, entered the College of San Ildefonso and graduated as a Bachelor of Laws on 24 April 1811.

In 1812 he joined the insurgents and fought beside José María Morelos at the siege of Cuautla. For his part in the assault on Oaxaca on 25 November 1812 he was given command of the insurgent army in Veracruz, and he took the name Guadalupe, for the Virgin of Guadalupe, and Victoria, for the victory. Using guerrilla tactics, he held the Puente del Rey, the crossing between Xalapa and the port of Veracruz, and attacked royalist convoys until 1815, when he was defeated.

He then spent almost four years hiding in the jungle, while most insurgents accepted a viceregal pardon and only Vicente Guerrero kept fighting. He reappeared on 30 December 1820 and joined the Plan of Iguala in 1821. When Agustín de Iturbide became emperor, Victoria wanted a republic and was jailed in 1822, but escaped. He joined Antonio López de Santa Anna's revolt in December 1822, and the Plan of Casa Mata forced Iturbide to abdicate on 19 March 1823. On 31 March Congress made Victoria, Nicolás Bravo and Pedro Celestino Negrete the Supreme Executive Power.

Seventeen states voted for Victoria in the presidential election of 1824, and on 2 October 1824 he was declared the first president of the United Mexican States. His constitutional term began on 1 April 1825. He had to rebuild an economy devastated by the war and the Spanish embargo. Spending averaged about 18 million pesos a year against half that in revenue, and two British loans, each of over 3 million pounds, averted bankruptcy.

He won recognition from the United Kingdom, the United States, the Federal Republic of Central America and Gran Colombia, and ratified the border with the United States under the Adams-Onís Treaty. In 1829 he handed the presidency to Vicente Guerrero, and he was the only president to complete his term in more than 30 years of independent Mexico. He later served as senator, governor of Puebla and president of the Senate, and died on 21 March 1843 at the fortress of Perote, where he was being treated for epilepsy.
guadiana: The Guadiana defines a long stretch of the border between Portugal and Spain, separating Extremadura and Andalusia from Alentejo and the Algarve. Its basin reaches from La Mancha and the eastern part of Extremadura to the southern provinces of the Algarve, and about 82 per cent of the basin lies in Spain and about 17 per cent in Portugal. The river runs east to west across the southern Iberian plain until near Badajoz, where it turns south, and it enters the Gulf of Cádiz between Vila Real de Santo António in Portugal and Ayamonte in Spain.

Its exact source in Castilla-La Mancha is disputed, but it is generally believed to rise at the Ojos del Guadiana, in Villarrubia de los Ojos, about 608 metres above sea level. Pliny the Elder introduced a classic theory that the river rose from the Lagunas de Ruidera and ran underground for part of its course. The belief that it disappeared and reappeared persisted until the 19th century, although no such underground course exists. The Cigüela and Záncara rivers are now regarded as part of its headwaters.

Ptolemy's Geography recorded the Celtiberian name as Anas, meaning a marshy area. The Romans adapted it as Flūmen Anās and explained it as the River of Ducks. After the Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula the name became Wādī Āna, which Portuguese and Spanish settlers passed on as Ouadiana and then Odiana. From the 16th century it slowly took the form Guadiana, like other Andalusi river names beginning with wadi, such as Guadalquivir, Guadalete and Guadarrama.

The river marks the border twice on its way to the sea, between the Caia and the Ribeira de Cuncos and again from the Chança to the mouth. Between the Olivença and Táliga ravines the border is a disputed section, claimed by both countries and administered in practice by Spain as part of Extremadura.

The Guadiana is navigable from the Atlantic as far as Mértola, 68 kilometres inland, and above Mértola lies Pulo do Lobo, the highest waterfall in southern Portugal. Its flow varies greatly from year to year, with large floods and severe droughts, in a semi-arid climate. The estuary is a saltmarsh with a maximum width of 550 metres, and two nature reserves protect parts of it, the Marismas de Isla Cristina in Spain and the Castro Marim and Vila Real de Santo António marsh in Portugal. More than 30 dams stand in the basin. The Alqueva Dam, near Moura, creates a reservoir of 250 square kilometres, the largest in Western Europe.
guadix: Guadix lies at an altitude of 913 metres in the centre of the Hoya of Guadix, a high plain at the northern foothills of the Sierra Nevada, in a landscape of gullies and badlands formed by erosion from small rivers. The sediments of the rivers Fardes and Guadix have made the area fertile, and its land is used for fruit trees, especially peaches, for poplar groves and for cereals, legumes and vegetables.

Evidence of settlement around Guadix goes back to at least the Bronze Age. Guadix el Viejo, 6 kilometres to the north-west, was the Roman Acci, mentioned by Pliny and by Ptolemy, who placed it among the Bastetani. Excavations have documented an oppidum with a well-defined urban plan from the 6th century BCE. Julius Caesar established the Roman colony of Julia Gemella, which minted coins and left a Roman theatre and a network of sewers. According to tradition it was the seat of the first bishopric in Hispania, in the 2nd century, and the city was among the first on the Iberian Peninsula to adopt Catholicism.

After 711 it became a Moorish fortress and trading station, renamed Wadi 'Ashi. After the decline of the Caliphate it lay on the border between the territories of the Zirids of Granada and the Banu Jayrán of Almería, and it later passed through the Almoravid and Almohad empires into the Emirate of Granada. The poet Ḥamda bint Ziyād lived there. In January 1362 a small Castilian army was routed there by the forces of Muhammed VI, Sultan of Granada. Civil wars in the kingdom of Granada made Guadix the capital of a short-lived kingdom under Muhammad XII, and in 1489 it surrendered without a siege to Ferdinand and Isabella.

The main sights are the cathedral, built from the 16th to the 18th century over a Moorish mosque with a Baroque façade, the Church of Santiago of 1540 with a Plateresque portal, the Moorish Alcazaba and the Barrio de Santiago, whose houses are cut into the tuff rock. The novelist Pedro Antonio de Alarcón was born there in 1833. By the end of the 19th century Guadix was known for its cutlery.
guaimar-iv-of-salerno: Guaimar was the eldest son of Guaimar III of Salerno and Gaitelgrima, daughter of Duke Pandulf II of Benevento, and was made co-prince in 1018. When Emperor Henry II campaigned in southern Italy in 1022, his father submitted and sent the boy as a hostage; he was handed to Pope Benedict VIII and released. He succeeded his father in 1027, aged fourteen or sixteen, perhaps under his mother's regency. He married Gemma, daughter of the Capuan count Laidulf, before 1032.

In 1036 Rainulf Drengot, a vassal of Pandulf IV of Capua, did homage to Guaimar, bringing him Norman support. Guaimar asked the emperors to judge Pandulf's fitness to rule, and Emperor Conrad II came south in 1038, took Capua and gave it to Guaimar, making Rainulf Count of Aversa as his vassal. In April 1039 Guaimar forced John II of Amalfi into exile and made himself duke; in July he took Sorrento and gave it to his brother Guy. He also received the homage of Duke John V of Naples and in June 1040 took Gaeta.

Guaimar sent Lombard and Norman warriors to the Byzantine expedition to Sicily under Giorgio Maniace, among them William Iron Arm. When the Normans turned on Greek Apulia, he backed them; they acclaimed him Duke of Apulia and Calabria, and he granted them Melfi. From 1042 to 1047 he was at war with Pandulf, who had returned from exile in Constantinople. In 1047 Emperor Henry III returned Capua to Pandulf, took Aversa and Melfi under his own suzerainty and stripped Guaimar of his title over Apulia and Calabria. Guaimar won back Aversa in 1048 by installing Richard Drengot there as regent.

In June 1052 the four brothers of his wife Gemma killed him in the harbour of Salerno; the sources give 2, 3 or 4 June. They seized the city, but Guy of Sorrento and the Normans besieged them, and after they surrendered on Guy's promise the Normans, holding themselves not bound by it, killed the four brothers and thirty-six others, one for each wound on Guaimar's body. His son Gisulf II succeeded him. The historian Lord Norwich praised his good faith, while his contemporary Peter Damian wrote that he died by the sword for his violence and tyranny.
guan-daosheng: Guan Daosheng, whose courtesy name was Zhongji, was born into a landed family in Huzhou, believed to descend from the high-ranking Wuxing official Guan Zhong. She grew up on the family's ancestral lands, nicknamed the Roost of the Esteemed, and was a well-educated child. In 1286, at the age of 24, she married Zhao Mengfu, a scholar-official and leading artist of the earlier Yuan period. They bought a town house with gardens in Huzhou and a country retreat at Dongheng village near Deqing, and they had two sons and two daughters, who were raised alongside Zhao's children from his first marriage.

Zhao served at the court of Kublai Khan, and the couple travelled widely, especially between the northern capital at Dadu and the south. These journeys let Guan meet leading artists of the era and see places that upper-class women usually could not. Both held a deep Chan Buddhist faith.

Guan seems to have become active as a painter around 1296 and as a calligrapher in 1299. She painted ink bamboo and plum with delicate strokes, and it is believed that she and her husband sometimes painted together. Bamboo was an unusual subject for a woman, since it was thought to carry masculine qualities: it bends without breaking and stays green through the winter. On a bamboo scroll of 1301 she wrote that using brush and ink was a masculine thing to do, and asked whether she had transgressed. Critics praised the strength of her brushwork and said that it did not betray the hand of a woman.

She painted bamboo among the thickets where it grows rather than as isolated branches close to the picture plane. Emperor Renzong had her calligraphy, with her husband's and their son Zhao Yong's, collected in a scroll for the imperial archives, and commissioned her to copy the Thousand Character Classic. Many aristocratic women commissioned works from her, and she also painted Buddhist murals for Yuan temples.

Guan died in 1319, aged 58, after a long illness, on board an official boat in Shandong while on the way home. Zhao is said to have painted mostly bamboo in her memory during the three years he lived after her, and he did not marry again. Her tombstone was marked as for one buried as a feudal lord. Few of her paintings survive, and most of her scrolls appear to have been made for women of similar rank, her relatives or the wives of her husband's colleagues. She appears in a nineteenth-century compilation on women painters by T'ang Sou-yu and is one of the few women named in early Western surveys of Chinese painting.
guan-hanqing: Guan Hanqing, whose art names were Yizhai and Yizhaisou, was a dramatist, playwright and poet of the Yuan dynasty who lived from about 1241 to 1320. He has been described as among the most prolific and highly regarded dramatists of the period, and as the most productive and creative playwright of northern plays.

Jia Zhongming called him the leader of the Pear Garden. He was fully immersed in the theatre of his time and well known among actors and fellow writers, and he is even said to have painted and powdered his face to act on stage. He spent much of his later life in Dadu and also lived in Hangzhou in the south.

Guan is credited with a large number of plays, of which only 18 survive, three in fragments. They were written mostly in the vernacular of the time, and in some cases the attribution is highly disputed. He is also said to have been a master of songs, or sanqu. Of these 57 short songs and 14 song suites survive. Above all he is known for his sympathetic portrayal of the downtrodden. Surviving titles include Saving the Prostitute, the Conference of a Single Dao, in which Lord Guan goes to a feast alone, The Pavilion of Moon-Worship, The Wife-Snatcher, The Riverside Pavilion and The Jade Mirror-Stand.

The Injustice to Dou E That Touched Heaven and Earth, also called Snow in Midsummer, is one of his most popular plays. Dou Duanyun is sold as a child bride so that her father can pay for a journey to the capital for an official exam, and renamed Dou E. Her husband dies two years into the marriage.

Zhang Lü'er, who had rescued her mother-in-law, tries to force Dou E to marry him and plans to poison her mother-in-law, but his own father eats the soup and dies. Dou E is framed, tortured and sentenced to death after confessing to spare her mother-in-law. She swears that her innocence will be proved by three events: her blood will rise onto white ribbons, snow will fall in summer and Chuzhou will have drought for three years. All three happen.

Guan wrote many courtroom dramas in which morality and legality work together. A Butterfly Dream differs. Three brothers accidentally kill a nobleman whose horse trampled their father, and the family is acquitted after each tries to accept blame for the others. The play shows a more flexible and complex view of justice than traditional Confucian law allowed and explores the grey area between moral culpability and lawful justice.
guan-yu: Guan Yu came from Xie County in Hedong Commandery, in present-day Yuncheng, Shanxi. His original courtesy name was Changsheng. He fled his hometown for unknown reasons and went to Zhuo Commandery. When the Yellow Turban Rebellion broke out in the 180s, he and Zhang Fei joined a volunteer militia formed by Liu Bei and helped a colonel, Zou Jing, to suppress the revolt. The main historical source for his life is Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms, annotated in the fifth century by Pei Songzhi.

After Liu Bei seized Xu Province, he left Guan Yu in charge of the provincial capital Xiapi. In 200 Guan Yu served briefly under Cao Cao. At the Battle of Boma in 200 he recognised the parasol of Yuan Shao's general Yan Liang, charged, killed him and returned with his head; Emperor Xian made him Marquis of Hanshou Village. He told Zhang Liao that he had sworn to follow Liu Bei until death, and he rejoined Liu Bei at about the time of the Battle of Guandu.

From 212 to 214, while Liu Bei campaigned in Yi Province, Guan Yu guarded Jing Province. In 219 Liu Bei made him General of the Vanguard, and he besieged Cao Ren at Fancheng. Autumn floods on the Han River destroyed Yu Jin's seven armies; Yu Jin surrendered and Pang De refused and was executed. Cao Cao allied with Sun Quan, and Xu Huang broke the siege. Lü Meng's troops, hidden in disguised vessels, disabled Guan Yu's river watchtowers and took Jiangling.

Most of Guan Yu's soldiers deserted to rejoin their families. He withdrew to Maicheng and was captured in an ambush with his son Guan Ping, and both were executed at Linju. Sun Quan sent Guan Yu's head to Cao Cao, who buried it with a noble's honours. Chen Shou judged that Guan Yu was unrelenting and conceited, and that this contributed to his downfall.

He was deified as early as the Sui dynasty. Taoist worship began in the Song dynasty, and Chinese Buddhists revere him as Sangharama Bodhisattva, a protector of monasteries. As Emperor Guan or Lord Guan he has temples across China and elsewhere. The 14th-century Romance of the Three Kingdoms, in which he is one of the most altered and aggrandised characters, shaped his popular image as a model of loyalty and martial courage.
guan-zhong: Guan Zhong, whose given name was Yiwu and Zhong a courtesy name, was a descendant of either Shu Xian of Guan or King Mu of Zhou and was born in Yingshang. He became acquainted early with Bao Shuya, and they were business partners. The Shiji records that Guan Zhong often took more than his share of the profits, but Bao, recognising his poverty, was not offended. Guan became tutor to Prince Jiu, younger brother of Duke Xiang of Qi, while Bao tutored Prince Xiaobai. In 686 BCE Duke Xiang was murdered in a palace coup, and both princes fled with their tutors, Jiu to Lu and Xiaobai to Ju.

In 685 BCE the ministers of Qi, after another coup, sought to bring Xiaobai home. Guan Zhong intercepted him and shot an arrow that struck his belt buckle, and Xiaobai pretended to be mortally wounded. Xiaobai won the race to Qi and became duke. Lu was defeated in battle and forced to execute Prince Jiu and return Guan Zhong as a prisoner. Bao Shuya urged that Guan be spared and made chancellor, though he would outrank Bao, and the duke agreed.

Duke Huan had inherited a treasury drained by three years of civil war. Guan Zhong divided the capital into 21 districts, six of merchants and fifteen of attendants who formed the core of the army, and organised the countryside from villages of 30 households into counties and five regions, with administrators reporting yearly to the duke. He ended the Zhou well-field system and taxed land by its productivity, expanded fisheries and salt production, and exempted some traders from tolls.

He held that monopolising salt, iron and other goods of the mountains and seas would bring revenue with fewer complaints than taxes, and he unified the coinage. The Zuo Zhuan records that in 660 BCE he urged the duke to attack the State of Xing, which was under attack by Quan Rong nomads. Duke Huan came to be recognised as the first Hegemon.

Duke Huan gave him the honorary title of Godfather. Guan Zhong died in 645 BCE. His administrative reforms later linked him to the Legalist school, although legalist philosophy developed hundreds of years afterwards. He was a controversial figure among Confucians: one passage has Confucius calling him mediocre for lack of frugality and ritual knowledge, yet when his students criticised him Confucius credited him with allowing Duke Huan to assemble the feudal lords without war chariots, adding that without him we would be folding our lapels right over left. The Guanzi, a later encyclopedia, was compiled under his name by the Jixia Academy during the Warring States period.
guanabara-bay: Guanabara Bay is an oceanic bay in south-eastern Brazil, in the state of Rio de Janeiro. Rio de Janeiro and Duque de Caxias lie on its western shore, and Niterói and São Gonçalo on its eastern shore. It is the second largest bay in Brazil by area, after All Saints' Bay, covering 384 square kilometres with a perimeter of 143 kilometres. It is 31 kilometres long and 28 kilometres wide at most. Its mouth, 1.5 kilometres wide, is flanked by the Pico do Papagaio on the eastern tip and the Pão de Açúcar, or Sugar Loaf, on the western tip.

The name comes from the Tupi language, goanã-pará, from gwa, bay, nã, similar to, and ba'ra, sea. Other suggested meanings include hidden water, lagoon of the sea and bosom of the sea. More than 130 islands dot the bay.

Tamoio and Tupiniquim people lived on the shores of the bay when the Portuguese explorers Gaspar de Lemos and Gonçalo Coelho first reached it on 1 January 1502, and they named it Rio de Janeiro. It is widely believed that they mistook the bay for a river mouth, but they probably knew it was a bay and called it a river because the term was then applied to other bodies of water, such as bays and rias.

No significant European settlement followed until 1555, when French colonists and soldiers under the Huguenot admiral Nicolas Durand de Villegaignon invaded to found France Antarctique. They stayed briefly on Lajes Island and then moved to Serigipe Island, near the shore, where they built Fort Coligny. After Portuguese military expeditions expelled them, the colonial government built fortifications at several points on the bay, among them the forts of Santa Cruz, São João, Lajes and Villegaignon, which formed a crossfire of heavy naval guns and made the bay almost impregnable to attack from the sea. Other islands were later fitted by the Navy for storehouses, hospitals, drydocks, oil reservoirs and the National Naval Academy.

The Rio-Niterói Bridge, 13.29 kilometres long, crosses the bay, and ferries and ships use it heavily. The Port of Rio de Janeiro and the city's two airports, Galeão on Governador Island and Santos Dumont on reclaimed land, stand on its shores, and the main campus of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro is on the artificial Fundão Island. The Guapimirim Environmental Protection Area protects part of it, chiefly in the municipality of Guapimirim.

Urbanisation, deforestation and pollution have damaged its mangroves, and an oil leak from a Petrobras pipeline in 2000 released 1,300,000 litres into the bay. It was once a whaling ground, and a population of botos, river dolphins, still lives there.
guanaja: Guanaja is one of the Bay Islands of Honduras in the Caribbean, about 70 kilometres off the north coast of Honduras and 12 kilometres from the island of Roatan. A cay off the island, also called Bonacca or Low Cay, or simply The Cay, lies near the main island and holds most of the approximately 5,538 people who live in Guanaja. Its waterways have led to its description as the Venice of Honduras. The other main settlements are Mangrove Bight and Savannah Bight, with smaller ones at Pelican Reef, East End and North East Bight. Fishing and shrimping are the islanders' chief income, and the warm waters support a coral reef that is part of the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef.

Columbus landed on Guanaja on 30 July 1502 on his fourth voyage, at Soldado Beach on the north side, the first time he came across cacao. He called it Isla de Los Pinos, though its inhabitants already knew it as Guanaca, a name that appears on the Peter Martyr map in 1511. English pirates, privateers and settlers changed it to Bonacca, and when the Honduran government took the islands it made Guanaja the official name, though older inhabitants still say Bonacca. Spanish slave raids ran from 1516 to 1526 and buccaneers were active in the 16th and 17th centuries, and there was a British Colony of the Bay Islands in 1852.

The Cay was first settled by the Haylocks, who moved to the little cays to escape the flies that plagued them on calm nights, and by the 1880s a thriving community had grown there. Savana Bight was founded by families from Olancho, and settlers from Grand Cayman, including the Tatums and Bennetts, later settled East End. Hurricane Mitch destroyed most of the buildings and homes on the island in late October 1998, and the forests were damaged by the storm.
