On 2 October 2021 a dawn fire swept the island, engulfing some 200 structures, with no casualties.

Guanaja municipality had a population of 5,445 at the 2013 census. English is the first language of native islanders, with Spanish second. The Caracol people, English-speaking and mainly of African descent with some European admixture, have lived in the Bay Islands since the early 19th century, having come from the English-speaking Caribbean to build railroads and work on banana plantations. Since 2021 the whole island and its cays have been a protected Ramsar site, and the island belongs to the Islas de la Bahía y Cayos Cochinos Important Bird Area.
guangdong: Guangdong faces the South China Sea on the south and has 4,300 km of coastline. The Leizhou Peninsula lies at its south-western end. The Pearl River Delta, where the East River, North River and West River converge, is filled with hundreds of small islands. A few mountain ranges collectively called the Nan Mountains separate the province from the north, and its highest peak is Shikengkong, at about 1,900 metres. The name means east of Guang: the Chinese character guang, meaning wide, has been linked with the region since Guang Prefecture was created in 226, and under the Song the Two Guangs were separated into Guangnan East and Guangnan West circuits.

The Neolithic began in the Pearl River Delta about 7,000 years ago, and in the north of the province the Shixia culture dates from about 4600 to 4200 years ago. The region was originally inhabited by a mixture of tribal groups known to the Chinese as the Baiyue, the Hundred Yue. It first became part of China under the Qin dynasty, which after unifying China expanded southwards and set up Nanhai Commandery at Panyu, near present Guangzhou. Chinese administration and reliable historical records began with the Qin. An independent kingdom, Nanyue, then controlled the region between the fall of Qin and the reign of Emperor Wu of Han.

The Han administered Guangdong, Guangxi and northern Vietnam as Jiaozhi Province, and its southern part was a gateway for traders from the west, as far away as the Roman Empire. Under the Wu Kingdom of the Three Kingdoms period, Guangdong was made its own province, Guang Province, in 226. After the Qin unified Lingnan, immigrants from the Central Plains moved in and formed a local culture of its own, whose languages, music, cuisine and opera spread across China and Southeast Asia.

In the early 1920s Guangdong was the staging area where the Kuomintang prepared the Northern Expedition against the warlords, and the Whampoa Military Academy near Guangzhou trained its commanders. Sun Yat-sen, born in the province, declared a military government there. At the end of the Chinese Civil War Guangzhou was briefly the Kuomintang's provisional capital before the People's Liberation Army took the province.

Guangdong is the most populous province of China, with a population of 126,012,510 in the 2020 census, and Guangzhou is its capital. Shenzhen, the first special economic zone, lies in the Pearl River Delta, and Hong Kong borders the province to the south. The Cantonese, Hakka and Teochew make up much of the Han population, and Guangdong is the traditional heartland of Yue Chinese. It is the ancestral home of many overseas Chinese, including most of the 19th-century railroad labourers in Canada, the western United States and Panama.
guangxi: Guangxi is in the far south of China, bordering Vietnam and the Gulf of Tonkin, with Yunnan to the west, Guizhou to the north, Hunan to the northeast and Guangdong to the east. Its mountainous terrain placed it on the frontier of Chinese civilisation for much of history. Karst landforms, with steep mountains and large caverns, cover 37.8 per cent of the land. The name Guang means expanse and has been associated with the region since the creation of Guang Prefecture in 226; the abbreviation Gui comes from Guilin, the provincial capital under the Ming and Qing.

The region was originally inhabited by tribal groups the Chinese called the Baiyue and first became part of China under the Qin. In 214 BCE the general Zhao Tuo claimed most of southern China for Qin Shi Huang, and after the emperor's death he set up the separate kingdom of Nanyue, which collapsed in 111 BCE when the Han expanded south. The Southern Han gained minimal control and was annexed by the Song in 971. The name Guangxi comes from the Song circuit Guangnanxi. The Zhuang leader Nong Zhigao led a revolt in 1052, but his kingdom was short-lived.

The Yuan established Guangxi as a proper province. The Zhuang Cen clan ruled parts of it under the Ming and Qing as recognised local rulers, and the Qing imposed direct rule in 1726. The 19th century was one of constant unrest, including the Jintian Uprising, the beginning of the Taiping Rebellion, in January 1851. The Guangxi Army repulsed the French at the Battle of Zhennan Pass on 23 March 1885. After the Wuchang Uprising Guangxi seceded from the Qing on 6 November 1911. It joined the People's Republic in December 1949. The Guangxi Massacre of 1967 and 1968 during the Cultural Revolution killed 100,000 to 150,000 people.

Guangxi became an autonomous region in 1958, and its capital is Nanning. It has the largest ethnic minority population in China, and a 2021 report put the Zhuang at 31.36 per cent. Languages spoken include Zhuang, Pinghua, Kam, Cantonese, Hakka and Min alongside Mandarin. Major cities are Nanning, Liuzhou, Guilin and Beihai.
guangxu-emperor: The Guangxu Emperor, personal name Zaitian, was born on 14 August 1871, the second son of Yixuan, Prince Chun, and of Yehenara Wanzhen, a younger sister of Empress Dowager Cixi. When the Tongzhi Emperor died without a son on 12 January 1875, the dowager empresses Ci'an and Cixi chose Zaitian, breaking the convention that a new emperor must belong to a generation after his predecessor. The sons of Prince Gong were passed over because they were distrusted as a bad influence on Tongzhi, while Zaitian was younger, Cixi's nephew, and the son of a prince known as a scholar and a supporter of patriotic policies.

The Sino-French War broke out in 1884 over influence in Vietnam. By 1885 the French had destroyed the Chinese fleet at Fuzhou, occupied part of Taiwan and ended Vietnam's status as a tributary of China. Even after Guangxu began to rule in his own right, the court still depended on Cixi, who decided appointments to the Grand Council and the Six Ministries. In 1894 the First Sino-Japanese War began over influence in Korea. Guangxu was associated with the pro-war faction, in contrast to Cixi and the Viceroy Li Hongzhang, who wanted a peaceful settlement.

In early June 1898 the grand councillor Weng Tonghe introduced Guangxu to the reformer Kang Youwei, and the emperor began issuing reform decrees on 11 June. The first edict called on all subjects to strengthen China through Western learning while respecting traditional morals, and Cixi approved it. The programme proved too radical for the conservative elite and did not win the army's support. Cixi rallied its opponents in a coup in late 1898, and Guangxu was confined on Yingtai Island at Zhongnanhai, never ruling alone again.

Guangxu died without children on 14 November 1908, aged 37, a day before Cixi. Her choice of heir, his nephew Puyi, succeeded him. In 2008 forensic tests found that the arsenic in his remains was 2,000 times the level in ordinary people. Most historians have inclined to think that Cixi poisoned him, though another theory names Yuan Shikai, and there are no reliable sources to show who did it. Imperial power in the Qing dynasty reached its lowest point under Guangxu, and he was the only Qing emperor put under house arrest during his own reign.
guangzhou: Guangzhou lies on the Pearl River in south-central Guangdong, about 120 km northwest of Hong Kong and 145 km north of Macau. The old town stood near Baiyun Mountain on the east bank, about 130 km from the river's junction with the South China Sea, and commanded the alluvial plain of the Pearl River Delta, with its link to the sea guarded at the Humen Strait. The city name comes from the ancient Guang Prefecture, whose seat it became.

Before the Han conquest the area was inhabited by non-Chinese tribes known collectively as the Baiyue. A settlement now called Nanwucheng was present by 1100 BCE, and some traditional Chinese histories place its founding in the reign of King Nan of Zhou. Under the name Panyu the city was founded on the east bank of the Pearl River in 214 BCE. Incorporated into the Han dynasty, Panyu became a provincial capital, and in 226 CE it became the seat of Guang Prefecture, which gave it its modern name. The Old Book of Tang describes it as an important port.

Relations with foreign traders were sometimes violent. Arab and Persian pirates sacked the city on 30 October 758, during the An Lushan Rebellion. In 878 the rebel Huang Chao killed about 200,000 foreigners there, along with the city's Jews, Christians and Parsis, and the port was closed for fifty years. For a long time Guangzhou was the only Chinese port accessible to Europeans. It was captured by the British in the First Opium War and lost its monopoly, though it remained a major entrepôt. In the late Qing period it was the site of the revolutionary uprisings of 1895 and 1911.

Guangzhou, also called Canton, is the capital and largest city of Guangdong and a major port and transport hub. The 2020 census recorded a registered population of 18,676,605. Cantonese culture, including Cantonese cuisine and Cantonese opera, is its main cultural heritage. The Canton Fair, formally the China Import and Export Fair, was inaugurated in the spring of 1957 and is held each April and October. Its metro, the fourth underground railway in mainland China, opened in 1997.
guanica: Guánica lies in southern Puerto Rico on the Caribbean Sea, between Lajas to the west and Yauco to the east, about 20 miles (30 kilometres) west of Ponce. The town stands at the head of a deep harbour bordered by rugged hills, barely a quarter-mile wide but about two miles long, which has been likened to a tropical fjord. The ridge of the Cordillera Central keeps rain from the area: the north-east of the island receives over 100 inches a year, Guánica less than 30. Its dry forest reserve was designated an international Biosphere Reserve in 1981.

Juan Ponce de León landed in the harbour on 12 August 1508 and founded a town called Guaynía, from a Taíno word popularly said to mean here is a place with water. Considered the first capital of the island, then named Isla de San Juan Bautista, it was destroyed in the indigenous uprising of 1511, and Europeans left the area for some years while San Juan became the capital. The municipal coat of arms recalls the Taíno chief Agüeybaná, whose territory lay in this region.

In the landing of 1898 the Gloucester was the first ship to anchor in the bay. Twenty-eight sailors and Marines under lieutenants H. P. Huse and Wood came ashore on rafts, replaced the Spanish flag with the American one and set up a machine gun post. Lt. Méndez López and his men of the Puerto Rican militia attacked them in the first land skirmish of the campaign; López and three of his men were wounded, and the unit fell back to Yauco. July 25 was long kept in Puerto Rico as Occupation Day, later renamed Constitution Day.

A census of 1899 by the United States Department of War counted 2,700 people in Guánica, which was at first a barrio of Yauco and became a separate municipality on 13 March 1914, with Víctor Ángel Sallaberry Safini as its first mayor. Its economy was long dominated by the sugar plantations of Central Guánica.

The town centre is a compact grid of twelve streets around the main square, where the Catholic church and city hall stand. The municipality had 13,787 inhabitants in 2020. Hurricane Maria damaged or destroyed 951 homes there on 20 September 2017, and earthquakes of magnitude 5.8 and 6.4 struck on 6 and 7 January 2020.
guanqiu-jian: Guanqiu Jian, whose courtesy name was Zhonggong, came from Wenxi County in Hedong Commandery, present-day Wenxi County in Shanxi. His father, Guanqiu Xing, served Cao Cao as Administrator of Anding Commandery and Cao Pi as Administrator of Wuwei Commandery, and held the peerage Marquis of Gaoyang District. Guanqiu Jian inherited the peerage and served as a clerk to the Marquis of Pingyuan, and he had been an assistant official to Cao Rui while the future emperor was crown prince.

When Cao Rui became the second emperor of Wei in 226, he made his former official a Gentleman of Writing and supervisor of the Imperial Guards. As Agricultural Officer of Luoyang, Guanqiu Jian urged the emperor to scale down his palace building. He was later Inspector of Jing Province, and in the Qinglong era (233-237), when Cao Rui planned to conquer Liaodong, Inspector of You Province and Colonel Who Protects the Wuhuan.

In 237 he marched against the warlord Gongsun Yuan, a former vassal who had rebelled, but heavy flooding ended the campaign. The next year he and Sima Yi defeated Gongsun Yuan, and he was raised to county marquis as Marquis of Anyi. In the war against Goguryeo he defeated King Dongcheon near the Tongjia River; parts of his army reached the eastern coast of the peninsula and northern Manchuria before withdrawing. A fragment of the stele carved for the victory was found in 1905.

The regent Sima Shi, in power since the death of his father Sima Yi in 251, purged Xiahou Xuan and Li Feng in 254. Chen Shou records in the Sanguozhi that Guanqiu Jian, close to both, rebelled out of loyalty to the emperor Cao Mao and for fear of sharing their fate. He rose at Shouchun with Wen Qin, but the revolt was crushed within months; fleeing to Shen County, he was killed by one Zhang Shu. Most of his family were killed, and the survivors defected to Eastern Wu.

His surname is often read as Wuqiu, as in Sima Guang's Zizhi Tongjian. The scholar Wu Jinhua argued that Guanqiu was a copyist's error of the Tang and Song dynasties, and that Wuqiu and Manqiu were readings of an original Muqiu.
guantanamera: Guantanamera is a Cuban patriotic song, an expression of love for Cuba and of solidarity with the poor people of the world. Its lyrics come from the poet José Martí. Official writing credits are given to Joseíto Fernández, who first popularized it on radio as early as 1929 and used it regularly in one of his programmes; consensus puts 1929 as its year of origin, although it is unclear when the first record was released. The music is sometimes attributed to him alone, but some claim the structure came from Herminio El Diablo García Wilson. García's heirs took the matter to court decades later and lost, and in 1993 the People's Supreme Court of Cuba credited Fernández as sole composer of the music.

The version created by Martí and Julián Orbón was the basis for the reworking by Pete Seeger, who in turn drew on a performance by Héctor Angulo. Seeger combined Martí's verse with the tune, intending it for use by the peace movement at the time of the Cuban Missile Crisis. He urged people to sing the song as a symbol of unity between the American and Cuban peoples and asked that it be sung in Spanish. Shortly after the Weavers' reunion concert at Carnegie Hall in May 1963, Seeger included it on his album We Shall Overcome, also performed live at Carnegie Hall; AllMusic's Stewart Mason calls his recording the definitive version.

The most commercially successful version in the English-speaking world was recorded in 1966 by the vocal group the Sandpipers, based on the Weavers' 1963 rendition and arranged by Mort Garson, with narration by the producer Tommy LiPuma. It reached No. 9 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 7 on the UK singles chart. Celia Cruz, whose earliest commercial recording of it was made for the Mexican label Tico Records in 1968, appears with it on at least 241 records or compilations. Wyclef Jean's version incorporated additional lyrics and music, with Cruz and a rap verse by Lauryn Hill, and was nominated for a Grammy Award.

The song has been recorded by many other artists, among them Joan Baez, Julio Iglesias, Nana Mouskouri, Tito Puente and the Gipsy Kings, and Bárbara y Dick took it to No. 1 in Argentina. Its tune is commonly used in British football chants of the form There's only one player's name. The Pakistani singer Alamgir recorded an adaptation in the 1980s, with unrelated Urdu lyrics, called Albela Rahi.
guantanamo-bay-naval-base: The base occupies 45 square miles (117 km2) of land and water on the shore of Guantánamo Bay, at the south-eastern end of Cuba. It is the oldest overseas American naval base. The bay divides the station into sections: Leeward Point holds the airfield, while Windward Point holds most of the base's activities. The highest point is John Paul Jones Hill, at 495 feet (151 m), and many coves and peninsulas along the shore provide anchorage for ships.

The area was first inhabited by the Taíno people. Christopher Columbus arrived on 30 April 1494, on his second voyage, spent the night and named the bay Puerto Grande. During the War of Jenkins' Ear a British expeditionary force held the bay briefly and renamed it Cumberland Bay, but withdrew after an attempt to march to Santiago de Cuba was repulsed by Spanish troops. In 1898, during the Spanish–American War, the American fleet attacking Santiago secured the harbour for protection during the hurricane season, and marines landed with naval support.

The war ended with the Treaty of Paris of 1898. In 1901 the Platt Amendment provided that Cuba would sell or lease to the United States lands for coaling or naval stations. After initial resistance by the Cuban Constitutional Convention it was incorporated into the Cuban constitution, which took effect in 1902, and land at Guantánamo Bay was granted the following year. The lease of 1903 has no fixed expiration date. It left ultimate sovereignty with Cuba while giving the United States sole jurisdiction during its occupation, at a rent of $2,000 a year in gold coin.

Since the Cuban Revolution the Cuban government has protested against the American presence, arguing that the base was imposed by force and is illegal under international law; only one rent payment has been accepted since 1959. In 1961 both sides completed minefields around the perimeter, some 55,000 mines in all, and at least ten people died in explosions between 1961 and 1965. President Bill Clinton ordered the American field cleared in 1996. In 1964 Cuba stopped the flow of water to the base, and the commander had the pipelines cut. Water was first imported from Jamaica by barge, and a desalination plant was then moved from San Diego.
guanzhong: Guanzhong is a crescent-shaped basin in central Shaanxi, bounded by the Qinling Mountains to the south and by the Huanglong Mountain, Meridian Ridge and Long Mountain ranges to the north. Its central flatland, the Guanzhong or Wei River Plain, is made of alluvial plains along the lower Wei River and its tributaries, at 300 to 700 metres above sea level. Xi'an, the capital of Shaanxi, lies at its centre, and Baoji, Xianyang, Tongchuan and Weinan are its other main cities.

The name means within the passes, after the fortresses that guarded it: Hangu Pass to the east, Wu Pass to the south-east, Xiao Pass to the north-west and Dasan Pass to the west, later joined by Tong Pass, built by the warlord Cao Cao, and Jinsuo Pass, built under the Tang. Hangu Pass, on a narrow corridor along the south bank of the Yellow River, was long the only passage into the region from the North China Plain, and its strength helped Qin defeat the alliances of its eastern rivals.

Guanzhong became the heartland of the Zhou after the Jī clan leader Gugong Danfu led his people south from Bin to escape nomad raids, and from there the Zhou conquered the Shang in 1046 BCE. After the Quanrong sacked the Zhou capital Haojing in 771 BCE and the court fled east, the Yíng clan, rewarded for escorting King Ping of Zhou, built up the Qin state in the basin and moved its capital east by stages to Xianyang. Irrigation works such as the Zhengguo Canal made the region highly productive, and Qin unified China in 221 BCE.

In 206 BCE the rebel leader Liu Bang entered Guanzhong and received the surrender of the last Qin ruler, Ziying, but had to yield it to Xiang Yu, who sacked Xianyang. Four months later Liu Bang returned with Han Xin, retook the region and used it as his base against Xiang Yu, and as founder of the Han he built a new capital, Chang'an, across the Wei from ruined Xianyang. Guanzhong was the capital region of twelve dynasties. By the Tang the economic centre of China had shifted south to the Yangtze basin, and after the destruction of Chang'an at the end of the Tang, Guanzhong declined politically and economically.
guaram-i-of-iberia: Guaram was the son of Leo, the younger son of King Vakhtang I Gorgasali and his Roman consort Helene. He thus belonged to the younger, non-royal branch of the Chosroid dynasty, which held the south-western Iberian duchies of Klarjeti and Javakheti. The medieval Georgian author Sumbat Davitis-Dze reports him as the first ruler of the Bagrationi line, a claim that has not been accepted as credible. He is commonly identified with the Gurgenes of the Byzantine chronicler Theophanes, a Hellenized form of the Middle Persian name Gurgēn.

When war between the Roman and Sasanian empires resumed under the Emperor Justin II, Guaram, as Gurgenes, joined the Armenian prince Vardan III Mamikonian and the Romans in 572 in a desperate attempt to break free of Sasanian control. When the uprising failed he apparently fled to Constantinople, and he remained there until he reappeared on the political scene in 588.

According to the Georgian chronicler Juansher, the Iberians revolted against Sasanian rule again in 588. Their nobles asked the Emperor Maurice for a ruler from the Iberian royal house, and Maurice sent Guaram to Mtskheta with the dignity of curopalates. The presiding principate of Iberia thus took the place of the Chosroid kingship, which had lain dormant since its suppression by the Sasanids around 580. Tradition credits Guaram with founding the Jvari Monastery at Mtskheta. He was succeeded by his son, Stephen I.

Guaram was the first Georgian ruler to take the unusual step of issuing coins modelled on the silver drachms of the Sasanids. These coins, known as Iberian-Sasanid, bear the initials GN, for Gurgen. It seems that Guaram, the name the Georgian chronicles record, was the name for use at home, while Gurgen was the official name of this ruler in foreign relations, the one found on his coinage and in foreign sources.
guarani-language: Guarani, called avañe'ẽ in the language itself, belongs to the Tupi-Guarani branch of the Tupian family. It was written down only after the arrival of Jesuit missionaries, so its earlier stages can be reconstructed only by comparison with related languages. Written records begin with the Jesuits Antonio Ruiz de Montoya and Alonso de Aragona. Montoya's Tesoro de la Lengua Guaraní, a dictionary of 1639, gave examples of how words were used, and his grammar, the Arte de la lengua Guaraní of 1640, is regarded as the starting point for all later grammatical work. Aragona's teaching grammar was finished in 1629 but not printed until 1979.

Guarani is one of the two official languages of Paraguay, with Spanish, and is spoken by the majority of the population; half of the rural population speak only Guarani. It is one of the most widely spoken Native American languages, with more than four million speakers. In South America it is the indigenous language most widely spoken among non-indigenous people, and unlike most American languages it has resisted a shift to the colonial language. Variants are spoken in north-eastern Argentina, south-eastern Bolivia and south-western Brazil, and it is one of the three official languages of Mercosur.

The language is highly agglutinative, often described as polysynthetic. Its syllables are open, consisting of a consonant and a vowel or a vowel alone, and it shows an unusual degree of nasal harmony. Everyday speech in Paraguay is Jopará, a mixture of Spanish and Guarani, spoken by an estimated 90 per cent of the population, with more Spanish used in official and business matters and more Guarani in art and daily life.

Modern scholarship shows that Guarani was always the main language of colonial Paraguay, inside and outside the Jesuit reductions. The Jesuits avoided direct loans from Spanish and built new terms from Guarani parts, rendering communion as Tupârahava, from Tupâ, God, while speakers outside the missions simply took in Spanish words, so that communion became komuño. After the Jesuits were expelled in the 18th century, the residents of the reductions moved gradually towards Asunción, and the regulated Jesuit variety gave way to the spoken form that became Jopará.

Since independence Paraguayan governments have repressed Guarani for most of the time, and it was forbidden in state schools for over 100 years, though populists used pride in the language to appeal to nationalist feeling. The constitution of 1992, with the arrival of democracy, made it equal to Spanish. It is also an official language of Bolivia.
guarani-people: The Guaraní are a group of culturally related Indigenous peoples, distinguished from the related Tupi by their use of the Guaraní language. Their traditional range lies in what is now Paraguay between the Paraná River and the lower Paraguay River, the Misiones Province of Argentina, southern Brazil and parts of Uruguay and Bolivia. Before they met Europeans they called themselves Abá, meaning men or people. When Europeans first met them they are estimated to have numbered about 400,000. They were sedentary farmers living on manioc, maize, game and honey, in communal houses that each held several families under a chief.

In 1537 Gonzalo de Mendoza met the Guaraní and founded Asunción. The first governor encouraged intermarriage between European men and Indigenous women, but modern historians describe the process as one of sexual and economic coercion: the Guaraní custom of giving women to newcomers to cement alliances gave way after 1541 to violent mass seizures, and women were sold and exported as slaves to Portuguese settlements on the coast.

In the early 17th century Jesuit missionaries, backed by the Spanish crown after protesting against the enslavement of Indigenous people, gathered Guaraní into mission towns. The first Guayrá mission, Loreto, was founded in 1610. Slave raiders from São Paulo attacked them, and within two years of 1629 about 60,000 converts had been carried off to be sold. In 1732 there were 30 missions with 141,252 Guaraní, defended by an army of 7,000. The Treaty of Madrid of 1750 transferred seven Uruguay missions to Portugal, and the Guaraní, who were absent from the negotiations, resisted in a war from 1754 to 1756. After the Jesuits were expelled in 1767 the missions declined, and the census of 1801 counted fewer than 45,000 Guaraní.

The Guaraní number around 280,000 and live mainly in Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil and Paraguay. Guaraní is one of the two official languages of Paraguay, with Spanish, and is learned there at school and in daily life. It is also an official language of Bolivia. In Paraguay Guaraní lineage predominates in the population, and in modern Spanish Guaraní can also mean any Paraguayan national. The Bolivian Guaraní, once called Chiriguanos, are represented by the Assembly of the Guarani People.
guarino-guarini: Camillo Guarino Guarini was born in Modena on 17 January 1624 into a deeply religious family; he and his four brothers all joined the Theatine Order. At fifteen he became a novice and was sent to the monastery of San Silvestro al Quirinale in Rome, where he stayed from 1639 to 1648 and studied the work of Francesco Borromini, Gian Lorenzo Bernini and Pietro da Cortona.

From Borromini he learned to use complex geometry as the basis of floor plans. He also trained in theology, philosophy and mathematics. Back in Modena as an ordained priest in 1648, he became a lecturer in philosophy at the Theatine College two years later, and in 1649 he began his career as an architect for the Order with the rebuilding of San Vincenzo.

In 1655 Guarini was elected provost of the Theatine house in Modena against the wishes of Alfonso IV d'Este, who banished him from the city. He reached Messina in 1660, where he built the façade of Santa Maria Annunziata, and in 1665 he published in Paris a large mathematical and philosophical treatise, the Placita Philosophica. When he arrived in Turin towards the end of 1666 he submitted a new design for San Lorenzo, and work on it began in 1668. The church has a centralized nave and a dome of criss-crossing hyperbolic ribs, with windows of different shapes breaking up the surfaces between them.

In 1679 Guarini was commissioned by Prince Emmanuel Philibert of Carignano to build the Palazzo Carignano outside the medieval walls of Turin. It was completed in 1683 as a three-winged building, not the four wings first planned. Its brick façade is formed of two S-curves around a tall oval pavilion, an innovation in Italian Baroque palace design. He also built the Chapel of the Holy Shroud (1668-94), the Castle of Racconigi and the Colegio dei Nobili. He wrote on mathematics, astronomy, fortification and architecture, roughly a book every other year.

Guarini died on 6 March 1683. In 1686 the Theatines published 33 engraved plates of his designs, and in the 1730s, with the help of the architect Bernardo Antonio Vittone, his treatise Architettura civile appeared in 1737. In it he wrote that vaults are the main thing in architecture and that architecture aims at the gratification of the senses.

His diaphanous domes found no imitators among his contemporaries in Italy outside Piedmont, and in the later 18th century Neoclassicism led to attacks such as Francesco Milizia's. His book was widely read in Austria and Germany and influenced Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach, Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt and Balthasar Neumann.
guatemala: Guatemala is mountainous. Two mountain chains enter it from west to east and divide it into three regions: the highlands, the Pacific coast to the south and the Petén region, a sparsely populated northern lowland. All major cities lie in the highlands and on the Pacific coast. The highlands lie along the Motagua Fault, which produced a 7.5 magnitude earthquake on 4 February 1976 that killed more than 25,000 people. Two of the three moves of the capital were caused by volcanic mudflows in 1541 and earthquakes in 1773.

The first evidence of human habitation dates to 12,000 BCE, and maize cultivation had been developed by 3500 BCE. Archaeologists divide the pre-Columbian past into the Preclassic period (2000 BCE to 250 CE), the Classic (250 to 900) and the Postclassic (900 to 1500). The Classic period matches the height of Maya civilisation, with the largest concentration of sites in Petén. That civilisation collapsed around 900 and many cities of the central lowlands were abandoned; the cause is debated, though the drought theory is gaining currency. In the Postclassic, regional kingdoms such as the Itza and Kowoj in Petén and the K'iche', Kaqchikel and Mam peoples in the highlands preserved many aspects of Maya culture.

Most of the territory was conquered by the Spanish in the 16th century and claimed as part of the viceroyalty of New Spain. Guatemala became independent from Spain and Mexico in 1821 and was part of the Federal Republic of Central America from 1823 to 1841. Jorge Ubico was overthrown in 1944, beginning a decade of reform that ended with a military coup in 1954. A civil war ran from 1960 to 1996 and included genocidal massacres of the Maya population by the military; 83 percent of the victims of the 626 massacres reported in the 1980s were Maya. A peace accord negotiated by the United Nations ended it.

Guatemala is a constitutional democratic republic with its capital and largest city at Guatemala City. The sole official language is Spanish, and twenty-one Mayan languages, Xinca and Garifuna are recognised as national languages. Indigenous Guatemalans, mostly Maya, are 43.6% of the population according to the 2018 census. The country is divided into 22 departments.
guatemala-city: Guatemala City lies in a mountain valley called the Valle de la Ermita, in the south-central part of Guatemala. Four stratovolcanoes are visible from the city, two of them active, and the nearest and most active, Pacaya, at times sends up a considerable amount of ash. The Guatemalan highlands lie on the Ring of Fire and are frequently shaken by earthquakes; the last large one to strike the region came in 1976, on the Motagua Fault.

Human settlement on the site began with the Maya, who built a large ceremonial centre at Kaminaljuyu. It was the biggest Maya settlement outside the lowlands of the Yucatán Peninsula and rose to prominence about 300 BCE through the mining and trade of obsidian, a volcanic glass valued across Mesoamerica. The centre is now a park within the city.

The old colonial capital, now Antigua Guatemala, was left in ruins by the earthquakes of 1773, the third to strike it after those of 1717 and 1751, and the Spanish decided to move to a safer place. In 1776 the capital was moved to the valley where Guatemala City stands. The Metropolitan Cathedral on the central plaza was built mostly between 1782 and 1815 and completed in 1871. The Act of Independence of Central America, declared in the city in September 1821, ended Spanish rule, and for several decades the city was the capital of the federation of the United Provinces of Central America. In August 1847 Guatemala declared itself an independent republic and Guatemala City became its national capital.

The earthquakes of 1917 and 1918 almost completely destroyed the city, and its reconstruction brought wider streets and grid layouts. Under President Jorge Ubico, who held power for 13 years, the National Palace was built between 1939 and 1943. He was overthrown in the Guatemalan Revolution of 1944.

Guatemala City is the national capital and largest city of Guatemala, and its metropolitan area is the largest in Central America. Its formal name is Nueva Guatemala de la Asunción, in honour of the Virgin of the Assumption, whose feast on 15 August is the city's feast day. The University of San Carlos of Guatemala, founded in 1676, is the oldest institution of higher education in Central America.
guatemalan-national-revolutionary-unity: The civil war is usually dated from a failed coup by dissident officers on 13 November 1960; it lasted 36 years and claimed an estimated 200,000 lives. The first guerrilla group, the Rebel Armed Forces (FAR), was founded in 1962. In the early 1970s two splinters of the FAR, the Organization of People in Arms (ORPA) and the Guerrilla Army of the Poor (EGP), turned to indigenous communities as their base, the EGP influenced by liberation theology and strong in El Quiché.

In 1978 the EGP, the FAR and a faction of the Guatemalan Party of Labour (PGT) agreed to cooperate. The Cuban and Nicaraguan governments, which supported the guerrillas, pressed for a fuller merger, and on 8 February 1982 the EGP, ORPA, the FAR and the National Directing Nucleus of the PGT formed the URNG under Cuban mediation.

A month after its founding the URNG faced the scorched-earth campaign of General Efraín Ríos Montt, who held power until August 1983. In the Guatemalan genocide of mid 1981 to 1983 about 150,000 civilians were killed and 1.5 million displaced. The guerrillas retreated to remote zones and their leaders fled to Mexico City. They fought by ambushes, raids, bombings and assassinations, while government death squads hunted prominent leftists.

Negotiations began in 1986, moderated by the United Nations, and led to an agreement on a political settlement signed in Mexico in 1991. The final accord was signed before about 50,000 people in front of the National Palace of Culture, in the presence of Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali. The URNG leader Rolando Morán and President Álvaro Arzú shared the UNESCO Peace Prize, and the URNG later apologised to the victims of the war.

During the war the URNG drew on the rural poor and urban intellectuals; 82% of its demobilised combatants and half of its political activists were indigenous. It was closely tied to the Committee for Peasant Unity (CUC), founded on 15 April 1978. Registered as a party in December 1998, it entered the 1999 elections in the New Nation Alliance, whose candidate Álvaro Colom came third with about 12.4% of the vote. Its support later fell to a few seats in Congress.
guayaquil: Guayaquil stands on the west bank of the Guayas River, about 60 km north of the Gulf of Guayaquil and near the Equator. The climate is tropical savanna: hot, humid and rainy from January to April, and dry from May to December because of the cooling Humboldt Current. The city lies on soft sediments and on the ring of fire, so it faces a serious earthquake threat.

After several failed attempts and fires, the Spanish settled the city as a port and shipyard. The name is older than the Spanish. A local tradition derives it from a leader called Guayas and his wife Quil, while historians point to a chief named Guayaquile, whose lands were held by the chonos of the Milagro-Quevedo culture. In colonial times it was the chief Spanish shipyard in the Pacific and a stopover for the Manila galleons. Most of the region's enslaved people lived there in the late eighteenth century, and María Chiquinquirá won her freedom in court in 1794. English and French pirates looted it on 20 April 1687, and Woodes Rogers and William Dampier did so in 1709.

On 9 October 1820 civilians and soldiers under the Peruvian Colonel Gregorio Escobedo arrested the Spanish authorities almost without bloodshed and declared the Free Province of Guayaquil, with José Joaquín de Olmedo as civil chief. Antonio José de Sucre sailed from the city to lead the army that won the Battle of Pichincha. On 26 July 1822 José de San Martín and Simón Bolívar met there. Peruvian troops occupied it for seven months in 1829. A fire destroyed large parts of it in 1896, and a three-day general strike in 1922 ended after at least 300 people were killed by the military and police.

Guayaquil is the capital of Guayas Province and the largest city of Ecuador, with more than 3,000,000 inhabitants. Its port handles most of the country's international trade. The oldest part of the city, with the cathedral, the Malecón along the river and the Las Peñas neighbourhood, draws visitors. The University of Guayaquil was founded in 1867.
guayas-province: Guayas lies on the Pacific coast of Ecuador, bordered by Manabí, Santa Elena and the Gulf of Guayaquil to the west, Los Ríos and Bolívar to the north, Chimborazo, Cañar and Azuay to the east, and El Oro to the south. Its capital, Guayaquil, is the largest city and main port of Ecuador. The province has no elevations except the Coastal Range, which runs from Guayaquil to Manabí. The land west of the range is desert, with an average temperature of 23 °C, while the land east of it belongs to the Guayas watershed and is humid and fertile.
The Daule River flows from the north to join the Babahoyo River and form the Guayas river. The province is part of the largest river basin in South America west of the Andes.

The native culture living in the province before the European arrival was the Huancavilca, and their descendants make up a large part of the population. Guayaquil was founded on 14 August 1534, although its foundation is marked on 25 July, and during the Spanish conquest it became one of the most important ports in South America. The city became free on 9 October 1820, and the Guayaquil Department, one of the original subdivisions of Ecuador, was founded soon afterwards. It consisted of Manabí Province and Guayaquil Province, which was later renamed Guayas.
The Guayaquil Province included the area of what is now Peruvian Tumbes and today's Los Ríos and El Oro. The provinces were separated from Guayas in 1860 and 1884, respectively.

Guayas is the most populous province in Ecuador, with a census population of 4,391,923 in 2022, and the seventh largest by area. It has grown rapidly, from 612,417 in 1950 to over 1.4 million by 1970, as people moved from rural areas to Guayaquil. The 2010 census recorded 67.5% of residents as mestizo, 11.3% as Montubio, 9.8% as white, 9.7% as Afro-Ecuadorian and 1.3% as indigenous, and there are also communities descended from Italians, Lebanese and German people. The province is divided into 25 cantons.
gubazes-ii-of-lazica: Gubazes was of Byzantine descent through his mother, Valeriana; his uncle Opsites was married to a Byzantine noblewoman, Theodora. His father's name is not recorded, though the historian Cyril Toumanoff has suggested he was the son and direct successor of King Tzath I. He had a younger brother, Tzath, and was married with children whose names are unknown. Before his accession he very likely lived for some years in Constantinople, since he is recorded as a silentiarius, an influential post at the imperial palace.

Lazica had been a Byzantine client since 522, but under Emperor Justinian I the trade monopoly run by the general John Tzibus from the new fortress of Petra made Byzantine rule unpopular. In spring 541 the Persian shah Khosrau I and his army, led by Lazi guides, crossed the mountains, and Gubazes submitted; Petra fell after Tzibus was killed. The Christian Lazi soon resented the Zoroastrian Persians and the loss of the Black Sea trade, and according to the historian Procopius of Caesarea Khosrau planned to resettle them and to have Gubazes killed. Warned, Gubazes returned to Byzantium.

In 548 Justinian sent 8,000 men under Dagisthaeus, who besieged Petra with the Lazi until a Persian relief force under Mihr-Mihroe raised the siege. The next spring Gubazes and Dagisthaeus destroyed the army of Phabrizus and later defeated a force under Khorianes. The Byzantines took and razed Petra in 551, but Mihr-Mihroe then won control of eastern Lazica, and Gubazes and his family took refuge in the mountains, where he rejected Persian peace offers through the winter of 551/552.

Gubazes quarrelled with the Byzantine generals and wrote to Justinian accusing them of incompetence. Bessas was recalled, but Martin and the sacellarius Rusticus accused Gubazes of dealings with Persia and were authorised to arrest him. In September or October 555 they invited him to watch a siege, and Rusticus's brother John stabbed him. The Lazi stopped fighting for a time, and an assembly asked Justinian for an inquiry and for Tzath as king. The senator Athanasius cleared Gubazes of treachery; Rusticus and John were executed in autumn 556, and Martin was deposed.
gubbio: Gubbio lies in an upland valley of the Apennines, on the lowest slope of Monte Ingino, in the north-east of Umbria. The area is a transitional one, close to Marche on the east and Tuscany on the west, and Gubbio has historically had strong political and cultural ties to both. The valley floor is a basin that was once a lake. The surrounding land is fertile and is especially productive for olives.

The oldest evidence of human habitation in the valley dates to the Middle Palaeolithic, and relatively permanent settlements appear in the Neolithic, between 6000 and 3000 BCE. By the Archaic period settlement had moved to the lower slopes of Monte Asciano, and Monte Ascoli served as a religious sanctuary, where dozens of bronze figurines dated between the 5th and 3rd centuries BCE have been found.

Coins struck in the Umbrian period carry the forms Ikvvini and Ikvvins, which show that the Umbrian and Roman towns were the same community. Iguvium obtained Roman citizenship before the Social War, and its inhabitants were enrolled in the Clustumina tribe. Roman accounts say the Iguvini were entrusted with the custody of the captured King Gentius.

In the early Middle Ages the city came under the Heruli and then the Ostrogoths. A general of Totila captured and destroyed it, and it was rebuilt with help from Narses. In the 11th century it became a free municipality with civic institutions, though conflicts with feudal lords and bishops continued. In 1516 Pope Leo X appointed Lorenzo de' Medici as duke and forced Francesco Maria I into exile, but Francesco Maria recovered the duchy on Leo's death. Gubbio joined the Kingdom of Italy on 14 September 1860.

Gubbio is a municipality in the province of Perugia with a population of about 30,000. The Palazzo dei Consoli, built between 1332 and 1349 to a design by Angelo da Orvieto, and the Palazzo dei Priori stand opposite one another and show the medieval commune's civic life. The Roman theatre, completed around 20 BCE, held about 6,000 spectators. Every year on 15 May the Festa dei Ceri takes place on the eve of the feast of the patron, Saint Ubald, who died in 1160. Three wooden structures called Ceri are carried through the town to the Basilica of Sant'Ubaldo on Monte Ingino.
guben: Guben lies in the south-east of the state of Brandenburg, in the district of Spree-Neiße. The town sits on the banks of the Lusatian Neisse between two plateaus, a position that favoured its early economic development. The plateaus are ground moraines left by the Weichselian glaciation, and the surrounding land is covered with pine forests and lakes. Its coat of arms shows a red wall with three gates and three towers, with small shields for the Kings of Prussia, the Kings of Bohemia and the Electors of Saxony, its historic rulers.

A trade settlement existed here from the 11th century, and in the early 11th century it belonged to the early Polish state under Bolesław I the Brave before falling to the March of Lusatia. A document of Duke Henry the Bearded mentions it as Gubin in 1211. On 1 June 1235 Henry III, Margrave of Meissen, granted the settlement on the eastern bank Magdeburg rights and declared it a town, while a Benedictine nunnery developed on the western bank as a suburb. King John of Bohemia besieged the town unsuccessfully in 1319. It passed to the Kingdom of Bohemia in 1368, and in 1635 Elector John George I of Saxony received Lower Lusatia and Guben in the Peace of Prague.

Textile making began in the 16th century and flourished in the 19th, with leather gloves from 1849. From 1822 Guben's hat production covered 65% of German demand, and rugs and shoes followed. Lignite processing began in the eastern half of the city in 1847. The railway between Frankfurt (Oder) and Breslau opened in 1846, and a tram ran in the city from 1904 until 1938. After the Margravate of Lower Lusatia was abolished in 1815, Guben became the capital of a district in the Province of Brandenburg.

At the Potsdam Conference in 1945 the boundary between Germany and Poland was fixed on the Oder–Neisse line. Because Guben stood on the Lusatian Neisse, the town was split into German Guben and Polish Gubin, and the old centre fell to Gubin. The western suburbs that had grown from the nunnery stayed in Guben, which grew after 1945 with a chemical plant and new housing. From 1961 to 1990 East Germany named it Wilhelm-Pieck-Stadt Guben after its president Wilhelm Pieck, born in what is now Gubin. Guben has 20,049 inhabitants and is twinned with Gubin, Cittadella in Italy and Laatzen in Germany.
gudea: Gudea ruled the city-state of Lagash in southern Mesopotamia during the Second Dynasty of Lagash, after the fall of the Akkadian Empire and before Lagash was incorporated into the Third Dynasty of Ur. His reign is estimated at between 20 and 25 years, and its exact dates cannot be fixed. He bore the title ensi, ruler or governor, and became ruler as the son-in-law of his predecessor Ur-Bau, having married his daughter Ninalla. His name means the one who is called, and may be a throne name that expresses his claim to have been chosen by the gods. After the end of Akkadian rule, southern Mesopotamia split apart; the Gutians held the north, and Ur-Namma later unified the region from Ur.

Gudea presents himself above all as a pious king. His ten attested year names and his inscriptions commemorate rebuilt temples, offerings to the gods and the consecration of a high priestess, and only one military campaign, in Elam, is mentioned. He turned away from the warlike image of the kings of Akkad, and historians often see his reign as the start of a Sumerian renaissance. His chief god was Ningirsu, whose temple Eninnu at Girsu he rebuilt, and he made Ningishzida his personal god and claimed the goddesses Gatumdug and Ninsun as his divine mothers.

He is best known for his statues, most of them carved from diorite imported from Magan, in southern Arabia. Specialists put the corpus at between 24 and 27 statues, many of them headless. They were first found at Telloh, ancient Girsu, in the French excavations of 1878 to 1909, and others turned up at Nippur and Tell Hammam. His inscriptions and two clay cylinders are among the finest examples of Sumerian literature.

Lagash was incorporated into the kingdom of Ur III after his reign, apparently under his fifth successor Nam-mahani, probably peacefully. Gudea was deified and received offerings at festivals and a priest of his own, and his name was used in personal names. In the 2nd century BCE a local ruler named Adad-nadin-ahhe, who admired the past, built a palace at Telloh and moved several statues of Gudea there, where they remained until modern excavations. The objects Gudea left, unearthed in the last quarter of the 19th century, played a decisive part in the rediscovery of Sumerian civilisation.
gudfred: Gudfred is the first ruler of Denmark about whom contemporary sources say much, but nearly all of it comes from hostile Frankish texts, and he leaves no clear trace in the later Norse sagas. His father is unknown; he may have been closely related to Sigfred, king of the Danes from about 770 to 804. He had at least five sons, of whom only Horik I is named, and at least five nephews, among them the later king Hemming. A rival royal branch, represented by Harald Klak, claimed kinship with an earlier King Harald.

In 804 a Frankish army reached the Eider, Denmark's southern boundary. Gudfred came to Sliesthorp (Hedeby) with his fleet and all his cavalry to meet Charlemagne, but on his men's advice never appeared. He then attacked the Obodrites, allies of the Franks, by sea; his nephew Ragnvald, second man in the kingdom, fell in a siege, but Gudfred took several Slavic strongholds and made two districts pay him tribute. The Obodrite prince Drożko was driven out, and another chief, Godelaib, was captured by trickery and hanged.

The Danevirke he strengthened was older, begun around 450 to 500; his work was an improvement, an earthen bank with a wooden stockade and a deep ditch, with a single gate. Talks with Frankish envoys at Badenfliot in 809 failed, and when Drożko returned and reclaimed his lands, assassins sent by Gudfred killed him in the rebuilt Reric. In 810 a Danish fleet of 200 ships ravaged Frisia, defeated the local forces in three battles and exacted 100 pounds of silver.

The Frankish annals say he was murdered by one of his housecarls. The later and unreliable Notker of St Gall has him cut down by his own son while hunting ducks, to avenge his abandoned mother. His nephew Hemming succeeded him and made peace with the Franks in 811. Some scholars have identified him with Gudrød the Hunter of Vestfold in the Ynglingatal, but most dismiss the link as speculative; the poem La Chevalerie Ogier de Danemarche makes him the father of Ogier the Dane.
guelma: Guelma is the capital of Guelma Province in north-eastern Algeria, about 52 kilometres from the Mediterranean coast. It lies 290 metres above sea level, surrounded by mountains and at the heart of a fertile agricultural region watered by the Seybouse River and a large dam. It is a crossroads linking the coast, around Annaba, El Taref and Skikda, with inland areas such as Constantine and Souk-Ahras. Its industries include the manufacture of cycles and mopeds, sugar refining, ceramics, canning and semolina milling. Nearby hot springs such as Hammam Debagh draw visitors.

The region was occupied from the Paleolithic, as the Roknia remains of more than 3,000 dolmens show, and was inhabited by a Libyan-Berber population. It was established as a town under the Phoenicians, who called it Malaca, probably a word meaning salt. The Romans renamed it Calama, in the province of Numidia. Calama prospered as Christianity rose, and Saint Possidius was its bishop in the 5th century. The Vandal invasion devastated the area, and the Byzantines then built city walls and included it in the Exarchate of Africa.

After the Islamic conquest of Algeria the site was long abandoned as a formal settlement, even under Ottoman rule. French troops under General Bertrand Clausel discovered and briefly occupied the ruins of Calama from 10 to 15 November 1836. Guelma was established as a city that year and developed by French settlers, who built a modern town around the Roman ruins, inside the restored Byzantine walls and later beyond them. Its communal constitution dates from 17 June 1854, and its Roman theatre was restored in 1905. On 8 May 1945, during the Sétif massacre, numerous settlers were killed.

After the independence of Algeria the European settlers and the local Jews left, and the synagogue and the church were converted into mosques. The population grew at a rapid pace. The oldest religious building still used for worship is the El-Atik Mosque, the Great Mosque of Guelma, built in 1837. The painter Bettina Heinen-Ayech and the opera singer Henri Médus are among its notable natives.
guelphs-and-ghibellines: The conflict grew out of the Investiture Controversy, which began in 1075 and ended with the Concordat of Worms in 1122, over whether secular rulers or the pope could appoint bishops and abbots. After the death of Emperor Henry V the German dukes elected Lothair III, which displeased the Hohenstaufen. War followed in Germany, and after Lothair's death the Hohenstaufen Conrad III was elected while Henry the Proud of the House of Welf kept fighting.

The names are said to come from rallying cries at the Siege of Weinsberg in 1140: the Welfs used their family name, and the Hohenstaufen under Conrad III used Wibellingen, the name of the town now called Waiblingen. In Italian these became Guelfo and Ghibellino. The Guelph Lombard League defeated Emperor Frederick Barbarossa at Legnano in 1176.

In the reign of Frederick II the Guelphs became more strictly associated with the papacy and the Ghibellines with the Empire. Pope Gregory IX excommunicated Frederick in 1227 and again in 1239, and Frederick died on 13 December 1250. At Montaperti in 1260 the Ghibellines of Siena defeated the Florentine Guelphs. After Charles I of Anjou executed the Hohenstaufen Conradin in 1268, the terms came to mark individual families and cities rather than the conflict between empire and papacy.

The Tuscan Guelphs defeated the Ghibellines at Campaldino in 1289, and the Florentine Guelphs then split into Black and White Guelphs. Dante, among the supporters of the Whites, was exiled in 1302 when the Blacks took control of Florence. In 1334 Pope Benedict XII threatened users of either name with excommunication. The names survived into the Italian Wars, and cities and families used them until Charles V consolidated imperial power over Italy in 1529.

Loyalties were local. Smaller cities tended to be Ghibelline if the larger city nearby was Guelph, as Siena stood against Florence. Within cities allegiance differed between guilds and districts, and a city could change party after an upheaval. In Florence and elsewhere the Guelphs usually included merchants and burghers and the Ghibellines noblemen. People marked their side by customs such as wearing a feather on a particular side of the hat. In Genoa the Guelphs were called rampini and the Ghibellines mascherati.

Families signalled allegiance in their coats of arms: Guelphs by a chief of Anjou with yellow fleurs-de-lys on blue, Ghibellines by a chief of the empire with the black imperial eagle on gold. Ghibelline buildings had swallow-tailed crenellations and Guelph ones square.
guerande: Guérande lies in the heart of the Guérande Peninsula, which is surrounded by water: the Atlantic Ocean to the west, the Brière Regional Nature Reserve to the east, the Vilaine to the north and the Loire estuary to the south. The peninsula has two contrasting landscapes, the Pays Blanc, named for its salt marshes, and the Pays Noir, with the Brière peat bog. The salt marshes began before the 9th century, and around 1500 they reached 80 per cent of their present surface. Guérande salt was traded throughout Brittany tax-free until Napoleon Bonaparte decided to tax it, and a decline set in during the middle of the 19th century.

About half of the surviving megalithic monuments of Loire-Atlantique stand on the peninsula, and the structures date from around 5200–2200 BCE. At the end of the Iron Age the Veneti held the north and the Namnetes the south. Around 848, under Nominoë, the town became the head of a temporary bishopric, and Salomon built a canon college there. In 1343, during the Breton War of Succession, troops of Charles of Blois commanded by Luis de la Cerda took Guérande and plundered it, and about 8,000 inhabitants were reported killed. Charles had twenty-four of the main culprits hanged.

The war ended in the first Treaty of Guérande, concluded before the high altar of Saint-Aubin on Holy Saturday in 1365, when Joanna of Penthièvre gave up her claims to the duchy in favour of John V of the House of Montfort. The second Treaty of Guérande (1381), between Duke John V and King Charles VI of France, established Brittany's neutrality in the Anglo-French conflict. John IV had meanwhile ordered the fortifications improved, and the ramparts, begun soon after the sack, were inaugurated in 1488 under Duke Francis II, father of Anne of Brittany.

The old walled town is enclosed by almost intact ramparts 1,434 metres long, with ten towers and four fortified gates, the largest being the 15th-century Porte Saint-Michel. They were listed as a historic monument in 1877. The collegiate church of Saint-Aubin, rebuilt around 1200 and extended in the 15th and 16th centuries, is one of the main sights. Guérande is the traditional source of fleur de sel, and its marshes have been on the Ramsar list of protected wetlands since 1971. Since 2004 the town has belonged to the national network of Villes et Pays d'Art et d'Histoire.
gueret: Guéret, called Garait in Occitan, is the largest town in the Creuse department and a light industrial town. It has a big woodland and some farming not far from the town centre. It lies approximately 80 kilometres by road northeast of Limoges, at the junction of the D942, D940 and N145 roads. The climate is oceanic, influenced by its elevation and by the Gulf Stream air that reaches it from the Bay of Biscay, and is mild for its latitude, wet and relatively gloomy.

The town grew up round an abbey founded in the 7th century, and in later times it became the capital of the County of La Marche. Buildings that survive show its later centuries. The Presidial, dating from the seventeenth century, houses the town hall. The Hotel de Moneyroux, a building in the Gothic style, is incorrectly called the Castle of the Counts of Marche, since no count ever lived in Guéret; it now houses the General Council of the Creuse.

The Museum of the Sénatorerie was partly built in the eighteenth century and served as the residence of senators under Napoleon. Since 1832 it has housed the Society of Archaeological and Natural Sciences of the Creuse, one of the oldest learned societies of France, which brings together natural history collections and works of art.

The church of St Pierre and St Paul dates from the thirteenth century. South of the town lie the artificial Courtille lake, about 3 kilometres round and used for sports and leisure, and the large Chabrières forest. The forest holds a zoo opened in 2001 where wolves live in large enclosures, some great natural monoliths linked to local myths, such as the Pierre Grole, and old granite quarries once used mainly for the cobblestones of Paris streets.
The historian Antoine Varillas was born in Guéret in 1624, and the writer Marcel Jouhandeau in 1888. The town is twinned with Stein in Bavaria, Germany, since 1991, and with Puck in Poland.
guernica: Guernica, officially Gernika, is part of the municipality of Gernika-Lumo in the province of Biscay, in the region of Busturialdea, in the valley of the Oka River, whose estuary lies at its mouth. Tello Alfonso, Lord of Biscay, founded the town on 28 April 1366, at the crossing of the road from Bermeo to Durango with that from Bilbao to Elantxobe and Lekeitio. A river estuary where vessels could dock at the port of Suso added to the site's strategic importance. It took the typical Basque form of parallel streets, with a church at each end of the built-up area.

Each administrative district of Biscay had its appointed tree for assemblies, but the Tree of Guernica gained particular importance. The laws of Biscay were drawn up beneath it until 1876, with each town and village sending two representatives to the General Assemblies. When the Domain of Biscay was incorporated into Castile, the king visited and swore an oath beneath the tree to uphold the fueros, or local laws. King Ferdinand's oath of 30 June 1476 is depicted in a painting by Francisco de Mendieta, and the pretender Don Carlos swore it on 3 July 1875. By 1512 the oak, the Gernikako Arbola, symbolized the traditional rights of the Basque people as a whole. The current assembly house was built in 1826.

The parishes of Guernica and Lumo quarrelled over land until 1882, when they joined as Gernika-Lumo. The town grew from 4,500 inhabitants in 1920 to around 7,000 in 1936. On 26 April 1937, during the Spanish Civil War, the Condor Legion of Nazi Germany and the Italian Aviazione Legionaria bombed the town at the request of Francisco Franco, for about three hours. According to official Basque figures, 1,654 civilians were killed. The town was devastated, though the assembly house and the oak survived. The attack is considered the beginning of the Luftwaffe doctrine of terror bombing of civilian targets. Pablo Picasso painted Guernica to commemorate it, and it also inspired poems by Paul Eluard and a 1950 short film by Alain Resnais.

In 1987 the town hosted the preliminary congress of the World Association of Martyr Cities. Eduardo Chillida's monument Gure Aitaren Etxea was set up in 1988, and Henry Moore's Large Figure in a Shelter beside it in 1990, as symbols of peace. Gernika-Lumo is twinned with Berga, Pforzheim and Boise, Idaho.

A Monday market has long been a tradition, and the saying lunes gerniqués, golperik ez, roughly that not a stroke of work gets done on Mondays, reflects it. The jai alai court, designed by Secundino Zuano and opened in 1963, is described as the biggest operational court of its type in the world.
guerrero: Guerrero is mountainous and rugged, with flat land limited to small mesas and the Pacific coastline. It covers 63,794 km2 and has three regions: La Montaña in the north and east, Tierra Caliente in the lowlands along the Balsas River, and La Costa, divided into the Costa Chica, which runs from Acapulco to the border with Oaxaca, and the Costa Grande, which extends west of Acapulco to the Balsas. The coast has long mattered economically, first through the port of Acapulco in the colonial and post-independence eras.

The first people inhabited caves about 20,000 years ago. Scholars debate whether the earliest civilizations were Olmecs who migrated there or native peoples heavily influenced by them; Olmec influence appears in cave paintings at Juxtlahuaca and Cacahuaziziqui. The last Aztec emperor, Cuauhtémoc, came from Ixcateopan. After the fall of Tenochtitlan the peoples of the area offered little resistance to the Spanish, and some, such as the Amuzgos, sided with them.

In the War of Independence the peoples of the territory supported Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla, and José María Morelos fought in the south. The insurgents never took Acapulco, but Morelos took Chilpancingo and convened the Congress of Anáhuac, which issued the Sentimentos de la Nación on 6 November 1813. The Mexican flag was designed and first sewn at Iguala after Agustín de Iturbide and Vicente Guerrero joined forces under the Plan of Iguala in 1821. The modern state did not exist until 1849, when it was carved from the states of Mexico, Puebla and Michoacán; it is the only Mexican state named after a president.

Guerrero has about 3.5 million people. Its capital is Chilpancingo and its largest city Acapulco. Nahuas, Mixtecs, Tlapanecs and Amuzgos live there, with Afro-Mexican communities in the Costa Chica, and over 20 indigenous languages are spoken. Taxco is the centre of the silversmiths' craft.
guerrilla-warfare: The Spanish word guerrilla means little war. It became popular in the Peninsular War of the early 19th century, when Spanish and Portuguese people rose against Napoleonic troops after their regular armies had been beaten, combining guerrilla methods with scorched earth. Arthur Wellesley took the word into English in 1809. The methods are far older. Sun Tzu proposed guerrilla-style tactics in The Art of War, the Roman general Quintus Fabius Maximus used evasion and ambush against Hannibal, and in China Peng Yue raided Chu convoys during the Chu-Han contention. Classical Greeks looked down on such warfare and preferred decisive battles in the open.

Byzantine commanders practised it along the eastern frontier between the eighth and tenth centuries, and a later tenth-century manual, De velitatione bellica, set it down. In the 17th century Shivaji, founder of the Maratha Kingdom, used guerrilla tactics against the much larger armies of the Mughal Empire.

Guerrilla warfare is unconventional warfare in which small irregular groups use ambushes, sabotage and raids against regular forces. Guerrillas avoid head-on battle, usually because their arms or numbers are inferior, and fight limited skirmishes meant to exhaust the opponent and force a withdrawal. They depend on intelligence, on terrain, and above all on the support of the local population or of foreign backers. Rural guerrillas favour forests and mountains, while urban ones blend into the population. Organisations often have political and military wings, and the Chinese and Vietnamese communists elaborated the fullest structure.

Theory followed practice. Matías Ramón Mella wrote a Guerrilla Warfare Manual in 1864. T. E. Lawrence concluded in Seven Pillars of Wisdom that Arab warriors could not defeat the Turks in pitched battle. Mao Zedong divided a people's war into three phases: winning the population's support, escalating attacks on the government's forces, and finally conventional war to seize the cities. Võ Nguyên Giáp applied this in Vietnam. Che Guevara, after the Cuban Revolution, argued in his foco theory that small mobile groups could focus popular discontent and bring about a general insurrection.

Examples from the 20th century include the Irish War of Independence of 1919–1921, where Michael Collins developed urban tactics in Dublin and Tom Barry led rural flying columns in County Cork, and the Algerian Revolution, which began in 1954 with a handful of guerrillas and lasted over eight years. The 1977 First Additional Protocol to the Geneva Conventions recognises combatants who do not wear uniforms if they carry arms openly during military operations.
guglielmo-embriaco: Guglielmo Embriaco, whose name in English means William the Drunkard, gained fame only when he and his brother Primo di Castello landed at Jaffa in June 1099 with a squadron of galleys: two according to the Annales of Caffaro di Rustico, six or nine according to Raymond of Aguilers. The expedition was a private undertaking. An Egyptian army turned the brothers from their march towards Ascalon inland to the Siege of Jerusalem, where he earned the nickname Caputmallei or Testadimaglio, mallet head.

After the fall of Jerusalem on 15 July 1099 he commanded a naval contingent offshore at the Battle of Ascalon on 12 August. He and Primo then returned to Genoa with letters from Godfrey of Bouillon and Daimbert of Pisa describing the crusaders' success and the need for reinforcements, arriving on 24 December. The Compagna made him consul of the Genoese army and sent him back with a fleet of twenty-six or twenty-seven galleys and three to four thousand men; he sailed on 1 August 1100, carrying the new papal legate, the cardinal-bishop of Ostia.

At Laodicea he met King Baldwin I of Jerusalem, wintered there and fought skirmishes with Saracen corsairs. In March 1101 he slipped past a large Egyptian fleet near Haifa and landed at Jaffa on Easter Monday. Promised a third of the booty, the Genoese marched on Arsuf, which fell after three days on 9 May, while Caesarea held out until 17 May. A thousand Arab merchants who had taken refuge in its mosque paid the Genoese for their release.

After making a treaty with Tancred, Prince of Galilee, Embriaco sailed home in July 1101, met a Byzantine fleet in the Ionian Islands and sent ambassadors to Constantinople from Corfu. He entered Genoa in triumph in October. He was elected consul in February 1102, the last recorded trace of him. For his part at Jerusalem he was remembered as a liberator of the Holy Sepulchre, and he is considered one of the founders of what became the Republic of Genoa.
guglielmo-gonzaga-duke-of-mantua: Guglielmo Gonzaga was born on 24 April 1538, the second son of Federico II Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua, and Margaret Palaeologina of Montferrat. He ruled Mantua from 1550 to 1587. In 1574 Montferrat was elevated to a duchy and he became its first duke, holding it until his death.

Guglielmo was particularly interested in sacred vocal music, and music historians know him above all for his extensive correspondence with the composer Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina. He built a large new church in Mantua dedicated to Santa Barbara, engaged in an unprecedented negotiation with the Papacy to create his own rite for Mantua, and devoted considerable resources to developing a musical repertoire for the church, commissioning works from Giaches de Wert and Palestrina.

Part of his correspondence with Palestrina discusses the commissioned work in detail and states Guglielmo's requirements, which gives a sense of his tastes. His tastes were conservative for the day. He enjoyed imitative contrapuntal music but wanted the text to remain clear, which shows the influence of the Tridentine reforms. After his death his son Vincenzo invited followers of the more modern trends to his court. Three months before his death Guglielmo wounded Ruggier Trofeo, the organist of the ducal basilica, in an encounter over a woman; Trofeo survived.

On 26 April 1561 Guglielmo married Eleonora of Austria, the sixth daughter of Emperor Ferdinand I and Anna of Bohemia and Hungary. Their son Vincenzo I (1562–1612) married Eleonora de' Medici, their daughter Margherita Barbara (1564–1618) married Alfonso II d'Este, and their daughter Anna Caterina (1566–1621) married her maternal uncle Ferdinand II, Archduke of Austria. Guglielmo died on 14 August 1587 and was succeeded as duke of both duchies by Vincenzo.
guglielmo-marconi: Guglielmo Marconi was born on 25 April 1874 in Bologna, the son of Giuseppe Marconi, an Italian landowner, and his second wife, Annie Jameson, a granddaughter of the founder of Jameson Irish Whiskey. Between the ages of two and six he lived in Bedford, England. He had no formal schooling and learned chemistry, mathematics and physics from private tutors. At 18 he met Augusto Righi, a professor of physics at the University of Bologna, who let him attend lectures and use the university's laboratory and library.

At 20 Marconi began experiments with radio waves, building much of his equipment in the attic of the Villa Griffone at Pontecchio. At Righi's suggestion he used a coherer, a detector that changed resistance when exposed to radio waves. In the summer of 1895 he found that raising the antenna and grounding the transmitter and receiver gave a much greater range, about 3.2 kilometres over hills. After a demonstration for the British government in July 1896 he sent Morse signals across Salisbury Plain, and on 13 May 1897 sent the first wireless message over open sea, across the Bristol Channel. He founded The Wireless Telegraph & Signal Company, later the Marconi Company, in 1897.

The reported reception at Signal Hill in 1901 met scepticism then and since: the signals were faint, there was no independent confirmation, and the daytime path was a poor choice for the wavelength used. The sinking of the Titanic on 15 April 1912 showed the value of wireless and brought Marconi fame. He became an Italian senator in 1914 and a marquess in 1929, joined the National Fascist Party in 1923, and defended the invasion of Ethiopia in 1935.

Marconi died in Rome on 20 July 1937, aged 63, after nine heart attacks in three years. At the hour of his funeral transmitters around the world observed two minutes of silence. His remains lie in a mausoleum at Sasso Marconi, beside his former villa, now a museum. On 21 June 1943 the Supreme Court of the United States held the broad claims of one of his patents invalid, because earlier patents of Oliver Lodge, John Stone Stone and Nikola Tesla anticipated them.
guiana-space-centre: The centre lies north-west of Kourou, about 500 km north of the equator at a latitude of 5°. Its position brings two advantages. Launching towards the east takes advantage of the Earth's rotation, and a near-equatorial site requires substantially less energy to reach geostationary orbit; rockets can be launched into orbits with an inclination as low as 6°, whereas from Cape Canaveral, at 28.5°, the inclination is fixed at 28.5° unless propellant is spent changing it. Open sea to the east and north also reduces the risk that rocket stages or debris from a failed launch fall near human settlements. The Ariane 5 could send more than 10,000 kg to geostationary transfer orbit from Kourou, against 6,270 kg for the Proton launched from Russia.

In 1964 Guiana was chosen to become the spaceport of France, replacing the launch site at Hammaguir in Algeria after the independence of Algeria. In 1975 France offered to share Kourou with the European Space Agency, which pays two thirds of the annual budget and financed the upgrades made as the Ariane launchers developed. The land is managed by the French agency CNES. A pad for the Diamant rocket was built in 1969, and on 10 March 1970 a Diamant-B launched the first satellites from Kourou. It was decommissioned in 1975.

A pad built in the 1960s for the Europa-II rocket saw one failed launch in 1971 before that programme was cancelled; it was rebuilt as the first Ariane complex, used for Ariane 1, 2 and 3 until 1989, and refurbished for the Vega rocket, which first flew on 13 February 2012. ELA-2 served Ariane 4 from 1988 until 2003. ELA-3 launched the Ariane 5 from 4 June 1996 until 5 July 2023, and among its payloads was the James Webb Space Telescope on 25 December 2021. ELA-4 was built for the Ariane 6, which first flew on 9 July 2024.

ESA built a separate complex, ELS, for Russian Soyuz rockets, with the first launch on 21 October 2011 carrying two Galileo satellites. The centre also contains the Îles du Salut, a former penal colony that includes Devil's Island; the islands lie under the launch trajectory for geosynchronous orbit and are evacuated during launches. Fire safety is provided by a detachment of the Paris Fire Brigade, and security by the French Gendarmerie assisted by the 3rd Foreign Infantry Regiment of the Foreign Legion.
guianas: The Guianas, also spelled Guyanas or Guayanas, are a region of north-eastern South America. In the broad sense the term covers the coast from the mouth of the Orinoco to the mouth of the Amazon: the former Spanish or Venezuelan Guiana, British Guiana (now Guyana), Dutch Guiana (now Suriname), French Guiana and the former Portuguese or Brazilian Guiana, now the state of Amapá in Brazil. In contemporary use the term usually means Guyana, Suriname and French Guiana. Dense jungle in the south leaves the population concentrated along the coast.

Before European colonisation the Guianas were inhabited by scattered Lokono bands and by Kalinago, whose cultures had blended so far that the two peoples were almost indistinguishable to outsiders. Columbus first sighted the coast in 1498, and real interest began only at the end of the sixteenth century, when it became known as the Wild Coast. Walter Raleigh began the exploration in earnest in 1594, searching for the city of Manoa, the seat of the king known as El Dorado. His Discoverie of the Large, Rich, and Bewtiful Empyre of Guiana was published in 1596.

The Dutch, concerned more with trading outposts than with conquering territory, expanded their colonies under the Dutch West India Company, established in 1621. The English founded a larger settlement in what is now Suriname in 1650. French attempts failed repeatedly, and in 1645 only two survivors of the settlers near Cayenne reached the Dutch settlement on the Pomeroon. The Treaty of Breda of 1667 let the Dutch keep the sugar plantations of Suriname; during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries all the coastal colonies were converted to sugar plantations.

Wars among the British, Dutch and French continued until the Convention of London of 1814, which favoured the British. The Dutch lost Berbice, Essequibo and Demerara, which were united under one British administration and called British Guiana after 1831, while the Dutch kept Suriname. Guyana became independent in 1966 and Suriname in 1975, and French Guiana is an overseas department and region of France. The population descends from Indigenous peoples, enslaved West Africans, Maroons, indentured labourers from India and Java, and Chinese and Portuguese settlers.
guidobaldo-ii-della-rovere: Guidobaldo was born on 2 April 1514, the son of Francesco Maria I della Rovere, Duke of Urbino, and Eleonora Gonzaga, and belonged to the House of La Rovere. In 1535, defying a papal ban, he married Giulia da Varano, daughter of the Duke of Camerino and Caterina Cybo. Pope Paul III answered by excommunicating Guidobaldo, his bride and his mother-in-law, and when Guidobaldo was installed as Duke of Camerino the pope placed the duchy under interdict. He became Duke of Urbino in 1538 on the assassination of his father. With Giulia he had a daughter, Virginia, who married Frederico Borromeo.

Like his father, a commander for the Republic of Venice in the Italian Wars, Guidobaldo was a condottiero, and in 1546 Venice gave him a condotta as its military governor. The armourer and artist Bartolomeo Campi made him a suit of armour. After Giulia's death in 1548 he married Vittoria Farnese, daughter of Pier Luigi Farnese, Duke of Parma, and Gerolama Orsini. He was later papal governor of Fano, captain general of the Papal States and Prefect of Rome. In 1559 he entered the service of the King of Spain, helping his son-in-law, a Sanseverino married to his daughter Isabella, in the war against the Ottoman Turks.
