On 1 January 1573 Urbino rose against the heavy taxes he laid on his state, and he put the revolt down with bloodshed. He fell ill on a journey to Ferrara and Pesaro and died at Pesaro on 28 September 1574. His son by Vittoria, Francesco Maria II, who married Lucrezia d'Este, succeeded him as duke, and Vittoria's daughter Lavinia married Alfonso Félix de Ávalos, Marquis del Vasto. Besides the Venus of Urbino, Guidobaldo commissioned his own portrait from Titian.
guild: The word derives from medieval Europe, where guilds were probably at their most extensive, but it has been used for similar groups before and after that period and in other parts of the world. Naram-Sin of Akkad, grandson of Sargon of Akkad, promulgated common Mesopotamian standards for length, area, volume, weight, time and shekels, which artisan guilds used in each city. Laws 234, 275, 276 and 277 of the Code of Hammurabi, from about 1755–1750 BCE, set wages and freight rates in contracts between shipbuilders, shipowners, charterers and shipmasters.

In ancient Rome a collegium or corpus was any association that acted as a legal entity, and many were voluntary groups of merchants specialising in a craft. One example is the corpus naviculariorum, a collegium of merchant mariners at the port of Ostia. The Roman guilds did not survive the collapse of the Roman Empire.

Evolving from earlier fraternities for protective or religious purposes, merchant and craft guilds became structured organisations that regulated trade, upheld quality and protected members' economic interests, and grew more common across Europe during the High Middle Ages. Craft guilds transmitted skills through apprenticeship, journeymanship and mastery. Their authority rested on charters or letters patent granting monopolies on production in their locality. Key privileges included control of trade in a city, and rules might cover prices, hours of trading and numbers of apprentices. In Florence, Paris, Barcelona and the German free cities guilds were central to economic and civic life, and many exercised influence in municipal governments, sometimes challenging patrician elites.

They also kept welfare funds for sick or elderly members, supported widows and orphans, organised feasts and reinforced communal religious life. Most were male-dominated and admitted women mainly as wives, widows or daughters of masters, though Étienne Boileau's Livre des métiers records several Parisian guilds as female monopolies. In Rouen women were full masters in 7 of the city's 112 guilds.

Critics argued that guild rules reduced free competition, while defenders held that they protected professional standards. Enlightenment thinkers such as Adam Smith argued that guild monopolies inhibited trade and innovation. The French Revolution abolished guilds in 1791, and most European countries followed during the 18th and 19th centuries as industrialisation made guild production less viable.

Comparable bodies existed elsewhere: the śreṇi of ancient and early medieval India, the Akhiya fraternities of the Ottoman Empire, the gongsuo of late-imperial China, the za and later kabunakama of Japan, the pochteca merchants of the Aztec Empire and the Igun guilds of artists in the Benin Kingdom. In London the medieval guilds survive as livery companies with ceremonial and charitable roles, and professional associations in law, medicine and academia have been compared to guilds.
guilford-connecticut: Before European settlement the land was the site of Menunkatuck, a Quinnipiac village. The Quinnipiac spoke Quiripi, one of the Eastern Algonquian branches of the Algonquian language family. By 1614 the Dutch had charted New Netherland, with claims over Quinnipiac territory, but they had no significant presence there; the claims lasted until the Treaty of Westminster of 1674. In June 1637, during the Pequot War, 100 English soldiers and Narragansett, Mohegan and Montauk allies arrived from Long Island in pursuit of the Pequot grand sachem Sassacus, and at Sachems Head they captured and executed three Pequot sachems.

In 1639 a group of 24 English Puritan families led by Rev. Henry Whitfield, after landing at the plantation of Quinnipiaic, later New Haven, chose to settle about 13 miles away near Menunkatuck. During the voyage they signed the Plantation Covenant on 1 June 1639 (O.S.), and on 29 September 1639 (O.S.) they obtained a land grant from Shaumpishuh, the female sachem of Menunkatuck.

The settlement first shared the name Menunkatuck. On 6 July 1643 (O.S.) the records of the General Court at New Haven note that the name had changed to Guilforde, with no reason recorded; it is assumed to refer to Guildford in England, the home of some of the first settlers. In 1664 the New Haven Colony, including Guilford, joined the Connecticut Colony. In June 1781, during the American Revolution, a skirmish was fought on Leete's Island between the Associated Loyalists and local militia.

Guilford lies on Interstate 95 and the Connecticut coast, and borders Madison, Branford, North Branford and Durham. Some count its historic homes as the third largest collection in New England. There are five historic house museums, including Dudley Farm and the Henry Whitfield House, built in 1639, the oldest dwelling house in Connecticut and the oldest stone house built by English settlers in North America. The Comfort Starr House of 1695 is one of the oldest wooden framed private dwellings in the state. In 1981 the Guilford Preservation Alliance identified 450 buildings of architectural significance.
guillaume-farel: Farel was born in 1489 at Gap in the French province of Dauphiné, the son of Antoine Farel, a papal notary, and Anastasie d'Orcières. He moved to Paris in 1509 and studied with pro-reform Catholic clergy at the University of Paris. There he met the humanist scholar Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, who helped him obtain a professorship of grammar and philosophy at the Collège du Cardinal Lemoine.

With Lefèvre he joined the Cercle de Meaux, gathered from 1519 by the reform-minded bishop Guillaume Briçonnet, and by 1522 the bishop had appointed him a diocesan preacher. The circle emphasized the study of the Bible and a return to the theology of the early Church. Farel came under the influence of Lutheran ideas there and, after condemnation by the Sorbonne, evangelized in the Dauphiné.

Writings against the use of images in worship forced Farel to flee to Switzerland. In 1524, in Basel, he wrote thirteen theses sharply criticizing Roman doctrine, and the argument was so heated that even Erasmus joined in the demand for his expulsion. He went on to Strasbourg and Montbéliard, then to Zürich to Huldrych Zwingli, to Metz, and back to Strasbourg, where he met Martin Bucer. He preached through Vaud, in Aigle, Lausanne, Orbe, Grandson and Yverdon, and Neuchâtel adhered to the Reformation in 1530. At the Synod of Chanforan in 1532 he took part in the discussions that led the Waldensians to merge with the Reformation.

Farel began preaching in Geneva in 1532 under the protection of Bern. After a hostile reception he gained followers, and the General Council adopted the Reformation. In 1536 he persuaded John Calvin, who was passing through, to stay. In 1538 Farel and Calvin were banished after conflict with the city's government over the authority of Church and State, and Farel settled in Neuchâtel as its first pastor for the rest of his life. He returned to Geneva after Calvin did in 1541. In 1558, aged 69, he married the 18-year-old Marie Thorel; Calvin refused to bless the marriage. He died in Neuchâtel on 13 September 1565.

Martin Bucer named Farel, with Calvin and Pierre Viret, one of the triumvirate of the Francophone Reformation. In 1533 he installed the first fully Reformed printer, Pierre de Vingle, in Neuchâtel. He published around fifteen works, all in French, among them the first French-language work of the Reformation, Le Pater noster et le Credo en françoys of 1524, and the first systematic exposition of Reformed doctrine in French, of 1529. His doctrine was Christocentric, and on the Last Supper he stressed, like Zwingli, that the bread and wine signify the body and blood of the Lord. A monument to him was unveiled at Neuchâtel on 4 May 1876.
guillaume-henri-dufour: Guillaume Henri Dufour was born on 15 September 1787 in Konstanz, where his parents, from Geneva, were living in exile for their part in the Revolution of 1782. The family returned to Geneva when he was two. In 1807 he went to Paris to join the École Polytechnique, graduated fifth in his class in 1809 and studied military engineering at Metz. In 1811 he joined the French Army and was sent to defend Corfu, where he mapped the old fortifications, and he was wounded in a naval battle against the British in June 1813. In 1817 he resumed Swiss citizenship and returned to Geneva.

From 1819 to 1830 Dufour was chief instructor at the military school of Thun, which he had largely brought into being. As state engineer of Geneva he arranged the first steamboat on Lake Geneva and introduced gas streetlights, and his Saint Antoine Bridge, designed in late 1822, became the first permanent wire-cable suspension bridge in the world. After he became chief of staff in 1831 the Federal Diet commissioned him to direct a trigonometrical survey of Switzerland. His Topographic Map of Switzerland, in 25 sheets at 1:100,000, appeared between 1842 and 1865.

The Federal Diet appointed him General on 21 October 1847. He led a federal army of 100,000 against the Catholic Sonderbund under Johann-Ulrich von Salis-Soglio in a campaign from 3 to 29 November that claimed fewer than a hundred lives. He ordered his troops to spare the wounded and sent an emissary to Fribourg urging surrender to avoid a battle. He was named General again in 1849, 1856 and 1859.

Dufour's moderation after the Sonderbund War prevented intervention by foreign powers and laid a basis of reconciliation that let the cantons agree on a federal state in 1848. In 1863 he sat on the committee with Gustave Moynier, Henry Dunant, Louis Appia and Théodore Maunoir that took up Dunant's idea of a voluntary relief society for the wounded, which led to the Red Cross, and in 1864 he presided over the conference that framed the First Geneva Convention.

He died on 14 July 1875, and 60,000 people attended his burial in Geneva, where an equestrian statue of 1884 also stands. The Dufourspitze, the highest mountain in Switzerland, was named for his cartography.
guillermo-endara: Guillermo Endara was born in Panama City on 12 May 1936. His father was an ally of Arnulfo Arias, founder of the Authentic Panameñista Party, and the family went into exile after Arias was overthrown in 1941. Endara studied in Argentina and the United States, then at the University of Panama Law School, and returned in 1963 to practise labour law. He served two terms in the National Assembly and in 1968 was minister of planning and economic policy in Arias's brief third government. When Arias was overthrown again that October, Endara went underground, was jailed briefly in 1971 and joined Arias in exile until 1977.

After Arias died in 1988, Endara became a leading opponent of the military ruler Manuel Noriega. In the 1989 presidential election he headed the Democratic Alliance of Civic Opposition against Noriega's candidate, Carlos Duque. The opposition's own count showed Endara ahead by nearly three to one, and observers led by former US President Jimmy Carter agreed that he had won decisively. Noriega annulled the results, citing foreign interference. The next day Endara and his running mates were beaten by the paramilitary Dignity Battalions, and images of the attacks were credited with building US public support for the invasion that followed.

The United States invaded Panama in December 1989, and Endara was sworn in at Fort Clayton, a US base, on 20 December. He had opposed US military action during his campaign, but said later that he had no other choice. He purged Noriega loyalists from the Panamanian Defense Forces and turned them into a national police, and in October 1994 the National Assembly, at his urging, passed an amendment abolishing the military. His term brought economic recovery, with growth of about 8 per cent a year on average, though unemployment rose to nearly 19 per cent. He was succeeded in 1994 by Ernesto Pérez Balladares.

Endara ran again for president in 2004, finishing second behind Martín Torrijos, and in 2009, when Ricardo Martinelli won. He died of a heart attack at his apartment in Panama City on 28 September 2009, at the age of 73, and was given a state funeral on 30 September.
guimaraes: Guimarães lies in the historical province of Minho in northern Portugal, in a valley surrounded by hills at some distance from the sea. The Ave river divides the municipality in half, and the Monte da Penha to the south is its highest point, at 613 m.

The city was settled in the 9th century under the name Vimaranes, which may come from the warrior Vímara Peres, who chose it as the seat of the County of Portugal, which he conquered for the Kingdom of Galicia. The medieval foundations of the present city date from the 10th century. The Countess Mumadona Dias built a monastery on her property of Vimaranes, which drew settlers to the area called the vila baixa, or downtown. She also ordered a castle on the hill known as the vila alta, or uptown, to defend the settlement. Henry, Count of Portugal, approved the first national foral, possibly in 1096, and chose Guimarães as capital of the County of Portugal.

In 1128 events that led to Portuguese independence took place in the city. On 24 June of that year the Battle of São Mamede, regarded as the seminal event for the foundation of the Kingdom of Portugal, was fought in its vicinity. Afonso Henriques, Portugal's first king, was born in Guimarães,.

Under King Denis the expanding town was partly surrounded by a wall, and under John I the wall was torn down and the uptown and downtown were united. A notable Jewish community lived around the present Praça do Peixe. After the decree of King Manuel I in 1496 requiring all Jews to convert or leave Portugal, some of its members became Marranos, and public Jewish life ended after the Inquisition. Queen Maria II promoted the town to a city on 23 June 1853.

Guimarães is a city and municipality of northern Portugal and the capital of the Ave Subregion, one of the most industrialised in the country. Its historic centre has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2001. The city is called the birthplace of Portugal, and its main festivities are the Nicolinas, held in honour of Saint Nicholas.
guinea: Guinea is a coastal country in West Africa, roughly the size of the United Kingdom, with 320 kilometres of coastline. It forms a crescent curving from the southeast to the north and west. It is divided into four regions: Maritime Guinea on the Atlantic coast, populated mainly by the Susu; the cooler, mountainous Fouta Djallon in the middle, populated by the Fula; Upper Guinea, a Sahelian region in the northeast, populated by the Malinké; and the forested southeast with several ethnic groups. The Guinea Highlands are the source of the Niger, the Gambia and the Senegal rivers, and the highest point is Mount Nimba at 1,752 metres.

The country is named after the Guinea region along the Gulf of Guinea. The English term comes from the Portuguese word Guiné, which emerged in the mid-15th century for the lands of the Guineus, a generic term for the African peoples south of the Senegal River. In 1978 the official name became the People's Revolutionary Republic of Guinea, and in 1984, after the death of the first president, Ahmed Sékou Touré, it was renamed the Republic of Guinea.

What is now Guinea sat on the fringes of various West African empires. The Ghana Empire grew on trade and fell after repeated incursions by the Almoravids, and Islam first arrived in the region in this period through North African traders. The Sosso Empire held the area in the 12th and 13th centuries. The Mali Empire followed after Soundiata Kéïta defeated the Sosso ruler Soumangourou Kanté at the Battle of Kirina, c. 1235. Its rulers included Kankou Moussa, who made a hajj to Mecca in 1324. After his reign it declined and was supplanted by its vassal states in the 15th century.

The Songhai Empire expanded its power from about 1460 and fell to invaders from Morocco in 1591. Fulani Muslims migrated to Futa Jallon in central Guinea and established an Islamic state from 1727 to 1896, with a written constitution and alternating rulers. The Wassoulou Empire, led by Samori Toure from 1878 to 1898 in the Malinké area of upper Guinea and southwestern Mali, moved to Ivory Coast before the French occupied it. France claimed the territory in the 1890s as part of French West Africa, and Guinea declared independence on 2 October 1958.

Guinea is the Republic of Guinea, with its capital and largest city at Conakry. French is the language of schools and administration, and more than 24 indigenous languages are spoken, the largest being Susu, Pular and Maninka. Most of the population is Muslim. Guinea has large reserves of bauxite, and the Nimba Massif is a UNESCO strict nature reserve on the Guinean and Ivorian sides.
guinea-bissau: Guinea-Bissau lies on the West African coast, bordered by Senegal to the north, Guinea to the south and east and the Atlantic Ocean to the west. Its area of 36,125 square kilometres is larger than Belgium's. The terrain is mostly low coastal plains with Guinean mangrove swamps, rising to a forest and savannah mosaic in the east, and the highest point is Monte Torin at 262 metres. The Bijagós Archipelago of 88 islands and islets lies off the mainland. A rainy season from June to September or October alternates with a dry season, and from December through April the country experiences drought.

The ancient history of the area is poorly understood. The earliest inhabitants were the Jola, Papel, Manjak, Balanta and Biafada peoples, and the Mandinka and Fulani migrated into the region in the 13th and 15th centuries, pushing the earlier inhabitants toward the coast and onto the Bijagós islands. The Balanta and Jola had weak or non-existent kingship and placed power in the heads of villages and families, whereas the chiefs of the Mandinka, Fula, Papel, Manjak and Biafada were vassals to kings. Trade was widespread between groups in pepper and kola nuts, iron utensils, salt and dried fish, and Mandinka cotton cloth.

The Biafada lived in three kingdoms, Biguba, Guinala and Bissege, and were subjects of the Mandinka mansa of Kaabu. According to oral tradition the Kingdom of Bissau was founded by a son of the king of Quinara. It defended its sovereignty against Portuguese 'Pacification Campaigns', defeating them in 1891, 1894 and 1904, but was fully absorbed in 1915 by the Portuguese under Officer Teixeira Pinto and the warlord Abdul Injai. On the Bijagós Islands, Bijago society was warlike: men built boats and raided the mainland and other islands, while women cultivated the land and built houses.

Guinea-Bissau is the Republic of Guinea-Bissau. Its capital, Bissau, was added to its name after independence, declared in 1973 and recognised in 1974, to prevent confusion with Guinea. Portuguese is the official language, and Guinea-Bissau Creole is the national language. The music most associated with the country is the polyrhythmic gumbe, and the film director Flora Gomes made Mortu Nega in 1988, the first fiction film made there.
guizhou: Guizhou is an inland province of south-western China on the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau, with an average altitude of about 1,100 metres. Its capital and largest city, Guiyang, lies in the centre. More than 60 per cent of the province is mountains and another 31 per cent hills, leaving very little flat land. A saying holds that sunny weather never lasts more than three days and flat ground never continues for more than three miles. Its rivers lie in the upper reaches of the Yangtze and Pearl River basins.

Stone artefacts found at Guanyindong Cave show that humans lived in the area between about 170,000 and 80,000 years ago. The area was first organised as an administrative region of a Chinese empire under the Tang, when it was named Juzhou. In the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty the character ju, meaning a carpenter's square, was changed to gui, meaning precious. The region formally became a province in 1413 under the Ming dynasty. In 1832 the population was estimated at five million.

During the Long March of 1934 and 1935 the Chinese Communist Party took refuge in the province. The People's Liberation Army took Guiyang on 15 November 1949, and the People's Government of Guizhou Province was established on 26 December. Mao Zedong later promoted the relocation of heavy industry to inland provinces such as Guizhou, to protect it from possible foreign attack.

Guizhou is one of China's most diverse provinces: minority groups make up more than 37 per cent of the population, among them the Miao, Bouyei, Dong, Tujia and Yi, and the main language is Southwestern Mandarin. The Dong people built the covered bridges known as Wind and Rain Bridges. The province is the home of the liquor Moutai.
gujarat: Gujarat lies along the western coast of India and has the longest coastline of any Indian state, most of it on the Kathiawar peninsula. It borders Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and the Arabian Sea, and on the northwest the Pakistani province of Sindh, from which the Rann of Kutch, a seasonally marshy saline clay desert, separates it. Historically the north was known as Anarta, the Kathiawar peninsula as Saurastra and the south as Lata. The name is generally believed to derive from the Gurjars: parts of modern Rajasthan and Gujarat were known as the Gurjarat region for centuries before the Mughal period.

Gujarat was one of the central areas of the Indus Valley Civilisation, and about fifty settlements of that civilisation have been found there, among them Lothal, believed to have been one of the first seaports, Dholavira, one of the largest archaeological sites in India, and Gola Dhoro. Coastal cities, chiefly Bharuch and Khambhat, were ports and trading centres under the Maurya and Gupta empires and the Saka dynasties of the Western Satraps. In the early 8th century the Arabs of the Umayyad Caliphate tried to expand southeast from Sindh; campaigns fought in 730 ended in their defeat, probably by a coalition of Indian rulers.

Qutbuddin Aibak tried and failed to annex Gujarat in 1197. From 1297 to 1300 Alauddin Khalji, Sultan of Delhi, destroyed the city of Anhilwara and brought it into the Delhi Sultanate. After Timur sacked Delhi, the governor Zafar Khan Muzaffar asserted independence, and his son Sultan Ahmed Shah (ruled 1411 to 1442) made Ahmedabad the capital. In 1664 and again in 1672 the Maratha ruler Shivaji attacked Surat. By then the Portuguese, followed by the Dutch and English, had bases on the coast; after the Battle of Diu the Portuguese held enclaves including Daman and Diu until India took them on 19 December 1961.

Gujarat is a state of India with its capital at Gandhinagar, a planned city, and its largest city at Ahmedabad. Gujarati is the official language, and the 2011 census counted 60,439,692 people. Its tradition of seafaring and long-distance trade carried Gujarati merchants to the Persian Gulf, the Horn of Africa and Indonesia. Somnath, the Sun Temple at Modhera, the Jain pilgrimage mountain of Shatrunjaya at Palitana and the Gir forest, the only home of wild Asiatic lions, are among its lasting sites, and Mahatma Gandhi was born at Porbandar.
gulab-singh: Gulab Singh was born in October 1792 into the Hindu Dogra Rajput family that had ruled Jammu since the medieval period. His father was Kishore Singh Jamwal. In 1808, after the battle of Jammu, Ranjit Singh annexed the Dogra kingdom. Gulab Singh joined Ranjit Singh's army in 1809 and earned a jagir worth 12,000 rupees and 90 horses. In 1820 Ranjit Singh gave Jammu as a hereditary fief to Kishore Singh, and in 1821 Gulab Singh captured Rajouri and Kishtwar and took part in the Sikh conquest of Dera Ghazi Khan.

Kishore Singh died in 1822, and Ranjit Singh confirmed Gulab Singh as raja of Jammu, one of the most powerful chiefs of the Sikh Empire, entitled to a personal army of 3 infantry regiments, 15 light artillery guns and 40 garrison guns. In 1837 he was given the task of crushing a revolt in Hazara and Poonch led by Shams ud-Din Khan, who was betrayed and beheaded in his sleep; contemporary British commentators state that the local population suffered immensely.

After Ranjit Singh's death in 1839 Lahore became a centre of intrigue in which the three Jammu brothers were involved. In January 1841 Gulab Singh held the fort against Sher Singh's attempt to seize the throne, and he is said to have taken a large amount of Lahore's treasure to Jammu. When the Sandhawalia Sardars murdered Dhian Singh and Sher Singh in 1842, the Lahore court in 1844 ordered an invasion of Jammu to extract money from him, but he negotiated an indemnity of 27 lakh Nanakshahee rupees.

He sided with the British in the First Anglo-Sikh War and briefly became prime minister of the Sikh court in 1846. The same year he signed the Treaty of Amritsar, which established Jammu and Kashmir under British suzerainty, and the British recognised him as a maharaja tributary to them. In the second Sikh War of 1849 he let his Sikh soldiers desert to fight in Punjab.

Gulab Singh died on 30 June 1857 and was succeeded by his son Ranbir Singh. Diwan Kirpa Ram wrote the first biography, the Gulabnama, in Persian in the 19th century, which K. M. Panikkar called a valuable historical document whose facts and chronology are beyond dispute.
gulag: The Russian Empire already used exile and forced labour as punishment. Katorga, reserved for the most serious crimes, involved confinement and hard labour, though according to the historian Anne Applebaum it was not common: about 6,000 convicts were serving it in 1906. The camps on the Solovetsky Islands in the White Sea, begun soon after the Revolution, were presented as a way of re-educating class enemies through labour. In 1929 the Politburo created a system of self-supporting camps to replace the existing prisons, and the agency that ran them was set up in 1930. Colonising remote regions and exploiting their resources were among its goals.

The population of the camps reached 1.5 million by the end of 1940, and in March 1940 there were 53 camp directorates and 423 labour colonies. Mining and industrial towns such as Karaganda, Norilsk, Vorkuta and Magadan originated as blocks of camps built by prisoners. The camps held ordinary criminals and political prisoners, many convicted by simplified procedures such as NKVD troikas.

Conditions varied with time and place, and were harshest during the famine of 1932–1933, the war and waves of terror. The system grew again after the war, reaching about 2.5 million inmates in prison camps and colonies by the early 1950s, partly because of the tightening of laws on property offences in 1947.

Estimates of the numbers are disputed. Many scholars hold that about 14 million people passed through the camps and 4 million through the colonies between 1930 and 1953, and that roughly 1.5 to 1.7 million died there or soon after release. Orlando Figes gives 25 million prisoners for 1928–1953, and writers who rely on memoirs give higher death tolls.

Archival researchers have found no plan to destroy the prisoners. Soon after Stalin's death a mass amnesty freed non-political prisoners and those serving up to five years, and Nikita Khrushchev's rehabilitations followed. The system was officially abolished on 25 January 1960.

Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, who survived eight years in the camps, gave the term its international reputation with The Gulag Archipelago in 1973, likening the camps to a chain of islands. Released political prisoners often faced discrimination, surveillance and bans on returning to large cities. Memorials made of boulders from Solovki stand in Moscow, on Lubyanka Square, and in St Petersburg, and people gather at them each year on the Day of Victims of the Repression, 30 October.
gulf-coast-of-the-united-states: The Gulf Coast, also called the Gulf South, runs along the shores of the five Gulf States: Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama and Florida. It is a coast of inlets, bays and lagoons cut by many rivers, the largest the Mississippi, and much of it is or was marshland. Barrier islands and peninsulas line the west, among them Padre Island off Texas, 130 miles long; marsh dominates from eastern Texas through Louisiana, and bays and inlets mark the Florida coast. The climate is humid subtropical, and the coast is exposed to hurricanes, floods and severe thunderstorms.

Before Europeans arrived, the peoples of the coast traded widely: shark and alligator teeth and Gulf shells have been found as far north as Ohio, in the mounds of the Hopewell culture. The first European settlers were mainly French and Spanish. The Louisiana Purchase of 1803, the Adams-Onís Treaty of 1819 and the Texas Revolution of 1835-1836 brought the coast into the United States. Sugar and cotton grown by enslaved people made the region rich, and by the mid-19th century New Orleans was the fourth largest city in the country and the largest away from the Atlantic seaboard.

The American Civil War damaged the economy of the South, and the Galveston Hurricane of 1900 struck a city that had the third busiest port in the country. In the 20th century the discovery of oil in Texas and in the Gulf waters made the coast the centre of the American petrochemical industry, while tourism grew from the 1920s. Hurricane Katrina, which struck on 29 August 2005, left over 1,800 dead, and Hurricane Ike in 2008 killed 112 people and left some 300 missing.

The coast's economy rests on energy, petrochemicals, fishing, aerospace, agriculture and tourism, and its marshes are nurseries for the fishing and shrimping industries. Its main cities, from west to east, include Brownsville, Corpus Christi, Houston, Galveston, New Orleans, Biloxi, Mobile, Pensacola, St. Petersburg and Tampa, and the Port of Houston and the Port of South Louisiana handle some of the largest cargo volumes in the world.
gulf-cooperation-council: Sheikh Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah of Kuwait, with the support of Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan of the United Arab Emirates, did much to promote closer cooperation among the Arab states of the Persian Gulf. The charter was signed in Arabic at Abu Dhabi on 21 Rajab 1401 of the Islamic calendar, which corresponds to 25 May 1981. An economic agreement between the six countries followed on 11 November 1981, also at Abu Dhabi. The six signatories remain the only members, and their territories are often called the GCC states. All are monarchies: Qatar, Kuwait and Bahrain are constitutional monarchies, Saudi Arabia and Oman absolute ones, and the United Arab Emirates a federation of seven emirates.

In 2001 the Supreme Council set the goals of a customs union by January 2003, a common market by 2007 and a common currency by 2010. The customs union was begun in 2003 and was fully operational by 1 January 2015, and a common market was launched on 1 January 2008, though implementation lagged after the financial crisis of 2008. The currency plan did not succeed. Oman said in December 2006 that it could not meet the 2010 date, and after the decision to place the central bank in Riyadh the United Arab Emirates and Oman withdrew from the project. On 15 December 2009 Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar and Saudi Arabia announced a Monetary Council, which first met on 30 March 2010.

The Unified Military Command, formerly the Peninsula Shield Force, was formed in 1984. Other joint bodies include a patent office, approved in 1992 and based in Riyadh, which granted its first patent in 2002, and an interconnection grid that began to link the power systems in 2009, by 2013 connecting all six members. Relations within the council have at times been strained. In March 2014 the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Bahrain recalled their ambassadors to Qatar. On 5 June 2017 Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Egypt cut diplomatic ties with Qatar, and the rift ended at the Al-Ula summit on 4 January 2021, after three years and seven months.

The Supreme Council, made up of the heads of state, is the highest decision-making body. Important decisions need unanimous approval, procedural ones a majority, and each state has one vote. The presidency rotates in the Arabic alphabetical order of the states' names. The Ministerial Council of foreign ministers meets every three months and prepares the Supreme Council's meetings. The Secretariat General in Riyadh is the executive arm. The council's emblem shows two concentric circles, with the words Bismillah above and the full name below, and a hexagon for the six countries enclosing a map of the Arabian Peninsula.
gulf-of-aden: The Gulf of Aden is a deepwater gulf of the Indian Ocean. Yemen lies to its north, Djibouti to the west, and the Guardafui Channel, the Socotra Archipelago and Somalia to the south. In the northwest it joins the Red Sea through the Bab-el-Mandeb strait, and to the east it opens onto the Arabian Sea. Tectonic activity at the Aden Ridge along its middle is widening the gulf by about 15 mm a year. The coast supports many isolated fishing towns, and local fishing takes sardines, tuna, kingfish and mackerel.

The ancient Greeks regarded the gulf as one of the most important parts of the Erythraean Sea. In antiquity it was a thriving area of trade between Ptolemaic Egypt and Rome in the west and Classical India, its Indonesian colonies and Han China in the east, and Yemeni incense, tortoiseshell and other goods were in demand in both directions. After Egyptian sailors discovered the monsoon winds and began to trade directly with India, caravan routes and their kingdoms began to collapse, and piracy rose. The 1st-century Periplus of the Erythraean Sea documents one Egyptian captain's experiences in this era.

After the collapse of the Roman economy direct trade ceased, but the Awsan port of Crater, just south of modern Aden, remained an important regional centre. In late antiquity and the early medieval period Ethiopia invaded Yemen several times, and after the rise of Islam the area around the gulf converted to Islam. Abu'l-Fida and, in the 15th century, the navigator Ibn Majid called it the Gulf of Berbera, which shows the importance of Berbera in medieval trade; the port has been prominent since antiquity. The gulf lies on the Suez Canal route, and its importance revived when Egypt reopened the canal in 1975.
gulf-of-aqaba: The gulf, also called the Gulf of Eilat, lies at the northern tip of the Red Sea, southeast of the Sinai Peninsula and west of the Arabian Peninsula. It stretches some 160 kilometres north from the Straits of Tiran and is 24 kilometres wide at its widest point, reaching a maximum depth of 1,850 metres in its central area. Geologically it is one of two gulfs formed where the Sinai Peninsula divides the northern Red Sea, the other being the Gulf of Suez to the west, and it forms the southern end of the Dead Sea Transform. Three small pull-apart basins lie between left-lateral strike-slip faults.

Trade across the Red Sea between Thebes' port of Elim and Elath at the head of the gulf is documented as early as the Fourth Dynasty of Egypt, and expeditions south to Punt are mentioned in several dynasties, among them the eighteenth, when Hatshepsut built a fleet and journeyed to Punt on a six-month voyage. Egyptian settlements near Timna at the head of the gulf date to the Eighteenth Dynasty. At the northern edge the ancient city of Ayla, in present-day Aqaba, was a commercial hub for the Nabateans, and the Romans built the Via Traiana Nova, which joined the King's Highway at Aqaba and connected Africa to Asia and the Levant.

Aqaba was a major Ottoman port, connected to Damascus and Medina by the Hejaz railway. During World War I the Battle of Aqaba, led by Lawrence of Arabia, was the key battle that ended 500 years of Ottoman rule over Syria.

Its coast is divided among Egypt, Israel, Jordan and Saudi Arabia. At its northern end stand Taba in Egypt, Eilat in Israel and Aqaba in Jordan, the largest population centre. The gulf is the only access to the Red Sea for Israel and Jordan, and Jordan's 26 kilometres of shoreline is the only part of its borders that keeps it from being landlocked. Haql is the largest Saudi city on it, and Sharm el-Sheikh and Dahab are the major centres on Sinai. The gulf is a major diving destination, rich in coral and marine life.
gulf-of-corinth: The Gulf of Corinth, Korinthiakós Kólpos in Greek, is bounded in the east by the Isthmus of Corinth, which carries the Corinth Canal built for shipping, and in the west by the Rion Strait, which widens into the shorter Gulf of Patras. Its coasts belong to several regional units: Aetolia-Acarnania and Phocis in the north, Boeotia in the north-east, Attica in the east, Corinthia in the south-east and south, and Achaea in the south-west. In the Middle Ages it was known as the Gulf of Lepanto, the Italian form of Naupactus.

The gulf was created by the expansion of a tectonic rift, caused by the westward movement of the Anatolian Plate, and it is widening by about 10 mm a year. The surrounding faults can produce earthquakes up to a magnitude of about 6.5, though these are relatively uncommon; one of magnitude 6.2 struck near Aigion on 15 June 1995. The northern margin has gentle gradients of 10 to 20 degrees, while the southern margin is mostly steep, at 30 to 40 degrees.

Shipping routes from Piraeus to ports of the western Mediterranean pass along the gulf, and a ferry links Aigio and Agios Nikolaos near its western end. The Rio–Antirrio Bridge has crossed the narrowest point of the Rion Strait since 2004. The main towns on the northern shore include Antirrio, Nafpaktos, Galaxidi and Itea, and on the southern shore Loutraki, Corinth, Xylokastro, Aigio and Diakopto. Trizonia is the only inhabited island. Rivers such as the Mornos and Pleistos flow in from the north and the Vouraikos, Krathis and Asopos from the south.
gulf-of-finland: The Gulf of Finland covers 30,000 km2 and runs about 400 km from the Hanko Peninsula to Saint Petersburg. It is shallow, averaging 38 m deep, and its water has very low salinity because of the rivers that flow into it, above all the Neva. Parts of it can freeze from late November to late April. The northern coast is high and winding, with many skerries, while the southern shore is smooth and shallow and runs along a limestone escarpment, the Baltic Klint, up to 55 m high.

People settled the shores soon after the glaciers retreated, and sites up to 9,000 years old have been found. Finnic peoples later settled the coast: Estonians, Votes, Izhorians and the Korela. From the 8th to the 13th century the gulf and the Neva formed part of the waterway from Scandinavia to the Byzantine Empire, and from the 9th century Veliky Novgorod controlled the eastern coast. Swedes conquered the Finnish tribes to the north in the 12th and 13th centuries, and in 1293 Torkel Knutsson founded Vyborg Castle. The Treaty of Nöteborg of 1323 set the border between Sweden and Russia. Reval, now Tallinn, was established in the 13th century, and northern Estonia passed to Denmark after the crusade of 1219.

Russia reclaimed the eastern part in the Great Northern War (1700–1721). Saint Petersburg was founded at the mouth of the Neva on 16 May 1703, and the fortresses of Kronstadt, nicknamed the Russian Dardanelles, were built to protect it. Peter the Great took Vyborg in 1710, and the Treaty of Nystad in 1721 gave Russia the lands along the Neva and the gulf, as well as Estland and Swedish Livonia. The Treaty of Fredrikshamn after the war of 1808–1809 gave Russia Finland, which became a Grand Duchy. Finland declared independence on 6 December 1917 and Estonia in 1918.

The bottom of the gulf is one of the largest ship cemeteries in the world, since cold, low-salinity water and the absence of shipworms preserve wrecks well. In 1721 more than 100 vessels were lost within three months during the evacuation of Russian troops from Finland. Helsinki and Tallinn both face the gulf, as does Saint Petersburg at its eastern end.
gulf-of-gabes: The gulf spans the coast roughly from Sfax to Djerba. Sources differ on its limits. Most place its entrance between the north-western tip of Djerba and Ras Yonga, about 52 kilometres south-west of Sfax. Strabo placed it at the Kerkennah Islands and Djerba, which gives a larger area about 150 kilometres across. The whole gulf lies on the continental shelf of the African Plate and is nowhere deeper than 200 metres. At its head is the city of Gabès, where the tides range up to 2.1 metres at spring tides.

The Latin name Syrtis Minor is used by Pliny the Elder, who quotes an earlier description by Polybius that uses the Greek equivalent. The name contrasts with the Greater Syrtis in Libya. Strabo gave an alternative name, the Syrtis of the lotus-eaters, and called Tacape, the modern Gabès, an important entrepôt of the Lesser Syrtis.

The Syrtis is mentioned in the New Testament in the account of the Apostle Paul being sent in chains to Rome to stand trial before Nero. The crew of his ship feared being driven by a storm into the Syrtis and took precautions, and the ship was eventually wrecked on the island of Malta. In the fourth book of his Histories Herodotus describes a violent ritual in the region, held at a festival of Athena, in which young women divided into two camps and fought with stones and wooden clubs; those who died of their wounds were called false virgins.

Gabès and Sfax are both major ports on the gulf, supporting sponge and tuna fisheries, and Gabès is its economic and administrative centre. Carbonate minerals and evaporites deposited in the Permian and Triassic periods now form salt domes and diapirs beneath the gulf, and hydrocarbons deposited with them form the basis of an oil and gas industry. The Ashtart and Chergui fields are among the important ones.
gulf-of-guinea: The Gulf of Guinea is the north-easternmost part of the tropical Atlantic Ocean, from Cape Lopez in Gabon north and west to Cape Palmas in Liberia. Null Island, defined as the intersection of the Equator and the Prime Meridian, lies within it. Many rivers drain into the gulf, among them the Niger, the main river, and the Volta, and its coastline includes the Bight of Benin and the Bight of Bonny.

The largest of its islands form a south-west to north-east chain that is part of the Cameroon line of volcanoes. They include Annobón, Bioko and Corisco, all belonging to Equatorial Guinea, and Bobowasi Island, which belongs to the Western Region of Ghana. São Tomé and Príncipe, two islands about 140 kilometres apart that are part of an extinct volcanic range, became an independent nation in 1975 after Portuguese rule.

The origin of the name Guinea is disputed. Some have said it is a corrupt form of Ghana, but the historian Bovill finds this unacceptable, since the name was in use in the Maghrib and Europe long before Prince Henry's time. It appears as Gunuia on a map of about 1320 by the Genoese cartographer Giovanni di Carignano and as Ginyia in the Catalan atlas of 1375. A passage in Leo Africanus suggests it may be a corrupt form of Jenne, a city on the Niger long famed as a market and seat of learning. Bovill thinks it more probable that it derives from the Berber aguinaou, meaning Negro.

The modern use of the name for the coast dates only from 1481, when the Portuguese built the fort of São Jorge da Mina, now Elmina, on the Gold Coast and King John II was permitted to style himself Lord of Guinea. Today the word appears in the names of Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Equatorial Guinea and Papua New Guinea.
gulf-of-izmir: The gulf opens to the Aegean between the Karaburun Peninsula and the mainland near Foça. It is 64 kilometres long and 32 kilometres wide, with an excellent anchorage. Its northern limit is a line of 13 nautical miles from Cape Kanlıkaya on the Karaburun Peninsula to Cape Aslan at Foça. The surface area is 960.4 square kilometres and the shore is 464 kilometres long. The gulf formed in the Quaternary period, when faults broke along an east-west line.

Seventeen rivers flow into it, the Gediz and the Meles most notably, and the Gediz Delta in the north-east is a Ramsar site. Among its islands, Uzunada is the fourth largest island of Turkey. The Mediterranean monk seal lives along the north-eastern coast, and birds breed at the İzmir Birds Paradise in the north and the Çakalburnu Lagoon in the south.

The first settlements around the gulf date to the Neolithic. The best known is Smyrna, established around present-day Bayraklı in the 3300s BCE. After the Battle of Ankara, Timur came to İzmir and in December 1402 seized the Port Castle and the area around it, and he ordered the castle destroyed. During the First World War there were naval battles between Sancakburnu Castle and Urla in March 1915 and around Uzunada in May 1916. Two ships of 118 and 86 metres collided and sank off Sancakburnu Castle in 1957.

As the population around the gulf grew past 500,000 and then 1.7 million in the 1990s, waste discharged into the water outran its capacity to renew itself, swimming stopped and heavy metal traces were found in fish. The Grand Canal Project, a sewage and treatment system begun by İZSU in 1992 and launched in October 2002, ended the discharge of waste water, and by the 2010s marine life had returned to normal.

The Port of İzmir, on the eastern side of the gulf, handles cargo and passengers, and nine passenger ferry quays operate on the gulf. Sailing, rowing and canoe races are held on its waters, and nine beaches around it fly the Blue Flag.
gulf-of-mannar: The Gulf of Mannar is a large shallow bay, part of the Laccadive Sea in the Indian Ocean, with an average depth of 5.8 metres. It lies between the south-eastern tip of India and the west coast of Sri Lanka, in the Coromandel Coast region. The chain of low islands and reefs called Adam's Bridge or Rama Setu, which includes Mannar Island, separates it from Palk Bay to the north. The Thamirabarani and Vaippar rivers of southern India and the Malvathu Oya of Sri Lanka drain into the gulf, and the dugong is found there.

The gulf has been known for its pearl banks, of the species Pinctada radiata and Pinctada fucata, for at least 2,000 years. Pliny the Elder, who lived from 23 to 79 CE, praised its pearl fishery as one of the most productive in the world. Extracting natural pearls is considered too expensive in most parts of the world, but it is still carried out in the gulf.

The chief seaports on the gulf are Thoothukudi, also called Tuticorin, in Tamil Nadu, and Colombo in Sri Lanka. They can take deep-draft vessels, whereas the shallow Palk Strait can take only small shallow-draft vessels.

The gulf harbours more than 3,600 species of plants and animals and is one of the richest coastal regions in Asia; about 117 species of hard coral have been recorded. Sea turtles, sharks, dugongs and dolphins visit it. In 1986 a group of 21 islets off the Tamil Nadu coast was declared the Gulf of Mannar Marine National Park, and in 1989 the park and its 10 km buffer zone became a Biosphere Reserve. The reserve covers 10,500 square kilometres of ocean, the 21 islands and the adjoining coast, with seaweed and sea grass communities, coral reefs, salt marshes and mangroves. Some 47 villages with about 50,000 people live along it and rely on the reef for food.
gulf-of-mexico: The Gulf of Mexico is an oceanic basin and marginal sea of the Atlantic, roughly oval and about 1,500 kilometres wide, with an area of about 1.6 million square kilometres. Almost half of it is shallow continental shelf. It connects to the Atlantic through the Straits of Florida and to the Caribbean Sea through the Yucatán Channel, and the narrow connections keep its tidal range very small. Its shores lie along the United States, from Florida to Texas, along the Mexican states from Tamaulipas to Quintana Roo, and along Cuba. The basin began to form in the Late Triassic, about 215 million years ago, as a result of plate tectonics; before then the area was dry land in the middle of the supercontinent Pangaea.

The earliest people on the coast found an arid landscape and hunted mostly rabbits, hare and rodents, with foraged plants. After climatic changes around 5,000 BCE, stable waterways, lagoons and shoals made fishing, agriculture and permanent settlement viable. In Florida, human remains date back to 10,000 BCE, and the Glades culture developed a complex society relying on fishing and shellfish. The Maya used the gulf as a major trade route and probably called it nahá, great water. The Aztecs called it Chalchiuhtlicueyecatl, the house of Chalchiuhtlicue, the deity of the seas.

Columbus reached Cuba but is not recorded entering the gulf. In 1517 Francisco Hernández de Córdoba discovered the Yucatán Peninsula, the first European encounter with an advanced civilisation in the Americas. Two further expeditions followed, in 1518 under Juan de Grijalva and in 1519 under Hernán Cortés, leading to the Conquest of Mexico. Hernández died in 1517 from the injuries and thirst suffered on the voyage.

European maps up to 1530 drew the gulf unlabelled. Cortés called it the Sea of the North in his dispatches, other Spanish explorers the Gulf of Florida or Gulf of Cortés, and early maps used names such as the Gulf of New Spain. At one point New Spain encircled the gulf.

The gulf receives water from 33 major rivers on the United States side. Its warm surface waters, averaging around 28 °C in summer, can feed powerful Atlantic hurricanes. It is one of the largest offshore petroleum production regions in the world and supports major fishing industries for the United States, Mexico and Cuba.
gulf-of-riga: The Gulf of Riga is also known as the Bay of Riga or the Gulf of Livonia. The island of Saaremaa partially separates it from the rest of the Baltic Sea, and its main connection with the open Baltic is the Irbe Strait. As a sub-basin of the Baltic it also includes the Väinameri Sea in the West Estonian archipelago. The International Hydrographic Organization draws its western limit as a line from Lyser Ort in Latvia to the southern extreme of Saaremaa, through that island and Hiiumaa, and on to Spithamn Point in Estonia.

The northern part of the gulf is shallow and the southern part slightly deeper, with the deepest point, 66 metres, opposite Mērsrags. In the central part a bank rises to form the island of Ruhnu. The major islands in the gulf are Saaremaa, Kihnu and Ruhnu, all in Estonian territory; Kihnu covers 16.4 square kilometres.

Notable cities around the gulf include Riga and Jūrmala in Latvia, and Pärnu and Kuressaare in Estonia. The main rivers flowing into it are the Daugava, Pärnu, Lielupe, Gauja and Salaca. Because Saaremaa partly shields the gulf from the Baltic, its water is brackish, with a salt concentration of around six to ten parts per thousand, the average for the Baltic Sea; freshwater has about 0.5 and seawater about 30.

The surface water has large annual temperature changes. In July and August the central part reaches about 18 °C, and the low coast can warm to 25 or 26 °C on hot, sunny days. In winter most or all of the gulf occasionally freezes, owing to the low salinity and the partial closure of its entrance, and many people walk over the bay. The thickest recorded ice was 90 centimetres. Fishing through holes in the ice has long been a traditional source of winter food, and the ice usually melts between March and April.
gulf-of-salerno: The Gulf of Salerno, also called the Bay of Salerno, is a coastline on the Tyrrhenian Sea facing the province of Salerno in Campania. Its northern part is the Costiera Amalfitana, which ends at Punta Campanella and includes Amalfi, Maiori, Positano and the city of Salerno itself. To the east lies the Piana del Sele, and to the south the Cilento coast, which ends at Punta Licosa. The distance from Punta Campanella to Punta Licosa is about 61 kilometres, and the gulf covers some 2,450 square kilometres.

The Amalfi Peninsula separates it from the Gulf of Naples. On the north the coast, also called the Divina Costiera, is rugged, with the rocky slopes of the Lattari Mountains falling into the sea, while the coast of the Sele plain is low and sandy and partly covered by pine forests. The climate is Mediterranean, with mild winters and hot, humid summers.

The gulf was inhabited by ancient Italic tribes long before the rise of the Roman Empire, and the foundation of Poseidonia, later Paestum, dates to the ancient period. In Roman times Salerno was known as Salernum, an important colony known for its productivity, and the gulf was a hub of trade and transport. According to one account Amalfi was founded by a Roman family bound for Constantinople, whose ship ran aground on a nearby shore.

In the Middle Ages the area belonged to the Lombard Duchy of Salerno. A diocese was established there in the 5th to 7th centuries, and the Schola Medica Salernitana, a medical school, was established in the 9th and 10th centuries. Alfano I invited Constantine the African from Carthage to help translate Arabic medical treatises. The town of Amalfi was the capital of the maritime Duchy of Amalfi, an important trading power in the Mediterranean between 839 and around 1200.

In 1076 the Normans under Robert Guiscard conquered Salerno and the surrounding region, incorporating it into the Kingdom of Sicily. Pope Gregory VII consecrated the Cathedral of Saint Matthew in 1084, and the university was founded in 1150. Forces of the Holy Roman Emperor Henry VI sacked Salerno in 1194. The region's importance declined as Naples and Palermo became more prominent. In World War II the gulf served as a landing point for the Allied forces during the Italian Campaign.
gulf-of-sirte: The Gulf of Sirte, also called the Gulf of Sidra, lies on the northern coast of Libya and takes its name from the oil port of Sidra or from the city of Sirte on its western coast. In antiquity it was known as the Great Sirte or Greater Syrtis, in Latin Syrtis Major, in contrast to the Syrtis Minor on the coast of Tunisia. It measures 439 kilometres from the promontory of Boreum, now Ras Teyonas, in the east to the promontory of Cephalae, Ras Kasr Hamet, in the west, reaches 177 kilometres inland and covers about 57,000 square kilometres. It has been a major centre of tuna fishing in the Mediterranean for centuries.

Ancient writers regarded the Syrtes as notorious sandbanks that sailors took pains to avoid. The greater Syrtis is unusually tidal, with a strong clockwise current at the rising tide, and the landward side was a featureless plain, in contrast to the fertile land of Tripolitania to the west. Strabo describes the march of the Roman general Cato the Younger in 47 BCE as thirty days through deep and scorching sand. The reputation also appears in Roman poetry, for example in Catullus and Virgil.

These sources should not be taken at face value. Pomponius Mela claimed that the greater gulf had no ports, but Pseudo-Scylax, writing in the early 4th century BCE, records one. Plutarch tells of Cato's march more calmly than Strabo, saying that it took seven days and that locals were engaged to protect the troops from serpents. Strabo himself says that sailors kept to the coast at a distance and took care not to be driven into the gulfs by winds, so they took precautions rather than avoided the area.

Two naval battles between the Regia Marina and the Royal Navy were fought in the gulf in the Second World War, in December 1941 and March 1942. In 1973 Muammar Gaddafi claimed much of the gulf as Libyan internal waters, drawing a line that he called the Line of Death, and the United States held naval exercises there to assert that these were international waters. American fighters shot down Libyan aircraft in the gulf in 1981 and 1989.
gulf-of-st-lawrence: The Gulf of St. Lawrence connects the Great Lakes to the Atlantic Ocean by way of the St. Lawrence River. It is bounded on the north by the Labrador Peninsula and Quebec, on the east by Saint-Pierre and Newfoundland, on the south by the Nova Scotia peninsula and Cape Breton Island, and on the west by the Gaspé Peninsula, New Brunswick and Quebec. Half of Canada's ten provinces adjoin it: New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Quebec. It contains many islands, among them Anticosti, Prince Edward Island, Cape Breton, Miquelon-Langlade and the Îles-de-la-Madeleine.

There is no consensus on where the river ends and the gulf begins, or whether it is hydrographically a gulf or an estuary. Geographers since Samuel de Champlain have treated Pointe des Monts as the dividing point, and a lighthouse was built there in 1829–1830. The waters leave the gulf by several straits: the Jacques Cartier Strait, the Honguedo Strait, the Strait of Belle Isle between Labrador and Newfoundland, and the Cabot Strait, about 56 miles wide, between Cape Ray and Cape North. The Laurentian Channel, formed in earlier ice ages by the erosion of the St. Lawrence River when sea level fell, is about 290 m deep and about 1,250 km long.

The gulf has long been an important fishery for the First Nations who have lived on its shores for millennia and used its waters for transport. Basque whalers from Saint-Jean-de-Luz entered it in 1530 and began whaling at Red Bay, on the Strait of Belle Isle, where they worked closely with the Iroquois. In 1579 the English government closed all English ports to Spanish oil imports, so that a third of Basque whale oil could not be sold, and Basque whaling in the gulf collapsed and never recovered.

The French explorer Jacques Cartier made a documented voyage in its waters in 1534. He named the shores of the St. Lawrence River the Country of Canadas, after an indigenous word meaning village or settlement, and the word became the name of Canada. In winter large quantities of ice form in the river and drift towards the gulf, which is covered by ice in January and February. The island of Saint Paul, off Cape Breton Island, is known as the Graveyard of the Gulf for its many shipwrecks.
gulf-of-thailand: The gulf is a shallow inlet lying between the southwestern shores of mainland Southeast Asia and the northern half of the Malay Peninsula. It is about 800 km long and up to 560 km wide, with a surface area of 320,000 square kilometres, and it is the largest gulf in Southeast Asia. About 70 percent of its coastline is Thai, 16.5 percent Cambodian, 13 percent Vietnamese and 0.67 percent Malaysian. Its northern tip is the Bay of Bangkok at the mouth of the Chao Phraya River, and its southern limit runs from Cape Bai Bung in southern Vietnam to the Malaysian coast. The Mae Klong, Bang Pakong and Tapi rivers also empty into it.

The mean depth is 58 metres and the maximum only 85 metres, so water exchanges slowly, and the inflow of river water lowers the salinity and enriches the sediments. The International Hydrographic Organization treats it as a sea. Its larger islands include Ko Chang, Ko Samui, Ko Pha Ngan, Ko Samet and Phu Quoc.

During the Last Glacial Maximum, 26,000 to 20,000 years ago, global sea level stood about 120 metres lower, and there was no seawater in the gulf. The area lay within Sundaland, a subcontinent joining the mainland with the western islands of Indonesia, and the gulf was a large paleolake filled by rivers, the Chao Phraya being the biggest. Sundaland existed until about 15,000 years ago and disappeared as the sea rose.

The gulf is generally identified with the Great Gulf, Magnus Sinus, known to Greek, Roman, Arab, Persian and Renaissance cartographers, a name it bears on the 1486 Ulm edition of Ptolemy's Geographia. The phantom Dragon Tail peninsula left European world maps in the 16th century after the Portuguese arrived. It was long called the Gulf of Siam after the kingdom of Siam. The country renamed itself Thailand in 1939, and Gulf of Thailand gradually became the more common name, though Gulf of Siam is still occasionally used.

The gulf is popular with divers and visitors, with destinations including Ko Samui, Ko Pha Ngan, Pattaya, Cha-am, Hua Hin and Ko Samet. Five species of sea turtle have been found on the coasts of the gulf and the Andaman Sea. About 41 percent of Thailand's marine catch is taken in the gulf. Malaysia and Thailand have chosen to develop jointly the areas they dispute, and Cambodia and Vietnam have a long-standing dispute over the island of Phu Quoc, known in Khmer as Koh Tral.
gulf-war: After the Iran-Iraq War, the Saudis had lent Iraq 26 billion dollars, and Saddam Hussein felt he should not have to repay it. The talks at Jeddah ended with an Iraqi demand for 10 billion dollars to cover revenue lost from the Rumaila oil field; Kuwait offered 500 million. Iraq responded by ordering an invasion, which began on 2 August 1990 with the bombing of Kuwait City. The UN Security Council demanded withdrawal on the day of the invasion and authorized a total embargo four days later. On 29 November 1990 Resolution 678 authorized all necessary means if Iraq was not out of Kuwait by 15 January 1991.

The coalition's operation had two phases: Desert Shield, the build-up from August 1990, and Desert Storm, which began with the bombing of Iraq on 17 January 1991. The air campaign lasted five weeks, with over 100,000 sorties and 88,500 tonnes of bombs, which widely destroyed military and civilian infrastructure. Iraq answered with Scud missile attacks on Israel and then Saudi Arabia, which failed to turn Muslim-majority states against the coalition.

The ground offensive began on 24 February 1991. The US Marines and other forces crossed into Kuwait, where trenches and minefields were poorly defended and most Iraqi troops surrendered. Meanwhile the US VII Corps attacked into Iraq just west of Kuwait, and the XVIII Airborne Corps swept across the southern desert, its flank guarded by the French Division Daguet. The 101st Airborne Division made an air assault 249 km behind Iraqi lines, cutting Highway 8 between Basra and the Iraqi forces. Kuwait was liberated on 28 February, and a ceasefire was declared within 100 hours of the ground attack.

A revolt broke out in Basra on 1 March 1991, one day after the ceasefire, and the Iraqi government suppressed a series of uprisings until 5 April, using helicopters it had been allowed to fly. The coalition countries set up no-fly zones over the north and south of Iraq, and the UN Special Commission sought to end Iraq's programmes for weapons of mass destruction. Iraqi forces had set over six hundred oil wells on fire in Kuwait, and over 1,000 Kuwaiti civilians were killed by Iraqis during the occupation. The war was also marked by live news broadcasts from the front, mainly by CNN.
guna-people: The Guna, also spelled Kuna or Cuna, are an Indigenous people of Panama and Colombia who call themselves Dule or Tule, meaning 'people'. Their language is Dulegaya, literally 'people-mouth'. At the time of the Spanish invasion they lived in northern Colombia and the Darién Province of Panama, in the region of Urabá.

Centuries before the conquest the Guna had arrived in South America as part of a Chibchan migration moving east from Central America. Alonso de Ojeda and Vasco Núñez de Balboa explored the coast in 1500 and 1501 and made contact with them in the Gulf of Urabá. Later, after conflict with the Spanish and other Indigenous groups, they moved westward toward what is now Guna Yala.

In the first decades of the twentieth century the Panamanian government tried to suppress many Guna customs. The Guna resisted bitterly, and in 1925 the Dule Revolution, led by Iguaibilikinya Nele Kantule of Ustupu and supported by the American adventurer Richard Oglesby Marsh, brought a short-lived but successful revolt. A treaty followed in which the Panamanians agreed to give the Guna some degree of cultural autonomy.

The Guna flag was adopted after that rebellion. Its centre shows an ancestral symbol called Naa Ukuryaa, explained as the four sides of the world or as the octopus that created the world; in 1942 a red ring, for the traditional nose-ring, was added around it to avoid Nazi associations.

The Guna live in three autonomous comarcas in Panama, Guna Yala, Guna de Madugandí and Guna de Wargandí, and in a few small villages in Colombia. Most live on small islands off Guna Yala known as the San Blas Islands. Each community is led by a saila, customarily both political and religious leader, who memorizes and sings the sacred history of the people in the Onmaked Nega, the Congress House, helped by voceros who interpret. The region is governed by the Guna General Congress, led by three Saila Dummagan. Families are matrilineal and matrilocal.

The Guna are known for molas, colourful appliqué textiles that form the blouses of women's dress. Their economy rests on agriculture, fishing and trade, with coconuts and lobsters the main exports. Dulegaya, of the Chibchan family, is spoken by 50,000 to 70,000 people, and most Guna children speak it. Albinistic people, called sipu, hold a special place and are the only ones to go out on the night of a lunar eclipse, to shoot the dragon that tries to eat the moon.
guna-yala: Guna Yala is a comarca indígena in north-eastern Panama with its capital at Gaigirgordub. It runs as a narrow strip about 373 kilometres long along the Caribbean coast, bordered by Colón province to the west and Colombia to the east, and covers about 2,306 square kilometres. An archipelago of 365 islands lies off the coast, of which 50 are inhabited. The area was formerly known as San Blas and later as Kuna Yala, and in October 2011 the government of Panama adopted the present name, accepting the people's claim that Guna is closer to their own word.

When the Spaniards arrived in the 1600s the Kuna lived near the Gulf of Urabá, in present-day Colombia. Contact brought significant violence and limited trade, and they fled towards Darién. They first settled along rivers flowing into the Caribbean, but from the mid-1800s they began to move to islands near the river mouths, which sheltered them from illness, snakes and mosquitoes and gave access to coastal trade in coconuts and turtle-shell. They kept farms on the mainland. In the late 1690s Scottish colonists founded New Edinburgh on the Bay of Caledonia as part of the Darien scheme; the town surrendered to a Spanish siege in March 1700.

A Colombian act of 4 June 1870 created the Tulenega Shire and recognised the Guna as owners of the land. After Panama separated from Colombia in 1903 the act was ignored. Incursions by outsiders seeking gold, rubber and sea turtles, banana concessions and police abuse of the Guna, including suppression of their customs, led to the rebellion of 1925, led by Nele Kantule of Ustupu and Ologintipipilele of Ailigandi.

The Guna proclaimed the independent Republic of Tule for a few days. A peace agreement was signed on 4 March 1925 in the presence of the American minister John G. South, and Panama committed itself to protecting Guna customs. Legislation of 1938 created the Guna District of San Blas, and Act No. 16 of 1953 finalised its boundaries and administration.

Under Law 16 of 1953 the highest authority is the General Congress, made up of representatives of all communities, which meets twice a year. The comarca is divided into four corregimientos with 51 communities, most of them on islands. The economy rests on farming for subsistence, fishing, tourism and crafts, and the making of molas is the main activity of Guna women and the chief income of many families. 32,016 people lived there in 2023, more than 95 per cent of them indigenous.
gundahar: Gundahar is the first king of the Burgundians to be historically attested. Most of his people crossed the Rhine into Roman Gaul in 406 or 407, together with numerous other Germanic tribes. Olympiodorus of Thebes gave him the title phylarchos, which may suggest that he was not the sole ruler, while Prosper of Aquitaine calls him rex, king. He appears as an ally of Goar, king of the Alans, in proclaiming the usurper Jovinus emperor on the lower Rhine, and he took part in Jovinus's campaigns in southern Gaul.

After Jovinus was defeated, the Roman general Constantius settled the Burgundians on the left bank of the Rhine as foederati. Many scholars place the settlement around Worms, following the later heroic tradition, though some have argued for other places. The Lex Burgundionum, issued by King Gundobad, names four earlier kings, Gibica, Gundomar, Gislaharius and Gundahar, without stating any family relationship.

In the 430s the Burgundians came under growing pressure from the Huns, and Gundahar, probably in reaction, attacked the Roman province of Belgica Prima, based around Trier. The general Flavius Aetius defeated him but at first confirmed his people's rights to their kingdom. In 436 Aetius, accompanied by Hunnish mercenaries, destroyed the Burgundian kingdom. According to Prosper of Aquitaine, Gundahar and most of his people died in the attack, and Aetius resettled the survivors in Savoy, on the upper Rhone.

His fall became the basis of Germanic heroic legend, where he appears as Gunther in the Nibelungenlied of about 1200 and as Gunnar in the Old Norse Poetic Edda and the Völsunga saga. He is a king at Worms who has Siegfried (Sigurd) killed and is himself killed at the court of Attila, called Etzel or Atli. In the Latin Waltharius he is a greedy antagonist of Walter of Aquitaine. Scholars generally take his role in these other tales to be a later development. Richard Wagner also made him a character in his Ring cycle.
gunderic: Gunderic was a son of Godigisel, king of the Hasdingi, a Vandal people originally living near the Oder River. On the last day of 406 the Vandals breached the Rhine frontier of the Western Roman Empire. That year they had become heavily involved in a war with the Franks, who were settled as allies of the Romans and tried to keep the Vandals out. Godigisel was killed in the fighting and Gunderic succeeded him.

Gunderic and his people crossed the Pyrenees into the Iberian Peninsula in October 409 and established a kingdom in the Roman province of Gallaecia, in the north-west. In 418 the Visigoths, acting for the Romans, drove them out. In the same year Attaces, king of the Alans, fell in battle against the Visigoths, and most of the surviving Alans appealed to Gunderic, who accepted them and so became king of the Vandals and Alans.

Conflicts with the Suebi drove the Vandals south into Baetica in 420 and 421, where Gunderic joined the surviving Silingi portion of the Vandals. In 422 they defeated a Roman army led by the magister militum Castinus outside the walls of Córdoba. In 425 the Vandals attacked Mauretania Tingitana and the Balearics and sacked Cartagena and Seville, though they did not remain in those cities.

Gunderic died early in 428. Hydatius wrote that after he laid hands on the church of Seville, he was seized by a demon and died by the will of God. How he died is unclear, but it has been suggested that Hydatius referred to an attempt to convert a Catholic church into an Arian one. The Vandals then chose his half-brother Genseric as successor. Genseric left Iberia in 429 to invade Roman Africa, and for the next ten years Roman Spain remained intact except for Galicia, which was under the control of the Sueves.
gundestrup-cauldron: Peat cutters found the cauldron on 28 May 1891 in a small peat bog called Rævemose. The finders were paid a large reward by the Danish government. It lay dismantled, with five long rectangular plates, seven short plates, one round base plate and two fragments of tubing stacked inside the curved base; an eighth short plate is assumed to be missing. Investigation of the bog showed that the land had been dry when the cauldron was deposited and that peat grew over it, and the stacking suggests an attempt to hide it. Sophus Müller worked out the traditional order of the plates from traces of solder at the rim. Timothy Taylor questions this, but Larsen concluded that his study confirmed the order.

The cauldron is 69 centimetres across and 42 centimetres high and weighs just under 9 kilograms. It is made almost entirely of silver, with gold for the gilding, tin for the solder and glass for the figures' eyes. The plates were hammered into repoussé relief, detailed with punches and tracers and partly gilded. Lead isotope studies indicate that the silver came mostly from northern France and western Germany and was recycled in three to six batches; the tin matches ingots from Cornwall. Benner Larson identified 15 punches in three distinct tool sets, fitting at least three different silversmiths. Silver was uncommon in Celtic art, and Celtic cauldrons are usually plainer and smaller.

The silverworking techniques are consistent with the Thracian sheet-silver tradition, while much of the depiction, especially of the human figures, relates to the Celts. The figures include players of the carnyx, a Celtic war horn, and men wearing torcs. The antlered figure on plate A is commonly identified as Cernunnos, who is named on the 1st-century Gallo-Roman Pillar of the Boatmen. Other details derive from the art of the ancient Near East, and scholars mostly regard these as motifs borrowed for their visual appeal. Attempts to tie the scenes closely to Celtic mythology remain controversial.

Its origin is debated. Taylor and Bergquist suggest that the Celtic Scordisci commissioned it from Thracian silversmiths, and that the Cimbri, who attacked the Scordisci in 118 BCE, carried it north. Olmsted argues that its art style matches Armorican coinage of 75-55 BCE from northwest Gaul, between the Seine and the Loire. Nielsen holds that a single ethnic group is unlikely to have produced it and that it reflects a fusion of cultures.
gundobad: Gundobad, born about 452, was the son of the Burgundian king Gundioc and the nephew of Ricimer, who had been the power behind the throne of the Western Roman Empire. When Ricimer died on 18 August 472, Gundobad took the title of patrician. According to John of Antioch, he had earlier executed the deposed emperor Anthemius on his uncle's orders. He raised the comes domesticorum Glycerius to the western throne, then left for Burgundy after his father's death.

The early decades of the reign are poorly known; the main source, Gregory of Tours, wrote almost a century later. He says Gundobad rid himself of his brothers, killing Gundomar and then Chilperic, whose wife he had drowned and whose daughters he exiled. One of them, Clotilde, married Clovis I, king of the Franks, though Danuta Shanzer and Ian Wood read a letter of Bishop Avitus of Vienne as showing that she was offered as an act of diplomacy.

The earliest firm date is 490, when the Burgundians invaded north-western Italy while Odoacer and Theodoric the Great fought over Pavia, devastated Liguria and carried off captives. Bishop Epiphanius of Pavia ransomed more than six thousand of them. Gundobad's brother Godegisel allied with Clovis against him, and Gundobad was defeated and pursued to Avignon, where he bought peace with a yearly tribute; Marius of Avenches dates this to 500.

Gundobad later broke the promise, besieged Godegisel in Vienne and, according to Gregory, killed him in 501 in an Arian church. After Clovis died in 511 the court of Constantinople favoured Gundobad and gave him the title magister militum. He died in 516 and was succeeded by his son Sigismund.

The Lex Burgundionum, which combined Roman law with Germanic custom, is attributed to Gundobad, though doubts surround its date. L. R. deSalis proposed a text without a date, which would better suit Sigismund's reign, and Katherine Fisher Drew holds that a core of the code came from Gundobad or his chancellery. Avitus, a Nicene bishop, answered an Arian's religious questions in several letters, showing considerable tolerance; Gregory of Tours later thought Gundobad had secretly become a Nicene Christian.
gung-ye: The date of his birth is unknown. Records make him a son of King Heonan or King Gyeongmun of Silla by a beloved lady of the court, but the claim cannot be fully verified, and some historians hold that he descended instead from Ko Ansŭng, ruler of a failed Goguryeo revival state. Legend says he was born on the holiday of Dano, which a royal seer declared would bring disaster, so the king ordered him killed. His mother threw him from an upper floor to a maid, who caught him but poked out his left eye. Raised in secret, he became a monk at the temple of Sedalsa.

Silla was then in decline under Queen Jinseong. After a year of famine taxes were raised sharply in 889, revolts spread, and local aristocrats called hojok became the real rulers of many provinces. He joined the rebel Ki Hwŏn in 891 but soon left him, and in 892 joined Yang Kil, whose leading general he became; many local lords, Wang Geon among them, submitted to him. He rebelled in present-day Kaesŏng in 898, subdued Yang Kil, and in 901 proclaimed himself king of Later Goguryeo. With Kyŏn Hwŏn's Later Paekche in the south-west, this opened the Later Three Kingdoms period.

He renamed the state Majin in 904, moved his capital to the mountain fortress of Cheorwon the next year, settled people there from Cheongju and extended his rule over almost two-thirds of the former Silla lands, also taking Pyongyang. Around 905 he began to present himself as the Maitreya Buddha, come to save the suffering, and in 911 he renamed the kingdom Taebong.

In his later years he is recorded as growing paranoid, claiming to read minds and putting officials to death on charges of treason. He accused his wife, Consort Kang, of infidelity and killed her, and their two sons were executed. In 918 four of his generals, Hong Yu, Pae Hyŏn-gyŏng, Sin Sung-gyŏm and Pok Chigyŏm, deposed him in favour of Wang Geon. He is said to have fled the palace and been killed soon after, by a soldier or by peasants who took him for a thief. Because Goryeo historians sought to justify the coup, the records of him are hostile, and some scholars now reassess his rule.
gungunum: According to the traditional king list of Larsa, Gungunum was the fifth ruler of the city, and his own inscriptions call him a son of Samium and brother of his predecessor Zabaya. His name is Amorite, from gungun, meaning protection or shelter. His reign of 27 years is far better documented than those before it: a complete list of his year names and four royal inscriptions survive. When he succeeded Zabaya in 1932 BCE, Larsa was a minor power beside Isin, dominant in southern Mesopotamia since the fall of Ur in 2002 BCE.

In his third year he destroyed Bašime, an Elamite region probably on the Iranian coast of the Gulf, and in his fifth year Anšan, one of Elam's chief cities, perhaps to secure his eastern flank against an ally of Isin. His capture of Ur shows in the documents found there, where the year names of Lipit-Ištar of Isin give way to his. He kept Ur's institutions in place, leaving Enanatuma, daughter of Ishme-Dagan of Isin, as high priestess of Nanna. Kisurra, close to Isin, was his by 1923 BCE but was retaken by Ur-Ninurta of Isin by 1921 BCE.
