In his 19th year, 1914 BCE, he destroyed the army of Malgium on the Tigris, reaching further north than Larsa ever had. The same year name invokes An, Enlil and Nanna, the gods of Uruk, Nippur and Ur, and bricks with his name found near Uruk suggest he held that city too. Two years later an inscription commemorating the great wall he built around Larsa calls him king of Sumer and Akkad, and copies of a hymn he composed were found in Nippur, which he almost certainly ruled for a time before Isin regained it.

His later year names record fortifications, temples, a silver statue for Nanna at Ur, and canals such as the Išartum and the Ba-ú-hé-gál near Girsu. Documents from Kisurra show it was again under Larsa in his 23rd year. He died around 1906 BCE and was succeeded by Abisare, whose relation to him the sources do not state, though many royal officials kept their posts. He had turned Larsa from a minor state into a regional power that broke Isin's hegemony.
gunpowder: Gunpowder, also called black powder, is the earliest known chemical explosive. It is a mixture of sulphur, charcoal and potassium nitrate, or saltpetre. The sulphur and charcoal act as fuels and the saltpetre as an oxidiser. It is one of the Four Great Inventions of China, and it was originally developed by Taoists for medicinal purposes.

The first confirmed reference in China is of the 9th century, in the Tang dynasty: a formula in the Taishang Shengzu Jindan Mijue of 808, and about fifty years later a Daoist text, the Zhenyuan miaodao yaolüe, which describes alchemists who burned their hands and faces and even a whole house. Gunpowder was therefore probably an accidental by-product of the search for an elixir of life. It was first used in warfare around 904.

Gunpowder is a low explosive: it deflagrates, burning at subsonic speed, and does not detonate. Ignited behind a projectile it forces the shot from the barrel without usually rupturing it, which makes it a good propellant. It was used in firearms, artillery and rockets, and it filled fused artillery shells until the second half of the 19th century.

Knowledge of it spread widely. Hasan al-Rammah in Syria wrote recipes and instructions for purifying saltpetre between 1240 and 1280, and his terms, such as Chinese snow for saltpetre and Chinese arrows for rockets, suggest a Chinese source. The earliest Western accounts are by Roger Bacon in 1267, and the oldest recipes in continental Europe are in the Liber Ignium of 1280 to 1300. Cannons reached Majapahit with Kublai Khan's army in 1293, and the Ayutthaya Kingdom used them in 1352 against the Khmer Empire.

Historians widely believe that gunpowder and the gun originated in China, because a large body of evidence documents the change of gunpowder from a medicine to an incendiary and an explosive, and of the gun from the fire lance to a metal gun. Tonio Andrade notes that the variation among Chinese recipes suggests experimentation there. How gunpowder travelled is less clear. Some sources mention gunpowder weapons used by the Mongols at the Battle of Mohi in 1241, but Timothy May says there is no concrete evidence that the Mongols used them regularly outside China, though they did use them against the Jin and the Song and in their invasions of Japan.

In Southeast Asia true firearms came after the middle of the 15th century, most probably from Arabs, and Portuguese influence after the capture of Malacca in 1511 produced the hybrid matchlock called the istinggar.
gunther-victor-prince-of-schwarzburg: Günther Victor was born in Rudolstadt on 21 August 1852, the son of Prince Adolf of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt and Princess Mathilde of Schönburg-Waldenburg. His mother was the daughter of Otto Victor, Prince of Schönburg-Waldenburg, and of Princess Thekla of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt, a cousin of his father. On his father's death on 1 July 1875 he became heir presumptive to the principality of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt.

He succeeded his first cousin once removed, Prince Georg, as sovereign prince on 19 January 1890. On 9 December 1891 he married, at Rudolstadt, Princess Anna Louise of Schönburg-Waldenburg, the daughter of his uncle Prince Georg of Schönburg-Waldenburg and Princess Luise of Bentheim-Tecklenburg. When Prince Leopold of Schwarzburg-Sondershausen died in 1906, Günther Victor became heir presumptive to the neighbouring Schwarzburg principality as well.

The death of Prince Karl Günther on 28 March 1909 united the two principalities under him in a personal union. It was the first time since their partition in the 16th century that the two territories had been ruled by a single monarch. After the union he dropped Rudolstadt from his title and styled himself Prince of Schwarzburg.

After the outbreak of the German Revolution, Prince Günther resigned his throne on 22 November 1918. Once the monarchy had been abolished, he reached a settlement with the Free State of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt over the ancestral assets of his house.

Günther Victor died in Sondershausen on 16 April 1925. His marriage had been childless, and he was succeeded as head of the House of Schwarzburg by his cousin Sizzo, Prince of Schwarzburg. In 1942 his widow, Princess Anna Luise, adopted her nephew Prince Wilhelm of Schönburg-Waldenburg together with his son, Prince Ulrich.
gunther-von-schwarzburg: Günther XXI was born around 1304, the younger son of Henry VII, Count of Schwarzburg-Blankenburg, and his wife Christine von Gleichen. On 9 September 1331 he married Elisabeth von Honstein-Klettenberg, daughter of Count Heinrich IV. They had five children, among them his heir Heinrich XIII, who died childless in 1357.

Günther distinguished himself as a diplomat in the service of the Emperor Louis IV. After Louis died in 1347, the throne was offered to Günther once Edward III of England had refused it. Four electors, partisans of the house of Wittelsbach and opponents of Charles of Luxembourg, chose him king at the Dominican monastery in Frankfurt on 30 January 1349: Louis, Margrave of Brandenburg, the Duke of Saxe-Lauenburg, the Elector Palatine and the deposed Elector of Mainz, Heinrich III von Virneberg.

Günther based his legitimacy on having been chosen at the right place, Frankfurt, whereas Charles had been elected at Rhens and crowned at Bonn rather than Aachen. Frankfurt itself had recognised Charles after the death of Louis and kept Günther waiting a week in the field. Only on 6 February did he enter the city, where he was installed in his office in the old manner, confirmed the city's privileges and received the homage of its citizens.

Charles won over many of Günther's adherents and defeated his army at the Battle of Eltville on the Rhine. Günther, by then seriously ill, renounced all claims to the throne in the Treaty of Eltville on 26 May 1349 in return for 20,000 marks of silver and an amnesty for his followers. He died three weeks later at the Johanniter monastery in Frankfurt, presumably of the Black Death. He himself suggested that he had been poisoned, but this cannot be proven.

At the instigation of Charles IV he was buried with royal honours in Frankfurt Cathedral, where his gothic headstone was erected in 1352. Streets and a school in Frankfurt are named after him, and he is the subject of a Singspiel in three acts by Ignaz Holzbauer, first performed in 1777.
guntram: Guntram was born about 532 at Soissons, the third-eldest and second-eldest surviving son of Chlothar I and Ingunda. On his father's death in 561 he became king of a fourth of the Kingdom of the Franks. After his brother Charibert I died in 567, the surviving brothers, Guntram, Sigebert I and Chilperic I, shared his lands, at first holding Paris in common. Charibert's widow Theudechild proposed marriage to Guntram, but he lodged her in a monastery at Arles instead.

In 573 he was drawn into civil war with Sigebert I of Austrasia and in 575 called on Chilperic for help, but changed sides and remained Sigebert's ally. When Sigebert was assassinated in 575 and Chilperic invaded, Guntram sent his general Mummolus, who defeated Chilperic's general Desiderius. After his two surviving sons died of dysentery in 577, he adopted his nephew Childebert II, Sigebert's son, as heir.

About 584 or 585 a man named Gundowald, claiming to be an illegitimate son of Chlothar I, took cities including Poitiers and Toulouse; Guntram besieged him, and his followers gave him up for execution. In 587 Fredegund attempted to have Guntram assassinated, without success. That year he concluded the Treaty of Andelot with Childebert, Brunhilda and others, which lasted until his death. He also compelled the Breton ruler Waroch II to renew his oath, but the Bretons stayed independent. In 590 he put down a rebellion of his niece Basina at the Holy Cross abbey in Poitiers.

Gregory of Tours, the chief chronicler of the period, calls him the good king Guntram. He describes a man who after a period of intemperance repented, fasted and prayed, protected the oppressed, cared for the sick, gave generously in plague and famine, and built and endowed churches and monasteries. Guntram died at Chalon-sur-Saône on 28 March 592 and was succeeded by Childebert II. He was buried in the Church of Saint Marcellus, which he had founded. He was soon proclaimed a saint, and his feast day is 28 March.
guntur: Guntur is the administrative headquarters of Guntur district and lies on the Eastern Coastal Plains, about 23 kilometres south-west of the state capital Amaravati, at an average elevation of 33 metres. It is part of the Andhra Pradesh Capital Region. The climate is tropical with dry winters, with an annual rainfall of about 905 millimetres; the hottest months are May and June, followed by the monsoon, and cyclones are common between May and November. The name is explained in two ways. Telugu gunta means a pond, so Guntur may be a pond village, while another source points to kunta, a unit of land measure. Sanskrit documents call the place Garthapuri.

The region was historically known for Buddhism. Inscriptions in Naga Lipi, a script of the third century CE, on a sculpture unearthed in 2018 at the Agastyeshwara temple lead the archaeologist Emani Sivanagi Reddy to think the area was a Buddhist site contemporary with Nagarjunakonda. The earliest reference to Guntur is in inscriptions of the Vengi Chalukyan king Ammaraja I (922 to 929 CE). An inscription at Ramachandra Agraharam records that in 1485 Tirumala Dasa Mahapatra, local ruler under Kapileswara Gajapathi, made donations to a temple.

Before the British, Guntur was ruled by the Satavahanas, Andhra Ikshvakus, Vishnukundinas, Pallavas, Vengi Chalukyas, Kakatiya kings, Reddy kings, Gajapathi kings, Vijayanagar kings, the Nizams of Hyderabad and French India. The British East India Company took Kondaveedu Fort in 1788 and abandoned it in the early 19th century in favour of Guntur, which became the headquarters of a district named after it; the district was abolished in 1859 and reconstituted in 1904. A railway link opened in 1890 made the city a major market for the produce of the surrounding countryside.

The Guntur Municipal Corporation traces its origin to 1886, when the city had a population of 25,000. The city's limits were expanded in 2012 by merging ten surrounding villages. Observations of the solar eclipse of 18 August 1868 by the French astronomer Pierre Janssen link Guntur to the discovery of helium.

The 2011 census recorded a population of 743,354, mostly Telugu speakers, with Urdu speakers the largest minority. Guntur is a hub for the export of chilli, cotton and tobacco, and its Agriculture Market Committee Market Yard is the largest chilli yard in Asia. The Tobacco Board and the Spices Board have their headquarters in the city. Ancient temples and sites near the city include Kondaveedu Fort, the Undavalli Caves and the Amareswaraswamy temple. Hindu College and Andhra Christian College date from the British period, and Guntur Medical College is one of the oldest medical colleges in the state.
gunzburg: Günzburg was founded in about 70 BCE by the Romans to defend their lands along the Danube and was known as Castellum Guntia, Gontia or Contia, a name taken from the Celtic goddess Gontia. It consisted of a fort, later replaced by at least one other on the same site, a fairly large civilian settlement and most likely an important bridge over the Danube. After the Romans left in the fifth century the Alamanni settled there. The town itself first appears in documents in 1065 as Gunceburch.

In 1301 the town passed to the House of Habsburg and was developed as the centre of the Margraviate of Burgau. From 1803 to 1805 it was for a time the capital of all Further Austria. In 1525, very near the town, the Swabian army defeated the Leipheim Horde in the German Peasants' War.

In 1770 Marie Antoinette stopped there for two days on her journey to France. On 9 October 1805 troops of the Sixth Corps of Napoleon's Grande Armée stormed the Austrian positions in Günzburg and took about a thousand prisoners and six guns. Through the Franco-Bavarian alliance the town was then integrated into the Kingdom of Bavaria. In April 1945 the Allies bombed it, damaging the castle and a munitions train in the station.

Günzburg has about 20,350 inhabitants and is the capital of the Swabian district of Günzburg, formed in 1972. Its sights include the Church of Our Lady, built by Dominikus Zimmermann, the margraves' castle, which is the only Habsburg castle built in Germany, the Reisensburg fort, now the congress centre of the University of Ulm, and a nearly intact old town centre. Legoland Deutschland Resort opened nearby in 2002.
guo-shoujing: Guo Shoujing, courtesy name Ruosi, was born in Xingtai, in present-day Hebei province, into a poor family. His paternal grandfather, Guo Yong, raised him and was known for expertise ranging from the Five Classics to astronomy, mathematics and hydraulics. As a child prodigy, Guo obtained a blueprint for a water clock that his grandfather was working on and worked out how it operated. He improved a type of water clock called a lotus clepsydra. At the age of 16 he began to study mathematics, which led him to hydraulics and astronomy.

At 20 Guo became a hydraulic engineer, and in 1251 he helped repair a bridge over the Dahuoquan River as a government official. Kublai Khan, who thought that irrigation and water transport could ease uprisings within the empire, sent Liu Bingzhong and his student Guo to survey the area between Dadu, now Beijing, and the Yellow River. To give Dadu a new water supply, Guo had a channel of 30 km built from the Baifu spring, joining water across different river basins with sluices to control the level. Kublai then sent him to manage similar projects elsewhere.

Guo also built instruments. He is credited with the gnomon, the square table, the simplified armilla and a water-powered armillary sphere called the Ling Long Yi. Kublai ordered him, Zhang and Wang Xun to prepare a more accurate calendar, and they built 27 observatories across China for their observations. The calendar reckoned the year at 365.2425 days. Guo became director of the Observatory in Beijing in 1283 and head of the Water Works Bureau in 1292, and he continued as adviser to Kublai's successors.

Guo worked extensively on spherical trigonometry. Scholars debate whether this built wholly on the earlier work of Shen Kuo or was partly influenced by Islamic mathematics, which was widely accepted at Kublai's court; Jamal ad-Din is recorded as having cooperated with him. His calendar remained in use for 363 years, the longest span for any calendar in Chinese history. Johann Adam Schall von Bell, impressed by the surviving instruments, called him the Tycho Brahe of China. An asteroid is named after him.
guo-wei: Guo Wei was born on 10 September 904 in Yaoshan, in present-day Longyao County, Hebei, as the Tang dynasty broke apart into warring regions. His father, Guo Jian, prefect of Shunzhou under the warlord Li Keyong, was killed when the forces of Liu Rengong took the city, and his mother, Lady Wang, died soon after; a distant relative, Lady Han, raised him. He grew into a strong young man more drawn to war than farming, fond of drinking, gambling and brawls, and was nicknamed Sparrow Guo for a sparrow-shaped tattoo on his neck.

At about 17, fleeing arrest, he joined the army of Li Jitao at Luzhou, who wanted brave soldiers more than he cared for the law and let him go free after he stabbed a butcher to death in a drunken quarrel.

After Li Cunxu founded the Later Tang in 923 and Li Jitao was killed, Guo Wei, then 19, was placed in the cavalry. Being literate and good at mathematics, he soon became an officer, and he read what he could on military strategy, guided by his sworn brother Li Qiong. In 927, when the emperor Li Siyuan put down the rebellion of Zhu Shouyin, Guo was among the first to scale the wall of Xun under the general Shi Jingtang, who then put him in charge of military records. Under the Later Han of Liu Zhiyuan he served as Assistant Military Commissioner.

After the teenage Liu Chengyou came to the throne in 948, court intrigue let Guo Wei seize power in a coup, and he proclaimed the Later Zhou on New Year's Day of 951, 11 February in the modern calendar. Two of his sons, Guo Qingge and Guo Yige, had died on 24 December 950. He was the first Han Chinese emperor in northern China since 923. His rule was stable and well organised, and he passed reforms meant to ease the burdens on the peasantry. He died of illness on 22 February 954, three years into his reign.
gurage-people: The linguist Marcel Cohen held that the Gurage descend from an isolated group of ancient Semitic-speaking settlers from South Arabia who settled around Lake Zway and mixed with the local peoples. Other historians stress that they were never a single group: Ulrich Braukhamper sees the eastern Gurage (Siltʼe, Wolane, Zay) as an extension of the Harla, and oral tradition tells of a military colony planted in northern Gurage by Emperor Amda Seyon. Their languages fall into at least three groups, Northern, Eastern and Western, and the Eastern group is closest to Harari.

The Gurage first appear in the chronicle of Amda Seyon I, and by the 15th century their region was part of the Ethiopian Empire. In the 1520s the Portuguese priest Francisco Alvares described them as fiercely independent and as raiders of the royal camp of Lebna Dengel. During the wars of Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi the region was briefly occupied, an occupation that ended soon after his death in 1543. Later the Gurage were often raided for slaves by neighbouring Oromo, while many Oromo and Gurage also intermarried.

Most Gurage resisted the expansion of Menelik II of Shewa; only the Soddo Gurage submitted, in 1876. From 1874 they fought for 14 years, and at the Battle of Aräkit in 1875 Hassan Enjamo of Kebena defeated a large Shewan force. They were subdued only after Gobana Dacche defeated Hassan Enjamo at Jebdu Meda in 1888. Taxes under the neftenya system then drove many to work in Addis Ababa, where they became the city's main labour force and the driving force of the Addis Mercato, and between the 1950s and 1970s outcompeted the foreign traders who had dominated Ethiopia's economy.

Enset is part of every side of Gurage life: its fronds wrap the dead, its fibre ties the newborn's umbilical cord, and it is exchanged in social life and given as payment for services. The pounded root is fermented in pits between the rows of plants, where it keeps for years as a store against famine, and is eaten as kocho bread with cabbage, cheese, butter and grain. Households keep zebu cattle chiefly for butter, which is also taken as medicine. The Gurage hold overeating to be coarse, and guests leave some of the bread passed round.
gurkhas: Historically the terms Gurkha and Gorkhali were synonymous with Nepali, and they come from the hill principality of Gorkha, from which the Kingdom of Nepal expanded under Prithvi Narayan Shah, the last ruler of the Gorkha Kingdom and the first monarch of Nepal. The name may be traced to the medieval Hindu warrior-saint Guru Gorakhnath, who has a shrine in Gorkha District. The Gorkhali conquests of the Kathmandu Valley gave the British an exaggerated view of Nepal's strength, which helped lead to the Anglo-Nepalese War of 1814 to 1816 against the East India Company, ended by the Treaty of Sugauli. The Gorkhali soldiers impressed the British, who called them Gurkhas.

David Ochterlony and the political agent William Fraser were among the first to see the soldiers' potential. During the war the British used defectors from the Gurkha army as irregular forces, and in April 1815 Fraser proposed forming them into a battalion called the Nasiri Regiment, which later became the 1st King George's Own Gurkha Rifles. About 5,000 men entered British service in 1815. Fraser and Frederick Young also raised the Sirmoor Battalion, and a Kumaon battalion followed. Gurkhas served the Company in the Pindaree War of 1817, at Bharatpur in 1826 and in the Anglo-Sikh Wars of 1846 and 1848.

After the Indian Rebellion of 1857, British authorities feared the influence of Hindu castes in the army, discouraged Thakuri and Khas recruits and refused to recruit tribes other than Gurungs and Magars. They pressed Nepal's prime minister Bir Shamsher Jang Bahadur Rana to ensure that at least 75 per cent of new recruits were Gurungs and Magars. Between 1901 and 1906 the regiments were renumbered one to ten as the Gurkha Rifles. In the First World War more than 200,000 Gurkhas served, with about 20,000 casualties, and many served in non-combatant roles in labour battalions.

After Indian independence a Tripartite Agreement between the United Kingdom, India and Nepal divided the ten pre-war regiments. Six went to the Indian Army and four, transferred on 1 January 1948, to the British Army, forming the Brigade of Gurkhas, first stationed in Malaya. Most Gurkhas given a choice opted for the Indian Army, where roles and terms were familiar. The agreement set Gurkha pay on the Indian scale, lower than British rates. British Gurkhas have since served in Borneo, the Falklands and peacekeeping missions. Gurkha soldiers have been awarded 26 Victoria Crosses, the first in 1858 and the last in 1965. They are closely associated with the khukuri, a forward-curving knife.
gurs-internment-camp: The camp stood at Gurs, not far from Pau. It was about 1.4 km long and 200 m wide, with a single street along its length and thirteen fenced blocks, called îlots, on either side, holding 382 cabins in all. The cabins, a type designed for the French army in the First World War, were thin planks covered with tarred fabric, without windows or insulation, and up to 60 people slept on sacks of straw in each 25 square metres. Heavy rain kept the clay ground permanently muddy, and there was no running water or plumbing.

From April 1939 the camp received Basques, ground crews of the Republican air force and members of the International Brigades, and that July some 17,000 internees of Spanish origin were held there. Most of the Spanish farmers were encouraged to return to Spain, where they were handed to the Francoist authorities at Irún. From May 1940 the French government also interned German nationals, many of them Jews who had fled the Nazi regime, along with left-wing activists, pacifists, sympathisers of the Nazis and ordinary prisoners, known together as the undesirables.

Under Vichy the camp held foreign Jews, political dissidents, stateless persons and others. In October 1940, in Operation Wagner-Bürckel, the Gauleiter Josef Bürckel had the Jews of Baden sent there, the only deportation of Jews westward by the Nazi regime, and typhus and dysentery were rife. Aid organisations, among them the Quakers, the YMCA and the Oeuvre de Secours aux Enfants, which took many children out, worked in the camp, and 755 internees escaped. After the SS captain Theodor Dannecker inspected Gurs on 18 July 1942, its Jews were sent in convoys to Drancy from 6 August, most of them on to Auschwitz.

After the liberation the camp briefly held German prisoners of war, accused collaborators and Spaniards who had fought in the French Resistance, whom the French feared might take up arms against Franco on the border. It was dismantled in 1946; some 64,000 people had been held there over the years.

A reconstructed cabin and several monuments stand on the site, and a commemorative ceremony is held each year. The Jewish cemetery is maintained at the expense of the German cities that deported their Jews to Gurs, among them Karlsruhe, Freiburg, Mannheim and Heidelberg, and since 1985 a memorial has honoured the fighters of the Spanish Civil War interned there.
guru-arjan: Arjan was born in Goindval to Bibi Bhani, daughter of Guru Amar Das, and Jetha Sodhi, who later became Guru Ram Das. He had two brothers, Prithi Chand and Mahadev. Scholarly consensus accepts 1563 as his birth year, with 15 April as the date. He spent his first eleven years in Goindwal and the next seven with his father in Ramdaspur.

Guru Ram Das chose Arjan, the youngest son, as his successor, and Arjan became the fifth Guru in 1581 at the age of 18. Mahadev chose the life of an ascetic. The choice led to disputes and divisions among the Sikhs. Prithi Chand is remembered in the orthodox tradition as vehemently opposed to Arjan, and Arjan's followers called the breakaway faction Minas. Competing texts written by the Minas tell the story differently.

Arjan completed the Darbar Sahib at Amritsar, in the town his father had founded and the pool his father had built. The town grew during his time as Guru, financed by donations and built by voluntary work. He is credited with founding Tarn Taran, Kartarpur and Hargobindpur, and with the water reservoirs Santokhsar and Gongsar. He asked Sikhs to give, if possible, one tenth of their income, a practice known as dasvandh, which financed gurdwaras and langars.

According to Sikh tradition he compiled the Adi Granth by collecting hymns of past Gurus from many places and rejecting those he considered spurious. The collection was completed on 30 August 1604 and installed in the Harmandir Sahib on 1 September. It holds hymns of the first four Gurus, his own, and those of 17 Hindu and 2 Muslim bards. Arjan composed 2,218 hymns, the largest part of the Guru Granth Sahib, among them the Sukhmani Sahib.

Arjan died in Mughal custody in 1606, after being imprisoned in Lahore Fort on the orders of the Emperor Jahangir. Sikh tradition holds that Jahangir demanded a fine of 200,000 rupees and the removal of hymns he found offensive, and that Arjan refused. Sources are unclear on whether he died by execution, under torture or by drowning in the Ravi River.

Sikh tradition holds that before his death Arjan told his son Hargobind to take up arms and resist tyranny. Hargobind became the sixth Guru in 1606. Arjan is regarded as the first of the two Gurus martyred in the Sikh faith, and his death is remembered as Shaheedi Divas.
guru-gobind-singh: Guru Gobind Singh was the only son of Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Sikh Guru, and Mata Gujri, and was born into the Sodhi clan of the Punjabi Khatri community. He was born in Patna, Bihar, while his father was visiting Bengal and Assam, and his birth name was Gobind Das. His family returned to Punjab in 1670 and in March 1672 moved to Chakk Nanaki in the Sivalik range, where he was schooled. In 1675, at the age of nine, he was formally made leader of the Sikhs after Aurangzeb had his father executed.

In 1699 the Guru asked the Sikhs to gather at Anandpur on Vaisakhi. According to Sikh tradition he asked for a volunteer and took him into a tent, returning with a bloody sword, and repeated this four more times. After the fifth volunteer, he came back with all five unharmed and called them the Panj Pyare, the first Khalsa. He is credited with introducing the Five Ks, the articles of faith that Khalsa Sikhs wear at all times.

The Guru is credited in Sikh tradition with finalizing the Kartarpur manuscript of the Guru Granth Sahib, including the compositions of his father, and with declaring it the eternal Guru. He is also credited with the Dasam Granth, which some Sikhs treat as a second scripture and others consider its authority disputed.

He fought 21 battles against the Mughal Empire and the kings of the Siwalik Hills, among them Bhangani in 1688 and Nadaun in 1691. He held that war was a last resort, a Dharamyudh fought in defence of righteousness. Mughal court historians wrote in a hostile tone, holding that he had corrupted the Sikh tradition by creating a military order willing to resist the imperial army.

His four sons died in his lifetime. The elder two, Ajit Singh, aged 17, and Jujhar Singh, aged 13, were killed in the Battle of Chamkaur in December 1704, and the younger two were executed by the Mughal governor of Sirhind. He then wrote the Zafarnama, a defiant Persian letter to Aurangzeb, stern yet conciliatory, which accuses the emperor of immorality in governance and in war and predicts that the Mughal Empire would soon end.

After Aurangzeb died in 1707 the Guru supported Bahadur Shah I in the Battle of Jajau, and then stayed near the imperial camp for nearly a year hoping to recover Anandpur, but Bahadur Shah kept postponing any restoration. Guru Gobind Singh died on 7 October 1708. He is remembered as the tenth and last human Sikh Guru, and he established the concept of Guru Panth as his spiritual successor, though it is rarely invoked today.
guru-granth-sahib: Guru Nanak's compositions were gathered in a book known as a pothi, which passed to his successor Guru Angad, and the later gurus added their own works and those of others. The text reached its canonical form after major expansions in about 1570, 1604, 1675 and the 1690s. Guru Arjan found that his eldest brother Prithi Chand, a rival claimant to the guruship, was circulating hymns of the earlier gurus alongside his own, and he judged these spurious.

He sent his associates across the Indian subcontinent to collect the circulating hymns and obtained from Mohan, the son of Guru Amar Das, the writings of the first three gurus. The compilation was completed on 29 August 1604 and installed in the Golden Temple on 1 September 1604, with Baba Buddha as its first granthi.

The text has 1,430 angs, a word meaning limbs, and 5,894 shabads. It opens with the Mul Mantar, the Japji Sahib, the So Dhar and the Sohila, all by Guru Nanak. The rest is arranged by the rāgas, or musical settings, in which the hymns are sung, and each raga section gives the gurus' compositions first, in order, followed by those of the bhagats.

Recurring forms include the vaars, which are longer ballad poems, as well as poems on the four parts of the day, the days of the week and the twelve months. Guru Arjan wrote 2,218 hymns, Guru Nanak 974, Guru Amar Das 907 and Guru Ram Das 679. The script is Gurmukhi, which according to Sikh tradition Guru Nanak invented and Guru Angad standardised.

In 1708 Guru Gobind Singh conferred the title of Guru of the Sikhs on the Adi Granth. An eyewitness, the bard Narbud Singh, recorded the event in a Bhatt Vahi. Sikhs have since regarded the scripture as their eternal living guru and as the embodiment of the ten human gurus. In a gurdwara it sits on a raised throne beneath a canopy, with a chaur, or fan whisk, waved above it. Worshippers cover their heads, remove their shoes and prostrate themselves before it, and it is never touched with unwashed hands or put on the floor.

At dawn in major gurdwaras such as the Golden Temple it is carried in a palanquin to the sanctum in the ritual of prakash, and a page is opened at random to give the day's mukhwak. At night the ritual of sukhasan carries it to its bedroom. Before the late 19th century only handwritten copies were made. Ernest Trumpp published an incomplete English translation in 1877, and a standard printed edition of 1,430 angs has been used since the early 20th century.
guru-nanak: Nanak was born on 15 April 1469 at Rāi Bhoi Dī Talvaṇḍī, now Nankana Sahib, in the Lahore province of the Delhi Sultanate, into the Bedi branch of the Punjabi Khatri clan. One tradition places his birth in the month of Kārtik, around November. His father wished him to lead an ordinary life of success, while his mother Tripta and his elder sister Nanaki recognised his contemplative nature. He married Sulakhani on 24 September 1487 at Batala, and they had two sons, Sri Chand and Lakhmi Das. Through Nanaki's husband, Jai Ram, he found work at Sultanpur in the storehouse of the Lahore governor Daulat Khan.

According to Sikh belief, Nanak disappeared into the Bein river while bathing and was presumed drowned. On the third or fourth day he returned, silent, and answered questions only with the words There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. The Janamsakhis, the hagiographies of his life, say that he was brought before God and charged to teach remembrance of the name, charity, cleansing and selfless service. He then left government employment.

The Janamsakhis describe long journeys, the udasis, across the Indian subcontinent and beyond. Scholars dispute these stories: Callewaert and Snell note that early Sikh texts do not contain them, and they grew more elaborate over the centuries. Nanak held discourses with Hindu and Muslim figures and drew followers from both backgrounds. By about the age of 50 he had a following known as the Nanak Panth, and on the Ravi he founded an ashram on donated land that became Kartarpur.

Nanak wrote in a composite vernacular called Sant Bhasha rather than only in Arabic, Persian or Sanskrit. His 974 hymns were gathered by Guru Arjan in the Ādi Granth in 1604, with the Japji opening the work. The Japji asks about the nature of the universe without claiming final answers. Nanak held that it was more important to be a good human being than a good Muslim or a good Hindu. He chose neither of his sons as successor, and his compositions passed to Guru Angad when he became guru. Recent scholarship places his movement within the Sant and Bhakti traditions of medieval India rather than seeing it as a blend of Hinduism and Islam.
gurugram: Gurugram lies in the south-eastern part of Haryana, on the border with Delhi. It is about 30 kilometres south-west of New Delhi and 268 kilometres south of Chandigarh, the state capital. The city covers 333 square kilometres at an average elevation of 237 metres above sea level. It stands on the Sahibi River, a tributary of the Yamuna that rises in the Aravalli range, and its climate is hot and semi-arid, with a monsoon from late June to September. Mangar Bani, a sacred grove between Gurgaon and Faridabad, is among the last surviving natural forests of the National Capital Region and is protected by Gurjars of the nearby area.

The region originally fell under the Kuru kingdom, and in the late 4th century BCE it was absorbed by the Maurya Empire in the early expansion of Chandragupta Maurya. Gurgaon may be the Gudapura mentioned in the 12th-century Prithviraja Vijaya, where Nagarjuna, a cousin of King Prithviraj Chauhan, rebelled and seized the town before the king recaptured it. Alexander Cunningham recorded a stone pillar of a local lord, Durgga Naga, with an inscription dated to 672 CE or 871 CE.

In the Mughal period and in the early British period Gurgaon was a small village in the Jharsa pargana of the Delhi subah. The pargana passed to Begum Samru in 1776-77 and came under direct British rule in 1836 after her death, when the British set up a civil lines at Jharsa and a cavalry cantonment at Hiyadatpur. Gurgaon became a district in 1818 after the Bharawas district was disbanded. British-era buildings include the Church of the Epiphany and Kaman Serai, built in 1925, and the Gurgaon Club. On 12 April 2016 the chief minister of Haryana, Manohar Lal Khattar, proposed the name Gurugram, meaning village of the Guru, citing the city's association with Drona; the Union Government approved it on 27 September 2016.

Gurugram is the administrative headquarters of Gurgaon district and a satellite city of Delhi within the National Capital Region. It had 876,969 inhabitants at the 2011 census, and Hindi was the first language of 74.18 per cent of them. The city is divided into 36 wards and 115 sectors. Its economy grew around the Maruti Suzuki plant and, later, outsourcing operations set up by General Electric with the developer DLF, and it adjoins the manufacturing and real-estate areas of New Gurgaon, Manesar and Sohna. The Sheetla Mata Mandir, dedicated to Kripi, the wife of Dronacharya, stands at the centre of the city.
gurung: The Gurung call themselves Tamu, and Gurung is the name used by outsiders. According to oral tradition, Gurung derives from a Tibetan word, gru-gu, meaning to bring down, which reflects a migration from the Tibetan plateau to the southern slopes of the Himalayas. The origin of the people has been traced back to the Qiang people of Qinghai in China. The Gurung have historically lived a semi-nomadic life, herding sheep and yaks in the Himalayan foothills, although many have since taken up other occupations.

They live mostly in the hills and mountains of Gandaki Province in Nepal. In the census of 2011, 798,658 people, 2.97 per cent of the population of Nepal, identified as Gurung. They form a large share of the people of Manang, Lamjung, Kaski, Mustang and Gorkha districts.

After the Anglo-Nepalese War ended and the Treaty of Sugauli was signed in 1816, the British began to recruit soldiers for the British Army from the northern villages of Nepal. Most came from four peoples, one of which was the Gurung. Gurungs served in the Gorkha regiments of the British and Indian armies and in the Singapore Police Force, and they played a prominent part in both world wars. Their service brought decorations, among them Victoria Crosses. Gurungs are still recruited into the British, Indian and Bruneian armies, and they retire after serving between 15 and 35 years. In 1999 the British government changed its policy and allowed Gurkha retirees of the British Army to settle in the United Kingdom with their families.

The Gurung language, also called Tamu Kyi, is a tonal Tibeto-Burman language. It was traditionally passed on by word of mouth and is now also written in Devanagari and in community-developed scripts. Most speakers are also fluent in Nepali, and migration and urbanisation have reduced its use among younger people. The main festival is Tamu Lhosar, which marks the new year on the 15th of Poush, in December or January.

Gurung religion includes the traditions called Ghyabri and Pachyu. Lamas perform Buddhist rites at births, funerals and Lhosar, mainly in Lamjung, Parbat, Kaski, Manang and Mustang, while some villages keep remnants of the pre-Buddhist Bon religion and of an older shamanic belief system. Traditional dress was made of handwoven wool and plant fibres such as nettle. Women wear the cholo blouse, the phariya skirt and the patuki sash, with ornaments; men wear the kachhad, a white wrap, with the bhoto shirt. It is now worn mainly at festivals and rituals.
gushi-khan: Güshi Khan was born Torobaikhu, the third son of Akhai Khatun and Khanai Noyan Khonggor, chief of the Khoshuts, and was descended from Qasar, a younger brother of Genghis Khan. At twelve he had already won renown in battle against the Turkistanis. In 1625 a quarrel over inheritance between the Khoshut chief Chöükür and his brother Baibaghas left Baibaghas dead; Güshi and Köndölön Ubashi pursued Chöükür from the Ishim River to the Tobol, and Güshi succeeded Baibaghas as chief of the Khoshut.

Sonam Rapten, chief attendant of the young 5th Dalai Lama, planned to end the persecution of the Gelug school and unify Tibet with Güshi's help, and the Gelug monasteries appealed to him against the Khalkha prince Choghtu Khong Tayiji. With the Dzungar prince Erdeni Batur, Güshi marched into Qinghai with 10,000 Oirat troops in 1636, and in 1637 he defeated Choghtu's 30,000 men in the Battle of the Bloody Hill; Choghtu was found hiding and killed. Visiting Lhasa as a pilgrim in 1638, he was proclaimed Holder of the Doctrine Chogyal.

When the Bön king of Beri in Kham, Donyo Dorje, plotted with the Tsangpa ruler Karma Tenkyong against the Gelug, Güshi invaded in 1639; the Beri ruler was executed and Kham subdued by 1641. His troops then besieged Shigatse, which an eyewitness described as a cremation ground heaped with corpses, and the castle surrendered on 25 March 1642. After further resistance in Kongpo, Güshi had Karma Tenkyong executed and his army killed 7,000 rebels, while many Karma Kagyu monasteries were forcibly converted to the Gelug.

Under the new order, a renewal of the patron and priest relationship of the Yuan era, Güshi kept the armed forces but did not interfere much in the affairs of Central Tibet, spending summers at Dam by Tengri-nor and winters at Lhasa, while Sonam Rapten acted as regent. An expedition into Bhutan in 1644 ended in a major defeat. Güshi died on 14 January 1655, leaving ten sons; his eldest, Dayan, succeeded him as Dharma king, and the system of a Khoshut protector over Tibet lasted four generations, until 1717.
gusinje: Gusinje lies at an elevation of 1,014 m in the Plav-Gusinje area of the upper Lim valley, in the Accursed Mountains. It stands on the Vermosh River, the first tributary of the Lim, which flows east towards Lake Plav. Zla Kolata, the highest mountain in Montenegro, rises about 10 km to the south in Prokletije National Park. The town is the seat of Gusinje Municipality, which covers 157 km2, much of it mountain land used in the past for herding.

A medieval settlement stood here, and Gusinje was a caravan station on the route from Ragusa and Cattaro through Scutari to Peć in the 14th century. In 1485 Ottoman records list it as a village of 96 households in the imperial domain of Plav. The Venetian diplomat Mariano Bolizza reported that a fortress was finished late in 1612, built at the request of the Ottoman bey of Podgorica to check raids by the Kelmendi on the trade routes. Kelmendi and other highland groups later formed many of the town's neighbourhoods, and largely converted to Islam by the middle of the 18th century. In 1852 it had 1,500 households, 350 shops and five mosques.

The Treaty of San Stefano and then the Congress of Berlin awarded Gusinje and Plav to Montenegro. Albanians there protested and formed the League of Prizren. Ali Pasha Shabanagaj, a landowner and commander from Gusinje, led its forces at the Battle of Novšiće, where they defeated a Montenegrin force under Marko Miljanov. More than 140 of about 300 League casualties came from Gusinje. The annexation was stopped and Ulcinj was given to Montenegro as compensation.

Montenegrin forces entered Plav on 19 and 20 October 1912. The harsh military rule that followed caused, by one account in the sources, up to 1,800 killings and 12,000 forced conversions to Orthodoxy by March 1913. After the Balkan Wars the town was assigned to Montenegro and its border with Albania was closed. In 1919 an Albanian revolt rose against inclusion in the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, and about 450 civilians were killed after it was put down.

Gusinje had 1,673 inhabitants at the 2011 census and has been a municipality of its own again since 2014, after belonging to Plav Municipality from 1953. Most of its people are Muslim, speaking Albanian or a Slavic dialect that shows strong Albanian influence. The oldest surviving mosque is the Čekića džamija of 1687; the Vezir's mosque dates from 1765 and the New Mosque from 1899.
gustav-adolf-von-gotzen: Gustav Adolf Graf von Götzen was born on 12 May 1866 at Scharfeneck Castle, his comital family's seat in the Kingdom of Prussia, now Sarny Castle in Poland. He studied law at Paris, Berlin and Kiel from 1884 to 1887 and became a lieutenant in the 2nd Garde-Ulanen regiment in 1887. While stationed in Rome in 1890-1891 he made his first African journey, a hunting trip to Mount Kilimanjaro, and in 1892 he travelled to the Ottoman Empire with Major Walther von Diest.

To claim the unexplored interior of East Africa for Germany, Götzen set out from Pangani on 21 December 1893 with Georg von Prittwitz und Gaffron and Hermann Kersting. On 2 May 1894 they crossed the Kagera at Rusumo Falls into the Kingdom of Rwanda, which Oscar Baumann had briefly entered in 1892, and met the mwami at his palace in Kageyo. After climbing in the Virunga Mountains they pushed west through the Congo forest, reached the Congo River on 21 September and the Atlantic on 29 November. From 1896 to 1898 he was attaché in Washington and observed the Spanish-American War beside Theodore Roosevelt.

Appointed governor of German East Africa in March 1901, he faced the Maji Maji Rebellion in 1905, which soon spread over about half the colony. He called for reinforcements and crushed it by force. Official figures gave his own losses as 15 Europeans and 389 African soldiers; estimates of the Africans who died in the famine that followed range from 75,000 to 300,000. The historian Mark Levene compares his method, starvation, with the Herero and Nama genocide in German South-West Africa.

Götzen left the colony on 14 June 1906, officially for ill health, after a report on the rising's causes that the Foreign Office accepted to avoid a scandal, and civilian control of the colonies followed. As envoy in Hamburg he wrote a defence of his actions, published in 1909. He died in Schöneberg on 1 December 1910. The steamer Graf von Götzen, scuttled on Lake Tanganyika in 1916, was refloated and returned to service in 1927 as the MV Liemba.
gustav-husak: Gustáv Husák was born Augustin Husák on 10 January 1913 at Pozsonyhidegkút in the Kingdom of Hungary, now Bratislava-Dúbravka. His father, a quarryman and farmer, had been disabled in World War I, and his mother died of tuberculosis when he was one year old. He studied at boarding schools in Bratislava, worked odd jobs to help his family and joined the Communist Youth Union in 1929. He began law studies at Comenius University in Bratislava in 1933 and joined the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia. During World War II the government of Jozef Tiso jailed him several times, and he was a leader of the Slovak National Uprising of 1944.

From 1946 to 1950 Husák headed the devolved administration of Slovakia. He contributed strongly to the suppression of the Democratic Party of Slovakia, which had won 62 per cent in Slovakia in 1946. In 1950 he fell victim to a Stalinist purge, was arrested in 1951 and was sentenced in 1954 to life imprisonment, serving in Leopoldov Prison until 1960. His conviction was overturned in 1963. In April 1968 he became a vice-premier under Alexander Dubček.

After the invasion of August 1968 he took part in the negotiations in Moscow with Leonid Brezhnev and became a leader of those who wanted the reforms reversed. He succeeded Dubček as head of the party in April 1969, purged liberal members in 1969-1971 and was elected president in 1975. The secret police ran a campaign of repression against dissidents, later represented by Charter 77. In December 1987 he gave up the party leadership to Miloš Jakeš.

On 24 November 1989, during the Velvet Revolution, the entire Presidium of the Communist Party, Husák included, resigned. On 10 December he swore in a government with a non-communist majority and resigned the same day. The party expelled him in February 1990, and he died on 18 November 1991, aged 78. His moral responsibility for the last two decades of communist rule remains in question. He later said he had tried to lessen the effects of the Soviet invasion and resist hardliners, while critics note that he was nominal head of the repressive apparatus and gave almost no attention to appeals from the persecuted.
gustav-i-of-sweden: Gustav Eriksson was probably born in 1496, the son of Cecilia Månsdotter Eka and Erik Johansson Vasa, most likely at Rydboholm Castle. He and his father supported the party of Sten Sture the Younger, regent from 1512, against King Christian II of Denmark in the struggle over the Kalmar Union. Taken hostage by the Danes, Gustav escaped from Kalø in 1519 and reached Lübeck on 30 September, perhaps disguised as a drover. Returning to Sweden on 31 May 1520, he declined an invitation to Christian's coronation in Stockholm. Close to 100 people, among them his father, were then executed in the Stockholm Bloodbath.

Gustav went to Dalarna, where the stories of his adventures rest largely on Peder Svart's strongly biased chronicle and cannot be verified. After first being refused, he was appointed military commander, and in February 1521 his force of about 400 men came mainly from the Lake Siljan area. A rebel victory at Brunnbäck's Ferry in April and the sacking of Västerås, with its copper and silver mines, brought him resources and supporters. In August the leading noblemen of Götaland declared him regent at Vadstena. Lübeck joined the war in 1522.

At Strängnäs in June 1523 the leading men of Sweden chose him as king, and on 17 June the rebels entered Stockholm. The Treaty of Malmö of 1524 made Denmark-Norway acknowledge Swedish independence, though Gustav failed to win Gotland and Blekinge.

When the Pope refused to accept Gustav's choice of archbishop and demanded the reinstatement of the exiled Gustav Trolle, Gustav appointed Laurentius Petri himself in 1531, and the Pope lost any influence over the Swedish Church. Olaus Petri's New Testament appeared in 1526, and a full Bible, the Gustav Vasa Bible, in 1540–41. The Church's assets were nationalised and the Lutheran Church placed under his control. He replaced the prerogatives of local landowners, nobles and clergy with centrally appointed governors and bishops, and began a standing army and navy.

He met resistance: Dalarna rebelled three times in the first ten years, and peasants in Småland under Nils Dacke rose in 1542 over taxes, church reform and the confiscation of church bells, until Gustav defeated them in the spring of 1543 with German mercenaries. He fought an inconclusive war with Ivan the Terrible of Russia in 1554 to 1557. He summoned representatives of the four estates, including peasants, to the Riksdag assemblies of 1527 and 1544.

Gustav died on 29 September 1560 and was buried in Uppsala Cathedral. Historians note the brutality of his methods, and the stories of his adventures are considered largely legend and his own propaganda. The annual Vasaloppet ski event and the founding of Helsinki in 1550 are linked with his name.
gustav-iii: Gustav was born in Stockholm on 24 January 1746, the eldest son of King Adolf Frederick and Queen Louisa Ulrika. He was educated under two governors who were among the most eminent Swedish statesmen of the day, Carl Gustaf Tessin and Carl Fredrik Scheffer, though he perhaps owed most to the poet and historian Olof von Dalin. His parents taught him to despise the governors the Riksdag had imposed. On 4 November 1766 he married Princess Sophia Magdalena of Denmark in Stockholm. As heir he forced the dominant Cap faction in the December Crisis of 1768 to summon an extraordinary diet, hoping to increase the power of the crown, but the Hat party refused to keep its pledges.

When he became king the Riksdag held more power than the monarchy and was divided between the Hats and Caps. The attempts of the Caps to reduce him to a powerless king, and fears of Russian influence, led him to the coup d'état of 1772, which ended the Age of Liberty. His reforms followed those of other enlightened sovereigns: torture to gain confessions was abolished, the death penalty restricted, and an ordinance of 1774 allowed the press liberty within certain limits. He founded the Royal Swedish Opera in 1773 and later the Royal Dramatic Theatre, and in 1777 he was the first formally neutral head of state to recognise the United States.

From 1786 he increasingly ruled without a parliament. After Catherine the Great refused to support his plan to acquire Norway, he declared war on Russia in June 1788 without the consent of the estates, which provoked the Anjala Conspiracy among his officers in Finland. The Act of Union and Security of 17 February 1789 reinforced royal authority and abolished most of the privileges of the nobility. The Swedes broke a Russian blockade at Svensksund on 9 July 1790, and the Treaty of Värälä followed on 14 August.

The war and the Act of 1789 deepened the nobility's hatred of the king, and in the winter of 1791-92 nobles plotted his murder. He was shot in the lower back at a masked ball at the Royal Opera House in Stockholm at midnight on 16 March 1792 and died on 29 March of sepsis, after receiving apologies from many political enemies. A regency under his brother Prince Carl and Gustaf Adolf Reuterholm ruled until his son came of age in 1796. The assassination was the basis of Verdi's opera Un ballo in maschera. His funeral took place on 14 May 1792.
gustav-iv-adolf: Gustav Adolf was born in Stockholm on 1 November 1778, the son of King Gustav III and Queen Sophia Magdalena. He was raised by his father and by the liberal-minded Nils von Rosenstein. When Gustav III was assassinated in March 1792 he succeeded to the throne at the age of 13, under the regency of his uncle Prince Charles, Duke of Södermanland.

In August 1796 the regent arranged for him to visit Saint Petersburg to arrange a marriage with Grand Duchess Alexandra Pavlovna, a granddaughter of Catherine the Great. The plan failed because Gustav Adolf refused to let his intended bride worship according to Russian Orthodox rites. On 31 October 1797 he married Friederike Dorothea of Baden instead, and they had five children.

When he came of age in 1796 he dismissed Gustaf Adolf Reuterholm, the regent's detested adviser, which added to his popularity. His horror of Jacobinism was intense, and he postponed his coronation for some years to avoid calling a diet. State finances, disordered by Gustav III's war against Russia, and crop failures in 1798 and 1799 forced him to summon the estates to Norrköping in 1800. He met serious opposition and resolved never to call the Riksdag again.

In 1805 he joined the Third Coalition against Napoleon, and the French occupied Swedish Pomerania. After Russia made peace and an alliance with France at Tilsit in 1807, Sweden was left, with Portugal, as Great Britain's only ally on the Continent. Russia invaded Finland on 21 February 1808, and Denmark declared war on Sweden. In a few months almost all of Finland was lost. By the Treaty of Fredrikshamn on 17 September 1809 Sweden surrendered the eastern third of its territory, and the Grand Duchy of Finland was established within Imperial Russia.

On 7 March 1809 Lieutenant-Colonel Georg Adlersparre raised a rebellion at Karlstad and began to march on Stockholm. On 13 March seven conspirators led by Carl Johan Adlercreutz seized the king and imprisoned him and his family at Gripsholm Castle, and his uncle accepted the leadership of a provisional government. Gustav Adolf abdicated on 29 March to save the crown for his son, but on 10 May the Riksdag declared that his whole family had forfeited the throne. His uncle was proclaimed Charles XIII on 5 June and accepted a new constitution, the Instrument of Government, ratified the next day. It remained in force until 1974.

In exile Gustav Adolf used titles such as Count Gottorp and divorced his wife in 1812. He settled in St Gallen in Switzerland, living in a small hotel under the name of Colonel Gustafsson, where he suffered a stroke and died on 7 February 1837. His body was later brought to Sweden and buried in Riddarholm Church.
gustav-klimt: Gustav Klimt was born on 14 July 1862 in Baumgarten, near Vienna, the second of seven children. His father, Ernst Klimt the Elder, was a gold engraver from a peasant family in Bohemia who often struggled to find work, and the family lived in poverty and moved address at least five times between 1862 and 1884. Klimt's brother Ernst, later an engraver like their father, enrolled with him at the Kunstgewerbeschule. With their friend Franz von Matsch, Klimt and Ernst formed by 1880 a team called the Künstlercompagnie, which secured many commissions, including murals in the Kunsthistorisches Museum and decorations for theatres built by the firm Fellner & Helmer.

In 1897 Klimt became a founding member and president of the Vienna Secession and of its periodical, Ver Sacrum. The group aimed to give exhibitions to unconventional young artists and to bring the best foreign artists to Vienna, and it declared no manifesto, so that Naturalists, Realists and Symbolists coexisted. Klimt painted his version of its symbol, Pallas Athena, in 1898, and he remained with the Secession until 1908. His paintings for the ceiling of the Great Hall of the University of Vienna, completed around 1900, were criticised as pornographic, after which he accepted no more public commissions.

From 1900 Klimt became known above all as a painter of women, producing about one large portrait a year in which flatness, decoration and gold leaf followed the principles of Art Nouveau. His golden phase included Judith I (1901), Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I (1907), The Kiss (1907–08) and the Stoclet Frieze (1905–1911), and it brought positive critical reaction and financial success. In 1911 his Death and Life won first prize at the world exhibition in Rome. On 11 January 1918 he suffered a stroke that paralysed his right side, and he died in Vienna on 6 February from pneumonia brought on by an early case of Spanish flu, aged 55, leaving many paintings unfinished.

Klimt's primary subject was the female body, and his work is marked by frank eroticism. He treated Old Testament heroines as dangerous femmes fatales and took life, love and death as important themes. Among the Secession artists he was the most influenced by Japanese art. He also painted landscapes. His work was an important influence on the younger Egon Schiele, and Klimt supported Schiele's 1917 plan for an artists' association, the Kunsthalle, which failed for lack of funding.

The Nazis looted many of Klimt's works during the Second World War, and several were destroyed. In 2006 an Austrian arbitration board ordered five paintings, among them Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I, returned to an heir of the Jewish family that had owned them, and that portrait was then sold to Ronald Lauder for the Neue Galerie New York.
gustav-landauer: Gustav Landauer was born in Karlsruhe on 7 April 1870, into a well-to-do middle-class Jewish family of assimilated, non-religious parents. His father, a shoe store owner, intended him for a commercial career, but he turned to music and literature, drawing his real education from the theatre, books and music, and from the philosophies of Baruch Spinoza, Arthur Schopenhauer and Friedrich Nietzsche. Between 1888 and 1891 he studied Germanics, philosophy and history at Heidelberg, Berlin and Strasbourg. Returning to Berlin in 1891, he was driven from the Social Democratic Party by its strictly Marxist Erfurt program and turned towards anarchism, joining the staff of the newspaper Der Sozialist.

Der Sozialist under Landauer became the country's only anarchist newspaper. In 1893 he was sent to prison for an article advocating disobedience of the law, and he was jailed again in 1899. In prison he translated the sermons of Meister Eckhart, and his Skepsis und Mystik (1903) argued that once skepticism has cleared away old illusions, new self-created illusions are necessary for life. In Die Revolution (1907) he portrayed the Middle Ages as an age of organic community destroyed by the modern state.

In 1908 he launched the Socialist Bund, a federation of autonomous communities meant to begin socialist construction outside the capitalist state. Its members included Martin Buber and Erich Mühsam. In Aufruf zum Sozialismus (1911) he rejected historical materialism, arguing that socialism arises from human will and ethical necessity, and that the state is a relationship between people that can be replaced by behaving differently. A committed pacifist, he advocated a general strike against war and opposed the First World War.

In late 1918 Kurt Eisner called Landauer to Munich, where he advocated a socialist democracy based on workers' and soldiers' councils. After the first Bavarian Räterepublik was proclaimed on 7 April 1919, he served as Commissioner for Enlightenment and Public Instruction. When Freikorps and Reichswehr troops moved against the republic, he was arrested on 1 May, and on 2 May he was beaten to death by soldiers in Stadelheim Prison. A monument to him in Munich's Waldfriedhof, erected in 1925, was destroyed by the Nazis in 1933. His ideas influenced Martin Buber, Ernst Toller and the socialist wing of the German youth movement.
gustav-mahler: Mahler was born on 7 July 1860 in the village of Kaliště in Bohemia, the second son of a German-speaking Jewish family of humble circumstances. His father, Bernhard Mahler, rose from a pedlar's family to become a coachman and then an innkeeper, and married Marie Herrmann in 1857. They had 14 children. In December 1860 the family moved to Jihlava, where Bernhard built up a distillery and tavern business and where Gustav heard street songs, dance tunes, folk melodies and the trumpet calls of the local military band. These sounds later fed his musical vocabulary. He studied at the Vienna Conservatory from 1875 to 1878.

Mahler's first professional conducting job, in the summer of 1880, was an operetta season at the spa town of Bad Hall. Posts followed at Laibach, Prague, Leipzig, Budapest and Hamburg, each larger than the last. In Leipzig he took charge of most of Wagner's Ring cycle when a senior colleague fell ill, and scored a public success, though the orchestra resented his dictatorial manner and heavy rehearsals. In 1897 he became director of the Vienna Court Opera, having converted to Catholicism to secure the post. He also led the Vienna Philharmonic's subscription concerts from 1898 to 1901, and the anti-Semitic press attacked him throughout his ten years in the city.

Mahler made his New York debut at the Metropolitan Opera on 1 January 1908, conducting Wagner's Tristan und Isolde, and later led the New York Philharmonic. He gave his last concert at Carnegie Hall on 21 February 1911 with a fever. Diagnosed with bacterial endocarditis, he was taken back to Europe and died in a Vienna sanatorium on 18 May 1911, aged 50.

Composing was for most of his life a part-time activity, done in summer studios while conducting paid his living. Apart from juvenilia he wrote only songs and symphonies, and the two forms are closely linked: melodies of the song cycle Lieder eines fahrenden Gesellen appear in the First Symphony, and Wunderhorn songs form movements of the Second, Third and Fourth. He told Sibelius that the symphony must be like the world and embrace everything, and his music mixes bird calls, bugle fanfares and street tunes with solemn matter. He left Das Lied von der Erde unnumbered, hoping to escape the curse of the Ninth Symphony.

His symphonies were often controversial when first performed. By his death there had been more than 260 performances of them. Nazi-era bans kept the music from much of Europe, but after 1945 a new generation rediscovered it. Arnold Schoenberg, Alban Berg and Anton Webern of the Second Viennese School were among his early admirers. The International Gustav Mahler Society was founded in 1955.
gustav-nachtigal: Gustav Nachtigal was born on 23 February 1834 at Eichstedt in the Prussian province of Saxony-Anhalt, the son of a Lutheran pastor. His father died of pulmonary tuberculosis in 1839, when the boy was five. He studied medicine at the universities of Halle, Würzburg and Greifswald and practised for several years as a military surgeon in Cologne. After contracting a lung disease he moved to Annaba in Algeria in October 1862, and in 1863 he went to Tunis, where he studied Arabic.

After returning to Germany, Nachtigal met Friedrich Gerhard Rohlfs, who asked him to go to the Bornu Empire. King Wilhelm I of Prussia commissioned him to carry gifts to Umar Kura, the ruler of Bornu, in acknowledgment of the kindness shown to German travellers such as Heinrich Barth. He set out from Ottoman Tripoli in 1869 with eight camels and six men. On the way he visited Tibesti and Borku, regions of the central Sahara not previously known to Europeans.

From Bornu he went on to Baguirmi, then to Wadai and to Kordofan. He emerged at Khartoum in the winter of 1874, after having been given up as lost. His account, Saharâ und Sûdân, appeared in Berlin from 1879, and in 1882 the Royal Geographical Society awarded him its Founder's Medal.

After the establishment of a French protectorate over Tunisia, Nachtigal served as the German Empire's consul-general there until 1884. Chancellor Otto von Bismarck then appointed him special commissioner for West Africa, to establish a German claim before the British could advance their own. He established Togoland and Kamerun as Germany's first colonial possessions.

Nachtigal died at sea aboard the gunboat Möwe off Cape Palmas on 20 April 1885, and in 1888 his remains were moved from Grand Bassam to a ceremonial grave at Duala. He is regarded, with Heinrich Barth, as one of the two important German explorers of Africa, and his work is noted for its detail and for his view that Africans were not inferior to Europeans. Having seen slave hunts carried out by African rulers, he believed that European domination might end them, which drew him into colonial work. In 2022 Berlin's Nachtigalplatz was renamed Manga-Bell-Platz, after the Duala king and resistance leader Rudolf Duala Manga Bell.
gustav-noske: Gustav Noske was born on 9 July 1868 in Brandenburg an der Havel, Prussia, the son of a weaver and a manual labourer. He was apprenticed as a basket maker and travelled as a journeyman to Halle, Frankfurt, Amsterdam and Liegnitz. He joined the Social Democratic Party in 1884, and in 1892 he became chairman of the Brandenburg SPD. From 1902 to 1918 he was chief editor of the Volksstimme in Chemnitz, and from 1907 he sat in the Reichstag.

He was the party's expert on military, navy and colonial questions and a reformist. During the First World War he supported the war loans and, in 1916 to 1918, spoke for a commission that investigated military procurement and excess profits.

In early November 1918 Prince Max von Baden sent him to Kiel to negotiate an end to the mutiny. The mutineers elected him chairman of the Soldiers' Council, but within days he had restored the officers' authority. On 30 December 1918 he joined the Council of the People's Deputies, responsible for military affairs. When the Spartacist uprising began in Berlin on 5 January 1919, Friedrich Ebert ordered it quashed and Noske used regular forces and Freikorps units, and around 165 people died. On 15 January Freikorps men under Captain Waldemar Pabst abducted and murdered Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg. Noske had earlier ordered Liebknecht's telephone line monitored and reported to Pabst.

In February 1919 he became Reichswehrminister in Philipp Scheidemann's government, and he stayed in Gustav Bauer's. Over the first half of 1919 left-wing uprisings were put down by army and Freikorps across the Reich. He supported signing the Treaty of Versailles despite misgivings. On 28 February 1920 he dissolved two Freikorps naval brigades on the orders of the Allied commission, and General Walther von Lüttwitz's refusal led to the Kapp Putsch. When the unions demanded his resignation as a condition for ending the general strike, he resigned on 22 March 1920.

Noske was governor of the Province of Hanover from 1920. The Nazi government dismissed him on 1 October 1933. The Gestapo arrested him on 22 July 1944 on suspicion of involvement in the 20 July plot, and he spent seven months in camps, among them Ravensbrück. He died in Hanover on 30 November 1946 from a stroke. He remains controversial. Some historians credit him with the courage to be, in his own words, the bloodhound who spared Germany chaos, while another called him a primitive brute in love with violence.
gustav-simon: Simon was the son of a railway official whose family farmed small plots in the Hunsrück. He trained as a schoolteacher in Merzig but found no post, worked as a railway assistant in Hermeskeil and a customs broker, and then studied economics and law at the Johann Wolfgang Goethe University in Frankfurt am Main from 1922 to 1925. He joined the Nazi Party on 14 August 1925 and led its student group in Frankfurt.

After a short time as a business teacher in Völklingen he worked full-time for the party at the invitation of Robert Ley. He became district leader for Koblenz-Trier in 1929, entered the Reichstag in 1930 and was appointed Gauleiter on 1 June 1931. He was known as a corrupt administrator, and his short stature earned him the nickname the Toadstool of Hermeskeil.

In Luxembourg he suspended the constitution, introduced the Reichsmark, banned all parties except the Ethnic German Movement and dissolved the Parliament and Council of State. He also banned Luxembourgish, and from 1941 required Luxembourgers to take German given names. After the general strike of 1942 he declared martial law; 20 strike leaders were executed at the Hinzert concentration camp, some 2,000 people were arrested and 290 students deported to camps in Germany. Of about 3,500 Jews in Luxembourg at the start of the occupation, about 1,945 had perished by the war's end.

Simon fled Luxembourg on 9 September 1944 and later commanded the Volkssturm in Moselland. After the war he hid in Upsprunge, Westphalia, under his mother's maiden name, posing as a gardener, until British Captain Hanns Alexander arrested him on 10 December 1945. He tried to cut his wrists in the prison at Paderborn and died on 18 December.

The official version holds that he hanged himself in his cell before being handed over to Luxembourg. Another account, investigated in studies of British and Luxembourgish archives, holds that he was killed after being taken from Paderborn prison, and the family of Hanns Alexander believed him involved. His death prevented any trial.
gustav-stresemann: Gustav Stresemann was born on 10 May 1878 in southeast Berlin, the youngest of seven children. He studied political economy, history and international law at the University of Berlin and Leipzig University, where he wrote a doctoral thesis on the bottled beer industry in Berlin. In his early writings he combined liberalism with strident nationalism, a mixture that marked his views for the rest of his life. In 1907 he was elected to the Reichstag for the National Liberal Party, and he became the party's leader after the death of Ernst Bassermann in 1917.

During the First World War he supported the Hohenzollern monarchy and German annexations. Germany's defeat and the revolution of 1918–1919 drove him into a mental and physical breakdown, and he abandoned his earlier militarism. Refused entry to the German Democratic Party because of his wartime record, he gathered the right wing of the National Liberals into the German People's Party. At first it opposed the Weimar Republic, but by late 1920 he was moving towards cooperation with the centre and left, though he remained a monarchist at heart.

On 13 August 1923 he became chancellor and foreign minister of a grand coalition. On 26 September he announced the end of passive resistance to the French and Belgian occupation of the Ruhr, and his government introduced the Rentenmark to end hyperinflation, which peaked in November. After the Social Democrats left the coalition he lost a confidence vote on 23 November 1923 and resigned, but stayed on as foreign minister in eight successive governments.

His policy rested on fulfilling the Treaty of Versailles in good faith so as to show that its reparations were beyond Germany's means, and on close economic ties with the United States. The Dawes Plan of 1924 reduced reparations and ended the Ruhr occupation. The Locarno Treaties, signed in October 1925, confirmed Germany's western borders; he refused a similar guarantee for the east, saying there would be no Locarno of the east. Germany joined the League of Nations in September 1926 and signed the Kellogg-Briand Pact in 1928.

Stresemann shared the 1926 Nobel Peace Prize with Aristide Briand. Nationalists attacked him as a fulfilment politician, and he was seen as a republican by reason rather than by conviction. His health worsened after 1928. He died of a series of strokes on 3 October 1929, aged 51, hours after persuading the Reichstag to accept the Young Plan. The Great Depression soon undid the American credit on which his strategy depended.
gustav-struve: Struve was born in Munich, the son of Johann Christoph Gustav von Struve, a Russian diplomat of the lesser nobility who served at embassies in Warsaw, Munich and The Hague and later as ambassador at the court of Baden in Karlsruhe. He studied law at Göttingen and Heidelberg, worked in the civil service of Oldenburg from 1829 to 1831 and in 1836 settled as a lawyer in Mannheim. As editor of the Mannheimer Journal he defended Baden's liberal deputies, was repeatedly sentenced to prison and was forced to give up the paper in 1846. He married Amalie Düsar in 1845 and dropped the aristocratic von in 1847.

After the Pre-Parliament rejected his demand for a federal republic of all Germany, Struve and Hecker organised a revolutionary assembly in Konstanz on 14 April 1848. Few joined their march, which troops from Frankfurt halted in the Black Forest, and both men fled to Switzerland. There Struve published Die Grundrechte des deutschen Volkes and, with Karl Heinzen, drew up a plan for the republicanisation of Germany. His rising at Lörrach on 21 September 1848 failed. Freed in the May Uprising of 1849, he helped overthrow the hesitant Lorenz Brentano before Prussian troops defeated the revolutionaries at Rastatt on 23 July.

In exile in the United States from 1851, Struve lived in Philadelphia and New York, edited German papers and wrote Weltgeschichte, a universal history from a radical republican standpoint and the main work of his career. He supported John Frémont in 1856 and Abraham Lincoln in 1860, and served briefly as a Union captain under Blenker, resigning rather than serve under Prince Felix Salm-Salm. An abolitionist, he opposed plans to settle freed slaves in Liberia.

A general amnesty of 1863 allowed Struve to return to Germany. Lincoln named him US consul at Sonneberg in 1865, but the Thuringian states refused him recognition because of his radical writings. He settled in Vienna in 1869 and died there on 21 August 1870. A vegetarian since 1832 under the influence of Rousseau's Émile, he wrote the first German vegetarian novel, Mandaras Wanderungen, in 1833 and founded the Stuttgart Vegetarian Society in 1868. The historian Corinna Treitel notes that he linked vegetarianism to republican self-government.
gustave-flaubert: Gustave Flaubert was born in Rouen on 12 December 1821, the second son of Anne Justine Caroline Fleuriot and Achille-Cléophas Flaubert, director and senior surgeon of the major hospital in Rouen. He began writing at an early age, as early as eight according to some sources. He was educated at the Lycée Pierre-Corneille and in 1840 went to Paris to study law, where he was an indifferent student and found the city distasteful. In 1846, after an attack of epilepsy, he left Paris and abandoned the study of law. He then returned to Croisset, near the Seine and close to Rouen, and lived there for the rest of his life.

His first finished work was a novella, November, completed in 1842. In September 1849 he completed the first version of The Temptation of Saint Anthony and read it aloud to Louis Bouilhet and Maxime Du Camp over four days. They told him to throw the manuscript in the fire and to write about day-to-day life instead. After returning from Egypt in 1850 he began Madame Bovary, which took five years to write and was serialised in the Revue de Paris in 1856. The government brought an action against publisher and author on a charge of immorality, but both were acquitted in 1857, and the book was warmly received.

In 1858 he travelled to Carthage to gather material for Salammbô, completed in 1862. Sentimental Education, published in 1869 after seven years, was his last complete novel; it follows a young man, Frédéric Moreau, through the Revolution of 1848 and the founding of the Second French Empire. Between 1875 and 1877 he wrote Three Tales, and he spent the rest of his life on the unfinished satire Bouvard et Pécuchet, published after his death in 1881. He was a prolific letter writer, and his Correspondence is among the works for which he is best known.

Flaubert pursued the principle of le mot juste, the right word, and avoided the inexact, the abstract and the cliché. He worked in solitude, sometimes spending a week on one page, and wrote that he wished to forge a style rhythmic as verse and precise as the language of the sciences.

He published far less than peers such as Balzac or Zola, and Walter Pater called him the martyr of style. Madame Bovary was followed by more scandal than admiration at first, but its scrupulously truthful portraiture of life was gradually accepted, and at his death he was widely regarded as the most influential French Realist. Guy de Maupassant, Émile Zola and Alphonse Daudet were among those he influenced. He died at Croisset of a cerebral haemorrhage on 8 May 1880, aged 58, and was buried in the family vault at Rouen.
gustavia: France first claimed Saint Barthélemy in 1648. In 1784 the island was given to Sweden in exchange for trade rights in Gothenburg, and Sweden founded the Swedish West India Company to run it. The site of the later town was known as Le Carénage, the Careening, because it offered shelter to damaged ships. Archival records show the name Gustavia appearing between 28 December 1786 and 9 February 1787. The island prospered during the Napoleonic Wars, but its assets were low afterwards, and it was sold back to France in 1878.

Gustavia remains a reflection of the Swedish period, during which about 4 per cent of the population was of Swedish origin. Three forts built in the mid to late 18th century protected the harbour: Fort Oscar, formerly Fort Gustav Adolf, Fort Karl and Fort Gustav. The town has two main churches, the Roman Catholic Our Lady of the Assumption, built in 1829, and St Bartholomew's Anglican Church on the harbour front, built in 1855.

Gustavia is the main town and capital of Saint Barthélemy, an island of 24 square kilometres, whose currency is the euro. Fort Oscar, at the tip of the Gustavia peninsula, houses the gendarmerie, while the sites of Fort Karl, above Shell Beach, and Fort Gustav, at the foot of the lighthouse, are visited by walkers. A museum stands at the end of Victor Schœlcher Road on the peninsula, and there is a Royal Swedish consulate in the town. The climate is tropical, with air and water temperatures around 27 °C, a dry season called Lent and a more humid summer season from May to November.
gustavo-gutierrez: Gustavo Gutiérrez was born in the Montserrat barrio of Lima on 8 June 1928 to mestizo parents of Hispanic and Quechua descent. As an adolescent he had osteomyelitis and used a wheelchair from the age of 12 to 18, a period he called formative.
