He studied medicine at the National University of San Marcos, intending to become a psychiatrist, and joined Catholic Action. Realising he wanted to become a priest, he studied theology at Leuven in Belgium and at Lyon in France, under teachers including Henri de Lubac and Yves Congar. He was ordained in 1959. In Europe he also read Karl Marx, whose account of class struggle gave him a framework for understanding economic inequality.

Back in Peru in the late 1950s he began to work out his understanding of Latin American reality. He drafted an outline of his proposal at a conference at Chimbote between 21 and 25 July 1968, and refined it until A Theology of Liberation appeared in 1971. He located the source of Latin America's problems in sin made visible in unjust social structures. He distinguished two forms of poverty, a scandalous state that God abhors and a spiritual childhood that is valued, and argued for a preferential option for the poor.

He described Christian liberation on three interdependent levels, political, psychological and theological, supported socialism and called for social revolution rather than reform. In 1974 he founded the Lima branch of the Bartolomé de Las Casas Institute. His later books include On Job (1986).

In 1984 the Holy See under Pope John Paul II criticised aspects of liberation theology, taking particular issue with its use of Marxist economic theory, and Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger asked the Peruvian bishops to examine Gutiérrez's writings. His propositions were never censored, though he was asked to modify some. He later held the John Cardinal O'Hara Professorship of Theology at the University of Notre Dame. He died of pneumonia in a convent in Lima on 22 October 2024, aged 96, and Pope Francis called him a great man of the Church.
gustavus-adolphus: Gustavus Adolphus was born in Stockholm on 9 December 1594, the eldest son of Duke Charles of the House of Vasa and Christina of Holstein-Gottorp. His tutor was the intellectual Johan Skytte. His father, a Protestant, fought a war against his Catholic nephew Sigismund III Vasa, king of Poland-Lithuania and Sweden, and took the throne as Charles IX in 1604. Gustavus Adolphus succeeded in October 1611 at the age of sixteen. Axel Oxenstierna acted briefly as regent until the young king was declared of age in January 1612.

The king inherited three wars: with Denmark–Norway, with Russia and with Sigismund III of Poland. The Kalmar War ended in 1613 with the Treaty of Knäred, by which Sweden paid a heavy indemnity and bought back Älvsborg Castle. The war in Russia ended in 1617 with the Treaty of Stolbovo, which excluded Russia from the Baltic Sea. The Polish war ended in 1629 with the Truce of Altmark, which gave Sweden the province of Livonia and freed its forces for Germany. He also began parish registration of the population so that the central government could tax and conscript more efficiently.

In June 1630 he landed in northern Germany and Pomerania with about 4,000 troops, marking Sweden's entry into the Thirty Years' War. On 17 September 1631 he won a decisive victory over the army of Count Tilly at the First Battle of Breitenfeld, using cavalry, disciplined infantry and mobile artillery. In April 1632 he crossed the Lech at the Battle of Rain, where Tilly was severely wounded, and Munich fell on 17 May. His army used shallow infantry formations, light mobile guns and combined arms. Historians such as B. H. Liddell Hart argue that he improved existing techniques rather than inventing them.

On 6 November 1632 Gustavus Adolphus met the Imperial army under Albrecht von Wallenstein at Lützen. He was killed while leading a cavalry charge, and his body was found an hour or two later. Lützen was a Protestant victory, but the loss of their leader left the campaign without direction. His young daughter Christina succeeded him. The Riksdag of the Estates named him Gustavus Adolphus the Great after his death, the only Swedish monarch so styled. Protestants in Europe commemorate him as a defender of their cause, and Gustavus Adolphus Day is kept in Sweden on 6 November.
gustrow: Güstrow lies 45 kilometres south of Rostock on the Nebel, an arm of the Warnow. The Bützow-Güstrow-Kanal gives a navigable link to the Warnow, and five lakes, the Inselsee, Sumpfsee, Parumer See, Grundloser See and Gliner See, and several forests lie around the town. Its name comes from the Polabian Guščerov and means lizard place.

The Wendish castle Güstrowe was built in 1219 on the site where the Renaissance palace now stands. The town is said to have been founded between 1219 and 1226 by Heinrich Borwin II, a grandson of Henry the Lion, who donated the cathedral as a collegiate church in 1226. It was first mentioned in 1228 and was a residence of the lords of Werle from 1229 until 1436. A host desecration trial in 1330 ended with the burning of 23 Jews and the destruction of the synagogue, and the Chapel of the Holy Blood was built on its site. Fires destroyed the town in 1503, 1508 and 1512.

After the division of Mecklenburg in 1621 Güstrow became the capital of the small Duchy of Mecklenburg-Güstrow, whose dukes included Albrecht von Wallenstein, the imperial general of the Thirty Years' War. When the last duke died in 1695 the duchy ceased to exist. The sculptor Ernst Barlach lived in the town from 1910 until his death in 1938. During the Second World War it held a labour camp of the Reich Labour Service and a Gestapo-operated prison.

Güstrow Palace, built in 1589 in Renaissance style as a residence for the dukes, is one of the most important works of its era in the Baltic region. The brick Gothic cathedral, built between 1226 and 1335, has a late Gothic high altar of about 1500 and Barlach's sculpture the Floating Angel, made in 1926 as a tribute to the victims of the First World War. The town also has Barlach's studio house, which exhibits a large collection of his works. Güstrow has been styled Barlachstadt since 2006 and has 28,999 inhabitants.
gusuku-sites-and-related-properties-of-t: The World Heritage Site consists of nine sites, all in Okinawa Prefecture, Japan. They are two utaki, or sacred sites, one a gate and the other a grove, the Tamaudun mausoleum, one garden, and five gusuku castle sites, four of which are ruins and one a reconstruction. The sites were inscribed as a fine representation of the culture of the Ryukyu Kingdom, whose blend of Japanese and Chinese influence made it a crucial economic and cultural junction between neighbouring states.

Gusuku were built throughout the Ryukyu Islands in the Gusuku Period (1187–1314), as chieftains and feudal lords called aji rose to power. People living on low coastal ground moved inland to higher ground and built villages, and agriculture, including paddy rice, wheat and millet, developed. Certain groves were set aside as utaki for praying to the guardian spirits of cultivation. The aji mainly oversaw taxes and conducted religious rites together with Noro priestesses, and trade drew them to good harbours such as Naha, Yomitan, Itoman, Katsuren, Sashiki and Unten.

In the Sanzan Period (1314–1429) Okinawa was divided between three rival kingdoms: Hokuzan in the north with its capital at Nakijin Castle, Chūzan in the centre with its capital at Urasoe Castle, and Nanzan in the south. They competed for territory and for recognition from Ming China. The period ended in 1429 when King Shō Hashi conquered the three and was recognised by the Chinese emperor as King of Ryukyu. The new kingdom, capital at Shuri Castle, took the Amami Islands by the mid 15th century and the Sakishima Islands by 1500. Nakagusuku Castle and Yarazamori Castle were among the gusuku built in this period, and the Hanta Road was laid for travel between them.

In 1609 the Satsuma Domain of Japan invaded Ryukyu. It destroyed Nakijin and Urasoe castles and captured Shuri Castle, made the kingdom a vassal and annexed the Amami Islands. Gusuku-building stopped after the 17th century. After Japan annexed Ryukyu in 1879, the Imperial Japanese Army used some gusuku, and in the Battle of Okinawa most of those it used, especially Shuri Castle, were damaged or destroyed.

Shuri Castle was rebuilt during the 1990s. On 30 November 2000 UNESCO inscribed the sites on the World Heritage list, along with 60 others. The listing represents more than 500 years of Ryukyuan history, from the 12th to the 17th century, and rests on three criteria: the exchange of human values over a span of time, an exceptional cultural tradition of a civilisation that has disappeared, and the linking of events and traditions with ideas, beliefs and literary and artistic works.
gutasaga: The saga survives in a single manuscript, Codex Holm. B 64 of about 1350, kept at the National Library of Sweden in Stockholm. In its story Gotland lay under a spell, under water by day and rising only at night, until Þieluar broke it by lighting a fire. His son Hafþi married Hwitastierna, White-star, who dreamed of three snakes entwined in her bosom; Hafþi read the dream as a prophecy of three sons and named them in an old alliterative verse, probably from oral tradition: Guti, Graipr and Gunfiaun. The brothers divided the island into northern, middle and southern thirds, though prose and verse disagree over which was eldest.

When their descendants grew too many for the land, every third person was chosen by lot to leave, taking everything they owned except their land. The emigrants went to Þorsburg, then to Faroy, then to Dagaiþi, an island close to Estonia, and up the Dyna through Russia until they came to Greece, where, the writer says, they still lived and still kept something of the islanders' language. The saga also names Awair Strabain as the man who arranged the agreement with the king of Sweden, and sets out the duties of the Swedish king and bishop towards Gotland.

The emigration story is associated with the migration of the Goths, whose first appearance in classical sources fits it: Eusebius of Caesarea reported that they devastated Macedonia, Greece, the Pontus and Asia in 263. The mention of the Dvina may reflect the Viking Age, when the Dvina-Dniepr waterway replaced the Vistula as the main trade route to Greece for the Gutes. Because it presents Gotland's ties with Sweden as resting on mutual agreement, the saga is read as an assertion of the island's independence as well as a history.

The threefold division it describes remained in law until 1747 and survives in the church's three deaneries. A stone ship at Boge is called Tjelvar's Grave, and in 2011 an Apollo asteroid was named 137052 Tjelvar after the first man to bring fire to the island.
guthrum: Guthrum, a native of Denmark born about 835, was a nephew of Horik II of Denmark and a failed candidate for a share of the Danish throne. Viking raids on England began in the late 8th century, with small-scale raiding continuing until 865, when a much larger army landed in East Anglia to conquer it. In April 871 Guthrum was one of the leaders of the Great Summer Army that joined the Great Danish Army at Reading. The combined army conquered Mercia in 874, deposing Burgred of Mercia, and then split, with Halfdan going north against the Picts and the Britons of Strathclyde and Guthrum going south against Wessex.

On Epiphany, 6 January 878, Guthrum made a surprise night attack on Alfred and his court at Chippenham. Alfred fled with a few retainers and took shelter in the Somerset marshes at Athelney, where, according to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, he built a fortress at Easter and fought the army from there with the men of Somerset. It is possible that Wulfhere, Ealdorman of Wiltshire, allowed the attack through negligence or intent, since he and his wife lost their lands once Alfred returned to power.

Alfred then gathered his loyal men at Egbert's Stone and went to Edington, where in 878 he defeated the Viking army. Guthrum retreated to his stronghold, and Alfred besieged it for fourteen days until he gave in.

Under the surrender Guthrum had to be baptised and leave Wessex with his army. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says he came to Alfred with thirty of the army's most honourable men at Aller, near Athelney, and that the unloosing of his chrism took place at Wedmore. A second agreement, the Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum, set the boundaries between the two kings' territories and made provisions for peaceful trade and for the weregild of their peoples. It is seen as the foundation of the Danelaw.

Guthrum returned to East Anglia and ruled for more than ten years, as a Christian king for his Saxon subjects and as a Norse king for his Viking ones, and he issued coins in his baptismal name of Æthelstan. Records show Viking raiding parties in the 880s, but he and his forces ceased to be a threat. When he died in 890 the Annals of St Neots recorded that he was buried at Hadleigh in Suffolk.
gutians: The Guti were a people of the ancient Near East, and their homeland was known as Gutium. Little is known of their origins, material culture or language, since contemporary sources give few details and no artifacts have been positively identified. The names of their kings suggest a language not closely related to Sumerian, Akkadian, Hurrian, Hattic, Eblaite, Amorite or Elamite. Boris Piotrovsky and Grigory Bongard-Levin suggested it may have been cognate with Hurrian. Most scholars have not accepted attempts to link the royal names to Indo-European languages.

The Gutians appear in a later copy of an inscription of Lugal-Anne-Mundu of Adab, among the nations giving him tribute. Year-names of Shar-kali-sharri of Akkad record that in one year he captured Sharlag, king of Gutium, and in another that "the yoke was imposed on Gutium". The later composition Great Revolt against Naram-Sin has Naram-Sin of Akkad defeating the Gutian king Gula'an, although 90,000 of his soldiers were slain.

During the Akkadian period the Gutians grew in strength and established a capital at Adab. They eventually overran Akkad, and the Sumerian King List says their army subdued Uruk for hegemony of Sumer, in about 2147–2050 BCE. Autonomous rulers soon arose again in several city-states, notably Gudea of Lagash, and Upper Mesopotamia and Assyria appear not to have been overrun. On a statue at Nippur the Gutian king Erridupizir styles himself "King of Gutium, King of the Four Quarters". The King List credits Utu-hengal of Uruk with defeating the Gutian ruler Tirigan and removing the Guti from the country in about 2050 BCE.

Later writers portrayed the Guti as uncouth. The Weidner Chronicle, written about 500 BCE, calls them unhappy people who did not know how to revere the gods, and the Victory Stele of Utu-hengal describes Gutium as a fanged snake of the mountains. By the middle of the 2nd millennium BCE the name had been extended to all foreigners from north-western Iran between the Zagros Mountains and the Tigris, so that Assyrian annals call Hurrians, Medes or Mannaeans Gutians. As late as the reign of Cyrus the Great the general Gubaru was described as "governor of Gutium", after which the name disappears.
guwahati: Guwahati lies between the south bank of the Brahmaputra River and the foothills of the Shillong plateau, with several hills inside the city limits. The Bharalu River, a tributary of the Brahmaputra, flows through the centre, and the freshwater lake of Dipor Bil to the south-west acts as a natural stormwater reservoir. The city is known as the gateway to North East India. Its name comes from the Assamese guwa, areca nut, from the Sanskrit guvaka, and hati, rows: the rows of areca nut trees.

The ancient cities of Pragjyotishpura and Durjaya, the latter now North Guwahati, were capitals of the ancient state of Kamarupa. Legend ascribes the founding of Pragjyotisha to the asura king Naraka, who appears in the Mahabharata and is said in later texts to have been slain by Krishna and Satyabhama. The Kamakhya temple on Nilachal hill, an important seat of Tantric and Vajrayana Buddhism, and the Navagraha temple on Chitrachal hill lie within the city, which is called the City of Temples.

The Koch king Parikshit had his capital at Pragjyotishpur during his conflicts with the Mughals. The area came under Mughal occupation in 1633-59, 1662-69 and 1679-81, and its vestiges were removed after the Battle of Itakhuli. Pandu, on the Brahmaputra in the west of the city, served as the chief military base of the Ahoms against external invasions, protected by fortifications called gorh. When Assam was ceded to the British in 1826, Guwahati became the seat of British administration there, until the headquarters moved to Shillong in 1874. The Gauhati High Court was established in 1948, and in 1972 the government of Assam decided to move its capital from Shillong to Dispur, where the Assembly first sat on 16 March 1973.

Guwahati is the largest city of Assam and of north-eastern India, with 962,334 people at the 2011 census. Dispur, the state capital, lies within it. The core area has an old city with Pan Bazaar, Paltan Bazaar, Fancy Bazaar and Uzan Bazaar. Pandu port is the largest river port in Assam. The city is a centre of education, with the Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati, Cotton University and Gauhati University among its institutions. The Gauhati High Court serves Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh.
guy-i-de-la-roche: Guy held the whole of Thebes, for which, together with Argos, he owed homage to the prince of Achaea, while Athens itself answered to no sovereign but the Latin emperor after the fall of the Kingdom of Thessalonica in 1224. The duchy prospered from its silk industry, centred at Thebes, and from its trade with Venice and Genoa. In 1240 Guy gave half of the lordship of Thebes to Bela of St. Omer, the husband of his sister Bonne. In 1251 he bought the lordship of Argos and Nauplia from his brother Othon, lord of Ray, for 15,000 hyperpyra and his own lands and claims in France.

When Prince William II of Achaea disputed the suzerainty over Euboea with the Venetians and the local triarchs, Guy took their side. In the spring of 1258 William defeated him at the foot of Mount Karydi, besieged him in Thebes and forced him to surrender. Guy did homage at Nikli, but the barons of Achaea, not being his peers, sent him to France for judgement, and he left in the spring of 1259. The court of France found that he did not owe liege homage and so could not be deprived of his fief; the journey was to be his punishment.

Setting out for Greece in the spring of 1260, Guy learned that Emperor Michael VIII Palaeologus had defeated and captured William II at the Battle of Pelagonia, and soon after his return came news that Constantinople had fallen to the Byzantines. Guy administered Achaea while William was held prisoner.

Guy survived these upheavals of the Frankish states in Greece until his death in 1263 and was succeeded by his son John I, who died unmarried and childless in 1280. His wife, whose name does not survive, was a niece of William II of Villehardouin from Champagne or Burgundy. Their son William followed John as duke and, by Helena Angelina Komnene, was the father of Guy II. Of their daughters, Alice, regent of Beirut, married John II of Beirut, and Marguerite married Count Henry I of Vaudémont.
guy-iii-of-spoleto: Guy was the second son of Guy I of Spoleto and Itta, a daughter of Sico of Benevento, and a descendant of Pepin of Italy, son of Charlemagne. The Duchy of Spoleto had been revived by the Franks in 842 as a border territory against the Byzantine catapans to the south. His family had been important in Italian politics since the early ninth century, and its interests were generally hostile to the papacy, a policy Guy at first followed.

He became Margrave of Camerino in 880 and supported his nephew Guy II of Spoleto's invasion of the Papal States in 882. Emperor Charles the Fat dispossessed him that year at Verona and declared him guilty of high treason. Guy rebelled and allied himself with the Saracens. In 883 he inherited Spoleto and reunited the dukedom as Spoleto and Camerino, and by the end of 884 Charles was forced to make peace and restore his titles.

After Charles was deposed in late 887, Guy tried to win the West Frankish throne but lost to Odo, Count of Paris, and was crowned king at Langres in an attempt to gain Lotharingia. He then went to Italy, where Berengar of Friuli, crowned king in 887, was his chief opponent. Guy, closer to Rome and allied with Pope Stephen V, gained control of much of northern and central Italy in the second half of 888, and was crowned King of Italy at Pavia in 889.

Stephen crowned him emperor in Rome on 21 February 891 and crowned his son Lambert as King of Italy. After Pope Formosus was elected in 891 he distrusted Guy, so on 30 April 892 at Ravenna Guy forced him to crown Lambert co-emperor. Formosus then invited Arnulf of Carinthia to Italy. In 894 Berengar and Arnulf's forces defeated Guy at Bergamo and took Trento and Milan, and Guy died that autumn, leaving his son under the care of his wife.

Guy died on 12 December 894, and Lambert succeeded him. His power barely extended beyond his hereditary lands, and he never firmly held northern Italy. The imperial title, with its claim of universal rule, had by then become a token of the pope's favour contested by Italian nobles. Guy tried to continue Carolingian practice by issuing capitularies, and in 891 demanded army service of all arimanni, whether they owned land or not. His motto was Renovatio Regni Francorum.
guy-of-lusignan: Guy was born around 1150, the youngest son of Hugh VIII of Lusignan, in Poitou, which belonged to the territories of Henry II of England. His family had long taken part in the Crusades, and his father died in Muslim captivity in the 1160s after the Battle of Harim. On 27 March 1168 Guy and his brothers ambushed and killed Patrick, 1st Earl of Salisbury, who was escorting Eleanor of Aquitaine to Poitiers, and the brothers were banished from Poitou. Guy went to Jerusalem between 1173 and 1180. In 1180, to forestall a coup by Raymond III of Tripoli and Bohemond III of Antioch, he was hastily married to Sibylla, the sister of Baldwin IV, whose leprosy made the succession uncertain.

In June 1183 Baldwin made Guy regent, but the leading nobles refused to cooperate with him, and Baldwin, who had recovered, judged him incompetent, dismissed him and had Sibylla's five-year-old son crowned as Baldwin V. Baldwin IV died in 1185 and Baldwin V in 1186. Sibylla was crowned queen after agreeing to annul her marriage, on condition that she could choose her next husband, and she then chose Guy and crowned him. Raymond of Tripoli refused him homage until after the Battle of Cresson on 1 May 1187.

On 2 July 1187 Saladin besieged Tiberias. Raymond advised against battle, but Gerard of Ridefort and Raynald of Châtillon accused him of cowardice, and Guy marched against Saladin. At the Battle of Hattin the crusader army was annihilated and most of its commanders, Guy among them, were captured. Saladin beheaded Raynald and spared Guy, and in the following months the whole kingdom fell to Saladin except Tyre. Guy was released in 1188.

Conrad of Montferrat, who held Tyre, refused Guy entry, so Guy began the siege of Acre in 1189. Sibylla and her daughters died in an epidemic in 1190, and Conrad married her half-sister Isabella and claimed the throne. Philip II of France backed Conrad and Richard I of England backed Guy. After Acre fell on 11 July 1191, the nobility chose Conrad at an assembly on 16 April 1192. Richard gave Guy Cyprus, and the Assassins killed Conrad on 28 April 1192.

Guy ruled Cyprus until his death around the end of 1194, and he proved a competent ruler there. With no surviving heir, he left Cyprus to his brother Geoffrey, but his vassals elected his brother Aimery. Guy was highly unpopular among the nobles of Jerusalem and is often blamed for the fall of the kingdom to Saladin.
guyuk-khan: Güyük was the eldest son of Ögedei Khan and a grandson of Genghis Khan, and he served as an officer under both. He married Oghul Qaimish of the Merkit clan. In 1233, with his maternal cousin Alchidai and the general Tangghud, he conquered the short-lived Dongxia Kingdom of Puxian Wannu, a rebellious Jin official. According to Ata-Malik Juvayni he was a Christian, though Juvayni does not name the denomination.

He took part in the invasion of Eastern and Central Europe from 1236 to 1241 with his cousin Batu and his half-brother Kadan, leading his corps at the siege of Ryazan and the siege of the Alanian capital Maghas. At the victory banquet he quarrelled violently with Batu, and Ögedei recalled him to Mongolia, threatened him with execution and reprimanded him for fighting within the family and mistreating his soldiers.

After Ögedei died in 1241 his widow Töregene acted as regent and worked to secure the throne for Güyük. Batu withdrew from Europe to influence the succession, but Güyük was elected in 1246 and enthroned on 24 August near Karakorum. Between 3,000 and 4,000 visitors came from across Asia and eastern Europe, among them the papal envoy Giovanni da Pian del Carpine, Grand Prince Yaroslav II of Vladimir and the future Seljuk sultan Kilij Arslan IV. In reply to the envoy he sent a letter demanding that Pope Innocent IV and the kings of Europe come and pay homage.

Güyük reversed several unpopular edicts of his mother and ordered an empire-wide census. He had Töregene's favourite Fatima executed, had Genghis Khan's brother Temüge put to death, and executed several high officials of the previous regime. He confirmed Andrey II as grand prince of Vladimir and made David Ulu senior king of Georgia. In 1247 Cilician Armenia became a vassal state, and in Korea Amuqan's force pillaged the peninsula until 1250.

In 1248 Güyük launched an expedition against the ulus of Jochi, Batu's territory and later the Golden Horde, but he died on the outskirts of Samarkand, before reaching the lower Volga. Some sources say the Jochids poisoned him, and some modern historians think he died of natural causes, as his health had declined. William of Rubruck reports a violent brawl with Shiban. His widow Oghul Qaimish became regent, but the succession passed in 1251 to Möngke, nominated by Batu. When Kublai Khan established the Yuan dynasty in 1271 he had Güyük placed on the official record as Dingzong.
gwadar: Gwadar stands on a natural hammerhead-shaped tombolo peninsula, forming two curved semicircular bays on either side. The city lies on a narrow sandy isthmus 12 kilometres long and 240 metres wide, which joins the Pakistani coast to the rocky Gwadar Promontory, or Koh-e-Batil, rising to 150 metres. The eastern bay, the Demi Zirr, is deep and is where the port was built. The name combines the Balochi words gwát, wind, and dar, gateway, so that Gwadar means the gate of wind. The climate is hot desert, moderated by the cool currents of the Arabian Sea, with about 100 millimetres of rain a year.

People have lived on this coast since the Bronze Age, around the area's oases, and the name Makran derives from this settlement pattern. It was for a time part of the Achaemenid Persian Empire and is believed to have been conquered by Cyrus the Great. After Alexander the Great's march through Gedrosia in 325 BCE, his admiral Nearchus led a fleet along the coast and described a dry, mountainous land inhabited by the Ichthyophagoi, the fish-eaters. The region came under Mauryan rule around 303 BCE, after Seleucus made peace with Chandragupta and ceded the territory. The Rashidun Caliphate captured Makran in 643 CE.

In 1783 Nasir Khan I, Khan of Kalat, handed Gwadar to Sultan bin Ahmad, a prince of Muscat who had fallen out with his brother, on the understanding that it would return to Kalat when the prince took the throne. He became ruler of Muscat in 1797 but never returned it, and the British helped Muscat keep Gwadar. From 1863 to 1879 it was the seat of a British Assistant Political Agent. Makran acceded to Pakistan in 1947 without Gwadar, and on 8 September 1958 Oman handed Gwadar over to Pakistan, after Prince Karim Aga Khan IV contributed about 3 million US dollars.

The United States Geological Survey identified the site as suitable for a deep-water port in 1954, while it was still under Omani rule. Construction of the port began in 2007, and its first phase cost 248 million US dollars. The 653-kilometre Makran Coastal Highway, completed in 2004, links Gwadar with Karachi, and Pakistan and China announced the China–Pakistan Economic Corridor in April 2015, with Gwadar at its centre. Before that, the economy rested largely on artisanal fishing. The population is predominantly Baloch, and 96.2 per cent of the people of Gwadar tehsil speak Balochi as their mother tongue.
gwageo: Silla's Gukhak, or National University, already graded its aristocratic graduates by their knowledge of the Confucian classics in the 7th century. The examinations of 788, known as Sambun-gwa, followed the Ten Urgent Points of Reform that the scholar Ch'oe Ch'i-wŏn submitted to Queen Jinseong; they opened the tests to lower nobility outside the Gukhak, though still only to aristocrats. In the 9th century as many as 88 Sillans passed the Tang examinations in China.

In Goryeo, King Gwangjong set up the system on Shuang Ji's advice and asked him to stay at court. The examinations widened the bureaucracy and broke the hold of a few powerful families, strengthening the throne against the aristocracy. Composition was more prestigious than the classics test: some 6000 men passed the first, about 450 the second. Unlike in China, candidates sat in the open under sunshades, and there were examinations on Buddhism.

Under Joseon the literary and military examinations had three stages: a qualifying test in the provinces, a second in the capital and a third before the king, who ranked the successful men; the top scorer in the literary examination, the jangwon, received a post of the 6th junior rank. The higher literary examination chose 33 men from a pool of 240 sent by the Seonggyungwan, the capital and the Eight Provinces. A yangban family that produced no official for four generations lost its status.

The military examination tested archery, horsemanship and texts such as Sun Tzu's Art of War, and in time it was opened even to the cheonmin. The miscellaneous examinations in translation, medicine, natural science and record-keeping were taken mostly by the chungin; under yangban pressure their certificate was changed from crimson to white. Besides the triennial singnyeonsi, special examinations grew in weight: 581 irregular examinations were held over the dynasty against 163 regular ones.

Under Jungjong of Joseon the official Cho Kwangjo added an examination of the Sage and Good, for men recommended by their magistrates. In later Joseon the system grew corrupt, and scholars who failed formed a class of disaffected yangban, among them the early 19th-century rebel Hong Gyeong-nae. The Gabo Reforms abolished it along with legal class distinctions and the old rank system.
gwalior-fort: The date of the fort's construction is unknown. A local legend tells of a king, Suraj Sen, who around the third century CE was cured of leprosy by a sage named Gwalipa; the king walled the sacred pond whose water healed him, built the fort and named it after the sage. Sanskrit inscriptions call the hill Gopgiri or Gopachala Durg, names meaning cowherd's hill. An inscription of the Huna emperor Mihirakula records a sun temple built there in the 6th century, and the fort certainly existed by the 8th century, when historical records first mention it.

From the 11th century Muslim dynasties attacked the fort. Mahmud of Ghazni besieged it for four days in 1022 and, according to the Tabaqat-i-Akbari, withdrew for a tribute of 35 elephants. Bahauddin Tourghil, a slave commander of Muhammad of Ghor, took it in 1196, and Iltutmish recaptured it in 1232. The Tomars held it from 1398; Sikander Lodi failed to take it in 1505, but after Ibrahim Lodi's attack of 1516, in which Maan Singh died, the Tomars surrendered following a year-long siege. Babur took the fort within a decade, Sher Shah Suri in 1542 and Akbar in 1558.

Akbar made the fort a prison for political prisoners. The Mughal emperor Jahangir held the young Sikh Guru Hargobind there from 1609; Sikh tradition places his release on Diwali, now marked as Bandi Chhor Divas. Murad Bakhsh and Sulaiman Shikoh were executed in the Man Mandir palace under Aurangzeb. The fort then passed between the Ranas of Gohad, the Marathas and the British East India Company, whose men took it in a night raid on 3 August 1780, before the British handed it to the Scindias in 1886.

The fort stands on Gopachal, a long, narrow ridge of Vindhyan sandstone overlain by basalt, and its ramparts follow the edge of the hill, linked by six bastions. The main entrance is the Hathi Pol, or Elephant gate, the last of a series of seven. The Man Mandir is known as the Painted Palace for its turquoise, green and yellow tiles, and the Gurjari Mahal, built by Man Singh Tomar for his wife Mrignayani, is now an archaeological museum. The Teli ka Mandir, built by the Pratihara emperor Mihira Bhoja, is the oldest part of the fort, and the Saas Bahu temples date from 1092–93.
gwanggaeto-stele: Carved from a single mass of granite with a girth of almost four metres, the stele stands near Gwanggaeto's tomb at Ji'an on the Yalu River. Its Classical Chinese text, covering all four sides, falls into three parts. The first tells how the founder, King Ch'umo, came from Northern Buyeo as son of the Celestial Emperor and the daughter of Habaek, crossed a river on floating turtles and founded his capital, the throne passing down to the seventeenth king, Gwanggaeto.

The second part lists Gwanggaeto's campaigns from the conquest of the Paeryeo in 395, among them the surrender of the Baekje king in 396, who gave captives and a thousand bolts of cloth, and the defeat of Wa troops on the southern border in 404, followed by the conquest of Eastern Buyeo in 410. Its seven conquests agree with the Samguk sagi. The third part names the Sumyoin, the households appointed to guard the king's tomb.

After the fall of Goguryeo in 668 the region lay outside Korean and Chinese politics, and the Qing closed it to settlement. When settlers arrived in the 19th century, a local official, Guan Yueshan, found the stele around 1876 under centuries of mud and growth. In 1882 the county magistrate had the vegetation burnt off, damaging the surface. In 1883 the Japanese officer Sakō Kageaki, travelling disguised as a herbalist, took a tracing of the text home, and the Japanese General Staff had scholars decode it, publishing their findings in 1889, before Korea knew of the monument.

The stele has become a focus of national rivalry in East Asia, above all over the sinmyo passage for the year 391. Japanese scholars traditionally read it as saying that the Wa crossed the sea and made Baekje and Silla their subjects; Korean scholars, beginning with Chŏng In-bo in 1955, read Goguryeo as the subject. In 1972 Lee Jin-hui claimed the Japanese army had altered the stele with lime, but Chinese scholars such as Wang Jianqun and Xu Jianxin, who found a rubbing made before 1881, concluded there was no evidence of deliberate damage. An exact replica stands at the War Memorial of Seoul.
gwanggaeto-the-great: Gwanggaeto was born in 374, three years after the kingdom of Baekje under Geunchogo defeated Goguryeo, killed King Gogukwon and sacked Pyongyang. His father was King Gogukyang and his grandfather Gogukwon. Goguryeo avoided conflict with Baekje in these years and cultivated good relations with the Former Qin, the Xianbei and the Rouran. Gogukwon's successor Sosurim made peace with Baekje, spread Buddhism through the kingdom's institutions and carried out military reforms after the defeats by Baekje and the Xianbei. Gogukyang then invaded Later Yan in 385 and Baekje in 386. These arrangements prepared the ground for Gwanggaeto's expansion.

Gwanggaeto took the throne in 391, adopting the era name Yeongnak and the title Taewang, equivalent to emperor, which presented him as the equal of China's rulers. In 392 he attacked Baekje with 40,000 troops and took ten walled cities. Baekje's king Asin counterattacked in 393 and invaded again in 394 but was defeated both times. In 396 Gwanggaeto assaulted the Baekje capital Wiryeseong by land and by sea along the Han River, and Asin submitted, surrendering a prince and ten ministers.

In the west and north he destroyed three tribes and between 600 and 700 camps of the Khitan Baili clan on the Liao River in 395, and conquered the Sushen in 398. In 400 Silla asked for help against an invasion by Baekje, Gaya and Wa. Gwanggaeto sent 50,000 troops and defeated the coalition, after which Silla stood under his influence and Gaya declined. In 402 he returned Prince Silseong, held as a hostage since 392, to Silla as its king.

He beat back Later Yan attacks, took a fortress near its capital in 402 and conquered all of Liaodong, which Goguryeo held until the mid to late 7th century. In 404 he defeated a Wa attack on the former Daifang commandery, and in 410 he attacked Eastern Buyeo.

Gwanggaeto died of an unknown illness and was succeeded by his eldest son Jangsu. He is credited with taking 64 walled cities and 1,400 villages. His deeds are recorded on the Gwanggaeto Stele, a monument 6.39 m tall that Jangsu erected in 414 at the supposed site of his tomb in Ji'an, and which was rediscovered in the late 19th century. Not all its characters survive, and Korean and Japanese scholars disagree on how to read its passages about the Wa. Koreans regard him as a hero and he is often taken as a symbol of Korean nationalism.
gwanghaegun-of-joseon: Gwanghaegun, personal name Yi Hon, was the second son of King Seonjo and Concubine Gong, a royal consort who died a year after his birth. When Toyotomi Hideyoshi's Japan invaded Joseon in the Imjin War of 1592 to 1598, he was installed as crown prince. While the king fled north towards the Ming border, he set up a branch court, fought defensive battles and, from 1592, acted as the de facto ruler, directing the reconstruction of the country in place of his elderly father. His position remained unstable, since he had an elder brother, Prince Imhae, considered incompetent, and a younger legitimate half-brother, Grand Prince Yeongchang, backed by the Lesser Northerners faction.

Before Seonjo died in 1608 he named Gwanghaegun his successor. Yu Yeong-gyong of the Lesser Northerners hid the decree and plotted to put Yeongchang on the throne, but was discovered and executed. Gwanghaegun then tried to include officials of different factions, yet the Greater Northerners, including Yi I-cheom and Chŏng Inhong, purged their rivals. In 1613 Yeongchang's maternal grandfather and uncles were executed for treason, and Yeongchang was exiled and killed in 1614. In 1618 Queen Inmok was stripped of her title and imprisoned. Gwanghaegun, though head of government, could not stop this.

He rebuilt Changdeokgung and other palaces, revised land rules, restored the hopae identification system and encouraged publishing, which produced the medical work Donguibogam. The Daedong law eased tax payment, though it applied only in Gyeonggi Province and took a century to spread across the kingdom. He reopened relations with Japan in 1609 through the Treaty of Giyu with the Sō clan of Tsushima. Judging Joseon unable to match Manchu power, he kept friendly ties with the Jurchens, angering the Ming and strict Confucian Koreans. In 1619 he sent ten thousand soldiers to aid the Ming, but the Manchu forces won the Battle of Sarhū and General Gang Hong-rip surrendered to Nurhaci. Gwanghaegun then negotiated peace with the Jurchens himself.

On 11 April 1623 the Westerners faction deposed him in a coup, justified by the freed Queen Inmok, and installed his nephew Neungyanggun as King Injo. He was held on Ganghwa Island and then on Jeju, where he died in 1641, and has no royal mausoleum or temple name. Injo's pro-Ming, anti-Manchu policies were followed by two Manchu invasions. Historians remain divided: Oh Hang-nyeong criticised his spending on palaces and his absence from meetings, while Lee Duk-il praised the Daedong law and the Donguibogam, and most historians judge his foreign policy favourably.
gwangjong-of-goryeo: Gwangjong was born in 925 as Wang So, fourth son of King Taejo, who had founded Goryeo in 918. Because he had three older brothers he was far from the succession, but Wang T'ae died early and Wang Mu died in 945, three years after being crowned. The throne passed to Wang Yo, who ruled for four years as Jeongjong and, before dying, chose Wang So as heir instead of his own son. As a prince he helped remove those opposed to the sovereigns, among them Wang Kyu and the general Pak Surhŭi.

Gwangjong took the throne on 13 April 949, at the age of 25. His father had made alliances through marriage with powerful families that kept their own armies, so he set out to consolidate royal power. He married within the royal family, taking his half-sister as Queen Daemok, rather than a noble clan. His reforms began in 956 with a law of emancipation of slaves, mainly prisoners of war who served noble families as private soldiers and paid no taxes to the crown. Freed, they became commoners who paid taxes to the king and could serve in his army.

In 957 the envoy Shuang Ji arrived from Later Zhou and stayed as an official, and with his advice the king instituted the civil service examination in 958, based on the Tang model and the Confucian classics. It was open to free-born men, though in practice only sons of the gentry could prepare for it. In 960 he introduced colours of court robes to distinguish ranks. He also built twelve garrisons on the borders, named Goryeo an empire with himself as emperor, and called Kaesong the Imperial Capital.

Nobles who had helped found the kingdom resisted, and after a failed rebellion Gwangjong began purges in 960. They killed his brother Wang Won and the sons of Hyejong and Jeongjong. At the end of them only forty of Taejo's 3,200 meritorious subjects were still alive.

Gwangjong grew more reliant on Buddhism in later years. He fell ill in July 975 and died within days, aged 50, and his son Gyeongjong succeeded him. Seongjong later retracted the emancipation law, and the bureaucracy became a hereditary class. The thinker Ch'oe Sŭng-no condemned him as a tyrant for cruelty, public projects and Buddhist devotion, while praising his first eight years.
gyebaek: The general, whose name is also written Kyebaek, served as a general of Baekje in the early to mid-7th century. Little is known of his personal life, not even the year or place of his birth. In 660 Baekje was invaded by a Silla army of 50,000 men supported by 144,000 Tang soldiers, and he, with only 5,000 troops under his command, met them on the battlefield of Hwangsanbeol.

Before entering the battle he reportedly killed his wife and children so that they would not be enslaved if he lost. His forces won the first four engagements and inflicted severe casualties on the Silla army. In the end, exhausted and surrounded, his outnumbered army was overwhelmed, and the Baekje force was annihilated together with its commander. He died on 20 August 660, and Baekje itself was destroyed shortly afterwards.

As Neo-Confucian philosophy grew more influential under the later Korean dynasties, historians and scholars held him up as an example of the Confucian ideals of patriotism and devotion to his king, Uija, and praised him on those grounds. Although little else is known of his life, the events leading up to his last battle are known to many Koreans.

His name is carried by Ge-Baek, the 12th pattern, or hyeong, in the teul of the International Taekwon-Do Federation, the forms of the Korean martial art Taekwon-Do. It is practised by holders of the 1st Dan black belt and has 44 moves, and its diagram is said to represent his severe and strict military discipline. He has been portrayed in Korean television series and films, among them the 2003 film Once Upon a Time in a Battlefield and the 2011 MBC series Kyebaek.
gyeon-hwon: Most accounts make him the eldest of six children of Ajagae, a farmer and rebel leader surnamed Yi, born in what is now Gaeun-eup in Mungyeong; he later changed his surname to Kyŏn, perhaps to start afresh as a founder. Legends say he grew up drinking a tiger's milk. Under Queen Jinseong, Silla was torn by corruption and famine, and his father led a peasant revolt based at Sangju. Kyŏn Hwŏn is said to have joined the Silla army at fifteen and to have risen to command its forces in the Jeolla region.

In 892 he seized Wansanju and Mujinju, the old lands of Baekje, whose people were hostile to Silla, and in 900 he declared himself king with his capital at Wansanju, saying he would avenge the destruction of Baekje by Silla and Tang in 660. He fought Kung Ye of Later Goguryeo, failing to retake Naju from Wang Kŏn in 910. Kung Ye was overthrown in 918, and Wang Kŏn founded Goryeo. Peace with Goryeo, sealed by an exchange of hostages, broke down in 926 when Kyŏn killed the hostage Wang Shin after his own nephew's death.

Attacking Gyeongju in 927, he captured King Gyeongae, forced him to kill himself, raped his chief consort and let his men assault the royal concubines, then enthroned Gyeongsun of Silla. On the way home he defeated Wang Kŏn, who escaped only through the sacrifice of his general Sin Sung-gyŏm and Kim Nak. Later Baekje never recovered from its heavy defeat at the Battle of Gochang in 930, and a further attack on Goryeo failed in 934. Kyŏn was confirmed as ruler by Wuyue and Later Tang, sought an alliance with the Liao dynasty and sent envoys to Heian Japan.

His eldest son Sin-gŏm, passed over in favour of Kŭm-gang, killed his brother and confined his father in the temple of Geumsansa, but Kyŏn Hwŏn escaped to Wang Kŏn, who gave him land and slaves. After the Goryeo army destroyed Later Baekje, he died the same year of an inflamed tumour. His reputation has been largely negative, shaped by the Samguk sagi of Kim Bu-sik, whose work historians note has a pro-Silla bias. Through his daughter Lady Kuktae his descendants married into the Goryeo royal house.
gyeongbokgung: After founding Joseon in 1392, King Taejo decided in 1394 that Hanyang, now Seoul, would be the capital. The first phase of the palace was completed in 1395, and the official Chŏng Tojŏn named it Gyeongbokgung, meaning great blessings palace, after the last characters of a poem in the Classic of Poetry. Its site weighed access to water, farmland and roads, and followed the Rites of Zhou, which put the ancestral temple on the left and the soil and grain temple on the right. Feng shui placed a mountain behind it and water in front.

The layout is mostly symmetrical along a north–south axis, with three gates and three courtyards: the first for government offices, the second for the king's dealings with his subjects, and the third where the king's family lived. Chŏng named the main buildings from the Book of Documents to express Neo-Confucian principles, and his arguments for the site were preferred to those of the Buddhist monk Muhak.

In 1398 the capital moved to Kaegyŏng and the palace stood abandoned for about ten years. King Taejong, who returned in 1405, preferred Changdeokgung. In 1421 Sejong the Great made Gyeongbokgung his primary palace and expanded it. It then held a water clock, a facility for producing movable type, the observatory Ganuidae, and the Hall of Worthies, which helped him develop Hangul. In 1592, during the Imjin War, the palace was completely burned. Who set the fire is debated, since it was intact when the Japanese entered the city. For about 270 years it went mostly unused, because money was short and other palaces sufficed.

The regent for King Gojong ordered reconstruction, which was finally completed in 1888, after fires in 1873 and 1876. In 1887 the first electric light in Korea was lit there. After Queen Min was assassinated in 1895, Gojong did not live there again.

In 1907 the palace became a public park, and in 1910 its property was auctioned off. Of around 500 buildings in 1888, only 40 remained by the end of the colonial period. The Government-General of Chōsen Building, built in the palace between 1916 and 1926, was demolished in 1995–1996. The First Restoration Plan, begun in 1990, restored 89 buildings and was completed in 2010, when about 25% of the original buildings stood. A second plan, running to 2045, will recreate 90 more. The authenticity of recreated buildings remains debated, partly because Joseon builders left few records. The palace now houses the National Palace Museum of Korea and the National Folk Museum of Korea.
gyeongdeok-of-silla: Gyeongdeok was the 35th ruler of Silla, a son of King Seongdeok and Queen Sodeok of the Kim clan, and grandson of King Sinmun. He succeeded his elder brother, King Hyoseong, the 34th ruler. His queens were Sammo, a daughter of Kim Sun-jeong, and Gyeongsu, a daughter of Kim Ui-chung. Besides his son and heir, the future King Hyegong, born in 758, he had a daughter, Lady Kim.

His reign is regarded as a golden age of Unified Silla, above all for Buddhist art and architecture, and he was a keen patron of Buddhism. Work on the Seokguram Grotto, Bulguksa and the Dabotap Pagoda began in 751 under the prime minister Kim Dae-seong. Gyeongdeok completed the tomb of his father in a style aligned with the Great Stupa of Sanchi and the Bharhut Stupa, and raised a jangsaengpyo at Borimsa in gratitude to Master Wanpyo for his help in government. He probably also built one of the lotus ponds south-west of Wolseong Castle, about forty metres from east to west and fifty from north to south.

He sought to govern the regions through officials appointed by the court rather than through local nobles, on the Chinese model, and to standardise names. Offices of artisans were renamed with the suffix bang in place of jeon. In 757 the place names of Silla and of the conquered kingdoms of Goguryeo and Baekje were given Chinese forms; the Samguk sagi records both the new name and a transcription of the old one, which were generally close in meaning.

Gyeongdeok was succeeded by his son Hyegong, with Hyegong's mother acting as regent. A tomb in Gyeongju believed to be his is a Historic Site of South Korea, No. 23, though its true occupant is debated.
gyeongju: Gyeongju lies in the far south-eastern corner of North Gyeongsang Province, 370 kilometres south-east of Seoul and 55 kilometres east of Daegu. It covers 1,324 square kilometres, and the Sea of Japan lies to its east, while low mountains, outliers of the Taebaek range, are scattered around it. Ulsan borders it on the south and Pohang on the north. Between 1895 and 1955 the area was called Gyeongju County. The city and the county were united in 1995, and it is now an urban and rural complex.

Gyeongju first enters non-Korean records as Saro-guk, in the Samhan period. Korean records, probably based on the dynastic chronicles of Silla, say that Saro-guk was founded in 57 BCE, when six small villages in the area united under Bak Hyeokgeose. As the kingdom grew it took the name Silla. In the Silla period the city was called Sŏrabŏl, a name that was to evolve into a Korean word for a capital city, as in Seoul, and also Gyerim, meaning rooster's forest, and Geumseong, meaning city of gold or metal, that is, an impenetrable fortress.

At its height, between the 7th and 9th centuries, Silla ruled about two-thirds of the Korean peninsula. According to the Samguk yusa, Sŏrabŏl had more than 170,000 households, or between 800,000 and 900,000 inhabitants, and the city is estimated to have had a million residents, with later Silla ranking Gyeongju as the fourth largest city in the world. The Hwarang, a military cadet corps of young aristocrats trained in the academic and martial arts, are associated with the city, and generals such as Kim Yu-sin played a central part in Silla's unification of the peninsula. Gyeongju's notable figures included the scholars Seol Chong and Ch'oe Ch'i-wŏn.

Gyeongju is the main destination in South Korea for visitors interested in the heritage of Silla and the architecture of Joseon, and is often called the museum without walls. Its tumuli, Buddhist sites, fortresses and palace sites include the Royal Tomb Complex, the Cheomseongdae observatory, one of the oldest surviving astronomical observatories in East Asia, and the Anapji royal pond garden. The Seokguram grotto, Bulguksa temple, the Gyeongju Historic Areas and Yangdong Folk Village are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The city has 31 National Treasures, and its national museum houses 16,333 artefacts. Namsan, the sacred mountain, is covered with Buddhist shrines and statues, and Gyeongju is the birthplace of Cheondoism.
gyeongsun-of-silla: Gyeongsun was born in 897 with the personal name Kim Pu. A sixth-generation descendant of King Munseong, he was the son of Kim Hyo-jong and of Princess Gyea, a daughter of King Heongang. His wife was Lady Jukbang of the Juksan Park clan; his eldest son was Crown Prince Maui and his youngest Beomgong.

Later Baekje forces sacked Gyeongju in 927 and forced his predecessor to kill himself, and the Later Baekje king placed Gyeongsun on the throne in order to break Silla's alliance with Goryeo. The kingdom was already gravely weakened, and Gyeongsun ruled over a small remnant of its former territory until 935, when he abdicated in favour of Taejo of Goryeo. He led his officials to Songak for the ceremony at the head of a convoy of treasures and women said to stretch for more than thirty li, and Taejo waited for him in the suburbs of his capital.

Taejo sealed the submission with marriages. He gave Gyeongsun his eldest daughter, Princess Nangrang, as a wife and appointed him sasim-gwan, or inspector-general, of Gyeongju, the first holder of what became Goryeo's sasim-gwan system. Taejo in turn married a daughter of Gyeongsun's uncle, who became one of his queens and later the grandmother of King Hyeonjong of Goryeo.

Gyeongsun spent the rest of his life near the Goryeo capital, modern Kaesong, and died in 978. His tomb lies in Jangnam-myeon, Yeoncheon County, in Gyeonggi Province, South Korea. According to the Samguk sagi, Crown Prince Maui objected to his father's submission and withdrew to Mount Kumgang as a hermit. In Korean shamanism Gyeongsun is worshipped as one of the Wangshin, or king gods, and he has been portrayed in the KBS television series Taejo Wang Geon.
gyges-of-lydia: Nothing is known of Gyges's origins except Herodotus's claim that he was the son of a man named Dascylus. His name is the Greek form Gugēs of the Lydian Kukas, which means grandfather, and the annals of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal refer several times to Gu(g)gu, king of Luddi, who is identified with him. He is regarded as the first known Lydian king to attempt to turn the kingdom into a powerful empire.

He seems to have taken the throne by overthrowing King Candaules of the Heraclid dynasty, helped by a Carian prince from Mylasa named Arselis. His rise came in a time of turmoil after the Cimmerians, nomads from the Eurasian Steppe, destroyed the kingdom of Phrygia, the previous major power in Anatolia, around 675 BCE.

Immediately after Gyges seized the throne, the oracle of Apollo at Delphi confirmed his kingship, and he thanked it with lavish offerings of gold and silver, including six gold crates weighing thirty talents together. Herodotus, who saw them there, called them the Gygadas. Gyges attacked the Ionian cities of Miletus, Smyrna and Colophon. He could not take Miletus or Smyrna and made peace with both, granting the Milesians the right to found colonies on Lydian coasts; he seized only the lower city of Colophon. In the south he kept alliances with Carian dynasts and, according to Herodotus's account of the length of his reign, ruled for 38 years.

In 665 BCE he faced a war with the Cimmerians. Neo-Assyrian records say that the god Aššur appeared to him in a dream and told him to seek help from Ashurbanipal. Gyges sent envoys to Nineveh, but offered presents rather than tribute and so did not become an Assyrian vassal. He defeated the Cimmerians without Assyrian help and sent captured Cimmerian soldiers to Nineveh. Afterwards he took the Troad without much resistance, settled Lydians there and made a hunting reserve at Cyzicus. Around 662 BCE he established contact with Psamtik I of Egypt, and until 658 BCE sent him Carian and Ionian Greek soldiers who helped Psamtik unite Egypt.

The Cimmerians invaded again in 657 BCE, which Assyrian oracular reports call a bad omen for the Westland. In 644 BCE a third attack, led by their king Lygdamis, defeated the Lydians, sacked Sardis and killed Gyges. Assyrian records blamed his death on his decision to act apart from Assyria, which they took for arrogance. His son Ardys succeeded him and resumed diplomacy with Assyria. His great-grandson Alyattes put the legend Kukalim, meaning I am of Kukas, on coins, declaring that he belonged to the dynasty of Gyges.
gylippus: Gylippus was the son of Cleandridas, adviser to King Pleistoanax, who was expelled from Sparta in 446 BCE for taking Athenian bribes and fled to Thurii, a pan-Hellenic colony then being founded in southern Italy with Athenian help. His mother may have been a helot, which would have made him a mothax, a man of lower status than a full Spartiate. He was nonetheless raised for war in the Spartan way and, on reaching manhood, elected to a military mess, with a wealthier Spartiate patron paying his dues. For a man of marginal origins, war offered a path to honour.

When Alcibiades urged Sparta to send a general to lead the Syracusan resistance to the Athenian expedition, Gylippus was chosen. His arrival turned the struggle: more daring than the Athenian commander Nicias, he drove the Athenians from key positions and in effect broke their siege, and when Demosthenes came with reinforcements he defeated him too. The sources differ on his part in the fate of the captured Athenian generals. Diodorus, probably following Timaeus, says he persuaded the Syracusans to condemn them to death, while Thucydides and the Syracusan Philistus, who fought in the defence, say he tried in vain to save them to take them to Sparta as proof of his success.

Like his father, he fell through money. Lysander entrusted him with a shipment of silver coins for the ephors at Sparta, and he embezzled part of it. When the theft was discovered he fled into exile, was condemned to death in his absence, and disappears from the record.
gympie: Gympie lies on the Mary River in the Greater Sunshine Coast, about 170.7 km north of Brisbane. Its name derives from the Gubbi Gubbi word gimpi-gimpi, meaning stinging tree, which refers to Dendrocnide moroides, a tree with large round leaves that have properties similar to stinging nettles. Gubbi Gubbi is the Aboriginal language formerly spoken by the peoples of the Sunshine Coast and Gympie regions.

The river floods the city from time to time. Floods are recorded in 1870, 1873, 1893, 1955, 1968, 1974, 1989, 1992, 1999, 2011, 2013 and 2022, most of them between December and April after heavy rain in the headwaters to the south. The highest peak was on 2 February 1893, at 25.45 m. On 27 February 2022 the river reached 22.96 m, more than a metre above the 1999 peak of 21.9 m.

Graziers were the first European settlers. On 16 October 1867 James Nash reported the discovery of payable alluvial gold, at a time when Queensland was suffering a severe economic depression. The settlement was first called Nashville, and the name was changed to Gympie in 1868 after the local tree. The Gympie Creek Post Office opened on 1 December 1867 and took the new name in 1868.

The goldfield filled quickly with institutions. In 1868 a slab hut called the Miner's Bethel served the Anglican, Catholic and Methodist congregations until each had built its own church, and a Cobb & Co coach service between Brisbane and Gympie began, running twice a week. The first school, One Mile Boys State School, opened on 20 September 1869. The railway from Maryborough was completed in 1881, and the North Coast railway linked Gympie to Brisbane in 1891. The state declared Gympie a town in 1903.

In 1882 a handful of macadamia seeds taken from trees at Gympie went to Hawaii. Researchers who compared the genetic profiles of Queensland and Hawaiian trees in 2019 concluded that essentially all the Hawaiian trees descend from a small population of Gympie trees, possibly a single tree.

Gympie had an urban population of 22,424 at the 2021 census and is the administrative centre of the Gympie Region. Gold mining, dairy farming, timber and tourism have all figured in its economy. Many buildings of the gold-rush era are on the Queensland Heritage Register, among them the Town Hall, built in 1890, the Court House, the Old Gympie Post Office and the Railway Hotel of 1915. The Gympie Gold Rush Festival marks Nash's discovery each October, and the Valley Rattler tourist train has run along the Mary Valley since 1996.
gyorgy-dozsa: György Dózsa was of Székely origin and was known to his contemporaries as György Székely. Probably in his forties or fifties when he died, he must have been born around 1470; nothing more specific is known of his family or early life. He probably received little education and seems to have been illiterate, and his younger brother, Gergely, was executed alongside him. Sándor Márki identified him with a man named in a 1507 court document over a violent robbery at a market in Medgyes, but it remains unclear whether that case concerns him.

Márki, and after him Pataki, held that Dózsa took part in John Zápolya's 1513 campaign against the Ottomans and then in the defence of Nándorfehérvár, where he was a cavalry captain. Sources tell of a duel on 28 February 1514 in which he beat the Ottoman champion Ali, though there is no decisive proof of how it happened. King Vladislaus II rewarded him with a noble title, a village and a coat of arms.

On 17 June 1513 Pope Leo X published a bull authorising a crusade, appointing Archbishop Tamás Bakócz to organise it. Franciscan friars recruited, and around 15,000 volunteers were in the camp at Pest within two weeks. Whether Bakócz appointed Dózsa commander is unproven: no contemporary source mentions him before 3 June 1514, and recent scholarship suggests a man named Menyhért led the camp at first. Within a few weeks Dózsa had an army of some 40,000, mostly peasants, students, friars and priests.

When landlords ordered the volunteers home to the harvest and mistreated their families, they refused, and Bakócz cancelled the crusade. Dózsa, Gergely and several friars disobeyed, and the movement became a war against the landlords. Hundreds of manor houses were burnt; at Csanád Dózsa impaled the bishop and the castellan, and at Arad the treasurer István Telegdy was tortured to death.

On 15 July 1514 an army of 20,000 under John Zápolya and Stephen Báthory routed Dózsa at Temesvár. He was captured and condemned to sit on a heated iron throne, wearing a heated iron crown and sceptre. Gergely was cut in three, and surviving rebels were forced to bite flesh torn from Dózsa with hot pliers. Some 70,000 peasants were tortured. The Tripartitum drawn up under István Werbőczy elaborated peasants' old rights but greatly raised the status of the gentry. Ferenc Erkel wrote an opera about Dózsa, and streets in Hungary and Romania bear his name.
gytheio: Gytheio lies at the northeastern corner of the Mani Peninsula, on the northwestern end of the Laconian Gulf, about 40 km southeast of Sparta and linked to it by Greek National Road 39. It was built on a hill called Koumaros or Laryssio near the mouth of a usually dry river nicknamed Xerias. Offshore lies the small island of Cranae, where myth says Paris and Helen spent their first night together before leaving for Troy; it now has a causeway to the mainland. The town is the seat of the municipality of East Mani.

Myth names Heracles and Apollo, and Castor and Pollux, as founders of ancient Gythium. Phoenician traders from Tyre may have used it for a purple dye trade based on the gulf's murex. In classical times it was a community of perioikoi, dependent on Sparta. The Athenian admiral Tolmides burned it in 455 BCE with 50 ships and 4,000 hoplites, during the First Peloponnesian War. It was rebuilt and probably became the shipyard of the Spartan fleet; in 407 BCE Alcibiades saw thirty triremes being built there. Epaminondas took it in 370 BCE after three days, and the Spartans recaptured it three days later. Philip V of Macedon failed to take it in 219 BCE.

Under Nabis, Gythium was a major naval arsenal and port, and it fell to Rome only after a long siege. It then became the leading community of the Union of Free Laconians, a league of twenty-four, later eighteen, communities declared free by Augustus. It exported purple dye, porphyry and rose antique marble, and the Romans built a theatre that survives. The city was destroyed in the 4th century, whether by Alaric and the Visigoths, by Slavs or by the earthquake of 375, which is not recorded. It remained a small village through Byzantine and Ottoman times. It grew after Tzannetos Grigorakis built his tower on Cranae, and during the Greek War of Independence refugees made it a major town.

Gytheio opened a modern port in the 1960s, with ferries to Kythira and Crete, and is the seat of the Orthodox Diocese of Gytheion and Oitylo. The ancient theatre and acropolis were found by Dimitris Skias in 1891. Most ruins of ancient Gythium lie under the gulf, and the Dimitrios shipwreck rests in shallow water by Valtaki beach. Cranae's Tzannetakis Tower is now the Historical and Cultural Museum of Mani.
gyula-andrassy: Gyula Andrássy was born on 8 March 1823, according to the usual account at Oláhpatak, now Vlachovo in Slovakia, though his date and place of birth are somewhat disputed; the registry of Košice records his baptism on 3 March 1823. His father, Count Károly Andrássy, was a liberal who belonged to the political opposition, and Gyula threw himself into the political struggles of the day at an early age. In 1845 he became president of the society for the regulation of the waters of the Upper Tisza River, and in 1846 he published critical articles on the government in Lajos Kossuth's Pesti Hírlap.

In 1848 Andrássy entered military service when the Croats under Josip Jelačić sought the return of Međimurje, served with distinction at Pákozd and Schwechat as adjutant to Artúr Görgei, and was sent to Constantinople to seek Ottoman neutrality. After the defeat at Világos he emigrated to London and then Paris. On 21 September 1851 he was condemned to death in absentia and hanged in effigy by the Austrian government. He returned to Hungary in 1858, never petitioned for amnesty and supported Ferenc Deák's party. In 1866 he presided over the sub-committee that drew up the Compromise of 1867, and originated the idea of the Delegations.

After the Prussian victory at Königgrätz, Emperor Franz Joseph I consulted him for the first time, and on 17 February 1867 appointed him first prime minister of the Hungarian half of the Dual Monarchy, after Deák had declined. He reorganised the Honvéd army. On the fall of Beust on 6 November 1871 he became Foreign Minister of Austria-Hungary, turning policy towards Germany. After the Andrássy Note of 30 December 1875 on the uprising in Bosnia and Herzegovina, he was the principal Austrian delegate at the Congress of Berlin in 1878, where he obtained the occupation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and garrison rights in the Sanjak of Novi Pazar.

The occupation of Bosnia-Herzegovina was unpopular in Hungary, where the opposition moved his impeachment on 5 November 1878; it was defeated by 179 votes to 95. He resigned on 8 October 1879, the day after signing the alliance with Germany. In retirement he took part in the Delegations and the Upper House, defended the Compromise of 1867, regained his popularity and died on 18 February 1890, aged 66, at Volosko. His death was mourned as a national calamity, and he is described as the first Magyar statesman in centuries to hold a European position.
